foundation_of_rome.detail: The date is a learned construct: Varro's friend L. Tarutius of Firmum even cast Rome's horoscope. Archaeology shows Iron Age huts on the Palatine from the 9th-8th centuries, a fortification wall on the north slope of the Palatine (Carandini's excavations, dated c. 730-720 by him, contested), and the first beaten-earth Forum floors around 700-650. The synoecism of village communities into a single city is a process of the 8th-7th centuries, not an act. Romulus, the twins, the asylum and the Sabine women are etiological legend.
foundation_of_rome.debate: Carandini reads the Palatine wall as evidence of a real founding act c. 750; most (Cornell, Forsythe, Smith) prefer gradual state formation.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 70-80
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 78-93
Carandini, Rome: Day One (2011)

numa_religious_institutions.detail: The story that Numa was a pupil of Pythagoras was already rejected on chronological grounds by Cicero and Livy (Pythagoras flourished c. 530). In 181 BC 'books of Numa' were allegedly found in a chest on the Janiculum and burned by the praetor Q. Petillius as subversive. The Regia in the Forum, traditionally Numa's house, has building phases from the late 7th century.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 118-119

destruction_of_alba_longa.detail: The story explains Rome's later presidency of the Latin festival on the Alban Mount (feriae Latinae) and the presence of Alban gentes (Julii, Servilii, Quinctii, Cloelii) among the patricians. No urban site of Alba Longa has been securely identified; scattered Iron Age cemeteries around Lake Albano suggest villages rather than a city.

draining_of_the_forum.detail: The Cloaca was originally an open channel; the surviving vaulted conduit in peperino and travertine is of the late Republic. The Comitium, Regia and the Volcanal/Lapis Niger area also show 6th-century monumental phases; the Lapis Niger cippus carries one of the oldest Latin inscriptions (mid-6th century) naming a 'recei' (rex).
scholarship: Holloway, The Archaeology of Early Rome and Latium (1994)
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 102

servian_reforms.detail: The full 193-century system with its bronze-asses ratings is anachronistic for the 6th century (coinage begins c. 300); Cornell and Forsythe accept a simpler early classis/infra classem division tied to hoplite equipment. Claudius' Lyons speech (ILS 212) preserves an Etruscan tradition identifying Servius with Mastarna, companion of Caelius Vibenna, whom the François Tomb paintings at Vulci show freeing Caile Vipinas and killing a 'Cneve Tarchunies Rumach' (Gnaeus Tarquinius of Rome). The so-called Servian wall of cappellaccio tufa may be 6th century in parts, but the surviving circuit is of 378 BC.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 173-197
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 108-115

battle_of_alalia.detail: Herodotus records that the Caeretans stoned their Phocaean prisoners to death, were afflicted with a plague, and consulted Delphi, which ordered annual funeral games; this links Caere to Delphi a generation before Rome. The battle shows the Etrusco-Punic alignment that underlies the Pyrgi tablets and the first Rome-Carthage treaty. Date c. 540-535.

destruction_of_sybaris_510.detail: The quarrel began when the Sybarite tyrant Telys drove 500 rich citizens into exile and Croton, persuaded by Pythagoras, refused to surrender them. Diodorus' figures of 300,000 Sybarites against 100,000 Crotoniates are fantasies, but the outcome was real: Sybaris' coinage ends abruptly, Croton became the leading power of the Ionian coast, and the survivors' attempts to refound the city culminated in the pan-Hellenic colony of Thurii (444/443). Herodotus heard a Sybarite version in which Dorieus of Sparta helped Croton, which the Crotoniates denied. The fall of Sybaris is the backdrop to Pythagorean political dominance in Croton and to the later anti-Pythagorean revolts.
destruction_of_sybaris_510.debate: Ancient numbers are absurd; whether the river was really diverted is doubted, but excavation at Sibari shows heavy alluviation over the archaic city.

dedication_temple_jupiter_capitolinus.detail:
The temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus, with Juno and Minerva in side chambers, was the central monument of Roman religion and politics. Tradition said Tarquinius Priscus vowed it in a Sabine war and levelled the summit, Tarquinius Superbus built it with Etruscan craftsmen, financing it from the spoils of Suessa Pometia, and the gods Terminus and Iuventas refused to leave the site, an omen of permanence. The terracotta cult statue of Jupiter, painted red with minium, and the quadriga on the roof were commissioned from Vulca of Veii, the only named Etruscan artist known from Roman literature. On the Ides of September of the first year, the consul M. Horatius Pulvillus dedicated it; told mid-ceremony that his son had died, he kept his hand on the doorpost and finished the prayer.

The building was huge. Excavations under Palazzo Caffarelli and in the Capitoline Museums (Mura Sommella, 1998-2000s) have exposed foundations of cappellaccio tufa measuring roughly 54 by 62 m, larger than any other temple of the 6th century west of Greece except the Sicilian giants. Its Tuscan plan, with a deep columned porch and three cellae on a high podium, became the model for Roman temples in Italy and the provinces, and its dedication date became an era: an old law said the praetor maximus should fix a nail in the wall on the Ides of September, and Pliny dates Cn. Flavius' shrine of Concord 204 years after the dedication. Triumphs ended there, consuls sacrificed there on taking office, and the Senate met there at the start of the year.

The original temple burned in 83 BC and was rebuilt by Sulla and Q. Lutatius Catulus (dedicated 69 BC) on the old plan; it burned again in AD 69 and 80 and was rebuilt by Vespasian and Domitian. Debate continues over whether the vast foundations carried a temple of the same size or a smaller building on a broad platform, and whether the scale reflects Tarquin's ambition or later enlargement. Either way, the dedication in 509 or 507 shows that the expulsion of the kings did not interrupt the great building programme of archaic Rome.
dedication_temple_jupiter_capitolinus.debate: Dedication in 509 or 507 is disputed in antiquity; modern debate concerns the reconstruction of the superstructure on the 54 x 62 m foundations.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 128
Hopkins, The Genesis of Roman Architecture (2016)
A. Mura Sommella, 'Il tempio di Giove Capitolino', Mitteilungen des DAI Rom 2008

expulsion_of_the_kings.detail:
The Roman story is a drama in three acts. Tarquinius Superbus is besieging Ardea when his sons and their cousin L. Tarquinius Collatinus, bored in camp, wager on whose wife is the most virtuous; riding home at night they find the princesses at a banquet and Collatinus' Lucretia spinning wool among her maids. Sextus Tarquinius returns days later, rapes her at sword-point by threatening to kill her beside a dead slave, and Lucretia summons her father Sp. Lucretius and her husband, who come with P. Valerius and L. Junius Brutus. She tells them what happened and stabs herself. Brutus, who had feigned stupidity (brutus, 'dullard') to survive the king's purges, draws the knife from her body and swears to drive out the Tarquins and never again suffer a king at Rome. The body is displayed in the forum of Collatia and then in Rome; the people vote the king's deposition, Brutus wins over the army at Ardea, Queen Tullia flees, and Tarquin finds the gates shut and goes into exile at Caere. Sextus is killed at Gabii.

Livy and Dionysius tell the tale with deliberate echoes of Athenian history: in 510 the Peisistratids were expelled after a sexual insult provoked Harmodius and Aristogeiton, and Roman annalists consciously aligned the two liberations. The Varronian date of 509 puts the event 244 years after the foundation; Polybius dates the first consuls 28 years before Xerxes' invasion, which gives 508/507. What can be checked supports a date around 500: the monarchy's sacral functions survived in the rex sacrorum and the Regifugium ritual of 24 February, the Capitoline temple was dedicated in the first year of the new regime, the Carthage treaty presupposes a Rome that still claimed Tarquin's Latin hegemony, and the Fasti, whatever their early distortions, begin then.

Modern debate concerns the how rather than the whether. Alföldi and Gjerstad argued for a later date (c. 470 or 450) on archaeological grounds now largely abandoned. Many scholars think Lars Porsenna, not a Roman aristocratic coup, ended Tarquin's rule, and that the transition passed through a phase of chief magistrates (praetor maximus, dictator) before annual collegial consuls became fixed. The result, in any case, was an aristocratic republic whose ideology was built on hatred of the name rex: Caesar's enemies in 44 BC would invoke Brutus at his statue on the Capitol.
expulsion_of_the_kings.debate: Alföldi (Early Rome and the Latins, 1965) argued for a later date c. 470 and Etruscan rule continuing; Gjerstad down-dated the kings too. Cornell defends a date c. 509-505 because the Fasti and the Polybian treaty fit it.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 215-239
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 147-155
Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 218-232
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) ch. 9
Alföldi, Early Rome and the Latins (1965)

institution_of_the_consulship.detail:
Livy says the first two consuls were elected by the centuriate assembly 'according to the commentaries of Servius Tullius', and that they received all the king's powers and insignia except that only one held the fasces at a time, alternating month by month so that the people would not see two kings. Brutus made the people swear never to allow a king, and Valerius added the right of appeal (provocatio). The office was annual and collegial, each consul able to veto the other; it carried imperium, the power of command and coercion, and the auspicia, the right to consult the gods on the state's behalf.

Our main documentary source, the Fasti Capitolini compiled under Augustus from earlier lists, credits 509 with five consuls: Brutus and Collatinus, then Sp. Lucretius (who died in office), Valerius and M. Horatius. The crowding betrays later reconstruction, and Polybius' treaty, which names Brutus and Horatius, does not match the traditional pairs of 509. Livy himself notes that the chief magistrates were at first called praetors, and an old law on the Capitol ordered the 'praetor maximus' to drive the annual nail; Festus explains praetor maximus as the senior of several. Scholars such as De Martino and Mazzarino therefore suggested that the Republic began with a single annual chief magistrate, or with a dictator-like praetor maximus assisted by junior colleagues, and that two equal consuls emerged only in 449 or even 367. Others, following Cornell, accept the dual magistracy from the start but agree that its title was praetor until the 4th century.

The early Fasti also contain many non-patrician names (Cassius, Genucius, Minucius, Sempronius, Volumnius): about a third of the consuls of 509-486 bear names later known as plebeian. This has fuelled the theory of a 'closing of the patriciate' (serrata) in the 5th century, when a narrower group monopolised office, against which the plebeian struggle was directed. The consular year began on varying dates until 153, when 1 January was fixed. Dating by consular pairs, the habit that made the Fasti the backbone of Roman chronology, began with this office.
institution_of_the_consulship.debate: Whether the dual collegial consulship goes back to 509 or developed later (De Martino, Heurgon) is unresolved.
scholarship: Broughton, MRR I 1-3
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 218-223, 226-230
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 226-230
Broughton, MRR I 1-2

first_treaty_rome_carthage.detail:
Polybius found the treaty in the treasury of the aediles beside the Capitoline temple, engraved on bronze, in Latin so archaic that the best experts could barely understand it, and he gives a Greek paraphrase. It dates, he says, to the consulship of L. Junius Brutus and M. Horatius, 28 years before Xerxes crossed to Greece. Its terms: there shall be friendship between the Romans and their allies and the Carthaginians and theirs. The Romans shall not sail beyond the Fair Promontory unless forced by storm or enemies; if forced, they may take only what is needed for repairs or sacrifice and must leave within five days. Merchants trading in Libya or Sardinia may do business only in the presence of a herald or scribe, and the state guarantees the price. In the part of Sicily ruled by Carthage, Romans have equal rights. The Carthaginians shall not harm Ardea, Antium, Laurentum, Circeii, Tarracina or any other Latin city subject to Rome; if they take a Latin city not subject to Rome, they must hand it over undamaged; they shall build no fort in Latium, and if they enter it in arms shall not spend a night there.

The treaty is the single most important document for early Rome. It shows a Rome claiming hegemony over the coastal Latin cities as far as Tarracina, as Livy says Tarquin had held, and a Carthage already organising exclusive trading zones, with the 'Fair Promontory' (probably Cape Farina, north of Carthage, or less likely Cape Bon) marking the closed waters of the Gulf of Tunis and the coast beyond. It parallels the Etrusco-Punic agreements known from Aristotle and the Pyrgi tablets.

Mommsen and many 19th-century scholars rejected the date and identified it with the treaty of 348 mentioned by Diodorus and Livy, which Diodorus calls the first. Most modern historians (Scullard, Walbank, Cornell) accept Polybius: the archaic language, the Latin cities named and the absence of the restrictions of 348 all fit c. 509. The treaties of 348, 306 (if Philinus' version is accepted) and 279 followed, and Polybius cited the series to judge responsibility for the First Punic War.
first_treaty_rome_carthage.debate: Mommsen and others redated it to 348 because Livy and Diodorus know no treaty before 348; most now accept Polybius' date (Walbank, Cornell), not least because the archaic language and context make better sense c. 509.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) 337-345
Scardigli, I trattati romano-cartaginesi (1991)
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 210-214

battle_of_silva_arsia.detail: The Roman matrons mourned Brutus for a year. Publicola celebrated the first triumph of the Republic (the Fasti Triumphales record a triumph over the Veientes and Tarquinienses on 1 March 509). The story belongs to the patriotic legend of the founding year.

lex_valeria_de_provocatione_509.detail: Livy reports three Valerian laws of appeal (509, 449, 300) and himself notes that the 300 law was 'the third, always by the same family'. Most scholars regard the 509 and 449 laws as retrojections of the 300 law (or of the Twelve Tables' rule that only the comitia maximus could pass capital sentence).
lex_valeria_de_provocatione_509.debate: Doublet of the lex Valeria of 300.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) on 10.9

conspiracy_of_the_vitellii_aquilii.detail: The story is the founding exemplum of Republican severitas: the consul's duty to the state overrides the father's love. The plotters met in the house of the Aquilii, nephews of Collatinus, and wrote letters to Tarquin that were seized. Vindicius was rewarded with freedom and citizenship, and later Romans derived the word vindicta (the rod used in manumission) from his name, an obvious aetiology. The Senate first voted to return the Tarquins' goods, then, after the plot, gave them to the plebs to plunder. Livy places the trial on the consuls' tribunal; Dionysius gives a much longer set-piece with Collatinus pleading for his nephews, which helps explain his fall. Modern scholars treat the episode as legend built round the Junii Bruti, though plotting by exiled kings is entirely plausible.
conspiracy_of_the_vitellii_aquilii.debate: Vindicius and the vindicta are an aetiological invention; the Junii Bruti of the later Republic were plebeian, which raised doubts already in antiquity about descent from the patrician first consul.

rex_sacrorum_instituted.detail: The rex sacrorum, with his wife the regina, kept archaic duties: on the Kalends he announced the dates of the month, and after the Regifugium of 24 February he performed a sacrifice in the Comitium and fled. He was barred from all magistracies and from addressing the people. The survival of the office, attested down to the 4th century AD, is one of the strongest arguments that the monarchy really did end, and that its religious functions were split off rather than abolished. Some scholars argue that the king's sacral powers passed in stages, with the rex sacrorum dating from the early Republic but the pontifical supremacy over him developing later.

exile_of_collatinus.detail: Livy makes Brutus plead with his colleague in a public assembly, and Collatinus' father-in-law Sp. Lucretius add his entreaty; Collatinus took 20 talents from Brutus as a gift (Livy) and went into exile. P. Valerius was elected in his place. The episode shows the tradition grappling with the fact that a Tarquin stood in the first consular college, and may reflect a real purge of the royal clan.

campus_martius_and_tiber_island.detail: Livy, Dionysius and Plutarch tell the same aetiology. Geologically the island is a volcanic tufa outcrop, far older than Rome, but the story records a genuine memory that the Campus Martius had once been crown land. The Campus became the mustering ground of the centuriate assembly and the site of the censors' lustrum; the island later received the cult of Aesculapius (291), which is why it was faced in travertine as a ship.
campus_martius_and_tiber_island.debate: The island story is pure aetiology; whether the Campus was really royal property is uncertain.

publicola_house_on_the_velia.detail: The episode is the origin legend for two conventions: magistrates' fasces were lowered (fasces summittere) before the sovereign people, and the axes were removed from the fasces inside the city, since there a citizen could appeal (provocatio). It is tied to the lex Valeria de provocatione, the first of three such laws attributed to the Valerii (509, 449, 300), and almost certainly reflects Valerian family propaganda transmitted by the annalist Valerius Antias.

aerarium_saturni_quaestors.detail: The attribution is anachronistic: the Temple of Saturn was dedicated only in 498 or 497, and Tacitus believed quaestors already existed under the kings, chosen by them, and were first elected in 447. What is not in doubt is the long association of the quaestors with the aerarium in the podium of the temple, where state funds, the military standards and copies of laws and senatus consulta were kept.
aerarium_saturni_quaestors.debate: Origins of the quaestorship disputed: royal appointees, consular assistants chosen from 509, or elected from 447.

siege_of_rome_508.detail:
In Livy's patriotic narrative Lars Porsenna, king of Clusium, marched on Rome to restore Tarquin. He seized the Janiculum in a rush, and only Horatius Cocles, with Sp. Larcius and T. Herminius, held the far end of the Pons Sublicius while the Romans hacked it down behind them; Horatius then swam the Tiber in full armour. The blockade that followed caused famine. The young noble C. Mucius slipped into the Etruscan camp to kill the king, stabbed his secretary by mistake, and, when threatened with torture, thrust his right hand into a brazier, telling Porsenna that 300 young Romans had sworn to try in turn; he was released and took the name Scaevola, 'Lefty'. Porsenna made peace, receiving hostages and the return of the seven pagi on the right bank taken from Veii. The hostage Cloelia escaped across the Tiber with other girls; returned by Rome under the treaty, she was freed by the admiring king with half the hostages, and an equestrian statue of her stood on the Via Sacra.

Other evidence tells a different story. Tacitus, describing the burning of the Capitol in AD 69, says the temple had survived 'when the city was surrendered' (dedita urbe) to Porsenna. Pliny quotes the treaty with Porsenna, which forbade the Romans to use iron except for agriculture, a typical condition imposed on a defeated people. Dionysius records that Rome sent Porsenna a throne, sceptre and crown, tokens of submission. The custom at Roman auctions of announcing 'the goods of King Porsenna for sale' was explained by Livy as a memory of the king's generosity in leaving his camp's supplies.

Most modern scholars conclude that Porsenna took Rome. Whether he came to restore Tarquin or to replace him is unclear; some suggest he removed Tarquin himself and that the Roman aristocracy seized power when his son Arruns was defeated by the Latins and Aristodemus of Cumae at Aricia (504). The heroic stories are aetiologies for monuments (the statues of Cloelia and Horatius) and family names. The Clusine king's legendary tomb, a labyrinth crowned by pyramids described by Varro, shows how large he loomed in Etruscan memory.
siege_of_rome_508.debate: Whether Porsenna took Rome. Livy's dating to 508/507 depends on the inflated Varronian fasti.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 215-218
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 147-149
Alföldi, Early Rome and the Latins (1965) 72-84

census_508.detail: Rome's territory around 500 was about 820 km2 (Beloch's estimate), able to feed perhaps 25,000-40,000 people in all. The early census totals in Dionysius and Livy are thus best read as later reconstructions, or as including women and children, or as projections back from 3rd-century figures. They matter because Roman antiquarians believed them and used them to describe the Republic's growth.
census_508.debate: Totals are unreliable; Brunt and others reject all census figures before the 4th century.
scholarship: Beloch, Die Bevölkerung der griechisch-römischen Welt (1886)
Brunt, Italian Manpower (1971)

sabine_war_505_503.detail: Livy reports the Sabine victories briefly; the war is notable for its ritual firsts. Pliny says Postumius Tubertus was the first to celebrate an ovation, wearing a crown of myrtle sacred to Venus Victrix, because he had won 'without bloodshed'. The Fasti Triumphales list triumphs of M. Valerius (505) and P. Valerius (504) over the Sabines. The secession of Attus Clausus and his clients to Rome in 504 was a by-product of Sabine divisions over the war.

battle_of_aricia.detail: The battle is attested independently in a Cumaean chronicle used by Dionysius (book 7), which makes it one of the best-founded events of the period and the start of Aristodemus' tyranny at Cumae, where he later sheltered Tarquin. Dionysius places it some 20 years before 492, Livy right after Porsenna's peace; c. 505-504 is usual.
battle_of_aricia.debate: The 'Cumaean chronicle' (Alföldi) is hypothetical but widely accepted.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 217
Alföldi, Early Rome and the Latins (1965) 56-72

migration_of_attus_clausus.detail: A key piece of evidence for archaic horizontal mobility of elites with private armies of clients, comparable to the Lapis Satricanus 'suodales' of Publius Valerius and the Fabii at the Cremera. Tacitus (Ann. 11.24) has Claudius cite it in his speech on admitting Gauls to the Senate. Suetonius (Tib. 1) dates it to the time of Romulus with Titus Tatius instead.
scholarship: Smith, The Roman Clan (2006)
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 144-145

death_of_publicola_503.detail: Plutarch reports that the Valerii marked the right by setting a torch under a body at the family site and then removing it, a symbolic claim rather than a real burial. The poverty motif recurs in Menenius Agrippa (493) and Cincinnatus, and expresses a later ideal of early Roman frugality.

siege_of_suessa_pometia_502.detail: Livy admits that his sources confused this siege with others, and the Fasti Triumphales record a triumph over the Aurunci in 503. Suessa Pometia had been rich enough for Tarquinius Superbus to fund the Capitoline temple from its booty (40 talents according to Fabius Pictor, 400 per Piso). The site has never been located with certainty; candidates lie around Cisterna and Latina, near Satricum.
siege_of_suessa_pometia_502.debate: Location unknown; Livy himself suspects duplication with the capture of Pometia under Tarquin and in 495.

first_dictatorship.detail: Livy admits his sources disagree on who was first dictator and when; some named M'. Valerius. The dictatorship (originally magister populi, with a magister equitum) was a six-month emergency office named by a consul; it may reflect an archaic Latin office (the dictator of Lanuvium, the dictator Latinus who dedicated the Diana grove at Aricia per Cato).
scholarship: Broughton, MRR I 9-10

lapis_satricanus.detail: Poplios Valesios is the archaic form of Publius Valerius, and some identify him with Publicola himself. Whether or not, the stone documents a warlord's sodales operating outside any state structure, the kind of band seen in the Fabian clan war at the Cremera and Attus Clausus' migration, and it shows that names in the early Fasti correspond to real archaic gentes.
lapis_satricanus.debate: Identification of Poplios Valesios with Publicola is possible but unprovable.
scholarship: Stibbe et al., Lapis Satricanus (1980)
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 144-145

pyrgi_tablets_dedication.detail: The bilingual is the longest Etruscan-Phoenician text known and shows a Caeretan ruler courting Carthage, the same Tyrrhenian world in which the first Rome-Carthage treaty was concluded. Pyrgi's temples were plundered by Dionysius I of Syracuse in 384.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 212, 232
Serra Ridgway, 'Etruscans, Greeks, Carthaginians: the sanctuary at Pyrgi', in Descœudres (ed.), Greek Colonists and Native Populations (1990)

aes_rude_and_weighed_bronze.detail: Timaeus, quoted by Pliny, knew that the Romans used aes rude before any coin, and Pliny credited Servius Tullius with first 'marking' bronze. The Twelve Tables fix penalties in asses (25 for an iniuria, 300 for breaking a free man's bone) and the lex Aternia Tarpeia (454) converted livestock fines at one ox = 100 asses and one sheep = 10. Transactions by bronze and scales (per aes et libram) survived as ritual in mancipatio and nexum, with a libripens holding the balance. Fragments of aes rude occur in votive deposits across central Italy (at sanctuaries such as Lavinium and Vicarello) and continue in hoards alongside aes grave into the 3rd century. Words such as aestimare, stipendium (from stips, small bronze) and expendere preserve the system.
scholarship: Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974)
Burnett, Coinage in the Roman World (1987)

aes_signatum_ramo_secco.detail: Ramo secco bars typically weigh 1-2 kg when whole and are found mostly as fragments in hoards and votive deposits, showing that value lay in weight, not in the mark. Their distribution from the Po valley to Latium shows that central Italy shared a bronze-weight economy long before coinage, which explains why Roman cast coinage of c. 280 began at such a heavy standard.
scholarship: Crawford, Coinage and Money under the Roman Republic (1985)
Burnett, Coinage in the Roman World (1987)

lucus_dianae_arician_dedication.detail: The fragment, preserved by Priscian, is the clearest evidence for a Latin federal cult and for a common Latin chief magistrate. Many scholars date it to c. 500, after the expulsion of the Tarquins, when the Latins under Tusculan and Arician leadership organized against Rome; others place it in the 6th century as a rival to the Servian Diana cult on the Aventine. The sanctuary on Lake Nemi, with its rex Nemorensis who held office by killing his predecessor, became famous through Frazer's Golden Bough.
lucus_dianae_arician_dedication.debate: Date (6th century or c. 500) and whether the list represents an anti-Roman league are disputed.

carthaginian_etruscan_treaties.detail: The partnership shaped Rome's world. The first Roman treaty with Carthage (509) belongs to the same family of agreements, regulating trade and protecting coastal Latin cities. The Pyrgi gold tablets, in Etruscan and Phoenician, show the ruler of Caere honouring Astarte (Uni) around 500. The alliance ended with Etruscan sea power after Cumae (474) and Syracusan raids (453, 384).

capture_of_crustumerium_499.detail: Crustumerium's territory became the Clustumina tribe, the only early rustic tribe named after a place rather than a gens. Excavated cemeteries show the town was largely abandoned in the early 5th century, matching the tradition.

census_498.detail: The figure fits the pattern of inflated early census totals (130,000 in 508, 110,000 in 493, 103,000 in 474) and was probably derived by later antiquarians from family archives or invented.
census_498.debate: Chronology of the first dictatorship (501 Livy, 498 Dionysius) and the census total are both suspect.

temple_of_saturn_497.detail: Its podium is under the eight Ionic columns of the 4th-century AD rebuilding. The temple's early date is one of several dedications clustered in the first decades of the Republic (Saturn 497, Mercury 495, Ceres 493, Castor 484) that suggest a still-prosperous city before the 5th-century recession visible in imports.
scholarship: Ziolkowski, The Temples of Mid-Republican Rome (1992)

battle_of_lake_regillus.detail:
After the Tarquins' last hope in Etruria faded, the Latin cities under Octavius Mamilius of Tusculum, Tarquin's son-in-law, went to war with Rome, sheltering the old king. The Senate appointed A. Postumius Albus dictator with T. Aebutius Elva as master of horse. The armies met at Lake Regillus in the territory of Tusculum, probably the drained crater of Pantano Secco below Frascati. Livy describes a heroic battle of leaders in Homeric style: the aged Tarquin, charging Postumius, was wounded; Aebutius and Mamilius wounded each other; Mamilius was finally killed by T. Herminius, himself slain moments later; the Roman exiles' cohort under Tarquin's son fought ferociously. Postumius ordered the cavalry to dismount and fight on foot, vowed a temple to Castor, and promised rewards to the first men over the Latin camp's rampart.

Later tradition added that two tall youths on white horses fought at the head of the Roman cavalry, and that the same evening two horsemen were seen washing their mounts at the spring of Juturna in the Forum, announcing the victory before vanishing: Castor and Pollux. Their temple beside the spring was dedicated by Postumius' son in 484, and the annual parade of the equites on 15 July (transvectio equitum), reorganised by Q. Fabius Rullianus in 304, commemorated the battle's anniversary.

The Dioscuri were Greek gods, but an inscribed bronze from Lavinium of the late 6th century (Castorei Podlouqueique qurois) shows they were already worshipped in Latium, perhaps as patrons of aristocratic cavalry. Livy noted that his sources dated the battle to 499 or 496. The outcome was less decisive than the legend: the Foedus Cassianum of 493 created an alliance of equals rather than Roman supremacy, and Tusculum later became Rome's closest Latin friend. Macaulay's 'Battle of the Lake Regillus' in his Lays of Ancient Rome (1842) made the story famous to Victorian readers.
battle_of_lake_regillus.debate: Date (499 or 496), site of the lake, and the decisiveness of the victory are disputed; the Dioscuri epiphany is an aetiological legend tied to the Juturna spring and the transvectio.
scholarship: Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 285-289
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 293-294
Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 285-291
Weinstock, 'Two Archaic Inscriptions from Latium', JRS 50 (1960)

temple_of_mercury_495.detail: The placement outside the pomerium by the Aventine and the river harbour links it to trade with Greek and Etruscan merchants; the episode is also an early instance of popular assertion against the consuls before the secession of 494.

death_of_tarquinius_superbus.detail: Aristodemus inherited Tarquin's property and later seized Roman grain ships sent to buy corn during the famine of 492, using it as a claim against Rome.

colony_at_signia.detail: Signia's polygonal walls (late 6th-4th century) and the temple on its acropolis survive. Early 'Latin colonies' like Signia, Norba, Velitrae and Circeii were joint foundations of Rome and the Latin League placed on the Volscian front.

twenty_one_tribes_495.detail: The rustic tribes bearing gentile names (Aemilia, Camilia, Claudia, Cornelia, Fabia, Galeria, Horatia, Lemonia, Menenia, Papiria, Pollia, Pupinia, Romilia, Sergia, Voltinia, Voturia) suggest districts where those clans held land, a striking picture of aristocratic territorial power in the early Republic. The Claudia was tied to the arrival of Attus Clausus in 504. The tribe was a unit for the census, levy and tributum, and from 471 for the plebeian assembly. The sixteen gentile tribes all lay within about 8-10 km of Rome, mapping the ager Romanus antiquus. Taylor's reconstruction of tribal geography remains standard.
twenty_one_tribes_495.debate: Whether 21 includes the Clustumina, and whether Dionysius' figure (21 in 491) reflects the same reform; the origins of gentile-named tribes are debated.
scholarship: L. R. Taylor, The Voting Districts of the Roman Republic (1960)

battle_against_the_aurunci_495.detail: Livy uses the campaign to dramatise the debt crisis: the soldiers who had won the war returned to find Appius Claudius enforcing debt judgments, leading to the secession of 494. The Fasti record no triumph for Servilius, whom the Senate refused one; Livy says he triumphed by popular decision, perhaps a retrojection of later practice.

debt_riots_495.detail: Livy's scene is a literary set-piece, but it captures the mechanism of nexum: a citizen who could not repay pledged his own labour and person, and the creditor could chain and beat him. The consul Appius Claudius enforced debt judgments harshly, his colleague Servilius promised relief, and the Senate's failure to legislate produced the First Secession the following year.

first_secession_of_the_plebs.detail:
Debt bondage (nexum), harsh debt judgments and the burden of continual war produced the crisis. When the consuls of 494 tried to march out the legions, still bound by their military oath, the soldiers instead withdrew in arms to the Mons Sacer, a hill beyond the Anio three miles from Rome, though the annalist Piso placed the secession on the Aventine. They camped peacefully for some days while the patricians, fearing both the plebs inside the city and enemies outside, negotiated. Menenius Agrippa, himself of plebeian origin according to Livy, told the fable of the limbs that starved the belly and found they starved themselves, a story that already existed in Greek literature.

The settlement created the tribunes of the plebs: two at first, by Livy's account C. Licinius and L. Albinus, who co-opted three more including L. Sicinius, the leader of the secession; other versions name five from the start. The tribunes' power rested not on law but on the sworn oath of the whole plebs (lex sacrata) to kill anyone who harmed them: they were sacrosanct. Their function was auxilium, protecting individual plebeians against magistrates, which grew into a general veto (intercessio). Plebeian aediles and the cult centre of Ceres, Liber and Libera on the Aventine slope followed.

Modern historians see the secession as the birth of a 'state within the state', with its own assembly, officers, archive and treasury, a model unparalleled in the Greek world. Who the plebs were is debated: not simply the poor, since wealthy plebeians led the movement, and perhaps not originally including the patricians' clients. The secession, a military strike, became the plebs' ultimate weapon, repeated in 449, in the mutiny of 342 and in the final secession to the Janiculum in 287. The story's details are later reconstructions, often coloured by the tribunician politics of the Gracchan age, but the creation of the tribunate early in the 5th century is generally accepted.
first_secession_of_the_plebs.debate: Mons Sacer vs Aventine. Dionysius turns the episode into long Thucydidean speeches. Mitchell (Patricians and Plebeians, 1990) denies the patrician-plebeian division is archaic at all.
scholarship: Raaflaub (ed.), Social Struggles in Archaic Rome (1986; 2nd ed. 2005)
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 256-271
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 170-177
Raaflaub (ed.), Social Struggles in Archaic Rome (2nd ed. 2005)
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 256-265

dictatorship_of_manius_valerius_494.detail: The dictator's edict suspended debt actions during the war, the device that made the levy possible. His resignation rather than a betrayal of his pledge earned him plebeian gratitude; the soldiers, still under oath, marched out and seceded to the Mons Sacer. Livy's 'ten legions' is an anachronism of the 'legion' as a later unit; the early army was a single legio of perhaps 3,000-6,000.
dictatorship_of_manius_valerius_494.debate: Some sources (DH) make Manius Valerius brother of Publicola; the scale of the levy is anachronistic.

colony_at_velitrae_494.detail: Velitrae was the home town of the Octavii, Augustus' paternal family. The Tabula Veliterna, a Volscian inscription of the 3rd century, shows that Volscian speech survived there long after colonisation.

foedus_cassianum.detail:
After Lake Regillus the consul Sp. Cassius made a treaty with the Latin cities that defined relations in Latium for 150 years. Dionysius gives its text: there shall be peace between the Romans and all the Latin cities as long as heaven and earth keep their place; they shall not make war on one another, nor bring in enemies, nor give them passage; each shall help the other with all its strength when attacked; each shall have an equal share of the spoils of joint wars; private lawsuits shall be decided within ten days in the city where the contract was made; and nothing shall be added or removed except by agreement of Romans and Latins together. Cicero says the treaty was engraved on a bronze column behind the Rostra and had been seen there not long before his time. Festus preserves an archaic clause about booty (pecuniam quis nancitor habeto).

The command of joint armies probably alternated: Cincius, quoted by Festus, describes the Latins meeting at the spring of Ferentina to decide on years when a Roman commander would lead them. Shared rights, later called Latin rights, allowed intermarriage (conubium), legally valid trade and contracts (commercium) and the right to migrate and take up citizenship (ius migrandi). Joint Latin colonies were planted on the frontiers: Signia, Velitrae, Norba, Ardea, Satricum, Setia, Circeii, Sutrium and Nepet. The Hernici joined the system in 486.

Scholars disagree on how equal the alliance was. Dionysius' text presents a bilateral treaty between Rome and 'the Latins' as one party, and some think Rome was already the dominant partner, as the first Carthage treaty implies. The alliance held through the Volscian and Aequian wars of the 5th century, frayed after the Gallic sack, was renewed in 358, and ended in the revolt of 340 when the Latins demanded one consul and half the Senate. Its rights and obligations became the template for the status of Latin colonies across Italy and, through the ius Latii, for provincial communities under the Empire.
foedus_cassianum.debate: Whether booty was split equally between Rome and the League collectively (thus Rome as half) or among all members; whether command alternated (Festus' 'praetor' at the Ferentine spring).
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 299-301
Alföldi, Early Rome and the Latins (1965) 111-122
Sherwin-White, The Roman Citizenship (2nd ed. 1973)

temple_of_ceres_liber_libera.detail: Pliny says the Greek artists Damophilus and Gorgasus decorated it with painting and terracotta and signed their work in Greek verse, the earliest attested Greek artists at Rome. The triad mirrors the Eleusinian Demeter, Iacchus and Kore, probably via Cumae, and the temple's Greek priestesses were recruited from Naples and Velia (Cicero).
scholarship: Spaeth, The Roman Goddess Ceres (1996)
Ziolkowski, The Temples of Mid-Republican Rome (1992)

siege_of_corioli.detail: Livy remarks that the consul's name had been eclipsed so thoroughly that only the treaty with the Latins preserved it. Corioli was already forgotten by Pliny's day (he lists it among vanished peoples of Latium). The cognomen derived from a place is anachronistic for 493.

plebeian_aediles_493.detail: The name derives from aedes, the temple. The aediles policed markets and grain supply, administered fines collected by the plebs, and organised the plebeian games. From 449 copies of decrees were deposited with them at the Ceres temple to prevent consular tampering. The temple of the Aventine triad thus acted as a plebeian counter-Capitol, with its own treasury and archive.

census_493.detail: The drop from his figure of 150,700 for 498 may reflect a tradition of losses in the Latin war and the secession, or simply inconsistent invented numbers.

famine_of_492.detail: Dionysius names Gelon of Syracuse as the Sicilian donor, an anachronism (Gelon took Syracuse in 485) already noticed by Dionysius himself, who criticised Licinius Macer and Gellius for it; Livy merely says 'the tyrant'. The annalistic record of famines (492, 456, 440-439, 411) and grain purchases from Etruria, Campania and Sicily probably derives from the pontifical tables and is among the more credible 5th-century data.
scholarship: Garnsey, Famine and Food Supply in the Graeco-Roman World (1988) 167-181
Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 320-322

colony_at_norba.detail: Norba's superb polygonal walls and gates (2.5 km circuit) survive; the town was destroyed by Sulla's forces in 82 BC and never reoccupied, so the street grid is visible from the air.

lex_icilia_492.detail: The law, if genuine, protected the tribune's ius agendi cum plebe, the right to convene and address the plebs, which became the basis of plebeian legislation. It fits a cluster of early laws in which the plebs, as a sworn community, protected their officers by a lex sacrata.
lex_icilia_492.debate: Known only from Dionysius; its authenticity is doubtful.

trial_of_coriolanus_491.detail: Livy names the donor vaguely as a Sicilian tyrant; Dionysius makes it Gelon, whereas other annalists named Dionysius I, an anachronism Dionysius himself pointed out. Dionysius presents the trial as the first before an assembly voting by tribes, a procedure scholars think he retrojected from the 4th century. Coriolanus went to Antium and to Attius Tullius, chief of the Volsci, with whom he planned the war of 488. The legend of a patrician war hero turned traitor through hatred of the plebs became a model in Plutarch and Shakespeare; modern scholars suspect a Volscian war leader called Marcius was fused with a Roman aristocratic myth.
trial_of_coriolanus_491.debate: Historicity of Coriolanus and of a tribal trial in 491 is widely doubted; the grain donor's identity was already contested in antiquity.

instauratio_ludi_romani_490.detail: The episode is the classic example of instauratio: any ritual flaw required the whole ceremony to be repeated. Cicero cites it from Fabius Pictor, which makes it one of the oldest recorded stories of Roman religion. Livy places it on the eve of Coriolanus' war; Macrobius used it to explain the festival called the 'Day of the Slave'.

fall_of_aristodemus_of_cumae.detail: Dionysius gives a long, partly romantic narrative based on a Cumaean chronicle, which is also an important independent source for the battle of Aricia (504). Aristodemus confiscated the Roman grain ships of 492 as compensation for Tarquin's property. Plutarch preserves a story that the courtesan Xenocrite helped the plotters.

anaxilas_takes_zancle.detail: Anaxilas married his daughter to Hiero of Syracuse but was the father-in-law and ally of Terillus of Himera, whose appeal brought the Carthaginian invasion of 480. His coinage at Rhegium and Messana shows a hare and a mule-car, commemorating an Olympic victory with mules. The control of the Strait recurs in Roman history: the Mamertines' seizure of Messana in 288 and their appeal of 264 began the First Punic War.
anaxilas_takes_zancle.debate: Chronology of the Samian seizure (c. 494-493) and the renaming (c. 488 or later) is disputed.

coriolanus_march_on_rome.detail: The temple of Fortuna Muliebris at the fourth milestone of the Via Latina was said to commemorate the women. The story has a real background: the Volscian advance into Latium in the early 5th century, which took Satricum, Antium, Velitrae, Circeii and the Pontine plain from Latin control. But the hero is probably fictitious, or a much reworked folk figure; the list of towns he captured mirrors later Volscian conquests.
coriolanus_march_on_rome.debate: Historicity of Coriolanus; Fabius Pictor had him live to old age in exile.
scholarship: Cornell, 'Coriolanus: myth, history and performance', in Braund & Gill (eds.), Myth, History and Culture in Republican Rome (2003)

treaty_with_hernici.detail: The Hernici held the strategic wedge between Volsci and Aequi; the triple alliance enabled the slow 5th-century counter-offensive. Livy's land confiscation is probably a confusion; Dionysius describes an equal treaty.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 299

temple_of_fortuna_muliebris.detail: Dionysius gives a detailed foundation narrative: the Senate offered the women a reward, they asked for a temple, and it was dedicated at public expense with a second statue paid for by the matrons. The cult and its location at the boundary of the early ager Romanus are real; the connection to Coriolanus is aetiology. The temple was restored under Augustus by Livia. It is one of a cluster of women's cults (Mater Matuta, Pudicitia, Venus Verticordia) whose foundation legends served as exempla of matronly virtue.
temple_of_fortuna_muliebris.debate: Dates of vow (488) and dedication (487 or 486) vary in the sources.

fall_of_spurius_cassius.detail: The tale of the first agrarian law looks heavily coloured by the Gracchan crisis; but the motif of the aristocrat who courts the plebs and is killed for 'regnum' (Cassius 485, Maelius 439, Manlius 384) seems to be a real archaic pattern of elite self-policing. A bronze statue of Ceres made from his confiscated property bore the inscription 'ex Cassia familia datum'.
fall_of_spurius_cassius.debate: Gracchan retrojection of the agrarian law is likely.
scholarship: Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 192-193

gelon_takes_syracuse_485.detail: Herodotus describes the deportations in detail: the rich of Megara were made citizens, the common people sold abroad. Gelon could field 20,000 hoplites and 200 triremes when the Greek allies asked his help against Xerxes in 481, and he refused unless given command. The resources concentrated at Syracuse explain the victory at Himera (480), and the city's later role as Rome's partner and rival.

fabian_consulships_485_479.detail: The Fabii first appear as hard-line opponents of Sp. Cassius' agrarian law (Caeso as quaestor prosecuted Cassius in 485, according to one version), then switch to conciliating the plebs: Caeso proposed in 479 that conquered land be distributed. Livy explains the Cremera expedition as the gens offering to fight Veii at its own cost. The run of consulships may be genuine, reflecting a gens with its own tribe (Fabia) and huge clientela, or partly the work of Fabius Pictor, Rome's first historian, glorifying his family.
fabian_consulships_485_479.debate: Possible family embellishment by Fabius Pictor.

temple_of_castor_484.detail: Excavations (Danish-Italian, 1980s) found the 5th-century podium under the Augustan-Tiberian rebuilding whose three standing columns are a Forum landmark. The temple was a meeting place of the Senate and later a weights-and-measures office.
scholarship: Nielsen & Poulsen (eds.), The Temple of Castor and Pollux I (1992)

vestal_oppia_483.detail: Vestals convicted of incestum were buried alive in an underground chamber at the Campus Sceleratus by the Colline Gate, so that no one shed their blood. The early cases (Oppia 483, Urbinia 472, Postumia accused 420, Minucia 337, Sextilia 273) cluster in years of crisis, showing that Vestal chastity was felt as the city's safety.

battle_of_himera_480.detail: Carthage paid 2,000 talents indemnity, and Gelon's Demareteion coinage and the Himera victory temple (the 'Temple of Victory', Doric) commemorate it. Carthage withdrew from Sicilian expansion for seventy years, turning to its African hinterland. The battle frames the western Greek world into which Rome's first contacts (grain from Sicily, Cumae) fall.
scholarship: CAH IV2 (1988) ch. 17 (Asheri)

olympieion_of_acragas.detail: Diodorus says some private Acragantines owned 500 prisoners each. The Olympieion, the largest Doric temple ever begun, was left unroofed when the Carthaginians sacked the city in 406; one reconstructed telamon is 7.6 m tall. The prisoners also built the temple at Himera. The scale of the programme illustrates how much wealth the defeat of Carthage transferred to the Sicilian tyrants.

peace_of_gelon_480.detail: Diodorus says Damarete coined silver from the crown, the 'Damareteion' worth ten Attic drachmas, which numismatists long identified with the magnificent Syracusan decadrachms showing Arethusa and a lion; modern die studies date those coins to the 460s, after the fall of the Deinomenids. The peace held for seventy years, until Carthage returned in 409.
peace_of_gelon_480.debate: Identification and date of the Damareteion decadrachm disputed (c. 479 or c. 465).

battle_of_veii_480.detail: Veii was supported by contingents from all Etruria, according to Livy. Fabius' refusal to triumph in a year of public mourning, and his care of the wounded in patrician houses, are presented as the turning point that reconciled the Fabii with the plebs, leading to the clan's volunteer war at the Cremera. The battle cost Rome heavily; the war continued until the forty-year truce of 474.

battle_of_the_cremera.detail: Ovid dates the disaster to the Ides of February; Livy (6.1.11) and Tacitus treat 18 July as the day of both the Cremera and the Allia. The '306' and the surviving child are legend (and modelled on the 300 Spartans), but the clan war of a gens with its clients against a neighbour fits the archaic world of the Lapis Satricanus. The Fabii vanish from the Fasti for a decade after 479, which may reflect a real catastrophe. The Porta Carmentalis through which they marched was thereafter ill-omened (the 'Porta Scelerata').
battle_of_the_cremera.debate: Date (13 Feb vs 18 July) and the role of the gens as a private army.
scholarship: Richardson, 'The Fabii and the Cremera', in Richardson & Santangelo (eds.), Andreas Alföldi in the Twenty-First Century (2015)
Smith, The Roman Clan (2006) 290-295

hiero_founds_aetna_476.detail: Hiero wanted to be honoured as a founder (oikistes) with hero cult after death, and was. After the Deinomenid fall the original Catanians returned (461) and the Aetnaeans moved to Inessa, renamed Aetna.

veientine_occupation_of_the_janiculum_47.detail: The occupation caused a grain shortage in Rome. The fighting shows how close the Veientine frontier lay: the right bank of the Tiber (ripa Veiens) was Etruscan territory, and control of the salt road and Tiber crossings was the issue in the Veientine wars.

trial_of_titus_menenius_476.detail: These are the first tribunician prosecutions of ex-consuls in Livy, a weapon of plebeian pressure that became regular. The 2,000-asses fine is expressed in bronze by weight, since Rome had no coins.

battle_of_cumae_474.detail: Hiero dedicated captured Etruscan helmets at Olympia; two survive, one in the British Museum inscribed 'Hiaron son of Deinomenes and the Syracusans to Zeus, Tyrrhenian spoils from Cumae'. Pindar's first Pythian celebrates the victory. Syracuse then planted a short-lived base on Pithecusae (Ischia). Weakened by the defeat, Etruscan Capua fell to the Samnites in 423.
scholarship: Meiggs & Lewis, Greek Historical Inscriptions no. 29 (helmet)

truce_with_veii_474.detail: Truces of fixed length (Veii 474, 40 years; Tarquinii 351, 40 years; Caere 353, 100 years; Volsinii 308, 30 years) were archaic Italian practice that pre-dated the formal foedus.

census_474.detail: Lower than his earlier figures, the total may preserve a tradition of losses in the Veientine war.

iapygian_defeat_of_tarentum.detail: Diodorus adds that the Iapygians pursued the Rhegines to Rhegium itself. Aristotle cites the defeat as a case where loss of the notables changed a constitution. Tarentum recovered and, with new dedications at Delphi from Messapian spoils, became the dominant Italiote power of the 4th century.

murder_of_the_tribune_genucius_473.detail: Livy implies patrician murder without proof. The episode led directly to Volero Publilius' defiance of the levy and to the lex Publilia of 471 transferring tribunician elections to an assembly by tribes. It shows sacrosanctity as a sworn plebeian protection that did not stop secret violence.

vestal_urbinia_472.detail: Dionysius is the only source. The double punishment of Vestal and seducer became standard. The Campus Sceleratus lay inside the Colline Gate near the later Baths of Diocletian.

lex_publilia_voleronis.detail: The consul Appius Claudius' resistance led to a battle in the Forum; his army then deserted against the Volsci and he decimated it, the first recorded decimation. The tribal assembly of the plebs (concilium plebis tributum) based on residence weakened patrician clientage in the curiate system. Number of tribunes may have been raised to four or five at this time.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 259-260

trial_and_death_of_appius_claudius_470.detail: Livy's Claudii are consistently arrogant patricians, a stereotype that Mommsen and later Wiseman traced to hostile annalists, notably Licinius Macer. The case belongs to the run of tribunician prosecutions of the 470s.
trial_and_death_of_appius_claudius_470.debate: The Claudian stereotype in Livy is likely literary.

tomb_of_the_diver_paestum.detail: The diver is usually read as a metaphor for the passage from life to death. Poseidonia was still Greek; around 410 the Lucanians took the city, and the painted tombs of the Lucanian period (4th century) show armoured horsemen and women mourners in Oscan dress.
scholarship: M. Napoli, La Tomba del Tuffatore (1970)

capture_of_antium_468.detail: Antium alternated between Roman and Volscian hands until its final capture in 338, when the beaks of its ships were fixed to the speakers' platform in the Forum.

colony_at_antium_467.detail: Livy presents the colony as a patrician alternative to distributing public land near Rome. The mixed settlement shows that early 'Latin' colonies were federal and multi-ethnic, and help explain why Antium could revert to the Volsci.

temple_of_dius_fidius_466.detail: Dionysius saw the Gabine treaty there. The temple also held a bronze statue of Gaia Caecilia (Tanaquil) with her distaff and spindle, and Varro said oaths 'me Dius Fidius' were sworn under its open roof. A base inscribed to Semo Sancus found on the Tiber Island led Justin Martyr to think Romans worshipped Simon Magus.

fall_of_the_deinomenids_466.detail: The new democracy faced civil strife with Gelon's enfranchised mercenaries, who were finally expelled. It experimented with petalism, an ostracism by olive leaves (454). Syracusan democracy lasted until Dionysius I seized power in 405, and fought off the Athenian expedition of 415-413.

census_465.detail: Early census figures (Servius 80,000; 508 c. 130,000 per Dionysius; 465 104,714; 459 117,319) are far too high for a city-state whose territory in c. 500 was about 822 km2 (Beloch's estimate): even counting all free males they imply a population greater than the land could carry. They are probably later inventions or back-projections, though the mid-Republican figures (from 293 onward) are generally taken seriously.
census_465.debate: Figures generally considered unreliable for the 5th century.
scholarship: Beloch, Römische Geschichte (1926)
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 204-208

plague_of_463.detail: Livy's sequence of 5th-century epidemics (463, 453, 436-433, 412, 399-398) is plausibly drawn from the pontifical annals; the 433 epidemic produced the vow of a temple to Apollo Medicus.

rogatio_terentilia_462.detail: Livy portrays Terentilius' rogation as the opening of the campaign that produced the Twelve Tables: an attack on the arbitrary coercive power (coercitio) of patrician magistrates and on the secrecy of law held by the pontiffs. Year after year the same tribunes were re-elected to push it, and the patricians answered with levies, violence by young nobles such as Caeso Quinctius, and religious obstruction. By 454 the plebs had shifted to demanding a general codification for both orders, which the patricians accepted on condition that the codifiers be patricians. The details are annalistic reconstruction, but a long agitation for written law preceding 451 is plausible and mirrors developments in the Greek world.
rogatio_terentilia_462.debate: The repeated tribunician colleges and the pattern of annual agitation are probably annalistic elaboration.

trial_of_caeso_quinctius_461.detail: The key witness, the former tribune M. Volscius Fictor, said Caeso had beaten his brother so badly that he died; in 459 Volscius was convicted of perjury and exiled. The impoverishment of Cincinnatus, reduced to four iugera beyond the Tiber, sets up the famous plough scene of 458. Livy uses Caeso to show patrician youth violence as a political weapon against the tribunate.

rain_of_flesh_461.detail: The Books warned of danger from foreigners gathering in the city and urged avoidance of sedition, an answer the patricians used against the tribunes. The episode is an early example of the prodigy-and-expiation cycle that structured Roman religious life.

ducetius_sicel_league.detail: Ducetius' movement is the one serious attempt by an indigenous Sicilian people to build a state against the Greek cities. He exploited the turmoil after the fall of the Deinomenids, sited his federal capital beside the sacred lake of the Palici (the twin gods of oaths), and in 451 took the Acragantine fort of Motyon. Syracuse spared him, which caused a war with Acragas. Diodorus, drawing on Timaeus, is the only narrative source; excavations at Rocchicella di Mineo have found the sanctuary.

seizure_of_the_capitol_460.detail: Like Attus Clausus, Herdonius illustrates the archaic warlord with a private following; a Turnus Herdonius of Aricia appears in the Tarquin saga. The tribunes had initially obstructed the levy, arguing the threat was a patrician trick.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 144

census_459.detail: See census_465 on the reliability of 5th-century census figures. Dionysius gives slightly different numbers.

battle_of_mount_algidus_458.detail: The tale became the paradigm of Republican virtue, but Livy's account of an army enclosing the besiegers with a ditch and stockade overnight, each man carrying twelve stakes, is a stock motif. The Algidus pass, carrying the route from the Aequian hills to the Alban plain, was the recurrent front of the 5th-century Aequian wars. Dionysius gives a different chronology.
scholarship: Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 437-444

tribunes_increased_to_ten.detail: A larger college made intercession (veto by a single colleague) a tool that the patricians could exploit by winning over one tribune, a tactic used against the Licinio-Sextian rogations and the Gracchi.

lex_icilia_de_aventino.detail: Dionysius says the bronze text was set up in the temple of Diana on the Aventine. The Aventine became the plebeian quarter par excellence and the site of the second secession.

lex_aternia_tarpeia.detail: The law is a precious glimpse of a pre-monetary economy in which value was reckoned in livestock (pecus, whence pecunia) and uncoined bronze by weight.

embassy_to_athens_454.detail: Most scholars doubt an Athenian mission: the Twelve Tables show few specifically Solonian features (a funerary restriction and the rule on boundary strips, which Gaius compared to Solon, are the strongest). Influence via the Greek cities of southern Italy, and the tradition that Hermodorus of Ephesus, an exile, helped the decemvirs (a statue of him stood in the Comitium per Pliny), are more plausible.
embassy_to_athens_454.debate: Historicity of the embassy widely doubted.
scholarship: Crawford (ed.), Roman Statutes II (1996) 555-721
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 275

syracusan_raid_on_etruria_453.detail: Elba (Aethalia) was the source of Etruscan iron, smelted at Populonia. The raids continued the Syracusan offensive begun at Cumae in 474 and weakened Etruscan sea power at the moment when Rome was consolidating against Veii. Dionysius I repeated the exercise with the sack of Pyrgi in 384.

plague_of_453.detail: Livy's notice comes from priestly lists, which recorded deaths in the colleges, and is therefore one of the more credible early items.

first_decemvirate.detail:
After a decade of tribunician agitation for written law, the patricians agreed in 452 to a codification, provided the codifiers were patricians. For 451 the consulship and the tribunate were suspended and ten men were elected 'for writing the laws' (decemviri legibus scribundis) with consular power and no appeal: Ap. Claudius and T. Genucius, the consuls-designate, the three envoys sent to Greece, and five others. Livy says they governed with moderation, each in turn holding the fasces for a day while his colleagues were attended only by an orderly, and that Appius was the dominant figure. At year's end they displayed ten tables in the Forum and invited citizens to propose amendments, after which the laws were passed by the centuriate assembly.

The embassy of 454, which supposedly studied the laws of Solon at Athens and other Greek cities, is controversial. The Twelve Tables do contain rules with clear Greek parallels: Gaius compared the rule on boundary spaces to a law of Solon, the rule on associations to another, and Cicero noted that the limits on funeral luxury were borrowed from Solon. Pliny says Hermodorus of Ephesus, an exile who advised the decemvirs, was honoured with a statue in the Comitium. Many scholars think the Greek influence came through Magna Graecia, especially Cumae and the law codes of Zaleucus and Charondas, rather than from Athens directly.

The first decemvirate was so satisfactory, according to Livy, that a second board was elected for 450 to complete the work, with fatal results. The suspension of the tribunate shows that the plebs had accepted giving up their protective office in exchange for written law, a sign of how much they valued certainty against patrician arbitrariness.
first_decemvirate.debate: The historicity of the embassy to Athens and the extent of Greek influence on the code are debated; some doubt that the tribunate was really suspended.
scholarship: Broughton, MRR I 45-46
Crawford (ed.), Roman Statutes II (1996) no. 40
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 272-276

twelve_tables.detail:
The Twelve Tables were Rome's first and only comprehensive codification before Justinian. Ten tables were enacted in 451 and two more in 450; they were displayed in the Forum, on bronze according to Livy, on wood or ivory according to other writers, and are said to have perished in the Gallic sack. The text survives only in quotations by Cicero, Festus, Gellius, the jurists and Gaius' lost commentary, and modern reconstructions (the standard edition is Crawford's Roman Statutes no. 40) assign fragments to tables by guesswork.

The fragments are terse commands in archaic Latin. 'If he summons to court, let him go' (si in ius vocat, ito) opens the code. A judgment debtor had thirty days' grace; then the creditor could lay hands on him, take him home in chains for sixty days, display him at three market days, and then, the code says, 'cut shares' (partes secanto) among several creditors or sell him abroad across the Tiber. A father who sold his son three times lost his power over him, a clause later used as a fiction for emancipation. Possession of land for two years and of other things for one gave ownership (usucapio); a wife who stayed away three nights a year avoided falling into her husband's power (manus). Breaking a free man's bone cost 300 asses, a slave's 150; a simple insult 25; maiming was punished by retaliation unless settled. A thief caught at night could be killed; a false witness was thrown from the Tarpeian Rock; a patron who defrauded his client was declared sacer. No one was to be buried or cremated inside the city, women were not to tear their cheeks at funerals, and gold was not to be buried with the dead, except gold binding the teeth. Magical spells against crops or persons were capital, and capital cases could be decided only by the 'greatest assembly'.

The code was not a constitution but a statement of existing custom on procedure, family, property, debt and delict, removing it from pontifical secrecy. Livy called it 'the fount of all public and private law', and Cicero recalled learning it by heart as a boy. Its authenticity, doubted by Pais and Lambert, is now accepted on linguistic grounds, and its picture of an agrarian society of farmers, debtors, clients and slaves is our best window on 5th-century Rome.
twelve_tables.debate: The text is a modern reconstruction; the attribution of fragments to individual tables and some clauses (e.g. the literal cutting of debtors) are disputed.
scholarship: Crawford (ed.), Roman Statutes II (1996) 555-721
Watson, Rome of the XII Tables (1975)
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 272-292
Crawford (ed.), Roman Statutes II (1996) no. 40

second_decemvirate_450.detail: Livy contrasts the moderate first board with a second that appeared with 120 lictors, all carrying axes, and ruled by terror. Cicero called the conubium ban 'most inhuman'. The plebeian names in the college (Poetelius, Duillius, Rabuleius, Oppius, Antonius) have led modern scholars to suspect that the tyranny story distorts a genuinely mixed board, and that the conubium clause was itself a codification of existing patrician exclusivity. The decemvirate fell in 449 after the Verginia affair and the Second Secession.
second_decemvirate_450.debate: Whether plebeians sat on the second board, and whether the tyranny narrative is a later construction, are debated (Cornell, Beginnings of Rome).

burning_of_the_pythagorean_houses.detail: Polybius says the burning of the Pythagorean synedria throughout Magna Graecia brought chaos until the Achaeans of the Peloponnese mediated and the cities adopted Achaean institutions. Later the Pythagorean Archytas governed Tarentum (c. 367-347). The episode shows how philosophical brotherhoods acted as oligarchic parties in the Greek West.
burning_of_the_pythagorean_houses.debate: Date (c. 510, c. 450 or several waves) disputed.

second_secession_of_the_plebs.detail:
The second decemvirate, re-elected in 450 with Appius Claudius at its head, ruled beyond its term into 449 with 120 lictors and axes in the fasces, according to Livy. While two armies fought the Sabines and the Aequi, Appius conceived a passion for Verginia, daughter of the plebeian centurion L. Verginius and betrothed of the former tribune L. Icilius. He had his client M. Claudius claim her in court as the child of one of his slave women, and then, as judge, awarded interim custody to the claimant, violating the decemvirs' own rule that liberty should be presumed pending trial. Verginius, summoned from the army on the Algidus, led his daughter aside near the shrine of Cloacina in the Forum, seized a butcher's knife from a stall and stabbed her, crying that this was the only way to keep her free.

He rode to the army, which marched to Rome and occupied the Aventine; the Sabine army, roused by Icilius and Numitorius, joined it. When the decemvirs refused to resign, the plebs withdrew to the Mons Sacer, leaving the city empty. The Senate sent L. Valerius and M. Horatius to negotiate; the decemvirs abdicated, tribunes were elected on the Aventine (including Verginius, Icilius and Numitorius), and Valerius and Horatius were elected consuls and carried their famous laws. Appius killed himself in prison awaiting trial.

The Verginia story closely mirrors that of Lucretia: an act of sexual violence by a tyrant against a virtuous woman, a male relative's sacrifice, and the overthrow of the oppressor. It is a moral drama about liberty (libertas) and the protection of the citizen body, with the legal point of vindiciae secundum libertatem at its centre. Modern historians treat the details as legend. Some argue that the image of a tyrannical second decemvirate is itself a construction to explain why the last two tables included the unpopular ban on patrician-plebeian intermarriage, and that the reforms attributed to 449 were partly retrojected from later centuries.
second_secession_of_the_plebs.debate: The tyranny of the second decemvirate and the Verginia story are widely seen as legend modelled on Lucretia; the extent of the 449 restoration is debated.
scholarship: Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 476-497
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 222-225
Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 476-500
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 274-275

leges_valeriae_horatiae.detail:
The consuls of the restoration, L. Valerius Potitus and M. Horatius Barbatus, carried three laws in the centuriate assembly that Livy presents as the charter of plebeian liberty. First, what the plebs resolved in its tribal assembly (plebiscitum) should bind the whole people. Second, no one should create a magistracy without appeal (provocatio), and anyone who did so might be killed without crime. Third, the tribunes of the plebs, the plebeian aediles and 'the judges, the decemvirs' were declared sacrosanct by statute, anyone harming them to be sacer to Jupiter and his property sold at the temple of Ceres. The tribune M. Duillius then carried a plebiscite threatening flogging and beheading for anyone who left the plebs without tribunes or created a magistrate without appeal. The consuls also began the practice of depositing copies of senatorial decrees with the plebeian aediles at the temple of Ceres, to prevent the patricians from altering them.

The first law poses a famous puzzle. Livy credits the same rule to Q. Publilius Philo in 339 and to the dictator Q. Hortensius in 287, and only the last is universally accepted as decisive. Explanations include: the 449 law required senatorial approval (auctoritas patrum) for plebiscites, and 339 and 287 progressively removed conditions; the 449 law referred to the tribal assembly of the whole people (comitia tributa) rather than the plebeian council; or the 449 and 339 laws are annalistic doublets. The second law similarly duplicates the leges Valeriae de provocatione of 509 and 300, the latter generally regarded as the first genuine one.

Whatever their exact content, the laws of 449 mark the moment when the plebeian institutions created by oath in 494 began to be recognised by the state as a whole. The Valerii and Horatii appear in the tradition as the patrician houses friendly to the plebs, a pattern that owes much to family historians such as Valerius Antias.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 277-278
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 230-233
Lintott, The Constitution of the Roman Republic (1999) 33-37

murder_of_siccius_dentatus_449.detail: Siccius had been urging the troops to secede. His record (120 battles, nine triumphs following generals) is preserved in Pliny, Dionysius and Gellius with variants; it is a later catalogue of military virtue but expresses the idea that plebeian valour carried the early Republic. The murder, with the Verginia affair, triggered the mutiny of the armies.

triumph_of_horatius_449.detail: The episode reinforces the image of Valerius and Horatius as the pro-plebeian consuls of the restoration. It became a precedent: in 356 C. Marcius Rutilus, the first plebeian dictator, and in 223 C. Flaminius triumphed by popular vote against the Senate.

trial_of_the_decemvirs_449.detail: M. Claudius, the client who had claimed Verginia as his slave, was condemned but allowed to go into exile at Tibur. The tribune M. Duillius then declared an end to prosecutions, a kind of amnesty. Livy's account builds the restoration of 449 as a constitutional reset, with the leges Valeriae Horatiae guaranteeing appeal and tribunician sacrosanctity.

lex_trebonia_448.detail: Co-optation had allowed patricians into the college. The law also shows the tribunate as an elected office of the concilium plebis, distinct from the magistracies of the whole people.

quaestors_elected_447.detail: The quaestores parricidii (criminal investigators) and the treasury quaestors may originally have been separate; numbers rose to four in 421, with plebeians eligible, and eight in 267.

ardea_aricia_arbitration.detail: Rome made amends to Ardea in 442 by sending a colony there, ostensibly to protect it from Volscian pressure and internal strife. The territory may be the origin of the tribus Scaptia (created 332).

battle_against_aequi_and_volsci_446.detail: Livy claims the booty was claimed by the Roman people in the notorious Ardea-Aricia arbitration of the same year. The episode illustrates how close the Aequian frontier still lay in the 440s.

lex_canuleia.detail:
In 445 the tribune C. Canuleius proposed that patricians and plebeians be allowed to intermarry, repealing the clause of the last two tables, while his colleagues proposed that one consul might be plebeian. The patricians objected that mixed marriages would confuse the gentes and pollute the auspices, which only patricians could take, since children of a mixed marriage would not know to which order they belonged. Livy gives Canuleius a celebrated speech: Rome's kings themselves had been outsiders, Numa a Sabine, Tarquinius Priscus the son of a Corinthian exile, Servius Tullius the son of a captive woman; why should a plebeian not marry a patrician or hold the consulship if the people elected him? The marriage law passed; the consulship proposal was deflected by the creation of military tribunes with consular power in 444.

The consequences were long-term rather than immediate. Intermarriage allowed the formation of a mixed elite of patrician and wealthy plebeian families, linked by marriage alliances, that became the nobilitas of the 4th and 3rd centuries. Because patrician status passed through the father, plebeian men who married patrician women did not change their children's status, which explains episodes like the story of Fabia (377) and Verginia's shrine of Plebeian Chastity (296).

Scholars disagree about what was banned. Cicero says the decemvirs added the prohibition to the last two tables, but many think patricians had long been endogamous by custom, and that the decemvirs only codified it. Others suggest the ban concerned the sacral form of marriage (confarreatio) required for certain priesthoods, rather than all unions. Whether there was real social mixing before 445 is uncertain: the plebeian names among the early consuls suggest a more open early elite, which had closed by the mid-5th century and was now reopened.
lex_canuleia.debate: Whether the decemvirs introduced a new ban or codified patrician endogamy, and whether the ban applied to all marriage or only confarreatio, are debated.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 252-256, 292
Linderski, 'The Auspices and the Struggle of the Orders', in Eder (ed.), Staat und Staatlichkeit (1990)

consular_tribunes_444.detail:
From 444 to 367 Rome was governed in most years not by two consuls but by a college of military tribunes with consular power (tribuni militum consulari potestate): three in the early years, four in some, and six from 405 onward. Livy counts about fifty such years. The first college of 444 abdicated after three months because of a flaw in their election, and suffect consuls took over, which Licinius Macer confirmed from the treaty with Ardea and the linen books.

Ancient writers offered two explanations, both recorded by Livy. The political one: the patricians, under pressure from the Canuleian agitation, created an office that plebeians could hold without opening the consulship itself. The military one: Rome needed more commanders than two consuls to fight the Aequi, Volsci and Veii at once. The facts fit the second better. No plebeian was elected until P. Licinius Calvus in 400, after which plebeians appear frequently, and the larger colleges of six coincide with the multi-front wars of 405-396 and the 380s. Consular tribunes never triumphed, suggesting that their auspices or imperium differed from the consuls'. Modern scholars (for example Cornell, Ridley, Bastien) generally combine the explanations: a flexible military command structure that also became an arena of plebeian ambition.

The years without consuls (375-371) belong to the same period and are now thought to be an artefact of the later chronographers. The Licinio-Sextian laws of 367 abolished the consular tribunate and restored the consulship, with one place open to plebeians, alongside a new praetorship. The episode shows Roman institutional pragmatism: the Republic changed its top magistracy for seventy years without any formal constitution.
consular_tribunes_444.debate: Political vs military explanation of the consular tribunate.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 334-339
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 234-239
Broughton, MRR I 52-53
Ridley, 'The consular tribunate: the testimony of Livy', Klio 68 (1986)

foundation_of_thurii_444.detail: The original Sybarite settlers claimed privileges and were expelled or killed. The citizens were organised in ten tribes by origin (Athenian, Arcadian, Achaean and others), and the city soon broke with Athens, Delphi declaring Apollo its founder. Thurii fought Tarentum over the Siritis, and its appeals to Rome against the Lucanians in the 280s helped draw Rome into southern Italy.

treaty_with_ardea_444.detail: Livy notes that the annals and the lists of magistrates omitted these consuls, which shows how Roman historians reconstructed the Fasti from documents. The libri lintei were magistrate lists on linen, consulted by Macer and Tubero in the 1st century BC; their authenticity was questioned already by Livy.
treaty_with_ardea_444.debate: Value of the libri lintei and the suffect consulship of 444 are disputed.

censorship_created.detail: The first censors held the census in the Villa Publica on the Campus Martius from 435. The lex Aemilia of 434 limited the censorship to 18 months within a five-year cycle, the lustrum.
scholarship: Suolahti, The Roman Censors (1963)
