Broughton, MRR I 53-54

colony_at_ardea.detail: Ardea, on a tufa spur near the coast, was one of the Latin cities named in the 509 Carthage treaty. Camillus later went into exile there (391).

spurius_maelius_439.detail: L. Minucius, praefectus annonae, was honoured with a column outside the Porta Trigemina; the columna Minucia appears on a denarius of 135 BC. Cicero celebrated Ahala as a tyrannicide (Brutus the assassin claimed descent from him). An older version (Cincius, Piso) had Ahala act as a private citizen without a dictatorship; the dictatorship may be later justification.
scholarship: Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 240-241
Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974) no. 243

foundation_of_campanian_league_438.detail: The Campanians kept Oscan as their language and the meddix tuticus as chief magistrate. Their cavalry was famous and their mercenaries served in Sicily for Carthage and Dionysius, later seizing Entella, Aetna and Messana. The distinction between lowland Campanians and highland Samnites became the fault line of the First Samnite War.

murder_of_roman_envoys_at_fidenae_438.detail: Cicero and Pliny saw the statues, which stood until the late Republic and were among the oldest portrait statues in Rome. Killing envoys violated the ius gentium and justified the war in which A. Cornelius Cossus killed Tolumnius and won the spolia opima.

battle_of_fidenae_437.detail: Livy reports that Augustus told him he had read on the linen corslet in the temple of Jupiter Feretrius that Cossus was consul when he won the spoils (so 428). The emperor's interest was political: in 29-27 BC Augustus denied M. Licinius Crassus (proconsul, not commander under his own auspices) the right to dedicate spolia opima. Statues of the four murdered envoys stood on the Rostra.
battle_of_fidenae_437.debate: Date of Cossus' feat (437 as military tribune, 428 as consul or 426 as magister equitum); Augustus' evidence is suspect.
scholarship: Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 563-567
Rich, 'Augustus and the spolia opima', Chiron 26 (1996)

plague_of_436_433.detail: Livy notes that the plague kept Rome from exploiting the destruction of Fidenae. The vow to Apollo, Rome's first Greek healing cult with its own temple, was fulfilled in 431 by the consul Cn. Julius.

villa_publica_435.detail: The Villa Publica remained the census office and the place where returning generals awaiting a triumph and foreign envoys were lodged outside the pomerium; Sulla massacred Samnite prisoners there in 82.

concilium_at_fanum_voltumnae_434.detail: The Fanum Voltumnae near Volsinii hosted annual assemblies, games and the election of a federal priest. Livy records later council meetings in 405, 403 and 389. Excavations at Campo della Fiera below Orvieto since 2000 have found a large sanctuary with temples, a sacred way and votives, now widely accepted as the Fanum.
scholarship: Stopponi, excavations at Campo della Fiera (2000-)

lex_aemilia_de_censura_434.detail: The law fixed the shape of the censorship for the rest of the Republic: censors elected every five years (later) but holding office only eighteen months, long enough to complete the census and let contracts. Livy says the people were outraged by the censors' revenge; Mamercus reportedly bore it calmly.

foundation_of_heraclea_433.detail: The Heraclea Tablets, bronze inscriptions of c. 300 recording temple land surveys, and the later Tabula Heracleensis with Roman municipal law were found nearby. Pyrrhus defeated the Romans on the Siris plain in 280; in 278 Heraclea obtained an unusually favourable treaty with Rome.

lex_de_ambitu_432.detail: The word candidatus comes from the chalk-whitened toga (toga candida). Livy calls this the first law on ambitus; later ones followed in 358, 181, 159 and onward.

temple_of_apollo_medicus.detail: Apollo came to Rome via the Sibylline Books, purchased from the Cumaean Sibyl according to legend. The temple stood near the later Theatre of Marcellus; its Augustan rebuilding by C. Sosius (the Apollo Sosianus) survives in three restored columns. The Senate met there to hear generals and envoys outside the pomerium.
scholarship: Ziolkowski, The Temples of Mid-Republican Rome (1992)

battle_of_mount_algidus_431.detail: Livy tells that Postumius had his own son executed for leaving his post to fight, a story he doubts (and which recurs with Manlius Torquatus in 340, 'imperia Manliana'). Rome now began to take the offensive: Labici (418), Bolae, Ferentinum (413).
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 307-309

imperia_postumiana_431.detail: Livy argues that the proverb belongs to Manlius Torquatus (340), whose execution of his son was certain, and doubts the Postumian version for lack of evidence. The doublet shows how family traditions competed for famous exempla.

first_athenian_expedition_to_sicily_427.detail: Gorgias' speeches at Athens introduced Sicilian rhetoric to the city. Athens' motive, according to Thucydides, was to stop Sicilian grain reaching the Peloponnese and to test the conquest of the island. The intervention set the precedent for the great expedition of 415.

siege_of_fidenae_426.detail: Fidenae controlled the Tiber crossing and the salt route upstream; its loss severed Veii from the Sabine and Faliscan hinterland and gave Rome both banks of the lower Tiber. A 20-year truce with Veii followed.

samnite_seizure_of_capua.detail: Part of a wider movement of Sabellian peoples (the ver sacrum, 'sacred spring', migrations) from the Apennines into the lowlands and Greek south in the later 5th century: Lucanians took Poseidonia (Paestum) c. 410-400, the Bruttii emerged c. 356. The Campanians soon diverged from their Samnite kin and appealed to Rome against them in 343.
scholarship: Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967) 37-39
Frederiksen, Campania (1984) 134-157

battle_of_sextus_tempanius_423.detail: Tempanius was honoured by the plebs and elected tribune; Sempronius was prosecuted and in 420 fined 15,000 asses. The story illustrates the early cavalry's habit of dismounting, which Livy repeats elsewhere.

fall_of_cumae_421.detail: Survivors fled to Neapolis. Cumae retained its oracle of the Sibyl, but Oscan inscriptions dominate from now on. Livy and Diodorus give 421/420.
scholarship: Frederiksen, Campania (1984)

quaestors_increased_421.detail: Patricians won all quaestorships until 409, when three of four went to plebeians, an index of the gradual erosion of the patrician monopoly.

vestal_postumia_420.detail: Livy's terse story is valuable because it shows suspicion of incestum resting on manner rather than evidence, and the pontifex maximus' disciplinary power over the Vestals.

colony_at_labici.detail: The first colony recorded after the Algidus victory, it consolidated Rome's hold on the north side of the Alban Hills. The small allotment size (about half a hectare) is a striking datum for archaic Roman smallholding.

agrarian_rogation_416.detail: The 'divide the tribunes' tactic became a standard patrician defence and foreshadows the deposition of Octavius by Ti. Gracchus in 133.

athenian_siege_of_syracuse_415.detail: The expedition is part of Italian history as well as Greek. Thucydides notes that some Etruscan cities, hostile to Syracuse since the raids of 453, sent three penteconters, and Etruscan troops fought in the battles of 413, at one point routing the Syracusans on the shore. Several Italiote cities refused Athens supplies; Rhegium stayed neutral; Thurii and Metapontum sent troops. Syracuse emerged as the leading Greek naval power of the West, and Hermocrates' career led, through his son-in-law Dionysius, to the 4th-century tyranny. The cost to Athens (perhaps 40,000 men including allies and rowers) helped decide the Peloponnesian War.

murder_of_postumius_at_bolae.detail: The episode was entangled with tribunician demands for an agrarian law dividing the territory of Bolae.

elogia_tarquiniensia_spurinna.detail: The Elogia Tarquiniensia, found in 1948 in the temple area of the Ara della Regina and published by Torelli (1975), also commemorate Aulus Spurinna, who deposed a king of Caere and fought Arretium and the Latins. They are rare Etruscan family memory surviving into Roman times, and show a Tarquinian aristocracy acting in Mediterranean wars, confirming Thucydides' note on Etruscan contingents at Syracuse.
elogia_tarquiniensia_spurinna.debate: Identification of the Sicilian expedition with 414-413 is likely but unproven; some date it to the 5th-century raids of Syracuse instead.
scholarship: M. Torelli, Elogia Tarquiniensia (1975)

famine_of_411.detail: Livy's detail that Cumae had become hostile reflects the Oscan conquest of 421. Repeated famines show the narrow agricultural base of 5th-century Rome.

lucanians_take_poseidonia.detail: Archaeology shows continuity: the temples stayed in use, Oscan names appear in inscriptions, and the painted tombs show Lucanian warriors with Samnite-style belts and crested helmets. Alexander of Epirus briefly recaptured the city (c. 332). Rome founded the Latin colony of Paestum there in 273.

first_plebeian_quaestors_409.detail: Livy presents this as the plebs' first success in winning a regular office of the whole people. The quaestorship later became the entry point to the Senate.

carthaginian_destruction_of_selinus_409.detail: Diodorus gives the Carthaginian army as 100,000 (Timaeus) or 200,000 (Ephorus), both inflated. Selinus had been an ally of Carthage in 480; its fall ended seventy years of peace and opened a century of Punic-Syracusan warfare. The city survived as a small Punic settlement until its final evacuation in 250; its great temples (Temple C, G) stand in ruins today.

destruction_of_himera_409.detail: A Syracusan relief force under Diocles evacuated part of the population by sea. Excavations at Himera have found mass graves from both 480 and 409. The poet Stesichorus had been Himera's most famous son; the Roman-era town of Thermae preserved its statue until Verres stole it.

siege_of_anxur_406.detail: Anxur changed hands repeatedly (lost 402, retaken 400); Rome planted a citizen colony at Tarracina in 329. The Temple of Jupiter Anxur on Monte S. Angelo overlooks the site.

introduction_of_stipendium.detail:
In 406, Livy reports, the Senate on its own initiative decreed that the soldiers should be paid from public funds, a measure greeted with joy by the plebs. To finance it a property tax (tributum) was levied on citizens according to their census rating; the senators led the way by paying first, and since there was as yet no coined money, they carried their bronze by weight to the treasury in wagons. The tribunes complained that the tax was a disguised burden on the poor. Diodorus also reports that during the Veientine war the Romans voted annual pay for their soldiers.

Pay made possible the long siege of Veii, including the first winter campaigns (Livy dates the first winter camp to 403). In the same years citizens of equestrian census without a public horse volunteered to serve on their own mounts, and cavalry pay was fixed. Livy also links the change from the round hoplite shield to the oblong scutum with the introduction of pay, a crucial step toward the manipular legion.

Tributum was not a regular annual tax but an extraordinary levy, sometimes treated as a forced loan to be repaid from booty, as happened after major victories; it was suspended entirely after 167 when the treasury filled with Macedonian wealth. Pay (stipendium, from stips, a small coin or bronze piece) remained modest, covering subsistence rather than providing a wage. Scholars have doubted that pay could exist before coinage, but payment in weighed bronze, or in grain and equipment, is plausible. Whatever the exact date, a state able to sustain armies beyond a summer season was a precondition of the conquest of Veii and of Rome's later expansion.
introduction_of_stipendium.debate: Some scholars think pay before coinage is anachronistic, or that Livy has antedated a later practice; the nature and amount of early pay are unknown.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 187, 313
Nicolet, The World of the Citizen in Republican Rome (1980) ch. 4
Rosenstein, Rome at War (2004)

siege_of_acragas_406.detail: Diodorus, drawing on Timaeus, dwells on Acragantine luxury: the citizen Gellias who entertained 500 horsemen at once, the 300 white horses of a wedding procession, the tombs built for racehorses and pet birds. The army included Campanian and Iberian mercenaries. Phalaris' bronze bull was carried off to Carthage, to be returned by Scipio Aemilianus in 146. The Syracusan generals' failure led to the rise of Dionysius I. Acragas was refounded by Timoleon in 338 and became a Punic base in the First Punic War.

siege_of_veii.detail:
Veii stood on a tufa plateau of about 190 hectares, as large as Rome, 15 km north of it, controlling the right bank of the lower Tiber, the salt route from the coast and a territory (ager Veientanus) of some 560 km2. The two cities had fought intermittently for a century. The final war began in 406, and the tradition made the siege last ten years, like the siege of Troy. Its episodes mark real changes in Roman warfare: soldiers' pay from 406, winter camps from 403, volunteer cavalry, the loss of the siege lines in 402 through the quarrel of Sergius and Verginius, and the isolation of Veii when the Etruscan league refused help because the Veientes had chosen a king.

Religion frames the climax. In 398 the Alban Lake rose without rain; a captured Veientine haruspex and the Delphic oracle both declared that Veii would not fall until the water was drained, and the Romans cut the emissarium tunnel. In 396 M. Furius Camillus, named dictator with P. Cornelius Scipio as master of horse, had a tunnel dug under the walls to the citadel temple of Juno. Livy's anecdote has Roman soldiers emerging just as the Veientine king was sacrificing, and snatching the entrails so that Camillus could complete the sacrifice and claim its promise of victory. Camillus summoned Juno Regina to leave her city by evocatio; when a young soldier asked the statue if she wished to go to Rome, she nodded. The city was sacked, the free population sold, and Camillus triumphed in a chariot drawn by four white horses, offending the plebs by imitating Jupiter. A tenth of the booty was vowed to Apollo, and a gold bowl was sent to Delphi.

The conquest nearly doubled Roman territory. Four new tribes were created in 387, and plebeian proposals to move to Veii were narrowly defeated. Archaeology shows that Veii was not wiped out: sanctuaries such as Portonaccio and Campetti continued in use, and Roman settlers lived among the survivors. The network of drainage tunnels (cuniculi) around Veii may have inspired the tunnel story. For the first time Rome had destroyed a major Etruscan city and absorbed its land, the beginning of territorial conquest.
siege_of_veii.debate: Duration and details; the evocatio story; the real scale of the war.
scholarship: Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 626-680
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 309-313
Ward-Perkins, 'Veii: the historical topography of the ancient city', PBSR 29 (1961)

dionysius_seizes_power_405.detail: He married the daughter of Hermocrates to link himself to the dead leader's party, failed to relieve Gela (405) and crushed a revolt of the Syracusan cavalry on his return. He fortified the island of Ortygia as a citadel and later enclosed Epipolae with the longest Greek fortification circuit (c. 27 km), built the Euryalus fort, and created the first catapults (399). His tyranny became the classic model for Greek political theory, from Plato to Aristotle.

treaty_of_405_carthage_syracuse.detail: Diodorus' text of the treaty is one of the few Greek-Punic agreements preserved. The clause recognising Dionysius' rule gave him legitimacy, which ancient writers saw as Carthage's error. He broke the treaty in 397 by attacking Motya.

six_consular_tribunes_405.detail: The larger colleges reflect military need: several fronts (Veii, the Volsci, the Aequi) required several commanders, a strong argument for the view that the consular tribunate was a military rather than a political compromise.

campanians_seize_entella_404.detail: The episode is the first of a sequence of Campanian mercenary seizures in Sicily and southern Italy (Aetna 403, Messana 288, Rhegium 280). Bronze tablets of the 3rd century from Entella record decrees of the Campanian-Greek community.

censorship_403_aes_uxorium.detail: The censorship of Camillus is known from Valerius Maximus and Plutarch, not Livy, and may be invented. The idea of penalising celibacy reappears in Augustus' marriage laws.

equites_equo_privato_403.detail: The episode explains the later distinction between equites equo publico, who received a state horse and were enrolled in the 18 centuries, and wealthy citizens who served on their own horses. Infantry volunteers also came forward, and pay was extended to those serving beyond their obligation. It fits the general shift to a paid army during the Veientine war.

veii_elects_a_king_403.detail: Livy's story indicates that most Etruscan cities were by then republics governed by annual magistrates (zilath), and that the league at the Fanum Voltumnae had a religious head. Veii's isolation sealed its fate in 396.

sergius_verginius_feud_402.detail: Livy uses the episode to show private enmity (inimicitia) destroying public interest. The Capenates and Faliscans, Veii's only allies, were punished in the following years.

eclipse_of_400.detail: The passage is precious evidence that the Annales Maximi recorded eclipses from at least c. 400 and that the pontifical calendar was then still roughly in step with the seasons (Nones of June = late June). Precise identification is debated; some prefer an earlier eclipse (e.g. 404) depending on calendar slippage.
eclipse_of_400.debate: Which eclipse is meant; calendar slippage.
scholarship: Skutsch, The Annals of Q. Ennius (1985) 311-313
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 69-70

first_plebeian_consular_tribune.detail: The sudden plebeian success during the Veientine war and its equally sudden reversal show how fragile plebeian access remained before 367. Some names in Livy's lists may be later interpolations by plebeian families.
scholarship: Broughton, MRR I 84-85

senones_settle_ager_gallicus.detail: Rich warrior graves at Montefortino, Filottrano and San Ginesio, with Etruscan bronzes and Greek pottery, show a Celtic elite in contact with Italy from the early 4th century. The Senones' raids peaked in 390 and the 360s-340s, and their territory was conquered by Rome in 283, becoming the first great block of ager publicus distributed by Flaminius in 232.

chimera_of_arezzo.detail: It was probably one figure from a group with Bellerophon, dedicated in a sanctuary. Cosimo I de' Medici acquired it, and Benvenuto Cellini restored parts; the serpent tail is an 18th-century replacement. Arretium was later a key Roman ally and producer of fine red pottery (terra sigillata).
scholarship: M. Cristofani, I bronzi degli Etruschi (1985)

mars_of_todi.detail: The statue embodies the mixed world of the central Apennines around 400: Umbrian language, Etruscan craftsmanship and script, Greek style, and a Celtic dedicant, perhaps a mercenary.
scholarship: F. Roncalli, Il 'Marte' di Todi (1973)

first_lectisternium.detail: A Greek rite (theoxenia) channelled through the Sibylline Books; householders kept open house and prisoners were unchained. Lectisternia recur in crises (364, 349, 217).

alban_lake_emissarium.detail: The tunnel (emissarium) is real: about 1,450 m long through the crater rim, still functioning, and probably of the 5th-4th century. It probably served agriculture and flood control; the prodigy legend rationalised the work.

siege_of_motya_397.detail: The siege is a landmark in Greek siege technology. Carthage replied under Himilco by recapturing the west and besieging Syracuse in 396, until plague destroyed his army. Survivors founded Lilybaeum nearby, later Carthage's chief Sicilian base against Pyrrhus and Rome.
scholarship: Marsden, Greek and Roman Artillery: Historical Development (1969) 48-56
Caven, Dionysius I (1990)

himilco_siege_of_syracuse_396.detail: The Carthaginians had pillaged the temple of Demeter and Kore in the suburb, which Greeks blamed for the plague. Himilco killed himself on return to Carthage; the Libyans revolted. Carthage atoned by introducing the cult of Demeter and Kore with Greek priests, a notable religious borrowing.

gauls_capture_melpum_396.detail: The synchronism is literary, but it marks the collapse of Etruscan power north of the Apennines under Celtic pressure in the early 4th century. Felsina (Bologna), Marzabotto and Spina followed over the next generations. Within six years Senonian Gauls reached Clusium and Rome.
gauls_capture_melpum_396.debate: Location unknown (near Milan has been suggested); the same-day synchronism is suspect.

temples_of_mater_matuta_and_juno_regina_.detail: The Sant'Omobono site in the Forum Boarium has twin temples identified as those of Fortuna and Mater Matuta, with an archaic phase of the 6th century and a rebuilding on a large platform datable to the 4th century, plausibly linked to Camillus. Mater Matuta was also worshipped at Satricum, where the Lapis Satricanus was found.

surrender_of_capena_395.detail: Lucus Feroniae was a major market and freedmen's cult centre on the Tiber; Hannibal plundered it in 211. The region formed part of the new tribes of 387.

delphi_bowl_394.detail: The bowl was placed in the treasury of the Massaliots at Delphi; Appian says it stood on a bronze base until melted down by Onomarchus in the Third Sacred War. When Rome took Lipara in 252 it exempted Timasitheus' descendants from tribute. The story places Rome in the network of Delphi, Massalia and the Tyrrhenian Greeks well before the 3rd century.

siege_of_falerii_394.detail: A moralising tale; in fact Falerii remained hostile into the 350s, and the town (Civita Castellana) was destroyed by Rome in 241 and its people moved to Falerii Novi on the plain. Capena had surrendered in 395.

colony_at_circeii_393.detail: Circeii's polygonal walls survive. It revolted with the Volsci in the 380s and was one of the Latin colonies in Rome's later network. The Monte Circeo promontory was reputed to be the home of Circe.

censor_death_convention_393.detail: The rule is an example of Roman religious reasoning from precedent: a replacement was deemed ill-omened. It was observed throughout the Republic.

italiote_league_alliance_393.detail: The league, initially led by Croton, was soon tested: in 389 the Thurians were crushed by the Lucanians at Laus, and in the same year Dionysius defeated the league at the Elleporus. Leadership later passed to Tarentum and the meeting place to Heraclea.

temple_of_juno_regina_aventine.detail: Evocatio, summoning the protecting deity of an enemy city with promise of a better cult in Rome, was used again at Carthage in 146 (Macrobius preserves a formula) and possibly at Volsinii (Vertumnus) in 264 and Isaura Vetus in 75.

census_392.detail: Pliny cites it to show how little gold Rome possessed then (the ransom was 1,000 pounds). The figure may refer to the lustrum of 392 or 393.

gauls_at_clusium_391.detail: Livy reports the story that a Clusine, Arruns, had lured the Gauls with wine to avenge his wife's seduction. The Fabii were then elected consular tribunes for 390, which gave the Gauls their casus belli. Diodorus says the Gauls had been in Iapygia (in Dionysius' service?) and were returning. The Gallic settlement of the Po valley (Insubres, Cenomani, Boii, Lingones, Senones) had begun at least a century earlier; Livy himself dates the first crossings to the time of Tarquinius Priscus.
scholarship: Williams, Beyond the Rubicon (2001) 140-150

truce_with_volsinii_391.detail: This is Rome's first recorded conflict with Volsinii, the leading city of the Etruscan league, which Rome destroyed in 264.

exile_of_camillus_391.detail: Plutarch adds that the charge concerned bronze doors from Veii, and that Camillus had lost a son just before. The exile sets up the legend of his recall as dictator to save Rome from the Gauls. Livy also records that Camillus had antagonised the plebs by triumphing with white horses like Jupiter and by insisting on a tithe of the booty for Apollo at Delphi, which forced soldiers to return plunder. The exile-and-return pattern, with Coriolanus as its negative counterpart, shaped Camillus as a 'second founder'.
exile_of_camillus_391.debate: The whole Camillus saga is heavily embellished; some scholars think the exile was invented to keep him out of the disaster of 390.

aius_locutius_391.detail: Cicero mocked the god who spoke when he was unknown and fell silent once he had a temple. An altar with a dedication 'sei deo sei deivae' on the Palatine has been associated with the cult. The story turns an anonymous divine warning into a cult and blames the elite's contempt for a plebeian witness.

battle_of_the_allia.detail:
The disaster began at Clusium, which the Senonian Gauls were besieging. Three Fabian envoys sent by Rome to mediate broke the law of nations by fighting in the Clusine ranks, one of them killing a Gallic chieftain. When the Gauls demanded their surrender, the Roman people instead elected them consular tribunes for 390. The Gauls marched straight on Rome. The Roman army met them at the Allia, a stream that flows into the Tiber about 11 Roman miles north of the city on the Via Salaria. Livy says the commanders neglected the auspices and sacrifices, did not fortify a camp, and stretched the line thin to avoid being outflanked, placing reserves on a hill on the right. The Gallic leader Brennus attacked the reserves first; the main line broke at the war cry without fighting, and most of the fleeing soldiers swam the Tiber and took refuge in Veii, leaving Rome defenceless. Diodorus puts the battle on the right bank of the Tiber, which would explain the flight to Veii.

The date, 18 July, became the dies Alliensis, the blackest day in the Roman calendar, on which no public business was transacted. Polybius synchronised the capture of Rome with the Peace of Antalcidas and the siege of Rhegium by Dionysius, that is 387/386, which is why most modern scholars place the Allia about four years after the Varronian 390. Diodorus says the Romans had 24,000 men; Plutarch's 70,000 Gauls is a rhetorical figure.

The defeat was the worst in Roman memory before Cannae. Later tradition blamed religious failure and the Fabii's violation of the ius gentium, making the catastrophe a moral lesson. Militarily, the Gallic charge against a Roman phalanx in close order may have been one reason for the gradual adoption of a more flexible manipular line during the 4th century. The 'Gallic terror' (metus Gallicus) became a permanent theme of Roman policy, justifying the special treasury reserved for Gallic wars and the levies en masse (tumultus) of later centuries.
battle_of_the_allia.debate: Varronian 390 vs Polybian 387/386; which bank of the Tiber.
scholarship: Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 715-722
Williams, Beyond the Rubicon (2001) 140-184
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 313-318
Williams, Beyond the Rubicon (2001)

siege_of_rome_390.detail:
Three days after the Allia (the day after, in some versions) the Gauls entered a city whose walls were undefended. The men of military age, the Senate and the treasures had gone up to the Capitol; the Flamen Quirinalis and the Vestals carried the sacred objects to Caere, helped by the plebeian L. Albinius. The aged ex-magistrates, says Livy, waited in their houses in their robes of office, sitting on ivory chairs; when a Gaul stroked the beard of M. Papirius, he struck him with his staff and was killed, and the massacre began. The city was plundered and burned. The Capitol held out. One night the Gauls climbed the cliff near the temple of Carmentis along a path found by following the Roman messenger Pontius Cominius, who had swum the Tiber to obtain the Senate's recall of Camillus from exile at Ardea. The sacred geese of Juno, spared despite the famine, woke M. Manlius, who threw the first Gaul down. After seven months, starving, the defenders agreed to pay 1,000 pounds of gold. When the Romans protested against false weights, Brennus threw his sword on the scale: 'vae victis', woe to the vanquished.

Livy has Camillus arrive as dictator at that moment, declare that Rome would be ransomed 'with iron, not gold', and destroy the Gauls. Other sources are less heroic. Polybius says the Gauls withdrew because the Veneti invaded their homeland and took the gold with them. Diodorus says the Caeretans ambushed them on the way home, and Strabo that Caere recovered the gold. Suetonius records that a Livius Drusus recovered the ransom in Gaul much later. The Gauls may have gone on south as mercenaries for Dionysius of Syracuse.

Archaeologically the sack left surprisingly little trace: the burnt layer in the Comitium once attributed to 390 is now dated to the 6th century. The trauma was nevertheless real. It produced the great wall of 378, a lasting fear of the Gauls, and the legend of Camillus as second founder. Greek writers of the 4th century, Heraclides Ponticus, Aristotle and Theopompus, knew of the capture, the first Roman event to enter Greek literature.
siege_of_rome_390.debate: Camillus' rescue is fiction; whether Caere defeated the Gauls; the scale of destruction; date 390 vs 387/386.
scholarship: Williams, Beyond the Rubicon (2001) 142-184
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 313-318
Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 719-748
Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 719-747

massilia_contributes_to_ransom_390.detail: The story may be Massiliot patriotic tradition, but the friendship between Rome and Massalia was old: Rome's golden bowl for Delphi after Veii was placed in the Massiliot treasury. Massalia remained Rome's most loyal Greek ally in the West, invoking Roman help against the Ligurians and Gauls in the 2nd century and keeping its freedom until it backed Pompey against Caesar in 49.

greek_notices_of_the_gallic_sack.detail: Plutarch quotes Heraclides and Aristotle. These fragments are precious because they show that by the mid-4th century Rome was known in the Greek world, though only vaguely, and that the sack was a real event independent of Roman tradition. Polybius synchronised it with the Peace of Antalcidas and the siege of Rhegium (387/386), which is why the Varronian date of 390 is thought to be about four years too early.

battle_of_the_elleporus.detail: Dionysius then destroyed Caulonia (389) and Hipponium, and after an eleven-month siege took Rhegium in 387, the year Polybius synchronises with the Gallic sack of Rome and the King's Peace. His empire spanned Sicily and the toe of Italy, and his fleet raided Pyrgi in 384 and founded posts on the Adriatic (Ancona, Issa, Lissos).
scholarship: Caven, Dionysius I (1990) 154-165

rebuilding_of_rome_389.detail: Livy blames the haste for Rome's irregular street plan, with sewers running under private houses; this is probably an etiological explanation of the city's archaic layout. The pontifical records were believed lost in the fire, Livy's explanation for the obscurity of earlier history (6.1.2), though much survived.

battle_of_maecium_389.detail: Livy's triple victory is patriotic inflation. Yet the period 389-358 does see Volscian, Aequian, Etruscan and Latin enemies probing a weakened Rome and Rome reasserting control.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. I (1997) 395-420

battle_of_laus_389.detail: The disaster showed the weakness of the new Italiote League against the Oscan peoples of the interior, and Dionysius' ambiguity: he backed the Lucanians against the Italiotes. Laus itself, a Sybarite foundation, passed to the Lucanians.

camillus_recovers_sutrium_389.detail: Livy says the city was 'twice captured on one day'. Sutrium and Nepet, 'the gates of Etruria', received Latin colonies in 383 (or 373).

temple_of_mars_porta_capena_388.detail: Armies leaving for the south assembled near this temple, and the stretch of road to it was paved in 296 by the aediles from fines. A 'lapis manalis' kept nearby was dragged into the city in times of drought.

four_new_tribes_387.detail: Livy reports that Veientine, Capenate and Faliscan deserters were given citizenship and land, a precedent for absorption of defeated peoples. Tribes were the units of the census, levy and the tribal assemblies; their creation registers Rome's territorial growth, ending with 35 in 241.
scholarship: Taylor, The Voting Districts of the Roman Republic (1960; rev. 2013)

siege_of_rhegium_387.detail: Rhegium had insulted Dionysius by refusing him a bride and offering the public hangman's daughter instead, according to Diodorus. With the Strait in his hands Dionysius dominated the toe of Italy, and Polybius dated the Gallic sack of Rome by this siege. Rhegium was later restored by Dionysius II as Phoebia and recovered its name.

colony_at_satricum.detail: Satricum, with its temple of Mater Matuta (findspot of the Lapis Satricanus), was the hinge between the Alban hills and the Pontine plain.

dionysian_adriatic_colonies.detail: The aim was control of the Adriatic trade in grain, timber, metals and horses from the Veneti, and perhaps a raid on Delphi. Strabo says Ancona was founded by Syracusans fleeing Dionysius' tyranny. These Greek settlements were the ones Rome later 'protected' against Queen Teuta in the First Illyrian War (229).

trial_of_manlius_capitolinus.detail: Livy notes the first trial was abandoned because the jury could see the Capitol he had saved, so it was moved to the Peteline grove outside the Porta Flumentana. His house on the Capitol was razed and the site later given to the temple of Juno Moneta (344). The episode belongs to the debt crisis that produced the Licinio-Sextian laws; the template of the ambitious patrician 'popularis' killed for regnum (Cassius, Maelius, Manlius) is suspiciously regular.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. I (1997) 476-567

dionysius_sack_of_pyrgi.detail: The raid funded Dionysius' war against Carthage. It may explain why Caere, weakened, sought Roman friendship, sheltering Rome's sacra in 390 and receiving hospitium publicum.
scholarship: Caven, Dionysius I (1990)

colonies_sutrium_nepet.detail: Velleius dates Sutrium to seven years after the Gallic sack and Nepet ten years later (373); Livy places Nepet's colony in 383. Sutrium was besieged by the Etruscans in 311-310 and became the base for Fabius Rullianus' march through the Ciminian forest.
colonies_sutrium_nepet.debate: Velleius and Livy disagree on Nepet's date.
scholarship: Salmon, Roman Colonization under the Republic (1969)

colony_at_setia_382.detail: Setia, Norba, Signia and Circeii formed a chain of fortified colonies around the Volscian Pontine plain. Setia's colonists joined the Latin revolt of 340.

tusculum_incorporation_381.detail: The incorporation of a whole community, retaining its own magistrates (the Tusculan dictator, later aediles), was a decisive innovation, the model for 338. Tusculum produced many noble families (Mamilii, Fulvii, Porcii, Juventii, Coruncanii) who reached the consulship.
tusculum_incorporation_381.debate: Some see the 381 grant as civitas sine suffragio upgraded later; most accept full citizenship.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. I (1997) 650-668
Sherwin-White, The Roman Citizenship (2nd ed. 1973) 29-31

battle_of_satricum_381.detail: Livy's set-piece shows ideal collegial conduct. The campaign uncovered Tusculan help to the Volsci and led to Tusculum's incorporation with Roman citizenship, the first municipium.

battle_of_the_allia_380.detail: The statue was placed on the Capitol with an inscription claiming he had taken nine towns, a boast corrected by Livy and Festus. Praeneste, with its huge territory and later the great sanctuary of Fortuna Primigenia, remained a rival until 338.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. I (1997) 669-686

servian_wall_378.detail:
Livy's terse notice under 378, that the censors let a contract for a wall 'of squared stone', is confirmed by the surviving stretches of the so-called Servian Wall, built of large blocks of yellowish Grotta Oscura tufa quarried in the territory of Veii, which Rome controlled only after 396. The wall ran for about 11 km and enclosed some 426 hectares, including all seven hills, the largest walled area of any Italian city of the time and comparable only to the Dionysian circuit of Syracuse. Where the plateau of the Esquiline, Viminal and Quirinal offered no natural defence, it took the form of an agger, a massive earth rampart faced with stone, fronted by a ditch about 30 m wide and up to 17 m deep. Blocks bear masons' marks in Greek letters, suggesting Greek contractors or workmen, perhaps from Syracuse or Magna Graecia.

Roman tradition attributed the city wall to King Servius Tullius, and remains of an earlier fortification in local cappellaccio tufa, probably of the 6th century, have been found beneath parts of the later circuit, so the 378 wall may have rebuilt and enlarged an archaic line. The best-preserved sections today are outside Termini station and on the Aventine in Via di Sant'Anselmo, where an arch for a catapult belongs to repairs of the early 1st century BC. Gates included the Porta Capena (start of the Via Appia), Collina, Esquilina, Viminalis, Caelimontana and Trigemina.

The wall answered the trauma of 390: never again would the city be open to raiders. It was repaired in 353, during the Second Punic War, when Hannibal reached the Anio in 211 and did not attempt an assault, and in the civil wars of the 80s. As the city outgrew it under the late Republic and Augustus it lost its function, and Rome remained unwalled until Aurelian's wall of 271-275.
servian_wall_378.debate: Whether the 378 wall replaced an earlier 6th-century circuit, and the precise extent of the original enclosure, are debated; the Grotta Oscura tufa gives a terminus post quem of 396.
scholarship: Säflund, Le mura di Roma repubblicana (1932)
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 331-332
Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. I (1997)
Cifani, 'The fortifications of archaic Rome', in Frederiksen et al. (eds), Focus on Fortifications (2016)

fabia_and_the_lictor_377.detail: Livy himself treats the story as a trivial cause for great events. It reflects the tradition that the Licinio-Sextian movement was led by wealthy plebeians allied by marriage with patrician houses, seeking office rather than social revolution.

battle_of_cronium.detail: Diodorus places the war under 383-382 but modern scholars prefer c. 378-375. The Halycus (Platani) frontier, giving Carthage Selinus and part of Acragantine territory, lasted with interruptions until the First Punic War and was confirmed by Timoleon.
battle_of_cronium.debate: Dating (383/2 in Diodorus, c. 378-375 by most moderns) and sites of both battles disputed.

solitudo_magistratuum.detail: Diodorus records only one year of anarchy, and many scholars see the five years as an artifice of chronographers padding the list to synchronise with Greek dates (like the dictator years of 333, 324, 309 and 301). The fasti for 376-367 are among the most manipulated in the record.
solitudo_magistratuum.debate: One year (Diodorus) or five (Livy); relevance to Varronian chronology.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. I (1997) 645-661
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 262-264

temple_of_juno_lucina_375.detail: Women celebrated the Matronalia there on 1 March. The date falls in the five-year 'anarchy' of the Fasti, a reminder that the annalistic gap is a chronological artefact and that the city continued its religious life.

gallic_mercenaries_of_dionysius_369.detail: The link suggests the Gallic bands in central Italy after 390 were partly mercenary companies moving south toward Apulia and Syracusan service. Gallic raids of the 360s-340s into Latium may relate to this traffic.

gallic_incursion_367.detail: A good case of Polybius' sober Gallic chronology (2.18) against Livy's glorifying annalists. Gallic bands raided Latium repeatedly in the 360s-350s (Livy has battles in 367, 361, 360, 358, 350, 349), probably reduced to a few real incursions, perhaps some of them mercenaries in the service of Dionysius I.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. I (1997) 727-735
Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) 184-186

licinio_sextian_laws.detail:
From 376 the tribunes C. Licinius Stolo and L. Sextius Lateranus proposed three bills together: that interest already paid be deducted from the principal of debts and the remainder repaid in three annual instalments; that no one should possess more than 500 iugera (about 125 ha) of public land; and that the consular tribunate be abolished and one consul be plebeian. According to Livy they were re-elected tribunes ten times, used their veto to prevent elections of curule magistrates for five years (the 'anarchy' of 375-371, now thought to be a chronological fiction), and finally, in 367, carried the laws against patrician resistance led by the aged Camillus, named dictator for the last time. A further law replaced the patrician duoviri sacris faciundis, keepers of the Sibylline Books, with a board of ten, half plebeian.

The compromise of 367 created two new patrician offices to compensate: a praetor with imperium for jurisdiction, and two curule aediles to manage the city and the Roman Games, which were extended by a day. Sextius became the first plebeian consul in 366, L. Genucius the second in 365. Camillus vowed a temple of Concord to celebrate reconciliation, though this tradition may be later invention. The law did not ensure a plebeian consul every year: patrician pairs appear in 355, 353, 351, 349, 345 and 343, until the lex Genucia of 342 made the arrangement permanent and even allowed both consuls to be plebeian.

The laws are the turning point of the Struggle of the Orders. They opened the consulship, and so the Senate, to wealthy plebeian families, creating the patricio-plebeian nobility (nobilitas) that dominated Rome for three centuries. The land clause is the most debated: many think the 500-iugera limit a retrojection of the Gracchan law of 133, which reaffirmed it, but Cato's speech for the Rhodians in 167 mentions a law forbidding the possession of more than 500 iugera, showing that some such rule existed by then. Livy records that Licinius himself was fined 10,000 asses under his own law in 357 for holding 1,000 iugera through his emancipated son.
licinio_sextian_laws.debate: Whether the 500-iugera law is authentic; whether the consulship law required or merely permitted a plebeian consul.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. I (1997) 645-661
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 327-340
Hölkeskamp, Die Entstehung der Nobilität (1987)
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 262-267
Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, I (1997) 645-661

temple_of_concord_367.detail: Momigliano argued the story was invented to give a respectable pedigree to the Temple of Concord rebuilt by L. Opimius in 121 after the murder of Gaius Gracchus, an act of 'concord' through bloodshed. Gnaeus Flavius dedicated a small bronze shrine of Concord in 304, the first securely attested.
scholarship: Momigliano, 'Camillus and Concord', CQ 36 (1942)

death_of_dionysius_i_367.detail: He left the most powerful Greek state of the West, with a large mercenary army, a navy of several hundred ships and an empire from the Adriatic to western Sicily. Athens had honoured him with citizenship and alliance in 368. His son lacked his authority, and the tyranny unravelled through the quarrels with Dion and Plato.

platos_sicilian_voyages.detail: The Seventh Letter, whether by Plato or an early follower, is the main narrative and a classic text on intellectuals and power. Plato had visited Sicily and met Dion around 388, when the elder Dionysius is said to have had him sold as a slave at Aegina. The Syracusan episode shaped ancient views of the relationship between philosophy and tyranny, and the Pythagorean friendship of Plato and Archytas is a rare glimpse of the intellectual life of Tarentum, Rome's future rival.
platos_sicilian_voyages.debate: Authenticity of the Seventh Letter disputed.

archytas_governs_tarentum.detail: Archytas solved the problem of doubling the cube, wrote on harmonics, and according to Favorinus built a wooden dove that flew. His leadership coincided with Tarentum's great silver horseman coinage and its growing army of hired condottieri after his death.

praetorship_and_curule_aediles_366.detail: Sp. Furius Camillus, son of the dictator, was the first praetor. The ludi Romani were extended by a day. The curule aedileship alternated between patricians and plebeians within a few years. The praetorship was opened to plebeians in 337 (Q. Publilius Philo).
scholarship: Brennan, The Praetorship in the Roman Republic (2000) I 58-69
Broughton, MRR I 114

plague_and_ludi_scaenici_364.detail: Livy traces a development from Etruscan dance to Fescennine-style improvised verse, saturae with music, and finally Livius Andronicus' plays with plot in 240. The word histrio came from Etruscan ister. In 363 a dictator was appointed solely to drive the annual nail into the temple of Jupiter as a plague remedy.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 40-72

plague_clavi_figendi_363.detail: Livy quotes an ancient law posted on the right side of the Capitoline temple, by the shrine of Minerva, that the 'praetor maximus' should fix a nail on the Ides of September; the antiquarian Cincius compared nails in the temple of Nortia at Volsinii used to count years. Further nail dictators followed in 331 and 313. The ritual is evidence for early year-counting and for the title 'praetor maximus'.

battle_against_hernici_362.detail: The dictator Ap. Claudius restored the situation. The Hernican revolt (362-358) shows that the alliance of 486 frayed as Rome grew stronger.

trial_of_lucius_manlius_imperiosus_362.detail: The people, admiring the son's piety, elected him a military tribune that year. The episode begins the legend of T. Manlius Torquatus, who in 361 won his cognomen by killing a Gallic champion and in 340 executed his own son.

marcus_curtius_chasm_362.detail: Livy gives this as one of three aetiologies of the Lacus Curtius, the paved spot in the Forum: the others tied it to the Sabine Mettius Curtius in Romulus' war, or to the consul C. Curtius fencing a place struck by lightning in 445 (Varro). A marble relief of a horseman sinking into a marsh, found in the Forum, is a copy of a Republican original. The story is a form of devotio.

elected_military_tribunes_362.detail: Livy's notice marks the people's growing role in military appointments. By 311 a law raised the number of elected tribunes to sixteen, and by the 2nd century the 24 tribunes of the four consular legions were all elected (tribuni militum a populo).

battle_of_the_anio_361.detail: The earliest version, by Claudius Quadrigarius (preserved verbatim by Gellius), is a vivid piece of Sullan-era prose and dates the duel to 361 (Livy) or 357. The torque motif appears on coins of the Manlii Torquati. The Gauls withdrew toward Tibur and Campania.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 113-148
Oakley, 'Single combat in the Roman Republic', CQ 35 (1985)

battle_of_the_colline_gate_360.detail: The Fasti Triumphales record a triumph of the consul C. Poetelius over the Gauls and Tiburtines in 360. Tibur's alliance with the Gauls reflects Latin resentment of Rome after 390, which ended only in 338.

battle_of_pedum_358.detail: Livy's report of the camp-follower ruse resembles stratagems told elsewhere. Rome's renewed treaty with the Latins this year is linked to the Gallic danger.

renewal_of_latin_treaty_358.detail: Livy's language implies the Foedus Cassianum had lapsed. The renewed treaty may have been less equal, with Rome now taking the lead; resentments built toward the war of 340.

tribes_pomptina_publilia_358.detail: The same year the tribune C. Poetelius carried the first law on electoral malpractice (lex Poetelia de ambitu), aimed against 'new men' canvassing at markets.

tarquinii_sacrifice_of_prisoners_358.detail: The ritual killing has been linked to Etruscan funerary iconography and the François Tomb fresco of Achilles slaughtering Trojan prisoners. The Elogia Tarquiniensia (inscriptions of the Spurinna family) may commemorate Etruscan leaders of these wars. Truce of 40 years in 351.
scholarship: Torelli, Elogia Tarquiniensia (1975)
Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998)

lex_poetelia_de_ambitu_358.detail: Livy reads it as a patrician measure to curb ambitious plebeians. It followed the toga law of 432.

lex_manlia_de_vicesima.detail: The vicesima libertatis endured into the Empire, and its revenue (aurum vicesimarium) was stored as a reserve in the aerarium sanctius, opened in 209 during the Hannibalic war. The tax implies a significant slave population and frequent manumission already by the mid-4th century.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 181-185

lex_duilia_menenia_357.detail: Tacitus says the Twelve Tables had already fixed the uncial rate, which complicates the tradition. A lex Genucia of 342 then banned interest altogether, a law impossible to enforce.

dion_liberates_syracuse_357.detail: Dion's rule disappointed the democrats led by Heraclides, who saw him as another tyrant. His death began a decade of civil wars and short-lived tyrannies (Callippus, Hipparinus, Nysaeus, Dionysius II restored in 346) that ended only with Timoleon. Dionysius II meanwhile ruled his mother's city of Locri in Italy.

first_plebeian_dictator_356.detail: Marcius went on to be the first plebeian censor (351) and held four consulships, a model of the plebeian noble whom the Licinio-Sextian settlement produced.
scholarship: Broughton, MRR I 123

rise_of_the_bruttii.detail: The name was interpreted as 'rebels' in Lucanian (Strabo). The Bruttian confederacy, centred on Consentia, fought Alexander of Epirus in 331 and later allied with Pyrrhus and Hannibal.

dionysius_ii_at_locri.detail: Later writers (Clearchus via Athenaeus, Strabo, Aelian) told lurid stories of his debaucheries at Locri, which belong to the moralising literature on tyrants. The episode shows how dynastic marriage tied Syracuse to the Italian cities: Dionysius I had married the Locrian Doris on the same day as a Syracusan wife.

treaty_with_samnites_354.detail: The treaty reflects Rome's arrival on the borders of Campania after subduing the Volsci, Hernici and Aurunci. It was renewed in 341 after the First Samnite War. Tibur and Praeneste submitted to Rome the same year.
scholarship: Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967) 187-193
Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998)

execution_of_tarquinian_prisoners_354.detail: The numerical symmetry is suspicious, but the brutality on both sides is plausible. Etruscan tomb paintings, notably the François Tomb at Vulci with Achilles killing Trojan prisoners, show that prisoner killing had a ritual dimension in Etruria.

truce_with_caere_353.detail: Gellius and Strabo say Caere was the first community to receive citizenship without the vote (civitas sine suffragio), and that the 'tabulae Caerites' (list of citizens without vote) took its name; whether this was a privilege of hospitium after 390 or a penalty imposed in 353 or 273 (when Caere lost half its territory) is debated.
truce_with_caere_353.debate: Date and character of Caere's civitas sine suffragio.
scholarship: Sherwin-White, The Roman Citizenship (2nd ed. 1973) 53-58
Humbert, Municipium et civitas sine suffragio (1978)

quinqueviri_mensarii_352.detail: A pragmatic response to the debt crisis that the Licinio-Sextian laws had not resolved; Livy praises its fairness. It anticipates the triumviri mensarii of the Hannibalic war.

first_plebeian_censor_351.detail: The lex Publilia of 339 later required one censor to be plebeian.

truce_with_tarquinii_and_falerii_351.detail: With the hundred-year truce granted to Caere in 353, the truces freed Rome to turn south to Campania in 343. Tarquinii renewed hostilities in 311.

battle_against_the_gauls_350.detail: Popillius triumphed, one of the first plebeian triumphs. The Gauls' wintering in the Alban hills set up the campaign of 349 with Valerius Corvus' duel.

boii_take_felsina.detail: The Boii controlled the central Po plain until Rome's conquest (196-191) and the Latin colony of Bononia (189). Mixed Etrusco-Celtic graves, such as the warrior burials of Monte Bibele, show coexistence rather than wholesale extermination.

battle_of_the_pomptine_plain_349.detail: Like the Torquatus duel, this is a family legend (the Valerii Corvini). In 350 M. Popillius Laenas had already defeated Gauls. Polybius (2.18.7-9) says that in this period the Gauls came again, the Romans met them, and the Gauls fled by night, after which there was peace for 13 years and then a formal peace treaty. The Latins refused troops this year, a sign of strain.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 237-255

greek_fleet_raid_349.detail: Probably a Syracusan expedition under Dionysius II; Antium itself was a notorious pirate base until 338, and Strabo says complaints from Alexander and Demetrius Poliorcetes reached Rome about Antiate pirates.

second_treaty_rome_carthage.detail: Polybius gives the text without a date; Livy (7.27.2) and Diodorus (16.69.1) record a treaty in 348, the first known to them. Carthaginian Sicily and Carthage itself remained open to Roman traders. The clause allowing Carthage to keep captives and movables but surrender captured Latin towns to Rome reveals a Rome still claiming hegemony in Latium yet unable to protect it at sea. Mastia is usually placed near later Cartagena.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) 345-349
Scardigli, I trattati romano-cartaginesi (1991)

interest_halved_347.detail: The relief measures of 357, 352 and 347 culminated in the lex Genucia of 342 banning interest altogether, a law soon ignored. The debt cycle of the 4th century underlay the abolition of nexum in 326.
interest_halved_347.debate: Whether the 'uncial' rate was annual (8 1/3%) or monthly is disputed.

battle_of_satricum_346.detail: The sale of prisoners as slaves begins to appear regularly in Livy in this period, reflecting Rome's growing captive labour force.

temple_of_juno_moneta_344.detail: Moneta was understood as 'the Warner' (from monere): Cicero says a voice from the temple advised expiating an earthquake with a pregnant sow, and the Suda claims Juno advised the Romans on financing the Pyrrhic war. The libri lintei, magistrate lists on linen, were kept in the temple. When the mint was set up there is debated: probably in the 3rd century, perhaps with the first Roman-struck silver of 269. The site lies beneath the church of Santa Maria in Aracoeli, where remains of a tufa podium have been identified.
temple_of_juno_moneta_344.debate: Date the mint moved to the temple, and the etymology of Moneta, are debated.

dictator_feriarum_constituendarum_344.detail: The dictatorship's range of causae (to hold elections, fix a nail, hold games, celebrate festivals) shows it developing into an all-purpose emergency office before its disappearance after 202.

timoleon_arrives_in_sicily_344.detail: Dionysius II retired to Corinth, where later anecdotes made him a schoolmaster and a fixture of the city's taverns. Timoleon razed the tyrants' citadel on Ortygia and built law courts on its site. Plutarch, using Timaeus, presents him as a man favoured by Fortune (Automatia, to whom he built a shrine); Diodorus is more matter-of-fact. The Crimissus victory (339) and the expulsion of the remaining tyrants followed.

deditio_of_capua_343.detail: Livy's story of a deditio is widely doubted as a pretext invented to excuse Rome's breach of the 354 treaty; but the appeal and Roman intervention began the century of Samnite wars. The Campanian aristocracy's links with Roman nobles (later intermarriage, the equites Campani) are a recurring factor.
deditio_of_capua_343.debate: Historicity of the deditio and of the whole war (Adcock and others doubted the First Samnite War entirely).
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 283-307
Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967) 197-200

battle_of_mount_gaurus.detail: Livy's narrative (Samnites asking what fire burned in Roman eyes) is rhetorical; the victory nonetheless saved Campania for the Romans. The Fasti Triumphales record triumphs of both consuls over the Samnites in 343.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 307-330

battle_of_saticula_343.detail: Decius received the corona obsidionalis (grass crown) from the rescued army and an ox with gilded horns. The episode resembles later stories (the Caudine Forks reversed; the tribune Calpurnius Flamma in Sicily in 258).

battle_of_suessula.detail: The Carthaginian embassy is often taken to reflect real diplomatic contact around the time of the 348 treaty. Faliscans asked to convert their truce into a treaty and the Latins turned their arms on the Paeligni.

carthaginian_gold_crown_343.detail: The gesture belongs to the treaty relationship renewed in 348 and shows Carthage watching Rome's expansion into Campania. In the 3rd century Philinus claimed a further treaty barring Rome from Sicily and Carthage from Italy, which Polybius denied.

mutiny_of_342_and_lex_genucia.detail: Livy confesses his sources disagree violently on the mutiny. From 342 one consul was regularly plebeian (both plebeian first in 172). The ten-year interval rule was often waived during the Samnite wars, and the Genucian package marks the effective end of the 'Struggle of the Orders' over the consulship.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 361-392

peace_with_samnites_341.detail: The diplomatic about-turn is the strongest evidence that the 'First Samnite War' was a short, limited conflict.

battle_of_vesuvius.detail:
When the Latins demanded, through their spokesman L. Annius of Setia, that one consul and half the Senate be Latin, the Romans refused and war followed. The consuls T. Manlius Torquatus and P. Decius Mus marched, according to Livy, through the land of the Marsi and Paeligni to join the Samnites and confronted the Latin and Campanian army near Mount Vesuvius on the road to Veseris. Before the battle Manlius' son, provoked by the Tusculan cavalry commander Geminus Maecius, fought him against orders and killed him; his father had him executed before the army, and 'Manlian commands' became a proverb for pitiless discipline. Both consuls dreamed that the general on one side and the army on the other were owed to the gods of the underworld.

In the battle the Roman left, under Decius, began to give way. Decius called the pontifex M. Valerius, who dictated the formula of devotio: veiled, his toga girt in the Gabine manner, standing on a spear, Decius invoked Janus, Jupiter, Mars, Quirinus, Bellona, the Lares, the Novensiles and Indigetes, and the Di Manes, devoting himself and the legions and auxiliaries of the enemy to the gods below. He then rode into the Latin ranks and was killed, and his body was found next day under a heap of enemy dead. Manlius held his triarii in reserve until the Latins were exhausted, then threw them in; Livy says scarcely a quarter of the enemy escaped. The victory at Trifanum soon after completed the campaign.

Livy uses the battle for his set-piece description of the manipular legion with hastati, principes and triarii, a passage historians treat as partly anachronistic. The devotio formula is precious evidence of archaic religion, whatever its historicity. Cicero knew of three Decii who devoted themselves (340, 295 and 279); some scholars think the first is a doublet of the second, better attested by the contemporary Greek Duris. The location is uncertain, since a march through the Abruzzi would bring the consuls toward northern Campania, and 'Veseris' has been sought near Vescia and Suessa rather than the volcano.
battle_of_vesuvius.debate: Site; historicity of the first Decian devotio (the 295 devotio of his son is better attested and the father's may be a doublet).
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 405-480
Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967) 206-208
Versnel, 'Two types of Roman devotio', Mnemosyne 29 (1976)
Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, II (1998) 477-487

battle_of_trifanum.detail: The Campanian equites (1,600) who had not revolted were rewarded with citizenship and a payment from the Campanian people; a bronze tablet recorded it in the temple of Castor at Rome.

campanian_equites_rewarded_340.detail: Livy's figure of 450 denarii per man is anachronistic, since the denarius dates from c. 211, but the bronze tablet suggests an authentic document. It shows Rome binding the Capuan aristocracy to itself against the Capuan commons, a policy that held until Capua's defection to Hannibal.

manipular_legion_reform.detail: Livy's description of the army of 340 (15 maniples of hastati, 15 of principes, 15 ordines of triarii with rorarii and accensi) is the earliest systematic account but is confused and partly anachronistic. A Greek fragment (the Ineditum Vaticanum) and Athenaeus state that the Romans took the scutum and the throwing javelin from the Samnites; Livy dates the switch from clipeus to scutum to the introduction of pay (406). Polybius describes the mature system of the late 3rd century: 1,200 hastati, 1,200 principes and 600 triarii per legion, with 1,200 velites and 300 cavalry. The manipular order suited broken Apennine terrain and allowed relief of the fighting line, a key reason Rome could absorb defeats and keep fighting. Most scholars now see a gradual evolution c. 350-300 rather than a single reform, possibly prompted by the Gallic victories of 390.
manipular_legion_reform.debate: Date, cause (Gallic defeats, Samnite influence, pay) and the reliability of Livy 8.8 are all debated.
scholarship: E. Rawson, 'The literary sources for the pre-Marian army', PBSR 39 (1971)
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)

leges_publiliae_philonis.detail: The advance auctoritas turned a patrician veto into a formality, and was extended to elections by a lex Maenia of uncertain 3rd-century date. The plebiscite clause appears again in 287; whether the 339 law imposed conditions is debated.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 522-530
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 341-342

battle_of_the_crimissus.detail: The victory confirmed Timoleon's restoration of Greek Syracuse after the Dionysian tyranny and led to a treaty fixing the Halycus river as the Punic boundary. Plutarch and Diodorus date it to 341 or 339. Carthage afterwards relied more heavily on mercenaries rather than citizen troops abroad.
scholarship: Talbert, Timoleon and the Revival of Greek Sicily (1974)

battle_of_the_fenectane_plains_339.detail: Publilius, returning to Rome, was named dictator and carried the leges Publiliae against patrician privilege.

battle_of_pedum_338.detail: Camillus then took every Latin town by storm or surrender, ending the League's resistance and opening the way for the settlement of 338.

settlement_of_338.detail:
After victories at Pedum and the Astura in 338, the consuls L. Furius Camillus and C. Maenius asked the Senate how to deal with Latium. The resulting settlement, preserved by Livy, treated each community separately and is the foundation of the Roman system of Italy. Lanuvium received full citizenship, its temple of Juno Sospita being shared with the Roman people; Aricia, Nomentum and Pedum received citizenship on the same terms as Lanuvium; Tusculum kept the citizenship granted in 381, its leaders of the revolt being punished. Velitrae, an old Roman colony that had revolted repeatedly, had its walls razed, its senate deported across the Tiber (any senator caught on the near side to be fined 1,000 asses) and its land given to new settlers. Antium received a colony, its warships were burned or taken to Rome's dockyards, their beaks adorned the Rostra, and its people were forbidden the sea. Tibur and Praeneste lost land but remained allies with their own treaties. The other Latin cities lost conubium, commercium and the right of assembly with each other, keeping those rights only with Rome. The Campanian cavalry were rewarded with citizenship, while Capua, Fundi, Formiae, Cumae and Suessula received citizenship without the vote (civitas sine suffragio).

The settlement created graded statuses that defined Roman Italy. Full citizen communities later became municipia; communities with citizenship without the vote shared the obligations (munera) of citizens, above all military service, while governing themselves; Latin communities, old and new, kept the Latin rights of the Foedus Cassianum; and the Latin status became transferable, so that new colonies such as Cales (334) were founded as Latin cities. Two new tribes, the Maecia and Scaptia, were added in 332. Roman territory grew to about 5,500 km2 and the citizen body to perhaps 350,000-400,000 people.

Modern historians see 338 as the moment Rome ceased to be a city-state leading a league and became the centre of a territorial state with a network of dependent allies. The divide-and-rule logic, combining generosity and severity, was applied to every later conquest in Italy, and the manpower it generated allowed Rome to absorb defeats like the Caudine Forks, Heraclea and Cannae.
settlement_of_338.debate: Whether civitas sine suffragio was a privilege or a burden at this date; the Campanian grant may be of 334 or 318.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 538-571
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 347-352
Sherwin-White, The Roman Citizenship (2nd ed. 1973) 38-58
Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, II (1998) 538-571
Afzelius, Die römische Eroberung Italiens (1942)

rostra_and_column_of_maenius.detail: Antium, notorious for piracy, was forbidden the sea; a citizen colony was planted there. The Maenian column (columna Maenia) by the Comitium became a landmark where thieves and debtors were tried by the tresviri capitales. Maenius as censor in 318 added balconies (maeniana) over the Forum shops for watching games.

colony_at_antium_338.detail: One of the first coastal citizen colonies (with Ostia and later Tarracina 329, Minturnae and Sinuessa 296), small garrisons of c. 300 families guarding the coast and exempt from legionary service.
scholarship: Salmon, Roman Colonization under the Republic (1969) 70-81

castrum_of_ostia.detail: The castrum's grid survives in the decumanus and cardo of the later city. Ostia was the base of one of the quaestores classici created in 267 and the port for Rome's grain imports; its fleet station served in the First Punic War. Excavations since the 1910s (Calza) and recent geophysics have refined the date, which some place nearer 300.
castrum_of_ostia.debate: Date of the castrum (c. 380-300) disputed; the regal foundation has no archaeological support so far.
scholarship: R. Meiggs, Roman Ostia (2nd ed. 1973)

battle_of_manduria_338.detail: He was the first of the Greek condottieri hired by Tarentum, followed by Alexander of Epirus, Cleonymus, Acrotatus and Pyrrhus. The Messapian walls of Manduria, with three circuits, are among the best preserved native fortifications in Italy.

timoleon_resettlement_of_sicily.detail: The annual priest of Zeus Olympios (amphipolos) became the eponymous official of Syracuse, a post that survived into Roman times. Archaeology shows a remarkable revival of Sicilian towns in the late 4th century: new houses and public buildings at Morgantina, Camarina, Gela and Heraclea Minoa, and a surge in coinage including the Corinthian-type Pegasus staters. The prosperity lasted until Agathocles' coup in 317.

vestal_minucia_337.detail: Vestal executions cluster at moments of military or social crisis (483, 337, 266, 216, 114). Publilius Philo went on to be the first proconsul (326).

aurunci_move_to_suessa_337.detail: Rome punished the Sidicini by taking Cales (334). Suessa received a Latin colony in 313 after the Aurunci joined the Samnites.

colony_at_cales.detail: The new-style Latin colony, with Latin rights but founded by Rome alone, became the principal instrument of Roman control: 19 more were founded by 263. Cales became famous for its black-gloss pottery (Calene ware) with relief medallions in the 3rd century.
scholarship: Salmon, Roman Colonization under the Republic (1969) 55-57

alexander_molossus_in_italy.detail: He fell out with Tarentum, planned to move the Italiote League's meeting place from Heraclea to Thurii, and was killed at Pandosia in 331. His campaign is the first of the great condottiere interventions (Cleonymus, Agathocles, Pyrrhus) that drew Rome into the affairs of Magna Graecia.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 665-690
Purcell, CAH VI2 (1994) ch. 9b

the_dictator_years.detail: They were almost certainly invented by Augustan-era (or late Republican) chronographers, together with the five-year anarchy of the 370s, to reconcile the Roman consular list with Greek synchronisms such as the sack of Rome in 387/386. As a result conventional Varronian dates before 300 are about four years too early relative to 'true' chronology: the Allia of 'Varronian 390' is probably 386. Modern handbooks retain Varronian dates for convenience while noting the problem. In this dataset all dates are Varronian.
the_dictator_years.debate: The fictitious character of the dictator years is generally accepted; how the Varronian system arose is debated.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. I (1997) 102-104
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 369-370
Drummond, CAH VII.2 (1989) 625-628

tribes_maecia_scaptia_332.detail: The Scaptia was probably on the old territory disputed between Ardea and Aricia (cf. P. Scaptius, 446).

gallic_peace_331.detail: Livy (8.20.2-3) reports that the Senones' threat in 329 proved empty. The treaty, probably with the Senones of the Adriatic coast, freed Rome to concentrate on the Samnites.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) 185-186

poisoning_trial_331.detail: Livy reports it with reluctance as an act of 'madness' rather than malice; a dictator was named to drive the annual nail as expiation. It was the first trial for veneficium and resembles later mass prosecutions (Bacchanalia 186, poisonings 184 and 180).
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 594-602

battle_of_pandosia_331.detail: His body was mutilated and parts sent to Consentia; a woman of Consentia ransomed the remains and sent them to his wife Cleopatra (sister of Alexander the Great) and mother Olympias in Epirus.

francois_tomb_vulci.detail: Discovered in 1857 by Alessandro François, the frescoes were detached and are now in the Villa Albani-Torlonia. They are the only Etruscan visual narrative of the archaic struggles that Roman tradition remembered as the reign of Servius Tullius. The emperor Claudius, an Etruscologist, told the Senate (ILS 212) that Servius Tullius was in Etruscan called Mastarna, companion of Caelius Vibenna, who gave his name to the Caelian hill. The paintings show a Vulcian aristocracy in the age of the Roman conquest asserting its heroic past, with the sacrifice of prisoners echoing the killings of 358 and 354.
francois_tomb_vulci.debate: Date of the paintings (c. 350-300) and the historicity of the Vipinas-Mastarna story are debated.
scholarship: F. Buranelli (ed.), La Tomba François di Vulci (1987)
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 133-141

ficoroni_cista.detail: Found in 1738 and named after the collector Francesco de' Ficoroni, it is in the Villa Giulia. It is one of the earliest Latin inscriptions to name a craftsman and proves that Rome had workshops of high Greek-influenced art in the later 4th century, when Praeneste was still a nominally independent ally. Its Greek model may be a painting by Cydias or Micon.
scholarship: T. Dohrn, Die Ficoronische Ciste (1972)

siege_of_privernum_329.detail: Vaccus was executed, Privernum's walls demolished and its senate deported beyond the Tiber. The new tribe Oufentina (318) was formed partly on Privernate land.

colony_at_tarracina_329.detail: With Antium and Ostia it formed the first group of small coastal citizen colonies (coloniae maritimae), whose settlers kept full citizenship and were exempt from legionary service but bound to guard their post. The Via Appia passed through it from 312, and the great temple of Jupiter Anxur crowned the cliff above.

colony_at_fregellae.detail: Fregellae was lost to the Samnites in 320, refounded in 313, and became one of the most prosperous Latin colonies until it revolted and was destroyed by the praetor L. Opimius in 125. Excavations have revealed its houses and a sanctuary of Aesculapius.
scholarship: Coarelli & Monti (eds.), Fregellae 1 (1998)
Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967) 214-216

siege_of_neapolis_327.detail: Neapolis received a favourable treaty (foedus aequum), supplying ships rather than troops, and remained a Greek city in name and language into the Empire. The prorogation became the key device for extending Roman commands beyond a year. The Samnite reaction to Rome's intervention was the formal start of the Second Samnite War; the Lucanians and Apulians allied with Rome in 326.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 628-665
Frederiksen, Campania (1984) 208-212

lex_poetelia_papiria.detail:
Nexum was a contract by bronze and scales (per aes et libram) by which a borrower pledged his own person and labour as security, becoming a bondsman (nexus) of his creditor until the debt was paid. Livy's story for 326 tells of a young man, C. Publilius, who had entered bondage to the moneylender L. Papirius for his father's debt. Papirius, attracted by his youth, tried first persuasion and then threats; when the young man resisted, he had him stripped and flogged. Publilius ran into the street showing the welts; a crowd gathered, the consuls were forced to convene the Senate, and a law was carried that no one should be kept in fetters or chains except those guilty of crime awaiting punishment, and that for money lent, the debtor's goods, not his body, should be liable. All nexi were released. Livy calls it 'as it were a second beginning of liberty' for the plebs. Dionysius tells a similar story with different names, and Varro dates the law to the dictatorship of C. Poetelius Libo Visolus in 313.

The law did not end all debt bondage: judgment debtors (addicti) could still be handed over to creditors to work off debts, a practice attested into the late Republic. What it ended was the voluntary self-pledge of citizens as a normal credit mechanism. Moses Finley argued that this was a turning point in Roman social history: once citizens could no longer be exploited as bonded labour, Roman landowners turned to chattel slaves imported through war, and the great slave society of the later Republic followed. The wars of the late 4th century supplied captives in quantity, from the 4,000 Satricans sold in 346 to the tens of thousands of Samnites enslaved in the 290s.

The law also strengthened the free peasantry as the backbone of the legions. Its anecdotal origin, a sexual assault on a free citizen's body like the Verginia story, expresses the Roman idea that libertas meant the inviolability of the citizen's person.
lex_poetelia_papiria.debate: Date (326 Livy, 313 Varro) and the scope of the abolition are disputed; debt bondage by judgment survived.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 688-700
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 330-333
Finley, Ancient Slavery and Modern Ideology (1980)
Finley, 'Debt-bondage and the problem of slavery', in Economy and Society in Ancient Greece (1981)
Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, II (1998) 688-700

romaion_bronze_of_neapolis.detail: Struck at Neapolis for Roman use in Campania, they show that Rome first acquired coinage through its Greek ally rather than at home. They are catalogued as RRC 1/1. Some numismatists prefer a later date in the early 3rd century. Rome's own cast bronze (aes grave) and silver didrachms followed.
scholarship: Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974) no. 1/1
Burnett, 'The coinages of Rome and Magna Graecia in the late fourth and third centuries BC', SNR 56 (1977)

alliance_with_apulians_and_lucanians_326.detail: Rome's eastern strategy, encircling Samnium from Apulia, depended on the Apulian cities (Arpi, Teanum Apulum, Canusium). Livy's story of Tarentine deceit anticipates the hostility of 282.

battle_of_imbrinium.detail: Livy cites Fabius Pictor here: Fabius burned the spoils so that the dictator could not use them in his triumph. The confrontation dramatises imperium versus popular appeal (provocatio) and the rivalry of two great generals of the Samnite wars.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 700-760

vestini_war_325.detail: The campaign opened Rome's route across the Apennines toward the Adriatic. The Vestini made a treaty with Rome in 302.

embassy_to_alexander_323.detail: Cleitarchus (per Pliny) also mentioned a Roman embassy. If real, it might relate to complaints about Antiate piracy (Strabo). Most scholars reject it as a later invention, though not all.

brutulus_papius_322.detail: Livy presents the rejection as Roman arrogance that the gods punished at the Caudine Forks the next year, and gives Gavius Pontius a speech appealing to divine justice. The Papii remained prominent: Papius Mutilus led the Samnites in the Social War.

battle_of_the_caudine_forks.detail:
In 321 the consuls T. Veturius Calvinus and Sp. Postumius Albinus were camped with four legions near Calatia in Campania when ten Samnite soldiers disguised as shepherds, posted by the Samnite general Gavius Pontius, told Roman foragers that the Samnite army was besieging Luceria in Apulia. Eager to relieve their ally, the consuls took the shortest route, through the Caudine pass. Livy describes the trap precisely: a grassy, enclosed plain between wooded ridges, entered and left by narrow defiles. The Romans passed through the first, found the exit blocked by felled trees and boulders, turned back and found the entrance blocked too, with Samnites on the heights. They fortified a camp and waited in vain.

Pontius consulted his aged father Herennius, who advised releasing the Romans unharmed to win their friendship, or else killing them all to cripple Rome for a generation; anything between, he warned, would earn hatred without weakening them. Pontius chose the middle course. The terms: the Romans would evacuate Samnite territory, withdraw their colonies at Cales and Fregellae, and restore the old treaty; 600 equites were given as hostages; and the whole army, consuls included, passed under a 'yoke' of spears, stripped to their tunics. Capua received the shamed soldiers kindly; they entered Rome by night.
