The disaster cost no lives but enormous prestige. Livy insists the agreement was only a sponsio, a personal pledge by the commanders, not a treaty sworn by fetials, and makes the Romans repudiate it in 320, handing over Postumius and the other guarantors, whom Pontius refused, and avenging themselves at Luceria. Modern scholars mostly believe Rome honoured the peace for some years, as Cicero and Appian imply, until the war resumed in 316 or 315. The location is traditionally the valley between Arpaia and Montesarchio (the Forchia di Arpaia preserving the name 'furculae'), though Salmon and others preferred the valley of Moiano. The Caudine Forks became shorthand for humiliation; passing 'under the Caudine yoke' is still an Italian idiom.
battle_of_the_caudine_forks.debate: Site of the pass; whether the Senate repudiated the sponsio; historicity of Roman revenge in 320.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005) 1-160
Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967) 225-232
Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967) 225-231
Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, III (2005) 1-21

siege_of_luceria_320.detail: Probably a doublet of the genuine capture of Luceria in 314, when a Latin colony was founded. The Fasti Triumphales do record a triumph of Papirius over the Samnites in 319.
siege_of_luceria_320.debate: Likely fictional or a doublet of 314.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005) 160-200

repudiation_of_caudine_peace_320.detail: Livy distinguishes a foedus, sworn by the people through fetials, from a sponsio given by magistrates, a distinction later repeated over Mancinus at Numantia (137). Pontius' speech denounces the trick as a mockery of the gods. Modern scholars, following Cicero, Appian and the evidence of Rome's quiet in Samnium until 316, widely believe that Rome in fact kept the peace for several years, ceding Fregellae and Cales, and that the immediate revenge (recapture of Luceria, Papirius Cursor's triumph and the 'yoke returned') was invented to soften the humiliation. Either way the episode became the classic case in Roman discussions of good faith (fides) in international law.
repudiation_of_caudine_peace_320.debate: Whether the peace was repudiated at once (Livy) or kept until c. 316 (Salmon, Cornell).
scholarship: E. T. Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967)

tarentine_mediation_320.detail: Livy paints the Tarentines as meddling and vain, anticipating the conflict of 282. Tarentum feared Roman expansion into Apulia, its hinterland.

prefects_for_capua_318.detail: The praefecti Capuam Cumas, later elected, became the template for prefectures administering communities of cives sine suffragio. The Apulian alliances outflanked Samnium from the east.

lex_ovinia.detail: Festus is the only source and does not date the law; most scholars place it between 339 and 312, often just before the censorship of Appius Claudius (312), whose controversial enrolment of freedmen's sons may have been the first under the new rules. Before Ovinius, consuls or consular tribunes had chosen their advisers each year, and senators could be dropped (praeteriti). Afterwards the Senate gained continuity and independent authority, while the censors' lectio senatus, with its notae marking expelled members, became a powerful moral instrument (as in the expulsion of P. Cornelius Rufinus in 275).
lex_ovinia.debate: Date (c. 339-312) and the meaning of 'ex omni ordine optimum quemque curiatim' are disputed.
scholarship: Cornell, 'The lex Ovinia and the emancipation of the Senate', in Bruun (ed.), The Roman Middle Republic (2000)

apulian_cities_submit_318.detail: Canusium was a rich Daunian city whose tombs, full of painted vases and gold, show a Hellenised native aristocracy. It remained loyal to Rome and sheltered the survivors of Cannae in 216.

agathocles_seizes_power_317.detail: He promised to cancel debts and redistribute land, and ruled as tyrant and from 304 as king until 289. Timaeus, whom he exiled, wrote a bitterly hostile history; Duris of Samos and Callias were more favourable. Polybius, criticising Timaeus, conceded that Agathocles must have had extraordinary abilities. For Rome he matters as the precursor of Pyrrhus: a Greek warlord whose wars weakened Carthage, whose Campanian mercenaries became the Mamertines, and whose death opened the Sicilian vacuum that led to 264.

capture_of_nerulum_317.detail: Nerulum lay on the later Via Popilia route through the Lucanian highlands.

battle_of_lautulae.detail: The defeat cut the coastal route to Campania and sparked a revolt among the Aurunci and part of the Campanian elite. Rome's response (Via Appia, colonies at Suessa, Pontiae, Interamna) was to secure the corridor permanently.
battle_of_lautulae.debate: Livy's indecisive result vs Diodorus' Roman defeat.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005) 290-310

siege_of_saticula_315.detail: A Latin colony was planted at Saticula in 313.

destruction_of_the_ausones_314.detail: Diodorus reports Roman victory near Tarracina in the same year. A Capuan conspiracy was investigated by the dictator C. Maenius; the Calavii brothers killed themselves. Roman citizen colonies followed at Minturnae and Sinuessa (296).

colony_at_luceria_314.detail: The far-flung Apulian colony embodied a strategy of encirclement. Luceria remained loyal during Hannibal's war and served as a base.

siege_of_sora_314.detail: Sora controlled the upper Liris valley, the route between Latium and Samnium; it was finally secured with a Latin colony in 303.

acrotatus_at_acragas_314.detail: Acrotatus belongs to the line of Spartan royals hired by western Greeks, from Archidamus (338) to Cleonymus (303).

colonies_313_312.detail: Together with Cales (334), Fregellae (328), Luceria (314) and the Via Appia (312), this ring of colonies isolated Samnium from Campania and Latium.
scholarship: Salmon, Roman Colonization under the Republic (1969)

capture_of_nola_313.detail: Nola became a loyal ally; it was the base from which Marcellus checked Hannibal in 216-214. Its coinage was Greek-style with the legend NOLAION.

censorship_of_appius_claudius.detail: The consuls of 311 refused to recognise his Senate list. Legend said the Potitii died out within a year and Appius was later struck blind (hence Caecus). Modern views range from Appius as a 'popular' reformer seeking a clientele among the urban and commercial classes (Mommsen) to a Hellenising aristocrat building state infrastructure for war against Samnium (Humm, Oakley). His secretary Gnaeus Flavius published the legal formulas in 304.
scholarship: Humm, Appius Claudius Caecus: la République accomplie (2005)
Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005) 349-415

via_appia.detail:
As censor in 312 Appius Claudius Caecus built, without waiting for Senate approval and draining the treasury, the road that bears his name, the first Roman highway named after its builder. It ran 132 Roman miles from the Porta Capena to Capua: through Bovillae and Aricia, across the Alban hills, then in a long straight line across the Pontine marshes to Tarracina, along the coast past Fundi and Formiae to Minturnae and Sinuessa, and inland to Capua. The 19-mile stretch through the marshes (the decennovium) ran beside a canal; Horace describes taking the night barge from Forum Appii to the shrine of Feronia near Tarracina, tormented by frogs and mosquitoes. At first the road was surfaced with gravel; in 296 the curule aediles laid a stone footpath from the Porta Capena to the temple of Mars, in 293 the road was paved with silex from there to Bovillae, and the familiar polygonal blocks of basalt gradually extended along the route.

The strategic logic is clear. The older route to Campania, the Via Latina, ran up the Sacco and Liris valleys through country exposed to Samnite attack; after Lautulae (315) Rome needed a secure coastal corridor to its Campanian allies, linking the colonies of Tarracina (329), Suessa (313), Minturnae and Sinuessa (296). The road was extended to Beneventum after 268, then to Venusia and Tarentum, and by the early 2nd century to Brundisium, the port for the East.

Ancient writers admired it as the 'queen of roads' (Statius). Procopius, travelling it 800 years after its construction, marvelled that the stones were fitted so tightly without mortar that they seemed to have grown together, and that it took five days for a traveller to cover it. Along its first miles outside Rome the aristocracy built its tombs, including the tomb of the Scipios, begun in the early 3rd century. Diodorus' claim that Appius paved most of it in stone in 312 is generally thought anachronistic, and some scholars think the censor improved an existing track rather than building a new road.
via_appia.debate: Whether the whole route was built new in 312 and when it was paved; Diodorus' account of stone paving in 312 is probably anachronistic.
scholarship: Humm, Appius Claudius Caecus (2005)
Laurence, The Roads of Roman Italy (1999)
Della Portella (ed.), The Appian Way (2004)

aqua_appia.detail: Only 60 paces near the Porta Capena ran on arches. Frontinus says Plautius resigned after 18 months but Appius remained in office to complete it and so the aqueduct bore his name alone. Its estimated daily discharge was some 73,000 m3 (Frontinus' 1,825 quinariae; conversions vary).
scholarship: Evans, Water Distribution in Ancient Rome (1994)
Ashby, The Aqueducts of Ancient Rome (1935)

potitii_ara_maxima_312.detail: The change made the cult of Hercules, closely tied to the cattle market of the Forum Boarium and to tithes from traders, a state cult supervised by the urban praetor. Modern scholars see Appius bringing a lucrative gentilicial cult under public control. The Ara Maxima lay near the church of Santa Maria in Cosmedin.

duoviri_navales_311.detail: The duoviri navales attest a small Roman squadron, used in 310 for a raid on Nuceria from Pompeii that went badly, and in 282 off Tarentum. The four-legion army is standard from here on. The same year the guild of tibicines (flute-players), banned from feasting in the temple of Jupiter, went on strike and withdrew to Tibur until tricked back drunk in carts, a famous religious-comic episode (Ovid, Livy).
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005) 382-405

battle_of_the_himeras_311.detail: The defeat prompted Agathocles' audacious decision to carry the war to Africa.

siege_of_sutrium_311.detail: The siege opened the second front of the Second Samnite War and set up Fabius' march through the Ciminian forest.

tibicines_strike_311.detail: The Quinquatrus minusculae of 13-15 June preserved the episode. It shows a professional collegium using withdrawal, the plebeian tactic of secession, to defend its privileges, and the practical dependence of public ritual on specialists.

capture_of_bovianum_311.detail: Bovianum fell again in 305 and 298, showing that Roman captures of Samnite towns were raids rather than permanent conquests until the 290s.

agathocles_invasion_of_africa.detail: The eclipse (Diodorus 20.5.5, Justin 22.6) is a fixed point of Hellenistic chronology. Agathocles captured Tunis and dozens of towns, allied with Ophellas of Cyrene (whom he then murdered), and nearly took Carthage, which in panic sacrificed 200 noble children to Baal Hammon (Diodorus). The expedition collapsed in 307 when Agathocles abandoned his army, whose sons he left behind to be killed. It showed Rome that Carthage was vulnerable at home, a lesson applied by Regulus (256) and Scipio (204).
scholarship: Consolo Langher, Agatocle (2000)
Lancel, Carthage: A History (1995)

eclipse_of_agathocles_310.detail: Astronomers identify it with the eclipse of 15 August 310 BC, one of the fixed points of Hellenistic chronology. It confirms Diodorus' dating of the African expedition, and illustrates the use of eclipses to date ancient events, as with the eclipse 'around the 350th year' in Ennius.

ciminian_forest_march.detail: The Senate, alarmed, sent envoys to forbid the crossing, but they arrived too late. The Camertes Umbri became Roman allies. Perusia, Cortona and Arretium sought a 30-year truce.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005) 450-500
Harris, Rome in Etruria and Umbria (1971)

battle_of_perusia_310.detail: Livy reports another victory near Perusia in 309 (9.40.18-20), perhaps a doublet. Diodorus says Fabius' raid reached Umbria.

battle_of_lake_vadimon_310.detail: Livy makes the dictator L. Papirius Cursor commander. The same small lake saw a decisive Roman victory over Etruscans and Boii in 283.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005) 500-520

battle_of_white_tunis.detail: Carthage reacted with religious panic, sending offerings to Melqart at Tyre and sacrificing children. Bomilcar attempted a tyranny in 308 and was crucified.

umbrian_treaties_310_308.detail: Cicero cites the foedus with Camerinum as a model of an equal treaty, and in 205 the Camertes sent a cohort to Scipio as allies of equal right. The treaties split Umbria and gave Rome a corridor to the Adriatic behind Etruria.

naval_raid_on_nuceria_310.detail: This is the first recorded operation by the fleet whose officers, the duoviri navales, had been created in 311. Nuceria surrendered in 308.

first_romano_campanian_didrachm.detail: The issue is RRC 13/1 and was accompanied by a bronze litra. It belongs to the 'Romano-Campanian' series, of which the later Hercules/wolf-and-twins didrachm (traditionally associated with Pliny's date of 269) and the quadrigati followed. These coins were made for use in the Greek monetary world of southern Italy rather than in Rome itself, where bronze by weight and, from c. 280, cast aes grave remained the money. The debate over dates depends on hoard evidence from southern Italy and on links between Roman and Neapolitan dies.
first_romano_campanian_didrachm.debate: Date: c. 310-300 (Burnett) or c. 280-276 (Crawford); place of minting (Neapolis or Rome).
scholarship: Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974) no. 13/1
Burnett, 'The coinages of Rome and Magna Graecia', SNR 56 (1977)
Burnett, Coinage in the Roman World (1987)

siege_of_syracuse_309.detail: The defeat of the Punic siege by Agathocles' brother Antander and the citizen defenders showed the success of Agathocles' gamble in carrying the war to Africa.

battle_of_longula_309.detail: Livy's battle has the hallmarks of later elaboration, but Papirius' triumph of 309 is in the Fasti and the gilded shields displayed in the Forum were real objects known to later Romans. The story is the earliest evidence connecting gladiatorial types with defeated enemies.
battle_of_longula_309.debate: Site unknown; details suspected to be annalistic decoration.

murder_of_ophellas_308.detail: Diodorus speaks of over 10,000 soldiers and as many non-combatants who suffered terribly in the two-month desert march. Ophellas had married an Athenian of the Philaid family, which drew settlers from Athens. Ptolemy recovered Cyrene soon after.

bomilcars_coup_308.detail: Aristotle had praised Carthage for never suffering a tyranny; Bomilcar's attempt was the nearest it came. The episode shows Carthaginian suspicion of successful generals, a recurring theme that later shaped Hannibal's career.

battle_of_mevania_308.detail: With the forty-year truce granted to Tarquinii and the treaty with Ocriculum, the victory closed the Etruscan-Umbrian war of 311-308.

roads_per_agros_307.detail: Five years after the Via Appia, the censors' road programme marks the start of state road-building as a regular instrument of control over newly won territory.
roads_per_agros_307.debate: Attribution of the Via Valeria to the censor of 307 is a modern inference.

agathocles_abandons_africa_307.detail: The expedition (310-307) had shown that Carthage's African heartland was vulnerable, a lesson Regulus (256) and Scipio (204) followed. In 306 a peace restored the status quo in Sicily, with Carthage paying Agathocles silver and grain.

hernican_revolt_306.detail: Livy notes the loyal towns preferred their own laws to Roman citizenship, an important datum for how civitas sine suffragio was perceived. An equestrian statue of Marcius stood before the temple of Castor.

third_treaty_rome_carthage.detail: Polybius denies such a treaty existed, saying no copy was in the archives. Modern opinion is split: many accept a 306 treaty with Philinus' spheres-of-influence clause (Cornell, Eckstein); others think Philinus misrepresented it or invented it. The issue bears directly on the 'war guilt' of the First Punic War.
third_treaty_rome_carthage.debate: Existence and content of the Philinus treaty.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) 354-355
Hoyos, Unplanned Wars (1998) 9-16
Serrati, 'Neptune's altars: the treaties between Rome and Carthage', CQ 56 (2006)

rhodes_friendship_306.detail: Rhodes had just resisted Demetrius Poliorcetes' great siege (305-304). The datum shows Rome's appearance in eastern Mediterranean diplomacy long before the Macedonian wars.

battle_of_bovianum_305.detail: Minucius died of wounds (or was replaced by M. Fulvius). Diodorus confirms the capture of Bovianum. Peace with the old treaty renewed followed in 304.

peace_of_304.detail: Treaties of alliance followed with the Marsi, Paeligni, Marrucini and Frentani (304) and the Vestini (302), extending Roman influence across the central Apennines to the Adriatic.

destruction_of_the_aequi_304.detail: Livy's 'nomen Aequorum prope ad internecionem deletum' is followed by Latin colonies at Alba Fucens (303) and Carseoli (302 or 298) and a new tribe (Aniensis, 299) on their land. A scattered remnant, the Aequiculi, survived around Cliternia.

gnaeus_flavius_publishes_the_law.detail: Pliny says the shrine's inscription dated it 204 years after the dedication of the Capitoline temple, a key datum for the Capitoline era. Nobles snubbed him: when he visited a sick colleague, young nobles refused to rise, so he had his curule chair brought in. The publication, followed by the first public legal teaching of Ti. Coruncanius (c. 250s), began secular jurisprudence.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005) 607-650
Humm, Appius Claudius Caecus (2005)

censorship_of_fabius_304.detail: Confinement to four of 31 tribes minimised the voting power of the urban poor in tribal assemblies and remained the rule for freedmen (with variations) for the rest of the Republic.

treaties_with_central_italian_peoples_30.detail: These peoples of the central Apennines became Rome's most valued allies, supplying contingents for two centuries, and led the revolt of the Social War in 91, when their federal capital at Corfinium was renamed Italia.

agathocles_takes_royal_title_304.detail: He presented himself as a Hellenistic ruler of the West, married Theoxena, a stepdaughter of Ptolemy I, and gave his daughter Lanassa to Pyrrhus, linking Syracuse to the Epirote who would later claim Sicily as her heir.

cleonymus_expedition_303.detail: Livy, a Paduan, notes with pride that the prows of Cleonymus' ships still hung in Padua's temple of Juno. Diodorus places him in 303/302. The 'Lacinian treaty' between Rome and Tarentum may date from these years.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) 41-60

treaty_with_tarentum_lacinium.detail: The date is unknown: c. 303 (after Cleonymus) is most often proposed, but the 330s (Alexander of Epirus) are possible.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) 41-60

colonies_sora_alba_fucens.detail: Alba Fucens, with its 3 km polygonal walls and later Roman forum and basilica (Belgian excavations), became a prison for royal captives: Syphax, Perseus and Bituitus.

colony_at_carseoli_302.detail: Carseoli and Alba Fucens (303) secured the route of the later Via Valeria across the Apennines. Carseoli was one of the twelve Latin colonies that refused troops in 209.

cilnii_of_arretium_302.detail: The episode is the clearest instance of Rome backing Etruscan aristocracies against their commons, a pattern repeated at Volsinii in 265. Maecenas, Augustus' minister, descended from the Cilnii on his mother's side.
cilnii_of_arretium_302.debate: Livy's sources disagreed on whether there was a war at all; the dictator is sometimes identified with Valerius Corvus.

temple_of_salus_302.detail: The paintings survived until the temple burned under Claudius. Pliny and Valerius Maximus treat Fabius' choice of art as unusual for a patrician. His grandson Q. Fabius Pictor wrote the first Roman history in Greek around 200.

lex_ogulnia.detail: With this the last major patrician monopoly fell, apart from a few archaic priesthoods (rex sacrorum, the major flamines, the Salii) that stayed patrician. Livy gives Appius Claudius Caecus a speech against it and P. Decius Mus a speech for it. Control of the calendar, auspices and sacral law now passed to a mixed patricio-plebeian nobility; the first plebeian pontifex maximus, Ti. Coruncanius, followed c. 254.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) 90-130
Beard, North & Price, Religions of Rome I (1998) 64-68

lex_valeria_de_provocatione_300.detail: Livy remarks that the only sanction was that violation would be 'improbe factum', a wicked act, showing how much early Roman law relied on social pressure. Most scholars regard this as the first historical lex de provocatione, the 509 and 449 laws being retrojections.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) 130-145
Lintott, 'Provocatio', ANRW I.2 (1972)

first_barbers_300.detail: Pliny adds that Scipio Aemilianus was the first to shave every day. The notice is a small but telling marker of the Hellenisation of Roman habits in the age of the Samnite wars.

statues_of_pythagoras_and_alcibiades.detail: Pliny wondered why Socrates and Themistocles were passed over. The choice reflects the strong influence of the Italiote world, where Pythagoras had taught, on 4th-century Rome, and the tradition linking King Numa to Pythagoras.

demetrius_complains_of_antiate_pirates.detail: The anecdote shows Rome already seen in the Hellenistic East as the power responsible for central Italy, and that Antium's seamen kept raiding despite the ban on its fleet in 338. Its date falls in Demetrius' years of power, roughly 306-288.

colony_at_narnia_299.detail: Narnia controlled the route into Umbria later followed by the Via Flaminia (220). The same year, Polybius says, Gauls joined by Etruscans plundered Roman territory and returned home unscathed.

agathocles_takes_corcyra.detail: The episode shows Syracuse playing in the politics of Alexander's Successors and explains Pyrrhus' later claims on Sicily through his son by Lanassa, Alexander.

gallic_raid_299.detail: Polybius places this after the thirty-year peace of 331; Livy says the Etruscans offered to pay the Gauls to fight Rome but they refused to settle. The episode foreshadows the Gallic-Samnite-Etruscan coalition defeated at Sentinum in 295.

treaty_with_picentes_299.detail: The Picentes revolted in 269 and were crushed in 268, part of them being deported to the Gulf of Salerno.

lucanian_alliance_298.detail: The war rapidly widened into a coalition of Samnites, Etruscans, Umbrians and Gauls, the greatest challenge Rome had yet faced in Italy.

scipio_barbatus_campaign_298.detail: The peperino sarcophagus, now in the Vatican, with its Saturnian verse inscription (CIL I2 6-7) is the earliest substantial Roman elogium and a rare documentary check on Livy, revealing family claims and annalistic confusion side by side. Barbatus' son L. Scipio (cos. 259) took Corsica.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) 154-170
Coarelli, 'Il sepolcro degli Scipioni', Dialoghi di Archeologia 6 (1972)

battle_of_volaterrae_298.detail: Livy's notice conflicts with Scipio's elogium, which mentions only Samnite and Lucanian successes, one of the classic problems in reconciling Livy with documentary evidence.
battle_of_volaterrae_298.debate: Conflict with the Scipio elogium over the consul's province in 298.

battle_of_tifernum_297.detail: Livy offers the usual inflated casualty figures (3,400 killed, 830 captured, 23 standards). The location of Tifernum in Samnium (perhaps the Matese massif or the upper Biferno) is uncertain.

temple_of_bellona_296.detail: Before the temple stood the columna bellica, over which the fetial hurled a spear into a plot deemed 'enemy territory' to declare war on distant foes; the Senate met there to receive returning generals and foreign envoys. Appius' elogium credits him with the vow.
scholarship: Ziolkowski, The Temples of Mid-Republican Rome (1992)

gellius_egnatius_coalition_296.detail: The strategic boldness of the plan is clear even through Livy's narrative: by uniting Rome's enemies north of the Tiber with the Samnites, Egnatius aimed to force Rome to fight on one decisive field against superior numbers. The Roman response was to raise perhaps six legions and arm freedmen.
scholarship: Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967) 263-268

ogulnian_she_wolf_296.detail: The first securely dated monument of the twins legend, which appears on Romano-Campanian silver didrachms c. 269. (The Capitoline Wolf bronze, long thought Etruscan, has been radiocarbon-dated to the Middle Ages, and the twins were added in the Renaissance.) The same year a patrician woman, Verginia, excluded from the cult of Pudicitia Patricia for marrying a plebeian, founded an altar of Pudicitia Plebeia in her house on the Vicus Longus.
scholarship: Wiseman, Remus: A Roman Myth (1995)
Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) 250-270

colonies_minturnae_sinuessa_296.detail: Minturnae's castrum-style rectangular fort (c. 2.5 ha) is a classic example of the 'coloniae maritimae'; Marius hid in its marshes in 88.

battle_of_the_volturnus_296.detail: The raid prompted the Senate to found citizen colonies at Minturnae and Sinuessa to guard the coastal plain.

battle_of_camerinum_295.detail: The disaster revealed the size of the coalition and caused the Romans to concentrate both consuls, Fabius and Decius, with four legions in Umbria.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) 280-300

battle_of_sentinum.detail:
In 296 the Samnite general Gellius Egnatius led an army north to join the Etruscans, Umbrians and Senonian Gauls in a coalition against Rome. Rome answered with an unprecedented effort: both consuls, Q. Fabius Rullianus (for the fifth time) and P. Decius Mus (for the fourth), marched with four legions and as many allies, while two propraetors, Cn. Fulvius and L. Postumius Megellus, ravaged the territory of Clusium to draw the Etruscans and Umbrians home. The Romans met the Samnites and Gauls in 295 at Sentinum, near modern Sassoferrato, on the Umbrian side of the Apennines.

Before the battle a hind chased by a wolf ran between the lines; the hind fled to the Gauls and was killed, the wolf, sacred to Mars, passed through the Roman ranks unharmed, an omen Livy reports. Fabius, on the right against the Samnites, held back to tire them; Decius, on the left against the Gauls, charged with his cavalry and was thrown back by Gallic war chariots, a weapon the Romans had not met, which terrified the horses. As his line broke, Decius summoned the pontifex M. Livius, recited the formula of devotio his father had used in 340, and rode to his death. The left steadied; Fabius sent reserves, then used the Campanian cavalry to take the Samnites in flank and rear, and stormed their camp. Gellius Egnatius was killed. Livy gives 25,000 enemy dead and 8,000 prisoners, Roman losses of 8,700 (7,000 in Decius' army). The Greek historian Duris of Samos, nearly contemporary, gives 100,000 enemy dead, a figure that shows how the battle impressed the Greek world.

Sentinum was the largest battle yet fought in Italy and decided its future. It broke the only coalition that might have contained Rome; the Etruscans and Umbrians soon sought truces, the Gauls were left isolated, and the Samnites fought on alone until 290. Fabius vowed a temple to Jupiter Victor; the curule aediles Ogulnii set up the bronze she-wolf with the twins in the same year. Polybius mentions the battle briefly in his account of the Gallic wars, which confirms its reality against those who doubt the annalistic details.
battle_of_sentinum.debate: Ancient casualty figures conflict (Livy 25,000 enemy dead, Duris 100,000); whether Etruscans and Umbrians fought, and the historicity of the second Decian devotio, are debated.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) 285-345
Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967) 268-270
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 359-362
Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, IV (2005) 277-345

temple_of_venus_obsequens_295.detail: The aedile's role in policing sexual morality and funding public buildings from fines is typical of the period (cf. the Ogulnii, 296). The same year the Fasti record plague and prodigies.

temple_of_jupiter_victor_295.detail: Sentinum produced several vows: the Ogulnii set up the she-wolf, Fabius dedicated Jupiter Victor, and Decius' devotio fulfilled a vow of a different kind.

agathocles_in_bruttium_295.detail: His Italian campaigns brought Syracusan power into the region Rome would contest with Pyrrhus fifteen years later. The Bruttii recovered Hipponion after his withdrawal.

temple_of_victoria_294.detail: The cult of the personified goddess Victoria reflects Hellenistic influence (Nike) at the height of the Samnite wars. Remains on the south-west Palatine have been identified.
scholarship: Ziolkowski, The Temples of Mid-Republican Rome (1992)

battle_of_luceria_294.detail: Livy admits that his sources disagreed on whether Atilius won or was refused a triumph. The temple was built near the Porta Mugonia on the Palatine slope, on the spot where Romulus had vowed one in the Sabine war.

capture_of_rusellae_294.detail: Rusellae's walls of large polygonal and squared blocks survive near Grosseto. It became a Roman ally and later supplied timber and grain for Scipio's fleet in 205.

truce_with_etruscan_cities_294.detail: The fines, expressed in bronze, show the scale of Etruscan wealth that Rome could extract. Megellus' illegal triumph was cited in his later trial.

battle_of_aquilonia.detail: When the sacred chickens would not eat, the pullarius lied that the omens were favourable; Papirius said the falsehood fell on the reporter's head, and the man was killed by a stray javelin at the start of the battle. Papirius vowed a cup of mead to Jupiter Victor if he won. Livy's account of the Samnite oath (an old priest named Ovius Paccius, a ritual from ancient linen books) is consistent with Oscan religious practice. Papirius' triumph displayed 2,533,000 pounds of bronze from the sale of captives and 1,830 pounds of silver. The site is disputed (Monte Vairano near Campobasso, or near Lacedonia).
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) 380-440
Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967) 182-186

temple_of_quirinus_293.detail: Pliny records an alternative tradition that the first sundial was brought from Catana in Sicily by M'. Valerius Messalla in 263, wrongly calibrated for Rome's latitude yet used for 99 years. The temple on the Quirinal was rebuilt by Augustus with 76 columns.

census_293.detail: Later figures: 287,222 (280/279), 271,224 (275), 292,234 (265). The dip after the Pyrrhic war suggests real losses. Rome's citizen manpower, plus the obligation of Latin and allied communities to send troops, gave it a military reserve of several hundred thousand by 225 (Polybius 2.24).
scholarship: Brunt, Italian Manpower 225 BC - AD 14 (1971) 13-14
Scheidel, 'Human mobility in Roman Italy I', JRS 94 (2004)

carvilius_colossus_293.detail: Carvilius also paid 380,000 asses of booty into the treasury, gave his soldiers 102 asses each and built a temple to Fors Fortuna across the Tiber. The colossus was among the first monumental bronzes made at Rome.

temple_of_fors_fortuna_293.detail: The festival of Fors Fortuna on 24 June was a popular holiday of boating and drinking, especially for the lower classes and slaves.

aesculapius_comes_to_rome.detail: The island sanctuary became Rome's healing centre: sick slaves abandoned there were declared free by Claudius if they recovered. In the 1st century BC the island was faced with travertine in the shape of a ship, with a carved snake-and-staff relief still visible at its prow. The episode marks the culmination of the 4th-3rd century importation of Greek cults.
scholarship: Beard, North & Price, Religions of Rome I (1998) 69-70

execution_of_gavius_pontius.detail: Known only from the Livian epitome and late sources, the execution became a stock example of Roman ruthlessness, criticised as unworthy by later writers. Rullianus rode as legate beside his son's chariot.
execution_of_gavius_pontius.debate: Whether the executed Pontius is the Caudine commander.

colony_at_venusia.detail: The figure may include families. Venusia controlled the Ofanto valley route to Tarentum; it sheltered survivors of Cannae in 216 and was the birthplace of Horace. The consul L. Postumius Megellus was later prosecuted for using his soldiers to clear his own estates.

trial_of_postumius_megellus_291.detail: Dionysius' fragments preserve the case. Megellus had already triumphed in 294 against the Senate's will; in 282 he led the embassy to Tarentum whose humiliation began the Pyrrhic war.

conquest_of_the_sabines_290.detail: Curius allegedly boasted he had taken so much land that it would have been a desert, and so many men that they would have starved, had he not taken both. He refused more than the seven iugera allotted to each settler, saying a man not content with seven iugera was a dangerous citizen. Peace was concluded with the Samnites the same year, ending the Third Samnite War.
scholarship: Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 334-335

velinus_drainage.detail: The diversion caused centuries of litigation between Reate and Interamna (Terni) over flooding; Cicero represented Reate before a commission in 54 BC. Some date the work to Curius' censorship of 272.

esquiline_historical_fresco.detail: Found in 1875, it is now in the Capitoline collections (Centrale Montemartini). The Q. Fabius has been identified with Fabius Rullianus. It illustrates the genre of 'triumphal painting' that Romans carried in processions and displayed in temples.
esquiline_historical_fresco.debate: Date (late 4th to mid 3rd century) and identification of the figures are uncertain.
scholarship: F. Coarelli, 'Frammento di affresco dall'Esquilino', in Roma medio repubblicana (1973)

lex_maenia_patrum_auctoritas.detail: Cicero says that M'. Curius as tribune had forced the patres to approve a plebeian consul in advance, 'a great thing before the lex Maenia'. With the lex Hortensia (287), the law reduced the patrician veto to a formality, completing the legal side of the Struggle of the Orders.

tresviri_capitales_created.detail: They were later elected in the tribal assembly and formed part of the vigintisexvirate, the junior magistracies before the quaestorship. The moneyers (tresviri monetales) may date from the same reform.

colony_at_hadria.detail: Hadria later minted its own heavy cast bronze (aes grave) with the legend HAT, and was the ancestral home of the emperor Hadrian's family.

aes_grave_and_tresviri_monetales.detail: The first Roman silver didrachms, with the legend ROMANO and types such as Mars/horse head, were struck c. 310-300 (Crawford dates the first to c. 280), probably at Neapolis or another Campanian mint, for use in the south. A Pomponius passage in the Digest dates the moneyers to the same reform as the tresviri capitales (c. 290). Coinage at Rome was thus a by-product of conquest and contact with the Greek south, not an archaic institution.
aes_grave_and_tresviri_monetales.debate: Exact date of the first moneyers and coins.
scholarship: Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974) 35-46
Burnett, Coinage in the Roman World (1987) 1-15

census_289.detail: From the 290s Livy's figures, preserved in the Periochae, are widely accepted as genuine records of adult male citizens: 262,321 (293), c. 272,000 (289), 287,222 (280), 271,224 (275), 292,234 (265).

death_of_agathocles_289.detail: Diodorus tells that the poison rotted his gums and that he was placed on the pyre while still alive. Syracuse fell into anarchy and the tyrannies of Hicetas and Phintias, until Pyrrhus (278) and Hiero II (275-215).

mamertines_seize_messana.detail: Their appeal to Rome (and to Carthage) in 264 against Hiero II of Syracuse triggered the First Punic War. Oscan-language coins of the Mamertines (legend MAMERTINΩN) and inscriptions survive.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) 52-53

lex_hortensia.detail:
After the Samnite and Sabine wars a debt crisis led the plebs, in 287, to secede for the last time, to the Janiculum. Livy's account is lost, and only the summary of book 11 survives: 'the plebs seceded to the Janiculum because of debt after serious and long seditions; it was brought back by the dictator Q. Hortensius, who died in office'. Hortensius, a plebeian, carried a law that resolutions of the plebeian assembly (plebiscita) should bind all citizens (ut quod plebs iussisset omnes Quirites teneret). Gaius and the jurist Laelius Felix, quoted by Gellius, record that the patricians had previously claimed not to be bound by plebiscites. Macrobius adds that a lex Hortensia made market days (nundinae) days on which legal business could be done, so that country people coming to town could settle their lawsuits.

The law has a puzzling history, since the same principle is credited to the Valerio-Horatian laws of 449 and the Publilian law of 339. The usual solution is that the earlier laws required the patrician senators' approval (auctoritas patrum) for plebiscites, and that Hortensius removed this condition, making the plebeian council a fully sovereign legislature. In the same secession, according to Byzantine tradition, the lex Aquilia on wrongful damage was passed.

Modern historians treat 287 as the formal end of the Struggle of the Orders. From then on most legislation was passed as plebiscites proposed by tribunes in the concilium plebis, and the tribunes, now drawn from the same noble families as the consuls, became instruments of senatorial government. The integration lasted until Tiberius Gracchus in 133 rediscovered the tribunate's revolutionary potential. The law also illustrates a paradox of the Roman constitution: the plebeian assembly, technically a meeting of part of the people, became the main legislature of the whole.
lex_hortensia.debate: Relationship to the laws of 449 and 339; the cause of the crisis (debt) is known only from the Periochae and Zonaras.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 341-344
Hölkeskamp, Die Entstehung der Nobilität (1987)
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 349-350
Hölkeskamp, 'The Roman Republic: government of the people, by the people, for the people?', SCI 19 (2000)
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 340-344

lex_aquilia_de_damno.detail: The law replaced scattered provisions of the Twelve Tables with a general regime of compensation for damnum iniuria datum. Over the following centuries jurists such as Labeo, Celsus and Ulpian extended it far beyond its words to cover negligence, indirect causation and personal injury to free persons, and it became the foundation of the law of delict in the civil-law tradition, still discussed in modern legal education. Ulpian notes it 'derogated from all earlier laws on damage'. The archaic valuation rules reflect a society of slaves and livestock and a period without coinage.
lex_aquilia_de_damno.debate: Date: Theophilus' 287 is widely accepted but some argue for the later 3rd century.
scholarship: Lawson and Markesinis, Tortious Liability for Unintentional Harm in the Common Law and the Civil Law (1982)

thurii_appeals_to_rome_285.detail: Pliny saw this as the first Roman statue set up by a foreign people. In 282 Fabricius relieved Thurii and received a statue too. Rome's acceptance of a Greek city's appeal broke the spirit, if not the letter, of its treaty with Tarentum, and led to the war with Pyrrhus.

battle_of_arretium.detail: Polybius dates it ten years after Sentinum; Livy's epitome places it in 283 and Orosius gives the figure of 13,000 dead and 7 military tribunes. M'. Curius Dentatus, as replacement, then ravaged the Senonian lands.
battle_of_arretium.debate: Year 284 or 283; Metellus praetor or consul.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) 187-188
Williams, Beyond the Rubicon (2001)

expulsion_of_the_senones.detail: Polybius says the Romans 'drove out the Senones and became masters of their country'. The ager Gallicus remained public land until C. Flaminius distributed it in 232, a step Polybius saw as a cause of the great Gallic war of 225.

battle_of_lake_vadimon_283.detail: Pliny, citing the same lake, describes its floating islands. The victory ended the Etruscan cities' capacity for coordinated resistance.

battle_of_populonia_282.detail: Polybius gives no location; later accounts (Dio/Zonaras) place a defeat of Etruscans and Gauls near Populonia, the Etruscan iron-smelting port opposite Elba, under Q. Aemilius Papus.

battle_of_thurii_282.detail: The Thurians set up a statue and a golden crown for Fabricius. Rome's emergence as protector of Greek cities in the Gulf of Tarentum, against the Lacinian treaty, alarmed Tarentum.

tarentine_incident_282.detail:
Tarentum, the richest Greek city of Italy, had long regarded the Gulf of Tarentum as its own water. A treaty, mentioned by Appian, forbade Roman warships to sail east of the Lacinian promontory near Croton; its date is uncertain, often put around 303 when Cleonymus campaigned in Italy. By 282 Rome had placed garrisons in Thurii and other Greek cities appealing for protection against the Lucanians, cities Tarentum considered its sphere. In that year a squadron of ten Roman ships, commanded by a duumvir whom Appian calls L. Cornelius and Dio L. Valerius, sailed into the gulf, perhaps on the way to the Adriatic, and appeared off Tarentum. The Tarentines, gathered in their theatre overlooking the harbour for the festival of Dionysus, were stirred by the demagogue Philocharis to attack; four ships were sunk, one captured with its crew, and the commander killed. The Tarentines then marched on Thurii, expelled the Roman garrison and plundered the city.

Rome sent an embassy led by L. Postumius Megellus to demand redress. The Tarentines laughed at his Greek and at the purple-bordered toga, and a drunken man named Philonides fouled the toga in front of the assembly. Postumius, holding up the stained garment, told them to laugh while they could: they would weep long, when it was washed clean with their blood. The Senate debated; the war party prevailed, and in 281 the consul L. Aemilius Barbula invaded Tarentine territory. Tarentum, unable to face Rome alone, sent for Pyrrhus of Epirus.

The anecdotes come from Dionysius, Appian and Dio, all writing under the influence of Roman tradition, which portrayed the Tarentines as frivolous and insolent. Modern historians debate whether the Roman squadron's appearance was innocent or a deliberate breach of the treaty to test Tarentine resolve, and whether the treaty itself existed in the form described. Either way the incident shows how Rome's acceptance of appeals from Greek cities in the south led to collision with Tarentum, just as its acceptance of the Mamertine appeal would lead to war with Carthage.
tarentine_incident_282.debate: Whether the Roman squadron deliberately violated the Lacinian treaty, the treaty's date and the identity of the Roman commander are all disputed.
scholarship: Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957)
Kent, A History of the Pyrrhic War (2020)
Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957) 238-252
Franke, 'Pyrrhus', CAH VII.2 (2nd ed. 1989) 456-462

roman_garrisons_in_magna_graecia_282.detail: The garrisons alarmed Tarentum and were the background to the attack on the Roman squadron. Locri soon expelled its Romans in favour of Pyrrhus, and the Campanian legion seized Rhegium for itself (280).

phintias_founds_phintias_282.detail: Phintias' rivalry with Hicetas of Syracuse, both defeated by Carthage, typifies the chaos in Sicily after Agathocles that opened the door to Pyrrhus and then to Rome and Carthage.

tarentum_invites_pyrrhus.detail: Pyrrhus, recently expelled from Macedon and seeking a western empire, obtained ships from Antigonus Gonatas, money from Antiochus I and 5,000 Macedonian infantry plus elephants on loan from Ptolemy Keraunos for two years. Plutarch's dialogue between Pyrrhus and Cineas ('and then we shall rest') dates from this moment.
scholarship: Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957)
Garoufalias, Pyrrhus, King of Epirus (1979)

aemilius_barbula_campaign_281.detail: Barbula's triumph of 280 over the Tarentines, Samnites and Sallentines is in the Fasti. His campaign shows that Rome tried a short punitive war before Pyrrhus turned it into a major one.

campanian_legion_seizes_rhegium.detail: Rome could do nothing during the Pyrrhic War; the city was recaptured in 270.

battle_of_heraclea.detail:
Pyrrhus landed at Tarentum in 280 after a storm scattered his fleet; Plutarch says he brought 20,000 infantry, 3,000 cavalry, 2,000 archers, 500 slingers and 20 elephants, of which not all arrived. He imposed military discipline on the Tarentines, closing their gymnasia and theatres. The consul P. Valerius Laevinus marched into Lucania to prevent the Samnites and Lucanians from joining the king, and the armies met on the plain between Heraclea and Pandosia, divided by the river Siris. Inspecting the Roman camp, Pyrrhus is said to have remarked that the order of these barbarians was not barbarian.

The Romans crossed the Siris, their cavalry fording upstream to outflank the Epirote position. Pyrrhus led his own cavalry, was nearly killed when his horse was struck down, and exchanged armour with his companion Megacles, whose death in the king's cloak and helmet caused panic until Pyrrhus showed himself bareheaded. The phalanx and the legions advanced and gave way seven times. Pyrrhus then sent in the elephants, which the Romans had never seen; the horses bolted, and the Thessalian cavalry completed the rout. A Roman soldier, C. Minucius of the fourth legion's hastati, is said to have wounded an elephant and caused disorder. The Romans fled back across the river; their camp was taken.

Losses are disputed. Dionysius gives 15,000 Romans and 13,000 of Pyrrhus' men, while Hieronymus of Cardia, who used the king's own memoirs, gives 7,000 Romans and just under 4,000 Pyrrhic dead, including many of the king's best officers. The victory brought the Lucanians, Samnites and Greek cities such as Locri and Croton over to Pyrrhus, and the Campanian garrison seized Rhegium. Pyrrhus advanced on Rome, reaching Anagnia or Praeneste, but Rome refused to negotiate. The battle introduced Rome to Hellenistic warfare and to elephants, the 'Lucanian oxen', and demonstrated that a beaten Roman army could be replaced almost at once.
battle_of_heraclea.debate: Casualty figures conflict (Hieronymus 7,000 Romans and under 4,000 Pyrrhic dead; Dionysius 15,000 and 13,000); the size of both armies is uncertain.
scholarship: Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957) 317-340
Kent, A History of the Pyrrhic War (2020)
Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957) 316-340
Garoufalias, Pyrrhus, King of Epirus (1979)

pyrrhus_march_on_rome.detail: Plutarch says he came within 300 stades (c. 55 km) of Rome; Eutropius has him reach Praeneste. No Latin colony or ally defected, the first demonstration that Rome's Italian system held under pressure.

cineas_embassy_and_speech_of_appius.detail: Cicero knew a written version of the speech, the earliest Roman oration preserved in his day, and Ennius versified it ('quo vobis mentes, rectae quae stare solebant antehac, dementes sese flexere viai?'). Cineas reported that the Senate seemed to him an assembly of kings and that fighting Rome was like fighting a hydra. Fabricius led a counter-embassy about prisoners, refusing Pyrrhus' gifts; Pyrrhus released prisoners on parole for the Saturnalia, and all returned. Chronology (280 or 279) is debated.
cineas_embassy_and_speech_of_appius.debate: Date and sequence of embassies (280 or after Ausculum in 279).
scholarship: Humm, Appius Claudius Caecus (2005)
Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957)

triumph_over_volsinii_and_vulci_280.detail: Coruncanius, from Tusculum, was the first plebeian pontifex maximus (c. 254) and the first to give public instruction in law. His Etruscan victory prevented a northern front during the Pyrrhic war.

census_280.detail: Plebeians had been eligible for the censorship since 351 and one censor had to be plebeian from 339, but the ritual act of the lustrum had remained in patrician hands. Domitius, consul in 283 and dictator in 280, was the founder of the Domitian line that later produced the emperor Nero.

fabricius_embassy_to_pyrrhus_280.detail: Plutarch adds a conversation in which Cineas explained Epicurean philosophy and Fabricius wished such doctrines on Rome's enemies. The prisoners all returned as promised when the Senate refused peace. These stories built Fabricius into the archetype of incorruptible Roman poverty.

battle_of_ausculum.detail:
After his march on Rome failed and Cineas' peace mission was rebuffed, Pyrrhus campaigned in Apulia in 279. The consuls P. Sulpicius Saverrio and P. Decius Mus met him near Ausculum (Ascoli Satriano), by a river later identified with the Carapelle. Dionysius gives a detailed order of battle: each side about 70,000 infantry and 8,000 cavalry, Pyrrhus with 19 elephants and his Macedonian and Epirote phalanx interspersed with Italian allies, a sensible reconstruction even if the numbers are inflated. The Romans had prepared 300 ox-drawn wagons armed with spikes, scythes and fire-pots to counter the elephants.

The first day was fought on rough, wooded ground near the river where the phalanx and the elephants could not operate freely, and ended inconclusively. On the second day Pyrrhus occupied the broken ground with light troops and forced the battle onto the plain. The legions fought the phalanx hard, the anti-elephant wagons were overwhelmed by the light troops escorting the elephants, and the elephants drove back the Roman line; the Romans retreated to their camp. Pyrrhus was wounded in the arm by a javelin. Meanwhile his Daunian allies plundered his own camp. Plutarch, using Hieronymus, gives 6,000 Roman dead and 3,505 on Pyrrhus' side according to the royal records, and records the king's remark, when congratulated, that one more such victory would ruin him, the origin of the phrase 'Pyrrhic victory'.

Roman tradition claimed a draw or even a victory, and Cicero believed that the third Decius devoted himself at Ausculum like his father and grandfather; Zonaras says Pyrrhus warned the Romans he would take alive anyone attempting the rite, and the story may be invented. Strategically the battle was decisive in the opposite direction: Pyrrhus could not replace his Epirote veterans, Rome replaced its losses, and the king turned to the invitation from the Sicilian Greeks against Carthage, leaving Italy for three years.
battle_of_ausculum.debate: Third Decian devotio; outcome (Roman sources claim a draw or victory).
scholarship: Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957) 370-392
Kent, A History of the Pyrrhic War (2020)
Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957) 370-398
Franke, CAH VII.2 (1989) 469-473

fourth_treaty_rome_carthage.detail: The Senate declined immediate naval help (Justin), but the treaty kept Rome and Carthage aligned while Pyrrhus turned to Sicily. A Carthaginian fleet ferried 500 Romans to Rhegium and burned timber Pyrrhus had collected.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) 349-351
Hoyos, Unplanned Wars (1998)

gallic_invasion_of_greece_279.detail: Greeks celebrated the deliverance with the Soteria festival at Delphi. The invasion is part of the same Celtic movement that brought new bands into Italy in 299 and 284. In Rome's tradition a Brennus also led the Gauls of 390, an identity of name that may reflect a title or later borrowing.

temple_of_summanus_278.detail: Summanus was a little-understood god already by Ovid's time. The episode shows the role of Etruscan haruspices in interpreting lightning, their speciality.

fabricius_and_the_poisoner.detail: An exemplum of Roman fides retold endlessly (Cicero, Valerius Maximus, Plutarch, Gellius citing Claudius Quadrigarius' text of the letter). It eased negotiations before Pyrrhus departed for Sicily.

pyrrhus_crosses_to_sicily.detail: His claim rested partly on his marriage to Lanassa, daughter of Agathocles, and on his son Alexander, Agathocles' grandson. The Syracusan factions of Thoenon and Sosistratus handed him the city and its fleet of some 120-140 ships.

foedus_heracleense_278.detail: Cicero's speeches for Balbus and Archias (the poet Archias was a citizen of Heraclea) are the source. The treaty illustrates how Rome detached Pyrrhus' Greek allies with generous terms.

siege_of_eryx_277.detail: By the end of 277 only Lilybaeum remained in Carthaginian hands. Eryx would later be the scene of Hamilcar Barca's long resistance (244-241).

siege_of_lilybaeum_277.detail: Pyrrhus then planned to invade Africa, demanded rowers and money from the Sicilian Greeks, and executed Thoenon; the cities turned against him, some inviting back the Carthaginians or Mamertines.

battle_of_the_cranita_hills_277.detail: Zonaras, abbreviating Dio, is the only source. The Samnites remained in arms until 272.

rufinus_takes_croton_277.detail: The ruse is in Frontinus' collection of stratagems. Rufinus was expelled from the Senate in 275 for owning ten pounds of silver plate.

battle_of_the_strait_of_messina_276.detail: A storm wrecked the ships carrying the temple treasure, which washed up at Locri; Pyrrhus, terrified, restored it (Dionysius, Livy 29.18 for the Locrian tradition). Pyrrhus' parting remark on Sicily, 'what a wrestling ground we leave for Carthaginians and Romans', is recorded by Plutarch.

pyrrhus_plunders_locri_276.detail: The story was told by the Locrians themselves in 204, when they complained to the Senate that Scipio's legate Pleminius had robbed the same temple, and Livy, Dionysius and Appian preserve it. Ancient writers saw Pyrrhus' later defeats as divine punishment.

plague_of_276.detail: The plague followed the introduction of Aesculapius (291) and coincided with the strains of the Pyrrhic war.

battle_of_beneventum.detail:
Pyrrhus returned from Sicily in 276 with a weakened army, having lost many ships in a sea battle with the Carthaginians in the Strait and fought off a Mamertine ambush near Rhegium; he plundered the treasury of Persephone at Locri to pay his men. In 275 the consul M'. Curius Dentatus was in Samnium near Maleventum, his colleague L. Cornelius Lentulus in Lucania. Pyrrhus detached a force to hold Lentulus and marched against Curius before the two could unite, planning to surprise his camp by a night march through wooded hills. The march went wrong: the torches burned out, the troops lost their way, and at dawn they arrived on the heights above the Roman camp, exhausted and in full view.

Curius led his men out, attacked the van and routed it, capturing some elephants. In the main battle on the plain the elephants drove the Romans back toward their camp, where reserves or camp guards attacked them with missiles; according to Florus, Orosius and Zonaras, a wounded elephant calf screamed, its mother rampaged through the Epirote lines, and the other elephants panicked. Pyrrhus withdrew to Tarentum and soon sailed for Epirus with 8,000 infantry and 500 cavalry, leaving a garrison under Milo. Curius' triumph displayed four captured elephants, the first seen in Rome.

The scale of the battle is unclear. Orosius' figures (80,000 Pyrrhic troops, 33,000 killed) are absurd, and Plutarch's account suggests a sharp defeat rather than annihilation. Some modern historians, like Lévêque, consider it a limited reverse and argue that Pyrrhus left because of shortage of money and the opportunity in Macedonia, where Antigonus Gonatas was vulnerable. The site is also disputed: Florus places it 'in Lucania, on the Arusine plains', while Plutarch and others place it at Maleventum. Rome renamed Maleventum, 'ill-come', as Beneventum, 'well-come', when it founded a Latin colony there in 268, a sign of how the battle was remembered.
battle_of_beneventum.debate: Location (Maleventum or the Arusine plains) and the decisiveness of the battle are debated; ancient casualty figures are unreliable.
scholarship: Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957) 505-520
Kent, A History of the Pyrrhic War (2020)
Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957) 535-560

census_275.detail: Rufinus, a capable general who had taken Croton in 277, was ancestor of Sulla. The anecdote became a staple of Roman moral nostalgia about early austerity, but it also shows that luxury silver was entering Rome with Greek contact.

hiero_ii_elected_general_275.detail: Polybius' account is admiring: Hiero became king after the victory at the Longanus (269) and ruled to 215 as Rome's most faithful ally from 263, the period of Archimedes, the Lex Hieronica grain tithe, and the great altar of Syracuse.

triumph_of_curius_275.detail: Pliny says Romans had first seen elephants at Heraclea in 280 and called them 'Lucanian oxen', and that they first appeared at Rome in this triumph. Florus contrasts it with earlier triumphs, which had displayed only cattle and Sabine wagons. Curius used his booty to build the Anio Vetus aqueduct (272).

curius_levy_275.detail: This is the earliest recorded case of a defaulter (infrequens) being sold into slavery, a penalty later used in exceptional crises. The story belongs to the exemplary tradition of Curius' severity and frugality.

locri_roma_pistis_stater.detail: The coin, usually dated c. 275-270, translates the Roman concept of fides into Greek visual language and anticipates the cult of Roma that Greek cities would establish in the 2nd century (Smyrna 195). It is a sought-after piece in the Magna Graecia series.
scholarship: R. Mellor, ThEA ROMH: The Worship of the Goddess Roma in the Greek World (1975)
HN Italy no. 2347

aes_signatum_elephant_sow_bar.detail: Crawford dated the currency bars to c. 280-242, alongside the earliest cast aes grave. The sow may allude to the story that the Romans routed Pyrrhus' elephants with squealing pigs, or simply to sacrifice. Pliny's belief that early bronze was 'marked with cattle' (nota pecudum), from which pecunia derived, may reflect such bars.
aes_signatum_elephant_sow_bar.debate: Dating and the meaning of the sow are disputed.
scholarship: Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974) nos. 3-12

vestal_condemnations_274_266.detail: The cases are recorded in the Periochae and Orosius from Livy's lost books. They fit the pattern of Vestal trials in periods of military strain.

embassy_from_ptolemy_ii.detail: The first formal Roman relationship with a Hellenistic great power. Lycophron's Alexandra, perhaps of these years (or a later interpolation), speaks of the descendants of Aeneas winning 'the sceptre and monarchy of land and sea'.
scholarship: Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984) 673-678

colonies_paestum_cosa_273.detail: Cosa, excavated by the American Academy (F. E. Brown), is the type-site of the Latin colony: hilltop polygonal walls, grid, forum and Capitolium, harbour below. At Paestum the colonists built a forum and comitium beside the old Greek temples.
scholarship: Brown, Cosa: The Making of a Roman Town (1980)
Fentress (ed.), Cosa V (2003)

death_of_pyrrhus.detail: With Pyrrhus dead, his garrison commander Milo surrendered Tarentum to Rome. Hannibal is said (Plutarch, Livy) to have ranked Pyrrhus first or second among generals. Pyrrhus' own memoirs were used by later historians.

siege_of_tarentum_272.detail:
When Pyrrhus left Italy in 275 he kept a garrison under his general Milo in the citadel of Tarentum, with his son Helenus. After the king's death in a street fight at Argos in 272, Helenus was recalled, and the consuls L. Papirius Cursor and Sp. Carvilius closed in on Tarentum, where pro-Roman and anti-Roman factions were fighting. A Carthaginian fleet appeared off the harbour, ostensibly to help the Tarentines; the Romans later cited it as a breach of the treaty of 279, and Carthage denied any hostile intent. Milo negotiated the surrender of the citadel to Papirius in return for safe passage for himself and his troops.

Tarentum surrendered its arms and fleet, its walls were demolished according to Zonaras, a Roman garrison occupied the acropolis, and the city became an allied state (socius navalis) obliged to supply ships rather than soldiers. Papirius triumphed over the Tarentines and Carvilius over the Samnites, Lucanians and Bruttii, completing the reduction of the south. The booty, including works of Greek art, enriched Rome; Papirius used his share for the temple of Consus. Among the captives was a young Greek, Andronicus, who became the slave and then freedman of a Livius and, as Livius Andronicus, translated the Odyssey into Latin and staged the first Latin plays in 240.

The fall of Tarentum, with the last resistance of the Samnites and the Bruttii in 272, left Rome master of the peninsula south of a line from Pisa to Ariminum, an alliance of perhaps 3 million people bound by treaties and colonies. Within eight years Rome crossed the Strait to Sicily. The Carthaginian fleet's appearance at Tarentum foreshadowed that conflict: each power now regarded the other with suspicion, and Polybius' treaty sequence breaks off with the alliance of 279.
siege_of_tarentum_272.debate: The Carthaginian fleet's intentions and whether Tarentum's walls were really demolished are uncertain.
scholarship: Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957)
Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957) 627-640
Franke, CAH VII.2 (1989) 481-484

samnite_final_submission_272.detail: Latin colonies at Beneventum (268) and Aesernia (263) were planted in Samnium. The Bruttian loss of the Sila forest gave Rome shipbuilding timber and pitch just before the First Punic War.

anio_vetus.detail: Curius died before completion, and the Senate appointed duumviri aquae perducendae (Curius and Fulvius Flaccus) to finish it. Frontinus records its daily discharge as 4,398 quinariae, more than double the Aqua Appia, though its water was turbid and later used for gardens and baths.
scholarship: Ashby, The Aqueducts of Ancient Rome (1935)
Evans, Water Distribution in Ancient Rome (1994)

temple_of_consus_272.detail: Festus records the painting along with that of M. Fulvius Flaccus in the temple of Vortumnus. Consus, the god of stored grain, also had an underground altar in the Circus Maximus.

siege_of_rhegium_270.detail: Polybius stresses that Rome thereby demonstrated fides to its allies. The contrast with Rome's acceptance of the Mamertines' similar crime six years later was noted by Polybius as Rome's embarrassment in 264.

battle_of_the_longanus.detail: The date is disputed: Polybius' narrative implies c. 269 (before Hiero's 54-year reign ending in 215, i.e. accession 270/269), while others place the battle in 265/264 immediately before the Mamertine appeal. Polybius praises Hiero's careful policy, and his long reign as a loyal Roman ally after 263.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) 54-55
Hoyos, Unplanned Wars (1998) 33-46

romano_campanian_silver_269.detail: The she-wolf didrachm echoes the Ogulnian monument of 296. Romano-Campanian silver was probably struck at Neapolis or Rome itself for payments in the south and Sicily.
scholarship: Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974) 39-41
Burnett, 'The beginnings of Roman coinage', AIIN 36 (1989)

battle_of_asculum_268.detail: Part of the Picentes were deported to the Gulf of Salerno, around Picentia. The temple of Tellus on the Carinae was built on the site of Sp. Cassius' razed house.

colonies_ariminum_beneventum_268.detail: Ariminum, later terminus of the Via Flaminia (220), was the leading Latin colony of the north and in 209 was among the eighteen colonies that stayed loyal when twelve refused troops. Cicero's 'ius duodecim coloniarum' (Pro Caecina 102), a restricted form of Latin rights, is associated with Ariminum and the colonies founded after it.

temple_of_tellus_268.detail: The temple became a meeting place of the Senate (Antony convened it there after Caesar's murder) and held a map of Italy painted on its wall, described by Varro.

quaestores_classici_267.detail: The new quaestors reflect the administrative demands of Roman Italy just before the First Punic War: naval contributions of the Greek allies (socii navales) and coastal defence. Triumphs over the Sallentini were celebrated in 267 and 266.
quaestores_classici_267.debate: Precise functions and seats of the quaestores classici.
scholarship: Harris, 'The development of the quaestorship 267-81 BC', CQ 26 (1976)

temple_of_pales_267.detail: Florus says that 'Pales herself demanded a temple' as the price of victory. The site of the temple is unknown.

apollonia_envoys_266.detail: The episode is evidence of Roman contact across the Adriatic decades before the Illyrian war of 229 and of Roman concern for the sanctity of envoys.

conquest_of_sarsina_266.detail: With the Sallentini and Picentes subdued, all of peninsular Italy south of the Arno-Rubicon line was now under Roman control or alliance.

siege_of_volsinii_264.detail: Fulvius triumphed on 1 November 264. A dedication by M. Fulvius at the sanctuary of S. Omobono in Rome was found in the 1960s, and he may have 'evoked' the Volsinian god Vertumnus (Voltumna) to a temple on the Aventine. Volsinii (Etruscan Velzna, modern Orvieto) was the site of the federal sanctuary of the Etruscans, the Fanum Voltumnae, now located at Campo della Fiera below Orvieto. Pliny says the statues were the real motive for the war.
scholarship: Harris, Rome in Etruria and Umbria (1971) 115-118
Stopponi, 'Campo della Fiera at Orvieto: new discoveries', in Turfa (ed.), The Etruscan World (2013)

census_265.detail: The figure, on the eve of the First Punic War, gives the Roman citizen manpower that would man the first fleets of 260. The rule against iteration held for the rest of the Republic.
scholarship: Brunt, Italian Manpower 225 BC - AD 14 (1971) 13

mamertine_appeal_264.detail:
The Mamertines ('sons of Mars') were Campanian mercenaries of Agathocles who seized Messana around 288, killed or expelled its men and took their wives and property. For two decades they raided eastern Sicily until Hiero, the new general of Syracuse, defeated them at the Longanus (c. 269 or 265) and besieged the city. One faction then admitted a Carthaginian garrison under Hanno; another appealed to Rome, citing kinship as Italians. Polybius (1.10-11) says the Senate could not decide, because Rome had just executed the Campanian legion that had seized Rhegium in exactly the same way (270), but feared that Carthage, already master of Africa, much of Spain, Sardinia and the western half of Sicily, would control the Straits and encircle Italy. The consuls, Appius Claudius Caudex above all, took the question to the people, holding out the prospect of booty, and the assembly voted to receive the Mamertines into alliance. The military tribune Gaius Claudius crossed the Straits; the Mamertines tricked or pushed Hanno out of the citadel, and Carthage crucified him for cowardice. Carthage and Hiero then allied and besieged Messana together, which turned a police action into war with both Sicilian powers.

The sources are thin and partisan. Polybius used Fabius Pictor, who blamed the war on Carthaginian aggression, and Philinus of Agrigentum, who claimed that Rome broke a treaty barring it from Sicily. Polybius denies that such a treaty existed (3.26), but many modern scholars accept a version of it, perhaps a misreading of the treaty of 306. Dio and Zonaras preserve a more elaborate annalistic narrative with negotiations in Messana. The decision to cross has become the classic test case for theories of Roman imperialism: Mommsen saw defensive necessity, Harris (1979) a society geared to war, gloria and plunder, Hoyos (1998) an 'unplanned war' that both powers expected to be short, and Eckstein (2006) normal behaviour in a multipolar anarchy. The role of the people, unusual in Polybius' account, is also debated: either the Senate really was split, or the historian (via Fabius) shifted responsibility for a fateful decision away from the governing class.
mamertine_appeal_264.debate: Polybius (3.26) rejects the 'treaty of Philinus' that allegedly barred Rome from Sicily and Carthage from Italy; if it existed, Rome broke it in 264. Modern opinion is split (Hoyos and others take it seriously as a misunderstanding of the 306 treaty). Whether the Senate truly abdicated the decision to the people, or Polybius (via Fabius Pictor) shifts blame onto the plebs, is also debated.
scholarship: Hoyos, Unplanned Wars (1998)
Harris, War and Imperialism in Republican Rome (1979)
Eckstein, Mediterranean Anarchy, Interstate War, and the Rise of Rome (2006)
Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957)
Lazenby, The First Punic War (1996)
Rich, in Rich and Shipley (eds.), War and Society in the Roman World (1993)

battle_of_messana_264.detail:
Messana was under siege by Hiero from the south-west and a Carthaginian army under another Hanno (son of Hannibal) from the north, with a Carthaginian fleet watching the Straits from Cape Pelorias. Appius Claudius Caudex, consul 264 with two legions and allies, perhaps 16,000 to 20,000 men, could not force the crossing by day. According to Polybius he crossed by night from Rhegium and entered Messana. He then sent envoys to both besiegers demanding that they lift the siege; when they refused, he attacked Hiero first, and after a hard fight drove the Syracusans back to their camp. Hiero, suspecting that the Carthaginians had betrayed him, withdrew to Syracuse that night. Appius then attacked the Carthaginian camp, defeated Hanno's forces and raided up to the walls of Syracuse.

The later tradition, preserved by Zonaras (from Dio) and partly by Frontinus, adds colour: a first attempt to cross ended in disaster when storms and the Carthaginian ships wrecked the Roman transports; Hanno returned the captured ships, warning that the Romans would not even wash their hands in the sea without Carthaginian permission; the Romans then crossed on rafts and triremes borrowed from Tarentum, Locri, Velia and Neapolis. Philinus, Polybius tells us, claimed instead that Appius was beaten by both enemies, and Polybius himself admits he cannot reconcile his sources (1.15). Modern accounts (Lazenby, Hoyos) accept the substance of Roman success but doubt that Appius won two separate battles on successive days; the Carthaginians may simply have pulled back to their fortresses at the end of the season.

The consequences were large. Hiero, isolated, made peace with Rome in 263 when the two consuls of that year marched on Syracuse with four legions. Messana remained a Roman base for the whole war and the start of Rome's Sicilian presence. Appius took no triumph, perhaps a sign that the victory was less complete than the Fabian tradition claimed, while his successor Valerius took the cognomen Messalla and triumphed.
battle_of_messana_264.debate: Polybius' victory narrative may be Fabian whitewash; Philinus (cited at Polybius 1.15) claimed Roman setbacks. The sequence of fighting is uncertain.
scholarship: Lazenby, The First Punic War (1996)
Goldsworthy, The Punic Wars (2000)

first_gladiatorial_munus_264.detail: The games were a funerary obligation (munus) owed to the dead, an import from Campania or Etruria. The scale grew rapidly: 22 pairs in 216, 25 pairs in 200, 60 pairs over three days in 183, and 120 gladiators at the funeral of P. Licinius Crassus in 183 (Livy 39.46).

colonies_firmum_castrum_novum_264.detail: Velleius dates Firmum and Castrum Novum to 264 and Aesernia to 263. The Picentes had been crushed in 268, and part of the population transplanted to the Gulf of Salerno (Picentia). Aesernia guarded the upper Volturnus routes into Samnium.

temple_of_vortumnus_264.detail: The evocatio of Vortumnus is one of the clearest Republican examples of the ritual by which a besieged city's patron god was promised a better cult at Rome. Pliny says the Romans carried off 2,000 bronze statues from Volsinii. A dedicatory base found in the area of Sant'Omobono in the Forum Boarium, inscribed with Flaccus' name and 'Volsinio capto', was probably a display of the spoils. The old city was destroyed and its people moved to a new site at Volsinii Novi (Bolsena).

alliance_with_hiero_263.detail:
In 263 both consuls, Manius Valerius Maximus and Manius Otacilius Crassus, crossed to Sicily with four legions, the full levy of the year. Polybius reports that 67 Sicilian towns, Greek and Sicel, went over to Rome and that the consuls advanced on Syracuse itself. Hiero, already ruling for nearly twenty years and realising that Carthage could not protect him, negotiated. He returned his prisoners without ransom, paid 100 talents (Diodorus has 150,000 drachmas, roughly 25 talents, and a later passage 100 talents to be paid over 15 years), and became Rome's friend and ally, keeping Syracuse and a strip of south-eastern Sicily, about 50 miles deep, including Leontini, Megara, Akrai, Helorus, Netum and Tauromenium. The treaty was renewed for life in 248.

The alliance transformed the war. Hiero's grain, siege technology (supplied at Agrigentum, Camarina and Lipara) and ships kept Roman armies supplied throughout, and Polybius praises his steady loyalty. Rome no longer needed to fight a war on two fronts and could concentrate on the Carthaginian west. For Hiero it secured his kingdom; he survived to 215, enriched by the Sicilian grain trade, gave Rome help again after Trasimene (a golden Victory weighing 320 pounds, grain and archers) and was the principal Greek benefactor of Rhodes after its earthquake. His tax law, the lex Hieronica, was later adopted by Rome for the province of Sicily.

The consul Valerius took the cognomen Messalla from Messana. From Catana he brought back a sundial, which was set up on a column by the Rostra; Pliny, following Varro, notes that it was calibrated for a latitude four degrees to the south and that the Romans used it for 99 years until Quintus Marcius Philippus installed one adjusted for Rome in 164. Valerius also displayed a painting of his victory over Hiero and the Carthaginians on the side wall of the Curia Hostilia, the first historical painting known at Rome. Modern scholars stress that by 263 Rome's aims had already grown beyond Messana: the scale of the army sent shows a decision to drive Carthage out of eastern Sicily at least.
alliance_with_hiero_263.debate: Diodorus gives a different indemnity figure (150,000 drachmas). Pliny's latitude claim for the sundial is approximately right (Catana c. 37.5 N, Rome c. 41.9 N).
scholarship: Eckstein, Senate and General (1987)
Serrati, Sicily in the Roman Republic (2000)

siege_of_agrigentum_262.detail:
Carthage responded to the loss of eastern Sicily by concentrating a mercenary army, including Ligurians, Celts and many Iberians, at Agrigentum, the second Greek city of the island and its western base for the land war. In 262 both consuls, Lucius Postumius Megellus and Quintus Mamilius Vitulus, laid siege with four legions. They built two fortified camps joined by double lines of ditches, one against the city and one against relief, and drew supplies through Herbessus with Hiero's help. The garrison commander, Hannibal son of Gisco, held about 50,000 people in the city; after five months he was starving.

Carthage sent Hanno with a relief army that Polybius puts at 50,000 foot, 6,000 cavalry and 60 elephants. Hanno took Herbessus and cut the Roman supply line, so that the besiegers too suffered famine and disease. After two months of stalemate Hanno offered battle. The Romans won: Hanno's Numidian cavalry first drew the Roman horse forward, but the Roman infantry broke the mercenaries in front, the elephants panicked and fled through the rear lines. That night Hannibal and the garrison slipped out through the Roman lines, filling the ditches with baskets of straw. The Romans entered Agrigentum the next day, plundered it and sold 25,000 inhabitants into slavery.

Polybius (1.20) says that the capture of Agrigentum changed Roman war aims: the Senate now hoped to expel Carthage from Sicily entirely. But it also exposed the limits of a land strategy. Many inland towns came over to Rome, while the coastal cities feared the Carthaginian fleet and stayed loyal; Carthaginian ships raided Italy at will. Hence the decision of 261 to build a fleet. Diodorus' version (23.8-9), from Philinus, gives the Roman losses in the siege as 30,000 foot and 540 cavalry and blames Roman cruelty for driving the Sicilians back to Carthage. The sale of the population, the first enslavement of an entire Greek city by Rome, was a grim precedent, and Agrigentum, rebuilt with new settlers, changed hands twice more before 210.
siege_of_agrigentum_262.debate: Diodorus' numbers (probably from Philinus) for both armies and Roman losses are inflated. Polybius' statement about the shift in war aims is often taken as Fabius Pictor's retrospective rationalisation.
scholarship: Lazenby, The First Punic War (1996)
Hoyos, A Companion to the Punic Wars (2011)

roman_fleet_built_261.detail:
Polybius (1.20-21) tells the story that became the founding myth of the Roman navy. Rome had never owned quinqueremes, and its shipwrights had no model; then a Carthaginian quinquereme that ran aground while attacking the Roman crossing in 264 was captured and copied. The Romans built 100 quinqueremes and 20 triremes in sixty days from the felling of the timber, while crews practised rowing on benches set up on land. Pliny echoes the speed; Florus says the fleet seemed to grow from the trees by divine intervention.

Modern scholarship qualifies the legend. Rome had naval officers (duoviri navales, from 311) and allied ships from Tarentum, Neapolis, Locri and Velia (the socii navales), and the Greek cities of southern Italy had long traditions of shipbuilding and naval architecture, so expertise was not lacking. What Rome lacked was the quinquereme, the 'five' with probably three banks of oars and two or three rowers to some oars, which required a different construction and a crew of 300 rowers and 120 marines. The Marsala Punic shipwreck, excavated by Honor Frost in the 1970s, revealed letters painted on timbers as assembly marks, which supports the possibility of rapid prefabricated construction; the Egadi rams recovered off Levanzo since 2004 show the scale of the warships, with rams of about 100 to 170 kilograms.

The 120 ships needed about 30,000 rowers and 12,000 marines, perhaps a quarter of all Roman and allied men of military age, drawn especially from the proletarii and allied coastal towns. The building programme marks the moment Rome became a naval power, a decision driven by the stalemate after Agrigentum. The first squadron of 17 ships under Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio was trapped at Lipara, but within months the corvus (a boarding bridge, Polybius' 'raven') allowed Duilius to win at Mylae.
