Some (Badian, Gruen) see it as a genuine policy based on Roman ideas of clientage, in which freedom meant freedom under Roman patronage; others (Harris) as a cynical instrument of domination; Eckstein emphasises the need for a stable Greek system that excluded the great powers. The meaning of 'freedom' became a point of contention: the Aetolians argued that Rome had simply replaced Macedon as master of Greece, and the subsequent decades of Roman arbitration, interference and finally the destruction of Corinth in 146, at the very place of the declaration, give the episode a tragic irony that Polybius felt keenly.
isthmian_declaration.debate: Badian saw Realpolitik behind philhellenism; Gruen stressed Roman adoption of Greek diplomatic language; Dmitriev traces the slogan's Hellenistic precedents.
scholarship: Badian, Titus Quinctius Flamininus: Philhellenism and Realpolitik (1970)
Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
Dmitriev, The Greek Slogan of Freedom and Early Roman Politics in Greece (2011)
Badian, Foreign Clientelae (1958)

conference_of_lysimachia.detail: The exchange (Polybius 18.49-52) frames the cold war that turned hot in 192. Rumours of Ptolemy V's death broke up the meeting.
scholarship: Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochus the Great (2002)

repeal_of_lex_oppia_195.detail: Livy (34.1-8) gives Cato a speech on the dangers of female luxury and assertiveness and Valerius a reply; both speeches are Livy's own compositions and reflect Augustan concerns with moral legislation. The episode is a key text in the history of Roman women.
repeal_of_lex_oppia_195.debate: The speeches are Livy's invention; whether Cato really spoke is uncertain.

battle_of_emporiae.detail: Cato boasted that he had taken more towns than he had spent days in Spain (Plutarch). His speeches and the Origines were Livy's sources and are full of self-praise; he also organised the taxation of the iron and silver mines, a major source of Roman revenue.
battle_of_emporiae.debate: Livy (34.15.9) notes that Valerius Antias put the enemy dead at 40,000; Cato's own self-aggrandising account is the ultimate source.

siege_of_sparta_195.detail: Livy (34.22-41) presents Nabis as a tyrant; Polybius (13.6-8) tells of his 'Apega', an iron maiden built in the likeness of his wife. Flamininus' moderation in leaving Nabis in place angered the Achaeans and Philopoemen.
siege_of_sparta_195.debate: Hostile sources dominate the image of Nabis; modern scholars see a social reformer in the line of Agis and Cleomenes.

cato_disarms_spain_195.detail: Livy says Cato's revenues from the mines, especially around New Carthage and in the north, made the province profitable (34.21). Plutarch claims Cato took 400 towns; Cato's own speeches survive in fragments and made the most of his campaign. The Celtiberian mercenaries whom the Turdetani hired against him he tried to buy off with double pay. Cato's settlement did not last: the Spanish wars resumed within two years, but his organisation of tribute and mining set patterns for the next generation.
scholarship: Astin, Cato the Censor (1978)
Richardson, Hispaniae (1986)

maritime_colonies_194.detail: Puteoli grew into the greatest port of Italy within a century. Several of these small colonies failed, and Sipontum and Buxentum were reported deserted by 186 (Livy 39.23).

triumph_of_flamininus_194.detail: Flamininus had gold staters struck in Greece with his own portrait, the first living Roman on a coin. Greek cities created cults for him with Roma.
scholarship: Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974)

porticus_aemilia_193.detail: Remains in the Testaccio district, about 487 m long, have traditionally been identified as the Porticus Aemilia, though some argue they belong to the Navalia (ship sheds).
porticus_aemilia_193.debate: Identification of the Testaccio ruins with the Porticus Aemilia has been challenged (Navalia hypothesis).

hannibal_and_scipio_at_ephesus_193.debate: Livy found the story in Claudius Quadrigarius, who followed Acilius' Greek history; many regard the meeting as a literary invention, though Villius' embassy and the Romans' talks with Hannibal, which made Antiochus distrust him, are accepted.

antiochus_lands_in_greece_192.detail:
Between 196 and 192, Antiochus III and Rome conducted a cold war of diplomacy over the status of the Greek cities of Asia Minor (notably Smyrna and Lampsacus, which appealed to Rome) and Antiochus' presence in Thrace. At the conference of Lysimachia (196) and in later negotiations at Rome (193) and Ephesus, the Romans demanded that Antiochus leave Europe and the autonomous cities of Asia; Antiochus replied that Rome had no more right to interfere in Asia than he had in Italy. Hannibal, who had fled Carthage in 195, was at Antiochus' court, which alarmed the Romans.

The Aetolians, embittered after Cynoscephalae, invited Antiochus to free Greece and in 192 seized Demetrias. In autumn 192 Antiochus crossed with only 10,000 infantry, 500 cavalry and six elephants, far too small a force, and landed at Demetrias, where the Aetolians elected him their supreme commander. He took Chalcis and won over Boeotia, Elis and part of Thessaly, but the Achaeans, Philip V and most of the Greeks sided with Rome or stayed neutral. He spent the winter at Chalcis, where he married a young local woman, a symbol, for Polybius and Livy, of his lost momentum.

Rome declared war in 191 and sent the consul Manius Acilius Glabrio with about 20,000 men, along with Philip V's support. The war was decided at Thermopylae in spring 191. Historians debate the war's causes: Badian saw a 'cold war' in which neither side wanted a real war, Gruen a series of misunderstandings, Grainger Antiochus' miscalculation in trusting the Aetolians' promises of Greek support. Antiochus' landing with so few troops suggests that he hoped to negotiate from strength rather than conquer Greece. Hannibal's advice, according to Livy, was to invade Italy with a large force and to secure the alliance of Philip; Antiochus did not follow it.
scholarship: Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochus the Great (2002)
Badian, Rome and Antiochus the Great: A Study in Cold War, CPh 54 (1959)
Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochos the Great (2002)
Ma, Antiochos III and the Cities of Western Asia Minor (1999)

battle_of_thermopylae_191.detail:
In spring 191 Antiochus III, with about 10,000 men, fortified the pass of Thermopylae against the consul Manius Acilius Glabrio, who had about 20,000 Roman and allied troops plus elephants and Philip V's support. Antiochus built a double rampart and ditch across the narrow pass between the mountains and the sea, placed his light troops on the heights, and asked the Aetolians to hold the mountain paths, including the path of Anopaea used by the Persians in 480, with 4,000 men in the forts of Callidromus, Teichious and Rhoduntia.

Glabrio sent two former consuls serving as military tribunes, Marcus Porcius Cato and Lucius Valerius Flaccus, with 2,000 men each to dislodge the Aetolians at night. Flaccus failed at Teichious and Rhoduntia, but Cato, after a difficult night march guided by a captured Aetolian, surprised and routed the Aetolians at Callidromus at dawn and appeared above the Seleucid camp as Glabrio attacked the front. Antiochus' army, caught between two forces, fled. Antiochus, wounded in the mouth by a stone, escaped with 500 cavalry to Chalcis and sailed to Ephesus. Livy reports that only 500 of his army escaped; the Romans lost 200 men.

Cato's role was decisive, and he made sure that it was known: Plutarch quotes his account, in which Glabrio embraced him before the army and said that neither he nor the Roman people could repay him. The battle ended Antiochus' European venture; he abandoned Greece and returned to Asia, leaving the Aetolians to face Rome alone. The parallel with Leonidas, whose last stand at the same place was outflanked by the same mountain path, was obvious to ancient writers. Glabrio then besieged Heraclea and Naupactus, and the war moved to Asia Minor in 190, where the Scipio brothers led the Roman army. Modern historians (Grainger) regard Antiochus' strategy as defensive and his defeat as the result of excessive reliance on unreliable allies.
scholarship: Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochos the Great (2002)
Astin, Cato the Censor (1978)

temple_of_magna_mater_191.detail: Excavations on the Palatine have found terracotta figurines of Attis in the temple's earliest deposits, showing the Phrygian cult was present from the start.

aetolian_deditio_191.detail: Polybius (20.9-10) uses the scene to explain the gulf between the Greek understanding of pistis as a reciprocal relationship and the Roman deditio in fidem as unconditional surrender. It is a central text for Roman diplomatic concepts.
scholarship: Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
Eckstein, 'Glabrio and the Aetolians: A Note on Deditio', TAPA 125 (1995)

defeat_of_the_boii_191.detail: The submission of the Boii ended Gallic independence south of the Po. Strabo (5.1.6) says the Boii were expelled and migrated to the Danube, but the Po valley names and archaeology show many remained under Roman rule.
defeat_of_the_boii_191.debate: Strabo's claim of total expulsion of the Boii is contradicted by later evidence.

lex_acilia_de_intercalando_191.debate: The interpretation is debated: whether the law granted discretion (and so allowed abuse) or tried to restore regular intercalation after wartime neglect.

carthage_offers_early_payment_191.detail: The offer shows how quickly Carthage recovered economically after 201, aided by Hannibal's reforms of state finance in 196. Archaeology of the circular military harbour and new residential quarters on the Byrsa slope belongs to this period of prosperity. Rome's refusal and its tolerance of Masinissa's encroachments reveal that it valued the dependency more than the money, and the prosperity later alarmed Cato.

battle_of_magnesia.detail:
In late 190 or early 189 (the Roman calendar date is late 190; in Julian terms perhaps January 189), the Roman army under the consul Lucius Cornelius Scipio, accompanied by his brother Africanus as legate, crossed the Hellespont and met Antiochus III on the plain near Magnesia ad Sipylum, in Lydia. Africanus was ill at Elaea, and the actual command was exercised by the experienced Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus. The Romans had about 30,000 men, including two Roman legions, two allied legions, Eumenes II's cavalry and Achaean light troops; Antiochus, according to Livy, had 60,000 infantry, 12,000 cavalry, 54 elephants and scythed chariots, including cataphracts, Arab camel riders, Galatians and a phalanx of 16,000.

The battle began badly for the Seleucids: Eumenes' archers and slingers panicked the scythed chariots on the Seleucid left, which turned back and disordered their own cavalry and the left flank of the phalanx. Eumenes then charged with his cavalry and routed the Seleucid left. Antiochus, commanding the cataphracts on his right, routed the Roman left and pursued it to the Roman camp, where he was stopped by the camp guard under Marcus Aemilius Lepidus. Meanwhile, the Seleucid phalanx, attacked by Roman missiles and its own panicked elephants, broke. Livy says 50,000 infantry and 3,000 cavalry of Antiochus were killed, 1,400 captured with 15 elephants; the Romans lost 300 infantry and 24 cavalry, and Eumenes 25 men.

The casualty figures are absurd, but the defeat was total. Antiochus sued for peace, accepting the Roman preliminary terms at Sardis, confirmed at Apamea in 188. Lucius Scipio celebrated a triumph and took the cognomen Asiaticus. Magnesia ended the Seleucid challenge to Rome and established Roman hegemony in the eastern Mediterranean. Modern historians emphasise the decisive role of Eumenes and the weaknesses of the Seleucid army, which, despite its size, was composed of disparate contingents, and debate the date, given the discrepancy between the Roman calendar and the solar year shown by the eclipse of 190.
battle_of_magnesia.debate: Seleucid numbers and losses are disputed; Bar-Kochva accepts Livy's order of battle (from Polybius) but not the loss figures. The role of Domitius is attested by Livy; Africanus' absence spared him the risk of a defeat.
scholarship: Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochus the Great (2002)
Bar-Kochva, The Seleucid Army (1976)
Briscoe, A Commentary on Livy XXXIV-XXXVII (1981)
Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochos the Great (2002)

eclipse_of_190.detail: This and the lunar eclipse before Pydna (Livy's 3/4 September, in fact 21 June 168) are the key anchors for converting Roman dates of the early second century: the calendar drifted far ahead during the Second Punic War, presumably because intercalation was neglected, and was brought back towards the seasons in the 180s and 170s, perhaps under the lex Acilia of 191. Battles such as Magnesia (late 190 or early 189 Julian) and Cynoscephalae have to be dated with this offset in mind.
scholarship: Derow, The Roman Calendar 190-168 BC, Phoenix 27 (1973)
Feeney, Caesar's Calendar (2007)

lascuta_decree_189.detail: The bronze tablet, found near Alcalá de los Gazules (Cádiz) and now in the Louvre (CIL II 5041 = ILS 15), is the oldest Latin document from Spain and the oldest original Roman magisterial decree to survive. It shows a governor intervening in local dependency relations to break the power of a hostile city.

siege_of_ambracia.detail: Polybius (21.27-28) describes the mine warfare in detail. Ennius accompanied Fulvius and wrote a play, Ambracia, on the campaign, which Cato attacked as unseemly. The Senate later ruled that the looting had been improper.

scholarship: Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)

battle_of_mount_olympus_189.detail: Polybius (21.38) tells the story of Chiomara, wife of a Galatian chief, who had a Roman centurion who had raped her beheaded and brought his head to her husband. Manlius' campaign was criticised at Rome as private war for plunder.

glabrio_censorship_trial_189.detail: The censors elected instead were Titus Flamininus and Marcus Claudius Marcellus. The episode is the first of the peculatus attacks that culminated in the trials of the Scipios two years later, and shows how the profits of eastern war became a political weapon in the competitive aristocracy. Livy notes the hostility of the nobility to a novus homo aspiring to the censorship.

census_189.debate: The low 194 figure probably reflects underregistration and men overseas rather than real losses (Brunt).

treaty_of_apamea.detail:
After Magnesia, Antiochus' envoys accepted the Roman terms at Sardis in early 189, and the final treaty was drawn up by the proconsul Gnaeus Manlius Vulso and ten commissioners at Apamea in Phrygia in 188. Polybius (21.42-45) and Livy (38.38) give the terms: Antiochus gave up all territory west of the Taurus mountains and north of the river Halys; he surrendered all his elephants and could keep no more; his navy was limited to ten decked ships, which could not sail west of Cape Sarpedon in Cilicia except to carry tribute, envoys or hostages; he was not to recruit mercenaries or receive fugitives from Roman territory; he paid 15,000 Euboean talents, 500 immediately, 2,500 on ratification, and 12,000 over twelve years; he handed over 20 hostages, including his son Antiochus (the future Antiochus IV), and Hannibal, the Aetolian Thoas and other enemies of Rome.

The territory surrendered was distributed among Rome's allies: Eumenes II received most of Asia Minor west of the Taurus, including Lydia, Phrygia, Lycaonia and the Thracian Chersonese, making Pergamon a major power; Rhodes received Lycia and Caria south of the Maeander. The Greek cities that had supported Rome were declared free; those that had supported Antiochus were given to Eumenes or Rhodes. Hannibal escaped to Crete and then Bithynia. The treaty's terms on the navy and elephants were later enforced brutally by Gnaeus Octavius in 162.

The indemnity, the largest in ancient history, and the territorial losses crippled the Seleucid state: Antiochus III died in 187 trying to plunder a temple in Elymais to pay it. Rome took no territory for itself, preferring to strengthen its allies, a policy that historians have described as hegemony without annexation. The treaty marked the high point of Pergamene and Rhodian power, both later reduced by Rome after the Third Macedonian War. Modern historians debate whether Rome deliberately sought to weaken the Seleucids permanently, or was simply establishing a balance of power in its favour in the Hellenistic world.
scholarship: Sherwin-White, Roman Foreign Policy in the East (1984)
Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochus the Great (2002)
McDonald, The Treaty of Apamea, JRS 57 (1967)
Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochos the Great (2002)

philopoemen_compasion_188.detail: Livy calls it the destruction of the 'sinews' of Sparta. The episode embittered relations between Sparta and the Achaeans for forty years: Spartan exiles and factions repeatedly appealed to the Roman Senate, which sent envoys (Caecilius Metellus 185, Appius Claudius 184) and sought to arbitrate without fully committing itself. Polybius, from Philopoemen's own circle, defends the action. The Spartan question was the immediate cause of the Achaean War of 146.

trials_of_the_scipios.detail:
The trials of the Scipios are among the most confused episodes in Roman history, because Livy (38.50-60) reports several conflicting versions, drawn from Valerius Antias, Claudius Quadrigarius and others, and admits he cannot decide between them. The core is clear: in 187, at the instigation of Cato, the tribunes Quintus Petillius and Quintus Petillius Spurinus demanded that Lucius Scipio Asiaticus account for 500 talents received from Antiochus III as the first instalment of the indemnity, or as money for the army's pay. Africanus, who had served as his brother's legate, produced the account books in the Senate and tore them up, saying it was unworthy to have to account for 500 talents when he had brought 15,000 into the treasury.

Lucius was condemned to a fine, and when he refused to give sureties, the tribune ordered him to prison; another tribune, Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, father of the Gracchi and a personal enemy of the Scipios, vetoed the imprisonment out of respect for the family's dignity. According to tradition, Gracchus was then betrothed to Africanus' daughter Cornelia. Lucius' property was sold, and it turned out to be insufficient to pay the fine, which some saw as proof of his innocence. Africanus himself was accused, perhaps in 184, by the tribune Marcus Naevius; on the day of the trial, the anniversary of Zama, he reminded the people of his victory and led them to the Capitol to give thanks to the gods, leaving the tribune alone. He then retired to his villa at Liternum, where he died in 183.

Modern historians (Scullard, Gruen, Astin) have tried to reconstruct the sequence, generally accepting that the attacks were part of a political campaign led by Cato and his allies against the dominant position of the Scipios after the Antiochus war, and against the increasing wealth and independence of the great generals. The trials marked the end of Africanus' political dominance and demonstrated the limits that the Roman aristocracy placed on individual pre-eminence. The many variants also show how Roman historical memory shaped the story of the 'ungrateful Republic'.
trials_of_the_scipios.debate: Chronology (187 or 184) and the sequence of trials are irrecoverable; Livy himself despairs. Scullard's model of 'Scipionic' and 'Catonian' factions has been heavily criticised.
scholarship: Scullard, Roman Politics 220-150 BC (1951)
Gruen, 'The Fall of the Scipios', in Malkin & Rubinsohn (eds.), Leaders and Masses in the Roman World (1995)
Gruen, The Fall of the Scipios, in Leaders and Masses in the Roman World (1995)
Astin, Cato the Censor (1978)

triumph_of_manlius_vulso_187.detail: Livy (39.6.7-9), probably following Piso Frugi, dates the beginning of Roman luxury to this triumph; other moralists chose 146 (Sallust) or 133. The topos of decline through eastern wealth is itself an important Roman historiographical idea.

via_aemilia_187.detail: The Via Aemilia gave its name to the region (Aemilia, modern Emilia-Romagna) and fixed the line of colonies at Bononia, Mutina, Parma and Placentia.

expulsion_of_latins_187.detail: The expulsions of 187 and 177 (lex Claudia), and again in 172, reflect the tension between the Latin right of migration (ius migrandi) and the allied obligation to supply troops by a fixed formula. As Italians moved to Rome and to the new colonies, the communities left behind struggled to meet their quotas, and Rome, needing the soldiers, sided with the local elites. The issue foreshadowed the citizenship question of the Gracchan age.
scholarship: Broadhead, Rome's Migration Policy and the So-called Ius Migrandi, CCG 12 (2001)

triumph_of_fulvius_nobilior_187.detail: The consul Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, Fulvius' enemy, tried to block the triumph by charging him with plundering Ambracia; Cato attacked him for taking a poet on campaign. The temple of Hercules Musarum, later rebuilt by Marcius Philippus (29 BC), introduced the Greek idea of the museum and of the poet as client of the general. Coins of Q. Pomponius Musa (c. 66) reproduce the Muse statues.

bacchanalia_affair.detail:
In 186 the consul Spurius Postumius Albinus learned from the freedwoman Hispala Faecenia, lover of the young Publius Aebutius, that Aebutius' mother and stepfather planned to initiate him into the Bacchic rites to get rid of him. Hispala, who had been initiated as a slave, described the rites: originally held three times a year for women only in daytime, they had been reformed by a Campanian priestess, Paculla Annia, who admitted men and held them at night five times a month; there was drunkenness, sexual excess, forgery, poisoning and murder. Postumius reported to the Senate, which ordered an inquiry throughout Italy.

Livy (39.8-19) describes a panic in Rome: 7,000 men and women were reportedly involved, many fled, and many were executed; women were handed over to their families for execution. The Senate's decree, known from a bronze tablet found at Tiriolo in Bruttium in 1640 (CIL I2 581, the senatus consultum de Bacchanalibus, now in Vienna), shows the measures. Bacchic groups were not banned outright, but placed under strict control: no man could be a priest; groups could have no common funds, officials or oaths; meetings had to be authorised by the urban praetor and the Senate, with no more than five people (two men and three women) present.

Modern historians have interpreted the affair in many ways: as a moral panic about a foreign cult (Gruen), as an assertion of Roman authority over Italian religion and communities (North), as a reaction against private associations independent of the state, or as a political attack by the Senate on the Campanian and southern Italian elites. The decree's application to the allies, who were formally independent, illustrates the growing interference of Rome in Italian affairs after the Hannibalic war. The cult of Bacchus was not suppressed: Bacchic imagery remained common, and Caesar is said to have restored the rites. The tablet of Tiriolo, in archaic Latin, is one of the most important Latin inscriptions of the Republic.
bacchanalia_affair.debate: The decree is dated to the Nones of October (7 October) 186. How far Livy's account reflects real events rather than a moralising novella, and why the Senate acted, are long debated.
scholarship: Gruen, Studies in Greek Culture and Roman Policy (1990)
Pailler, Bacchanalia (1988)
Beard, North & Price, Religions of Rome (1998)
North, Religious Toleration in Republican Rome, PCPhS 25 (1979)

transalpine_gauls_at_aquileia_186.detail: The Senate's reply to the Gauls, as Livy reports it, was that the Alps were a nearly impassable frontier which Rome intended to defend. Gallic chiefs from beyond the Alps disowned the migrants and Roman envoys went to them. The episode explains the foundation of Aquileia in 181 and is an early instance of Rome treating the Alps as Italy's boundary.

apulian_shepherds_conspiracy_185.detail: The episode is the first notice of trouble from the armed slave herdsmen who drove flocks between the Apulian lowlands and the Samnite mountains on transhumance routes (calles), a system that grew with the ager publicus confiscated after the Hannibalic war. The same population, along with Sicily's estate slaves, supplied recruits for the slave wars of 135 and 73.

censorship_of_cato.detail:
In 184 Marcus Porcius Cato and his friend Lucius Valerius Flaccus were elected censors after a bitter campaign against seven other candidates, including Lucius Scipio Asiaticus and Lucius Valerius Tappo, on a platform promising severe reform. Cato's censorship became legendary for its severity. He expelled seven senators from the Senate, including Lucius Quinctius Flamininus, consul 192 and brother of Titus, for killing a Gallic deserter (or a condemned prisoner) at dinner to please a favourite, and Manilius, who was expelled for kissing his wife in daylight in front of their daughter. He deprived Lucius Scipio of his public horse.

Cato and Flaccus imposed heavy taxes on luxury goods: jewellery, women's clothing and carriages worth more than 15,000 asses were assessed at ten times their value and taxed at three per thousand; expensive slaves bought recently were similarly assessed. They cut off public water that private individuals had diverted to their houses and gardens, and demolished buildings that encroached on public land. They let public contracts at the highest rents and lowest prices, which led to protests from the publicani; the Senate cancelled the contracts and ordered new ones, which were only slightly less strict.

Cato also built the Basilica Porcia next to the Curia, the first basilica in Rome, and reconstructed the city's sewers. Flaccus was chosen princeps senatus. Cato's censorship became a symbol of austerity and the Roman resistance to Hellenistic luxury, and gave him his traditional cognomen Censorius. Plutarch says the people set up a statue of him in the temple of Health with an inscription praising him for restoring the Republic through good guidance and sound principles. Modern historians (Astin) stress that Cato's measures, although harsh, were directed at the political and economic consequences of the eastern wars, especially the concentration of wealth among the elite, and that his attacks on rivals, such as the Flaminini and Scipios, were part of aristocratic competition. His speeches as censor, preserved in fragments, show his rhetorical force.
scholarship: Astin, Cato the Censor (1978)
Suolahti, The Roman Censors (1963)

basilica_porcia.detail: The basilica form, probably adapted from Hellenistic stoas and halls, spread rapidly: Basilica Aemilia (179), Basilica Sempronia (169) and Basilica Opimia (121).

death_of_plautus_184.detail: Gellius preserves the story that Plautus lost his money in trade and worked in a mill, writing plays in his spare time, a tale probably constructed from his plays. Varro sifted the 130 comedies circulating under Plautus' name to 21 accepted by all, which are those that survive (the Vidularia fragmentary). Plautine comedy, with its singing slaves, inversions of the Roman household and puns in Latin on Greek settings, shows a theatre audience thoroughly familiar with Greek culture by the 190s.

death_of_scipio_africanus.detail: Livy (39.52) records disagreement over the year (187 to 183) and the place of burial, noting monuments at both Liternum and the Tomb of the Scipios. Seneca visited the villa and its small dark bath (Epistles 86).
death_of_scipio_africanus.debate: Polybius places his death in the same year as Hannibal's and Philopoemen's (183); Valerius Antias put it earlier.

death_of_hannibal.detail:
After the battle of Magnesia, the treaty of Apamea required the surrender of Hannibal. He fled, first to Crete, where Nepos tells how he deceived the Gortynians by filling amphorae with lead and leaving them in the temple of Artemis while hiding his gold in hollow bronze statues, and then perhaps to Armenia, where Strabo and Plutarch say he advised King Artaxias on the founding of Artaxata. Eventually he took refuge with Prusias I of Bithynia, for whom he commanded a fleet against Eumenes II and won a naval victory using jars of snakes.

In 183 Titus Quinctius Flamininus, as Roman envoy to Prusias, demanded Hannibal's surrender (whether on the Senate's orders or on his own initiative is disputed). Prusias' soldiers surrounded Hannibal's house at Libyssa, on the Gulf of Nicomedia. Finding all exits guarded, Hannibal took poison that he kept in a ring, saying, according to Livy (39.51), 'let us free the Roman people from their long anxiety, since they think it too long to wait for the death of an old man'. He was about 64. Livy also mentions the year of his death as 183, the same as that of Scipio Africanus and Philopoemen, though other authors place it in 182 or 181.

Hannibal's tomb at Libyssa was still shown in Pliny's time; the emperor Septimius Severus, an African, is said to have covered it with white marble. Flamininus was criticised in Rome for hounding an old man to death. Polybius (23.13) concludes his portrait of Hannibal by praising his ability to hold together an army of many different nations for sixteen years without mutiny. Hannibal remained the greatest enemy in Roman memory; Juvenal mocked the futility of his ambition that ended in a ring. Modern biographers (Lancel, Hoyos, Seibert) debate his strategic choices, particularly his failure to march on Rome after Cannae, and his political role in Carthage after the war.
death_of_hannibal.debate: Year (183, 182 or 181) disputed in antiquity; Flamininus' role was criticised even by Romans (Plutarch).
scholarship: Lancel, Hannibal (1998)
Hoyos, Hannibal: Rome's Greatest Enemy (2008)
Seibert, Hannibal (1993)

pontic_war_183_179.detail: Polybius preserves the treaty text of 179 (25.2), listing the participants, including the Sarmatian king Gatalus and the free cities of Heraclea, Mesembria, Chersonesus and Cyzicus. Rome acted only by embassies, the 'diplomacy of the Senate' that let Eumenes, its favoured client, do the fighting.

founding_of_aquileia.detail: Its foundation followed the expulsion of a group of 12,000 Transalpine Gauls who had tried to settle nearby in 186-183.

books_of_numa_181.detail: The episode reflects the contemporary belief, rejected by Livy and Cicero on chronological grounds, that Numa was Pythagoras' pupil, and Roman anxiety about Greek philosophy.

lex_villia_annalis.detail:
In 180 the tribune Lucius Villius carried a law that, according to Livy (40.44), established the minimum ages for each magistracy; his family was later known as Annales for this reason. The precise provisions are not recorded, but they can be reconstructed from the careers of subsequent politicians: a minimum age of about 30 for the quaestorship (after ten years of military service), 36 or 37 for the aedileship, 39 or 40 for the praetorship and 42 or 43 for the consulship. The law probably also required a two-year interval (biennium) between curule offices, and made the praetorship a mandatory step before the consulship.

The law codified the cursus honorum, the established order of offices, which had been taking shape in the early second century. Before 180, young men like Scipio Africanus (aedile at about 22, consul at 31) and Flamininus (consul at about 29) could reach the highest offices quickly in exceptional circumstances. The law responded to the intensification of aristocratic competition and the risk of exceptional careers: it gave more men an opportunity to reach the consulship and limited the advantage of the great families. The lex Baebia of 181 on the number of praetors and the laws on ambitus of 181 and 159 were part of the same effort to regulate competition.

The law was not always respected: Scipio Aemilianus was elected consul in 147 at about 37, before the legal age, by a special dispensation, and again in 134, in violation of the prohibition on second consulships (c. 151). Sulla's lex Cornelia de magistratibus (81) reaffirmed and modified the rules. Modern historians (Astin, Evans and Kleijwegt) have debated the precise ages, using the careers of known politicians, and the motivations for the law, seeing it as an indication of the oligarchy's efforts to maintain equality among its members and to prevent the rise of a dominant individual, as seen with Africanus.
lex_villia_annalis.debate: The exact age limits of the Villian law are not stated by any source and are reconstructed from known careers.
scholarship: Astin, The Lex Annalis before Sulla (1958)
Evans & Kleijwegt, 'Did the Romans like Young Men?', ZPE 92 (1992)
Astin, The Lex Annalis before Sulla, Latomus 16-17 (1957-1958)
Evans and Kleijwegt, Did the Romans Like Young Men?, ZPE 92 (1992)
Beck, Karriere und Hierarchie (2005)

deportation_of_the_apuani.detail: The Ligures Baebiani were still a distinct community three centuries later: a bronze alimentary table of Trajan (AD 101) found at Macchia di Circello records loans to its landowners.

callicrates_embassy_180.detail: Polybius, himself a victim of Callicrates in 167, presents the embassy as a turning point: the Senate wrote to many Greek states urging them to back men like Callicrates, who returned home and was elected strategos. Whether Rome had a deliberate policy of building client factions or simply responded to Greek appeals is a central question in the work of Gruen and Eckstein, who stress Greek initiative, against older views (Badian) of Roman manipulation.
scholarship: Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
Derow, Rome, Polybius and the East (2015)

execution_of_demetrius_180.detail: Polybius treats the story as a tragedy sent by Fortune to punish Philip for his crimes (23.10). Livy's long version, with the brothers' speeches before their father, comes from him. Demetrius' embassy of 184/3 had been a diplomatic success, the Senate saying it forgave Philip for his son's sake, but this marked him as Rome's man. His death cleared the way for Perseus and fed the Roman narrative of Perseus as a usurping fratricide, used in the propaganda before the war of 171.

colony_luca_180.debate: Livy's text is suspected of confusion with Luna (177); some scholars think Luca was a citizen colony or not a colony until later.

temples_of_juno_regina_and_diana_179.detail: The tablet of the Lares Permarini, quoted by Livy, used Saturnian verse; a parallel tablet hung on the Capitol. The dedications illustrate the building programme of the censorship of 179, which also included the Basilica Aemilia (Fulvia), the piers of the Pons Aemilius and a harbour at Tarracina. The temples were set in the Circus Flaminius district, which became the showcase of triumphal monuments.

gracchan_settlement_in_spain.detail: Polybius (25.1) mocked claims that Gracchus had taken 300 towns, saying many were mere forts. The ban on new walled towns was the legal pretext for the war with Segeda in 154.
scholarship: Richardson, Hispaniae (1986)

censorship_of_lepidus_and_nobilior.detail: The Basilica, rebuilt by later Aemilii into the first century AD, preserves the family name. The voting reform (Livy 40.51.9) is obscure.

accession_of_perseus_179.detail: Polybius (23.10) treats the Demetrius affair as a tragedy sent by the Furies. Roman historians portrayed Perseus as planning war from the start; modern scholars see a cautious king whose popularity in Greece alarmed Rome and Eumenes.
accession_of_perseus_179.debate: Whether the letter incriminating Demetrius was forged is uncertain.
scholarship: Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
Walbank, Philip V of Macedon (1940)

sardinian_war_177.detail: Livy (41.28.8-10) quotes the dedicatory tablet, which bore a map of Sardinia with depictions of the battles, an early example of a Roman triumphal map.

murder_of_seleucus_iv_175.detail: An Athenian decree (OGIS 248) honours Eumenes and Attalus for installing Antiochus. Pergamon had every reason to want a friendly king in Antioch; Rome, holding Demetrius, the rightful heir, could keep the dynasty dependent. The usurpation, the boy co-ruler's murder in 170, and Demetrius' long detention set up the dynastic conflicts that fractured the Seleucid state over the next century.

censorship_of_flaccus_and_albinus_174.detail: Livy's account of the contracts (41.27) is the most detailed list of censorial public works from the Republic, showing the censors' use of revenue from the eastern wars to equip both Rome and the colonies. Postumius refused to let contracts paid by colonies without their consent, while Flaccus did so; inscriptions from Pisaurum honouring Flaccus as patron survive. The expulsion of his brother Lucius Fulvius, who had disbanded a legion without orders in Spain, illustrates censorial severity.

expulsion_of_epicureans_173.debate: The date depends on identifying the consul Postumius (173 or 155).

juno_lacinia_tiles_173.detail: Livy presents Flaccus' later suicide (172) after news of his sons' fates as divine punishment. The episode reveals the Senate's sense of responsibility for the sanctuaries of Italy, already seen in the Pleminius affair at Locri, and the growing temptation for Roman nobles to strip Greek sites to adorn their own monuments, which the Senate tolerated outside Italy but not within it.

postumius_at_praeneste_173.detail: Livy explains that magistrates had previously travelled at their own or the state's expense, with mules and tents provided from the treasury, and used private ties of hospitality (hospitium) with leading families. The episode became a classic illustration of the hardening of Roman superiority over the Italian allies in the second century, which Gaius Gracchus later dramatised with stories of magistrates flogging local officials.

eumenes_at_delphi_172.detail: Livy (42.11-18) gives Eumenes' speech. Polybius (22.18) said the true causes of the war went back to Philip's resentment; modern scholars see Rome as determined to eliminate a revived Macedon regardless of Perseus' conduct.
eumenes_at_delphi_172.debate: A Roman indictment of Perseus inscribed at Delphi (Syll.³ 643) lists the official charges. The degree of Perseus' aggression is disputed.
scholarship: Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
Harris, War and Imperialism in Republican Rome (1979)

sources.w: Roman letter to the Amphictyons on Perseus

marcius_deceives_perseus_172.detail: Livy's contrast (42.47) between ancestral fides, which waged war openly, and the new sophistication of men who preferred deceit to courage is one of the key texts on the supposed decline of Roman morality. The majority of the Senate approved Marcius' conduct. Envoys at the same time broke up the Boeotian League, separating its cities in individual alliances with Rome.

carteia_171.detail: Carteia is the first Latin colony founded outside Italy and a revealing glimpse of the social consequences of long Roman service in Spain.

spanish_extortion_trials_171.detail: The Senate also forbade Roman officials to fix the price of grain or to station prefects in Spanish towns to collect money. The procedure prefigured the permanent extortion court of 149.
scholarship: Richardson, Hispaniae (1986)
Lintott, Judicial Reform and Land Reform in the Roman Republic (1992)

battle_of_callinicus.detail: Polybius (27.8) uses the Roman refusal to illustrate a national characteristic: they were most unyielding in defeat. Greek sympathy for Perseus after the battle alarmed Rome.

spurius_ligustinus_171.detail: Livy's speech, with its six sons and two married daughters supported from one iugerum, is a celebrated, perhaps idealised, portrait of the citizen-farmer who fought Rome's overseas wars. It is used both to show the prolonged service demanded of the smallholder class (whose decline the Gracchi lamented) and, by others (Rosenstein), to argue that many such men could combine service and family farming.
scholarship: Rosenstein, Rome at War (2004)

lucretius_gallus_condemned_170.detail: The year 170 saw a cluster of such complaints, from Chalcis, Abdera, Coronea and the Spanish provinces, and the Senate issued a decree that no one should requisition supplies from Greek communities except by its order. The senatus consultum de Thisbensibus, inscribed at Thisbe, preserves the Senate's detailed settlement of one Boeotian town the same year.

sc_de_thisbensibus_170.detail: The inscription (dated by the praetor Quintus Maenius, 170) is one of the best surviving texts of a senatus consultum, showing the Senate's procedure, the formulas of the decree ('quod Thisbenses verba fecerunt...') and its micro-management of a conquered community, down to grants of the right to fortify the acropolis. It illustrates how Rome rewarded its local friends and created the 'pro-Roman' parties of Greek cities.
scholarship: Sherk, Roman Documents from the Greek East (1969) no. 2

antiochus_iv_invades_egypt_170.detail: Antiochus claimed to act as guardian of Ptolemy VI and may have been crowned at Memphis. His second invasion in 168, when the brothers had reconciled, ended with Popillius Laenas' ultimatum at Eleusis. The Ptolemaic envoys who came to Rome in 169 begging help, and the Senate's delay until Perseus was defeated, show how the two crises were linked. Antiochus' looting of the Jerusalem temple on his way home (1 Macc 1.20-24) preceded the measures that provoked the Maccabean revolt.

lex_voconia_169.detail: The law aimed to stop great fortunes passing to women; it was evaded by trusts (fideicommissa) and by not registering in the census. Cicero (Verrines 2.1.104-114) shows Verres' manipulation of it; St Augustine still found it unjust.

censorship_of_gracchus_and_claudius_169.detail: The clash with the publicani, who had bid for the new contracts of 169 and been excluded, is the first open conflict between censors and the equestrian contractors, a group whose interests would loom large in the Gracchan age. The registration of freedmen in a single urban tribe confined their voting weight in the tribal assembly; Livy's account of the dispute between the two censors over how to do it preserves the legal argument that a censor could not deprive a citizen of his tribe without a vote of the people.

basilica_sempronia_169.detail: It was Rome's third basilica, after the Porcia (184) and the Fulvia/Aemilia (179); with them it framed the Forum with covered halls for business, banking and law courts. Excavations under the Basilica Julia have identified remains of the Republican structure and of earlier houses. The purchase of Africanus' house by his son-in-law is a nice instance of the elite remodelling of the Forum.

death_of_ennius_169.detail: Born at Rudiae in Calabria in 239, trilingual in Oscan, Greek and Latin (he said he had 'three hearts'), Ennius served in Sardinia, was brought to Rome by Cato in 204, and attached himself to the Scipios and Fulvii. Beyond the Annales, he wrote tragedies, comedies, satires, a didactic Euhemerus and the Hedyphagetica on gourmet fish. Only some 600 lines of the Annales survive in quotations, yet the epic shaped Roman historical memory until Virgil; Cicero quoted it constantly, and lines such as 'moribus antiquis res stat Romana virisque' became proverbial.
scholarship: Skutsch, The Annals of Quintus Ennius (1985)
Goldberg and Manuwald, Fragmentary Republican Latin I (2018)

battle_of_pydna.detail:
After three years of indecisive campaigns, Lucius Aemilius Paullus, consul for the second time at about 60, took command in Macedonia in 168, restored discipline, outflanked Perseus' line on the Elpeus via Pythium thanks to Scipio Nasica's march, and forced him back to the plain near Pydna. On the night before the battle, the military tribune Gaius Sulpicius Galus predicted a lunar eclipse, which took place on 21 June 168 (Julian; Livy's date, 3/4 September, reflects the Roman calendar error), and the Macedonians were frightened by it. The battle began the next afternoon, apparently by accident, after a skirmish over a horse that had escaped near the river.

Perseus had about 44,000 men, including 21,000 phalangites; Paullus about 38,000, including two Roman legions and allied troops and 22 elephants. The Macedonian phalanx charged, and Paullus later said that he had never seen anything so terrifying as the advancing wall of sarissas. The Paelignian cohort and the first legion were pushed back. But as the phalanx advanced over uneven ground, gaps opened in its ranks, and Paullus ordered his maniples to penetrate these gaps and attack the phalangites from the sides, where their long spears were useless. The elephants and allied infantry routed the Macedonian left. The 3,000 elite peltasts, the agema, fought to the death. In about an hour the battle was over.

Plutarch and Livy say 20,000 Macedonians were killed and 11,000 captured; the Romans lost about 100. Perseus fled to Pella and then to Samothrace, where he surrendered. The battle ended the Antigonid monarchy, which had ruled Macedonia since 277. Polybius, who knew the participants, gave the main account, used by Livy and Plutarch. Paullus' victory monument at Delphi, a pillar originally intended for a statue of Perseus, survives with a frieze showing the battle, including the escaped horse. Modern historians see Pydna as confirmation of Polybius' analysis of the superiority of the legion over the phalanx, but stress the role of leadership and terrain.
battle_of_pydna.debate: The battle date is fixed by the lunar eclipse of 21 June 168 (Julian), which Livy (44.37.8) places on 3 September by the Roman calendar, showing the civil calendar was about 2.5 months ahead of the seasons. Exact site uncertain.
scholarship: Hammond, 'The Battle of Pydna', JHS 104 (1984)
Kähler, Der Fries vom Reiterdenkmal des Aemilius Paullus in Delphi (1965)
Hammond, The Battle of Pydna, JHS 104 (1984)
Taylor, The Battle Scene on Aemilius Paullus's Pydna Monument: A Reevaluation, Hesperia 85 (2016)

sources.w: Monument of Aemilius Paullus at Delphi

day_of_eleusis.detail:
In 168 Antiochus IV invaded Egypt for the second time, after the reconciliation of Ptolemy VI and Ptolemy VIII, occupied Memphis, sent a fleet to Cyprus, and advanced on Alexandria. At Eleusis, a suburb about six kilometres east of Alexandria, he was met by a Roman embassy led by Gaius Popillius Laenas, consul 172, which had waited at Delos until news of the Roman victory at Pydna arrived. Popillius handed Antiochus the Senate's decree ordering him to leave Egypt and Cyprus immediately. When Antiochus said he wanted to consult his advisers, Popillius drew a circle in the sand around the king with a vine stick and told him to give his answer before leaving the circle.

Antiochus, after a moment's hesitation, agreed to comply, and Popillius then gave him his hand as a friend. Polybius (29.27), who tells the story, explains that Antiochus yielded because he knew of the Roman victory at Pydna and did not want to risk war with Rome. He withdrew his army from Egypt within the time prescribed, and his fleet from Cyprus, bitterly resentful. The episode is the classic example of Roman hegemony exercised by diplomacy, based on the prestige of recent victories, without the use of force.

The 'Day of Eleusis' saved the Ptolemaic kingdom, which became dependent on Roman protection. Its consequences extended beyond Egypt: according to the Book of Daniel (11.30, 'ships of Kittim shall come against him'), Antiochus, frustrated in Egypt, took out his anger on Jerusalem, where he imposed the measures that triggered the Maccabean revolt. He then held the great festival at Daphne in 166 to restore his prestige. Modern historians (Gruen, Morgan) have discussed whether the Senate intended to take control of Egypt or simply to prevent a Seleucid takeover, and whether Polybius' account, which emphasises Roman superiority, is literally accurate. The phrase 'to draw a line in the sand' has been associated with this event.
day_of_eleusis.debate: The Book of Daniel refers to the 'ships of Kittim' turning back the king of the north; Antiochus' subsequent measures in Jerusalem (167) have been linked to his humiliation.
scholarship: Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
Morkholm, Antiochus IV of Syria (1966)
Morgan, The Perils of Schematism: Polybius, Antiochus Epiphanes and the Day of Eleusis, Historia 39 (1990)
Gruen, Rome and the Seleucids in the Aftermath of Pydna, Chiron 6 (1976)

nasica_outflanks_at_pythium_168.debate: Plutarch had Nasica's own letter describing the march; Polybius gave smaller numbers for the Macedonian detachment.

crates_of_mallos_168.debate: Suetonius dates it 'between the second and third Punic Wars, about the time of Ennius' death'; 168 or 159 have been proposed.

cato_origines.detail: The Origines was the first history of Rome in Latin and a deliberate counterpart to the Greek-language histories of Fabius Pictor and Postumius Albinus. Its interest in the origins of Italian communities reflected a vision of Roman history as the history of Italy. Only fragments survive, including the heroic stand of a military tribune (Caedicius or Calpurnius Flamma) in 258 and the speeches for the Rhodians (167) and against Galba (149).

triumph_of_aemilius_paullus.detail:
In November 167 Lucius Aemilius Paullus celebrated a three-day triumph over Perseus and Macedonia, described in detail by Plutarch (Aemilius 32-34) and Livy (45.40). On the first day 250 wagons carried statues and paintings; on the second, the finest Macedonian weapons and armour, followed by 3,000 men carrying silver coins in 750 vessels each containing three talents, and silver bowls, horns and cups. On the third day, 120 oxen for sacrifice, gold coins in 77 vessels, a sacred gold bowl weighing ten talents, the gold plate of Perseus, his chariot, armour and diadem. Then came the king's children with their attendants, and Perseus himself, dressed in black, followed by his friends. Then Paullus himself, in a gilded chariot and purple robe. Livy says that the money brought to the treasury amounted to 120 million sesterces (or 300 million in another version).

Before the triumph, the soldiers, encouraged by Servius Sulpicius Galba, opposed the triumph because Paullus had given them too little booty; it was saved by the speech of the elderly consular Marcus Servilius. Plutarch tells the tragic story of Paullus' two younger sons, who died during the triumph, one five days before and the other three days after; the other two had been adopted into the families of the Fabii and the Scipios. In his speech to the people, Paullus said that he had prayed that if Fortune envied Rome's success, she would turn her anger on him and his house rather than on the state, and that his prayer had been answered.

The triumph marked a turning point in Roman finances: the booty was so large that the tributum, the direct tax on Roman citizens, was suspended indefinitely. Paullus gave Perseus' library to his sons Scipio Aemilianus and Fabius, the start of the Scipionic interest in Greek culture. Perseus was imprisoned at Alba Fucens, where he died a few years later. The triumph is one of the best documented of the Republic and has served as a model for studies of the ceremony (Beard, The Roman Triumph).
scholarship: Beard, The Roman Triumph (2007)
Östenberg, Staging the World (2009)

settlement_of_macedonia_167.detail:
In 167, at Amphipolis, Lucius Aemilius Paullus and ten senatorial commissioners announced the settlement of Macedonia. The monarchy was abolished. Macedonia was declared free, but divided into four separate republics (merides), with capitals at Amphipolis, Thessalonica, Pella and Pelagonia. Each had its own council (synedrion) and magistrates. The Macedonians would pay Rome half the tribute they had paid the king, 100 talents a year. Marriage (conubium) and the acquisition of land (commercium) between citizens of different republics were prohibited.

The royal gold and silver mines were closed (only copper and iron mines remained open) to prevent them from being exploited by publicani or financing a revolt; the royal forests, which supplied timber for shipbuilding, were also closed and the import of salt restricted. The four republics, except those bordering the barbarians, were forbidden to maintain armies. The leading men of the old monarchy, the king's friends and officers and their sons over 15, were deported to Italy. Paullus then held great games at Amphipolis, which Polybius describes as a model of organisation, and drafted a constitution for the Macedonians, which Livy says lasted a long time.

The settlement shows Roman reluctance to annex territory directly in the East at that time; the four republics, with their restrictions, were designed to prevent the rise of a new monarchy. But the arrangement was unstable: the four republics were economically weakened, the mines were reopened in 158, and in 149 the pretender Andriscus, claiming to be the son of Perseus, easily reunited Macedonia. After his defeat in 148, Macedonia became a Roman province in 146. Silver tetradrachms of the merides, especially the First (Amphipolis) with Artemis on a Macedonian shield, are common in hoards and show the economic activity of the republics after 158. Modern historians (Gruen, Hammond) debate whether Rome intended to weaken Macedonia permanently or to establish free republics on the Greek model.
scholarship: Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
Gruen, Macedonia and the Settlement of 167 BC, in Philip II, Alexander the Great and the Macedonian Heritage (1982)
Hammond and Walbank, A History of Macedonia III (1988)

sack_of_epirus_167.detail:
During the Third Macedonian War, the Molossians of Epirus, under Cephalus and Theodotus, had joined Perseus, while other Epirote peoples remained loyal to Rome. In 167 the Senate ordered Aemilius Paullus to punish the Epirote cities that had defected and to give their plunder to his soldiers. Paullus sent centurions to the 70 towns of the Molossians, announcing that the Roman garrisons would be withdrawn and asking the towns to collect their gold and silver; then, on a pre-arranged day, his soldiers simultaneously plundered all the towns. According to Polybius (30.15), followed by Livy (45.34) and Plutarch, 150,000 people were sold into slavery and the walls of the towns were demolished.

The booty, Livy says, was so great that each infantryman received 200 denarii and each cavalryman 400, yet even this sum was criticised as meagre by the soldiers. Strabo, writing two centuries later, says that Epirus was still depopulated in his time, with the villages of the Molossians deserted. The episode was one of the most brutal acts of Roman warfare of the period, comparable to the massacres in Spain and the destruction of Carthage and Corinth twenty years later.

Modern historians have seen the sack of Epirus as an example of the Senate's use of terror to deter defection, and as evidence of the economic motive of Roman warfare: the massive supply of slaves fed the expanding villa economy of Italy. The figure of 150,000 has been questioned, since it would represent almost the entire population of Molossia, but most accept that the number was very large. The sack contrasts sharply with Paullus' reputation for personal integrity and his philhellenism, illustrating the coexistence of cultural admiration and military brutality in Roman attitudes towards the Greeks. It also shows the Senate's willingness to reward its armies at the expense of provincials, a practice that would contribute to the development of professional armies loyal to their commanders.
sack_of_epirus_167.debate: The figure of 150,000 may be inflated but is taken seriously by most historians; it fed the slave economy of Italy.
scholarship: Harris, War and Imperialism in Republican Rome (1979)
Ziolkowski, 'Urbs direpta, or how the Romans sacked cities', in Rich & Shipley (eds.), War and Society in the Roman World (1993)
Hammond, Epirus (1967)
Ziolkowski, Urbs direpta, or How the Romans Sacked Cities, in War and Society in the Roman World (1993)

achaean_hostages_167.detail:
After Pydna, Roman commissioners went to Greece to investigate the conduct of Greek politicians during the war. In Achaea, the pro-Roman politician Callicrates gave them a list of about 1,000 Achaeans who, he claimed, had favoured Perseus or had not supported Rome enough. They were deported to Italy for trial, although no trial was ever held, and were dispersed among the towns of Etruria. Among them was Polybius, son of Lycortas, who had been hipparchus of the Achaean League in 170/169.

Polybius, thanks to his friendship with Scipio Aemilianus and Fabius Maximus Aemilianus, the sons of Aemilius Paullus, was allowed to stay in Rome, where he became Scipio's mentor and friend, as he describes (31.23-30). This situation gave him access to the Roman political elite and to documents, and inspired him to write his history of the rise of Rome to world power in 53 years. The other hostages remained in Etruria; Achaean embassies repeatedly asked for their release, but the Senate refused, in part because of Callicrates' influence.

In 150, after 17 years, the Senate released the 300 survivors, after Scipio Aemilianus intervened and Cato made his famous remark about Greek old men. The returning exiles, embittered, became leaders of the anti-Roman party in the Achaean League, contributing to the Achaean War of 146. Pausanias (7.10) describes how Callicrates, called a traitor, was hated so much that the Achaeans would not bathe in the same baths as him. The deportation illustrates Rome's methods of control in Greece after 168: reliance on loyal local elites and removal of potential opponents. For historians, its main consequence was the work of Polybius, without which Roman history of the third and second centuries would be much less well known.
scholarship: Walbank, Polybius (1972)
Champion, Cultural Politics in Polybius's Histories (2004)

end_of_tributum_167.detail:
The tributum was a direct tax on the property of Roman citizens, levied according to census class to pay for the army, traditionally since the siege of Veii (c. 406). It was not a regular annual tax but was imposed by the Senate according to need, at a rate of usually one per thousand of assessed property (sometimes more in emergencies), and it could be refunded from booty if a war was profitable, as happened after some campaigns.

In 167, after the triumph of Aemilius Paullus, which brought to the treasury, according to Pliny and Plutarch, 300 million sesterces (Livy 120 million), the tributum was no longer collected. Pliny (33.56), Cicero (Off. 2.76) and Plutarch say that Paullus brought so much money from Macedonia that the people ceased to pay the tax. Revenue from the provinces, from the indemnities paid by Carthage and Antiochus, from the Macedonian tribute and mines, and from the Spanish silver mines, was enough to finance the state.

The tributum was not formally abolished but simply not levied again until the crisis of 43, during the civil wars after the death of Caesar. Its suspension had important consequences: the cost of empire was borne by the provincials and conquered peoples, not by Roman citizens; the relationship between military service and taxation was broken; and Roman citizens in Italy enjoyed a significant privilege, which made citizenship more attractive to the Italian allies, who continued to pay for their own contingents. The end of the tributum is often seen as a symbol of the profitability of Roman imperialism in the second century. Modern historians (Nicolet, Rosenstein) debate whether the end of the tributum reflected a deliberate policy or simply a fiscal surplus, and its effects on the relationship between the Roman state and its citizens.
end_of_tributum_167.debate: The booty totals vary by source; the tributum was technically suspended, not abolished.
scholarship: Nicolet, Tributum (1976)
Rosenstein, Rome and the Mediterranean 290 to 146 BC (2012)
Tan, Power and Public Finance at Rome (2017)

cato_pro_rhodiensibus_167.detail: The speech was included in Cato's Origines, book 5, and is the longest surviving piece of Republican oratory before Gracchus and Cicero. Tiro, Cicero's freedman, criticised it, and Gellius defends it at length. Its argument from Roman self-interest ('we too would not wish to be punished for wanting something') shows Cato as a pragmatic opponent of naked aggression, not the simple hawk of the Carthage debate. Rhodes received a formal alliance only in 164.
scholarship: Astin, Cato the Censor (1978)

maccabean_revolt_167.detail: The causes are debated: the sources present a religious persecution, but modern accounts (Bickerman, Tcherikover, Gruen) stress a civil conflict between Hellenising high priests (Jason, Menelaus) and traditionalists, Antiochus' need for money after Eleusis, and his punishment of a Jerusalem that had rebelled while he was in Egypt. The revolt was the start of the Hasmonean state, which sought Roman friendship in 161 and became Rome's client a century later.
scholarship: Bickerman, The God of the Maccabees (1937; Eng. 1979)
Gruen, Heritage and Hellenism (1998)

terence_andria_166.detail: Terence adapted Menander and Apollodorus with a polished style admired by the Scipionic circle; rumours that Scipio Aemilianus or Laelius wrote his plays circulated in his lifetime and he answered them in his prologues.

rhodes_and_delos_166.detail: Polybius (30.31) records the envoys' complaint. Delos became the great slave market of the Aegean, where 10,000 slaves could change hands in a day (Strabo 14.5.2). Rhodes became a formal ally in 164.

daphne_procession_166.detail: The review is the best evidence for the Seleucid army after Apamea and shows that the treaty limits on elephants were flouted (hence Gnaeus Octavius' mission of 163-162). The legionary-style unit suggests Hellenistic armies experimenting with Roman equipment. Polybius' hostile portrait of Antiochus 'Epimanes' (the mad) comes from the same section.

pergamon_great_altar.debate: Dating ranges from c. 180 to after 166; some link it to Eumenes' Galatian victory of 166, others to the 180s. The Ampelius notice of a great marble altar is the only literary reference.
scholarship: Queyrel, L'Autel de Pergame (2005)

rededication_of_the_temple_164.debate: The authenticity of the letter of the Roman envoys (2 Macc 11.34-38) is debated; if genuine it is the earliest Roman contact with the Maccabees.

census_164.debate: The decline to 328,316 (159), 324,000 (154) and 317,933 (136) has been read as evidence of rural impoverishment (the Gracchan diagnosis) or of evasion of registration to avoid the levy.

demetrius_i_escapes_rome_162.detail: Polybius (31.11-15) tells the story in the first person, one of the most vivid passages of his work.

consuls_of_162_abdicate.detail: Cicero uses the case as the model of scrupulous respect for augural law, set against Gracchus' earlier anger when the haruspices had first questioned the election. It shows how procedural flaws (vitium) could annul elections and how the augural college held real constitutional power, a power used politically in the following century.

murder_of_gnaeus_octavius_162.detail: Demetrius, the Seleucid hostage in Rome, used the crisis to ask again to be released. When refused, he escaped with Polybius' help and seized the throne (162), sending Leptines to Rome for punishment. The Senate refused to accept the murderer, a calculated refusal to absolve the new king. The episode shows Rome's willingness to impose disarmament clauses by bare authority and the risks its envoys ran.

masinissa_seizes_emporia_161.detail: Polybius (31.21) admits that Carthage had the better case but that Roman arbiters favoured Masinissa. Repeated encroachments over the next decade drove Carthage to the war of 150.
masinissa_seizes_emporia_161.debate: The date may be 162 or 161; Livy's epitomes place a later dispute in 157.

treaty_with_judas_maccabaeus_161.detail: The text of the treaty is given in 1 Maccabees 8 and Josephus. It was a cheap way to weaken the Seleucids and had no immediate practical effect (Judas was killed in 160), but it began a relationship that ended with Pompey's capture of Jerusalem in 63.
treaty_with_judas_maccabaeus_161.debate: Authenticity of the treaty text was once doubted but is now generally accepted, though its wording has been adapted. The Hasmonean polity formally dates from c. 140; the polity tag here anticipates it.

expulsion_of_philosophers_161.detail: Suetonius and Gellius quote the decree's wording. Like the expulsion of the Epicureans and the reaction to Carneades, it shows a conservative senatorial anxiety about Greek education that never stopped the elite from employing Greek teachers.

lex_fannia_161.detail: Lucilius mocked the law's 'miserable hundred asses'. Pliny (10.139) notes that the hen clause led Romans to fatten capons instead, a classic example of sumptuary law evasion.

terence_adelphoe_160.detail: The Hecyra prologues are unique evidence for the competitive conditions of the Roman stage: the first performance (165) was ruined by a tightrope walker and boxers, the second (160) by a rumour of gladiators. The Adelphoe, a debate between strict and indulgent fathers, has been read as reflecting the Scipionic household's own discussions of Greek education.

sources.r: Adelphoe and Hecyra didascaliae and prologues

cato_de_agri_cultura.detail: The work is a jumble of instructions rather than a treatise, but it is fundamental evidence for the market-oriented slave villa of central Italy in the generation after the Hannibalic war, the 'villa system' later excavated at sites like Settefinestre. Cato's estates were in Latium and Campania (Casinum, Venafrum); he also invested in pasture, fishponds and maritime loans through a freedman. The contrast with the smallholder ideal Cato celebrated in his speeches has fascinated historians.
scholarship: Astin, Cato the Censor (1978)
Marzano, Roman Villas in Central Italy (2007)

macedonian_mines_reopened_158.detail: Livy reports that the Senate feared that if the mines were let to the publicani the allies would lose their freedom, and if worked by the Macedonians, the profits would fund sedition. The reversal of 158 coincides with a large increase in Roman denarius output in the 150s.

will_of_ptolemy_viii_155.detail: The inscription (SEG IX 7), found in 1929, is the first known royal bequest to Rome and a model for the wills of Attalus III (133), Ptolemy Apion (96) and Nicomedes IV (74). Ptolemy VIII outlived its purpose and it never took effect.

embassy_of_philosophers_155.detail:
In 155 Athens, fined 500 talents by a Sicyonian arbitration for raiding the town of Oropus, sent three heads of philosophical schools to Rome to ask for a reduction of the fine: Carneades of Cyrene, head of the Academy; Diogenes of Babylon, head of the Stoa; and Critolaus of Phaselis, head of the Peripatos. The senator Gaius Acilius acted as their interpreter before the Senate, which reduced the fine to 100 talents.

While waiting, the philosophers gave public lectures that attracted huge crowds of young Romans. Carneades, a master of the sceptical method of arguing both sides of a question, spoke one day in praise of justice and the next day against it, arguing that if the Romans were just they would have to give back their empire and return to their huts. Cato, then 79, alarmed at the effect on Roman youth, urged the Senate to settle the business quickly and send the philosophers home, so that young Romans could listen to the laws and magistrates as before, according to Plutarch (Cato 22).

The embassy is considered a landmark in the introduction of Greek philosophy to Rome. It followed the expulsion of Epicureans in 173 and of philosophers and rhetoricians by senatus consultum in 161, and preceded the integration of Greek philosophy into Roman aristocratic culture with Panaetius and Scipio Aemilianus. Cicero (Republic 3) used Carneades' speech against justice as the basis for the argument of Furius Philus. Modern historians (Gruen, Powell) see the episode as reflecting the ambivalence of Roman attitudes to Greek culture: admiration, curiosity and a sense of threat to traditional values. Cato's opposition was not total rejection of Greek culture, since he himself learned Greek; it was an assertion that Roman values must have priority.
scholarship: Gruen, Culture and National Identity in Republican Rome (1992)
Powell, The Embassy of the Three Philosophers to Rome in 155 BC, in Kremmydas and Tempest (eds.), Hellenistic Oratory (2013)

theatre_demolished_154.detail: Rome had no permanent theatre until Pompey's of 55 BC, which was disguised as an approach to a temple of Venus Victrix.

cato_carthago_delenda.detail:
In 153 (some say 152), Cato served on a senatorial embassy sent to arbitrate a border dispute between Carthage and Masinissa. He was struck by the prosperity of Carthage: its fertile land, large population, abundant arms and supplies. According to Plutarch (Cato 26-27), he returned to Rome convinced that Carthage was a mortal danger, and, showing the Senate a fresh fig from Carthage, he said that the place where such fruit grew was only three days' sail from Rome. From then on he ended every speech in the Senate, whatever the subject, with the words 'ceterum censeo Carthaginem esse delendam' ('moreover, I think Carthage must be destroyed').

The exact formula 'Carthago delenda est' is a modern reworking; the ancient sources give variants, the earliest in Plutarch in Greek. Scipio Nasica Corculum opposed Cato, ending his speeches with the opposite sentiment, that Carthage should be preserved; he argued that fear of Carthage was necessary to maintain Roman discipline and unity (metus Punicus), an argument later developed by Sallust and Diodorus (via Posidonius) as an explanation for Roman moral decline after 146.

Modern historians have debated whether Carthage was really a danger to Rome in the 150s. Archaeology has confirmed Carthage's prosperity in this period: new residential quarters on the Byrsa hill (the 'Hannibal quarter') and the circular military harbour. Some (Harris) see Cato's campaign as a manifestation of Roman aggressiveness; others (Astin) argue that Cato genuinely feared Carthaginian revival, especially after Carthage built up its forces against Masinissa; still others see economic motives (competition in agricultural exports, such as wine and oil), although this is disputed. The Senate's decision for war in 150-149 was influenced by Cato's campaign, Masinissa's encroachments and Carthage's violation of the treaty of 201.
cato_carthago_delenda.debate: The date (153 or 152) and Nasica's motives are debated; the figs story is probably authentic in substance.
scholarship: Astin, Cato the Censor (1978)
Harris, War and Imperialism in Republican Rome (1979)
Miles, Carthage Must Be Destroyed (2010)
Little, The Origin of the Third Punic War, CPh 29 (1934)

foundation_of_corduba.detail: Polybius (35.2-4) describes the Senate's refusal of Marcellus' peace and the 'fiery war' in Spain; Marcellus nevertheless concluded it on his own terms.
foundation_of_corduba.debate: Strabo does not date the foundation: it may belong to Marcellus' praetorship (169/168) or to his third consulship (152).

marcellus_celtiberian_peace_152.detail: Polybius (35.2-3) describes the Senate's reception of the Celtiberian envoys and the Roman aristocrats who wanted war for glory, alongside the young men who evaded the levy. Marcellus was accused of being bribed; the peace held with the Arevaci until 143. It shows the senatorial division between negotiated settlement and wars of annihilation that ran through the Spanish wars.

levy_crisis_151.detail: Polybius (35.4) was in Rome and describes the panic. The iteration ban explains why Aemilianus' election in 134 required a special exemption.
levy_crisis_151.debate: The date of the law against iteration (c. 152-151) is inferred.

massacre_of_cauca.detail: Appian (Iberica 52) says Lucullus was never brought to account. The episode, with Galba's massacre a year later, fuelled the movement for an extortion court.

galba_massacre_of_lusitanians.detail:
In 151-150, the Lusitanians, who had raided Roman territory in Hispania Ulterior since 155, were attacked by the praetor Servius Sulpicius Galba, who had already suffered a defeat in 151, and by Lucius Licinius Lucullus, who had moved into Lusitania from Citerior after his massacre at Cauca. In 150 the Lusitanians sent envoys to Galba offering to renew the treaty made with the praetor Atilius in 152. Galba, according to Appian (Iberica 59-60), pretended to sympathise with their poverty, which forced them to raid, and promised to give them good land if they laid down their arms.

He divided the Lusitanians into three groups, settled them in three places, and told them to wait for him; then he went to each group in turn, ordered them to lay down their arms, surrounded them with a ditch, and had them massacred. Appian says that few escaped; Valerius Maximus and Orosius give figures of 8,000 killed or 30,000 Lusitanians killed and enslaved. Galba distributed little of the booty to his soldiers and kept most for himself. Among the survivors was Viriathus, who became the great leader of the Lusitanian resistance in the following years.

In 149 the tribune Lucius Scribonius Libo proposed a law to create a special court to try Galba, supported by Cato in one of his last speeches. Galba escaped condemnation by appealing to the pity of the people, presenting his young children and his orphaned ward. The failure of the prosecution led to the creation of the permanent court for the recovery of money extorted by governors, under the lex Calpurnia of 149. Galba became consul in 144 and was regarded by Cicero as one of the greatest orators of his time. Modern historians see the massacre as a symptom of the violence of Roman warfare in Spain and of the impunity of Roman commanders, and as the immediate cause of the long Lusitanian War.
scholarship: Richardson, Hispaniae (1986)
Simon, Roms Kriege in Spanien 154-133 v. Chr. (1962)

battle_of_oroscopa.detail: By waging war without Roman permission Carthage breached the treaty of 201, giving Rome its pretext. Appian gives 58,000 Carthaginians, few of whom returned.

release_of_achaean_exiles_150.detail: The returnees included embittered opponents of Rome, among them men who later led the Achaean League into the war of 146. Polybius himself spent the following years with Scipio, at Carthage in 147-146 and in the settlement of Greece in 146-145.

carthaginian_deditio_149.detail:
In 149, after Carthage's war with Masinissa (150), which violated the treaty of 201, Rome declared war. Utica, the second city of Carthaginian Africa, had already surrendered to Rome, giving it a base. Carthaginian envoys came to Rome and surrendered their city by deditio, an act by which they placed themselves entirely in Roman hands. The Senate promised that Carthage would keep its freedom, its laws, its territory and its property, on condition that it sent 300 hostages, children of the leading families, to the consuls in Sicily within 30 days, and obeyed the consuls' further orders.

The consuls Manius Manilius and Lucius Marcius Censorinus crossed with 80,000 infantry and 4,000 cavalry (Appian) to Utica. They demanded that Carthage surrender all its weapons; Carthage handed over 200,000 sets of armour and 2,000 catapults. Then Censorinus announced the final demand: the Carthaginians must abandon their city, which would be destroyed, and settle at least 80 stades (about 15 kilometres) from the sea. Appian (Punica 80-89) gives Censorinus' speech, arguing that the sea had corrupted Carthage and that the Senate had promised to preserve the Carthaginian state (civitas), not the city (urbs).

The Carthaginian envoys were horrified; when the demand was reported, the people of Carthage rioted, killed senators who had advised surrender, and killed the Italians in the city. They decided to fight, freed slaves, and worked day and night to make weapons: Appian says they produced 100 shields, 300 swords, 1,000 catapult bolts and 500 javelins a day, and the women cut their hair to make catapult ropes. Polybius (36.2-9) discusses the morality of the Roman behaviour, presenting the arguments of Greek critics who saw it as deceit, and of those who defended its legality. Modern historians see the series of demands as a deliberate policy to destroy Carthage without the risks of a major war, a cynical exploitation of the legal concept of deditio.
carthaginian_deditio_149.debate: Polybius 36.9 reports four Greek views on the morality of Rome's conduct. Modern debate pits Roman fear and Catonian ideology against greed for land and plunder and the desire to forestall Masinissa.
scholarship: Harris, War and Imperialism in Republican Rome (1979)
Astin, Scipio Aemilianus (1967)
Miles, Carthage Must Be Destroyed (2010)
Le Bohec, Histoire militaire des guerres puniques (1996)
Purcell, On the Sacking of Carthage and Corinth, in Ethics and Rhetoric (1995)

lex_calpurnia_149.detail:
In 149 the tribune Lucius Calpurnius Piso Frugi carried a law establishing a permanent court (quaestio perpetua) to hear cases of extortion (de pecuniis repetundis) by Roman magistrates in the provinces. The court was presided over by a praetor, with a jury drawn from the Senate. It was a civil procedure for the restitution of money extorted, not a criminal punishment; provincials could bring complaints through a Roman patron.

The background was a series of scandals: the complaints of the Spanish envoys in 171, who had to be heard by special panels (recuperatores) of senators, and the failure of the special court proposed against Servius Sulpicius Galba in 149 for his massacre of the Lusitanians. Previous cases had been handled through special commissions or popular trials, which were cumbersome and subject to political pressure. The new court gave a standing procedure for redress. Piso, later consul (133), censor and annalist, was known for his integrity (Frugi means 'honest').

The lex Calpurnia was the first of the permanent jury courts that would become the main forum of Roman political conflict in the late Republic. It was followed by the lex Junia (c. 126) and Gaius Gracchus' lex Acilia (123/122), which transferred the juries to the equestrians and made the procedure more effective, with a penalty of double restitution. Sulla and later Caesar reformed the extortion law. Cicero's prosecution of Verres in 70 is the most famous case. Modern historians (Lintott, Richardson) see the creation of the court as a sign of Senate concern over the conduct of governors and its effect on provincial loyalty, but also as a way of keeping the control of senatorial magistrates within the Senate itself. The court's effectiveness was limited: convictions were rare, since senators judged their peers.
lex_calpurnia_149.debate: J. S. Richardson argued that the law served Roman interests in controlling governors more than provincial redress.
scholarship: Lintott, Judicial Reform and Land Reform in the Roman Republic (1992)
Richardson, 'The Purpose of the Lex Calpurnia de repetundis', JRS 77 (1987)
