Lintott, The Leges de Repetundis and Associate Measures under the Republic, ZRG 98 (1981)
Richardson, The Purpose of the Lex Calpurnia de Repetundis, JRS 77 (1987)

siege_of_carthage_149.detail:
Carthage lay on a peninsula connected to the mainland by an isthmus about 4.5 kilometres wide, defended by a triple line of walls: a ditch, a palisade, and a wall 13.5 metres high and 9 metres wide, with towers and two storeys housing 300 elephants, 4,000 horses and 20,000 infantry (Appian). The city, with a population of perhaps 200,000 to 400,000, had the Byrsa citadel and two harbours: a rectangular commercial harbour and a circular military harbour. After refusing to abandon the city, the Carthaginians armed themselves and called back Hasdrubal (the Boetharch), who commanded an army of 20,000 outside the city at Nepheris.

In 149 the consuls Manilius and Censorinus attacked the walls on the isthmus and on the narrow strip near the lagoon (the Lake of Tunis). Censorinus breached part of the wall with rams but the Carthaginians repaired it overnight and burned his engines. Manilius was beaten at Nepheris, where the military tribune Scipio Aemilianus saved part of the army. In 148 the consul Lucius Calpurnius Piso besieged other towns without success. In 147 the people elected Scipio Aemilianus consul, though below the legal age, and gave him Africa without the usual lot. He restored discipline, took the suburb of Megara, built a siege wall across the isthmus to cut off supplies by land, and blocked the harbour entrance with a mole, while the Carthaginians cut a new channel to the sea.

In winter 147/146 Laelius and Gulussa destroyed the Carthaginian army at Nepheris. In spring 146, the Romans attacked the commercial harbour and fought their way through the streets towards the Byrsa, house by house, for six days. Appian's account (Punica 127-131), based on Polybius, an eyewitness, describes the horrors. The siege of Carthage, with Polybius present, is one of the best documented in antiquity. Excavations by the UNESCO campaign (1970s-1980s) have revealed traces of the destruction, including burnt houses on the Byrsa slopes and the circular harbour's shipsheds.
scholarship: Astin, Scipio Aemilianus (1967)
Lancel, Carthage (1992)
Hurst, Excavations at Carthage: The British Mission II.1, The Circular Harbour, North Side (1994)
Lancel, Carthage (1995)
Le Bohec, Histoire militaire des guerres puniques (1996)

trial_of_galba_149.detail: Cicero, who had read Galba's speeches, admired him as the first Roman orator to use digressions and appeals to the emotions. The failure of the prosecution prompted the lex Calpurnia of the same year, setting up a permanent court for provincial extortion. Galba, enriched by Lusitanian spoil, went on to the consulship of 144. The case is a prime example of the impunity of Roman commanders for atrocities against provincials.

death_of_masinissa_148.detail: Polybius' obituary credits Masinissa with turning Numidia from nomadism to settled agriculture, which the archaeology of the period partly supports, and remarks that he fathered a son at 86 and could still ride all day. The tumulus of Le Medracen and the monument at El Khroub (possibly Masinissa's tomb) illustrate Numidian royal display. The triple division kept Numidia weak and dependent; Micipsa outlived his brothers and left the kingdom to his sons and his nephew Jugurtha.

aemilianus_elected_consul_147.detail: The episode set a precedent for popular intervention in the allocation of commands, exploited later by Marius and others.
scholarship: Astin, Scipio Aemilianus (1967)

carthaginian_harbour_breakout_147.detail: Excavations of the circular military harbour (the cothon) at Carthage have revealed shipsheds for some 170 to 180 vessels around an island admiralty, and a channel matching Appian's account. The episode is a testimony to Carthaginian ingenuity in the last siege.

orestes_embassy_corinth_147.detail: Whether Rome intended to break up the League (Pausanias, Justin) or Orestes exceeded his instructions is debated; Polybius blames the demagogues Critolaus and Diaeus and the 'madness' of the masses. The episode moved the conflict from a quarrel over Sparta to war with Rome, ended by Mummius at Corinth.

destruction_of_carthage.detail:
In spring 146, after taking the harbour area, Scipio Aemilianus' troops advanced through the streets towards the Byrsa, the citadel, along three streets lined with six-storey houses. Appian (Punica 128-131), following Polybius, describes the fighting from roof to roof, the burning of the houses, and the bodies of the dead and living thrown into pits and trampled by the cavalry. After six days, 50,000 men, women and children came down from the Byrsa and surrendered, and were sold as slaves. 900 Roman deserters, who could expect no mercy, held out in the temple of Eshmun with Hasdrubal and his family. Hasdrubal surrendered to Scipio; his wife, cursing him, threw herself and her children into the flames of the burning temple.

Polybius, who was at Scipio's side, describes how Scipio wept as he watched the city burn and quoted Homer's lines on the fall of Troy (Iliad 6.448-449), saying that he feared the same fate would one day befall Rome. The city was plundered for days, and Scipio returned the art taken from Sicilian cities by the Carthaginians. The Senate sent ten commissioners who ordered the city to be razed completely; the site was cursed, and no one was to live there. The story that the Romans sowed the ground with salt is a modern invention (first attested in the 19th century).

The destruction of Carthage, the same year as that of Corinth, marked the end of the independent powers of the Mediterranean. Its territory became the province of Africa, governed from Utica. Modern historians have discussed Rome's motives: fear of Carthaginian revival, Cato's campaign, Masinissa's ambitions, economic rivalry, or the ruthlessness of a hegemonic power. The ancient tradition, particularly Sallust, saw the destruction as a turning point in Roman morality: freed from fear of an external enemy (metus hostilis), the Roman elite fell into greed and internal strife. Gaius Gracchus attempted to found a colony (Junonia) on the site in 122; Caesar and Augustus refounded Carthage as a Roman colony, which became one of the largest cities of the empire.
destruction_of_carthage.debate: The salting of Carthage is a myth; the curse on the site is attested. Sallust and others dated the moral decline of Rome to the removal of the Carthaginian threat (metus Punicus) in this year.
scholarship: Ridley, 'To Be Taken with a Pinch of Salt: The Destruction of Carthage', CPh 81 (1986)
Astin, Scipio Aemilianus (1967)
Ridley, To Be Taken with a Pinch of Salt: The Destruction of Carthage, CPh 81 (1986)
Purcell, On the Sacking of Carthage and Corinth (1995)
Miles, Carthage Must Be Destroyed (2010)

province_of_africa_146.detail:
After the destruction of Carthage, the Senate's commissioners organised the former Carthaginian territory, about 25,000 square kilometres in the north-east of modern Tunisia, as the province of Africa. Its boundary with the Numidian kingdom was marked by a ditch, the fossa regia, which ran from the coast near Thabraca to Thaenae on the Lesser Syrtis; traces of it, with boundary stones restored under Vespasian, have been found. Utica, which had surrendered to Rome before the war, became the seat of the governor, a praetor or propraetor, and received the land between Carthage and Hippo Diarrhytus.

Seven towns that had supported Rome, including Utica, Hadrumetum, Leptis Minor, Thapsus, Acholla, Usalis and Theudalis, were declared free (civitates liberae et immunes). The other communities paid a fixed tribute (stipendium) and their land became Roman public land (ager publicus), partly leased to Roman and Italian settlers or to the indigenous people. The site of Carthage was cursed and abandoned. Masinissa's sons kept the territories that Numidia had taken from Carthage in previous decades.

The province was the first Roman possession in Africa and the beginning of a long process of Roman settlement and agricultural exploitation. The lex agraria of 111, preserved on a bronze tablet, regulated the status of land in Africa. Gaius Gracchus' attempt to found the colony of Junonia on the site of Carthage in 122 failed, but Marius settled veterans in the region, and Caesar and Augustus refounded Carthage as a colony and greatly expanded the province (Africa Proconsularis), which became one of the main sources of grain for Rome. Modern historians (Lintott, Raven) see the province's creation as the result of Rome's refusal to leave the territory to Numidia, which might have become too powerful, and the beginning of a Roman presence that lasted until the Vandal conquest of 439.
scholarship: Raven, Rome in Africa (1993)
Lintott, Judicial Reform and Land Reform in the Roman Republic (1992)
Di Vita-Évrard, La Fossa Regia, in L'Africa romana (1986)

battle_of_scarpheia.detail: Polybius, whose account survives in fragments (38.9-18), blamed the Achaean leaders' demagoguery and the masses' folly, a judgement shaped by his own position as friend of Rome.
battle_of_scarpheia.debate: Polybius' hostility to Critolaus and Diaeus colours the tradition; Pausanias says Critolaus was never found.

battle_of_corinth_146.detail:
After Critolaus' defeat at Scarpheia in Locris by Quintus Caecilius Metellus in 146, the Achaean League's last general, Diaeus, mobilised all available men, freed and armed 12,000 slaves, and imposed heavy levies on the cities. The consul Lucius Mummius, who had replaced Metellus, arrived at the Isthmus with 23,000 infantry and 3,500 cavalry, reinforced by Cretan archers and Pergamene troops under Philopoemen (an Attalid officer), and camped near Corinth.

The Achaeans, encouraged by a minor success against the Roman outposts, attacked the Roman camp at Leucopetra on the Isthmus. According to Pausanias (7.16), the Achaean cavalry fled immediately when attacked by the Roman cavalry, and the Achaean infantry, after a short resistance, was taken in the flank by 1,000 Roman picked troops and routed. Diaeus fled to Megalopolis, killed his wife to prevent her from being captured, and committed suicide by poison. Many Achaeans took refuge in Corinth, but most fled the city at night.

Mummius waited three days before entering Corinth, fearing an ambush, then occupied the deserted city. The battle of Corinth (or Leucopetra) ended the Achaean War and the independence of the Achaean League. Pausanias is the main source, since the relevant books of Polybius and Livy are lost. Modern historians (Gruen, Kallet-Marx) emphasise the hopelessness of the Achaean position against Rome and the role of radical leaders in leading the League to war, although Polybius blamed them for madness. The battle marked the end of the last independent Greek power and is often regarded as the date of the end of Greek freedom. The destruction of Corinth that followed was ordered by the Senate as an example to Greece.
scholarship: Gruen, The Origins of the Achaean War, JHS 96 (1976)
Kallet-Marx, Hegemony to Empire (1995)

sack_of_corinth.detail:
After the defeat of the Achaean army at Leucopetra, Lucius Mummius entered Corinth, which had been largely abandoned, killed the men who remained, sold the women and children into slavery, and, on the orders of the Senate, razed the city and burned it. Corinth, one of the richest and most famous cities of Greece, with its two harbours on the Isthmus (Lechaeum and Cenchreae), had been the site of the Isthmian proclamation of Greek freedom in 196 and the seat of Achaean League meetings, where Roman envoys had been insulted in 147.

Polybius, who arrived after the sack, saw Roman soldiers playing dice on famous paintings thrown on the ground, including Aristides' Dionysus. Mummius, a new man with no interest in Greek art, shipped huge quantities of statues and paintings to Rome and Italy, warning the contractors, according to Velleius, that if they lost any, they would have to replace them with new ones. Statues from Corinth were dedicated in Rome and in many Italian towns; inscriptions recording Mummius' gifts have been found at Italica in Spain, at Parma and elsewhere. Attalus II bought Aristides' painting for 600,000 sesterces, which made Mummius suspect it had value and withdraw it.

The destruction of Corinth, in the same year as Carthage, horrified the Greek world and became the symbol of Roman brutality. Its territory became Roman public land, part given to Sicyon. Excavations show that the site was not entirely deserted: some buildings, like the temple of Apollo, survived, and squatters occupied it until Caesar founded the Roman colony Laus Iulia Corinthiensis in 44, which became the capital of the province of Achaea. Modern historians (Purcell) have compared the two sacks of 146, seeing in them a deliberate demonstration of Roman power, while others note that the destruction of Corinth was less complete than the literary sources suggest.
sack_of_corinth.debate: Archaeology shows some continued occupation at Corinth after 146, so the destruction was not total. Pliny's story that 'Corinthian bronze' was an alloy formed when the city burned is fanciful.
scholarship: Purcell, On the Sacking of Carthage and Corinth (1995)
Williams and Bookidis (eds.), Corinth: The Centenary 1896-1996 (2003)

province_of_macedonia_146.detail:
After the defeat of Andriscus by Quintus Caecilius Metellus in 148, Rome abandoned the system of four republics established in 167 and made Macedonia a permanent province, governed by a praetor or proconsul, with responsibility for the defence of the northern frontier against the Thracians, Dardanians and Scordisci. The governor also supervised Greek affairs, since Achaea was not organised as a separate province until 27. The precise date of the province's creation is debated; some put it in 148, others in 146 after the Achaean War, when the ten commissioners settled Greece.

The four merides continued to exist as administrative units with their own councils and coinage until the 1st century. A new era, the Macedonian provincial era, began in 148, used for dating inscriptions in the region. The Via Egnatia, built by the proconsul Gnaeus Egnatius in the following years (probably between 146 and 120), linked Dyrrachium and Apollonia on the Adriatic coast to Thessalonica, the capital of the province, and later to Byzantium. Milestones with the name of Egnatius and the distance in Roman miles, found near Thessalonica, are among the earliest Roman milestones.

The province was the first permanent Roman possession in the Greek East, and the beginning of Roman territorial rule there. It was a frontier province, with constant wars against the Thracians and Scordisci; several governors were defeated or killed (for example, Gaius Porcius Cato in 114). Polybius had seen the Roman settlement of Greece as the end of his history. Modern historians (Kallet-Marx) emphasise that the province's creation marked a shift from indirect hegemony to direct rule, although Rome's control of Greece remained loose until the Mithridatic Wars. The Via Egnatia became one of the main roads of the empire, connecting Italy and the East, and was used by armies, merchants and later Christian missionaries, including Paul.
province_of_macedonia_146.debate: Whether the province dates from 148 or 146, and the exact date of the road, are debated.
scholarship: Kallet-Marx, Hegemony to Empire (1995)
Romiopoulou, Un nouveau milliaire de la via Egnatia, BCH 98 (1974)
Papazoglou, Les villes de Macédoine à l'époque romaine (1988)

sources.w: Bilingual milestone of Cn. Egnatius near Thessalonica

temple_of_jupiter_stator_146.debate: Construction may have begun after Metellus' triumph of 146 and finished somewhat later.

triumph_of_mummius_145.detail: The surviving dedication (CIL I² 626) reads that Achaea was captured and Corinth destroyed under his leadership and auspices. Inscribed bases of Mummian dedications have been found at Italica, Parma, Nursia and elsewhere.

sources.w: Dedication of L. Mummius to Hercules Victor

lex_licinia_de_sacerdotiis_145.detail: The principle Crassus sought was achieved in 104 by the lex Domitia, which provided that 17 of the 35 tribes chosen by lot should elect priests from the colleges' nominees. Cicero's remark about Crassus turning to face the Forum symbolises a shift of oratory from the Senate to the people, a step towards popularis politics.

aqua_marcia.detail: Frontinus (De aquis 1.7) gives the figures. The Marcia was the longest and most admired of Rome's aqueducts, and its water was considered the best; Pliny calls it the most famous water in the world.

panaetius_in_rome_144.debate: The 'Scipionic Circle' as a coherent salon is largely Cicero's construction (Zetzel, Astin); the friendships themselves are well attested.

censorship_of_aemilianus_142.debate: The prayer story may be a later invention reflecting the 'limits of empire' theme.

temple_of_hercules_victor_142.debate: The inscription was found on the Caelian; the round marble temple of Hercules Victor/Olivarius in the Forum Boarium is later (c. 120-100) and is not Mummius' temple.

mithridates_i_takes_seleucia_141.detail: The loss of Mesopotamia cut the Seleucids off from their richest revenues and created the Roman-Parthian frontier zone of the next centuries. The Babylonian astronomical diaries record the transition month by month. Roman awareness of Parthia, as yet, was minimal: the first Roman-Parthian contact came only with Sulla in 96.

denarius_retariffed_141.detail: Pliny attributes the change to the dictatorship of Fabius Maximus in 217, but the coins (Crawford RRC 224 onwards) show the XVI marks around 141, which is the consensus date. The change devalued bronze relative to silver, reflecting the shift to a silver-based economy fuelled by Spanish and Macedonian mines. Polybius (6.39) gives legionary pay as two obols a day, about a third of a denarius.
scholarship: Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974)

battle_of_erisane.detail: Within months the next governor, Quintus Servilius Caepio, persuaded the Senate to let him renew the war.

laelius_agrarian_proposal_140.debate: The date is uncertain, during his praetorship (145) or consulship (140); the anecdote shows that the agrarian problem Tiberius Gracchus tackled in 133 was recognised a decade earlier.

lex_gabinia_tabellaria_139.detail:
In 139 the tribune Aulus Gabinius, grandson of a slave according to Cicero's hostile remark, carried a law introducing the secret written ballot (tabella) in the election of magistrates, replacing oral voting, in which each voter declared his choice to an official (rogator) who recorded it. Cicero (Laws 3.35) calls the lex Gabinia the first of the four ballot laws (leges tabellariae), followed by the lex Cassia (137) for popular trials except treason, the lex Papiria (131) for legislative assemblies, and the lex Coelia (107) for treason trials.

Under the new system, each voter received a small wooden tablet coated with wax, on which he wrote the initials of the candidates he chose, and dropped it into an urn (cista) as he crossed the narrow bridges (pontes) to the voting enclosures. Coins of the period, notably a denarius of Publius Licinius Nerva (c. 113), depict voters crossing the pons and receiving or depositing the tabella. The law was opposed by the aristocracy, who saw it as an attack on their influence over voters, especially their clients, who could no longer be observed and controlled.

Cicero, in On the Laws, has his brother Quintus attack the ballot laws for destroying the authority of the optimates, while Cicero defends a compromise in which the ballot is shown to the optimates. Modern historians debate the effect of the laws: some (Taylor, Yakobson) see them as increasing the independence of voters and the importance of popular politics; others (Gruen, Mouritsen) doubt their impact on elections, arguing that patronage and bribery continued. The lex Gabinia is also interpreted as a measure against bribery, since bribers could no longer verify that votes were delivered. It coincided with a period of political tension, with the Numantine War, the levy crises and the expulsion of Chaldaeans, preceding the Gracchan reforms.
scholarship: Yakobson, 'Secret Ballot and its Effects in the Late Roman Republic', Hermes 123 (1995)
Yakobson, Secret Ballot and Its Effects in the Late Roman Republic, Hermes 123 (1995)
Taylor, Roman Voting Assemblies (1966)
Mouritsen, Plebs and Politics in the Late Roman Republic (2001)

expulsion_of_chaldaeans_and_jews_139.detail: The passage survives only in two epitomes of Valerius Maximus (1.3.3); the reference to Sabazius may be a confusion with the Jewish divine title Sabaoth. It is the earliest notice of Jews in Rome.
expulsion_of_chaldaeans_and_jews_139.debate: Whether the expelled were Jews, worshippers of the Phrygian Sabazius or both is debated.

assassination_of_viriathus.detail:
Viriathus, a Lusitanian shepherd and survivor of Galba's massacre of 150, had led the Lusitanian resistance since 147, defeating a series of Roman commanders (Vetilius, Plautius, Unimanus, Nigidius) with guerrilla tactics and feigned retreats. In 140, after trapping the army of Quintus Fabius Maximus Servilianus at Erisane, he granted a peace treaty under which he was recognised as a friend of the Roman people and the Lusitanians kept their land; the treaty was ratified by the Roman people.

In 140/139 Servilianus' brother Quintus Servilius Caepio, consul for 140, obtained permission from the Senate to break the treaty secretly and then openly, and attacked Viriathus. Viriathus sent three of his friends, Audax, Ditalcus and Minurus, from the town of Urso, to negotiate with Caepio. Caepio bribed them with promises of great rewards to kill Viriathus. They returned to his camp and stabbed him in the throat while he slept in his armour. When they went to Caepio for their reward, he sent them to Rome, where the Senate refused to pay, saying 'Rome does not pay traitors' (a phrase attributed by later tradition).

Viriathus' followers gave him a magnificent funeral, burning his body on a great pyre with funeral games and gladiatorial combats around it. His successor Tautalus surrendered to Caepio soon after, and the Lusitanians were settled at Valentia (138) by Decimus Junius Brutus. Viriathus became a hero of the resistance against Rome; Diodorus (from Posidonius) praised his justice and frugality. In Portuguese national tradition he became a founding hero. Modern historians debate the nature of his leadership, some seeing him as a bandit chief, others as the leader of a social or national movement. The assassination, a clear violation of fides, was criticised by ancient writers (Velleius, Appian), and illustrates the brutality of the Roman wars in Spain. Caepio was refused a triumph.
assassination_of_viriathus.debate: The phrase usually quoted ('Rome does not pay traitors') is not ancient in that form; the refusal of reward is reported by Eutropius and Orosius.
scholarship: Pastor Muñoz, Viriato: la lucha por la libertad (2000)
Richardson, Hispaniae (1986)

hasmonean_embassy_139.debate: The date (142 or 139) and the identity of 'Lucius the consul' (probably Lucius Caecilius Metellus Calvus, cos. 142, or Lucius Calpurnius Piso, cos. 139) are debated, as is the relation to the decree that Josephus misplaces under Hyrcanus II.

surrender_of_mancinus.detail:
Gaius Hostilius Mancinus, consul in 137, took command of the war against Numantia, the Celtiberian town on the upper Douro that had defeated several Roman generals since 143. After several reverses, on hearing a false rumour that the Cantabri and Vaccaei were coming to help the Numantines, he abandoned his camp at night and withdrew to the site of Nobilior's old camp of 153. The Numantines, only 4,000 strong according to Appian, surrounded the Roman army of 20,000 and threatened to destroy it.

Mancinus negotiated a treaty with the Numantines through his quaestor Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, whose father had made the moderate treaties of 179 and who was respected by the Celtiberians. The treaty, sworn by Mancinus and his officers, recognised Numantine independence and Roman friendship, in exchange for the release of the Roman army. The Numantines also returned Gracchus' account books, which they had taken from the camp. According to Plutarch, Gracchus saved 20,000 Roman citizens, besides slaves and camp followers.

In Rome, the Senate rejected the treaty as shameful, following the precedent of the Caudine Forks (321). To free Rome from its oath, it decreed in 136 that Mancinus be handed over to the Numantines, naked and bound; the Numantines refused to accept him, and he returned to Rome, where he set up a statue of himself in chains. Gracchus, whose treaty was repudiated, became embittered towards the Senate, according to Plutarch, a factor in his later tribunate. The episode raised profound questions about Roman fides and the rights of commanders to make treaties, and was debated by lawyers like Publius Mucius Scaevola (Cicero, On Duties 3.109). Modern historians see it as a symptom of the crisis of the Roman army in Spain and of the political tensions that preceded the Gracchan era. Scipio Aemilianus took command in 134 to finish the war.
scholarship: Rosenstein, Imperatores Victi (1990)
Rich, The Fetiales and Roman International Relations, in Priests and State (2011)

mancinus_handed_over_136.detail: The case was debated by jurists for centuries: whether a man surrendered and refused had lost his citizenship (postliminium).

first_servile_war_outbreak.detail:
In 135 (or 136, or as early as 138), slaves on the estates of Sicily revolted. Diodorus (34/35.2), following Posidonius, explains the causes: after the Second Punic War, wealthy Sicilians and Romans bought large numbers of slaves, many of them recently enslaved from the eastern wars, to work on large estates and as herdsmen; they treated them harshly, branding them, underfeeding and overworking them; herdsmen were allowed to rob travellers to feed themselves. The revolt began at Enna, where the slaves of the cruel master Damophilus, led by Eunus, a Syrian slave from Apamea who claimed to have visions and could breathe fire (by hiding a nutshell of fire in his mouth), seized the city and killed Damophilus and his wife Megallis, sparing their daughter, who had been kind to them.

Eunus took the name Antiochus and the royal title, set up a court and a council, and minted coins with the image of Demeter and the legend 'King Antiochus'. Another revolt broke out in the south-west under Cleon, a Cilician herdsman, who joined Eunus. The rebels, said to number 70,000 to 200,000, defeated several Roman praetors and controlled much of the island, including Tauromenium and Enna. The Roman state was slow to respond, preoccupied with Numantia. Similar revolts broke out at Minturnae, Sinuessa, Delos and Attica, inspired by the Sicilian example.

The war was ended in 132 by the consul Publius Rupilius, who besieged and captured Tauromenium and Enna; Eunus was captured and died in prison at Morgantina, and Rupilius issued a law (lex Rupilia) for the administration of Sicily. The First Servile War was the largest slave revolt in antiquity before Spartacus. Modern historians (Bradley, Shaw) see it as a consequence of the development of the slave economy in the second century, and debate whether the revolt aimed to overthrow slavery or to establish a Hellenistic-style kingdom. It formed part of the background of social crisis that Tiberius Gracchus addressed in 133.
first_servile_war_outbreak.debate: The start date (136 or 135, or even 140s) is uncertain; Diodorus' figures are inflated; how far the revolt aimed at a Hellenistic-style kingdom rather than abolition of slavery is debated.
scholarship: Bradley, Slavery and Rebellion in the Roman World, 140 B.C.-70 B.C. (1989)
Shaw, Spartacus and the Slave Wars (2001)
Bradley, Slavery and Rebellion in the Roman World (1989)
Urbainczyk, Slave Revolts in Antiquity (2008)

siege_of_numantia.detail:
After a decade of Roman defeats at Numantia, the people elected Scipio Aemilianus consul for 134, setting aside the law banning second consulships, and gave him command in Spain. The Senate gave him no new legions, so he brought 4,000 volunteers, including friends and clients, and a cohort of 500 friends (cohors amicorum) including the historian Polybius, the young Gaius Marius, the future king Jugurtha, and the poet Lucilius. He found the army demoralised and spent months restoring discipline, expelling 2,000 prostitutes, traders and diviners, selling the soldiers' wagons, and training the men with marches and the construction of camps.

In summer 134 Scipio ravaged the lands of the Vaccaei to cut off Numantia's supplies, then surrounded the city, which sat on a hill at the confluence of the Douro and Merdancho, with a circuit of fortifications about nine kilometres long, with seven camps, towers, a wall 3 metres wide and 2.4 metres high, and a boom across the Douro. He had 60,000 men against perhaps 8,000 Numantines. The Numantines attempted sorties and sent the hero Retogenes Caraunius to seek help from other Celtiberian towns; the young men of Lutia agreed, but Scipio marched there and cut off the hands of 400 of them.

After eight months of famine, in which the inhabitants were reduced to cannibalism, Numantia surrendered in summer 133. Many inhabitants killed themselves; the survivors were sold, except 50 kept for Scipio's triumph, and the town was razed. Scipio took the cognomen Numantinus. Schulten's excavations (1905-1912) identified Scipio's camps and siege works, such as Castillejo and Peña Redonda, among the best preserved Roman siege works of the Republic; Schulten's interpretations have since been revised, and recent research has re-examined the circumvallation. The fall of Numantia ended the Celtiberian wars and is a symbol of resistance in Spanish national history. Appian's account (Iberica 84-98) comes from Polybius' lost monograph on the Numantine War.
siege_of_numantia.debate: Dobson's re-examination of Schulten's camps questions some of Schulten's camp plans and dates. Figures for the defenders vary widely.
scholarship: Schulten, Numantia: Die Ergebnisse der Ausgrabungen 1905-1912 (1914-1931)
Astin, Scipio Aemilianus (1967)
Dobson, The Army of the Roman Republic: The Second Century BC, Polybius and the Camps at Numantia (2008)
Schulten, Numantia I-IV (1914-1931)
Dobson, The Army of the Roman Republic: Polybius and the Camps at Numantia (2008)

pergamon_bequest.detail: A Pergamene decree (OGIS 338) issued soon after the king's death confirms the will and extends citizenship to various groups to secure the city against the rising of Aristonicus, an illegitimate son of Eumenes II who claimed the throne as Eumenes III and rallied the poor and slaves as 'Heliopolitans', with the Stoic Blossius of Cumae as adviser. The war lasted until 129, when Manius Aquillius organised the province of Asia, which became the richest source of Roman revenue.
pergamon_bequest.debate: Why Attalus made the bequest (fear of social revolution, ensuring the cities' freedom, or Roman pressure) is unknown. Some modern scholars doubt Attalus' reputation for eccentricity (gardening in poisonous plants, studying sculpture), which comes from hostile sources.
scholarship: Kallet-Marx, Hegemony to Empire: The Development of the Roman Imperium in the East from 148 to 62 B.C. (1995)
Sherwin-White, Roman Foreign Policy in the East (1984)

sources.w: Pergamene decree on the will of Attalus III

tribunate_of_tiberius_gracchus.detail:
Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus entered the tribunate on 10 December 134 with formidable connections: grandson of Scipio Africanus through his mother Cornelia, brother-in-law of Scipio Aemilianus, son-in-law of Appius Claudius Pulcher, the princeps senatus. His advisers included the consul of 133, the jurist Publius Mucius Scaevola, and Crassus Mucianus. His brother Gaius later claimed that Tiberius had conceived his programme while travelling through Etruria in 137 and seeing estates worked by imported slaves while free peasants had vanished.

The year moved through escalating confrontations. The agrarian bill was vetoed by the tribune Marcus Octavius; Tiberius responded by suspending public business and sealing the temple of Saturn, then took the unprecedented step of having the assembly depose Octavius. When the Senate refused funds for the land commission, he proposed that the treasure of Attalus III, just bequeathed to Rome, be used to equip new settlers, and that the people rather than the Senate decide the fate of the cities of Pergamon. This invaded the Senate's control of finance and foreign affairs. Finally he stood for re-election to a second consecutive tribunate, which his enemies represented as a bid for tyranny; it was not clearly illegal, but it was without recent precedent.

Our narrative sources are Plutarch's Life and Appian's Civil Wars Book 1, both drawing ultimately on accounts written in the heat of later controversy. Plutarch is sympathetic and personal; Appian frames the year as the beginning of the cycle of civil strife that ended with Augustus, and centres the Italian allies, who he says had most to lose. Cicero, who admired the Gracchi's eloquence but condemned their methods, alternates between praise and blame according to his audience.

Modern scholarship has moved away from seeing Tiberius as either a social revolutionary or a cynical demagogue. The problem he addressed was real, though its nature is debated: Brunt argued for a manpower crisis caused by long overseas service; Rathbone, de Ligt and Rosenstein question whether the free peasantry was declining at all, suggesting instead a problem of under-registration or of a growing population pressing on land. What is not in doubt is the political consequence. By using the assembly against a colleague's veto and against the Senate's prerogatives, Tiberius demonstrated a popularis method that was copied for a century, and his murder introduced lethal violence into Roman politics.
tribunate_of_tiberius_gracchus.debate: Was Tiberius a reformer responding to real rural depopulation (Brunt) or did he exaggerate a manpower crisis (Rich, Historia 1983)? Archaeological survey of the ager Romanus and Etruria does not show the wholesale disappearance of small farms that Appian and Plutarch imply. Whether the crisis Tiberius addressed was demographic decline, under-registration or rural overpopulation remains contested.
scholarship: Stockton, The Gracchi (1979)
Bernstein, Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus: Tradition and Apostasy (1978)
Brunt, Italian Manpower (1971)
Rosenstein, Rome at War (2004)

lex_sempronia_agraria.detail:
The lex Sempronia agraria revived the old limit, traditionally ascribed to the Licinian-Sextian laws of 367, on how much ager publicus any individual could occupy: 500 iugera (about 125 hectares) per head, with an additional 250 for each of up to two sons, so up to 1,000 iugera per family. Land held above the limit was to be surrendered; in compensation, holders received secure, rent-free title to what they kept. The recovered land was to be distributed in small allotments, probably of 30 iugera, which were inalienable and subject to a nominal rent, so that recipients could not simply sell to the rich. A board of three men with judicial power to determine what was public and what private, the tresviri agris iudicandis adsignandis, was elected annually: initially Tiberius, his brother Gaius and his father-in-law Appius Claudius.

The difficulty lay in the land itself. Much ager publicus had been occupied for generations, built on, inherited, mortgaged and sold, and boundaries were rarely recorded. Among the occupiers were wealthy Latins and Italians, who had no vote at Rome and whose access to public land had been tolerated. Appian, who makes the allies central to his narrative, says the rich protested that they would lose ancestral tombs and dowries invested in the land.

The commission survived Tiberius' death and worked actively for several years. Boundary stones (cippi) bearing the names of the commissioners Gaius Gracchus, Appius Claudius and Publius Licinius Crassus, and later of Carbo and Fulvius Flaccus, have been found in Lucania, Campania, Samnium and Apulia. The census figures, 318,823 in 131/130 and 394,736 in 125/124, are often linked to settlement, since allotment raised men into the propertied classes eligible for registration and service, but the inference is fragile. In 129 Scipio Aemilianus had the commission's judicial powers transferred to the consuls, which slowed its work.

A series of later laws, summarised by Appian and partly preserved in the epigraphic lex agraria of 111, dismantled the scheme: first allowing sale of allotments, then halting distribution and converting remaining public land into private property subject to rent, and finally abolishing the rent. By 111 most of Italy's ager publicus had become private land. Whether the Gracchan settlements lasted or simply accelerated the concentration of property is still argued.
lex_sempronia_agraria.debate: Whether allies were entitled to allotments and how large the lots were is disputed; the law's text does not survive, and the later lex agraria of 111 (CIL I2 585) is the main documentary witness to its effects. The size of the allotments (30 iugera) is inferred from later evidence; whether allies were eligible for allotments is disputed.
scholarship: Roselaar, Public Land in the Roman Republic (2010)
Stockton, The Gracchi (1979)
Lintott, Judicial Reform and Land Reform in the Roman Republic (1992)

deposition_of_marcus_octavius.detail:
Marcus Octavius was a fellow tribune and, according to Plutarch, a friend of Tiberius Gracchus; he was also a substantial occupier of public land, which Tiberius offered to compensate from his own purse. Octavius' veto blocked the agrarian bill at the concilium plebis. Tiberius first tried to persuade him, then retaliated with an edict suspending the activities of all magistrates and sealing the treasury in the temple of Saturn. When armed supporters of the wealthy appeared and the voting urns were seized, the dispute was referred to the Senate, which offered no solution.

At the next meeting of the assembly Tiberius proposed that a tribune who acted against the interests of the people had ceased to be a tribune, and put a motion to remove Octavius. The thirty-five tribes voted one by one; when seventeen had voted for deposition and one more would make a majority, Tiberius paused and pleaded with Octavius to give way. Octavius refused, the eighteenth tribe voted, and he was dragged from the rostra; his slave who tried to protect him lost his eyes. A client of Tiberius, Quintus Mummius, was elected in his place.

The act had no precedent in the history of the tribunate. Tiberius' defence, recorded by Plutarch, was that the tribune's sacrosanctity derived from the people and could be withdrawn by them, just as the kings had been expelled and Vestal Virgins could be punished. His opponents saw an attack on the veto, the principle of collegiality, and the sacrosanctity of the office, which removed the main constitutional brake on the assembly. Even sympathetic contemporaries were alarmed, and the episode was cited against Tiberius by Scipio Aemilianus and later by Cicero.

Modern historians see the deposition as the decisive escalation of 133. It turned a dispute about land into a dispute about popular sovereignty, the claim that the will of the assembly overrode other constitutional checks. That claim would be revived by Saturninus, Sulpicius, Clodius and Caesar's partisans, while the optimate answer, the senatus consultum ultimum and the right of the Senate to declare emergencies, developed in reaction to it.
deposition_of_marcus_octavius.debate: Whether Octavius' veto was itself an abuse of the tribunate, as Tiberius claimed, is a question already debated in antiquity.
scholarship: Morstein-Marx, Mass Oratory and Political Power in the Late Roman Republic (2004)
Badian, 'Tiberius Gracchus and the beginning of the Roman revolution', ANRW I.1 (1972)

murder_of_tiberius_gracchus.detail:
The consular elections of summer 133 coincided with Tiberius' campaign for re-election. Many of his rural supporters were busy with the harvest, and the urban crowd was less reliable. On the day of the tribunician election the assembly met on the Capitol before the temple of Jupiter. Rumours circulated that Tiberius intended to make himself king; when he touched his head to signal that his life was in danger, opponents claimed that he was asking for a diadem.

In the Senate, meeting nearby in the temple of Fides, Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica Serapio, the pontifex maximus and Tiberius' cousin, demanded that the consul Scaevola act against the tyrant. Scaevola refused to kill a citizen without trial. Nasica then declared that whoever wished the state to be safe should follow him, drew the hem of his toga over his head in the manner of a priest at sacrifice, and led senators and their attendants to the Capitol. Armed with clubs and the broken legs of benches, they routed Tiberius' supporters. Tiberius stumbled and was clubbed to death, by tradition by the tribune Publius Satureius and Lucius Rufus. Some three hundred others died, and the bodies were thrown into the Tiber; his brother's request to bury him was refused.

The ritual gesture of Nasica has attracted much attention. Linderski argued that the scene was staged as a consecratio, the killing of an enemy of the gods as a sacrificial victim, giving religious sanction to an act without legal basis. The sources disagree on details: Appian stresses the chaos and the Senate's role, Plutarch Nasica's personal leadership. Valerius Maximus and Velleius treat Nasica as a saviour; Cicero alternately praises him as the man who rescued the Republic and admits Tiberius was killed without trial.

The consequences were immediate and long-term. Nasica was sent to Asia on an embassy to escape prosecution and died at Pergamon. A special court under the consuls of 132 punished Tiberius' followers. Above all, as Appian observes, this was the first time since the expulsion of the kings that civil strife had ended in bloodshed at Rome, and it would not be the last.
murder_of_tiberius_gracchus.debate: Nasica's acting as pontifex maximus and the religious framing of the killing are interpreted differently; whether he had any legal standing to act is denied by most modern scholars.
scholarship: Lintott, Violence in Republican Rome (1968)
Linderski, 'The pontiff and the tribune: the death of Tiberius Gracchus', Athenaeum 90 (2002)

revolt_of_aristonicus.detail: He minted cistophori in his regnal name, and Blossius of Cumae, Tiberius Gracchus' Stoic adviser, joined him. The utopian label rests on Strabo and Diodorus; modern scholars see him primarily as a dynastic pretender exploiting social discontent. He held out until 129.
revolt_of_aristonicus.debate: The Heliopolitai as a social-revolutionary programme versus a dynastic war is debated.

siege_of_enna_132.detail: Lead sling bullets inscribed with the name of Lucius Calpurnius Piso, consul of 133, have been found at Enna, documenting the earlier Roman siege attempts.
scholarship: Bradley, Slavery and Rebellion in the Roman World (1989)

quaestio_against_the_gracchans_132.detail: The inquiry had no popular mandate, which is why Gaius Gracchus later passed his lex de capite civis and drove Popillius into exile (123). Scipio Nasica, the leader of the lynching, was sent on a face-saving embassy to Asia, where he died at Pergamon in 132. The land commission itself was left untouched: the Senate punished the man, not the law.
quaestio_against_the_gracchans_132.debate: Numbers executed are unknown; Plutarch's anecdotes about Villius and Diophanes may be embroidered.

lex_papiria_tabellaria.detail: Cicero (De legibus 3.35) regarded the ballot laws as undermining aristocratic influence. Carbo also proposed allowing tribunes to stand for immediate re-election, which failed, opposed by Scipio Aemilianus.

province_of_asia_organized.detail:
Attalus III of Pergamon died in spring 133 leaving his kingdom to the Roman people, while declaring the city of Pergamon itself free. The bequest was challenged at once by Aristonicus, an illegitimate son of Eumenes II, who claimed the throne as Eumenes III, won support among the rural population and slaves he promised to free as citizens of a 'City of the Sun', and defeated and killed the consul Publius Licinius Crassus Mucianus in 130. The consul Marcus Perperna captured him at Stratonicea in 129, and he was strangled in prison at Rome.

Manius Aquillius, consul in 129, then spent three years with a commission of ten senators organising the new province. The territory comprised the Attalid heartland: Mysia, Lydia, Ionia, Caria and the Thracian Chersonese. Some territories were detached: Greater Phrygia was granted, or by repute sold, to Mithridates V of Pontus, and Lycaonia went to the sons of Ariarathes V of Cappadocia, killed fighting for Rome. Aquillius built a road network from Pergamon to Side, recorded on milestones that are the earliest Roman milestones in Asia, and was later tried and acquitted for extortion.

The most consequential change came from Gaius Gracchus' law of 123, which established that the tithe and other taxes of Asia would be farmed out by the censors in Rome to companies of publicani for five-year periods. This created a vast source of profit for the equestrian order, and the companies became a powerful lobby. The provincials suffered from their abuses; the exploitation goes far to explain the welcome Mithridates received in 88 and the massacre of Italians known as the Asiatic Vespers.

The province was Rome's richest. Cicero in 66 called it the most fertile land, with tribute exceeding that of all other provinces. A senatus consultum preserved on stone from Adramyttium (the 'SC de agro Pergameno') shows Roman magistrates adjudicating disputes between Pergamon and the publicani over tax-exempt land. Scholars debate whether the annexation was the product of Roman greed or reluctant acceptance of a bequest whose refusal would have created chaos; the five-year delay before organisation suggests the latter.
scholarship: Kallet-Marx, Hegemony to Empire (1995)
Sherwin-White, Roman Foreign Policy in the East (1984)

death_of_scipio_aemilianus.detail: Rumour accused his wife Sempronia (the Gracchi's sister), Cornelia, Carbo and Fulvius Flaccus. Natural death is quite possible. The episode marks the moment the agrarian question became an Italian question: allies who possessed ager publicus had no vote and could only appeal to Roman patrons.
death_of_scipio_aemilianus.debate: Murder or natural death; ancient authors themselves were divided.

scipio_and_the_land_commission_129.detail: This is the first time the allied question appears as politics in its own right: the Gracchan law reclaimed public land that Latins and Italians had occupied, often for generations. The transfer effectively paralysed the commission's judicial work, though boundary stones (cippi) of the commissioners Carbo, Fulvius Flaccus and Gaius Gracchus show that assignations continued into the 120s.
scipio_and_the_land_commission_129.debate: How much land the commission actually redistributed is disputed; the census jump of 131-125 (318,823 to 394,736) is read by some as evidence of large-scale settlement, by others as better registration.

census_of_125.debate: Real population growth, better registration, or both? Brunt saw registration effects; the figures are also subject to textual corruption.
scholarship: Brunt, Italian Manpower (1971)

siege_of_fregellae.detail: Fregellae had been loyal through Hannibal's war. Excavation shows a prosperous town with Hellenistic houses and a sanctuary of Aesculapius abruptly destroyed. The revolt's isolation shows the allies were not yet ready for concerted action; its brutal suppression anticipated Opimius' role in 121.

fulvius_flaccus_salluvian_campaign_125.detail: Flaccus had just failed to carry his citizenship proposal, and his removal to Gaul was convenient to the Senate. The Salluvian oppidum of Entremont, with its sculptures of seated warriors and skull niches, shows a destruction layer that excavators link to Sextius' campaign; the Roman garrison at the springs nearby became Aquae Sextiae (122).

tribunate_of_gaius_gracchus.detail:
Gaius Gracchus, nine years younger than Tiberius, held the tribunate for 123 and was re-elected for 122, a second term now permitted. He was the greatest orator of his generation, pacing the rostra and turning to face the Forum rather than the Senate house, with a slave behind him sounding a pitch pipe to moderate his voice. His programme, carried in a torrent of laws, was far broader than his brother's: he sought to build a coalition of the urban plebs, the rural poor, the equestrian order and eventually the allies.

The legislation, whose chronology is uncertain, included: the lex de capite civis, outlawing capital sentences without the people's authority, which drove Popillius Laenas into exile; the grain law establishing a monthly ration at a fixed low price; the reinstatement of the agrarian commission; the founding of colonies, including Junonia at Carthage, Scolacium and Tarentum (Neptunia); a road-building programme with milestones; the military law; the law on consular provinces; the Asian tax law; and the judiciary law transferring the extortion court to equestrian juries. In 122 his citizenship bill, offering Roman citizenship to Latins and Latin rights to other Italians, was defeated after the consul Gaius Fannius warned the plebs that they would lose their seats at games and festivals.

The Senate's counterattack was subtle. The tribune Marcus Livius Drusus proposed twelve colonies of 3,000 poor citizens each, free of rent, and protection of Latins from flogging, outbidding Gaius without any intention of implementation. Gaius' absence for seventy days in Africa founding Junonia damaged his position, ill omens were reported there, and in the elections for 121 he failed to win a third term.

Ancient judgments were sharply divided. Cicero condemned his grain law as draining the treasury while praising his talent; Plutarch presents him as more passionate and radical than his brother. Modern scholars stress the coherence of his programme and his recognition of the equestrian order as a political force. His judiciary law in particular, according to Varro, made the state 'two-headed', setting senators against equites for half a century.
tribunate_of_gaius_gracchus.debate: Whether Gaius had a coherent plan to reshape the state (Mommsen) or reacted to events; the chronology of his laws between 123 and 122 is uncertain. The order and dates of the Gracchan laws across 123 and 122 cannot be fixed with confidence.
scholarship: Stockton, The Gracchi (1979)
Sherwin-White, 'The lex repetundarum and the political ideas of Gaius Gracchus', JRS 72 (1982)

lex_frumentaria_123.detail:
Gaius Gracchus' grain law obliged the state to sell a monthly ration of wheat to every adult male citizen resident in Rome who applied, at a fixed price of 6 1/3 asses per modius, a little over half the normal market price and, critically, stable regardless of harvest fluctuations. The ration was probably five modii (about 33 kg) a month, enough for one person. To support it, Gaius built public granaries, the horrea Sempronia, near the Tiber, among the first such state storehouses in Rome.

The measure answered a real need. Rome's population was growing rapidly from migration, and grain prices were volatile, especially in years of war or poor harvest in Sicily and Sardinia. A slave revolt in Sicily (135-132) and locust plagues in Africa in 125 had recently disrupted supplies. Gaius' law did not give grain away free, and it was not means-tested: Cicero tells the story of the wealthy consular Lucius Calpurnius Piso Frugi, who had opposed the law, queuing for his ration because, as he said, if Gracchus was going to divide his property among the citizens he wanted his share.

The grain law became the most durable of all Gracchan measures and a permanent fixture of politics. It was modified in a conservative direction by Marcus Octavius (perhaps in the 90s), abolished by Sulla, restored in limited form by the lex Terentia Cassia of 73, extended by Cato in 62 to win the plebs away from Caesar, and made free by Clodius in 58. Caesar cut the rolls from 320,000 to 150,000, and Augustus fixed them at some 200,000. The distribution, the frumentatio, continued into late antiquity, when bread and pork replaced grain.

Ancient conservatives condemned the law as a bribe that emptied the treasury and taught the plebs idleness; Cicero calls it a drain on the aerarium. Modern historians emphasise instead that the regular supply defused famine riots, tied the urban plebs to the state, and created the infrastructure of the annona that sustained the imperial capital.
lex_frumentaria_123.debate: The monthly quantity (five modii) is attested only for later laws and is assumed for Gaius'.
scholarship: Garnsey, Famine and Food Supply in the Graeco-Roman World (1988)
Virlouvet, Tessera frumentaria (1995)

lex_sempronia_iudiciaria.detail:
Gaius Gracchus' judiciary legislation transferred the juries of the permanent extortion court (quaestio de repetundis), established by the lex Calpurnia of 149, from senators to men of equestrian census. The cause was the notorious leniency of senatorial juries toward fellow senators accused of plundering provinces: three governors had recently been acquitted in suspicious circumstances, including Manius Aquillius, organiser of Asia.

A long bronze inscription, found in fragments in the fifteenth century and now in Naples and Vienna, preserves much of an extortion law of this period, usually identified with Gaius' law or with a closely related lex Acilia. It sets out procedure in remarkable detail: a praetor draws up an annual list of 450 jurors, excluding senators and their relatives and requiring a census qualification; prosecutors may be non-citizens; successful non-Roman prosecutors receive Roman citizenship; damages are doubled; and verdicts are by majority vote with a procedure for adjournment (ampliatio). It is the most important surviving Republican statute.

The political effect was enormous. Senators who governed provinces now faced judgment by equites, many of whom were connected with the publicani whose operations governors were supposed to restrain. The danger became clear in 92, when Publius Rutilius Rufus, who as legate in Asia had protected provincials against tax-farmers, was convicted by an equestrian jury and retired to Smyrna. Control of the courts became the central issue between the orders: Caepio's law of 106 tried to share juries, Glaucia's restored equestrian control, Drusus in 91 proposed a mixed scheme, Sulla returned the courts to the Senate in 81, and the lex Aurelia of 70 divided juries among senators, equites and tribuni aerarii.

Whether Gaius consciously sought to elevate the equites as a counterweight to the Senate, or simply to end senatorial collusion, is debated. Either way, the judiciary law is often seen as the moment the equestrian order became a political class.
lex_sempronia_iudiciaria.debate: Whether the lex Acilia is Gaius' own law or a colleague's, and whether Plutarch's version (adding equites to the senate) is a confusion with Drusus in 91. Identification of the epigraphic lex repetundarum with Gaius' law or with a lex Acilia is unresolved.
scholarship: Crawford (ed.), Roman Statutes (1996) no. 1
Lintott, Judicial Reform and Land Reform in the Roman Republic (1992)
Badian, Publicans and Sinners (1972)

lex_sempronia_de_capite_civis.detail: The law framed the arguments of 121, 63 and 58: Opimius' defence in 120, Cicero's execution of the Catilinarians and his exile under the lex Clodia all turned on whether the senatus consultum ultimum overrode it.

lex_sempronia_de_provinciis_consularibus.debate: Date (123 or 122) uncertain. It remained in force until replaced by Pompey's law of 52.

founding_of_aquae_sextiae.detail: Entremont, with its sculptures of heroes holding severed heads, was sacked c. 123; its destruction layer matches the literary record.

citizenship_bill_of_gaius_gracchus.debate: Appian and Plutarch differ on the scope; the bill's failure showed that the Roman plebs would not share its privileges.

senatus_consultum_ultimum_121.detail:
After Gaius Gracchus failed to win a third tribunate, the consul of 121, Lucius Opimius, a bitter enemy who as praetor had destroyed Fregellae in 125, moved to repeal the law founding Junonia. During a sacrifice on the Capitol on the day of the vote, an attendant of the consul, Quintus Antyllius, insulted Gracchan supporters and was stabbed to death. The Senate met the next day, with the body displayed in the Forum, and passed a decree that the consul 'should see to it that the state suffer no harm' (videret ne quid res publica detrimenti caperet).

This formula, later called the senatus consultum ultimum or 'final decree' after Caesar's phrase, had no basis in statute. It authorised nothing specific; it urged the consuls to act and implied that the Senate would back them if they used force against citizens. Opimius summoned senators and equites to appear armed with two slaves each, and recruited Cretan archers. When Gaius and Marcus Fulvius Flaccus occupied the Aventine, he offered an amnesty and then attacked.

The legal status of the decree was contested for the rest of the Republic. Opimius was prosecuted in 120 by the tribune Quintus Decius for killing citizens without trial, defended by the consul Carbo, a former Gracchan, and acquitted on the argument that he had acted under the Senate's authority. Its supporters regarded it as declaring a state of emergency that suspended the citizen's right of appeal; its opponents, invoking Gaius' own lex de capite civis, held that no decree could override a law. The decree was passed again against Saturninus (100), Lepidus (77), Catiline (63), during the disturbances of 52, against Caesar (49), and against Antony (43).

Cicero's execution of the Catilinarian conspirators under the decree in 63 led to his exile in 58, showing that the question was never settled. Modern scholars (Lintott, Ungern-Sternberg, Drogula) generally treat the decree as political rather than legal: it worked only when the consuls had the force and the political support to act.
senatus_consultum_ultimum_121.debate: Whether the senatus consultum ultimum gave any legal immunity to magistrates acting under it was disputed in antiquity and remains so.
scholarship: Lintott, The Constitution of the Roman Republic (1999)
Lintott, Violence in Republican Rome (1968, 2nd ed. 1999)
Ungern-Sternberg, Untersuchungen zum spätrepublikanischen Notstandsrecht (1970)

death_of_gaius_gracchus.detail:
Fulvius Flaccus, a former consul and one of the land commissioners, and Gaius Gracchus occupied the Aventine with their supporters on the day after Antyllius' death, invoking the hill's association with the plebeian secessions and the temple of Diana. Fulvius armed his men with Gallic spoils from his triumph; Gaius, according to Plutarch, went unarmed save for a small dagger. They sent Fulvius' younger son, a boy, to negotiate. Opimius detained him and attacked.

Opimius' force, including Cretan archers, stormed the hill. Fulvius was found hiding in a bathhouse and killed with his elder son. Gaius fled across the Tiber by the Sublician bridge, where his friends held off pursuers, and reached the grove of Furrina on the Janiculum, where he was killed by his slave Philocrates at his own request, the slave then killing himself. Opimius had offered his head's weight in gold; one Septimuleius is said to have filled the skull with lead to increase the reward. Some 3,000 of Gaius' supporters were killed then or executed afterward without trial, and their bodies thrown into the Tiber; their widows were forbidden to mourn, and Gaius' widow Licinia lost her dowry.

Opimius then rebuilt the temple of Concord in the Forum, an act seen by many as provocative: someone carved on it at night 'a work of madness makes a temple of concord'. The Senate also built a new basilica, the Basilica Opimia, beside it. Cornelia, mother of the Gracchi, withdrew to her villa at Misenum, where she received visitors and spoke of her sons without tears, according to Plutarch. Statues of the brothers were later set up and they were honoured with cult offerings at the places of their deaths.

The deaths of 121 established a pattern: the Senate's decree, armed force, mass executions and a subsequent trial that confirmed impunity. Opimius was acquitted in 120 but convicted in 109 by the Mamilian commission for taking bribes from Jugurtha and died in exile at Dyrrachium. The Gracchi became heroes of the popularis tradition and villains of the optimate one, and both sides of the late Republic defined themselves by their judgment of the brothers.
scholarship: Stockton, The Gracchi (1979)
Lintott, Violence in Republican Rome (1999)

temple_of_concord_rebuilt_121.detail: The temple later hosted the senate meeting of 5 December 63 that condemned the Catilinarians.

battle_of_vindalium.detail: Suetonius (Nero 2) says Ahenobarbus afterwards rode through the province on an elephant escorted by his troops, a scene of triumphal display remembered in his family.

battle_of_the_isara.detail: Ancient totals of 120,000 to 130,000 Gauls killed against 15 Roman dead are fantastical, but the victory ended Arvernian hegemony in southern Gaul. Fabius took the name Allobrogicus and, with Ahenobarbus, set up stone trophy towers on the battlefields, a novelty Florus remarks on.

trial_of_opimius_120.detail: The acquittal gave the senatus consultum ultimum practical force. Opimius was convicted in 109 by the Mamilian commission for taking Jugurtha's bribes and died in exile at Dyrrachium.

accession_of_mithridates_vi.debate: Mithridates VI probably took sole power about 116-113 by imprisoning his mother and killing his brother; the immunity-to-poison tales are later legend.

metellus_delmaticus_campaign_119.detail: Appian says bluntly that Metellus wanted a triumph. The Metelli were at their peak: between 123 and 109 six members of the family held the consulship, and four celebrated triumphs.

founding_of_narbo_martius.detail: Narbo was the first citizen colony outside Italy that survived (Junonia having been abolished). The Via Domitia, built by Ahenobarbus, ran through it; a milestone naming Gnaeus Domitius as imperator, found at Treilles near Narbonne, is the oldest Roman milestone known in Gaul.

death_of_micipsa.detail: In 116 a senatorial commission led by Opimius divided the kingdom: Jugurtha got the richer, more populous west; Adherbal the east with Cirta and its ports. Sallust says the commissioners were bought.

vestal_scandal_114.detail: This was the last recorded Roman human sacrifice of this ritual type (also performed in 228 and 216). Cassius was the judge famous for asking 'cui bono?'. The affair shows religious anxiety about the Cimbri and the political use of religious courts: the tribunal was set up by a tribune's law over pontifical jurisdiction.

battle_of_noreia.detail: This was the first Roman encounter with the Cimbri, a people whose origin the ancients placed in Jutland. Carbo was later prosecuted by Marcus Antonius and killed himself. Noreia's site is unknown; the Magdalensberg and sites near Neumarkt in Styria have been proposed.

siege_of_cirta_112.detail:
On the death of Micipsa in 118, Numidia passed jointly to his sons Adherbal and Hiempsal and his adopted nephew Jugurtha, who had won fame and Roman friendships serving under Scipio Aemilianus at Numantia. Jugurtha had Hiempsal murdered and defeated Adherbal, who fled to Rome. A senatorial commission under Lucius Opimius divided the kingdom in 116, giving Jugurtha the richer western part, but in 113 he attacked again and besieged Adherbal in his capital Cirta.

Cirta, on its gorge-ringed rock above the Ampsaga (modern Constantine), was a fortress of exceptional strength, and Jugurtha settled for a blockade with siege lines. Inside were many Italian merchants, the negotiatores who had settled in Numidia's trading towns, who organised the defence. Two Roman embassies came; the second, led by the princeps senatus Marcus Aemilius Scaurus, ordered Jugurtha to raise the siege, but he temporised and the envoys left. After some five months the Italians, believing they would be protected by their status, persuaded Adherbal to surrender on the promise of his life. Jugurtha tortured Adherbal to death and massacred all adult males of military age, including the Italians.

The killing of Italian and Roman businessmen caused outrage in Rome, where the tribune Gaius Memmius stoked suspicion that Jugurtha had bought the Senate's indulgence. Sallust's Bellum Iugurthinum makes the episode the starting point of his indictment of the nobility's corruption: Rome, he famously has Jugurtha say, was 'a city for sale and doomed to perish if it finds a buyer'. War was declared in 111.

Modern historians caution against Sallust's moralising. Senatorial reluctance may reflect a reasonable desire to avoid a costly war in Africa while the Cimbri threatened the north. But the massacre showed how the interests of Italian traders now shaped Roman foreign policy, as the Asiatic Vespers would do again in 88. Sallust's account, written seventy years later, remains our only detailed narrative.
siege_of_cirta_112.debate: The number of Italians killed is unknown; Sallust's charge of senatorial bribery is generally regarded as tendentious.
scholarship: Kraus, 'Jugurthine disorder', in Kraus (ed.), The Limits of Historiography (1999)
Morstein-Marx, 'The myth of Numidian origins in Sallust', AJPh 122 (2001)

jugurtha_in_rome_111.detail: Leaving the city, Jugurtha is said to have looked back and called Rome a city for sale and doomed to perish if it found a buyer. Sallust built his whole monograph around this theme of aristocratic venality.
scholarship: Paul, A Historical Commentary on Sallust's Bellum Jugurthinum (1984)

lex_agraria_111.detail: It is the longest surviving Republican statute text. Appian's account (BC 1.27) of three post-Gracchan laws, first allowing sale of allotments, then stopping distribution, then abolishing rent, is usually reconciled with it.
scholarship: Lintott, Judicial Reform and Land Reform in the Roman Republic (1992)

peace_of_bestia_111.debate: Sallust's whole account of senatorial venality is a moralising construct; modern scholars (e.g. Kraus, Morstein-Marx) suspect strategic caution played a part.

battle_of_suthul.detail: The senate repudiated the agreement. The humiliation produced the Mamilian commission and, indirectly, Marius' consulship.

battle_of_the_muthul.detail: Sallust's set-piece is the best tactical narrative of the war. The battle showed Metellus' disciplined army could beat Jugurtha in the open but not catch him; Jugurtha simply dispersed and reassembled.

marius_elected_consul_107.detail:
Gaius Marius of Arpinum, a novus homo from an equestrian family with links to the Metelli, had served with distinction at Numantia, held the tribunate in 119, the praetorship in 115 and governed Further Spain. In 109 he went to Africa as legate of Quintus Caecilius Metellus, consul and commander against Jugurtha. When he asked leave in 108 to return to Rome to stand for the consulship, Metellus told him to wait and stand alongside Metellus' young son, then about twenty, which would have meant waiting some twenty years.

Marius stayed, cultivated the equites and Italian traders in Utica by criticising Metellus' slow conduct of the war and promising to capture Jugurtha quickly, and wrote letters home attacking his commander. Sallust says that a soothsayer at Utica told him to trust the gods and to try his fortune. Metellus finally released him only twelve days before the elections; Marius travelled fast and won the consulship for 107 with the support of the equites and the plebs.

The tribune Titus Manlius Mancinus then proposed, and the assembly voted, that the command in Numidia be given to Marius, overriding the Senate's decision to extend Metellus' command. This was a serious breach of convention: the allocation of provinces was the Senate's prerogative. It anticipated the later use of popular legislation to give commands to Pompey (67, 66) and Caesar (59).

Sallust gives Marius a famous speech on taking office, in which he contrasts his own scars and military experience with the nobles' ancestral masks and Greek books, and declares that the nobles despise his newness while he despises their idleness. The speech is a Sallustian composition but captures the new man's resentment and the ideological claim that virtus, not birth, should qualify for command. Marius' election began a career of seven consulships, unmatched in Roman history, and a new style of politics built on military reputation and popular support.
scholarship: Evans, Gaius Marius: A Political Biography (1994)
Carney, A Biography of C. Marius (1961)

marian_recruitment_107.detail:
Having won the Numidian command, Marius needed reinforcements and found the Senate unwilling to obstruct him, assuming the levy would make him unpopular. Instead, Sallust records, he enrolled volunteers 'not according to the custom of our ancestors, nor from the classes, but whoever wished, mostly the capite censi', those registered only by head because they had property below the minimum qualification for legionary service. This is the most famous and most misunderstood military reform of the Republic.

Its significance lies less in a sudden change than in the culmination of a trend. The property qualification for service had already been lowered, from 11,000 asses perhaps to 4,000 in the second century and to 1,500 by Gaius Gracchus' time, and the state had begun to provide equipment. Marius' volunteers for 107 were probably only a few thousand. But the precedent was decisive. In the following decades armies were increasingly composed of poor volunteers who served for long periods and looked to their general, rather than the state, for a share of booty and for land on discharge, as Marius' veterans received in Africa through Saturninus' law of 103.

The other changes popularly called the 'Marian reforms' are a modern bundle. The cohort of about 480 men as the main tactical unit appears before Marius; the adoption of the eagle as the single legionary standard, ascribed to his second consulship by Pliny; the redesign of the pilum with a wooden rivet to break on impact (Plutarch); and the training of soldiers to carry their own kit, hence 'Marius' mules' (Frontinus, Festus), cannot all be dated or attributed with confidence. The disappearance of the old distinctions between hastati, principes and triarii, and of the citizen cavalry and velites, was gradual.

Modern scholarship (Gabba, Brunt, Gauthier, Cadiou) stresses continuity and argues that the 'proletarian army' of the late Republic was less proletarian than once thought. Yet the link between soldiers and commanders that enabled Sulla's march on Rome in 88 grew directly out of these developments.
marian_recruitment_107.debate: Gabba saw a decisive proletarianisation; Rich and Cadiou argue the 'Marian reforms' are largely a modern construct, the army changing gradually and recruitment of the poor being neither new nor universal after 107. How far the 'Marian reforms' were Marius' work at all, and how proletarian the late Republican army was, are central debates.
scholarship: Gabba, Republican Rome: The Army and the Allies (1976)
Cadiou, L'armée imaginaire (2018)
Matthew, On the Wings of Eagles: The Reforms of Gaius Marius (2010)
Rich, Historia 32 (1983)

battle_of_burdigala.detail: Caesar used the memory in 58 to justify attacking the Tigurini on the Arar, noting with satisfaction that the canton that had killed Lucius Piso, his father-in-law's grandfather, was the first to pay. Popillius was prosecuted for the surrender.

siege_of_capsa.detail: Sallust admits the act was contrary to the laws of war, justified as necessary against a fickle and hostile population. The exploit established Marius' reputation and his soldiers' loyalty.

battle_of_cirta_106.detail: Sallust describes Jugurtha in the second fight brandishing a bloody sword and shouting in Latin that he had killed Marius. After this Bocchus opened negotiations through Sulla.

lex_servilia_caepionis.debate: Whether juries were wholly senatorial or mixed is uncertain.

gold_of_tolosa.detail: Strabo, following Posidonius, rejects the legend that it was Delphic gold looted by Brennus' Gauls in 279. Caepio was condemned in 103 by a quaestio set up by the tribune Norbanus, partly over the treasure, partly over Arausio, and died in exile at Smyrna.

battle_of_arausio.detail:
In 105 two Roman armies were sent to the Rhône valley to stop the Cimbri, Teutones and their allies, who had defeated Roman forces at Noreia (113), in the Rhône valley under Silanus (109) and at Burdigala under Cassius Longinus (107), and had overrun the legate Marcus Aurelius Scaurus, whom they executed after he warned their king Boiorix not to cross the Alps. The proconsul Quintus Servilius Caepio, enriched, rumour said, by the gold of Tolosa, and the consul Gnaeus Mallius Maximus, a new man, commanded perhaps eight to ten legions with auxiliaries.

The two commanders refused to cooperate. Caepio, a patrician, would not serve under Mallius, and camped separately on the opposite side of the Rhône near Arausio (Orange). When Mallius began negotiations with the Cimbri, Caepio, fearing he would receive the credit, attacked alone on 6 October 105. His camp was overrun, and the Cimbri then destroyed Mallius' army, which was trapped against the river. Livy's epitomator and Orosius give 80,000 soldiers and 40,000 camp followers killed; Mallius lost two sons. Only a handful escaped, among them the young Quintus Sertorius, who swam the Rhône in armour.

Granius Licinianus says the Cimbri, fulfilling a vow, destroyed all the booty: gold and silver thrown into the river, horses drowned, armour broken, prisoners hanged from trees. The day was added to the calendar of ill-omened days. Arausio was the worst Roman defeat since Cannae, and the casualty figures, though inflated, reflect a genuine catastrophe for Roman manpower.

The political fallout was immediate. Caepio was stripped of his imperium, the first such deprivation since the kings, and expelled from the Senate; in 103 he was convicted by a court created by the tribune Gaius Norbanus and went into exile at Smyrna. The panic in Rome led to Marius' re-election, in his absence and against the law requiring a ten-year interval, as consul for 104 and every year until 100. Rutilius Rufus, consul of 105, introduced gladiatorial weapons training for the new levies.
battle_of_arausio.debate: Numbers of the dead and the exact site on the Rhône are uncertain; Plutarch (Luc 27) supplies the date, 6 October. The figure of 80,000 soldiers killed is widely considered exaggerated; the battle date of 6 October rests on Plutarch, Lucullus 27.
scholarship: Rosenstein, Imperatores Victi (1990)
Evans, 'Rome's Cimbric Wars (114-101 BC) and their impact on the Iberian peninsula', Acta Classica 48 (2005)

capture_of_jugurtha.detail:
Marius' campaigns of 107-106 took the war to the edges of the Numidian kingdom: he stormed Capsa in the desert, massacring its adult males, and captured a royal treasure fortress on a crag near the Mulucha river, the frontier with Mauretania, when a Ligurian auxiliary found a way up while gathering snails. But Jugurtha remained at large, now allied with his father-in-law Bocchus I of Mauretania, who had joined the war in return for a promise of a third of Numidia.

After two hard-fought battles near Cirta in late 106, in which the Roman army was surprised on the march, Bocchus opened negotiations. Marius' quaestor, the young patrician Lucius Cornelius Sulla, conducted them. In a series of dangerous journeys through Mauretanian territory with a small escort, Sulla persuaded Bocchus that Roman friendship was worth more than his son-in-law. Bocchus wavered between betraying Sulla to Jugurtha and Jugurtha to Sulla. Finally, at a meeting arranged as a peace conference, Jugurtha's companions were cut down and the king handed in chains to Sulla, probably in early 105.

Marius returned to triumph on 1 January 104, when Jugurtha walked before his chariot with his two sons; he was then lowered into the Tullianum, where, according to Plutarch, he remarked on the coldness of 'your bath' and died of starvation within six days. Western Numidia was given to Bocchus, and the rest to Jugurtha's half-brother Gauda.

Sulla made the capture the centre of his own legend. He wore a signet ring showing Bocchus surrendering Jugurtha to him, and in 91 Bocchus set up a gilded group on the Capitol depicting the scene, which nearly caused a riot between Marius and Sulla. Sulla's son Faustus put the image on a denarius in 56. The episode, Plutarch says, was the seed of the enmity between the two men that would end in civil war. Sallust's narrative of Sulla's diplomacy, with a famous character sketch of Sulla, is one of the finest passages of Roman historiography.
capture_of_jugurtha.debate: Whether Jugurtha died in 104 by starvation or strangulation varies between sources.
scholarship: Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974) no. 426/1
Keaveney, Sulla: The Last Republican (1982)

consecutive_consulships_of_marius.detail:
Marius was elected consul for 104 while still in Africa and without standing in person, and was then re-elected for 103, 102, 101 and 100, a run of five consecutive consulships without precedent. The law required a ten-year gap between consulships and personal candidature, and the lex Villia annalis had regularised the cursus. The people suspended these rules because the Cimbri and Teutones, after Arausio, could have descended on Italy at any time, and Marius was the only general who had won a war recently.

The Germans, however, turned away into Spain and northern Gaul in 104-103, giving Marius two years to train his army in southern Gaul. He built camps, dug the Fossa Mariana, imposed hard training and long marches, and promoted able officers including Sulla, who later moved to Catulus' staff. Each re-election required political management at Rome. In 103 his ally the tribune Saturninus helped secure his fourth consulship, and Marius was accused of staging a show of reluctance; in 102 Lucius Appuleius Saturninus again canvassed for him. His colleagues included the patrician Catulus (102), who held the Alpine passes, and Manius Aquillius (101), who suppressed the Second Sicilian Slave War.

After the victories at Aquae Sextiae (102) and Vercellae (101), Marius triumphed jointly with Catulus and was hailed as the third founder of Rome after Romulus and Camillus. His sixth consulship in 100, gained, Plutarch claims, with heavy bribery, ended in the debacle of Saturninus' death, after which he withdrew to Asia and lost political influence for a decade.

The consecutive consulships set a dangerous precedent: in an emergency a single general could monopolise command and office.
