Later precedents for Pompey's extraordinary commands and sole consulship, and Caesar's dictatorships, were justified in the same way. Sulla's legislation of 81 reinforced the ten-year rule specifically to prevent another Marius.
scholarship: Evans, Gaius Marius: A Political Biography (1994)
Broughton, MRR I 558-576
Shaw, Spartacus and the Slave Wars (2001)

lex_appuleia_de_maiestate.detail: Maiestas, vague by design, outlived the Republic and became the treason charge of the imperial age. Saturninus had turned popularis after being removed from charge of the grain supply at Ostia in 104.
lex_appuleia_de_maiestate.debate: Whether the maiestas law dates to 103 or 100 is disputed.

lex_appuleia_agraria_103.debate: Dated to 103 by most (Broughton); some argue 100. Evidence for the African settlements is largely epigraphic and later.

battle_of_aquae_sextiae.detail:
In 102 the migrating peoples divided: the Cimbri went round to cross the eastern Alps into Italy, while the Teutones and Ambrones marched toward Italy along the coast through the Roman province. Marius, in a fortified camp on the Rhône, refused to give battle and let his soldiers watch the Germans for days so as to lose their fear. The Teutones, Plutarch says, filed past the camp for six days, mocking the Romans and asking whether they had messages for their wives.

Marius followed them to Aquae Sextiae (Aix-en-Provence). A clash between Roman water-carriers and Ambrones bathing in the river escalated into a battle in which the Ligurian auxiliaries and then legionaries destroyed the Ambrones, some 30,000 by Plutarch's figure. Two days later Marius drew up his army on a hill and lured the Teutones into an uphill attack, while his legate Claudius Marcellus, with 3,000 men hidden in woods behind the enemy, attacked their rear at the decisive moment. The Teutonic host was annihilated; the ancient figures, 100,000 to 200,000 killed or captured, are fantastic, but the destruction was complete. Their king Teutobod was captured.

Plutarch, perhaps drawing on Posidonius, records that the people of Massalia fenced their vineyards with the bones of the dead, and that the soil was so enriched by decaying bodies that it gave extraordinary harvests for years. The women of the Teutones, refused their request to be given to the Vestal Virgins as slaves, killed their children and themselves. Marius was preparing to burn the spoils when news arrived of his election to a fifth consulship.

The battle site has been sought near Pourrières, east of Aix, whose name has been derived from campi putridi, 'rotten fields'; the nearby Mont Sainte-Victoire is often linked with the victory. The tactical use of terrain and a concealed reserve shows the quality of Marius' generalship and his trained army.
battle_of_aquae_sextiae.debate: Ancient figures are rhetorical; the precise battlefield is uncertain. Battle site (Pourrières area, Trets, or elsewhere east of Aix) and casualty figures are disputed.
scholarship: Goldsworthy, In the Name of Rome (2003)

catulus_retreat_from_the_atiso_102.detail: Plutarch, following Sulla's memoirs, says Catulus deliberately led the retreat himself so that the disgrace fell on him rather than the army; the young Sulla was his legate. The episode was later spun by both Catulus and Sulla against Marius.

battle_of_vercellae.detail:
While Marius destroyed the Teutones, the Cimbri had crossed the Brenner and driven the consul Catulus back from the Adige in early 102, overrunning the Po plain north of the river during the winter. In 101 Marius, consul for the fifth time, joined Catulus, now proconsul, and the combined army of some 52,000 men (Plutarch: 32,000 under Marius and 20,300 under Catulus) met the Cimbri on the Raudine Plain near Vercellae on 30 July 101. Boiorix, the Cimbric king, rode to the Roman camp to ask for land for his people and that of his brothers the Teutones; Marius replied that the Teutones already had land, which they would hold forever.

The battle was fought in summer heat and dust, which Plutarch says Marius used to his advantage, turning his men so that the sun was in the Cimbri's eyes. The Cimbric infantry, he says, formed a vast square, its front ranks chained together, while 15,000 cavalry tried to draw the Romans away. Marius' wings missed the enemy in the dust, and the decisive fighting fell on Catulus' centre, where Sulla served. Boiorix was killed fighting. The ancient figures, 120,000 to 140,000 killed and 60,000 captured, are inflated but signal annihilation. As at Aquae Sextiae, the Cimbric women killed their children and themselves on the wagon laager.

Credit was bitterly contested. Catulus' soldiers showed the Parmesan envoys that their javelins, inscribed with Catulus' name, were in most of the bodies; Catulus wrote a memoir, and Sulla's memoirs also minimised Marius' role. Plutarch's account, drawing on both, is partisan. Nevertheless the people regarded Marius as the saviour, and the two generals triumphed together. Catulus built the temple of Fortuna Huiusce Diei, probably Temple B in the Largo Argentina, and Marius the temple of Honos and Virtus.

The site of the Campi Raudii is disputed: near Vercelli in Piedmont, as the name suggests, or in the lower Po valley near Rovigo, which some scholars prefer because the Cimbri had come from the Adige.
battle_of_vercellae.debate: Location (Vercelli versus the lower Po) and numbers are disputed; Plutarch's figures derive from Sulla's hostile memoirs. Location of the Campi Raudii: Vercelli in Piedmont (traditional) or near Rovigo in the Po delta.
scholarship: Evans, Gaius Marius: A Political Biography (1994)

birth_of_caesar.debate: Mommsen preferred 102 to fit the minimum ages of his offices; most now accept 100 and suppose a privilege for patricians or exceptions granted later. Day 12 July (Dio) or 13 July (Macrobius).

lex_de_piratis_persequendis.detail: It followed Marcus Antonius' (the orator, grandfather of the triumvir) naval campaign against Cilicia in 102, for which he triumphed. The law is a rare documentary witness to Roman administrative language in the East and to the empire's first attempt at Mediterranean-wide anti-piracy policy.
scholarship: Crawford (ed.), Roman Statutes (1996) no. 12

death_of_saturninus.detail:
Lucius Appuleius Saturninus, tribune for the second time in 100, and the praetor Gaius Servilius Glaucia formed an alliance with Marius, consul for the sixth time, to provide land for his veterans of the German wars. Saturninus' agrarian law distributed land in Transalpine Gaul and founded colonies in Sicily, Achaea and Macedonia, and required every senator to swear within five days to obey the law; Metellus Numidicus alone refused and went into exile. Saturninus also carried a grain law, perhaps lowering the price, and, if the dating is right, the law on praetorian provinces known from inscriptions at Delphi and Cnidus.

The alliance fractured in the autumn. Saturninus was re-elected tribune for 99 and Glaucia sought the consulship, although as a sitting praetor he was ineligible. When Gaius Memmius seemed likely to win the second consular place, he was clubbed to death in the Campus Martius. The Senate passed the senatus consultum ultimum, and Marius, as consul, had to act against his allies. Saturninus, Glaucia and their followers seized the Capitol; Marius cut the water pipes, and they surrendered on a promise of safe conduct. Marius locked them in the Curia Hostilia for their protection, but a crowd climbed onto the roof, tore off the tiles and stoned them to death. Glaucia was dragged from a house and killed.

The episode wrecked Marius' political standing: the optimates mistrusted him and the populares felt betrayed. In 98 Metellus Numidicus was recalled, and Marius left for Asia to avoid witnessing his triumph. Thirty-seven years later the tribune Titus Labienus, prompted by Caesar, prosecuted the elderly senator Gaius Rabirius for Saturninus' murder, a test case on the validity of the senatus consultum ultimum.

Modern scholars differ on Saturninus. Ancient tradition, following optimate sources, depicts him as a violent demagogue; Badian and others see him as a serious legislator with a coherent programme who was destroyed by a collapse of his coalition, and question whether he authorised Memmius' murder.
death_of_saturninus.debate: Dating of the Saturnine laws (103 or 100) and Saturninus' responsibility for Memmius' murder are disputed.
scholarship: Lintott, Violence in Republican Rome (1968)
Badian, 'The death of Saturninus', Chiron 14 (1984)
Crawford (ed.), Roman Statutes (1996) no. 12

sources.r: Lex de provinciis praetoriis (Delphi and Cnidus)

recall_of_metellus_numidicus.detail: In Asia Marius met Mithridates VI and reportedly told him either to be stronger than Rome or do what he was told.

sulla_meets_orobazus.detail: A Chaldaean in the envoy's suite, reading Sulla's face, predicted he would be the greatest of men. The date is disputed between 96 and 92.
sulla_meets_orobazus.debate: Date of Sulla's Cilician command: c. 96 (Badian's later view, followed by many) or 92.

ariobarzanes_installed_in_cappadocia_95.debate: Date of Sulla's Cilician command disputed: 96 or 92 (Badian argued 96; Keaveney and others 92).

scaevola_governs_asia.debate: Date 97 or 94 (or his proconsulship after the praetorship).

trial_of_rutilius_rufus.detail: The verdict was a scandal that discredited equestrian juries and prompted Drusus' jury reform of 91. Cicero visited the old man in Smyrna in 78.

tribunate_of_livius_drusus.detail:
Marcus Livius Drusus, son of the tribune who had outbid Gaius Gracchus in 122, entered the tribunate in December 92 with the backing of leading senators, the orator Lucius Licinius Crassus and the princeps senatus Scaurus among them. His programme was a grand compromise. To restore senatorial control of the courts after the scandalous conviction of Rutilius Rufus, he proposed enrolling 300 equites in the Senate and drawing juries from the enlarged body; to win the plebs he offered colonies in Italy and Sicily and a grain law; and to settle the Italian question he promised citizenship to the allies. To pay for the grain he debased the coinage, mixing one part bronze in eight of silver, according to Pliny.

The first laws passed in the assembly, but opposition grew on all sides. The equites resented losing the courts; many senators distrusted the enlargement; Italian landholders, especially in Etruria and Umbria, feared the agrarian laws; and the consul Lucius Marcius Philippus attacked Drusus relentlessly, declaring in September that he could not govern with this Senate. Crassus answered with his last great speech and died days later. The Senate then annulled Drusus' laws on religious grounds, for having been passed against the auspices and in violation of the lex Caecilia Didia against combining unrelated measures.

An oath of loyalty to Drusus said to have been sworn by Italian leaders, preserved by Diodorus, shows the depth of his connections with the allies; Poppaedius Silo, the Marsic leader, was his guest-friend. Before he could bring the citizenship bill, Drusus was stabbed in the atrium of his house on the Palatine by an unknown assassin, uttering, it was said, 'When will the Republic have another citizen like me?' The allies concluded that Rome would never grant citizenship peacefully, and within weeks Asculum rose.

Ancient writers disagree on whether Drusus was a conservative reformer or an ambitious demagogue; modern scholars generally take him seriously as the last attempt at a negotiated settlement of the Italian question.
tribunate_of_livius_drusus.debate: The authenticity of the 'oath of Philippus' in Diodorus is debated; Mouritsen questions whether the allies wanted citizenship at all, rather than independence.
scholarship: Mouritsen, Italian Unification (1998)
Dart, The Social War, 91 to 88 BCE (2014)
Gabba, Republican Rome: The Army and the Allies (1976)

massacre_at_asculum_91.detail:
In late 91 the praetor (or proconsul) Quintus Servilius Caepio learned that hostages were being exchanged among the Italian communities and went to Asculum, the chief town of the Picentes, to investigate. During the Ludi Romani, when he addressed the people in the theatre with threats, the Asculans killed him and his legate Fonteius, then massacred all the Romans in the town and plundered their property. Diodorus preserves a story that a Roman actor and a Latin comic performer were caught up in the violence, the comic surviving by declaring himself no Roman.

The Asculum massacre was the signal for a general rising of the Italian peoples of the central and southern Apennines: the Marsi, Paeligni, Vestini, Marrucini, Picentes and Frentani in the north, and the Samnites, Hirpini, Lucanians, Apulians and others in the south. Latin colonies and most Etruscan and Umbrian communities stayed loyal, as did the Greek cities. The allies sent a final embassy to Rome requesting citizenship; the Senate refused to receive it unless they first laid down arms.

The rising took Rome by surprise despite the warnings, and the first campaigns of 90 went badly. Asculum itself was the last northern stronghold to fall: Gnaeus Pompeius Strabo besieged it through 90 and 89, and inscribed lead sling bullets from the siege, with messages from both sides, survive in their hundreds. When it fell in November 89, the leaders were executed and the rest expelled with nothing.

Appian makes the allies' grievance their exclusion from the rewards of an empire they had helped win, and their exposure to the abuses of Roman magistrates. The massacre fixed the war's character as a ferocious civil conflict fought between men who had served in the same armies. Modern estimates suggest a combined death toll in the war of perhaps 100,000 or more.
massacre_at_asculum_91.debate: Whether Caepio was praetor or proconsul, and the exact date in late 91, are uncertain.
scholarship: Dart, The Social War, 91 to 88 BCE (2014)
Zangemeister, Glandes plumbeae (CIL IX 6086)

battle_of_the_tolenus.detail: When the bodies of the consul and other nobles were brought to Rome the grief was so great that the senate decreed that the dead should be buried where they fell, so that others would not be deterred from enlisting.

italia_confederation.detail:
Having resolved on war, the allies created a state of their own. They chose Corfinium, the Paelignian town in the Aterno valley, as their capital, renamed it Italia, built a forum and senate house there, and set up a senate of 500 members drawn from all the insurgent peoples. Executive power lay with two consuls, the Marsic Quintus Poppaedius Silo and the Samnite Gaius Papius Mutilus, each with six praetors commanding in the northern and southern theatres respectively. The organisation deliberately copied Rome's: they had served in Roman armies for generations and knew its system intimately.

The confederation struck its own coinage on the Roman weight standard, with the legend ITALIA in Latin or VITELIU in Oscan, and images of the bull goring the wolf and of warriors swearing a common oath. The generals' names on the coins (C. PAAPI C., Q. SILO, and others) show the dual language of the alliance: Latin for the northern Marsic group, Oscan for the Samnites. Embassies were sent to Mithridates VI, who was reportedly asked to invade Italy, though he did not.

What the Italians wanted is debated. Appian and Velleius say they fought for the citizenship Rome had refused; the creation of an independent state with its own capital, coinage and magistrates suggests to some modern scholars, especially Mouritsen, that at least some leaders aimed at independence or at the destruction of Rome's hegemony. Others argue that the state was a war organisation designed to force Rome to concede. The Samnites in particular seem to have fought on after others accepted citizenship, and Velleius says Pontius Telesinus in 82 aimed at Rome's destruction.

As northern communities surrendered in 89, the capital moved to Aesernia in Samnium. The confederation dissolved after 88, though Samnite resistance continued and merged with the Marian side in the civil war.
italia_confederation.debate: Brunt: the allies fought for citizenship. Mouritsen: the citizenship narrative is a retrospective construct and many insurgents sought independence. Whether the confederation sought Roman citizenship or independence is the central interpretive question of the Social War.
scholarship: Mouritsen, Italian Unification (1998)
Brunt, The Fall of the Roman Republic (1988)
Pobjoy, 'The first Italia', in Herring and Lomas (eds.), The Emergence of State Identities in Italy (2000)

lex_julia_de_civitate.detail:
Late in 90 the consul Lucius Julius Caesar, after a year of defeats and with Etruria and Umbria wavering, carried a law granting Roman citizenship to the Latin communities and to those Italian allies who had remained loyal or who laid down their arms by a fixed date. It was the decisive political concession of the Social War. It was soon followed in 89 by the lex Plautia Papiria, which extended citizenship to individuals of allied communities who registered with a praetor in Rome within sixty days, and the lex Pompeia, which gave Latin rights to the communities north of the Po.

The law also allowed generals to grant citizenship to individual soldiers for valour, as the bronze of Asculum shows Pompeius Strabo doing for Spanish cavalrymen in 89. Communities had to accept the grant by vote; Appian reports that some Greek cities in Italy, such as Neapolis and Heraclea, hesitated because they would lose their treaty rights and institutions. Cicero later discussed the case of Heraclea in defending the poet Archias.

The new citizens were not immediately equal. They were first enrolled in a limited number of new tribes or in eight or ten of the thirty-five existing tribes (sources differ), so that their votes counted for less in the tribal assembly. The distribution of new citizens across all tribes became the political issue that Sulpicius Rufus took up in 88, and that the Cinnan regime implemented in 84. Census registration lagged: the count of 86 showed only 463,000 citizens; that of 70, 910,000.

Velleius noted the paradox that Rome, victorious in the field, granted to the defeated what it had denied to them when they were unbeaten. The law transformed Italy south of the Po into a single citizen body, with the old allied states becoming municipia under their own magistrates, a process of municipalisation that took decades. It created the unified Roman Italy on which the later Republic and the Empire rested.
scholarship: Sherwin-White, The Roman Citizenship (2nd ed. 1973)
Bispham, From Asculum to Actium (2007)

lex_varia_de_maiestate_90.detail: The aged Scaurus, accused under the law, is said to have answered with a single sentence: 'Varius of Sucro says Scaurus took bribes from the allies; Scaurus denies it; which do you believe?' The court suspended its sittings in the emergency of the war, and in 89 the lex Plautia iudiciaria replaced equestrian juries for it with juries elected by the tribes.

papius_mutilus_invades_campania_90.detail: Nola would remain in rebel hands until 80, long after the rest of Italy had surrendered; it was the last town of the Social War to fall. The Campanian campaign showed that the confederates aimed at Rome's resources, not only at defence: Capua's grain and the Campanian ports were vital to the city.

siege_of_acerrae_90.debate: Appian mentions that Mutilus dressed Oxyntas, a son of Jugurtha held at Venusia, in purple to win over the Numidian troops.

italia_coinage_90.detail: These coins are the confederation's most eloquent surviving documents. The oath scene echoes Roman treaty imagery but with the number of swearers varied; the bull trampling the wolf inverts Rome's founding symbol. Many were overstruck on or imitate Roman denarii, and hoards in central Italy show them circulating with Roman issues. Rare today, they are among the most sought-after Republican coins.
scholarship: Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974)
Campana, Corpus Nummorum Belli Socialis (1987)

turma_salluitana_decree_89.detail: The inscription is a snapshot of a Roman army headquarters in the Social War: 59 named officers, many of whom became prominent in the civil wars. It also proves that the lex Julia allowed generals to grant citizenship to individual non-Italians for bravery, the precedent for later grants to provincials.
scholarship: Criniti, L'epigrafe di Asculum di Gn. Pompeo Strabone (1970)

lex_plautia_papiria.detail:
Proposed by the tribunes Marcus Plautius Silvanus and Gaius Papirius Carbo in 89, this law extended citizenship beyond the communities covered by the lex Julia. Its key clause, preserved in Cicero's Pro Archia, granted citizenship to anyone enrolled as a citizen of an allied community, who had a domicile in Italy at the time of the law, and who registered with a praetor at Rome within sixty days. It thus reached individuals in communities still in arms or whose status was unclear, encouraging defection from the insurgent cause.

Plautius also carried a jury law, the lex Plautia iudiciaria, under which each tribe elected fifteen jurors annually from among senators, equites and even plebeians, ending the equestrian monopoly of the courts. Under this law the Varian court turned on its creators, condemning Quintus Varius himself.

The registration requirement created problems that echoed for decades. The poet Archias of Antioch, enrolled at Heraclea, claimed to have registered with the praetor Quintus Metellus in 89; when he was challenged under the lex Papia of 65, the records of Heraclea had burned in the Social War, and Cicero's speech in his defence depends on witnesses and the praetor's register. The episode shows how administrative the enfranchisement was: a new citizen needed documentary proof and a clerk's entry in Rome.

Combined with the lex Julia and the lex Pompeia on the Transpadanes, the lex Plautia Papiria effectively ended the Social War for most communities. The Samnites and Lucanians, who fought on, received citizenship only from Cinna in 87 or later. The law is a central document in debates over whether citizenship was what the Italians wanted: thousands rushed to register, which suggests it was valued, even if some insurgent leaders aimed higher.
lex_plautia_papiria.debate: The law may have covered only individuals already holding citizenship of federate cities, rather than whole communities; its exact scope is disputed.
scholarship: Sherwin-White, The Roman Citizenship (2nd ed. 1973)
Badian, 'Roman politics and the Italians (133-91 BC)', Dialoghi di Archeologia 4-5 (1970-71)

siege_of_asculum_89.detail: Hundreds of inscribed lead sling bullets survive from the siege, with taunts and the names of units and commanders. The bronze decree of Strabo's council granting citizenship to Spanish horsemen lists his staff, including his son Gnaeus Pompeius (the future Magnus, aged 17) and Lucius Sergius (Catiline). Cicero also served in this army.

battle_of_nola_89.debate: Appian's casualty figure is likely inflated; the grass crown is attested by Pliny, citing Sulla's own memoirs as the likely source.

lex_papiria_semuncial_as_89.debate: Crawford dates the semuncial standard to 91; the law's author is uncertain (perhaps the tribune Gaius Papirius Carbo of 89).
scholarship: Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974) II 596-597

nicomedes_raids_pontus_89.detail: Appian gives Pelopidas' speeches at length; they present Mithridates as the injured party and Aquillius as the aggressor, a view many modern historians share. Rome had just ordered Mithridates out of Cappadocia and Bithynia (where he had backed Socrates Chrestus) and he had complied. The Roman commissioners then encouraged a client king to provoke him, apparently believing Pontus too weak to respond and Asia too loyal to waver.

asiatic_vespers.detail:
In spring or summer 88, from his headquarters at Ephesus, Mithridates VI sent secret letters to the satraps and city magistrates of Asia ordering that on a fixed day, thirty days later, all Romans and Italians in the province, men, women, children and freedmen of Italian birth, be killed, their bodies left unburied, and their property divided between the killers and the king. Slaves who killed their masters were promised freedom, debtors who killed creditors remission of half their debts.

Appian describes the scenes city by city. At Ephesus fugitives were dragged from the temple of Artemis; at Pergamon those clinging to the statues of Asclepius were shot with arrows; at Adramyttium people were driven into the sea and drowned with their children; at Caunus, which owed its freedom from Rhodes to Rome, Italians were torn from the statue of Vesta, their children killed before their eyes; at Tralles the citizens hired a Paphlagonian, Theophilus, to do the killing so as not to stain their own hands, and he cut off the hands of those clinging to statues. Only a few cities, such as Magnesia on the Maeander and Stratonicea, refused, and Rhodes sheltered refugees.

Valerius Maximus and Memnon give 80,000 victims; Plutarch, citing others, 150,000. Both figures are surely exaggerated, but the number of Italian businessmen, tax-farmers, freedmen and their families in Asia was large, and the slaughter was real and thorough. The massacre bound the cities to Mithridates by complicity and secured him huge funds.

The Vespers were the culmination of Asian hatred for Roman tax-farmers and moneylenders, which Mithridates exploited with calculated brutality. Rome's reaction shaped its policy for a generation: Sulla's punitive indemnity of 20,000 talents in 84 and the debts the cities incurred to pay it were still crippling them when Lucullus intervened in 71. Modern scholars debate the role of local class conflict, Greek civic resentment, and royal compulsion.
asiatic_vespers.debate: Death toll figures are unverifiable and likely exaggerated. The 80,000 figure is widely regarded as inflated; the date (spring or summer 88) and the degree of local enthusiasm are debated.
scholarship: McGing, The Foreign Policy of Mithridates VI Eupator (1986)
Mayor, The Poison King (2010)

sources.w: De imperio Cn. Pompei (Pro lege Manilia)

sulpician_laws.detail:
Publius Sulpicius Rufus, tribune of 88, was a brilliant orator from the circle of Crassus and Drusus and initially a moderate conservative. In 88 he broke with the optimate leadership, perhaps over the consular candidature of Gaius Julius Caesar Strabo, which he opposed as illegal, and turned to radical legislation, allying with Marius. Plutarch calls him second to none in villainy; Cicero, who heard him as a young man, admired his eloquence.

His laws were: the distribution of the newly enfranchised Italians and of freedmen across all thirty-five tribes, rather than confining them to a few; the recall of those exiled by the Varian court; a ban on senators holding debts of more than 2,000 denarii, aimed at bankrupt nobles; and, most explosively, the transfer of the command against Mithridates from the consul Sulla, who had been allocated it by the Senate and lot, to Marius, then nearly seventy and a private citizen.

To push the laws through, Sulpicius gathered an armed following of 3,000 swordsmen and a 'counter-senate' of 600 young equites. The consuls Sulla and Quintus Pompeius Rufus declared a suspension of public business (iustitium) to prevent voting; Sulpicius' men attacked them, killing Pompeius' son, and Sulla, by one account, took refuge in Marius' house before agreeing to lift the suspension. The laws passed.

Sulla's response, the march on Rome, ended the programme. Sulpicius was betrayed by a slave at Laurentum and killed; his head was displayed on the rostra, and Sulla freed the slave and then had him thrown from the Tarpeian Rock for betraying his master. All Sulpicius' laws were annulled as passed by violence. The question of the new citizens' distribution was revived by Cinna and resolved in 84.
sulpician_laws.debate: What turned Sulpicius from optimate to popularis is disputed; the transfer of the command may have been the price of Marius' support for the tribal law.
scholarship: Mouritsen, Plebs and Politics in the Late Roman Republic (2001)
Powell, 'The tribune Sulpicius', Historia 39 (1990)
Keaveney, Sulla: The Last Republican (1982)

sullas_march_on_rome.detail:
Stripped of the Mithridatic command by Sulpicius' law, Sulla went to his army of six legions besieging Nola in Campania, veterans of the Social War who had expected to profit from the eastern campaign. When Marius' military tribunes arrived to take over, the soldiers stoned them to death. Sulla addressed the army and led it on Rome. All but one of his officers, the quaestor Lucius Licinius Lucullus, refused to follow, an index of how shocking the act was. Envoys asking why he marched on his country received the reply that he came to free it from tyrants.

His colleague Pompeius Rufus joined him. Marius and Sulpicius, unable to raise forces, offered freedom to slaves who would fight; only three joined. Sulla entered through the Esquiline Gate, fought a street battle in the Forum Esquilinum where his men were pelted from rooftops until he threatened to burn the houses, and took the city. It was the first time a Roman army had captured Rome.

Sulla had Marius, his son, Sulpicius and nine others declared public enemies; Sulpicius was killed, and Marius escaped to Africa after hiding in the marshes of Minturnae. Sulla then passed laws requiring the Senate's prior approval for legislation in the assembly and, according to Appian, voting by the centuriate rather than tribal assembly, and he enrolled 300 new senators. He allowed the election of Cinna as consul for 87 after making him swear to uphold his acts, and then left for Greece.

The march was the decisive breach in Roman political culture. Appian dates the end of shame about civil war to this moment; once an army had been led against Rome, there was no inherent restraint. Sulla's justification, that he acted to restore the legitimate decision of the Senate overturned by violence, would be echoed by Caesar in 49. Modern historians debate whether Sulla planned it or reacted to his soldiers' anger.
sullas_march_on_rome.debate: Whether Sulla's soldiers followed out of greed for eastern plunder (Appian) or genuine belief in the consul's legitimacy is debated. Whether the army's loyalty was to Sulla or to the prospect of eastern booty, and the legality claimed for the march, are discussed by Levick and Morstein-Marx.
scholarship: Keaveney, Sulla: The Last Republican (2nd ed. 2005)
Keaveney, Sulla: The Last Republican (1982)
Levick, 'Sulla's march on Rome in 88 BC', Historia 31 (1982)
Morstein-Marx, 'Consular appeals to the army in 88 and 87', in Beck et al. (eds.), Consuls and Res Publica (2011)

mithridates_occupies_asia_88.detail: The speed of the collapse reflects how hated Roman tax-farming and moneylending had become in the province created in 129. Mithridates presented himself as a new Alexander and liberator, remitted taxes for five years, and minted gold staters with an idealised, windswept portrait. The welcome turned sour within two years: the king's demands, executions and arbitrary confiscations drove cities such as Ephesus to revolt in 86.

sack_of_delos_88.debate: The 20,000 figure (Appian) is generally thought exaggerated; the 'Agora of the Italians' shows destruction layers.

aristion_seizes_athens_88.debate: Whether Athenion and Aristion were one man or two successive leaders is disputed; Posidonius' hostile portrait (preserved by Athenaeus) is our main source.

siege_of_rome_87.detail:
In 87 the consul Lucius Cornelius Cinna revived Sulpicius' proposal to distribute the new citizens across all tribes. His colleague Gnaeus Octavius, backed by the old citizens, drove Cinna's supporters from the Forum in a battle that left, by Plutarch's figure, 10,000 dead. The Senate deposed Cinna, an act without precedent, and replaced him with the flamen Dialis Lucius Cornelius Merula. Cinna went to the army besieging Nola, threw himself on the ground before them, and won them over.

Cinna appealed to the new citizens of Italy, raising money and men, and recalled Marius, who landed in Etruria with a band of Moorish horsemen and freed slaves and enrolled 6,000 men. Sertorius and Gnaeus Papirius Carbo also joined. The armies converged on Rome: Cinna and Carbo on the Tiber south of the city, Sertorius upstream, and Marius seizing Ostia to cut the grain supply. Pompeius Strabo, commanding the only substantial senatorial army, hovered outside the Colline Gate negotiating with both sides, until plague swept through the camps and he died.

The Senate sought help from Metellus Pius, fighting the Samnites, who demanded terms the Senate would not grant; the Samnites themselves came over to Cinna on the promise of citizenship. With Rome starving, the Senate negotiated, asking only that Cinna swear to shed no blood. He refused the oath. Octavius, refusing to flee, sat in his curule chair on the Janiculum and was beheaded; his head was the first consul's head displayed on the rostra.

The siege marked the second capture of Rome by a Roman army within a year. It brought the Cinnan regime to power for four years, during which Cinna held the consulship continuously (87-84), elections were controlled, and Sulla was declared a public enemy while he fought Mithridates in Greece.
scholarship: Lovano, The Age of Cinna: Crucible of Late Republican Rome (2002)

marian_massacres.detail:
When Marius and Cinna entered Rome in late 87, Marius, bitter from exile and his humiliation in 88, unleashed a five-day massacre. His bodyguard of freed slaves, the Bardyaei, killed whomever he indicated, or whomever he failed to greet. Among the victims were the consul Octavius, the orator Marcus Antonius, betrayed by a wine merchant's indiscretion and killed while charming his executioners with his eloquence, the brothers Lucius Julius Caesar (consul 90) and Gaius Julius Caesar Strabo, Publius Licinius Crassus (father of the triumvir) and his elder son, and Quintus Ancharius, killed while trying to greet Marius. Their heads were displayed on the rostra. Catulus and Merula killed themselves.

The Bardyaei raped and plundered in the houses of their victims until Cinna and Sertorius had them surrounded and killed, some 4,000 by one account, in their camp. Plutarch's narrative, drawing on Sulla's memoirs and other hostile sources, presents Marius as a deranged old man; modern scholars think the killings, though brutal, were more targeted than the sources suggest, aimed at those who had supported Sulla's outlawing of Marius in 88.

Marius and Cinna then appointed themselves consuls for 86 without election. Marius died on 13 January 86, days into his seventh consulship. The young Crassus fled to Spain and hid in a cave for eight months; he would return to fight for Sulla.

The massacres of 87, with heads on the rostra and killings of consulars, set a precedent of political murder that Sulla surpassed in his proscriptions. Their memory kept many nobles loyal to Sulla, whose return in 83 was framed as revenge for these deaths.
marian_massacres.debate: The number of victims and Marius' personal responsibility versus Cinna's are debated; Plutarch's portrait is heavily coloured by Sullan propaganda.
scholarship: Lovano, The Age of Cinna (2002)
Bauman, 'The Marian massacres', Antichthon 7 (1973)

death_of_pompeius_strabo_87.debate: Lightning (Plutarch) or epidemic (Velleius, Orosius); the two may be combined in the tradition.

sulla_plunders_greek_sanctuaries_87.detail: He promised to repay the gods and later assigned half the territory of Thebes to the sanctuaries as compensation. The bullion was minted on the spot: Sulla's quaestor Lucius Licinius Lucullus struck large issues of denarii and tetradrachms in Greece, the so-called 'Lucullan' coinage. For later Greeks the episode marked the moment when Roman generals stopped even pretending to respect the panhellenic shrines.

suicides_of_merula_and_catulus_87.detail: Merula's death left the flaminate of Jupiter vacant; the teenage Julius Caesar was designated to it in 84/83, a post with taboos (no horse riding, no sight of an army) that would have ended any military career. Sulla's victory voided the appointment. The office stayed empty until 11 BC.

death_of_marius.detail:
Marius entered his seventh consulship on 1 January 86, fulfilling, it was said, a childhood omen in which an eagle's nest with seven chicks fell into his lap. His first act was to have the senator Sextus Lucilius thrown from the Tarpeian Rock. He was nearly seventy-one, exhausted by exile and war, and Plutarch says he was tormented by fear of Sulla's return and by sleeplessness, drinking heavily. He fell ill with pleurisy and died on 13 January after seventeen days in office.

Posidonius, who was in Rome on an embassy from Rhodes and met him on his sickbed, is cited by Plutarch as the source for his final days, in which Marius was delirious and imagined himself fighting Mithridates. Livy says he had done more harm in peace than good in war.

Marius' career encapsulates the late Republic: the new man who became the greatest general of his age, saviour of Italy from the Germans, seven times consul, yet politically clumsy and ultimately destructive. His military innovations, real or attributed, created armies personally loyal to their generals; his alliance with tribunes against the Senate made the popularis method a vehicle for military power. His enmity with Sulla, born in Numidia, led directly to the civil wars.

After his victory in 82, Sulla had Marius' ashes dug up and scattered in the Anio and his monuments destroyed. His nephew by marriage, Julius Caesar, restored the trophies of his victories to the Capitol by night as aedile in 65 and displayed his images at his aunt Julia's funeral in 69, signalling that the Marian cause lived on. His adopted son, Gaius Marius the Younger, became consul in 82 at about twenty-six and died at Praeneste.
scholarship: Evans, Gaius Marius: A Political Biography (1994)

siege_of_athens_86.detail:
Sulla landed in Epirus in spring 87 with five legions and marched directly on Athens, which under Aristion had joined Mithridates, and on the Piraeus, held by the Pontic general Archelaus. He besieged both through the winter of 87/86. To build siege works he cut down the groves of the Academy and the Lyceum; to pay his army, cut off from Rome where his enemies now ruled, he took the treasures of Delphi, Olympia and Epidaurus.

The Piraeus, protected by the Long Walls and Themistocles' fortifications, was resupplied by sea; the Pontic and Roman engineers fought a duel of mines and countermines, and Archelaus' sorties burned Sulla's engines. Athens itself starved. Plutarch reports a medimnus of wheat selling for 1,000 drachmas, people eating boiled shoes and leather flasks, while Aristion feasted and mocked Sulla and his wife Metella from the walls. Sulla's spies discovered an unguarded section of wall near the Heptachalcon, between the Piraeus and Sacred Gates, and on the night of 1 March 86 his men broke in.

The sack was savage. Plutarch, citing eyewitnesses, says blood flowed through the Ceramicus out of the Dipylon gate; the number killed was never counted. Sulla stopped the slaughter, he said, sparing the living for the sake of the dead, in deference to Athens' past. Aristion held out on the Acropolis until thirst forced surrender and was executed. Sulla then stormed the Piraeus, burning the arsenal of Philo, and Archelaus withdrew by sea.

Archaeologists have found the destruction layer across the Agora and Ceramicus and thousands of sling bullets. Sulla took to Rome the library of Apellicon of Teos, containing manuscripts of Aristotle and Theophrastus that later formed the basis of Andronicus of Rhodes' edition of Aristotle.
siege_of_athens_86.debate: Date of the fall (1 March 86, the Kalends) rests on Plutarch citing Sulla's memoirs.
scholarship: Habicht, Athens from Alexander to Antony (1997)

battle_of_chaeronea_86.detail:
After the fall of Athens, Archelaus joined the Pontic army that had come down through Thessaly under Taxiles, giving a combined force that Plutarch and Appian put at 120,000 men, including scythed chariots, phalanx infantry with bronze shields, and freed slaves. Sulla had some 16,500 Romans plus Greek allies. He took up a position in western Boeotia near Chaeronea, scene of Philip II's victory in 338, and kept his men digging trenches to deny the Pontic cavalry room and to keep them from idleness.

Two men of Chaeronea guided a Roman detachment around Mount Thurium, from which they dislodged a Pontic force that fled down onto its own army. The Pontic chariots, launched without room to gather speed, were driven back by Roman javelins and stakes planted in front of the legions, to the derisive applause of the Roman soldiers, who called for more as at the circus. The Pontic phalanx, interspersed with freed slaves, was attacked from the flanks by Sulla's cavalry and by Murena and Hortensius. The rout drove the Pontic army against the hills; Archelaus escaped to Chalcis with 10,000 men.

Sulla claimed that only fourteen Romans were missing, and two of those turned up the next day, figures that surely come from his own memoirs. He set up two trophies, one on the plain and one on Mount Thurium, recording the names of Ares, Nike and Aphrodite, and his cognomen Epaphroditus. The base of the Thurium trophy was found in 1990, with an inscription naming the two Chaeroneans, Homoloichos and Anaxidamos.

Chaeronea, together with Orchomenus later that year, destroyed Mithridates' armies in Greece. Plutarch, himself a native of Chaeronea, describes local memories and finds of armour and weapons in the marshes generations later.
battle_of_chaeronea_86.debate: Sulla's casualty figures are self-glorifying; Pontic numbers vary widely. Pontic numbers and the near-zero Roman losses come from Sulla's memoirs and are not credible as given.
scholarship: Keaveney, Sulla: The Last Republican (2nd ed. 2005)
Camp et al., 'A trophy from the battle of Chaironeia of 86 B.C.', AJA 96 (1992)

battle_of_orchomenus.detail: Plutarch reports that two hundred years later bows, helmets and swords were still being found in the marshes.

sources.r: Ephesian decree of war against Mithridates

peace_of_dardanus.detail:
By 85 Mithridates had lost two armies in Greece, faced revolts in Asia, and was pursued by Fimbria, who had murdered the consul Flaccus and taken command of the Valerian legions. Sulla, for his part, needed to return to Italy to deal with his enemies. Negotiations began through Archelaus at Delium in the winter of 86/85, and Sulla crossed to Asia. In August 85 he met Mithridates at Dardanus in the Troad.

Plutarch describes the encounter: Mithridates came with 20,000 infantry, 6,000 cavalry and a fleet; Sulla with four cohorts and 200 horsemen. When the king held out his hand, Sulla demanded whether he accepted the terms, and when Mithridates tried to justify his actions, Sulla cut him off. The terms: Mithridates was to evacuate all his conquests and return to the borders of Pontus as before the war; surrender seventy (or eighty) warships with crews and 500 archers; pay an indemnity of 2,000 or 3,000 talents; release prisoners and deserters; and restore Nicomedes IV to Bithynia and Ariobarzanes to Cappadocia. In return Mithridates was recognised as a friend and ally of Rome and kept his kingdom.

Sulla's soldiers were angry, believing they had been cheated of the king who had massacred 80,000 Italians. Sulla's answer was that he could not fight Mithridates and Fimbria at once. He then marched on Fimbria, whose army deserted.

The treaty was never ratified by the Senate, and its informal status allowed Murena to provoke the Second Mithridatic War in 83. Mithridates lost nothing of his own kingdom and rebuilt his forces for the third war in 74. Modern scholars regard the peace as a pragmatic decision that sacrificed Rome's long-term interest in the East to Sulla's political needs at home, which is broadly how Mithridates' enemies saw it at the time.
peace_of_dardanus.debate: The indemnity (2,000 or 3,000 talents) and the number of ships vary in the sources.
scholarship: McGing, The Foreign Policy of Mithridates VI Eupator (1986)
Kallet-Marx, Hegemony to Empire (1995)

battle_of_tenedos_85.debate: Plutarch's claim that Lucullus let Mithridates escape out of loyalty to Sulla over Fimbria is often repeated; it may be a later rationalisation.

rhetorica_ad_herennium.debate: Author unknown (Cornificius has been proposed); date c. 86-82 inferred from internal references.

sullan_settlement_of_asia.detail: Sulla reorganised Asia into 44 districts for collection, a structure that lasted. Loyal cities (Rhodes, Chios, Stratonicea, Ilium) were rewarded; the Fimbrian legions stayed in Asia.

sullan_aurei_84.detail: This is the first time a Roman general put his own power, rather than his family's history, at the centre of coinage. The two trophies probably allude to Chaeronea and Orchomenus. The aureus became, with Caesar and the triumvirs, the instrument of army pay in the civil wars, and gold issues became normal only after 49.
scholarship: Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974) nos. 359, 367

enrollment_of_new_citizens_84.debate: The census figure of 86 (463,000) against 910,000 in 70 shows the real enfranchisement of Italy happened over a generation; why the 86 registration was so low (war, hostility of censors, refusal to register) is debated.

burning_of_the_capitol_83.detail: Sulla took columns from the temple of Olympian Zeus at Athens for the new temple (Pliny). Catulus' name on the rebuilt temple was a target of Caesar's in 62.

sulla_lands_at_brundisium.detail:
In spring 83 Sulla crossed from Dyrrachium to Brundisium with some 1,600 ships carrying perhaps 40,000 men: five legions of veterans, 6,000 cavalry and contingents from Macedonia and the Peloponnese. Before sailing, the soldiers swore to remain with him and not to plunder Italy, and offered him their own savings. Brundisium opened its gates without resistance, and Sulla rewarded it with an exemption from customs duties that it still held in Appian's day.

Sulla had written to the Senate in 84 listing his services and announcing that he would punish his enemies but not harm the new citizens, a crucial reassurance to Italy. The Cinnan government had prepared perhaps 100,000 men under the consuls of 83, Lucius Cornelius Scipio Asiaticus and Gaius Norbanus, and Carbo. But its legitimacy had collapsed with Cinna's murder by his own troops at Ancona in 84, and many nobles came over to Sulla: Metellus Pius from Africa, Marcus Crassus from Spain, the young Pompey with three legions raised in Picenum, Cethegus, Verres and others.

Sulla marched up the Via Appia. Near Canusium or at Mount Tifata outside Capua he defeated Norbanus, who withdrew to Capua; at Teanum the army of Scipio went over to him during a truce. Sertorius, who had warned against negotiation, left for Spain. A severe winter halted operations. In July the Capitoline temple burned down, a portent that both sides interpreted in their favour.

The landing opened the Second Sullan Civil War, fought across Italy through 83 and 82 and ending at the Colline Gate. Its outcome depended less on battles than on defections. Sulla later claimed in his memoirs that favourable omens and the support of the gods had accompanied every step, building his image as Felix, the fortunate.
scholarship: Keaveney, Sulla: The Last Republican (1982)
Seager, 'Sulla', CAH IX2 (1994)

defection_of_scipios_army_83.detail: Sertorius, serving with Scipio, had warned against the talks; the betrayal convinced him that the Marian cause in Italy was lost and he left for Spain. The episode, like the earlier defeat of Norbanus at Mount Tifata, showed that many Roman soldiers would not fight Sulla's veterans.

pompey_raises_legions_in_picenum_83.detail: The episode is the clearest example of the 'private army' of the late Republic: soldiers loyal to a family rather than to the state. Velleius and Plutarch tell it as heroic; Sallust and others later remembered the adulescentulus carnifex, the teenage butcher. Crassus and Metellus Pius also brought forces to Sulla at this time.

battle_of_the_colline_gate.detail:
In autumn 82, with the younger Marius besieged in Praeneste and Carbo's armies in the north collapsing, the Samnite leader Pontius Telesinus and the Lucanian Marcus Lamponius, together with the remnants of the Marian forces under Carrinas and Censorinus, broke away from the attempt to relieve Praeneste and marched on Rome itself, which was virtually undefended. Velleius records Telesinus riding along his lines declaring that the wolves who had ravaged Italy's liberty would never disappear until the forest that sheltered them was cut down: Rome must be destroyed.

Sulla raced back and arrived at midday on 1 November 82 outside the Colline Gate, at the north-east of the city, where Telesinus had camped. Against the advice of his officers, he attacked late in the afternoon with tired troops. His left wing, under his personal command, was broken and driven back against the city walls; the gates were shut on the fugitives, and Sulla himself narrowly escaped javelins, praying, it was said, to a small golden image of Apollo from Delphi he carried. On the right, however, Crassus routed the enemy and pursued them to Antemnae. The battle continued into the night.

Over 50,000 men are said to have died on both sides. The next day 3,000 to 8,000 prisoners, mostly Samnites, were herded into the Villa Publica on the Campus Martius and massacred while Sulla addressed the Senate in the nearby temple of Bellona; when the senators flinched at the screams, he told them to pay attention, it was only some criminals being punished. Telesinus' head was paraded before Praeneste, whose garrison surrendered; Marius the Younger killed himself.

Sulla then devastated Samnium, declaring that no Roman would be safe while the Samnites existed. Strabo, writing under Augustus, says that their towns had become villages. The battle ended the civil war in Italy, opened the proscriptions, and was later commemorated by Sulla's Ludi Victoriae.
battle_of_the_colline_gate.debate: Numbers of prisoners massacred in the Villa Publica range from 3,000 (Livy) to 8,000 (Plutarch).
scholarship: Keaveney, Sulla: The Last Republican (2nd ed. 2005)
Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967)
Keaveney, Sulla: The Last Republican (1982)

siege_of_praeneste.detail: Sulla displayed Marius' head with the gibe that one should learn to row before taking the helm. The great terraced sanctuary of Fortuna Primigenia was rebuilt, possibly in Sulla's colonial period, though its date is debated.

sullan_proscriptions.detail:
In November 82 Sulla posted a list (proscriptio, a public notice) in the Forum of men declared outlaws: anyone could kill them, their killers received two talents (12,000 denarii) from the treasury, informers received rewards, slaves who killed their masters were freed, and those who sheltered the proscribed were themselves put to death. The property of the proscribed was confiscated and sold at auction; their sons and grandsons were barred from public office.

The first list had eighty names; others followed, and the lists were closed only on 1 June 81 under the lex Cornelia de proscriptione. Estimates of the dead vary: 40 senators and 1,600 equites in Appian's first phase, 4,700 in all according to Valerius Maximus. Many more died outside Rome as local enemies settled scores. Plutarch reports the remark that a man was killed for his Alban villa, and that the young senator Gaius Metellus asked in the Senate when the killing would end, at least telling the living who was safe.

The proscriptions were also a vast transfer of property. Sulla's freedman Chrysogonus bought the estates of the murdered Sextus Roscius of Ameria, worth six million sesterces, for 2,000; Cicero exposed the case in 80. Crassus built his fortune by buying confiscated estates cheaply, and Catiline was later accused of murdering his own brother-in-law and having him added to the list. The young Caesar, Cinna's son-in-law, was threatened and went into hiding.

The proscriptions were remembered as the defining horror of the age, cited by Cicero, Sallust and every later writer, and their exclusion of the sons of the proscribed from office remained a grievance until Caesar repealed it in 49. The triumvirs revived the method in 43. Modern studies (Hinard) emphasise that the proscriptions were also a legal procedure, an attempt to define and limit vengeance that nonetheless escaped control.
sullan_proscriptions.debate: Numbers vary widely; Hinard's prosopography identifies only a fraction by name. The total number of proscribed is uncertain; Hinard's prosopography identifies only about 75 by name.
scholarship: Hinard, Les proscriptions de la Rome républicaine (1985)

sulla_dictator.detail:
With both consuls of 82, Carbo and Marius the Younger, dead, Sulla wrote to the Senate suggesting that an interrex be appointed, and that the times called for a dictator, not for six months as in the old Republic, but until the state was restored. The interrex Lucius Valerius Flaccus carried a law, the lex Valeria, in late 82, appointing Sulla dictator legibus scribundis et rei publicae constituendae, 'for writing laws and settling the constitution', with no fixed term. The law also ratified all his past acts, gave him power of life and death over citizens, and the right to found colonies, confiscate land and make war and peace.

The dictatorship had not been used since 202. Sulla's version transformed it: his title combined the old emergency office with a constituent mandate that had parallels only in the decemvirs of 451. Cicero later called the lex Valeria the most unjust of all laws. Sulla took twenty-four lictors, as many as the kings, and appointed Flaccus as his master of horse.

Sulla held the office probably until late 81 or early 80, during which he carried his programme of reforms and continued the proscriptions. He then held the consulship in 80 with Metellus Pius, and declined re-election for 79. His laying down of the dictatorship and retirement to private life became one of the great puzzles of Roman history; Caesar mocked him for it, saying Sulla had not known his political ABC.

The dictatorship of Sulla was the immediate model for Caesar's dictatorships, especially his dictatorship for ten years and then perpetual dictatorship, which went further by abandoning any constituent purpose or intention of laying down the office. The dictatorship itself was abolished by Antony's law in 44.
sulla_dictator.debate: When Sulla laid down the dictatorship (late 81, early 80, or 79) is disputed.
scholarship: Keaveney, Sulla: The Last Republican (2nd ed. 2005)
Hurlet, La dictature de Sylla (1993)
Keaveney, Sulla: The Last Republican (1982)

pompey_in_sicily_and_africa.detail: The elephants harnessed to his triumphal chariot could not fit through the city gate. Sulla's sarcastic remark that more people worshipped the rising than the setting sun is reported by Plutarch. The triumph's date is disputed between 81 and 79.
pompey_in_sicily_and_africa.debate: Date of Pompey's first triumph (12 March 81, 80 or 79).

damasippus_massacre_82.detail: The murder of Scaevola, the greatest jurist of the age and a man who had tried to stay neutral, horrified contemporaries; Cicero cites it repeatedly. It gave Sulla moral cover for the proscriptions, and Damasippus himself was killed after the Colline Gate.

pompeys_first_triumph.debate: Year disputed: 81 (Badian, Seager), 80, or 79 (Granius Licinianus' evidence read differently). Sulla reportedly gave way after Pompey told him more men worship the rising than the setting sun.

sullan_constitution.detail:
Sulla's legislation of 82-80, carried as dictator through the assemblies, aimed to make the Senate the permanent centre of government and to remove the instruments by which tribunes and generals had challenged it. He enlarged the Senate to about 600 by enrolling some 300 equites and making the quaestorship the qualification for entry, raising the number of quaestors to twenty and so supplying the Senate automatically without censorial selection.

The tribunate was gutted: tribunes lost the right to propose laws without the Senate's prior approval, their veto was limited to protecting individuals, and holders were barred from higher office, deterring ambitious men. The cursus honorum was fixed by law: quaestor, then praetor, then consul, with minimum ages (perhaps 30, 39 and 42) and a ten-year interval before re-election to the same office. The number of praetors rose to eight, and consuls and praetors were expected to remain in Rome during their year of office and govern provinces as promagistrates afterward.

Criminal justice was reorganised into seven or more standing courts (quaestiones perpetuae) with senatorial juries: extortion, treason (lex Cornelia de maiestate, which also forbade governors to leave their provinces or make war without authorisation), murder and poisoning (de sicariis et veneficis), forgery, electoral bribery, embezzlement and violence. This was the most durable part of the reform and the foundation of Roman criminal law. He also abolished grain distributions, increased the priestly colleges to fifteen, restored co-optation in place of election, extended the pomerium, and rebuilt the Senate house.

Most of the political reforms were undone within a decade: the tribunes' powers were restored in 70 by Pompey and Crassus, and the juries were shared in the same year. The court system and the cursus rules survived. Modern scholars debate whether Sulla was a reactionary restoring an idealised past or a pragmatist reinforcing the Senate against new realities.
sullan_constitution.debate: Was Sulla a reactionary restoring senatorial government (the traditional view) or a modernizer whose institutions shaped the next century? Flower treats his settlement as founding a new republic of its own.
scholarship: Keaveney, Sulla: The Last Republican (2nd ed. 2005)
Santangelo, Sulla, the Elites and the Empire (2007)
Flower, Roman Republics (2010)
Hantos, Res publica constituta (1988)

sullan_veteran_colonies.detail: Volaterrae held out against siege until 80/79. The dispossessed and the veterans who failed as farmers formed the reservoir that Lepidus in 78 and Catiline in 63 tried to tap; Faesulae was the base of Manlius' rising. At Pompeii, new public buildings (the covered theatre, the amphitheatre, built by two colonial magistrates) mark the colonists' arrival.
scholarship: Brunt, Italian Manpower (1971)

caesar_defies_sulla_81.debate: Sulla's prophetic remark is surely a later embellishment.

pro_roscio_amerino.detail: Cicero carefully exempted Sulla from blame while exposing the abuses under his regime. The case made his name; he then spent two years studying in Athens and Rhodes, partly for his health and perhaps partly for safety.

sertorius_returns_to_spain.detail:
Quintus Sertorius, a Sabine from Nursia, had served under Caepio at Arausio, swimming the Rhône to escape, under Marius against the Cimbri, where he spied in Celtic dress, and under Didius in Spain, where he lost an eye. He had joined Cinna in 87 but distanced himself from Marius' massacres. Sent as propraetor to Hither Spain in 83, he was driven out by Sulla's general Annius in 81, took to the sea with Cilician pirates, fought in Mauretania for the Moorish prince Ascalis, and captured Tingis, where he opened the supposed tomb of the giant Antaeus.

In 80 the Lusitanians, at war with Rome, invited him to lead them. He crossed the Strait with 2,600 Romans and 700 Libyans, defeated a Roman fleet off Mellaria, and joined 4,700 Lusitanians. Within a year he defeated the governor of Further Spain, Fufidius, on the Baetis, and the legates of Metellus Pius, who arrived with a proconsular army.

Sertorius combined guerrilla tactics, which the Iberians knew well, with Roman organisation. He presented himself as a legitimate Roman magistrate in exile, forming a counter-senate of 300 Roman emigrés, and as a charismatic leader to the Iberians, whose loyalty he cemented with the famous white fawn, a gift, he said, of Diana that brought him divine messages. He armed and drilled the Iberians in Roman fashion, established a school at Osca for the sons of chieftains, and restrained Roman extortion.

His return began the Sertorian War, which held two proconsular armies, including Pompey's, at bay for eight years. Modern scholars debate whether Sertorius was a Roman patriot preserving the Marian Republic in exile, as Plutarch suggests, or a warlord who aimed at an independent Spanish state; his alliance with Mithridates in 75 is cited for the latter.
sertorius_returns_to_spain.debate: Sertorius' aims, Roman restoration or Iberian independence, remain contested.
scholarship: Konrad, Plutarch's Sertorius: A Historical Commentary (1994)
Spann, Quintus Sertorius and the Legacy of Sulla (1987)

accession_of_ptolemy_xii_80.detail: The supposed will hung over Auletes' whole reign. Rome never formally acted on it, but it gave politicians such as Crassus (65) and Rullus (63) a pretext for proposing annexation, and it is the reason Auletes spent a fortune buying recognition as 'friend and ally of the Roman people' (59).
accession_of_ptolemy_xii_80.debate: Whether the will existed and which Alexander made it was uncertain even to Cicero.

sulla_abdicates.detail: Caesar later said Sulla did not know his political ABC in laying down the dictatorship (Suet. Iul. 77). Appian marvels that no one touched him.
sulla_abdicates.debate: The date of Sulla's abdication of the dictatorship (81, 80 or 79) is disputed.

ciceros_eastern_study_tour_79.detail: Cicero's own account in the Brutus tells how he returned 'not just better trained but almost transformed'. In Athens he befriended Titus Pomponius, henceforth Atticus. The trip was the formative moment of the Roman philosophical education; Caesar would go to Molon at Rhodes a few years later.

death_of_sulla.detail:
After his consulship of 80, Sulla retired to his estate near Puteoli, where he spent his last year writing twenty-two books of memoirs, fishing, hunting and enjoying the company of actors, among them the comedian Roscius, the mime Sorex and the female impersonator Metrobius. He was still active in local affairs, drafting a constitution for Puteoli, and on the day before his death he had the local magistrate Granius strangled in his presence for withholding funds owed for the Capitol's restoration. He died in 78, aged sixty, of a haemorrhage, apparently from liver failure; Plutarch's lurid story of a disease of lice (phthiriasis) is a literary convention for tyrants.

His funeral was the most magnificent Rome had seen. The consul Lepidus wanted to deny it; his colleague Catulus and Pompey insisted. The body was carried on a golden litter from Campania through Italy, escorted by his veterans; in Rome some 2,000 golden crowns from cities and legions accompanied it, and the ladies of Rome brought so much incense that a statue of Sulla and a lictor were modelled from it. He was the first patrician Cornelius to be cremated rather than buried, perhaps to avoid what he had done to Marius' remains. The pyre, on the Campus Martius, was lit as rain began to fall.

His tomb bore an epitaph he had written himself: no friend ever surpassed him in doing good, and no enemy in doing harm. His memoirs, dedicated to Lucullus, became a major source for Plutarch and others, ensuring his version of events, with its emphasis on Fortune and divine favour, endured.

Within months of his death, Lepidus was attacking his system, and the questions he had tried to settle by force reopened. Sulla's legacy was ambivalent: he restored the Senate's dominance but showed how to seize power with an army.
death_of_sulla.debate: The phthiriasis story is generally rejected as a topos; the exact date in 78 is uncertain.
scholarship: Keaveney, Sulla: The Last Republican (1982)

revolt_of_lepidus.detail: Lucius Marcius Philippus' speech for the senatus consultum ultimum survives in Sallust's Histories. It was the first test of Sulla's system and it held, but only through Pompey, a privatus with an army.

tabularium_78.debate: Whether the building was the tabularium of the state or a substructure for Capitoline temples has been questioned (Tucci, 2005).

battle_of_the_campus_martius_77.detail: Marcus Perperna took the remnant, Plutarch says 53 cohorts, to Sertorius in Spain. Brutus' son never forgave Pompey, yet joined him in 49.

scholarship: Vervaet, The High Command in the Roman Republic (2014)

sources.w: De imperio Cn. Pompei (Pro lege Manilia)

siege_of_lauro.detail: Sertorius is said to have remarked that a general should look behind as well as ahead. Frontinus preserves the ambush in detail.

battle_of_the_sucro.detail: Plutarch has Sertorius say that if the old woman had not turned up, he would have thrashed the boy and sent him back to Rome.

battle_of_saguntum_75.debate: Site disputed between Saguntum on the coast and Segontia (Sigüenza) inland.

sertorius_mithridates_treaty.detail: Mithridates is said to have exclaimed what a Roman Sertorius would demand if he ruled from the Palatine, when he set such terms as an exile. Cilician pirates linked the two.

sources.w: De imperio Cn. Pompei (Pro lege Manilia)

caesar_and_the_pirates.detail: Suetonius adds that, as a mercy, he had their throats cut before they were crucified. The story's details come from Caesar's own circle but its core is not doubted. Date 75 or 74.

scholarship: Ribera i Lacomba and Calvo Galvez, 'La primera evidencia arqueológica de la destrucción de Valentia por Pompeyo', JRA 8 (1995)

pompeys_letter_to_the_senate_75.debate: The text in Sallust's Histories is a Sallustian composition, not a verbatim letter.

antonius_creticus_command_74.detail: The command was the precedent for Pompey's lex Gabinia, but its failure was spectacular. Rome's retaliation came with Quintus Caecilius Metellus' conquest of Crete (69-67).

siege_of_cyzicus.detail:
In 74, after Nicomedes IV bequeathed Bithynia to Rome, Mithridates invaded with an army the sources put at 120,000 foot and 16,000 horse, defeated the consul Marcus Aurelius Cotta by land and sea at Chalcedon, and turned west to besiege Cyzicus, a wealthy city on an island joined to the mainland by bridges on the Propontis. He brought siege towers, including a hundred-cubit tower on ships, rams and a mole across the strait. The consul Lucius Licinius Lucullus, with five legions (about 30,000 men) and 2,500 cavalry, followed and occupied a hill behind the Pontic camp that controlled its supply routes, Mithridates having been persuaded by the renegade Lucius Magius, a Sertorian envoy, that the Roman soldiers would defect.

Lucullus' strategy was to starve the besiegers rather than fight. The Cyzicenes held out heroically: they burned the siege engines, cut the mole, and repaired breaches, helped by a storm that wrecked the Pontic siege towers, which the citizens attributed to Persephone, their patron goddess, whose sacrificial heifer swam across to the city. Winter came, famine and plague struck the huge Pontic army, and soldiers resorted to cannibalism. Mithridates sent his cavalry and baggage away, and Lucullus caught them at the Rhyndacus in snow, killing many and taking 15,000 prisoners and 6,000 horses.

In spring 73 Mithridates abandoned the siege. His fleet escaped by sea, but his land army retreated to Lampsacus and was cut to pieces by Lucullus at the Aesepus and Granicus. Of the invading force, Plutarch claims, perhaps 300,000 combatants and followers perished, an impossible figure that nonetheless reflects catastrophe.

Cyzicus was rewarded with freedom and territory, and its siege became a model of how to defeat a superior army by logistics. It was the turning point of the Third Mithridatic War.
siege_of_cyzicus.debate: Pontic army size and losses are grossly inflated in Plutarch and Appian.
scholarship: Keaveney, Lucullus: A Life (1992)
McGing, The Foreign Policy of Mithridates VI Eupator (1986)

sources.w: De imperio Cn. Pompei (Pro lege Manilia)

murder_of_sertorius.detail:
By 73 the tide in Spain had turned against Sertorius. Metellus Pius and Pompey had recovered the east coast and much of the Celtiberian interior, and Pompey's army, reinforced after his letter of 75, ground down Sertorian towns. Metellus offered a reward of 100 talents and 20,000 iugera of land for Sertorius' death. Sertorius himself, according to Plutarch, grew harsh and suspicious, surrounding himself with a Spanish bodyguard, punishing the boys of the Osca school and alienating Roman officers.

The plot was led by Marcus Perperna Veiento, the aristocratic former Lepidan who had joined Sertorius in 77 with his own army and resented his subordinate role. At a banquet at Osca, arranged by Perperna to celebrate a fictitious victory, the conspirators behaved with deliberate indecency to provoke Sertorius; when he turned away on his couch in disgust, Perperna gave a signal by dropping a cup, and they stabbed him to death. The Iberian devoti who had sworn to die with him killed themselves.

Perperna took command, but his army distrusted him. In 72 Pompey lured him into an ambush and destroyed his forces. Perperna offered Pompey Sertorius' correspondence, which supposedly incriminated leading Roman senators; Pompey burned the letters unread and executed him, an act widely praised as statesmanlike. The last Sertorian towns, Uxama, Clunia and Calagurris, fell soon after, Calagurris only after famine drove its people to cannibalism.

Sertorius' career fascinated ancient writers. Plutarch paired him with Eumenes of Cardia, another foreign general fighting for a cause in exile. Sallust, whose Histories gave him a central role, presented him as a talented Roman who deserved better. Spain was pacified by Pompey, who settled his veterans and rewarded supporters with citizenship, building a Pompeian clientele there that would fight for his sons a generation later.
murder_of_sertorius.debate: Date of the murder 73 or 72. Date (73 or 72) and place (Osca) of the murder are not certain.
scholarship: Spann, Quintus Sertorius and the Legacy of Sulla (1987)
Konrad, Plutarch's Sertorius (1994)

escape_from_capua.detail:
In 73 some seventy-eight gladiators broke out of the training school of Gnaeus Lentulus Batiatus at Capua, armed with kitchen knives and spits, seized a wagon carrying gladiatorial weapons and made for Mount Vesuvius, then a wooded mountain with a flat crater top. They chose three leaders: the Thracian Spartacus, who had served in the Roman army as an auxiliary before deserting, and the Gauls Crixus and Oenomaus. Plutarch says Spartacus' wife, a prophetess of Dionysus, had foretold his greatness when a snake coiled round his face as he slept.

Rome treated the outbreak as a police matter. The praetor Gaius Claudius Glaber, with 3,000 hastily raised men, besieged the fugitives on Vesuvius; Spartacus' men climbed down a cliff on ladders woven from wild vines and attacked Glaber's camp from behind, routing it. A second praetor, Publius Varinius, was defeated in several encounters, losing his lictors and horse. Slaves, herdsmen and free rural poor joined in thousands, and the movement spread through Campania, Lucania and Apulia, sacking towns such as Nola, Nuceria, Thurii and Metapontum.

The ancient sources disagree on Spartacus' aims. Plutarch portrays him as wanting to lead his followers home across the Alps; Appian says he sought to march on Rome; Sallust's fragments show internal disputes between Spartacus and the Gauls who wanted to plunder Italy. Modern interpretations range from the Marxist image of a revolutionary seeking to abolish slavery, influential in the twentieth century, to the view (Shaw, Strauss) that the revolt had no programme beyond survival and plunder.

The revolt grew because Rome's best armies were in Spain under Pompey and in Asia under Lucullus. By 72 Spartacus commanded perhaps 70,000 or more, and the third servile war had become a major military crisis in Italy.
escape_from_capua.debate: Spartacus' goals and the social composition of his army (slaves only, or free poor as well) are debated.
scholarship: Shaw, Spartacus and the Slave Wars (2001)
Strauss, The Spartacus War (2009)
Bradley, Slavery and Rebellion in the Roman World (1989)

battle_of_cabira.detail: Before fleeing he sent a eunuch to Pharnacia to kill his sisters and wives, including the Milesian Monime, rather than let them be captured.

battle_of_picenum_72.detail: Why he turned back is a mystery: Plutarch says the slaves refused to leave Italy, preferring plunder. Appian claims he considered marching on Rome. The senate stripped the consuls of command and gave it to Crassus.

battle_of_mutina_72.debate: Why Spartacus turned back (overconfidence, his followers' wish to plunder Italy, or fear of the Alpine crossing) is unknowable.

crassus_decimation.detail: Appian gives a second version in which 4,000 were executed. Either way the shock restored discipline. Crassus had been given an extraordinary command with six new legions plus the consular armies.

battle_of_the_silarus_71.detail:
After Spartacus broke through Crassus' fortified line in Bruttium in winter 72/71, his army divided again; Crassus destroyed the Gallic and German breakaway force under Castus and Gannicus at a Lucanian lake. Meanwhile the Senate had recalled Pompey from Spain and Lucullus' brother Marcus Lucullus from Thrace, giving Crassus every reason to finish the war before they claimed the credit. Spartacus, harried by Crassus' cavalry, turned to fight in Lucania near the headwaters of the Silarus (Sele) river in spring 71.

Plutarch reports that before the battle Spartacus killed his horse, saying that if he won he would have many fine horses from the enemy, and if he lost he would not need one. He then tried to reach Crassus himself, killing two centurions, but was surrounded and cut down. His body was never found. Appian says that he was wounded in the thigh and fought on his knees. The slave army was destroyed; Appian puts the dead at a figure that cannot be trusted, but the result was decisive. About 6,000 prisoners were crucified along the Via Appia from Capua to Rome, a distance of some 200 km, as a deterrent.

Five thousand fugitives fled north and were intercepted in Etruria by Pompey, returning from Spain, who wrote to the Senate that while Crassus had defeated the slaves, he had torn out the war by the roots. The rivalry this provoked shaped their joint consulship of 70. Crassus received only an ovation, not a triumph, because the enemy were slaves, though he was allowed a laurel wreath instead of the usual myrtle.

The site has been placed near the modern town of Quaglietta in the upper Sele valley, or near Paestum; neither is certain. Spartacus' death ended the last great slave revolt of antiquity.
battle_of_the_silarus_71.debate: The location in the upper Silarus valley is approximate; Appian's figure of 60,000 slaves killed is not credible.
scholarship: Strauss, The Spartacus War (2009)
Shaw, Spartacus and the Slave Wars (2001)

lucullus_debt_relief_in_asia.detail: Plutarch says the cities celebrated festivals in his honour, but the equestrian financiers at Rome began the campaign that eventually stripped him of command.
scholarship: Badian, Roman Imperialism in the Late Republic (1968)

crassus_wall_in_bruttium_71.debate: The line's location (Catanzaro isthmus or further north, near the Sila) is uncertain.

trial_of_verres.detail:
Gaius Verres had governed Sicily as propraetor for three years (73-71), extended because of the Spartacus war, and stripped the province systematically: manipulating the grain tithes, selling verdicts, extorting money from cities, and seizing works of art from temples and private houses, including the statue of Diana at Segesta and the silver of Sicilian families. The Sicilian communities, many of which had been clients of Cicero since his quaestorship at Lilybaeum in 75, asked him to prosecute under the extortion law. Verres was defended by Quintus Hortensius, the leading orator of the day and consul-elect for 69.

Verres' strategy was delay: if the trial could be pushed into 69, Hortensius would be consul, Quintus Metellus would preside over the extortion court, and a sympathetic jury could be drawn. His friends first tried to install a sham prosecutor, Quintus Caecilius Niger, whom Cicero defeated in a preliminary hearing (Divinatio in Caecilium). Cicero then gathered evidence in Sicily in fifty days. At the trial in August 70 he abandoned the usual long opening speech and presented his witnesses and documents immediately, speaking only briefly (the Actio prima). The evidence was overwhelming; after nine days Verres went into voluntary exile at Massilia without waiting for the verdict.

Cicero then published the five speeches of the Actio secunda, which he never delivered, a comprehensive indictment covering the grain tithes, the art thefts (De signis) and the crucifixion of the Roman citizen Gavius at Messana, who cried 'I am a Roman citizen' as he was flogged. The damages assessed were three million sesterces against the forty million Cicero claimed.

The case made Cicero the foremost orator in Rome, overtaking Hortensius, and occurred as jury reform was being debated; the lex Aurelia followed. Verres lived in exile until 43, when he was proscribed by Antony, allegedly for refusing to give up his Corinthian bronzes.
scholarship: Lintott, Cicero as Evidence (2008)
Frazel, The Rhetoric of Cicero's In Verrem (2009)
Miles, Art as Plunder (2008)

consulship_of_pompey_and_crassus_70.detail:
Pompey and Crassus both stood for the consulship of 70 while still commanding armies outside Rome. Pompey, at thirty-five, had held no previous magistracy and was not even a senator; the Senate waived the requirements of the lex annalis. Crassus, who had held the praetorship, was legally qualified. Though rivals, they made a temporary alliance, and both were elected. Pompey celebrated his second triumph, for Spain, on 29 December 71, and appeared before the censors as an eques to report his military service, leading his horse through the Forum to great applause.

Their consulship dismantled the core of Sulla's settlement. A law of both consuls restored the tribunes' full powers, including legislative initiative, a cause Pompey had promised in his election speech and which the plebs had demanded since 78. The praetor Lucius Aurelius Cotta carried the lex Aurelia iudiciaria, dividing juries equally among senators, equites and tribuni aerarii. The censors, Gellius and Lentulus, the first since 86, expelled 64 senators and registered 910,000 citizens.

The year was marked by the trial of Verres and by public quarrels between the consuls. At the end of the year, Plutarch says, a Roman knight, Gaius Aurelius, reported that Jupiter had appeared to him in a dream ordering him to tell the consuls to be reconciled before laying down office. Crassus offered his hand to Pompey, and they parted publicly friends. Crassus had also celebrated by feasting the people at 10,000 tables and giving each citizen three months' grain.
