siege_of_uxellodunum.detail: Excavations at Puy d'Issolud found the Roman diversion tunnel and quantities of Roman arrowheads, confirming the identification.

publication_of_the_commentarii.detail: They are the only first-person account by a Roman general of his own war to survive, and the classic case of propaganda disguised as reportage: inflated enemy numbers (368,000 Helvetii, 430,000 Usipetes and Tencteri), blame shifted to subordinates (Sabinus), omission of awkward legal issues, and silence on profits. Whether books were issued annually or all at once in 51 is debated.
publication_of_the_commentarii.debate: Annual versus single publication; extent of deliberate distortion (Rambaud) versus conventional generalship reporting.
scholarship: Rambaud, L'art de la déformation historique dans les Commentaires de César (1953)
Welch & Powell (eds), Julius Caesar as Artful Reporter (1998)
Riggsby, Caesar in Gaul and Rome (2006)

de_re_publica_51.detail: Composed 54-51, it reflects Cicero's anxiety about the dynasts. The Somnium Scipionis survived separately through Macrobius' commentary and shaped medieval cosmology. Whether the 'princeps' of Books 5-6 anticipates Pompey or Augustus has been debated since the nineteenth century.

accession_of_cleopatra_51.detail: A papyrus decree of 50 BC concerning grain shipments shows the queen's name ahead of her brother's at first, and early dated documents suggest Cleopatra ruled alone in 51-50. The Buchis bull stele of Hermonthis claims she personally rowed the sacred bull to its installation in her first regnal year. Low Nile floods in 50-48 caused famine, weakening her position.
accession_of_cleopatra_51.debate: The precise date of Auletes' death (before 22 March 51, per a Buchis stele) and the length of Cleopatra's sole rule are debated.

curio_and_the_vote_of_1_december_50.detail:
Throughout 50 the question of Caesar's recall paralysed Roman politics. The consul Gaius Claudius Marcellus and the optimates sought to name a successor to Caesar's Gallic provinces; the tribune Gaius Scribonius Curio, now in Caesar's pay, vetoed every attempt, proposing instead that Caesar and Pompey both give up their armies simultaneously. The proposal was popular, as it seemed to offer peace.

On 1 December 50 Marcellus put two questions to the Senate separately. On whether Caesar should be replaced, the Senate voted yes; on whether Pompey should be replaced, it voted no. Curio then demanded a vote on whether both should lay down their commands. The Senate voted 370 to 22 in favour. Marcellus dismissed the meeting, saying 'Have it your way: Caesar as your master!' The crowd showered Curio with flowers.

The next day, on a false rumour that Caesar was marching on Italy with ten legions, Marcellus went to Pompey's villa outside the city with the consuls-designate, handed him a sword, and asked him to take command of the two legions at Capua (those withdrawn from Caesar for the Parthian war) and raise more troops in defence of the state. Pompey accepted, 'unless something better could be found'. Curio's tribunate ended on 9 December; he went to Caesar at Ravenna and returned to Rome on 1 January 49 with Caesar's last offer.

The vote of 1 December shows that most senators wanted peace and were willing to strip both dynasts of power, but a small group of optimates, led by Cato, Marcellus and Lentulus Crus, preferred war to compromise. Modern accounts (Morstein-Marx, Raaflaub) emphasise this vote as evidence that the civil war was not inevitable.
scholarship: Gruen, The Last Generation of the Roman Republic (1974)
Morstein-Marx, Julius Caesar and the Roman People (2021)
Raaflaub, Dignitatis contentio (1974)

philodemus_and_the_villa_of_the_papyri.detail: The papyri, found in 1752-54, are the only intact library to survive from antiquity; since 2023 machine learning applied to X-ray scans has begun to read unopened scrolls. Virgil and Varius studied with Philodemus and Siro in the Epicurean circle on the Bay of Naples.
philodemus_and_the_villa_of_the_papyri.debate: Ownership of the villa by Piso is an inference, widely accepted but unproven.

caesar_overruns_picenum_49.detail: The speed and the lack of resistance shocked Pompey, who had boasted that he could raise legions by stamping his foot. Cicero's letters of these weeks show the panic of the propertied classes and the gradual realisation that Caesar's clemency (he released captured officers unharmed) was a deliberate policy contrasting with memories of Sulla.

senatus_consultum_ultimum_49.detail:
On 1 January 49 Curio delivered Caesar's letter to the new consuls, Lucius Cornelius Lentulus Crus and Gaius Claudius Marcellus. The tribunes Mark Antony and Quintus Cassius forced its reading: Caesar listed his services and offered to lay down his command if Pompey did the same, failing which he would defend his rights and the state's liberty. The consuls refused a debate on it. Metellus Scipio, speaking for Pompey, proposed that Caesar be ordered to disband his army by a fixed date or be considered a public enemy; Antony and Cassius vetoed it.

Private negotiations continued for a week. Caesar, through his friends and through Cicero, who had just returned from Cilicia hoping for a triumph, reduced his demands to keeping Illyricum and one legion until his consulship; Pompey seemed willing, but Lentulus, Cato and Marcellus refused. On 7 January the Senate passed the senatus consultum ultimum, instructing the consuls, praetors, tribunes and proconsuls near the city, that is Pompey, to see that the state came to no harm. Antony and Cassius, warned that their safety could not be guaranteed, fled the city disguised as slaves in a hired carriage, with Curio and Caelius, to join Caesar at Ravenna.

The Senate then assigned provinces: Domitius Ahenobarbus to succeed Caesar in Transalpine Gaul, Considius Nonianus in the Cisalpina, Metellus Scipio to Syria, and others. Levies were ordered throughout Italy, and money was voted to Pompey from the treasury.

Caesar used the treatment of the tribunes as his justification for invasion: the sacrosanctity of the tribunate had been violated, as in Sulla's time. His own account in the Civil War opens with this narrative, placing responsibility on the intransigence of a small faction. Modern historians debate the balance of responsibility; Raaflaub emphasises Caesar's concern for his dignitas, others the optimates' determination to destroy him.
scholarship: Raaflaub, Dignitatis contentio (1974)
Morstein-Marx, Julius Caesar and the Roman People (2021)

crossing_of_the_rubicon.detail:
On the night of 10/11 January 49 by the unreformed calendar (late November in solar terms), Caesar crossed the Rubicon, the small river that marked the boundary between his province of Cisalpine Gaul and Italy proper, with the Thirteenth legion. Leading an army out of his province without the Senate's authority was treason under Sulla's lex Cornelia de maiestate. He had spent the day publicly at Ravenna, attending a show and a dinner, before slipping away in a carriage drawn by mules from a nearby bakery, losing his way in the dark before finding the road.

Suetonius' account, probably from Asinius Pollio, who was present, describes Caesar hesitating at the bridge, saying to his companions that turning back was still possible but crossing meant war. Then a figure of extraordinary size and beauty appeared, playing a reed pipe; shepherds and soldiers gathered to listen, and he seized a trumpet from a soldier and sounded the advance as he crossed. Caesar exclaimed, 'Let us go where the signs of the gods and the injustice of our enemies call us. The die is cast.' Plutarch, also following Pollio, says Caesar spoke in Greek, quoting Menander: 'anerriphtho kubos', let the die be thrown.

Caesar himself does not mention the Rubicon in his Civil War; he simply says he addressed his soldiers at Ravenna and marched to Ariminum. The silence was deliberate: the crossing was the moment of illegality.

The identification of the river is uncertain. In 1933 Mussolini officially identified it with the Fiumicino near Savignano, renamed Rubicone, but the Pisciatello and the Uso have also been proposed. The phrase 'crossing the Rubicon' became proverbial for an irrevocable decision.
crossing_of_the_rubicon.debate: Exact date (10 or 11 January by the pre-Julian calendar; about late November 50 in Julian terms). The river's identity (Fiumicino, Pisciatello or Uso), and whether Caesar's words were Latin or Greek, are debated.
scholarship: Morstein-Marx, Julius Caesar and the Roman People (2021)
Beard, 'The Rubicon', in SPQR (2015)
Pelling, Plutarch: Caesar (2011)

siege_of_corfinium.detail: Domitius had tried to poison himself, but his doctor gave him a sleeping draught. Caesar's letter about his clemency survives in Cicero's correspondence (Att. 9.7C). Domitius promptly went to hold Massilia against him.

caesar_seizes_the_aerarium.detail: Pliny gives 15,000 gold bars, 30,000 silver bars and 30 million sesterces in coin. Caesar's De Bello Civili omits the episode.

battle_of_the_bagradas.detail: Caesar's account is unusually generous to a subordinate and reads as a eulogy. Juba killed many of the prisoners against Varus' wishes.

battle_of_ilerda.detail:
After securing Italy and Rome in 49, Caesar marched to Spain to destroy Pompey's legions there, 'going against an army without a general, before turning against a general without an army'. Pompey's legates Lucius Afranius and Marcus Petreius, with five legions plus Spanish auxiliaries, had concentrated at Ilerda (Lleida), a town on a hill above the river Sicoris (Segre). Caesar's legate Gaius Fabius arrived first with three legions, and Caesar joined in June with 900 cavalry.

The campaign was one of manoeuvre. An early Caesarian attempt to seize a hill between Ilerda and the Pompeian camp failed. Then floods swept away the bridges over the Sicoris, cutting Caesar off from his supplies; a large supply convoy from Gaul was nearly lost, and grain prices in his camp soared. In Rome the Pompeians celebrated. Caesar built boats of wicker and hides, on the British model, and established a new bridgehead upstream; his cavalry then harried the Pompeian foragers.

The Pompeians tried to withdraw south across the Ebro to Celtiberia. Caesar's men forded the Sicoris neck-deep, with the cavalry breaking the current, and overtook them in the hills. He refused to fight, despite his soldiers' eagerness, preferring to cut them off from water. Soldiers of the two armies began to fraternise, until Petreius massacred Caesarians in his camp. Finally, short of water and food, Afranius and Petreius surrendered on 2 August 49.

Caesar released the Pompeian soldiers, disbanding some and letting others return to Italy, and pardoned the commanders, who went straight to Pompey. Ilerda was a masterpiece of bloodless strategy and a propaganda triumph for Caesar's clemency. Further Spain, under Varro, surrendered soon after.
scholarship: Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (2006)
Carter, Julius Caesar: The Civil War Books I and II (1991)

caesars_debt_settlement_49.detail: The measures disappointed radicals such as Caelius and Dolabella, who agitated for cancellation in 48 and 47, but preserved the property order. Caesar boasted that he had spared creditors' principal; Suetonius estimates the overall reduction at a quarter.

caesar_elephant_denarius_49.debate: Meaning of the elephant (victory over evil, a pun on Punic 'caesai' for elephant per the Historia Augusta, or Africa) is debated.
scholarship: Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974) no. 443

caesar_crosses_to_epirus_48.detail: The crossing in winter, against a superior fleet, was a typical Caesarian gamble. Plutarch's story belongs here: impatient for reinforcements, Caesar tried to cross back in a small boat in disguise and told the frightened helmsman, 'You carry Caesar and his fortune.' Bibulus died of exhaustion and illness while maintaining the blockade.

battle_of_dyrrhachium.detail:
After crossing to Epirus in January 48 and receiving Antony's reinforcements in spring, Caesar, with some 22,000 men, confronted Pompey, whose army of perhaps 45,000 was encamped on the coast near Dyrrachium (Durrës), supplied by sea. Caesar attempted the extraordinary feat of besieging a larger army: he built a line of fortifications some seventeen miles long around Pompey's position on the hills south of the town, while Pompey built an inner line of fifteen miles. Caesar's men, short of grain, made bread from a root called chara, which they threw into Pompey's lines to show they could eat anything.

Pompey's cavalry suffered for lack of fodder, and his army from lack of water, as Caesar diverted the streams. But in July, informed by two Allobrogian deserters of a weak point at the southern end of Caesar's line near the sea, Pompey launched a combined land and sea attack. The Ninth legion was overwhelmed; Caesar's counterattack with thirty-three cohorts went astray in the maze of fortifications and was routed. Caesar lost 960 men and 32 military tribunes and centurions, and 32 standards. He seized a standard-bearer to halt the flight, and the man tried to strike him.

Caesar said afterward that the war would have been over that day if the enemy had had a commander who knew how to win; Pompey, suspecting a trap, did not pursue. Labienus executed the Caesarian prisoners. Caesar retreated to Apollonia and then into Thessaly to join Domitius Calvinus and find supplies, sacking Gomphi.

Dyrrachium encouraged the Pompeian leadership to press Pompey for a decisive battle, which led to Pharsalus. Their overconfidence was fatal: senators quarrelled over Caesar's priesthood and confiscated properties before the battle.
battle_of_dyrrhachium.debate: Casualty figures are Caesar's own; Orosius gives 4,000 dead.
scholarship: Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (2006)

battle_of_pharsalus.detail:
On 9 August 48 (by the unreformed calendar, about 7 June solar), on the plain of Pharsalus in Thessaly near the river Enipeus, Pompey, pressed by his senatorial advisers, offered battle. He had about 45,000 legionaries in 110 cohorts and 7,000 cavalry; Caesar, 22,000 legionaries in 80 cohorts and 1,000 cavalry. Pompey anchored his right on the river and massed his cavalry under Labienus on the left, planning to sweep around Caesar's right flank and roll up his line. He ordered his infantry to stand and receive the Caesarian charge rather than advance, to tire the enemy.

Caesar anticipated the plan. He took one cohort from the third line of each legion to form a fourth line of six cohorts, hidden behind his right-wing cavalry, with orders to use their pila as spears against the faces of the cavalry. When Labienus' horsemen drove back Caesar's cavalry, the fourth line charged; the inexperienced Pompeian horsemen, many young aristocrats, fled to the hills. The cohorts then turned on Pompey's archers and slingers and attacked the left flank of his infantry. Caesar's veterans, having halted in the middle of their charge to recover their breath when they saw Pompey's men stand, threw their pila and engaged. Caesar then committed his third line, and the Pompeian army collapsed.

Caesar claims he lost 200 men and 30 centurions; the Pompeians 15,000 dead and 24,000 captured. Asinius Pollio, present, gave 6,000 Pompeian dead. Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus was killed. Caesar, viewing the dead, said: 'They wanted it; after such deeds, I, Gaius Caesar, would have been condemned had I not sought help from my army.' He pardoned most prisoners, including Brutus, and burned Pompey's correspondence unread.

Pompey fled to the coast and sailed for Egypt. Pharsalus effectively decided the civil war, though resistance continued in Africa and Spain.
battle_of_pharsalus.debate: Battlefield location; Caesar's numbers (especially Pompeian losses) versus Pollio's. The battlefield's location north or south of the Enipeus is disputed; Caesar's casualty figures are certainly too low for his side.
scholarship: Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (2006)
Gelzer, Caesar: Politician and Statesman (1968)
Pelling, Plutarch: Caesar (2011)

death_of_pompey.detail:
After Pharsalus Pompey fled via Larisa and Amphipolis to Mytilene, where he collected his wife Cornelia and his son Sextus, and then along the coast of Asia Minor to Cyprus. Rejecting Parthia and Juba, he decided to seek refuge in Egypt, whose young king, Ptolemy XIII, owed his throne to Pompey's support of Ptolemy XII. He arrived off Pelusium on 28 September 48, where the boy king's army was facing that of his sister Cleopatra.

The king's advisers, the eunuch Pothinus, the general Achillas and the rhetorician Theodotus of Chios, debated whether to receive him. Theodotus argued that a dead man does not bite; to receive Pompey would make Caesar an enemy, to refuse him would make Pompey one. They sent a small boat with Achillas and two Roman officers, Lucius Septimius, a former centurion of Pompey's, and Salvius. As Pompey stepped ashore, Septimius stabbed him in the back; Pompey covered his face with his toga and died without a word, on the day after his fifty-eighth birthday. Cornelia watched from the ship. His head was cut off and preserved; his body was left on the beach, where his freedman Philippus burned it on a pyre made from a broken boat.

When Caesar arrived in Alexandria a few days later, Theodotus presented the head and Pompey's signet ring, showing a lion holding a sword. Caesar wept and turned away, ordered the head buried in a shrine of Nemesis near the city, and had Pompey's killers put to death in time. Theodotus fled and was later executed by Brutus.

Pompey's death became a moral exemplum of the reversal of fortune. Cicero commented that he could not doubt how Pompey's life would end; Lucan made the scene the centrepiece of Book 8. His ashes were returned to Cornelia, who buried them at his Alban villa.
death_of_pompey.debate: Date: Velleius and Plutarch agree on the day after his birthday (29 September, unreformed calendar).
scholarship: Seager, Pompey the Great (2002)

siege_of_alexandria_48.detail:
Caesar landed at Alexandria in early October 48 with only 3,200 infantry and 800 cavalry. He insisted on settling the dispute between Ptolemy XIII and Cleopatra under Ptolemy XII's will, and demanded repayment of the old debts. After Cleopatra's arrival and his decision in her favour, the Alexandrians and Ptolemy's army of 20,000 under Achillas, including many of Gabinius' former soldiers settled in Egypt, rose against him. Caesar was besieged in the palace quarter for some six months.

Caesar fortified the palace and the theatre, burned the Egyptian fleet in the harbour, with the fire spreading to the docks and possibly to warehouses of books, and seized the Pharos lighthouse. Cleopatra's younger sister Arsinoe escaped to the Egyptian army, was proclaimed queen, and had Achillas killed by her eunuch Ganymedes, who took command. Ganymedes tried to poison Caesar's water by pumping seawater into the cisterns; Caesar dug new wells. Caesar released Ptolemy XIII, who had been his hostage, hoping he would end the war, but he joined the Egyptian forces.

In a battle for the Heptastadion, the mole linking the Pharos to the mainland, Caesar's men were routed and he had to swim for safety. Reinforcements came from Asia: the Thirty-Seventh legion, formed from Pompey's surrendered troops, and a relief army under Mithridates of Pergamon, with 3,000 Jews under Antipater. Mithridates took Pelusium and marched up the Delta; Caesar joined him, and in March 47 they defeated the Egyptian army at the battle of the Nile, where Ptolemy XIII drowned.

The Alexandrian War was described in the Bellum Alexandrinum, probably by Hirtius. It was the most dangerous episode of Caesar's career after Dyrrachium, entered into, his critics thought, for Cleopatra's sake.
siege_of_alexandria_48.debate: Extent of damage to the Library of Alexandria.
scholarship: Roller, Cleopatra (2010)
Goldsworthy, Antony and Cleopatra (2010)
Hölbl, A History of the Ptolemaic Empire (2001)

cleopatra_meets_caesar_48.detail: Dio has her win Caesar by her beauty and wit; modern historians stress that Caesar needed Egyptian grain and money (he demanded 17.5 million denarii owed by Auletes) and that Cleopatra was the more capable partner. The carpet of modern films comes from Plutarch's strômatodesmon, a bag for bedding.

revolt_against_cassius_longinus_48.detail: The revolt showed how Caesarian government could alienate even loyal provinces. The disaffected legions later formed the core of the Pompeian army of Gnaeus Pompeius in 46-45.

fire_at_alexandria_48.debate: Most scholars think books stored in warehouses near the harbour burned, not the Library itself, which continued to function; Mark Antony's alleged gift of 200,000 scrolls from Pergamon (Plutarch, Antony 58) is reported as a hostile rumour.

battle_of_the_nile.detail: Caesar then spent weeks on a Nile cruise with Cleopatra, according to Suetonius nearly to Ethiopia. Antipater was rewarded with Roman citizenship and his son Herod's career began. A son, Ptolemy Caesar (Caesarion), was born in 47, whose paternity became political dynamite.

battle_of_zela.detail:
While Caesar was trapped in Alexandria, Pharnaces II, son of Mithridates and king of the Bosporus, exploited the civil war to reconquer his father's kingdom of Pontus and invade Lesser Armenia and Cappadocia. At Nicopolis in late 48 he defeated Caesar's legate Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus, whose army included Deiotarus' legions trained in the Roman manner, and then occupied Pontus, castrating Roman captives and massacring Romans at Amisus.

Caesar, after settling Egypt and Syria, marched rapidly through Cilicia and Cappadocia in summer 47, collecting troops: the veteran Sixth legion, reduced to under 1,000 men, Deiotarus' legion, and two others. Pharnaces, sending envoys and offering terms, tried to delay him; Caesar refused. Pharnaces took position on a hill near Zela in Pontus, the scene of his father's victory over Triarius in 67. On 2 August 47, while the Romans were fortifying a camp on the opposite hill, Pharnaces attacked uphill with scythed chariots and infantry. The surprised Romans recovered, the Sixth legion broke the Pontic line, and the army was routed within four hours. Pharnaces fled to the Bosporus, where he was killed by his governor Asander.

Caesar wrote to his friend Matius in Rome 'veni, vidi, vici', I came, I saw, I conquered; in his Pontic triumph the next year the words were displayed on a placard. He also remarked on Pompey's good luck in having won his reputation against such enemies.

The battle restored Roman control in Anatolia. Caesar rewarded Mithridates of Pergamon with the Bosporan kingdom and part of Galatia, and confirmed the arrangements of the client kings, fining those who had supported Pompey, including Deiotarus.
scholarship: Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (2006)

mutiny_of_the_tenth.detail: That same year Dolabella's agitation for debt cancellation led to street fighting in Rome that Antony, as master of horse, suppressed with troops.

caesar_and_cleopatra_on_the_nile_47.debate: The Nile cruise is doubted by some as romantic embroidery; Caesarion's paternity was contested by Caesar's partisans (Oppius wrote a pamphlet denying it).

caesar_rewards_antipater_47.detail: These privileges became the charter of Jewish communities across the empire, cited for centuries. Antipater appointed his sons Phasael and Herod governors of Jerusalem and Galilee; Herod's summary execution of the bandit chief Hezekiah got him summoned before the Sanhedrin.

varro_antiquitates_47.detail: Varro arranged Roman religion under the headings of men, places, times and rites, and distinguished the theology of the poets, of the philosophers and of the state. He is credited with fixing the 'Varronian' foundation date of Rome at 753, which this atlas uses. His output, some 74 works in 620 books, was proverbial; his De lingua Latina (c. 43) partly survives.
varro_antiquitates_47.debate: Date of publication (47 or 46) is uncertain.

suicide_of_cato.detail:
Marcus Porcius Cato commanded the Pompeian garrison at Utica, the capital of the province of Africa, during the campaign of 46, having led the remnants of Pompey's fleet from Corcyra and marched an army across the desert of Libya from Cyrenaica in thirty days. When news of Thapsus arrived, he tried to organise resistance among the 300 Roman merchants and senators in Utica, then, seeing that they wanted to surrender, helped them escape by sea and refused to seek Caesar's pardon himself, saying he would not accept a favour from a tyrant who had no right to grant it.

On the night of his death, in mid-April 46, he dined with friends and discussed the Stoic paradox that only the good man is free. He then retired and read Plato's Phaedo, on the immortality of the soul, twice. Finding his sword had been removed by his son, he demanded it back; at dawn he stabbed himself in the stomach. His doctor found him still alive and bandaged the wound, but Cato tore it open with his hands and died. He was forty-eight.

Caesar, on hearing the news, said: 'Cato, I begrudge you your death, as you begrudged me the chance to save your life.' The people of Utica buried him with honour and set up a statue of him with a sword.

Cato's death made him the martyr of the Republic. Cicero wrote a eulogy, Cato, Brutus another, and Caesar replied with the Anticato. Lucan made him the moral hero of the Pharsalia, Seneca the model Stoic sage, and Virgil placed him giving laws to the righteous in Elysium. In later centuries he became a symbol of republican virtue and resistance to tyranny, as in Addison's Cato (1713), admired by George Washington.
scholarship: Goar, The Legend of Cato Uticensis (1987)
Morrell, Pompey, Cato, and the Governance of the Roman Empire (2017)

battle_of_thapsus.detail:
In Africa the Pompeians regrouped under Metellus Scipio, with Labienus, Afranius, Petreius, and King Juba I of Numidia, with ten legions, 15,000 cavalry, light troops and 120 elephants. Caesar landed near Hadrumetum in late December 47 with too few troops and was nearly defeated at Ruspina in January 46. After months of manoeuvre in Byzacena, reinforced to ten legions, he besieged Thapsus, a coastal town on a narrow isthmus between the sea and a salt lagoon, to force Scipio to battle.

On 6 April 46 Scipio and Juba approached in two groups to relieve the town and began fortifying positions. Caesar deployed his legions in three lines, with five cohorts of the Fifth legion on each wing to face the elephants, which they had trained to fight using elephants imported from Italy. Before Caesar gave the signal, a trumpeter on the right, urged on by the eager veterans, sounded the attack. Caesar, seeing that he could not stop it, spurred his horse into the charge. Slingers and archers stampeded the elephants on the Pompeian left, which trampled their own men; a wounded elephant attacked a camp follower and was killed by a soldier of the Fifth, which afterwards bore an elephant on its standards.

The Pompeian army collapsed. Caesar's veterans, embittered by years of war, massacred those who tried to surrender, ignoring his orders; the Bellum Africum gives 10,000 Pompeian dead, against 50 Caesarians. Plutarch reports a story that Caesar suffered an epileptic seizure at the start of the battle and took no part.

Thapsus destroyed the Pompeian cause in Africa. Cato killed himself at Utica, Juba and Petreius killed each other, Scipio drowned himself, Afranius was killed. Labienus and Pompey's sons escaped to Spain.
battle_of_thapsus.debate: The epileptic seizure story in Plutarch and the casualty figures are uncertain.
scholarship: Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (2006)

caesars_quadruple_triumph.detail:
Between late July and early September 46, Caesar celebrated four triumphs on separate days over Gaul, Egypt, Pontus and Africa. He did not triumph over Roman citizens, framing the African victory as over Juba. The Gallic triumph displayed Vercingetorix, who was then executed; his chariot's axle broke as it passed the temple of Fortuna, and Caesar climbed the Capitoline steps on his knees, flanked by elephants carrying torches. The Egyptian triumph displayed Arsinoe IV, whose presence moved the crowd to pity, and images of the Nile and the burning Pharos. The Pontic triumph carried the placard 'veni vidi vici'. The African triumph showed the young son of Juba, the future Juba II, and caused offence with images of the suicides of Scipio, Petreius and Cato.

Caesar's soldiers marched singing obscene songs, including 'Citizens, lock up your wives: we bring the bald adulterer' and verses about his supposed affair with Nicomedes of Bithynia. Each veteran received 5,000 denarii, centurions twice and tribunes four times as much; each citizen 400 sesterces, plus grain and oil. The triumphs brought 65,000 talents in coin, 2,822 golden crowns.

Spectacles followed: a feast at 22,000 tables, gladiatorial combats in the Forum, a mock naval battle on an artificial lake in the Campus Martius with Tyrian and Egyptian fleets, a battle between armies of 500 infantry, 30 cavalry and 20 elephants each in the Circus, and the first giraffe seen in Rome. A silk awning protected spectators. On the final day he dedicated the Forum Iulium and the temple of Venus Genetrix.

The triumphs announced Caesar's supremacy. The Senate had voted him a dictatorship for ten years, a forty-day supplicatio, and 72 lictors, three times the normal number.
scholarship: Beard, The Roman Triumph (2007)
Östenberg, Staging the World (2009)

forum_iulium_dedicated_46.detail: The Forum Iulium was a colonnaded rectangle about 160 by 75 metres with the temple at its north-west end, the template for the imperial fora of Augustus, Vespasian, Nerva and Trajan. Its message was dynastic: Venus Genetrix was the mother of Aeneas and so of the Julii. An equestrian statue of Caesar stood in front of the temple, on a horse said to have had human forefeet. Caesar's plan to receive the Senate seated before the temple, without rising, was remembered as one of the gestures that turned opinion against him. The complex was completed by Augustus and rebuilt after the fire of AD 80 by Domitian and Trajan, whose rebuild of the temple and Basilica Argentaria survives in part today.
forum_iulium_dedicated_46.debate: Date of the temple's design (begun 54 as a forum, temple added after the Pharsalus vow) and the meaning of Cleopatra's statue are debated.
scholarship: Ulrich, 'Julius Caesar and the creation of the Forum Iulium', AJA 97 (1993)
Westall, 'The Forum Iulium as representation of imperator Caesar', MDAI(R) 103 (1996)

julian_calendar_reform.detail:
The Roman Republican calendar had 355 days, kept in line with the solar year by intercalating a month of 22 or 23 days in some years, a decision left to the pontifices, who had manipulated or neglected it for political reasons. By 46 the calendar was about three months ahead of the seasons: the 'harvest festival' fell in spring. Caesar, as pontifex maximus and dictator, with the advice of the Alexandrian astronomer Sosigenes and the scribe Marcus Flavius, introduced a solar calendar of 365 days, with an extra day every fourth year inserted after 23 February (the sixth day before the Kalends of March doubled, hence 'bissextile').

To realign the calendar with the seasons, 46 was given 445 days, the 'year of confusion' (annus confusionis): the regular intercalary month after February, and two extra months between November and December, totalling 67 extra days. The new calendar began on 1 January 45. The ten days added to the shorter months were placed at the end so as not to disturb the dates of festivals.

After Caesar's death, the pontifices misinterpreted the rule and intercalated every third year (counting inclusively), so that by 9 BC there had been three extra leap days; Augustus suspended intercalation until AD 8. In 44 the month Quinctilis was renamed Iulius in Caesar's honour; Sextilis became Augustus in 8 BC.

The Julian calendar, with a year of 365.25 days, was about eleven minutes too long; by the sixteenth century the error amounted to ten days, which led to Pope Gregory XIII's reform of 1582. It remained in use in Russia until 1918 and in Orthodox churches. Cicero, told that the constellation Lyra would rise the next day, remarked: 'Yes, by edict.'
scholarship: Feeney, Caesar's Calendar (2007)
Rüpke, The Roman Calendar from Numa to Constantine (2011)
Bennett, 'The early Augustan calendars in Rome and Egypt', ZPE 142 (2003)

africa_nova_46.detail: Sallust's governorship ended in charges of extortion from which Caesar shielded him; he retired to write history in the famous gardens on the Quirinal paid for, his enemies said, by Africa. Sittius' colonists at Cirta formed the nucleus of the later Cirtan confederation of four colonies.

reduction_of_the_grain_dole_46.debate: Some scholars think the 320,000 figure counted all male citizens in Rome and the cut was smaller; the closed list of 150,000 remained a model for Augustus' 200,000.

cleopatra_in_rome_46.debate: Whether she stayed continuously from 46 to 44 or made two visits is disputed.

scholarship: Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974) no. 466

battle_of_munda.detail:
In 46 the Pompeian cause revived in Further Spain, where the legions of Quintus Cassius' former army mutinied and invited Gnaeus Pompeius, Pompey's elder son, to lead them. With his brother Sextus and Labienus, he raised thirteen legions, many of them Spaniards and former slaves. Caesar arrived in December 46 after a journey of 27 days from Rome. After a winter campaign of sieges, including Ategua, Gnaeus offered battle on 17 March 45 at Munda, on a hill above a plain near modern Osuna or Montilla in Andalusia.

Caesar had eight legions and 8,000 cavalry; the Pompeians thirteen legions, 6,000 cavalry and light troops. The Pompeians held the high ground; Caesar attacked uphill across a stream. The fighting was desperate: the Pompeian soldiers, knowing they could expect no mercy as many were deserters or slaves, fought hard. Caesar's line wavered, and he dismounted, took a shield, and rushed forward, shouting that this would be his last day and their last campaign. He said afterward that he had often fought for victory but at Munda for his life.

The Tenth legion on the right finally broke the Pompeian left. When Labienus moved five cohorts to protect the camp against Bogud's Mauretanian cavalry, the Pompeian infantry thought it was a retreat and broke. The Bellum Hispaniense gives 30,000 Pompeian dead, including Labienus and 3,000 equites, against 1,000 Caesarians. The Caesarians built a rampart of corpses and shields with heads on spears around the town of Munda.

Gnaeus Pompeius fled and was killed a few weeks later; Sextus escaped and continued the struggle for a decade. Munda ended the civil war. Caesar's triumph over Spain in October 45, over fellow citizens, caused resentment.
battle_of_munda.debate: Location of Munda; casualty figures. Location disputed: near Osuna (La Lantejuela), Montilla, or elsewhere in the Campiña; recent finds near Osuna support that area.
scholarship: Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (2006)

caesars_spanish_triumph_45.detail: Cicero joked that in Caninius' consulship nobody had lunch and nothing bad happened, because the consul was so vigilant he never slept.

ciceros_philosophical_works_45.detail: Cicero presented the programme as a service to the state when politics was closed to him; he coined much of the Latin philosophical vocabulary (qualitas, essentia, moralis). The lost Hortensius later converted the young Augustine to philosophy. He told Atticus they were 'copies: they cost little effort, I supply only the words, of which I have plenty'.

tabula_heracleensis_45.debate: Whether the text is a single lex Iulia municipalis or a compilation of several measures is disputed.
scholarship: Crawford (ed.), Roman Statutes (1996) no. 24

caesar_dictator_perpetuo.detail:
Caesar's dictatorships multiplied: for elections in 49 (eleven days), for a year in 48/47, for ten years, renewed annually, from 46, and finally, probably on 14 or 15 February 44, dictator perpetuo, 'dictator for life'. The title appeared on coins of the moneyers of 44 with his portrait, CAESAR DICT PERPETVO. The dictatorship for life abolished the temporary character that had defined the office since the early Republic and that even Sulla had preserved.

It came with a cascade of honours voted by the Senate in late 45 and early 44: the title parens patriae, a golden chair in the Senate and on the tribunal, a triumphal dress at all times, the right to wear a laurel wreath, statues in all temples and among the kings on the Capitol, the month Quinctilis renamed Iulius, a temple to Caesar's Clemency with Antony as his flamen, his birthday a public holiday, and his person declared sacrosanct. Senators swore to protect him; he dismissed his Spanish bodyguard. When the Senate came to confer honours, he received them seated before the temple of Venus Genetrix, an insult remembered as a cause of his death.

Caesar also controlled elections, naming half the magistrates and recommending the rest; he appointed consuls for the years ahead, as he planned to be absent in the East for three years. When the consul Fabius Maximus died on 31 December 45, he appointed Caninius Rebilus for the remaining hours.

The dictatorship for life made it clear that the Republic would not be restored. Cicero, in his Philippics, called it the source of the tyranny. Within a month Caesar was dead, and in 44 Antony carried a law abolishing the dictatorship forever.
caesar_dictator_perpetuo.debate: Whether Caesar formally assumed the title on 14 or 15 February 44, and whether he sought kingship, are debated.
scholarship: Morstein-Marx, Julius Caesar and the Roman People (2021)
Weinstock, Divus Julius (1971)
Alföldi, Caesar in 44 v. Chr. (1985)

lupercalia_44.detail: Whether it was a staged test of opinion, a demonstration that Caesar did not want kingship, or Antony's own initiative was debated then and now. Cicero's Second Philippic makes the most of it.

ides_of_march.detail:
On 15 March 44 the Senate met in the Curia of Pompey, in the portico of his theatre on the Campus Martius, because the Curia Hostilia was being rebuilt. Some sixty senators had joined the conspiracy, led by Marcus Junius Brutus and Gaius Cassius Longinus, both praetors, and including Decimus Brutus, Gaius Trebonius, Servius Sulpicius Galba, Lucius Tillius Cimber, and the brothers Casca. They chose the Ides because Caesar was due to leave for the Parthian war on 18 March.

Omens were reported: the haruspex Spurinna had warned Caesar to beware the danger that would come no later than the Ides; his wife Calpurnia dreamed of holding his murdered body, and the doors of their bedroom flew open. Caesar, unwell, hesitated, but Decimus Brutus persuaded him to attend. On the way, Artemidorus of Cnidus handed him a scroll revealing the plot, which he did not read. Trebonius detained Antony outside.

When Caesar was seated, Tillius Cimber approached as if to petition for his exiled brother and seized his toga. Casca struck first, wounding him in the neck. Caesar fought back, stabbing Casca's arm with his stylus, until he saw Brutus among the assassins; Suetonius records the report that he said in Greek 'kai su, teknon' (you too, child), though he states that Caesar died without a word. Caesar covered his face with his toga and fell at the foot of Pompey's statue, with twenty-three wounds, of which, according to the doctor Antistius, only one, the second in the chest, was fatal.

The senators fled; the assassins marched to the Capitol proclaiming liberty, but the city did not rise for them. The murder led to fourteen more years of civil war and the establishment of monarchy under Caesar's heir. Archaeologists have identified the remains of the Curia of Pompey in the Largo Argentina.
ides_of_march.debate: Whether the assassination was a principled defence of republican liberty, an aristocratic reaction against a popular leader (Morstein-Marx), or factional resentment; Nicolaus of Damascus is the earliest narrative, from Augustus' court.
scholarship: Strauss, The Death of Caesar (2015)
Tempest, Brutus: The Noble Conspirator (2017)
Syme, The Roman Revolution (1939)
Woolf, Et Tu, Brute? (2006)
Toher, Nicolaus of Damascus: The Life of Augustus (2016)

funeral_of_caesar.detail:
Two days after the Ides, on 17 March, the Senate met in the temple of Tellus and, at Antony's and Cicero's urging, agreed a compromise: an amnesty for the assassins, while Caesar's acts, including future appointments, were ratified. Caesar's father-in-law Piso insisted that his will be read and that he receive a public funeral. The will, opened at Antony's house, named his great-nephew Gaius Octavius heir to three-quarters of his estate, adopted him as his son, and left 300 sesterces to every citizen and his gardens across the Tiber to the people. Decimus Brutus, one of the assassins, was named among the secondary heirs.

The funeral took place on about 20 March. The body was laid on an ivory couch in a gilded shrine modelled on the temple of Venus Genetrix, in the Forum before the rostra. Antony, as consul, delivered the eulogy: according to Suetonius, he simply had a herald read the Senate's decree voting Caesar all honours and the oath by which senators had sworn to protect him, with a few words of his own. Appian and Plutarch describe a more theatrical performance, in which Antony displayed Caesar's bloodstained toga and a wax effigy showing his twenty-three wounds rotated on a mechanical device.

The crowd, enraged, refused to let the body be burned on the Campus Martius and built a pyre in the Forum from benches, tables and whatever was at hand. Veterans threw their arms on it, musicians and actors their costumes, women their jewellery. Jews of Rome mourned at the pyre for nights. The mob tried to burn the houses of Brutus and Cassius and lynched the poet Helvius Cinna by mistake. The assassins left Rome.

An altar and column were set up at the site, later replaced by the temple of Divus Iulius.
funeral_of_caesar.debate: The content of Antony's funeral speech is disputed; Suetonius' minimal version contrasts with Appian's and Dio's elaborate ones.
scholarship: Strauss, The Death of Caesar (2015)

lynching_of_helvius_cinna_44.detail: Cinna's short epic Zmyrna, nine years in the making, was praised by Catullus (poem 95) as a masterpiece that would outlast the bulky annals of his rivals; only a few lines survive. Shakespeare's 'I am Cinna the poet' scene comes straight from Plutarch.

octavian_accepts_the_inheritance.detail:
Gaius Octavius, aged eighteen, was at Apollonia in Illyricum studying and waiting to join Caesar's Parthian campaign when news of the murder arrived. His mother Atia and stepfather Lucius Marcius Philippus urged caution, but he sailed to Italy, landing near Brundisium, and learned at Lupiae of the terms of the will. He immediately accepted the inheritance and the name, calling himself Gaius Julius Caesar, and ignored those who urged him to renounce it.

Arriving in Rome in May 44, he declared his acceptance before the urban praetor, Gaius Antonius, the consul's brother. Antony, who controlled Caesar's papers and much of his money, refused to hand over the estate and obstructed the adoption's formal ratification by a lex curiata. Octavian sold his own property and borrowed to pay Caesar's legacies of 300 sesterces to each citizen, winning popular favour. He organised Games of Caesar's Victory in July, during which a comet appeared, interpreted as Caesar's soul ascending to the gods.

Cicero met him at Puteoli in April and wrote that his friends called him Caesar, but Philippus did not, nor would Cicero; he judged him devoted to him. In autumn Octavian raised an illegal private army of 3,000 of Caesar's veterans in Campania by offering 500 denarii each, and two of Antony's legions, the Martia and the Fourth, defected to him.

The acceptance of the name Caesar was the most important decision of the young man's life. It made him the political heir of Caesar to the veterans and the plebs. Though Roman testamentary adoption was disputed in law, the name gave him a claim no rival could match.
scholarship: Syme, The Roman Revolution (1939)
Osgood, Caesar's Legacy (2006)
Toher, Nicolaus of Damascus (2016)

sidus_iulium.detail: Chinese records in the Han shu note a comet in the same year. It became a central image of Augustan ideology (Virgil, Horace, Ovid).
scholarship: Ramsey & Licht, The Comet of 44 B.C. and Caesar's Funeral Games (1997)

philippics.detail: Cicero described his strategy, in a quip that reached Octavian, as to praise the young man, honour him and remove him (tollere means both 'raise' and 'get rid of'). The speeches cost him his life.

defection_of_the_martia_and_fourth_44.detail: This was the moment Octavian became a military power. Raising a private army was illegal, and Cicero's Third Philippic of 20 December retrospectively praised it as saving the state, a precedent the Res Gestae opens with: 'At the age of nineteen, on my own initiative and at my own expense, I raised an army.'

lex_coloniae_genetivae.debate: The surviving copy was engraved in the Flavian period and may include later updates.
scholarship: Crawford (ed.), Roman Statutes (1996) no. 25

caesar_portrait_denarii_44.detail: The Senate's decree authorising the portrait was among the extravagant honours of early 44 that Dio lists. Hellenistic kings had put their heads on coins for centuries; for Romans it was a royal gesture. The series also shows Venus with Victory, the clasped hands of concord, and the wreath Caesar wore. After the Ides, coin portraits of the triumvirs, the Liberators and Sextus Pompey became normal, and the imperial coinage followed directly.
scholarship: Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974) nos. 480-481
Alföldi, Caesar in 44 v. Chr. II (1974)

de_officiis_44.detail: It became the most widely read work of moral philosophy in Latin for 1,500 years: the second book printed after the Gutenberg Bible, and a manual for Renaissance and Enlightenment gentlemen. Its denunciation of Caesar shows how the treatise was also a political pamphlet.

battle_of_forum_gallorum.detail: The legate Servius Sulpicius Galba's eyewitness letter to Cicero (Fam. 10.30) is one of the very few first-hand battle accounts from a Roman officer outside Caesar. Octavian, defending the camp, was hailed imperator.

battle_of_mutina.detail:
In late 44 Antony, as proconsul-designate, demanded that Decimus Brutus hand over Cisalpine Gaul, which a law of June had transferred to Antony; Decimus refused and shut himself in Mutina (Modena) with three legions. Antony besieged him through the winter. In Rome Cicero, in the Philippics, roused the Senate against Antony, who was declared a public enemy in April 43. The new consuls, Aulus Hirtius and Gaius Vibius Pansa, both Caesarians, marched north with the propraetor Octavian, given imperium by the Senate in January.

On 14 April Antony ambushed Pansa's recruits at Forum Gallorum on the Via Aemilia; Pansa was mortally wounded, but Hirtius arrived with veterans and routed Antony's tired troops in the evening. A letter of Servius Galba, one of the participants, to Cicero gives an eyewitness account of the fighting in marshes and woods. On 21 April Hirtius and Octavian attacked Antony's siege lines at Mutina; Hirtius was killed in the enemy camp, Octavian carried the eagle of a legion when its bearer fell. Antony abandoned the siege and retreated over the Alps with the remnants of his army, joined by Ventidius' three legions.

With both consuls dead, rumours circulated that Octavian had arranged their deaths. The Senate honoured Decimus Brutus with a triumph and gave him command of the consular armies, slighting Octavian, who refused to cooperate with one of his adoptive father's murderers. Cicero's remark that the young man should be 'praised, honoured and removed' (laudandum, ornandum, tollendum) reached Octavian.

The war of Mutina, the Senate's last attempt to assert itself against the Caesarian generals, ended in failure: within months Lepidus and Plancus joined Antony, Octavian marched on Rome for the consulship, and the three formed the triumvirate.
scholarship: Osgood, Caesar's Legacy (2006)

lepidus_joins_antony_43.detail: Cicero's correspondence with Plancus, Pollio and Lepidus in May and June 43 lets us watch the Senate's position dissolve as the western governors, with seventeen legions between them, joined Antony one after another. Plancus' letters are a masterpiece of hedging. Decimus Brutus, abandoned, fled and was killed.

octavian_first_consulship.detail:
After Mutina, Octavian, denied a triumph and passed over in favour of Decimus Brutus, sent a delegation of 400 centurions to Rome in July 43 demanding the consulship for him, though he was only nineteen, and rewards for his soldiers. When the Senate refused, one centurion threw back his cloak to show his sword: 'If you do not give it, this will.' Octavian then crossed the Rubicon with eight legions, as his father had, and marched on Rome.

The Senate yielded, then reversed when two legions from Africa arrived, then yielded again as the African legions defected. Cicero, who had hoped to guide the young man, went to greet him and received an ironic welcome as the last of his friends. On 19 August 43 Octavian and his cousin Quintus Pedius were elected consuls, an anniversary Augustus would later mark. He took the auspices and saw twelve vultures, as Romulus had.

Octavian's first acts: the lex curiata formally ratifying his adoption, making him Gaius Julius Caesar by law; the lex Pedia establishing a court to try the assassins of Caesar, who were condemned in absence, including Sextus Pompey; payment of his soldiers from the treasury; and revocation of the decrees outlawing Antony and Lepidus.

The consulship opened the way for the meeting at Bononia and the triumvirate. It also showed the young Caesar's ruthlessness: within weeks he abandoned the senatorial cause he had served, while presenting himself as the avenger of his father. Augustus' Res Gestae opens with the claim that he had saved the Republic from domination by a faction, and that the people elected him consul in the same year in which both consuls had fallen.
scholarship: Syme, The Roman Revolution (1939)
Osgood, Caesar's Legacy (2006)

meeting_at_bononia.detail:
In late October or early November 43, Antony, Lepidus and Octavian met on a small island in a river near Bononia (Bologna), either the Lavinius (Lavino) or the Rhenus (Reno), each bringing five legions, which they left on opposite banks. Lepidus inspected the island first and waved his cloak to signal safety; the three searched each other for daggers. For two days, from dawn to dusk, they negotiated in full view of their armies.

They agreed to form a board of three men for restoring the Republic, triumviri rei publicae constituendae, for five years, with powers equal to consuls, the right to make laws and appoint magistrates without consulting Senate or people. Octavian would resign his consulship to Ventidius. Provinces were divided: Antony took Cisalpine and Transalpine Gaul, Lepidus Spain and Narbonensis, Octavian Africa, Sicily and Sardinia, the least secure, as Sextus Pompey controlled the sea. Antony and Octavian would make war on Brutus and Cassius in the East while Lepidus held Italy. Eighteen of the richest Italian cities, among them Capua, Rhegium, Venusia, Beneventum, Nuceria, Ariminum and Vibo, were promised to their soldiers as rewards.

Above all, they agreed to proscribe their enemies, each sacrificing friends or relatives to the others' demands: Antony gave up his uncle Lucius Caesar, Lepidus his brother Paullus, and Octavian Cicero, after two days of resistance. Octavian was betrothed to Clodia, Antony's stepdaughter through Fulvia.

The meeting has been compared to the conference of Luca, but the triumvirate it created was a formal, legal institution, ratified by the lex Titia on 27 November 43. It effectively replaced the Republic's institutions with a junta.
meeting_at_bononia.debate: The river (Lavinius or Rhenus) and exact date (late October or early November) are uncertain.
scholarship: Syme, The Roman Revolution (1939)
Osgood, Caesar's Legacy (2006)

foundation_of_lugdunum_43.detail: Plancus' tomb at Gaeta records the foundation of Lugdunum and of Raurica (Augst). The site, a Celtic oppidum named after the god Lugus, had a natural strategic position for routes to the Rhine, the Atlantic and the Mediterranean. Augustus made it the hub of Agrippa's Gallic road network and in 12 BC the altar of Rome and Augustus was dedicated there.

proscriptions_of_43.detail:
Immediately after Bononia the triumvirs sent orders to Rome for the killing of seventeen prominent men, including Cicero; on their arrival in late November they published an edict, preserved by Appian, explaining that they would rather punish their enemies than be killed by them, as Caesar had been by those he pardoned. Lists followed: Appian gives 300 senators and 2,000 equites, Livy's epitomator 130 senators. Rewards for killing were 100,000 sesterces for a free man and 40,000 and freedom for a slave; heads were displayed on the rostra.

The proscriptions were also a fiscal measure, as the triumvirs needed money for the war against Brutus and Cassius. When sales of confiscated property raised too little, they imposed taxes, including one on 1,400 wealthy women, which Hortensia, daughter of the orator Hortensius, successfully contested in a speech before the triumvirs, the first recorded public speech by a Roman woman.

Appian's Book 4 collects stories of victims and escapes: Antony's uncle Lucius Caesar saved by his sister Julia; Lepidus' brother Paullus allowed to escape; the wife of Quintus Lucretius Vespillo who hid him in the roof; and the woman of the 'Laudatio Turiae', a funerary inscription of a husband to his wife who saved him and confronted Lepidus. Some were betrayed by slaves or relatives, others protected. Thousands fled to Sextus Pompey in Sicily or to Brutus and Cassius.

The proscriptions of 43 surpassed Sulla's in scale. Augustan writers tried to blame Antony and Lepidus, presenting Octavian as reluctant; Suetonius, however, says he proscribed with more severity than the others once he had decided. Their memory shaped the Augustan regime's need to present itself as a restoration of peace and law.
scholarship: Hinard, Les proscriptions de la Rome républicaine (1985)
Osgood, Caesar's Legacy (2006)

lex_titia.detail:
On 27 November 43 the tribune Publius Titius proposed a law, carried the same day without the customary interval of three market days (trinundinum), establishing Antony, Lepidus and Octavian as triumviri rei publicae constituendae, 'board of three for setting the state in order', until 31 December 38. The office gave them consular imperium, the right to issue edicts with the force of law, to nominate magistrates for years in advance, to administer justice without appeal, and to allocate provinces. It took effect immediately, the triumvirs entering office on 27 November.

The law legalised the arrangements of Bononia. Its model was Sulla's dictatorship to write laws and settle the state, but shared among three. The triumvirs controlled appointments to magistracies: lists of consuls were fixed for several years, and the consulship became an honour distributed to supporters, with suffect consuls replacing ordinary ones within the year. The Senate was swollen with their partisans to over 1,000 members.

The triumvirate was renewed at Tarentum in 37 for another five years, until the end of 33, though the date of expiry and whether Antony and Octavian continued to hold it after 33 were contested. Lepidus was deposed in 36 after his attempt to take Sicily.

The lex Titia marks the formal end of the free Republic, with constitutional authority vested in three men. Augustus' Res Gestae records that he was triumvir for ten consecutive years. Tacitus, at the opening of the Annals, summarises: Lepidus' and Antony's forces passed to Augustus, who took everything under the name of princeps.
lex_titia.debate: Whether the triumvirs' powers ended on 31 December 33 or persisted until resigned.
scholarship: Millar, JRS 63 (1973), 'Triumvirate and Principate'
Osgood, Caesar's Legacy (2006)
Lange, Res Publica Constituta (2009)
Millar, 'Triumvirate and Principate', JRS 63 (1973)
Bleicken, Zwischen Republik und Prinzipat (1990)

death_of_cicero.detail:
Cicero's name was on the first list of seventeen sent from Bononia, at Antony's insistence; Octavian, after resisting for two days, yielded. Cicero was at his Tusculan villa with his brother Quintus when they heard the news. They set out to join Brutus in Macedonia; Quintus went back for money and was killed with his son. Cicero reached Astura and took ship, but returned to land, seasick and undecided, and went to his villa at Formiae.

On 7 December 43 a band led by the centurion Herennius and the military tribune Popillius Laenas, whom Cicero had once defended on a charge of parricide, found him being carried in a litter through the woods toward the sea. Cicero ordered his slaves to set the litter down, looked his killers in the face, and stretched out his neck from the litter. He was sixty-three. Herennius cut off his head and, on Antony's orders, his hands, which had written the Philippics.

The head and hands were nailed to the rostra in the Forum, where Cicero had spoken. Fulvia, Antony's wife, is said to have pierced his tongue with her hairpin. Popillius received a reward of a million sesterces and set up a portrait of himself with Cicero's head.

Cicero's death became the defining tragedy of the end of the Republic. The elder Seneca preserved accounts of it from Livy, Aufidius Bassus, Cremutius Cordus and Asinius Pollio, and declamations debated whether he should have begged Antony for life. Plutarch tells that years later Augustus found a grandson reading Cicero, took the book, read it at length, and returned it saying: 'A learned man, my child, and a lover of his country.' Octavian made Cicero's son consul in 30, when the decree against Antony's memory was announced.
scholarship: Butler, The Hand of Cicero (2002)

okmok_eruption_and_the_cold_years.detail: Plutarch, Virgil and Pliny describe the sun's pallor through the year after the Ides as a portent; the volcanic explanation, published in 2020, ties the political crisis to a climate shock that worsened food shortages in Italy and Egypt during the triumviral wars.
scholarship: McConnell et al., PNAS 117 (2020)

battle_of_philippi_first.detail:
In 42 Brutus and Cassius, with some nineteen legions and 20,000 cavalry, took up strong positions astride the Via Egnatia west of Philippi in eastern Macedonia: Brutus on the north on hills near the town, Cassius on the south near marshes stretching to the sea, their camps linked by a wall. Their fleet controlled the sea and their supplies came from Thasos. Antony and Octavian arrived with nineteen legions and 13,000 cavalry, short of supplies. Antony, with Octavian ill, camped in the plain opposite Cassius and began building a causeway through the marsh to cut his communications.

On 3 October 42 (some date it late October) Cassius attacked Antony's working parties in the marsh. Antony responded with a direct assault on Cassius' camp, which he took. Simultaneously, Brutus' legions, without orders, attacked and stormed Octavian's camp, where Octavian was absent, having been warned by a dream of his doctor Artorius, or hiding in the marshes, as his enemies said. Each side was thus victorious on one wing and defeated on the other.

Cassius, short-sighted and seeing horsemen approaching, which were in fact Brutus' men sent to inform him of his victory, thought them enemies and believed Brutus defeated. He withdrew to his tent and had his freedman Pindarus kill him; it was his birthday. Brutus wept over his body, calling him the last of the Romans, and had him buried on Thasos lest his funeral demoralise the army.

On the same day the Liberators' fleet destroyed the triumviral reinforcements crossing the Adriatic under Domitius Calvinus. Had Brutus known, he might have waited for the triumvirs to starve. The first battle left Brutus in sole command of a still superior position.
battle_of_philippi_first.debate: The dates of the two battles (3 and 23 October 42, or later) depend on calendar reconstructions.
scholarship: Collart, Philippes, ville de Macédoine (1937)
Osgood, Caesar's Legacy (2006)

battle_of_philippi_second.detail:
After the first battle, Brutus held his strong position and refused to fight, intending to starve the triumvirs, whose supplies were running out as winter approached and whose reinforcements had been destroyed at sea. Antony extended his lines southward to cut Brutus off from the sea, and Brutus built forts to match. His officers and soldiers, many of them former Caesarians, grew restless and deserted; his allies pressed for battle. Plutarch says Brutus saw again the apparition that had visited him at Abydos, telling him 'You will see me at Philippi'.

On 23 October 42 Brutus gave battle. The fighting was close and bloody, with few missiles thrown; his left wing gave way and the triumviral legions, led by Antony, broke through and captured the gates of his camp. Octavian's troops took the camp itself. Brutus escaped with four legions to the hills, and that night, finding his men unwilling to continue, he asked his friends to kill him; when they refused, he fell on his sword, held by his friend Strato. He quoted, Plutarch says, a line of Euripides: 'O wretched virtue, you were only a word.'

Antony covered Brutus' body with his purple cloak and sent the ashes to his mother Servilia; Octavian, in Suetonius' account, had the head sent to Rome to be thrown at the feet of Caesar's statue, though it was lost in a storm. Many nobles fell or killed themselves, including Cato's son Marcus, Lucullus' son, and Quintus Hortensius. Survivors joined Sextus Pompey, or surrendered; Messalla Corvinus and the young Horace, a military tribune, made their peace with the victors.

Philippi ended the Liberators' cause and, for many, the Republic. Antony took the East, while Octavian returned to Italy to settle veterans. Philippi was refounded as a colony of veterans.
scholarship: Osgood, Caesar's Legacy (2006)
Tempest, Brutus: The Noble Conspirator (2017)

eid_mar_denarius.detail: The coin is a paradox: a self-proclaimed defender of liberty putting his own portrait on coinage, exactly as Caesar had. The pileus was the cap given to freed slaves, so the message is that Rome had been freed by the daggers. It was struck in 43-42 to pay the Liberators' army before Philippi. Many examples on the market are forgeries; an aureus sold in 2020 for over 3 million pounds.
scholarship: Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974) no. 508/3

sources.r: Plancus at the Temple of Saturn

antony_and_cleopatra_at_tarsus.detail: Plutarch's description, followed by Shakespeare almost word for word, is the most famous set piece in his Lives. The alliance gave Antony Egypt's wealth and Cleopatra Roman protection.
scholarship: Pelling, Plutarch: Life of Antony (1988)
Roller, Cleopatra (2010)

veteran_settlements_41.detail: The confiscations were the greatest transfer of land in Italy since Sulla and permanently changed the ownership of the countryside: many veterans sold up within a generation, but many settlements took. Virgil's First and Ninth Eclogues give voice to the dispossessed, and ancient biographers claimed (perhaps from the poems themselves) that the poet's own farm near Mantua was seized and restored through Pollio, Varus and Gallus. Propertius and Horace also lost family land.
veteran_settlements_41.debate: Whether Virgil's family estate was in fact confiscated is debated; the biographical tradition may have been read out of the poems.

execution_of_arsinoe_iv_41.debate: The identification of the Octagon at Ephesus with Arsinoe's tomb is widely doubted.

sallust_bellum_catilinae.detail: The paired speeches of Caesar and Cato in the Catiline debate of 5 December 63 became the classic statement of the two political temperaments of the age. Sallust's theme of moral decline (metus hostilis) shaped Livy, Tacitus and every later account of the Republic's fall.

siege_of_perusia.detail:
After Philippi, Octavian returned to Italy to settle some 50,000 veterans on land confiscated from eighteen cities and many individuals, causing widespread hardship and resistance. Antony's brother Lucius Antonius, consul in 41, and Antony's wife Fulvia championed the dispossessed and the propertied Italians, accusing Octavian of exceeding his powers, while also claiming to defend Antony's interests. Fighting broke out in late 41. Lucius, failing to hold Rome, was driven into Perusia (Perugia), a hill town in Etruria, by Octavian's generals Agrippa and Salvidienus, and besieged through the winter.

Octavian surrounded the town with a ditch and wall over fifty stades long and starved it out. Antony's generals in Gaul, Ventidius, Pollio and Plancus, failed to relieve it, uncertain of Antony's wishes. Hundreds of lead sling bullets found at Perugia bear obscene inscriptions aimed at Fulvia, Octavian and Lucius Antonius. Octavian's own verses on Fulvia are quoted by Martial.

Lucius surrendered in February or March 40. Octavian pardoned him and his soldiers, and sent him to govern Spain, but the town council of Perusia was executed, except for one who had voted to honour the murderers of Caesar. Suetonius reports, citing hostile authors, that Octavian sacrificed 300 senators and equites at an altar to Divus Iulius on the Ides of March, the 'arae Perusinae'; he answered pleas for mercy with 'You must die'. The town burned, whether by Octavian's soldiers or a citizen.

The Perusine War nearly provoked open conflict between Antony and Octavian, resolved by the Treaty of Brundisium. It was the low point of Octavian's reputation, remembered in Propertius' elegies 1.21-22, whose author's kinsman died there.
siege_of_perusia.debate: Historicity of the 'arae Perusinae' sacrifice. The human sacrifice at the 'Perusine altars' is generally regarded as hostile invention or exaggeration.
scholarship: Osgood, Caesar's Legacy (2006)

treaty_of_brundisium.detail:
After the Perusine War, Antony sailed from the East to Italy in summer 40, allied with Sextus Pompey and Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus, and besieged Brundisium, which refused him entry. Octavian came south with an army. But the veterans of both sides refused to fight, and mediators, Lucius Cocceius Nerva for both, Maecenas for Octavian and Asinius Pollio for Antony, negotiated an agreement in September or October 40. Fulvia's death at Sicyon removed an obstacle.

The empire was divided along a line at Scodra in Illyricum: Antony took the East, Octavian the West, including Gaul, Spain and Illyricum, while Lepidus kept Africa. Italy was shared as a recruiting ground. Antony would fight the Parthians, Octavian Sextus Pompey unless an agreement was made. The alliance was sealed by Antony's marriage to Octavian's sister Octavia, widowed in 40, the Senate waiving the period of mourning; Octavia was pregnant by her first husband at the time.

Antony revealed that Octavian's general Salvidienus Rufus had offered to defect; Octavian had him condemned. Both triumvirs celebrated ovations in Rome, and Antony was given the honour of a flamen of Divus Iulius. The treaty was celebrated on coins showing clasped hands and the heads of Antony and Octavia, and by Virgil's Fourth Eclogue, addressed to Pollio as consul, prophesying a golden age with the birth of a child.

Brundisium averted war and restored the triumvirate's unity, but Sextus Pompey, left out, intensified his blockade of Italy, causing famine and riots in Rome that forced the Treaty of Misenum in 39. The territorial division between East and West foreshadowed the conflict of 32.
scholarship: Osgood, Caesar's Legacy (2006)
Pelling, 'The triumviral period', CAH X2 (1996)

parthian_invasion_of_40.detail:
In 40, exploiting the triumvirs' divisions and Antony's absence in Egypt, Parthian forces invaded Roman territory under the crown prince Pacorus and Quintus Labienus, son of Caesar's general, who had gone to Parthia as an envoy of Brutus and Cassius and stayed after Philippi. Labienus, with former Republican soldiers among the garrisons of Syria, defeated and killed the governor Decidius Saxa, took Apamea and Antioch, and overran Cilicia, Caria and much of Asia Minor, sacking Mylasa and Alabanda, though Stratonicea held out. He struck coins as Q. Labienus Parthicus Imperator.

Pacorus took Syria and Phoenicia, though Tyre resisted, and entered Judaea, where he installed the Hasmonean Antigonus as king and captured Hyrcanus II and Phasael. Herod escaped to Masada, then to Rome. For a short period, Roman power east of the Taurus and in Syria collapsed.

Antony, recalled to Italy by the Perusine War, sent Publius Ventidius Bassus, a self-made man once captured as a child in the Social War and led in Pompeius Strabo's triumph, to deal with the invasion. In 39 Ventidius defeated Labienus in the Taurus and at the Cilician Gates, and Labienus was captured and killed in Cilicia; Ventidius then defeated the Parthian general Pharnapates at the Amanus pass. In 38 at Gindarus he defeated and killed Pacorus.

The invasion revealed the fragility of Roman control in the East and the danger of Roman civil wars spilling into external war. Ventidius became the first Roman to triumph over the Parthians, in November 38.
scholarship: Bivar, CHI 3.1 (1983)
Sherwin-White, Roman Foreign Policy in the East (1984)
Bivar, 'The political history of Iran under the Arsacids', CHI 3.1 (1983)

herod_named_king_40.detail: An Idumaean commoner with no Hasmonean blood, Herod owed his crown entirely to Rome. His betrothal to the Hasmonean princess Mariamme, granddaughter of both Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II, was meant to supply the legitimacy he lacked. Josephus dates his reign from this grant (40) and also from the capture of Jerusalem (37).

antigonus_takes_jerusalem_40.detail: Antigonus' coins, the last Hasmonean issue, carry the first depiction of the Temple menorah and shewbread table, with Hebrew legend 'Mattathias the high priest'. Hyrcanus was taken to Babylonia, where the Jewish community honoured him, and returned to Herod's court only to be executed in 30.

scholarship: Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974) no. 527
Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974) nos. 511, 483
Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974) nos. 525-535
Syme, 'Imperator Caesar: a study in nomenclature', Historia 7 (1958)
Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974) no. 524

treaty_of_misenum.detail: Sextus' admiral Menas whispered that he could cut the anchor cable and make Sextus master of the world; Sextus replied that he should have done it without asking. The peace broke down within a year.

virgils_eclogues.detail: The Eclogues were performed on stage to great acclaim. Tityrus in the First Eclogue thanks a 'god' in Rome, clearly Octavian, for restoring his land, while Meliboeus goes into exile. The child of the Fourth Eclogue was probably intended as a son expected from the marriage of Antony and Octavia (or Pollio's own son); Christian readers from Constantine onward read it as a prophecy of Christ, which made Virgil a quasi-prophet in the Middle Ages and Dante's guide.
virgils_eclogues.debate: Identity of the child of Eclogue 4 (Antony and Octavia's expected son, Pollio's son Saloninus or Asinius Gallus, Octavian's expected child by Scribonia) has never been settled.

battle_of_gindarus.detail:
In spring 38 Pacorus, the Parthian crown prince, invaded Syria again, crossing the Euphrates. Publius Ventidius Bassus, Antony's legate, who had driven out Labienus and the Parthians the year before, was short of troops, his legions in winter quarters. He used a ruse: through a Parthian sympathiser in his camp, the dynast Channaeus, he leaked false information that the Parthians should cross the Euphrates at Zeugma, the shortest route, which he feared least, so that they took the longer route, giving him time to concentrate.

Ventidius camped on high ground near Gindarus in Cyrrhestica, north-east of Antioch, and let the Parthians approach. Confident after their earlier successes, the Parthian cavalry charged uphill against the camp; Ventidius' legions sallied out and drove them down the slope, while slingers, whom he had deployed specifically against the horse archers, struck with lead bullets, outranging the bows. Pacorus was killed fighting, and the Parthian army broke, losing heavily as it tried to recross the Euphrates. Ventidius sent Pacorus' head around the cities of Syria, which had sympathised with him.

The battle was fought, the sources note, on 9 June, the anniversary of Crassus' defeat at Carrhae fifteen years earlier, which made it a symbolic revenge. Ventidius celebrated a triumph over the Parthians in Rome on 27 November 38, the first ever, and the only one until Trajan's victories, Gellius notes with irony that he had once walked as a captive child in Strabo's triumph.

Pacorus' death devastated his father Orodes II, who abdicated in favour of another son, Phraates IV; Phraates murdered his father and brothers. Antony, arriving, removed Ventidius from command, reportedly jealous, and besieged Samosata.
battle_of_gindarus.debate: The 9 June date depends on Dio's claim of the Carrhae anniversary.
scholarship: Sherwin-White, Roman Foreign Policy in the East (1984)

siege_of_jerusalem_37.detail: Josephus claims the city fell on the same day as to Pompey, 27 years before. Herod ruled as Rome's client king until 4 BC.

deposition_of_lepidus.detail: Octavian, now master of 40 legions, received the sacrosanctity of a tribune for life and an ovation. Rome would have two masters, not three.

battle_of_naulochus.detail:
Octavian's war against Sextus Pompey, who controlled Sicily, Sardinia and the sea with a fleet manned by many runaway slaves, resumed in 38 after Menodorus' defection. Octavian's fleet was defeated off Cumae and wrecked by a storm at Scyllaeum. Agrippa spent 37 building a new fleet with heavy ships and training 20,000 freed slave rowers in the Portus Julius near Puteoli; he also developed the harpax, a grapnel fired from a catapult to drag enemy ships alongside for boarding. Antony provided 120 ships in exchange for legions at Tarentum.

In July 36 a triple invasion of Sicily began: Octavian from Italy, Lepidus from Africa with twelve legions, and Statilius Taurus from Tarentum. Storms delayed it, and Octavian himself was defeated off Tauromenium, but Agrippa defeated Sextus' fleet off Mylae in August and the land forces established themselves in Sicily.

On 3 September 36 off Naulochus, near the north-eastern tip of Sicily, Agrippa and Sextus fought with about 300 ships each, as both armies watched from the shore. Agrippa's heavier ships and the harpax prevailed: Sextus lost 28 ships sunk and almost all the rest captured or burned, only 17 escaping. Sextus fled to the East, where he was killed by Antony's general Titius at Miletus in 35. His land army in Sicily surrendered to Lepidus, who then tried to claim the island for himself, but his soldiers deserted to Octavian, and Lepidus was stripped of his triumviral powers.

Agrippa received the naval crown, a gold crown with ship's prows. Octavian returned 30,000 slaves to their owners and crucified 6,000 whose owners could not be found. Naulochus secured the western Mediterranean and Italy's grain supply.
scholarship: Welch, Magnus Pius: Sextus Pompeius and the Transformation of the Roman Republic (2012)
Powell, Sextus Pompeius (2002)

siege_of_phraaspa.detail:
In 36 Antony launched the great Parthian expedition that Caesar had planned, with sixteen legions, some 60,000 legionaries, 10,000 Spanish and Gallic cavalry and 30,000 allies, the largest Roman army sent east. Instead of crossing Mesopotamia like Crassus, he marched north through Armenia, whose king Artavasdes II was his ally, to strike at Media Atropatene, an ally of Parthia, aiming at its capital Phraaspa (perhaps Takht-e Soleyman or near Maragheh).

Antony moved ahead with the army, leaving the siege train of 300 wagons, including an 80-foot ram, to follow under Oppius Statianus with two legions. Phraates IV's cavalry destroyed the train and killed 10,000 men; Artavasdes withdrew his cavalry. Antony besieged Phraaspa without siege engines, building earthworks, while Parthian cavalry harried his foragers. Supplies ran low, and an assault failed. Antony decimated the cohorts that fled.

In October, with winter coming, Antony abandoned the siege. The retreat of 300 miles to Armenia took twenty-seven days, guided by a Mardian who knew the hills, under constant Parthian attack; the legions formed the testudo against arrows. Hunger and disease, including poisoning from an unknown plant, struck the army. Antony lost some 24,000 men, a third of his force; Plutarch says he exclaimed 'O the Ten Thousand!' in admiration of Xenophon's retreat. In winter cold in Armenia 8,000 more died. Cleopatra brought supplies and money to the army at Leuce Come near Sidon.

The campaign was a disaster, though Antony avoided Crassus' fate. In Rome Octavian concealed the extent of the defeat while celebrating his victory over Sextus Pompey, and the contrast weakened Antony's prestige.
siege_of_phraaspa.debate: Site of Phraaspa (near Maragheh or Takht-e Soleyman); size of Antony's army. The location of Phraaspa (Takht-e Soleyman, Maragheh, or elsewhere) is uncertain; Plutarch's figures likely derive from Dellius' account.
scholarship: Pelling, Plutarch: Life of Antony (1988)
Bivar, 'The political history of Iran under the Arsacids', CHI 3.1 (1983)

octavian_tribunician_sacrosanctity_36.detail: This was the first element of the tribunician power that became, from 23, the basis of the Principate. A grant to Octavia and Livia of the same inviolability and freedom from guardianship followed in 35.
octavian_tribunician_sacrosanctity_36.debate: Appian dates the grant to 36, Dio to 36 or 35; whether a fuller tribunicia potestas was given in 30 is debated.

donations_of_alexandria.detail:
In autumn 34, after his capture of Artavasdes of Armenia, Antony celebrated a triumphal procession in Alexandria. A few days later, in the Gymnasium, before a crowd, he and Cleopatra sat on golden thrones on a silver platform, with their children seated on smaller thrones. Antony proclaimed Cleopatra 'Queen of Kings' and Caesarion, whom he declared Caesar's true son, 'King of Kings', ruling Egypt and Cyprus jointly. Alexander Helios, aged six, wearing Median dress and tiara, received Armenia, Media and Parthia, still unconquered. Cleopatra Selene received Cyrenaica and Libya. Ptolemy Philadelphus, two years old, in Macedonian cloak and boots, received Phoenicia, Syria and Cilicia.

Coins issued at the time showed Antony with ARMENIA DEVICTA and Cleopatra as 'Queen of Kings and of her sons who are kings'. The donations formalised the restoration of much of the old Ptolemaic empire, though most of the territories remained Roman provinces or were held by client kings, and it is unclear what practical effect they had.
