In Rome Octavian presented the donations as proof that Antony had become the tool of a foreign queen, giving away Roman territory to her children and claiming Caesarion as Caesar's son, which directly threatened Octavian's own position as Caesar's heir. Antony's dispatch asking the Senate to ratify his acts was suppressed by the consuls of 32, both his supporters, who judged it too damaging.

Modern historians see the donations as a reorganisation of the eastern client system along dynastic lines with Cleopatra at its centre, intended for Greek and Egyptian audiences rather than Roman. They became a central element in Octavian's propaganda campaign of 33-32.
donations_of_alexandria.debate: The date (autumn 34) and the legal effect of the donations are debated.
scholarship: Roller, Cleopatra (2010)
Pelling, Plutarch: Life of Antony (1988)
Roller, Cleopatra: A Biography (2010)
Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974) no. 543

capture_of_artavasdes_34.detail: The 'triumph' in Alexandria was presented by Octavian's propaganda as Antony giving a Roman rite to a foreign queen. Artavasdes refused to prostrate himself before Cleopatra and was executed after Actium. Antony's coins of 34 proclaim ARMENIA DEVICTA and show Cleopatra as 'Queen of Kings'.

antony_divorces_octavia.detail:
Relations between Antony and Octavian broke down in 33, with an exchange of propaganda: Octavian attacked Antony's subservience to Cleopatra, Antony replied that Octavian had deposed Lepidus and kept Sextus Pompey's provinces without sharing, and mocked his ancestry and cowardice. The triumvirate's term expired at the end of 33. On 1 January 32 the consul Gaius Sosius attacked Octavian in the Senate; Octavian returned with armed men and read documents against Antony, and the consuls and over 300 senators fled to Antony in the East.

In early summer 32, at Athens, Antony formally divorced Octavia, sending her a notice to leave his house in Rome, which she did with dignity, taking his children with her. The divorce gave Octavian his casus belli. Lucius Munatius Plancus and his nephew Marcus Titius, who had witnessed Antony's will, defected to Octavian and revealed its contents. Octavian seized the will illegally from the Vestal Virgins and read selected passages to the Senate: Antony had confirmed Caesarion as Caesar's son, made large bequests to his children by Cleopatra, and asked to be buried in Alexandria beside Cleopatra, even if he died in Rome.

The burial clause outraged opinion. Antony was stripped of his consulship for 31 and of his remaining powers. Octavian then organised a sworn oath of loyalty to him by all Italy (tota Italia), followed by the western provinces, demanding him as leader in the war. The Res Gestae records that all Italy swore the oath of its own accord.

The authenticity of the will has been questioned, but most historians accept that Octavian edited rather than forged it. The divorce and the will marked the final rupture and the transformation of a Roman civil war into a war against Egypt.
antony_divorces_octavia.debate: Whether the published will was authentic, edited or forged is debated.
scholarship: Syme, The Roman Revolution (1939)
Osgood, Caesar's Legacy (2006)

antony_cleopatra_denarius_32.detail: Its unflattering realism (hooked nose, prominent chin for Cleopatra; thick neck for Antony) has done more than any text to shape modern debate about Cleopatra's appearance. Its message, endorsing the Donations, was precisely the one Octavian exploited.
scholarship: Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974) no. 543

antony_legionary_denarii_32.detail: Lower silver content (about 92 per cent) kept them out of hoards for melting, which is why they are among the commonest Republican coins in hoards of the second century AD. The legion numbers are an invaluable source for Antony's order of battle, though LEG XXIV, XXV and XXX are modern forgeries or misreadings. Pliny notes Antony mixed iron into his denarii.
scholarship: Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974) no. 544

flight_of_the_consuls_32.detail: Augustus later claimed that more than 700 senators fought under his standards at Actium, implying that perhaps a third of the Senate went east. With both consuls in Antony's camp, Octavian's position rested on the oath of Italy rather than on any magistracy, since his triumviral powers had arguably lapsed at the end of 33.

battle_of_actium.detail:
Antony and Cleopatra spent winter 32/31 at Patrae with a fleet of some 500 warships, many very large, and an army of nineteen legions. In spring 31 Agrippa seized Methone and other bases, cutting their supply route from Egypt; Octavian landed in Epirus and camped on the north side of the Gulf of Ambracia, facing Antony's fleet and army on the south side at Actium. Through the summer Antony's position deteriorated: disease, desertion, hunger. Dellius, Amyntas of Galatia and Domitius Ahenobarbus defected. Canidius urged retreat into Macedonia for a land battle; Cleopatra pressed for a naval breakout.

On 2 September 31 Antony's fleet, reduced to about 230 ships after he burned those he could not man, came out of the gulf in three squadrons, with Cleopatra's squadron of 60 in the rear carrying the war chest. Octavian's fleet under Agrippa, about 400 lighter ships, waited in open water. The battle began around noon when the wind shifted. Agrippa extended his line to outflank Antony's right; a gap opened in the centre, and Cleopatra's squadron sailed through it and away to the south, under sail. Antony transferred to a smaller ship and followed her with a few dozen ships. The rest of the fleet fought on until late afternoon; many ships were burned. The army, under Canidius, surrendered a week later.

Plutarch's account, drawing on Augustan sources, presents Cleopatra's flight as treachery or cowardice and Antony's as abandonment of his men. Modern historians suggest the breakout, with the treasury, may have been planned. Losses were relatively small: about 5,000 dead.

Octavian dedicated a victory monument at his camp site, rebuilt the temple of Apollo at Actium, founded Nicopolis, and instituted the Actian games. Augustan poetry, notably Virgil's shield of Aeneas and Horace's Cleopatra ode, made Actium the founding battle of the new order.
battle_of_actium.debate: Was Cleopatra's flight treachery, panic or a planned breakout? Most moderns accept a planned breakout, as Tarn argued. Whether Cleopatra's departure was flight or a planned breakout has been debated since Tarn (1931).
scholarship: Tarn, JRS 21 (1931)
Gurval, Actium and Augustus (1995)
Murray & Petsas, Octavian's Campsite Memorial for the Actian War (1989)
Lange, Res Publica Constituta (2009)
Murray and Petsas, Octavian's Campsite Memorial for the Actian War (1989)
Tarn, 'The battle of Actium', JRS 21 (1931)

agrippa_takes_methone_31.detail: These operations, more than the battle itself, decided the war. By the summer Antony's forces at Actium were short of food and rowers, deserting in numbers, and his council was split between those who wanted to fight on land in Macedonia and those, led by Cleopatra, who wanted a naval breakout.

fall_of_alexandria_30.detail:
After Actium, Antony and Cleopatra returned to Egypt. Antony first went to Paraetonium to take over the legions of Cyrenaica, which had defected to Octavian under Pinarius Scarpus, then returned to Alexandria and spent the winter in the 'Inimitable Livers' club, renamed the 'Partners in Death'. Cleopatra tried to send her fleet across the Isthmus of Suez to the Red Sea, but the Nabataeans burned it. Both sent envoys to Octavian; he answered Antony's requests with silence and Cleopatra's with promises if she killed or expelled Antony.

In summer 30 Octavian advanced from Syria via Pelusium, which surrendered, perhaps on Cleopatra's orders, while Cornelius Gallus came from the west and took Paraetonium. On 31 July Antony won a cavalry skirmish near the Hippodrome east of Alexandria. On 1 August his fleet and remaining cavalry went over to Octavian, and his infantry was defeated. Antony, told falsely that Cleopatra had killed herself in her mausoleum, stabbed himself, was carried still alive to the mausoleum, hauled up through a window by Cleopatra and her women, and died in her arms.

Octavian entered Alexandria on 1 August 30, a date later celebrated as a holiday (feriae) at Rome. He addressed the Alexandrians in Greek in the Gymnasium, sparing the city for the sake of its founder Alexander, the god Sarapis, and his teacher Areius. He visited Alexander's tomb, placing a crown on the body, and broke off part of the nose, it was said; he declined to visit the Ptolemies, saying he had come to see a king, not corpses. Caesarion and Antyllus were killed.

The fall of Alexandria ended the civil wars. The Senate decreed that the day was to be a public holiday, and the month Sextilis was later renamed Augustus partly because of it.
scholarship: Goldsworthy, Antony and Cleopatra (2010)
Roller, Cleopatra: A Biography (2010)

death_of_cleopatra.detail:
After Antony's death, Cleopatra was captured in her mausoleum by Octavian's agents Proculeius and Gallus, who prevented her from burning herself with her treasures. She was allowed to bury Antony. Octavian visited her, she pleaded and tried to win him over, and he promised her kind treatment, but she learned from the Roman officer Cornelius Dolabella that Octavian intended to send her and her children to Rome within three days for his triumph.

On 10 or 12 August 30, she bathed, dined, and sent Octavian a letter asking to be buried with Antony. A peasant brought a basket of figs, said to conceal an asp, an Egyptian cobra. When Octavian's messengers arrived, they found her dead on a golden couch in her royal robes, with her servant Iras dead at her feet and Charmion, dying, arranging her diadem; asked if this was well done, Charmion replied 'Very well, as befits a descendant of so many kings.' She was thirty-nine and had reigned twenty-two years.

Plutarch admits that no one knew the truth: some said she kept the asp in a water jar, others that she used a poisoned hairpin; only two faint punctures were found on her arm, and no snake was found in the room. Octavian, disappointed, had Psylli, snake-charmers, try to suck out the poison. He gave her a royal burial beside Antony, as she wished. In his triumph an effigy of Cleopatra with the asp was carried.

The asp became inseparable from her legend, perhaps because the cobra (uraeus) was the symbol of Egyptian royalty. Horace's ode celebrates her death as noble, 'no humble woman'. She was the last active ruler of the Ptolemaic kingdom.
death_of_cleopatra.debate: Method of death (asp or poison) and exact date. The method of her death (asp, poisoned pin, or other poison) is unknown; the date is 10 or 12 August 30.
scholarship: Roller, Cleopatra (2010)
Pelling, Plutarch: Life of Antony (1988)
Roller, Cleopatra: A Biography (2010)

annexation_of_egypt.detail:
With Cleopatra dead, Octavian annexed Egypt, though not as an ordinary province. The Res Gestae says simply 'I added Egypt to the empire of the Roman people.' Egypt was governed not by a senator but by an equestrian prefect, the praefectus Alexandreae et Aegypti, appointed by and responsible to Octavian personally, the first being Gaius Cornelius Gallus. Senators and leading equites were forbidden to enter Egypt without the emperor's permission, because whoever held it, with its grain and strategic position, could starve Italy. Three legions were stationed there.

The administrative structure of the Ptolemies was largely retained: the nomes, the bureaucracy, the royal land and monopolies, and the Greek language of administration. Octavian appeared as pharaoh in temple reliefs, with Egyptian titles, though he never visited Egypt again. The treasure of the Ptolemies paid off his soldiers, and Roman interest rates fell from 12 to 4 per cent, Dio says, because of the influx of money.

Egypt's annual grain shipment, perhaps a third of Rome's needs under the empire, made it central to the city's supply. Octavian had the irrigation canals cleared by the army. The prefect Gallus campaigned in Upper Egypt, suppressed a revolt in the Thebaid, and set up a boastful trilingual stele at Philae; his self-glorification led to his disgrace and suicide in 27/26.

The anniversary of the capture of Alexandria (1 August) was celebrated, and in Egypt the years were counted from Octavian's conquest. The Augustan regime presented the conquest as the end of the civil wars. Egypt remained under Roman and then Byzantine rule until the Arab conquest of 641.
scholarship: Capponi, Augustan Egypt: The Creation of a Roman Province (2005)
Bowman, Egypt after the Pharaohs (1986)

philae_stele_of_gallus_29.detail: Such self-advertisement by a subordinate was exactly what Augustus could not allow; Gallus fell from favour in 27/26 and killed himself. The stele was later broken and reused in a temple foundation. Gallus' four books of elegies to Lycoris made him the founder of Latin love elegy; a papyrus from Qasr Ibrim published in 1979 preserved some ten lines.

triple_triumph_29.detail:
On 13, 14 and 15 August 29, Octavian celebrated three triumphs: for Illyricum (his campaigns of 35-33), for Actium, and for Egypt. The third was the most splendid. Effigies of Cleopatra on a couch with an asp were carried, and her children by Antony, Alexander Helios and Cleopatra Selene, walked in the procession. The Egyptian treasure was so vast that it lowered interest rates and raised land prices. Each soldier received 1,000 sesterces and each citizen 400. Octavian rode in the triumphal chariot with his stepson Tiberius and nephew Marcellus on the trace horses.

Unusually, the magistrates and the Senate followed the chariot rather than leading it, a break with tradition that marked Octavian's supremacy. On 18 August he dedicated the temple of Divus Iulius in the Forum, adorned with the rams of ships from Actium, and on 28 August the Curia Julia with the statue and altar of Victory, which had been brought from Tarentum. Games followed, including a Troy game by aristocratic boys and gladiatorial combats with Dacians and Suebi.

Octavian also closed the doors of the temple of Janus for the first time since 235, signifying peace throughout the empire. The Senate voted many honours: an arch at Brundisium and in the Forum, his name in the hymn of the Salii, and his birthday as a holiday.

The triple triumph marked the formal end of the civil wars and the beginning of the transition to the Principate. Virgil, in the Aeneid, placed the triumph at the climax of the shield of Aeneas, with Octavian receiving the gifts of the nations at the temple of Apollo. The settlement of 27 followed.
scholarship: Beard, The Roman Triumph (2007)
Lange, Res Publica Constituta (2009)

temple_of_divus_iulius_29.detail: The cult had been voted by the triumvirs in 42 under the lex Rufrena; a column and altar first marked the pyre site. The temple contained Apelles' Venus Anadyomene, bought from Cos. It made the Forum's eastern end a monument of the new dynasty, facing the Rostra at the other end, and Octavian's coinage of 36 already showed its design with a star in the pediment.

crassus_and_the_spolia_opima.detail: Crassus triumphed in 27 but disappeared from public life. Historians see the episode as Octavian refusing to let any other general outshine him.
crassus_and_the_spolia_opima.debate: Whether the corslet story was fabricated for the occasion.
scholarship: Rich, Chiron 26 (1996)

virgils_georgics.detail: Composed amid civil war, the poem frames hard labour (labor improbus) as the human condition, ends Book 1 with the portents after Caesar's murder, and closes with the myth of Aristaeus and Orpheus. Servius reports that the last half of Book 4 originally praised Gallus and was rewritten after his disgrace, a claim modern scholars mostly reject.

temple_of_apollo_palatinus_28.detail: Apollo had become Octavian's patron at Actium, where the god's temple overlooked the battle; the temple's doors showed the Gauls driven from Delphi and the death of Niobe's children. Excavations since the 1950s have revealed painted terracotta plaques of Apollo and Hercules struggling for the Delphic tripod. The complex fused the princeps' house with the sanctuary in a way that anticipated the imperial palace.

census_of_28.detail: The leap from 910,000 in 70/69 to over 4 million is among the most debated numbers in ancient demography: either women and children were now counted (the 'low count', Beloch and Brunt) or Italy's free population was far larger than usually thought (the 'high count', Lo Cascio).
census_of_28.debate: Low count versus high count of the Italian population.
scholarship: Brunt, Italian Manpower (1971)
Rich & Williams, Numismatic Chronicle 159 (1999)
Sutherland, Roman Imperial Coinage I2 (1984) Augustus 275, 476

division_of_the_provinces_27bc.detail: The division of provinces in January 27 BC created the administrative map of the Principate. Augustus received the "unpacified" provinces where armies were needed: Hispania Tarraconensis and Lusitania (then still one large command with the Cantabrian war under way), the Gallic territories, Syria with Cilicia and Cyprus, and Egypt. The Senate kept the rest: Africa, Baetica, Narbonensis (handed back in 22 BC along with Cyprus), Sicily, Sardinia and Corsica, Macedonia, Achaea, Illyricum (transferred to Augustus in 11 BC when war flared), Crete and Cyrene, Bithynia and Pontus, and Asia. Proconsuls of the "public" provinces were chosen by lot from ex-consuls (for Africa and Asia) and ex-praetors (for the others) and served for a single year, while Augustus governed his share through his own legati Augusti pro praetore, senators of his choice serving at his pleasure, often for three years or more, and through equestrian prefects in Egypt, where senators were barred from even visiting without permission. Financial administration followed the same split: proconsuls had quaestors and paid revenues to the aerarium Saturni, while imperial provinces were managed by equestrian procurators accountable to the emperor, who also placed procurators in public provinces to manage his estates. Strabo (17.3.25) and Dio (53.12-15) give the lists, which differ slightly, reflecting changes over time. In practice the line between the two categories blurred: the emperor's maius imperium after 23 BC allowed him to give orders to proconsuls, as the Edicts of Cyrene (7-6 BC) show, and the Senate's provinces could be reassigned when trouble arose (Achaea and Macedonia went to the emperor in AD 15 and back in 44; Bithynia passed to Pliny as a special imperial legate in 110). Africa was the only senatorial province with a legion until Caligula transferred command of III Augusta to an imperial legate in 39. The arrangement lasted in outline until the reforms of Diocletian, though new conquests (Britain, Dacia, Arabia) were always imperial.
scholarship: Millar, 'The emperor, the Senate and the provinces', JRS 56 (1966)

first_settlement_27bc.detail: At the Senate meeting of 13 January 27 BC Octavian, consul for the seventh time with Agrippa, formally laid down the extraordinary powers he had held since the triumvirate and "transferred the res publica from my power to the discretion of the Senate and people" (Res Gestae 34). The scene was carefully staged: senators, briefed in advance, begged him not to abandon the state, and he accepted a ten-year command over a large "province" comprising Spain (except Baetica), Gaul and Syria, together with Egypt, which he already held as personal possession. These were the regions where most of the legions stood. The remaining provinces, including Africa with its legion, Macedonia and Illyricum for the time being, returned to proconsuls chosen by lot. On 16 January the Senate voted him the name Augustus, a word with religious overtones (augur, augere) chosen over the suggestion of Romulus, together with the oak wreath (corona civica) over his door, laurels flanking the doorposts and a golden shield (clipeus virtutis) in the Curia inscribed with his virtues: valour, clemency, justice and piety. Dio (53.2-12) gives Octavian a long speech of renunciation and explains the arrangement as a sham that left all real power in his hands through control of the army and the treasury; Velleius (2.89) presents it as the restoration of the old Republic, and the coin legend LEGES ET IVRA P R RESTITVIT on an aureus of 28 BC shows the language of restoration. Modern historians since Mommsen have debated whether the settlement created a "dyarchy" of princeps and Senate, a disguised monarchy (Syme's "Roman Revolution"), or a genuine if evolving compromise with the aristocracy. Its key mechanisms, a provincial command delegated to legates and a continuous consulship, proved unstable and were revised in 23 BC. The ten-year grant was renewed in 18, 13 and 8 BC and AD 3 and 13, a rhythm later marked by decennalia celebrations.
first_settlement_27bc.debate: Sham restoration (Dio, Syme), dyarchy (Mommsen) or genuine compromise with the Senate.
scholarship: Syme, The Roman Revolution (1939)
Millar, 'Triumvirate and Principate', JRS 63 (1973)
Rich and Williams, 'Leges et iura p.R. restituit', Numismatic Chronicle 159 (1999)

name_augustus.detail:
On 16 January 27, three days after Octavian's formal restoration of the Republic, the Senate, on the motion of Lucius Munatius Plancus, voted that he be called Augustus. Some had proposed Romulus, as the second founder of Rome, but this was rejected, Suetonius says, because of Romulus' associations with kingship and fratricide. Augustus was a word of religious solemnity, used of holy places and things consecrated by augury. Ennius had written that Rome was founded 'augusto augurio', with august augury. The name implied that its bearer was more than human without claiming divinity.

The full name was now Imperator Caesar Divi filius Augustus: Imperator as a first name, an innovation emphasising military victory; Caesar as a family name; son of the deified Julius; and Augustus as a cognomen. Ovid's Fasti explains that the sacred things are called august, as are temples consecrated by priests, and that the word shares its root with augere, to increase.

Dio says the name signified something more than human, and that it was a title of honour rather than power. The month Sextilis, in which he had won his first consulship and conquered Egypt, was renamed Augustus in 8 BC. The name became the title of all subsequent emperors, and in Greek Sebastos, 'the revered one'.

The choice of 'Augustus' over 'Romulus' shows the care with which Octavian shaped his public identity. It distanced him from the bloodstained triumvir and from kingship, while giving him a unique and sacred standing. The name is the beginning of the imperial titulature.
scholarship: Syme, The Roman Revolution (1939)

triumph_of_crassus_27bc.detail: Livy (4.20.5-11) records that Augustus told him he had seen, in the restored temple of Jupiter Feretrius, the linen corslet of Aulus Cornelius Cossus inscribed to show that Cossus had won the spolia as consul, not military tribune, which would establish that only a commander with his own auspices could dedicate them. Crassus also took the title imperator, a privilege then being restricted to the princeps and his family. Crassus disappears from the record afterwards. Dessau and Syme saw a deliberate snub to a rival; Rich (1996) argues the issue was invented later or exaggerated.
triumph_of_crassus_27bc.debate: How far the Cossus episode was manufactured to block Crassus is contested.
scholarship: Rich, 'Augustus and the spolia opima', Chiron 26 (1996)

census_of_gaul_27bc.detail: Livy's Periocha 134 reports the conventus at Narbo and the census; Dio adds that Augustus organised the Gauls administratively, a task completed by the division into Aquitania, Lugdunensis and Belgica, usually dated 16-13 BC. Later censuses in Gaul (12 BC under Drusus, AD 14-16 under Germanicus, AD 61 and 83) were moments of tension; the census of 12 BC coincided with unrest and the dedication of the altar at Lugdunum.

livy_begins_ab_urbe_condita.detail: The date rests on the preface's gloomy mention of a time when "we can endure neither our vices nor their remedies", on Book 1.19.3, which mentions the closing of Janus after Actium and calls Octavian Augustus (so after January 27 BC) but not the closing of 25 BC, and on an aside in 4.20 recording Augustus's personal testimony about the linen corselet of Cossus. Livy reached the death of Drusus in 9 BC in Book 142. Augustus jokingly called him a Pompeian (Tacitus, Annals 4.34), and he encouraged the young Claudius to write history. Books 1-10 and 21-45 survive, with the Periochae and the Oxyrhynchus epitome for most of the rest.
livy_begins_ab_urbe_condita.debate: Some scholars date Book 1 as late as 25 or even 20 BC, or posit a second edition.

battle_of_vellica.detail: Florus says the Cantabri were defeated beneath Vellica and fled to the 'very lofty' Mons Vindius, believing the ocean would rise to it before Roman arms, where they were besieged into starvation. Augustus may not have commanded in person on the day; Suetonius (Aug. 20) says he conducted only two wars personally after Actium, the Dalmatian and Cantabrian, and Dio records a thunderbolt narrowly missing his litter during a night march, which led him to dedicate the temple of Jupiter Tonans on the Capitol (22 BC).
battle_of_vellica.debate: Vellica is usually placed at Monte Cildá near Olleros de Pisuerga, but this is not secure.

siege_of_aracillum.detail: Florus calls it Aracelium and says it resisted strongly; Orosius gives Racilium. Archaeologists have identified Roman siege works around the Iron Age hillfort of La Espina del Gallego (Cantabria), with three Roman camps (El Cildá, Cueto del Avellanosa, El Cincho), which many now equate with Aracillum, though the older candidate Aradillos near Reinosa still has supporters.
scholarship: Peralta Labrador, Los cántabros antes de Roma (2003)

downfall_of_cornelius_gallus.detail: Gallus had suppressed a revolt in the Thebaid and set up a trilingual stele at Philae (dated 15 April 29 BC; ILS 8995) claiming to have taken an army beyond the First Cataract 'where neither the Roman people nor the kings of Egypt had borne arms', and inscribed his deeds on the pyramids. The renuntiatio amicitiae by the princeps was followed by prosecutions in the Senate, showing how imperial disfavour could translate into legal ruin. A papyrus from Qasr Ibrim, published in 1979, preserves lines of his love-elegies, previously known only from one pentameter.
downfall_of_cornelius_gallus.debate: Jerome dates his death to 27 BC; Dio places it in 26.
scholarship: Anderson, Parsons and Nisbet, 'Elegiacs by Gallus from Qasr Ibrîm', JRS 69 (1979)

augustus_at_tarraco_26bc.detail: Augustus set out from Rome in 27 BC, held a census at Narbo, and in 26 opened the campaign from a base at Segisama (Sasamon) with a three-pronged advance into the Cantabrian mountains. Illness, apparently a recurrence of the complaint that nearly killed him in 23, forced him back to Tarraco, and the fighting was left to his legates Gaius Antistius Vetus and Gaius Furnius. At Tarraco he took up his consulship of 25 BC, and Orosius (6.21.19) places here the arrival of embassies from India and Scythia. Tarraco later dedicated an altar to him, on which a palm tree famously sprouted (Quintilian 6.3.77). He closed the temple of Janus on his return in 25 BC, although the war resumed almost at once.
augustus_at_tarraco_26bc.debate: The Cantabrian narrative depends on Florus and Orosius, both drawing on Livy, and the three-column plan is a reconstruction.

siege_of_marib.detail: Strabo reports that in the only real battle the Romans lost two men against 10,000 Arabs, and that the expedition's losses came from disease, heat and thirst, blaming the treachery of the Nabataean vizier Syllaeus. Augustus's Res Gestae (26.5) claims the army reached Mariba in the land of the Sabaeans. The expedition yielded geographical knowledge and showed that conquest of South Arabia was impractical; Rome turned to controlling the Red Sea trade instead, which boomed after Egypt's annexation (Strabo saw 120 ships a year sailing from Myos Hormos to India).
siege_of_marib.debate: Whether Syllaeus truly sabotaged the expedition or became Strabo's scapegoat is debated; Syllaeus was executed in Rome c. 6 BC for other crimes.

siege_of_lancia.detail: Florus says Carisius had to restrain his soldiers from burning the town, keeping it intact 'as a better monument of Roman victory'. Lancia lies at Villasabariego (León), where excavations have found a Roman town overlying the Asturian oppidum. Carisius founded Emerita and struck coins at a mint in the north-west showing captured Cantabro-Asturian weapons (caetra shields, double-axes).

subjugation_of_the_salassi.detail: Strabo says 8,000 of those sold were men of fighting age and that the buyers were forbidden to free them for 20 years. The colony (Aosta) retains its Augustan walls, gate (Porta Praetoria) and arch. Control of the Great and Little St Bernard opened direct routes to the Rhone and upper Rhine, indispensable for the coming German wars.

founding_of_augusta_emerita.detail: Mérida preserves one of the best ensembles of Roman architecture in the West: the theatre (dedicated by Agrippa, 16-15 BC), amphitheatre (8 BC), the 60-arch Guadiana bridge, two aqueducts (Los Milagros, San Lázaro) and the Proserpina reservoir. Its coinage under Carisius depicts the city gate.

annexation_of_galatia.detail: Galatia was the first of the great Augustan annexations of client kingdoms, setting a pattern of absorbing them on the death of the ruler. It was expanded with Paphlagonia (6/5 BC) and Pontus Galaticus (3/2 BC) and colonised with veteran colonies in Pisidia (Antioch, Lystra, Cremna, Comama, Olbasa, Parlais), linked by the Via Sebaste (6 BC). The best-preserved copy of the Res Gestae, in Latin and Greek, survives on the temple of Rome and Augustus at Ancyra (Monumentum Ancyranum).
scholarship: Mitchell, Anatolia I (1993)

agrippas_pantheon.detail: Dio says Agrippa wished to install a statue of Augustus inside and name the building after him; Augustus declined, so statues of Julius Caesar stood inside and of Augustus and Agrippa in the porch. The original was rebuilt after fires of 80 and c. 110, and Hadrian's version (c. 118-128) is the building that survives. Excavations by Beltrami in the 1890s were taken to show a south-facing Agrippan temple; work in 1996-97 suggests the original faced north on the same axis, though its plan (rectangular or circular) is still debated.
scholarship: Marder and Wilson Jones (eds), The Pantheon: From Antiquity to the Present (2015)

temple_of_janus_closed_25bc.detail: Res Gestae 13 boasts that Janus, closed only twice before his birth (under Numa and in 235 BC after the First Punic War), was shut three times while Augustus was princeps. The closing of 25 BC was premature: the Cantabri and Astures rose again almost immediately. The third closing is undated; Orosius puts it in 2 BC to coincide with the birth of Christ, a theological construction rather than evidence, and modern guesses range between 13 BC and 1 BC.
temple_of_janus_closed_25bc.debate: Date of the third closing is unknown.

marriage_of_julia_and_marcellus.detail: The match marked Marcellus as Augustus's intended successor in the eyes of contemporaries, and Velleius (2.93) and Dio (53.31-32) report Agrippa's resentment, which some ancient writers tied to his departure to the East in 23. Marcellus received the aedileship of 23 BC early and gave lavish games, but died that autumn at Baiae. The widowed Julia was then married to Agrippa (21 BC).

juba_ii_king_of_mauretania.detail: Mauretania had been without a king since Bocchus II died in 33 BC and had been administered through Roman agents; Augustus had also planted twelve veteran colonies there (Iulia Constantia Zilil, Banasa, Babba and others) which remained outside the king's jurisdiction. Juba, raised in Rome in Octavia's household and a prolific Greek author (on Libya, Arabia, the theatre, painting), turned Iol into Caesarea with a theatre, amphitheatre and Hellenistic court culture; the royal purple-dye works on the Iles Purpuraires off Mogador date from his reign. The kingdom remained a client state until his son Ptolemy was killed by Caligula in AD 40.

vitruvius_de_architectura.detail: Vitruvius had served Caesar as an artillery engineer and owed his pension to Octavia's recommendation. The work covers town planning, materials (including pozzolana concrete), temple orders and proportions, the basilica he himself built at Fanum Fortunae, water supply, sundials and astronomy, and siege engines. Its theory of symmetria based on the proportions of the human body produced the Renaissance image of the Vitruvian man. Vitruvius praises Augustus's building programme as already under way but does not know the great monuments of the 20s and teens, which gives the approximate date.

battle_of_pselchis.detail: Strabo says the Kushites were poorly armed, with large oxhide shields, axes, pikes and swords; some fled into the town, others into the desert, others swam to an island. Petronius then stormed Primis and marched on Napata, the residence of the queen's son, which he razed. He sent a thousand captives to Augustus. The Meroë head of Augustus, buried beneath the threshold of a victory shrine, is the Kushite counter-memorial of the same war.
battle_of_pselchis.debate: Whether the battle belongs to late 25 or 24 BC is uncertain; Petronius's prefecture is usually dated 25-21 BC.

second_settlement_23bc.detail: The settlement of 23 BC, following Augustus's near-fatal illness and the conspiracy of Fannius Caepio and Varro Murena, gave the Principate its lasting legal basis. On 1 July 23 Augustus resigned the consulship he had held continuously since 31 BC, freeing an annual place for senators and ending the anomaly of a permanent consul. In compensation he received two powers. The first was the tribunicia potestas for life, which gave him the right to convene the Senate and people, propose laws, veto any magistrate and offer protection to citizens, and from which his regnal years were henceforth counted (TR POT on coins and inscriptions, renewed each year, so that "TR P XXXVII" dates an inscription to AD 14). Augustus had held some tribunician privileges since 36 and 30 BC, but now took the full power as a substitute for office. The second was an imperium proconsulare that he could exercise inside Rome without laying it down at the pomerium, and which was declared greater (maius) than that of any proconsul, allowing him to intervene in senatorial provinces. Dio adds the right to convene the Senate first at any meeting (ius primae relationis). The tradition that he also received consular imperium in 19 BC rests on a disputed passage of Dio (54.10.5). In the same year Agrippa was sent to the East with an imperium of his own, perhaps also maius, a sign that the princeps intended to share power within his family. Tacitus (Annals 3.56) famously called tribunicia potestas the "title of the highest rank" invented by Augustus to avoid the name of king or dictator. Scholars disagree on the motive: a concession to senators alarmed by his monopoly of the consulship (Syme), a reaction to a real conspiracy among his own supporters, or the culmination of a long-planned constitutional design. Whatever the cause, the combination of tribunician power and maius imperium became the core of every later emperor's authority, conferred in a single package by Senate and people, as the Lex de imperio Vespasiani shows.
second_settlement_23bc.debate: Whether Augustus received consular imperium in 19 BC, and whether the settlement responded to a genuine crisis.
scholarship: Rich, Cassius Dio: The Augustan Settlement (1990)
Crook, CAH X2 (1996), ch. 2

conspiracy_of_caepio_and_murena.detail: Augustus appeared uninvited at Primus's trial and denied giving instructions; Murena's insolent questioning ('What are you doing here, who summoned you?') was remembered. Several jurors voted for acquittal of the conspirators, and Augustus responded with a law that votes in such cases be open. Caepio's slave who betrayed him was paraded with a placard; another who defended him was rewarded. The episode is commonly linked to the political crisis and constitutional reshaping of 23 BC.
conspiracy_of_caepio_and_murena.debate: Dio dates it to 22 BC; many scholars prefer 23. Whether the consul of 23 BC, who disappears from the Fasti, was the conspirator Murena is disputed. Maecenas reportedly leaked the danger to his wife Terentia, Murena's sister, cooling his relationship with Augustus.
scholarship: Swan, 'The consular fasti of 23 B.C. and the conspiracy of Varro Murena', HSCP 71 (1966)

death_of_marcellus.detail: Marcellus had been allowed to stand for office ten years early and gave lavish games as aedile in 23 BC. Rumour blamed Livia; Dio rejects this given the epidemic of that year. Virgil's lament at the end of Aeneid 6 ('tu Marcellus eris') reportedly made Octavia faint when he recited it before her (Donatus, Vita Vergilii 32). Augustus named the theatre near the Circus Flaminius after him and Octavia built a library in his memory. Julia was then married to Agrippa.

augustan_coinage_reform.detail: The system (1 aureus = 25 denarii = 100 sestertii = 400 asses) lasted, with modifications, until the third century. Brass, a zinc-copper alloy, was valued above copper, so sestertius and dupondius (yellow) were distinguished from the as (red) by colour, the dupondius later by a radiate crown. The SC on base-metal issues probably acknowledges senatorial authorisation. Precious-metal production soon shifted to Lugdunum (from c. 15 BC), close to the Rhine armies. Moneyers' names disappear from coins after c. 4 BC.
augustan_coinage_reform.debate: The exact date (23 or 19 BC) and the meaning of SC on bronze are debated.
scholarship: Sutherland, Roman Imperial Coinage I2 (1984)
Burnett, Coinage in the Roman World (1987)

horace_odes_published.detail: The collection includes the Cleopatra ode (1.37, "nunc est bibendum"), the six "Roman Odes" that open Book 3 and the closing claim to have built a monument "more lasting than bronze" (3.30). Lukewarm reception, Horace later implied, discouraged further lyric until Augustus commissioned the Carmen Saeculare for the Secular Games of 17 BC, sung by 27 boys and 27 girls on the Palatine and Capitol; Book 4 followed c. 13 BC, with odes celebrating the Alpine victories of Drusus and Tiberius. Augustus offered Horace a post as his private secretary, which he declined.

illness_of_augustus_23bc.detail: The illness came during the political crisis of 23 (the Murena-Caepio affair) and helps explain the reconstitution of his powers that summer, when he resigned the consulship and received tribunician power and an enhanced proconsular imperium. Musa was rewarded with a statue beside Aesculapius and the equestrian rank, and physicians at Rome were exempted from taxes, but the same treatment failed to save Marcellus in the autumn. Handing the ring to Agrippa signalled that the succession was not settled on Marcellus and caused tension in the household.

tiber_flood_23bc.detail: Floods of the Campus Martius, Velabrum and Forum Boarium were a structural hazard of the city; later records include AD 5 (Dio 55.22), AD 12 (when the Circus was flooded and the Ludi Martiales moved to the Forum of Augustus) and AD 15. Augustus cleared the river channel of rubbish and encroaching buildings (Suetonius, Augustus 30), but a permanent board of curatores riparum et alvei Tiberis was created only under Tiberius in AD 15.

cura_annonae_22bc.detail: Res Gestae 5 records both the refusal and the cura annonae. In the same year Augustus had censors elected, Paullus Aemilius Lepidus and Lucius Munatius Plancus, the last pair of private citizens to hold the office; the platform collapsed on the first day, an omen. The grain supply was later placed under an equestrian praefectus annonae (by AD 14), one of the great prefectures.

augustus_eastern_tour_22bc.detail: In Sicily he founded colonies at Syracuse and elsewhere; in Greece he rewarded Sparta with Cythera for sheltering Livia in 40 BC and punished Athens for its support of Antony by taking Aegina and Eretria from it. In 20 BC Cyzicus lost its freedom for flogging and killing Roman citizens, as did Tyre and Sidon for civil strife. He enlarged Herod's kingdom with the territory of Zenodorus (Ulatha and Paneas), and appointed client kings in Commagene, Cilicia and Lesser Armenia. The diplomatic climax was the Parthian surrender of the Crassus and Antony standards in May 20, while Tiberius installed Tigranes III in Armenia. On Samos he received an Indian embassy whose gifts included tigers and an armless boy. He returned to Rome on 12 October 19 BC, the day honoured by the Altar of Fortuna Redux.

marriage_of_julia_and_agrippa.detail: Dio (54.6.5) has Maecenas advise Augustus that he had made Agrippa so great that he must either kill him or make him his son-in-law. Julia accompanied Agrippa to the East in 16-13 BC, where the cities gave her divine honours. The birth of Gaius (20 BC) and Lucius (17 BC) provided the heirs whom Augustus adopted in 17 BC.

return_of_the_parthian_standards.detail: On 12 May 20 BC, according to the Fasti, the Parthian king Phraates IV handed back to Tiberius, acting for Augustus, the legionary eagles and standards lost by Crassus at Carrhae (53 BC), by Decidius Saxa (40 BC) and by Antony's lieutenant Oppius Statianus (36 BC), together with surviving prisoners. Augustus had gone to Syria in person, and a Roman army under Tiberius was moving into Armenia; Phraates, insecure on his throne and holding a pretender Tiridates who had fled to the Romans with Phraates's son, chose to negotiate. No battle was fought. The success was nonetheless presented as a military triumph that avenged the Republic's greatest humiliation in the East. Augustus refused a triumph but accepted an ovation and a triumphal arch; coins proclaimed SIGNIS RECEPTIS and CIVIB ET SIGN MILIT A PARTH RECVP, showing a kneeling Parthian offering a standard. The standards were deposited first in a small round temple of Mars Ultor on the Capitol, shown on coins, and in 2 BC in the great temple in the Forum of Augustus. The central scene of the Prima Porta statue's cuirass shows a Parthian handing an eagle to a Roman figure (Tiberius, Mars or a personification), surrounded by the subjected provinces and the cosmic order. Horace, Propertius and Ovid celebrated the event as the restoration of Roman honour. Res Gestae 29 claims that Augustus "compelled the Parthians to return the spoils and standards of three Roman armies and to seek the friendship of the Roman people as suppliants". In 10/9 BC Phraates sent four of his sons with their families to Rome as hostages, which Augustus represented as submission but which also removed rivals from Phraates's court. Modern scholars stress that the agreement was a negotiated compromise between equals that recognised the Euphrates as a de facto boundary, and that Augustus's propaganda transformed diplomacy into conquest, sparing him the risk of a real war.
return_of_the_parthian_standards.debate: Whether a Parthian arch was built in the Forum, and where, remains disputed.
scholarship: Rich, 'The Parthian Honours', PBSR 66 (1998)

treaty_of_samos_kush.detail: The frontier was fixed at Hiera Sykaminos (Maharraqa), with the Dodekaschoinos as a Roman military zone. The generosity reflects Augustus's preference for stable frontiers and the low value of Lower Nubia. The peace held, with minor exceptions (a Neronian exploration party reached Meroë and the Sudd c. 61-63), until the Blemmyes troubles of the third century.

herods_temple_begun.detail: To avoid profaning the sanctuary, 1,000 priests were trained as masons; the shrine itself took 18 months, the porticoes eight years, and work continued until c. AD 63, only seven years before its destruction. The Royal Stoa ran along the southern edge. A Greek warning inscription forbidding Gentiles to pass the balustrade on pain of death was found in 1871 (OGIS 598), confirming Josephus's description. Some ashlars of the retaining walls weigh over 500 tonnes.

tiberius_crowns_tigranes_iii.detail: Augustus advertised the event as the conquest of Armenia (Res Gestae 27: "Armenia maiore ... cum possem facere provinciam, malui ... regnum id Tigrani ... tradere"), and coins proclaimed ARMENIA CAPTA alongside SIGNIS RECEPTIS. The arrangement collapsed within a few years and Armenia remained the chronic fault line between Rome and Parthia for the rest of the period.

indian_embassy_zarmanochegas.detail: Nicolaus of Damascus, who met the envoys at Antioch, described a letter in Greek from a king who claimed to rule six hundred kings, gifts of tigers, a large river tortoise, snakes and a boy born without arms, and the ascetic's tomb inscription at Athens: "Zarmanochegas, an Indian from Bargosa, made himself immortal according to the ancestral customs of the Indians." Res Gestae 31 lists Indian embassies as something "never before seen" at a Roman commander's court. The name may reflect sramanacarya, a Buddhist or Jain teacher, and Bargosa is Barygaza (Bharuch), the main port of the Indian Ocean trade that boomed after the annexation of Egypt.

ius_respondendi.detail: Pomponius (Digest 1.2.2.48-50) says that before Augustus anyone confident in his learning gave opinions; Augustus wanted their authority enhanced and Tiberius gave the privilege to Masurius Sabinus, the first equestrian so honoured. How binding such responsa were on judges is unclear before Hadrian, who ruled that where licensed jurists agreed their view had the force of law. The date of Augustus's grant is unknown.
ius_respondendi.debate: Nature and date of the privilege are disputed; some doubt that it gave formally binding force.

triumph_of_cornelius_balbus.detail: Pliny lists the names of towns and peoples carried in the procession, including Cidamus (Ghadames) and Garama, and notes that the route over the mountains was unknown before. Balbus used his spoils to build the Theatre of Balbus and its crypta in the Campus Martius (dedicated 13 BC). After this, generals received only triumphal ornaments (ornamenta triumphalia); the Fasti Triumphales on the Arch of Augustus end with Balbus.

aqua_virgo.detail: Frontinus says the name came from a young girl who showed the source to soldiers searching for water. It is the only ancient Roman aqueduct to have functioned almost continuously to the present (restored by Pope Nicholas V in 1453 as the Acqua Vergine). Agrippa as aedile in 33 BC had already overhauled Rome's water system, creating 700 basins, 500 fountains and 130 reservoirs, and his slave water-gang of 240 was bequeathed to Augustus and then made public.

death_of_virgil.detail: The Aeneid's half-lines and inconsistencies betray its incomplete state. Its epitaph, supposedly composed by Virgil himself, ran 'Mantua me genuit, Calabri rapuere, tenent nunc Parthenope; cecini pascua rura duces'. The poem became the school text of the Latin West for the rest of antiquity and was quoted on graffiti at Pompeii and on writing tablets at Vindolanda.

conspiracy_of_egnatius_rufus.detail: Velleius, deeply hostile, presents him as a gladiator rather than a senator. The affair, during Augustus's absence in the East, and riots over consular elections led the Senate to send for Augustus; on his return Dio says he received consular power for life (54.10.5), a passage whose reliability is debated. Fire-fighting remained a political issue until Augustus created the vigiles in AD 6.

end_of_the_cantabrian_wars.detail: Dio notes that Agrippa declined a triumph and did not even report his success to the Senate, a sign of the new etiquette that triumphal honours belonged to the princeps. He degraded legio I Augusta, stripping it of its title. The pacified north-west was reorganised around new towns, Asturica Augusta (Astorga), Lucus Augusti (Lugo) and Bracara Augusta (Braga), and its gold fields were exploited by hydraulic mining (ruina montium) on a massive scale.

aeneid_published.detail: Virgil had been reading parts to Augustus since at least 23 BC, when Octavia reputedly fainted at the lament for Marcellus in Book 6. The ancient Life by Donatus (drawing on Suetonius) records the instruction to burn the manuscript and the editors' orders to add nothing. The poem became at once a school text: graffiti quoting its opening lines appear at Pompeii, and Virgil's epitaph ("Mantua me genuit, Calabri rapuere, tenet nunc Parthenope") was shown at his tomb near Naples. Propertius (2.34) had already hailed "something greater than the Iliad" in 26-25 BC.

augustan_marriage_laws_18bc.detail: In 18 BC, using his tribunician power, Augustus carried the Lex Julia de maritandis ordinibus and the Lex Julia de adulteriis coercendis, the first Roman statutes to regulate the family life of citizens on this scale. The marriage law required men between 25 and 60 and women between 20 and 50 to be married; widows and divorcees had to remarry within a period later fixed at two years and eighteen months respectively. Unmarried persons (caelibes) could not receive inheritances or legacies from outside their close kin, and the childless (orbi) only half; parents of three children (four for freedwomen) gained the ius trium liberorum, which freed women from guardianship and gave men advantages in the cursus honorum. The law also forbade senators and their descendants to marry freedwomen, actresses and prostitutes, while allowing other freeborn men to marry freedwomen. The adultery law turned a private family matter into a public crime with a standing jury court: a husband had to divorce an adulterous wife and prosecute within sixty days, or face a charge of pimping (lenocinium); the father could kill an adulterous daughter and her lover caught in his house, the husband only the lover and only if he was of low status. Penalties were relegation to separate islands and confiscation of half the man's property and a third of the woman's. The laws met fierce resistance: an earlier attempt seems to have failed c. 28 BC (Propertius 2.7), knights demonstrated at games in AD 9, and the Lex Papia Poppaea of that year, carried by two unmarried consuls, softened and supplemented the provisions. The most famous victims were Augustus's own daughter Julia (2 BC) and granddaughter Julia (AD 8). Tacitus (Annals 3.25-28) judged that the laws did not increase marriages or child-rearing and only enriched informers, who received a share of forfeited property. The penalties on the unmarried survived until Constantine abolished them in 320, but the adultery law lasted into Justinian's Digest.
augustan_marriage_laws_18bc.debate: Purpose of the laws: demographic (raising citizen birth rates), moral, or political control of the elite.
scholarship: Treggiari, Roman Marriage (1991)
Edwards, The Politics of Immorality in Ancient Rome (1993)

lectio_senatus_18bc.detail: This was the second Augustan purge after that of 29-28 BC (from about 1,000 to 800). A minimum census for senators was fixed, probably at 1 million sesterces, with Augustus subsidising worthy but poor members. A third revision followed in 11 BC and a committee of three (tresviri legendi senatus) in AD 4.

lex_julia_de_ambitu_18bc.detail: The bribery law shows that the popular assemblies still elected magistrates in a meaningful way, and Augustus himself handed out a thousand sesterces to the members of his tribes (Fabia and Scaptia) on polling days so that they would not take money from candidates (Suetonius, Augustus 40.2). The sumptuary law set limits on the cost of dinners that were soon ignored; Tiberius in AD 22 declined to revive such measures (Tacitus, Annals 3.52-55).

ludi_saeculares_17bc.detail: A long inscription recording the protocol (the Acta of the games, CIL VI 32323) was found in 1890 near the Tiber at the site of the Tarentum, giving prayers to the Moirai, Ilithyiae, Terra Mater, Jupiter, Juno, Apollo and Diana and naming 110 matrons. The calculation of a 110-year saeculum was itself a scholarly construction of the jurist Ateius Capito. Shortly afterwards Augustus adopted Agrippa's sons Gaius and the newborn Lucius as his own, signalling the dynastic purpose of the new age.
scholarship: Feeney, Literature and Religion at Rome (1998)
Schnegg-Köhler, Die augusteischen Säkularspiele (2002)

adoption_of_gaius_and_lucius_17bc.detail: The adoption, performed shortly before the Secular Games, publicly settled the succession on the next generation, with Agrippa as regent figure. Coins of the moneyer Gaius Antistius Vetus (16 BC) and later Lugdunum issues showing the two boys spread their images. Their early deaths (Lucius at Massilia in AD 2, Gaius in Lycia in AD 4) forced the adoption of Tiberius.

clades_lolliana.detail: Velleius calls it a defeat 'of greater disgrace than damage'; Suetonius pairs it with the Varian disaster as Augustus's only two serious and ignominious defeats, both in Germany. Augustus came to Gaul in person (16-13 BC), the Germans withdrew and gave hostages, and the episode led directly to Drusus's offensives across the Rhine from 12 BC. Lollius later served as guardian to Gaius Caesar in the East and was disgraced for taking bribes from the Parthians (AD 2).
clades_lolliana.debate: Dio dates it to 16 BC; the Livian tradition (Obsequens) may imply 17. Site unknown.

augustus_in_gaul_16bc.detail: Licinus, a Gaul enslaved by Caesar and freed, collected monthly tribute and argued that December (the tenth month) made the year fourteen months long. When the Gauls complained, he showed Augustus his treasure and claimed he had amassed it to keep it out of rebel hands, and was spared; his wealth became proverbial ("Licinus' marble tomb" in the epigram). Augustus's stay produced the census and road network radiating from Lugdunum and laid the ground for the Altar of the Three Gauls (12 BC). He returned in 13 BC, when the Senate voted the Ara Pacis.

conquest_of_raetia.detail: Horace (Odes 4.14) dates the decisive victory to the anniversary of the fall of Alexandria (1 August); Odes 4.4 compares Drusus to an eagle. Dio says the Romans deported most of the strongest men, leaving enough to farm. The Augustan legionary base at Dangstetten on the upper Rhine and the early camp at Augsburg-Oberhausen belong to this phase. Raetia was later governed by an equestrian prefect and procurator with its capital at Augusta Vindelicum.

annexation_of_noricum.detail: The hill-town on the Magdalensberg, with its Roman traders' quarter and inscriptions recording the export of Noric iron and steel (ferrum Noricum, praised by Ovid and Horace), was the centre of the region until Claudius founded Virunum in the plain below. Velleius treats the annexation as part of the Alpine war of 15 BC. Noricum received no legion until the Marcomannic Wars (legio II Italica, at Lauriacum).

agrippa_visits_jerusalem_15bc.detail: Herod had named one wing of the Temple fortress area and a hall of his palace after Agrippa, and the visit marked the high point of their friendship. In 14 BC, after Herod accompanied Agrippa's Black Sea expedition to the Bosporus, the Jews of Ionia petitioned against local interference with their Sabbath, their exemption from military service and their temple-tax collections; Nicolaus of Damascus pleaded their case and Agrippa upheld their privileges. Josephus preserves a series of such documents, the core of the later Roman protection of diaspora communities.

lugdunum_mint_15bc.detail: The Lugdunum series (IMP X, IMP XII etc. with bulls, Apollo of Actium, Diana and from 2 BC the C L CAESARES type with Gaius and Lucius) are among the commonest Augustan silver coins. Strabo (4.3.2) mentions the mint. Precious-metal coinage was moved back to Rome under Caligula or, more likely, Nero, after which Lugdunum struck mainly bronze. The ROM ET AVG altar asses circulated in huge quantities on the Rhine frontier and were widely imitated.

agrippa_bosporan_settlement.detail: On this eastern tour (16-13 BC) Agrippa visited Jerusalem with Herod (15 BC), sacrificing a hecatomb in the Temple, and in 14 BC heard the complaints of Ionian Jews, confirming their privileges, a speech Nicolaus of Damascus preserved through Josephus. Dynamis soon broke with Polemon and ruled alone, issuing gold staters with Augustus's portrait. Agrippa declined the triumph voted for the Bosporan success.

ara_pacis.detail: The Altar of Augustan Peace was vowed by the Senate on 4 July 13 BC, on Augustus's return from three years in Spain and Gaul, and dedicated on 30 January 9 BC, Livia's birthday. It stood on the Via Flaminia in the northern Campus Martius, near the Mausoleum and the meridian of the obelisk. The altar itself sits within a marble enclosure (11.6 by 10.6 m) carved inside and out. On the long sides, a procession moves westwards: Augustus with lictors, priests (the four major flamines in their spiked caps), Agrippa with his head veiled, a small boy clutching his toga (Gaius Caesar or a foreign prince), Livia, Tiberius, Antonia Minor with Drusus and the infant Germanicus, and other members of the family, as well as senators. The scene probably represents the vow ceremony of 13 BC rather than the dedication, which Agrippa did not live to see. The short ends carry mythological panels: Aeneas (or perhaps Numa) sacrificing a sow, the Lupercal with Romulus and Remus, a seated goddess with twins, animals and personified winds variously identified as Tellus, Italia, Pax or Venus, and Roma seated on arms. The lower register of the exterior is covered with a carpet of acanthus scrolls inhabited by swans, snakes and insects, an image of the fertile abundance of the new age. Inside, garlands and ox-skulls hang above a fence-like pattern recalling the wooden templum of the original consecration. The altar was buried by rising ground levels; fragments were found from 1568 onwards, and the monument was excavated beneath the Palazzo Fiano in 1937-1938 by freezing the waterlogged soil, then reassembled by Mussolini's regime for the bimillenary of Augustus near the Mausoleum. Since 2006 it has been housed in Richard Meier's pavilion. The altar's mix of Greek classical style (the procession recalls the Parthenon frieze), Roman ritual and dynastic portraiture makes it the key monument of Augustan ideology; its precise iconography, especially the identity of the "Tellus" figure and of the children, remains debated.
ara_pacis.debate: Identity of the female figure on the east panel (Tellus, Italia, Pax, Venus) and of the children in the procession.
scholarship: Zanker, The Power of Images in the Age of Augustus (1988)
Rossini, Ara Pacis (2006)

theatre_of_marcellus.detail: Its superimposed Doric and Ionic arcades on a radial concrete substructure anticipated the Colosseum. Pliny says a tame tiger was exhibited in a cage at its dedication, the first in Rome. In the Middle Ages it became a fortress of the Pierleoni and Savelli, and Baldassare Peruzzi built the Palazzo Orsini (Savelli) into its upper cavea in the 1520s.
theatre_of_marcellus.debate: Dio places the dedication in 13 BC, Pliny's evidence implies 11 BC.

terms_of_service_13bc.detail: Dio (54.25.5-6) says the measure was meant to stop soldiers from being an instrument of revolution by giving them a guaranteed reward. Between 7 and 2 BC Augustus paid some 400 million sesterces in cash to discharged veterans from his own funds (Res Gestae 16). The terms proved unaffordable and were lengthened in AD 5, when a separate military treasury was planned. The professional standing army of 25-28 legions dates from these measures.

theatre_of_balbus_13bc.detail: It was Rome's third and smallest permanent theatre (c. 7,700 places), with a colonnaded courtyard, the Crypta Balbi, behind the stage; Pliny admired four small onyx columns there. The Crypta excavations (now a branch of the Museo Nazionale Romano) are a key sequence for the city from antiquity to the Middle Ages. Together with the theatres of Pompey and Marcellus it gave Rome some 50,000 theatre seats.

thracian_war_of_piso.detail: The rebels used the Roman tactics and armament they had learned as auxiliaries. Velleius (2.98), who served in Thrace, praises Piso's handling of a war that threatened Macedonia and Asia; Antipater of Thessalonica wrote an epigram on his victory. The war shows how fragile the Thracian client kingdom remained until its annexation in AD 46.

death_of_agrippa.detail: Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa died in March 12 BC in Campania, aged about fifty, on his return from a winter mission to Pannonia, where his arrival had been enough to make the rebellious tribes submit. He was Augustus's oldest friend and indispensable partner: victor at Naulochus and Actium, three times consul, holder of tribunician power since 18 BC (renewed in 13) and of an imperium equal to Augustus's in the provinces, he was effectively co-regent and guardian of the dynastic future through his marriage to Julia and his sons Gaius and Lucius, adopted by Augustus. His public works transformed Rome: as aedile in 33 BC he repaired the sewers, sailing through the Cloaca Maxima, restored the aqueducts and built the Aqua Julia, followed by the Aqua Virgo (19 BC), the first Pantheon, the Baths of Agrippa with the Euripus canal and the Saepta Julia, and he left his gardens and baths to the Roman people. Augustus delivered the funeral oration, part of which survives in Greek translation on a papyrus from Egypt (P. Köln 249), and placed his ashes in his own Mausoleum. Dio says that Augustus received his estate, including the Thracian Chersonese, and gave each citizen a cash gift in his name. Agrippa's death left a vacuum that shaped the next decade. His posthumous son, Agrippa Postumus, was born months later. Augustus compelled Tiberius to divorce Vipsania and marry Julia (11 BC), and the burden of the northern wars fell on Tiberius and Drusus. Pliny the Elder records that Agrippa had urged that all paintings and statues be made public property, and his geographic commentaries became the basis for the world map in the Porticus Vipsania. Seneca (Epistles 94.46) quotes his maxim that harmony makes small states great and discord ruins the greatest. Modern historians emphasise that Agrippa's loyalty and administrative ability were as crucial as Augustus's political skill in creating the Principate, and that his low birth, which aristocrats despised, made him safely dependent.
scholarship: Koenen, 'Die Laudatio Funebris des Augustus für Agrippa auf einem neuen Papyrus', ZPE 5 (1970)

augustus_pontifex_maximus.detail: Rather than live in the official domus publica on the Via Sacra, he made part of his Palatine house public and dedicated a shrine of Vesta there (28 April 12 BC), joining the cult of the hearth of the state to his own household. As pontifex maximus he had over 2,000 anonymous prophetic books burned and deposited an edited set of Sibylline books in the temple of Apollo Palatinus. Every emperor until Gratian held the office.

altar_of_lugdunum.detail: The first priest was the Aeduan Gaius Julius Vercondaridubnus. The concilium Galliarum became a forum for provincial elites, who later built an amphitheatre on the site (AD 19); the martyrs of 177 died there. The altar appears on the 'ROM ET AVG' asses minted at Lugdunum. It was a model for an altar of the Ubii at Cologne (Ara Ubiorum) intended for the future province of Germany.
altar_of_lugdunum.debate: Livy's Periocha and Dio date the dedication to 12 BC, but Suetonius says Claudius was born at Lugdunum on 1 August 10 BC, the very day the altar was dedicated. Solutions include a two-stage inauguration.

fossa_drusiana.detail: The fleet sailed along the coast to the Ems, where it defeated the Bructeri on the river, and on to the Weser; the ships were stranded by the tide in the land of the Chauci and saved only by Frisian help. Germanicus used the canal again in AD 15 and 16. Its exact course is debated (most locate it near Arnhem/Doesburg, joining the Old IJssel). Drusus also built a mole (moles) on the Rhine that Civilis broke in AD 70.

pyramid_of_cestius.detail: The tomb reflects the fashion for things Egyptian after the conquest of 30 BC. An inscription records that the heirs could not place costly Attalid fabrics in the tomb because of a new sumptuary law, and instead sold them to pay for bronze statues. Aurelian built it into his wall in the 270s, which preserved it; it stands beside the Porta San Paolo and the Protestant Cemetery.

battle_of_arbalo.detail: Pliny the Elder cites the battle as a case where an evil omen (a swarm of bees settling on a tent-rope in Drusus's camp) proved false, for the battle was 'most fortunate'. After it Drusus built a fort at the confluence of the Lippe and Eliso (Aliso) and another among the Chatti on the Rhine. It is the only named battle of Drusus's campaigns.

marriage_of_tiberius_and_julia.detail: Suetonius says that when Tiberius once saw Vipsania afterwards he followed her with tearful eyes, and guards were set so that he would not see her again. The marriage was soon unhappy; their only child died in infancy at Aquileia. Vipsania married Asinius Gallus. Tiberius's withdrawal to Rhodes in 6 BC owed something to this estrangement.

caesarea_maritima_inaugurated.detail: The harbour moles, built with pozzolana shipped from Italy and set in wooden forms under water, enclosed some 20 acres; underwater excavation since the 1970s has confirmed Josephus's description and Italian hydraulic concrete. The city had a theatre, a hippodrome-stadium and an aqueduct, and was celebrated with quinquennial games. After AD 6 it became the residence of the Roman prefects and procurators of Judaea; the Pilate inscription was found in its theatre.

obelisks_brought_to_rome_10bc.detail: The Campus Martius obelisk of Psammetichus II (now on Montecitorio) cast its shadow on a bronze-inlaid pavement; Pliny says the mathematician Novius Facundus designed it and that it had gone out of true by his day. Edmund Buchner's claim that it formed a giant sundial whose shadow reached the Ara Pacis on Augustus's birthday has been strongly challenged; excavation found only a meridian line with Greek labels of Domitianic date. The Circus obelisk of Ramesses II now stands in the Piazza del Popolo.
obelisks_brought_to_rome_10bc.debate: Buchner's Horologium-Ara Pacis alignment theory versus a simple meridian (Heslin, Haselberger).

death_of_drusus_the_elder.detail: Tiberius walked before the body all the way to Rome. Drusus was cremated on the Campus Martius and buried in the Mausoleum; the Senate granted him and his descendants the hereditary cognomen Germanicus, and erected a marble arch with trophies on the Via Appia. A cenotaph (tumulus honorarius) was raised at Mogontiacum, around which the legions held annual ceremonies; the 'Drususstein' in Mainz citadel is traditionally identified with it. Dio reports that at the Elbe a superhuman woman told him in Latin to turn back as the end of his deeds and life was near. The pseudo-Ovidian Consolatio ad Liviam laments him.

deportation_of_the_sugambri.detail: The resettled Sugambri became the Cugerni around Vetera (Xanten). Suetonius records the deportation as an example of Augustan practice. Augustus himself came to the Rhine, and Tiberius received a triumph (celebrated 1 January 7 BC) and a second consulship. Dio says Augustus refused to treat with the Sugambri unless they sent envoys, then detained them.

month_of_augustus.detail: Macrobius preserves the text of the decree (Sat. 1.12.35). Since 45 BC the pontiffs, using inclusive counting, had inserted twelve leap days in 36 years instead of nine; Augustus suspended intercalation for about twelve years so that the calendar was back in step by AD 8. The exact years of the triennial leap days are reconstructed differently by modern chronologers, which affects the conversion of some Roman dates of 45-9 BC.
scholarship: Bennett, 'The Early Augustan Calendars in Rome and Egypt', ZPE 142-147 (2003-2004)

deaths_of_maecenas_and_horace.detail: Maecenas had been Octavian's agent in Rome during the civil wars and patron of Virgil, Horace and Propertius, but his influence waned after his brother-in-law Murena's conspiracy in 23 BC. Horace had named Augustus his heir in a dying declaration because he was too weak to sign a will (Suetonius, Life of Horace). The Horti Maecenatis, with their heated swimming pool and the so-called Auditorium, became imperial property.

census_of_8bc.detail: The jump from about 900,000 in the last Republican census (70/69 BC) to over four million in 28 BC is the central problem of Roman demography. The "high count" view holds that the Augustan figures, like the Republican ones, counted adult males only, implying a citizen population of over ten million; the "low count" view (Brunt, Scheidel) holds that Augustus counted women and children too, implying a much smaller Italy. The figures are recorded in Res Gestae 8.
census_of_8bc.debate: High count (Lo Cascio) versus low count (Brunt, Scheidel) interpretation of the Augustan census figures.

regions_and_vici_of_rome.detail: The reform turned neighbourhood cult into a vehicle of loyalty and gave freedmen honoured public roles; surviving compital altars, such as that of the vicus Sandaliarius (2 BC) in the Uffizi, show the Lares holding laurel branches. The regions also structured fire-fighting (two per cohort of vigiles from AD 6), grain distribution and later the fourth-century Regionary Catalogues. Augustus also enlarged the city's boundary with the regions extending beyond the Servian wall.
scholarship: Lott, The Neighborhoods of Augustan Rome (2004)

edicts_of_cyrene.detail: The edicts set up mixed juries of Greeks and Romans for capital cases involving Greeks, require Greek holders of Roman citizenship to continue performing local liturgies, and send cases of treason to the governor. The SC Calvisianum (4 BC) created a fast procedure in which five senators chosen by lot could assess restitution for provincials claiming extortion by a governor, without a full criminal trial. They show the princeps intervening in a public province, the practical meaning of his imperium maius.
scholarship: Oliver, 'On the edicts of Augustus at Cyrene', Historia 18 (1969)
Sherk, Roman Documents from the Greek East (1969) no. 31

porticus_liviae_7bc.detail: Vedius Pollio, an equestrian friend of Augustus, was notorious for feeding slaves to his moray eels; Augustus once broke his crystal cups to save a slave. The portico enclosed a shrine of Concordia dedicated by Livia, and was a public park with vines; it appears on the Severan Marble Plan.

herod_executes_his_sons.detail: Macrobius (Saturnalia 2.4.11) attributes to Augustus the quip that it was better to be Herod's pig than his son, a Greek pun (hys/huios) that also mocks Herod's Jewish abstention from pork. The executions removed the Hasmonean bloodline from the succession and left the kingdom to the sons of Malthace and Cleopatra of Jerusalem, divided between Archelaus, Antipas and Philip in 4 BC.

map_of_agrippa.detail: Pliny the Elder cites Agrippa's measurements (in Roman miles) for dozens of provinces and seas, often critically, and says Augustus completed the portico on Agrippa's plan. The form of the map (a painted or carved orbis terrarum, perhaps oval) is unknown; it lies behind later itineraries and has been connected with the ancestry of the Peutinger Table.

tropaeum_alpium.detail: The inscription is dated by Augustus's seventeenth acclamation and fourteenth tribunician power (7/6 BC). Pliny copied the full text (NH 3.136-137), allowing its reconstruction from fragments; the list begins with the Triumpilini and Camunni and ends with the peoples of the Maritime Alps. The monument, about 35 m high, was quarried in the Middle Ages and partly restored in 1929-1933 by Jules Formigé with funds from the American Edward Tuck.

tiberius_retires_to_rhodes.detail: Motives were debated even in antiquity: disgust with his wife Julia, resentment at the rapid promotion of Gaius and Lucius, a wish to avoid seeming their rival, or exhaustion (Suetonius gives several). Augustus complained publicly of desertion; Tiberius's tribunician power lapsed in 1 BC and he came close to danger when Gaius's entourage suggested killing him. He returned in AD 2 with Augustus's permission on condition he take no part in public affairs. On Rhodes he befriended the astrologer Thrasyllus, who remained his confidant until 36.

birth_of_jesus.detail: Matthew sets the birth under Herod, with the magi, the star and the flight to Egypt. Luke ties it to a universal census under Augustus "when Quirinius was governing Syria", but Quirinius's provincial census of Judaea took place in AD 6, ten years after Herod's death, and no empire-wide census of the kind Luke describes is attested. Attempts to rescue Luke with an earlier governorship of Quirinius, or to identify the star with the Jupiter-Saturn conjunctions of 7 BC or a comet of 5 BC, remain speculative. The AD era itself derives from Dionysius Exiguus (AD 525), whose reckoning puts the birth after Herod's death and is generally reckoned a few years too late. Many critical scholars regard the Bethlehem setting as theological (Davidic descent) and Nazareth as the actual place of birth.
birth_of_jesus.debate: Luke's census of Quirinius conflicts with Matthew's Herodian dating; the AD 6 census is securely attested by Josephus.

gaius_and_lucius_principes_iuventutis.detail: The Lugdunum denarius showing the two youths with shields, spears and priestly implements (C L CAESARES AVGVSTI F COS DESIG PRINC IVVENT) is one of the commonest Roman silver coins. The Maison Carrée at Nîmes was rededicated to them as 'principes iuventutis'. Res Gestae 14 records the honours. Their deaths in AD 2 and 4 wrecked Augustus's succession plans.

homonadensian_war.detail: Strabo describes their homeland as a fertile hollow surrounded by cliffs. The war secured the new Pisidian colonies and the Via Sebaste. Its date (between c. 12 BC and AD 1) and Quirinius's province at the time are disputed, a question entangled with the census of Luke 2.

death_of_herod_the_great.detail: Josephus dates the death shortly after a lunar eclipse and before Passover; the partial eclipse of 13 March 4 BC fits, though some argue for the total eclipse of 10 January 1 BC, a debate that also bears on the chronology of Jesus's birth. Risings across the kingdom on Herod's death were crushed by Publius Quinctilius Varus, governor of Syria, who crucified 2,000 rebels. Macrobius reports Augustus's quip that it was better to be Herod's pig than his son.
death_of_herod_the_great.debate: Date of Herod's death (4 BC conventional; 1 BC minority view).

waldgirmes_town.detail: Excavations from 1993 found a forum with a gilded bronze equestrian statue of Augustus, whose life-size horse head was recovered from a well in 2009; native Germanic potters and Roman houses coexisted. Dendrochronology dates the wells to 4/3 BC. The finds confirm Dio's statement (56.18) that the Romans held parts of Germany, that cities were being founded and the barbarians adapting to Roman ways, before Varus's attempt to impose tribute too quickly.
scholarship: Becker and Rasbach, Waldgirmes (2015)

pater_patriae.detail: Res Gestae 35, the culminating chapter, records that the title was inscribed in the vestibule of his house, in the Curia Julia and in the Forum of Augustus beneath the quadriga erected to him by decree of the Senate. Suetonius quotes Messalla's formula and Augustus's reply. The title had been given informally before (Cicero, Caesar) and became standard for emperors, who usually accepted it after an interval.

forum_of_augustus_dedicated.detail: The Forum of Augustus with its Temple of Mars Ultor was dedicated on 1 August 2 BC, forty years after Octavian had vowed the temple at Philippi in 42 BC to the avenging Mars if he defeated Caesar's murderers. The project was delayed because Augustus refused to expropriate the land he needed, and the irregular eastern edge of the precinct shows where owners would not sell (Suetonius, Augustus 56.2). A 33 m firewall of peperino separated the forum from the crowded Subura. The octastyle Corinthian temple, of Luna marble on a high podium, housed cult statues of Mars, Venus Genetrix and the deified Caesar, and from 2 BC the standards recovered from Parthia. Flanking porticoes opened into two great exedrae. Their niches held a sculptural gallery: on one side Aeneas carrying Anchises and the Alban kings and Julii, on the other Romulus with the spolia opima and the summi viri of the Republic, each with an inscription (elogium) summarising his career; copies of elogia survive at Rome and Arretium. A quadriga of Augustus stood in the centre, inscribed with the title pater patriae granted on 5 February of the same year. Augustus declared in an edict that he had set up the gallery so that citizens would judge him and later principes by the standard of these men. The forum was given a political function: the Senate met in the temple to decide on wars and triumphs, governors departed from it for their provinces, triumphing generals dedicated their insignia there, and boys assumed the toga virilis. The dedication was marked by spectacular games: a naumachia across the Tiber, gladiators, a Troy game and 260 lions and 36 crocodiles killed in the Circus Flaminius. The forum's caryatids copied from the Erechtheion and its programme of Roman history made it the architectural counterpart of the Aeneid and of Livy. Excavations under the Fascist Via dell'Impero and again since the 1990s have revealed the plan, including a colossal hall that probably housed a statue of the Genius of Augustus.
forum_of_augustus_dedicated.debate: Ovid places the dies natalis of Mars Ultor on 12 May; Velleius and Dio imply 1 August 2 BC. One view takes 12 May as the date of the earlier Capitoline shrine of 20 BC.
scholarship: Zanker, Forum Augustum (1968)
Spannagel, Exemplaria principis (1999)

exile_of_julia_the_elder.detail: Those named include Sempronius Gracchus, Appius Claudius Pulcher, Quinctius Crispinus and a Scipio. Pliny the Elder mentions a plot against Augustus's life in connection with Julia, and many scholars (Syme, Levick) argue the scandal concealed a political conspiracy around her and Iullus in favour of her sons and against Tiberius. She was moved to Rhegium after five years and died there in AD 14, shortly after Tiberius cut her allowance.
scholarship: Levick, 'The fall of Julia the Younger', Latomus 35 (1976)

augustan_manumission_laws.detail: Aelia Sentia also created the degraded status of dediticii for freed slaves who had been chained, branded or tortured, barring them from citizenship and from living near Rome, and annulled manumissions in fraud of creditors. Gaius's Institutes (1.13-46) are the main source. The laws aimed at controlling the influx of new citizens rather than stopping manumission, which remained common.

naumachia_of_augustus.detail: The basin was fed by the new Aqua Alsietina, a low-quality aqueduct from Lake Alsietinus (Martignano) that Frontinus says was fit only for the naumachia and for watering gardens. The show reenacted Salamis, an allusion to Actium. Crocodiles were also killed in the Circus Flaminius flooded for the occasion (Dio 55.10.8).
