The naumachia survived until at least the third century, when Titus and Nero had used it for shows.

ovid_ars_amatoria.detail: Published in the year of Julia's disgrace and soon after the adultery laws, its jokes about married women and the Augustan monuments as pick-up venues sat ill with official morality; Ovid insisted in the Tristia that the poem was written for courtesans only. The Remedia Amoris followed. The Metamorphoses, completed by AD 8, and the unfinished Fasti were the major works of his last years in Rome. The books were removed from the public libraries after his exile.

ahenobarbus_crosses_the_elbe.detail: Ahenobarbus, Nero's grandfather, received triumphal ornaments; Suetonius (Nero 4) describes him as arrogant and cruel, a lover of chariot racing. His intervention in Cherusci politics, trying to restore exiled nobles, was a failure. The pontes longi were reused, and nearly cost Caecina his army, in AD 15.
ahenobarbus_crosses_the_elbe.debate: Date uncertain (Dio's text is fragmentary); placed between c. 7 BC and AD 1.

death_of_lucius_caesar.detail: His death, and that of Gaius 18 months later, produced the Pisan decrees (cenotaphia Pisana, ILS 139-140), which preserve the honours voted by the colony of Pisa, including annual rites and the closing of temples on the anniversary, a rich source for municipal loyalism. Tacitus reports rumours that Livia was responsible.

gaius_caesar_meets_phraataces.detail: Velleius Paterculus, serving as a military tribune, witnessed it. At the meeting Phraataces revealed that Gaius's guardian Marcus Lollius had taken bribes from eastern kings; Lollius died soon after, perhaps by suicide, and Tiberius's partisan Sulpicius Quirinius replaced him. Gaius then installed Ariobarzanes of Media as king of Armenia, leading to the siege of Artagira where he was wounded.

return_of_tiberius_from_rhodes.detail: On Rhodes Tiberius had studied with the astrologer Thrasyllus, attended philosophical lectures and visited Gaius at Samos, where Gaius's companion Marcus Lollius poisoned the meeting. His tribunician power had lapsed and the people of Nemausus had thrown down his statues. Lollius's disgrace and death and then the death of Lucius at Massilia that summer cleared the way for his rehabilitation and adoption in AD 4.

siege_of_artagira_3.detail: Gaius had installed the Median prince Ariobarzanes as king of Armenia against the pro-Parthian faction after his meeting with Phraataces on the Euphrates in AD 2. Velleius says the wound left him in body and mind unfit for service and that he asked to retire to Syria; the Fasti Cuprenses give the date of the wound. His death removed Augustus's chosen heir and led to the adoption of Tiberius.

death_of_gaius_caesar.detail: His cenotaph at Limyra survives. The deaths of both grandsons left Augustus with no alternative to Tiberius; within four months he adopted him. Pisa decreed annual mourning on 21 February. Velleius blames Gaius's flatterers for his decline.

adoption_of_tiberius.detail: On 26 June AD 4, four months after the death of Gaius Caesar in Lycia, Augustus adopted Tiberius, then 44, together with his last surviving grandson Agrippa Postumus. Tiberius in turn was required to adopt his nephew Germanicus, son of his dead brother Drusus, although he had a son of his own, Drusus the Younger. The arrangement fixed the succession on two lines at once: Tiberius as immediate heir, and Germanicus, married to Augustus's granddaughter Agrippina, as the next generation, joining the blood of Livia's Claudii with Augustus's Julii. Tiberius received tribunician power for ten years and a major military command in Germany. Velleius, who served under him, describes the day as one of universal rejoicing and the soldiers' delight at seeing their old commander return; Augustus is said to have declared that he did it "for the sake of the state" (rei publicae causa), a phrase Suetonius read as betraying reluctance. Tacitus's account of Livia's scheming in bringing about this outcome, including insinuations that she had a hand in the deaths of Gaius and Lucius, has coloured the tradition but is not substantiated. As an adopted son Tiberius became legally Tiberius Julius Caesar, losing his own property and freedmen to Augustus, and his son Drusus also passed into the Julian family. Agrippa Postumus was soon disowned (AD 6) and banished to Planasia (AD 7), apparently for a violent temperament, possibly also for political associations. The adoption ended the "Julian" phase of succession planning, in which Augustus had relied on his daughter's children, and began the Claudian ascendancy that lasted until Nero. Tiberius spent most of the next eight years fighting in Germany and Illyricum, and his authority was progressively raised until in AD 13 he received an imperium equal to Augustus's in all provinces, making him co-ruler in all but name before Augustus's death.

immensum_bellum.detail: Velleius, an eyewitness, calls it an 'immense war' and describes an old German who paddled across the Elbe in a dugout to touch Tiberius and declare it the happiest day of his life. Res Gestae 26.4 claims the fleet sailed east from the Rhine mouth to the land of the Cimbri (Jutland), 'where no Roman had gone before', and that the Cimbri, Charydes and Semnones sent envoys. The legionary base at Anreppen on the upper Lippe, built of timber in AD 4-5, matches the winter quarters.

clemency_to_cinna.detail: Seneca's De Clementia (1.9) sets the episode in Gaul when Augustus was forty (c. 16-13 BC) and has Augustus lecture Cinna for two hours; Dio (55.14-22) places it in AD 4 and gives Livia a long speech on the benefits of mercy. Cinna was indeed consul in AD 5, which favours Dio's context. Corneille turned the story into his tragedy Cinna (1641).
clemency_to_cinna.debate: Seneca and Dio differ on the date (16-13 BC or AD 4); the story may be embellished as an exemplum of clemency.

maison_carree_nemausus.detail: The temple, a hexastyle pseudoperipteral Corinthian building on a high podium, was probably begun under Agrippa's patronage c. 20-12 BC and rededicated to the dead princes. Its decoration copies the Forum of Augustus workshops. The temple survived as a consular house, stable and church, and inspired Thomas Jefferson's Virginia State Capitol. The Pont du Gard brought water to the same colony a generation later.
maison_carree_nemausus.debate: The first phase may date to c. 16 BC with a dedication to Agrippa; the Gaius and Lucius inscription is the second.

military_service_reform_5.detail: The change acknowledged that the 13 BC terms were unaffordable; it led directly to the aerarium militare of AD 6, financed by a 5% inheritance tax and a 1% sales tax. Long service without promised discharge was a main grievance of the mutinous legions of AD 14, who complained of being kept on for thirty or forty years and paid in "swamps and mountainsides" instead of land.

lex_valeria_cornelia_5.detail: The law is known only from the Tabula Hebana (found 1947), which records the addition of five further centuries named after Germanicus in AD 19 and five after Drusus the Younger in AD 23. It shows how Augustus managed elections through the upper orders while preserving the assembly's formal role, a stage on the way to the transfer of elections to the Senate in AD 14.

aerarium_militare.detail: The military treasury (aerarium militare) was created in AD 6 to pay the discharge bounties (praemia) of veterans, which since 13 BC had been given in cash and since AD 5 amounted to 12,000 sesterces for a legionary after twenty years. The cost was enormous: with some 150,000 legionaries and perhaps 5,000-6,000 retirements a year, the treasury needed at least 60-70 million sesterces annually. Augustus opened it with a personal gift of 170 million sesterces (Res Gestae 17) and invited client kings and communities to contribute; none volunteered except, Dio says, some kings and cities. To provide regular income he introduced two new taxes on Roman citizens: the vicesima hereditatium, a 5% duty on inheritances and legacies above a threshold and excluding bequests to close relatives, and the centesima rerum venalium, a 1% tax on goods sold at auction. These were the first direct burdens on Italian citizens since the abolition of tributum in 167 BC, and they provoked strong opposition: Augustus asked senators to propose alternatives, and in AD 13 threatened a land tax on Italy, which persuaded them to accept the inheritance tax. The treasury was administered by three praefecti aerarii militaris of praetorian rank, chosen at first by lot and later by the emperor, serving three years. The arrangement shows how Augustus separated the army's finances from the old aerarium Saturni while keeping them formally public. The fiscal strain remained: the mutineers of AD 14 complained of being kept beyond their terms and settled on poor land, and Tiberius had to restore the twenty-year limit after briefly conceding sixteen. The sales tax was halved in 17 and abolished in Italy by Caligula in 38; the inheritance tax lasted, being doubled by Caracalla. The fund probably also absorbed confiscated property and windfalls. Modern estimates of Roman imperial budgets (Duncan-Jones, Hopkins) treat army costs of around 400-500 million sesterces a year as the largest single item of state spending.
scholarship: Corbier, L'aerarium Saturni et l'aerarium militare (1974)

annexation_of_judaea.detail: After Herod's death in 4 BC Augustus divided his kingdom among three sons: Archelaus received Judaea, Samaria and Idumaea as ethnarch, Antipas Galilee and Peraea, and Philip the north-eastern territories. Archelaus ruled harshly, provoking unrest at the outset that the governor of Syria, Varus, suppressed by crucifying 2,000 rebels. In AD 6 a joint embassy of Jews and Samaritans complained to Augustus, who deposed Archelaus and exiled him to Vienna in Gaul. His territory became a province governed by an equestrian prefect, Coponius, residing at Caesarea with auxiliary troops recruited mainly from Caesarea and Sebaste, under the general supervision of the legate of Syria. Publius Sulpicius Quirinius, then governing Syria, conducted a census of property for tribute, which provoked the resistance of Judas the Galilean and the Pharisee Saddok, whom Josephus links to the later Zealots; the High Priest Joazar persuaded most to comply. The census is the one mentioned by Luke 2.1-2, whose attempt to place Jesus's birth under it conflicts with Matthew's Herodian setting. The prefects controlled the appointment of High Priests and the vestments, held the right of capital punishment and kept the Antonia fortress garrisoned, while internal affairs remained largely with the High Priest and council. The title of the governor is confirmed by the Pilate inscription from Caesarea ("praefectus Iudaeae"); after 44 the governors were called procurators. Judaea remained a province, except for Agrippa I's kingdom (41-44), until the revolt of 66, after which it became a praetorian province with a legion. The arrangement of AD 6 is significant as a test of Roman indirect rule: the equestrian prefects lacked troops and local knowledge, and tension over images, taxation and temple funds recurred under Pilate, Cumanus and Florus. Josephus's narrative (Jewish War 2, Antiquities 18) is the main source, and his tendency to trace the revolt back to the "fourth philosophy" of AD 6 has shaped modern interpretations of a sixty-year path to war.
annexation_of_judaea.debate: Historicity and date of the Lucan census.

vigiles_created.detail: Each cohort had about 500 men (later 1,000) with specialists such as siphonarii (pump operators), aquarii, centonarii (with fire blankets) and doctors. Service in the vigiles brought freedmen of Junian Latin status full citizenship after six years (later three, under a lex Visellia of AD 24). The excubitorium of the seventh cohort in Trastevere, with its graffiti, survives. The same year saw famine, the expulsion of gladiators and slaves for sale to 100 miles from Rome, and Augustus's appointment of two consulars to oversee the grain supply.
scholarship: Rainbird, 'The fire stations of imperial Rome', PBSR 54 (1986)

outbreak_of_the_illyrian_revolt.detail: In AD 6, as Tiberius was moving twelve legions against Maroboduus, the Dalmatian and Pannonian peoples called up to serve as auxiliaries rose in revolt. The trigger, Dio says, was the levy itself and the burden of tribute: when Tiberius later asked Bato the Daesitiate why his people had rebelled, he answered "You are to blame, for you send as guardians of your flocks not dogs or shepherds but wolves." The Daesitiates of central Bosnia under Bato rose first and were joined by the Breuci of the Sava valley under another Bato and Pinnes. The rebels, some 200,000 infantry and 9,000 cavalry by Velleius's count, had served in Roman auxiliary units and knew Roman tactics and Latin. They massacred Roman traders and veterans, attacked Salona, where Bato was wounded, and moved on Sirmium, held by Aulus Caecina Severus from Moesia, and raided Macedonia. Velleius reports panic at Rome: Augustus told the Senate that the enemy could be at the gates within ten days, raised troops by emergency levies of freedmen and wealthy citizens' slaves (the first time since Cannae), and sent Germanicus with them. Tiberius made peace with Maroboduus and turned south, gathering at Siscia an army of ten legions, over seventy auxiliary cohorts, fourteen cavalry wings and 10,000 veterans, with Thracian cavalry under Rhoemetalces, the largest Roman force assembled since the civil wars, though too unwieldy to use as one. The war lasted three years (6-9), fought in a grinding campaign of attrition, sieges of hill forts and scorched earth, with famine and disease on both sides. Suetonius calls it the most serious foreign war since the Punic Wars. Its outbreak coincided with famine, fire and fiscal crisis in Rome, and the strain it imposed on manpower was one reason why the loss of Varus's three legions in AD 9 was so alarming. The revolt also marked the end of plans to annex Bohemia and pushed the empire towards consolidation along the Danube.

battle_of_sirmium_6.detail: Dio's brief account is the only source. The relief of Sirmium kept the key crossing of the Sava in Roman hands; the rebels then joined forces on Mons Almus (Fruška Gora) north of the city, where Rhoemetalces's Thracian cavalry skirmished with them.

famine_of_6.detail: Senators were allowed to leave the city and the courts were suspended. The famine coincided with the fire that led to the creation of the vigiles, the new taxes of the aerarium militare and the outbreak of the Illyrian revolt, which Dio (55.27) describes as a time of lampoons and talk of revolution; one Publius Rufus was suspected of circulating seditious pamphlets. Germanicus and his brother gave games in honour of the dead Drusus to soothe the people.

gaetulian_war_of_cossus.detail: An inscription from Lepcis Magna records the "freeing of Africa from the Gaetulian war" under Cossus. The war foreshadowed the much longer revolt of Tacfarinas, a Musulamian, from AD 17. Gaetulicus the younger, consul in 26, later commanded Upper Germany and was executed by Caligula in 39.

planned_invasion_of_bohemia_6.detail: Velleius (2.108-110), who served as Tiberius's officer, describes Maroboduus's army of 70,000 foot and 4,000 horse drilled in Roman fashion and his kingdom as a threat to Italy. A hasty peace recognised Maroboduus as a friend of Rome, and he stayed neutral in AD 9 after Varus's defeat. Recent finds of Roman marching camps in Moravia and Lower Austria (e.g. Musov) may relate to these or later operations.

revolt_of_judas_the_galilean.detail: The High Priest Joazar persuaded most to accept the census. Judas's fate is not recorded by Josephus, but Acts 5.37 says he perished. His sons James and Simon were crucified by Tiberius Julius Alexander c. 46-48, another son (or grandson) Menahem seized Masada and led a faction in 66, and his descendant Eleazar ben Yair commanded Masada to its fall in 73/74.

proculian_and_sabinian_schools.detail: Pomponius says Labeo was innovative and confident in his own learning, Capito conservative. The schools disputed dozens of questions until the mid-second century: for instance whether a new object made from another's material (specificatio) belonged to the maker (Proculians) or the owner of the material (Sabinians), and the age of puberty. Gaius, writing c. 161, still calls the Sabinians "our teachers". Labeo wrote some 400 books; Tacitus (Annals 3.75) contrasts his incorruptible freedom with Capito's servility.

battle_of_the_volcaean_marshes.detail: Velleius, who served in the war, says the legions saved the day 'by their own courage' after the Thracian cavalry of king Rhoemetalces was routed, the alae fled and cohorts turned; several senior officers, including a camp prefect and military tribunes, were killed. After the battle Tiberius had ten legions, more than 70 auxiliary cohorts, 14 alae, more than 10,000 veteran reservists and many volunteers at Siscia, which Velleius says was the largest army assembled since the civil wars; Tiberius judged it too large to supply and sent part away.

exile_of_agrippa_postumus.detail: The ancient sources describe him as brutish but not criminal; modern historians suspect political motives, perhaps connected to the conspiracies around his sister Julia the Younger (exiled in AD 8) and her husband Aemilius Paullus. Tacitus reports a rumour that Augustus secretly visited him on Planasia shortly before his death. He was killed immediately after Augustus died in AD 14.

surrender_of_the_breuci.detail: The Fasti record 3 August as the day of a victory of Tiberius in Illyricum, often linked to this surrender. Only the Dalmatian highlands remained in revolt into AD 9.

exile_of_ovid.detail: Ovid's exile poetry (Tristia, Epistulae ex Ponto) gives a vivid, if literary, picture of a frontier town raided by Getae and Sarmatians across the frozen Danube. He kept his property and citizenship (relegatio, not exilium) and died at Tomis c. AD 17, his appeals to Augustus and Tiberius unanswered. The same year Julia the Younger was banished to Trimerus for adultery with Decimus Junius Silanus; many link Ovid's 'error' to her circle. No contemporary source other than Ovid mentions the exile, and a minority has even doubted it took place.
exile_of_ovid.debate: The nature of Ovid's error; the authenticity of the exile (Fitton Brown 1985) is a fringe but persistent question.

battle_of_the_teutoburg_forest.detail: In September AD 9 Publius Quinctilius Varus, legate of Germany, was marching his army of three legions (XVII, XVIII, XIX), six cohorts and three cavalry wings, perhaps 15,000-20,000 soldiers plus camp followers, from their summer camp on the Weser back to winter quarters on the Rhine, when he was told of a rising among distant tribes and diverted his route. The informant was Arminius, a Cheruscan noble and Roman citizen of equestrian rank who commanded auxiliaries; his father-in-law Segestes had warned Varus the previous night, in vain. In wooded, marshy country, amid heavy rain, the strung-out column was attacked by the Cherusci, Marsi, Chatti and Bructeri. Dio describes a running fight of three or four days: the Romans built a camp, burned surplus wagons, pushed on, and were cut down in the forests. Varus and his senior officers killed themselves; the camp prefect Ceionius surrendered, the cavalry commander Numonius Vala fled and was killed, and Eggius fell fighting. Tribunes and senior centurions were sacrificed in groves, and the lawyers were reportedly tortured, one having his tongue cut out. Varus's head was sent to Maroboduus and then to Augustus. Only the fort at Aliso held out and broke through to the Rhine. Augustus, Suetonius says, let his hair and beard grow for months and banged his head against doors crying "Quinctilius Varus, give me back my legions!" The disaster, the worst since Carrhae, ended Roman occupation east of the Rhine, though Germanicus campaigned there in 14-16. The site was long sought in the Teutoburg Forest, the name in Tacitus; since 1987 excavations at Kalkriese near Osnabrück, prompted by an amateur's coin finds, have revealed a narrow passage between Kalkriese Hill and the Great Bog where a turf wall channelled the Romans, with over 6,000 Roman objects, including a cavalry face mask, coins ending with issues of Varus, and bone pits from later burial. Whether Kalkriese is the main battlefield or one phase of it (or even a site of Germanicus's campaigns of 15) remains debated. The legion numbers were never reused.
battle_of_the_teutoburg_forest.debate: Whether Kalkriese is the site of the main battle, one phase of it, or of the fighting of AD 15.
scholarship: Wells, The Battle That Stopped Rome (2003)
Wolters, Die Schlacht im Teutoburger Wald (2008)

siege_of_aliso.detail: Dio says the defenders' archers repulsed assaults and the Germans tried to starve them; the garrison slipped past two German posts but was detected at the third, and was saved by trumpeters sounding the signal for a relief force, which made the Germans fall back. Lucius Asprenas, Varus's nephew, secured the Rhine crossings with two legions and prevented a German advance into Gaul.
siege_of_aliso.debate: Aliso has been identified with Haltern, Oberaden, Anreppen and other Lippe sites.

siege_of_raetinium.detail: Dio describes the stratagem in detail. Germanicus then took Seretium and Splonum; at Arduba the women, refusing surrender, threw their children and themselves into the flames or the river.

siege_of_andetrium.detail: Asked by Tiberius why his people had rebelled, Bato replied that Rome sent 'wolves, not dogs or shepherds' to guard its flocks. Tiberius spared him and he lived out his life at Ravenna. The victory was announced in Rome only days before news arrived of Varus's disaster in Germany, which overshadowed the celebrations.

lex_papia_poppaea.detail: Lapsed legacies (caduca) of those incapable of inheriting went first to heirs with children and ultimately to the treasury, making the law a source of revenue and of informers (delatores). Before its passage Augustus harangued the unmarried and married equites in separate assemblies (Dio 56.1-10). Juristic commentaries on 'the lex Julia et Papia' fill whole books of the Digest; Constantine repealed the penalties on celibacy in 320.

temple_of_concord_10.detail: The temple, with its unusual wide cella, became a museum of Greek art: Pliny lists works by Zeuxis, Nicias, Theodorus and Sthennis, and Livia dedicated a sardonyx of Polycrates. It was a frequent meeting place of the Senate (Sejanus was condemned there in 31). Tiberius also rebuilt the Temple of Castor (dedicated AD 6) in the names of himself and Drusus, the twin dedications projecting fraternal concordia within the dynasty.

sc_silanianum_10.detail: The decree, named after the consul Gaius Junius Silanus, aimed to make every slave a guard over his master's life; a slave who could not have helped (being out of earshot or chained) was exempt. Its interpretation fills Digest 29.5. In AD 61, 400 slaves of the murdered urban prefect were executed after a famous debate in the Senate in which Gaius Cassius Longinus defended the custom.

tiberius_on_the_rhine_10.detail: Suetonius (Tiberius 18) describes his precautions: he limited baggage, checked the loading of every wagon, slept without a tent and gave orders in writing. Dio says he crossed the Rhine but did not advance far or win a battle. The two new legions on the Rhine (XXI Rapax and V Alaudae or I Germanica moved up) brought the force to eight, the largest concentration in the empire until the 80s. Tiberius returned to Rome for his Pannonian triumph in October 12.

tiberius_pannonian_triumph.detail: The Gemma Augustea, a sardonyx cameo in Vienna, is often interpreted as showing Tiberius stepping from a chariot before an enthroned Augustus and Roma, above Roman soldiers raising a trophy over captives, and may commemorate this triumph. Tiberius fed the people at 1,000 tables and gave each citizen 300 sesterces. In 13 his tribunician power was renewed and he received imperium equal to Augustus's in the provinces.

death_of_augustus.detail: Augustus died at Nola in Campania on 19 August AD 14, in the same room in which his father had died, a month before his 76th birthday. He had accompanied Tiberius, who was setting out for Illyricum, as far as Beneventum and fell ill on the return journey; by some accounts he had already visited Capri and enjoyed games at Naples. Tiberius was recalled and found him alive, or according to a rumour reported by Tacitus and Dio, arrived too late, Livia concealing the death until he came. Suetonius records his last words to friends, quoting the end of a comedy: "If I have played my part well, applaud and send me from the stage with your approval," and to Livia: "Livia, live mindful of our marriage, and farewell." Tacitus and Dio report rumours that Livia poisoned him with figs, fearing a reconciliation with Agrippa Postumus after a secret visit to Planasia with Paullus Fabius Maximus, a story modern historians generally reject. His body was carried by local magistrates by night to Bovillae and then by knights to Rome. At a Senate meeting Tiberius had the will read: two-thirds of the estate to Tiberius and one-third to Livia, who was adopted into the Julian family and named Augusta; legacies of 40 million sesterces to the people, 1,000 to each praetorian, 500 to urban cohort soldiers and 300 to legionaries. Three rolls accompanied it: instructions for the funeral, the Res Gestae, and a summary of the empire's resources (breviarium totius imperii) advising that the empire be kept within its existing boundaries. The funeral took place in the Campus Martius, with laudations by Tiberius and Drusus; a senator swore he had seen Augustus's spirit ascending, and he was consecrated as Divus Augustus on 17 September. His death tested the system he had built: there was no formal procedure for succession, and the mutinies on the Rhine and Danube and the murder of Agrippa Postumus followed immediately.

mutinies_of_14.detail: In Pannonia the ex-claqueur Percennius and the soldier Vibulenus led the movement; a lunar eclipse during the night of 26/27 September AD 14 (astronomically confirmed) terrified the soldiers and helped Drusus regain control. On the Rhine, at Ara Ubiorum, mutineers offered Germanicus the throne; when he drew his sword to kill himself one soldier offered his own as 'sharper'. Sending away his pregnant wife Agrippina and little son 'Caligula' shamed the troops, who then massacred their own ringleaders at Vetera. Germanicus led them across the Rhine to expiate their guilt. Tacitus's speeches for the mutineers (Ann. 1.17) are a rare articulation of soldiers' grievances: beatings by centurions, extortion for leave, being paid 10 asses a day for their bodies and souls.

deification_of_augustus.detail: An ex-praetor, Numerius Atticus, swore he had seen Augustus ascending to heaven from the pyre, and Dio claims Livia paid him a million sesterces. The decree set the model for the consecratio of later emperors, voted by the Senate after death and represented on coins with eagles and pyres. The Senate's act on the same day (17 September) also began the formal transfer of power to Tiberius.

accession_of_tiberius.detail: Tiberius's accession in AD 14 was the first transfer of power within the Augustan system, and its ambiguities fascinated ancient writers. Legally Tiberius already held tribunician power and an imperium equal to Augustus's, so on Augustus's death he immediately gave the watchword to the praetorians, sent dispatches to the armies and was escorted by soldiers, yet in the Senate he professed reluctance. At the meeting of 17 September, after Augustus's consecration, senators begged him to accept the whole of the state; he replied that only the mind of Augustus could bear such a burden and offered to take a share. Asinius Gallus asked which part he wanted, Quintus Haterius asked "How long, Caesar, will you let the state lack a head?" and Mamercus Scaurus provoked him by hoping he would not veto the Senate's prayers. Tacitus presents the scene as hypocrisy (the "dissimulation" that became Tiberius's defining trait), Velleius as genuine modesty, and Suetonius says Tiberius described himself as "holding a wolf by the ears". He finally accepted without ever formally saying so, declining the title imperator as praenomen and pater patriae. Meanwhile Agrippa Postumus was killed on Planasia by his guard, an act whose author (Augustus's posthumous order, Livia, Sallustius Crispus or Tiberius) was disputed even at the time; Tiberius disclaimed it. The legions in Pannonia and Germany mutinied, demanding shorter service and higher pay, and the German legions offered the throne to Germanicus, who refused. Another early measure transferred the election of magistrates from the popular assemblies to the Senate. Tiberius's handling of the accession established the pattern of the "reluctant" princeps (recusatio imperii) imitated by later emperors and showed that the Principate, though never defined as an office, had become a permanent position requiring a successor. Modern historians (Levick) see his reluctance as partly sincere, reflecting a conservative aristocrat's discomfort with autocracy and his loss of political skill after years at the front.
scholarship: Levick, Tiberius the Politician (1976)

lunar_eclipse_14.detail: Tacitus (Annals 1.28) describes the moon seeming to fade in a clear sky and the men interpreting the gods' anger. Astronomical calculation confirms a total lunar eclipse visible in Pannonia on 27 September AD 14, which fixes the chronology of the mutiny. The ringleaders Percennius and Vibulenus were then executed.

massacre_of_the_marsi.detail: The Bructeri, Tubantes and Usipetes ambushed the returning column in the forest but were beaten off by the twentieth legion. Tanfana is otherwise unknown. The raid was a punitive gesture rather than a campaign of conquest.

res_gestae_divi_augusti.detail: The Res Gestae Divi Augusti ("Achievements of the Divine Augustus") is Augustus's own account of his career, written in the first person and deposited with his will with the Vestal Virgins, to be inscribed on bronze pillars in front of his Mausoleum. Its final version dates from AD 13-14; chapter 35 notes that he was in his 76th year. The bronze originals are lost, but copies were set up in the province of Galatia: the Monumentum Ancyranum on the walls of the temple of Rome and Augustus at Ancyra (Ankara), with Latin text and Greek paraphrase, the "queen of inscriptions" in Mommsen's phrase, plus fragments from Apollonia (Greek) and Pisidian Antioch (Latin). The text is arranged in 35 chapters and an appendix written after his death. It falls into three parts: honours and offices (1-14), expenditure on the people, veterans and buildings (15-24), and achievements in war and diplomacy (25-33), ending with the settlements of 27 and the title pater patriae (34-35). It lists precise figures: 600 million sesterces paid for land for veterans, 400 million in cash bounties, 82 temples restored in 28 BC, three censuses with their citizen totals, 55 triumphal acclamations, the nations whose embassies reached him from India to the Scythians. Its silences are as telling as its claims: it never names Antony, Lepidus or Brutus and Cassius, calls Sextus Pompey's forces pirates and slaves, presents the triumviral proscriptions as vengeance for Caesar, and claims that after 27 BC he "excelled all in authority (auctoritas) but had no more power (potestas) than my colleagues in each magistracy". Scholars debate its genre (funerary elogium, political testament, an account to the people) and its audience. It is the single most important document for Augustan self-representation, and its rhetoric of restoration, consensus and modesty shaped the ideology of the Principate. The appendix, added by an editor, totals his expenditure at 2.4 billion sesterces. In 1938 Mussolini's regime reproduced the full Latin text on the wall of the pavilion of the Ara Pacis, where it remains.
res_gestae_divi_augusti.debate: Genre, intended audience and date of composition of successive drafts.
scholarship: Cooley, Res Gestae Divi Augusti: Text, Translation and Commentary (2009)
Scheidel, 'Roman population size: the logic of the debate' (2008)

murder_of_agrippa_postumus.detail: In AD 16 a slave of Postumus named Clemens, who resembled him, impersonated his dead master, gathered followers in Etruria and Gaul and even in Rome before being captured and executed in the palace; asked how he had become Agrippa, he reportedly answered 'as you became Caesar'.

elections_transferred_to_senate.detail: Tiberius commended four of the twelve praetorian candidates, who had to be elected. The procedure of destinatio by special centuries of senators and equites (named after Gaius and Lucius under the lex Valeria Cornelia of AD 5 and expanded for Germanicus and Drusus), known from the Tabula Hebana and Tabula Siarensis, had already narrowed the field. The comitia met for a ceremonial renuntiatio into the third century.
scholarship: Levick, 'Imperial control of the elections under the early Principate', Historia 16 (1967)

census_of_14.detail: Augustus took a vow for the next lustrum but declined to pronounce it, as he would not live to fulfil it (Suetonius, Augustus 97). The increase of some 700,000 over 8 BC reflects manumission, grants to provincials and natural growth. This was the last regular census of citizens; Claudius (47/48) and Vespasian (73/74) revived it.

battle_of_pontes_longi.detail: Tacitus says Caecina dreamt that Varus rose from the swamp and beckoned him. Panic in the camp at night was stopped by Caecina lying across the gate. A rumour that the army was lost nearly led to the destruction of the Rhine bridge at Vetera, which Agrippina personally prevented, distributing clothing and dressings to the returning wounded. Earlier that summer Lucius Stertinius recovered the eagle of legio XIX from the Bructeri, and Germanicus buried the Varian dead, laying the first sod of their mound.

germanicus_visits_teutoburg_battlefield.detail: Tacitus's account (Annals 1.61-62) is one of the most vivid passages in Latin historiography: Varus's first camp with its wide circuit, a half-ruined rampart and shallow ditch where the remnants had made a stand, whitening bones in heaps or scattered, skulls nailed to tree trunks, and the altars in nearby groves where tribunes and centurions had been sacrificed. Survivors pointed out where the eagles were taken and where Varus received his first wound. Tiberius disapproved, thinking a general with augural duties should not handle the dead. The Kalkriese excavations found bone pits containing remains of men and mules buried several years after death, consistent with this episode.
germanicus_visits_teutoburg_battlefield.debate: Identification of the site with Kalkriese is widely but not universally accepted.

recovery_of_the_varian_eagles.detail: The recoveries were advertised as balancing the disaster: the arch of Germanicus near the temple of Saturn (AD 17) commemorated the standards recovered "with Varus", and Claudius allowed Gabinius his victory name. The legion numbers XVII, XVIII and XIX were never used again, a unique case in the army.

tiber_flood_and_curatores_15.detail: Tacitus reports the delegations of Florentia, Interamna and Reate, who argued that nature had provided rivers with their courses and that the Velinus should not be dammed into the Nar. The scheme was dropped either from religious scruple or local opposition. Boundary stones (cippi) of the curators, beginning in AD 15 under Ateius Capito, line the riverbanks and record the delimitation of the public bank.

battle_of_idistaviso.detail: Before the battle Germanicus walked through the camp in disguise to hear the soldiers' mood, and eight eagles flying into the forest were taken as an omen for the eight legions. Arminius escaped by smearing his face with his own blood; his uncle Inguiomerus also got away. The soldiers hailed Tiberius imperator and raised a trophy of captured arms. Days earlier Arminius had argued across the Weser with his brother Flavus, a Roman officer who had lost an eye in Roman service, a famous scene in Tacitus.

battle_of_the_angrivarian_wall.detail: Afterwards he set up a trophy inscribed that the army of Tiberius Caesar, having subdued the nations between Rhine and Elbe, dedicated the monument to Mars, Jupiter and Augustus, without mentioning himself. On the way home much of the fleet was destroyed in a North Sea storm; survivors told tales of sea monsters and bird-men. Tiberius then recalled Germanicus to a triumph, saying the Germans could be left to their own quarrels.

trial_of_libo_drusus.detail: It was the first great maiestas trial of the reign, with informers rewarded from the accused's property. The Senate expelled astrologers and magicians from Italy, executing two. The Fasti Amiternini and Antiates mark 13 September as a holiday because on that day Libo's 'nefaria consilia' were condemned. Tacitus presents it as the beginning of the 'evil that would devour the state'.

false_agrippa_postumus_16.detail: Tacitus reports that when Tiberius asked "how did you become Agrippa?", Clemens replied "the same way you became Caesar". Tiberius did not investigate the many in his household and the Senate said to have supported him. The episode shows how fragile the succession still was two years after Augustus's death.

germanicus_fleet_wrecked_16.detail: Germanicus was cast ashore among the Chauci, reputedly ready to drown himself. Survivors told tales of sea monsters and half-human creatures. Albinovanus Pedo, a cavalry prefect, wrote a poem on the voyage, of which the elder Seneca preserves a fragment. The losses and cost confirmed Tiberius's decision to recall Germanicus and end the campaigns across the Rhine.

triumph_of_germanicus.detail: Strabo, writing at the time, lists the captives, including Thusnelda's brother Segimundus and the Chattan priest Libes, and notes that Thusnelda's father Segestes watched as an honoured guest. An arch near the temple of Saturn commemorated the recovery of the Varian standards. The war was officially over, but only two of the three eagles had been recovered; the third came back in 41.

annexation_of_cappadocia.detail: Tiberius used the new revenues to halve the 1% sales tax (centesima rerum venalium) that funded the military treasury. Germanicus was sent east with imperium maius to organise the new provinces and settle Armenia. Commagene was restored as a kingdom to Antiochus IV by Caligula in 38 and finally annexed in 72. Archelaus's offence, Tacitus says, was having neglected Tiberius during his retirement on Rhodes.

asian_earthquake_17.detail: Pliny calls it the greatest earthquake in human memory. A senator of praetorian rank was sent to oversee reconstruction. A statue base found at Puteoli (CIL X 1624), dedicated to Tiberius in 30 by the Augustales, carries relief personifications of fourteen Asian cities, the twelve of 17 plus Cibyra and Ephesus, damaged in later quakes (23, 29), probably copying a monument in Rome. Coins of Tiberius with CIVITATIBVS ASIAE RESTITVTIS celebrate the relief.

centesima_halved_17.detail: The inheritance tax was deeply resented; in AD 13 Augustus threatened a land tax instead, and the Senate accepted the 5%. Tiberius halved the sales tax to 0.5% after the annexation of Cappadocia in AD 17 and restored it in 31; Caligula abolished it in Italy in 38. Caracalla later doubled the inheritance tax to 10% and, according to Dio, extended citizenship partly to broaden its base.

furius_camillus_defeats_tacfarinas_17.detail: Tacitus notes the irony that the first military glory of the family since the great Camillus fell to a man thought unwarlike. Tacfarinas had divided his followers into a regular infantry and cavalry force and light raiding bands. The victory proved temporary: he resumed raiding in 20 and the war dragged on until his death in 24.

germanicus_in_the_east.detail: At Alexandria he opened the state granaries to relieve a famine. A papyrus (P.Oxy. XXV 2435) records his speech to the Alexandrians and an edict (SB I 3924) rejects divine acclamations as appropriate only to Tiberius and Livia. Tiberius rebuked him for both his dress and his entry into Egypt. Throughout, he feuded with Gnaeus Calpurnius Piso, governor of Syria, and his wife Plancina, whom many believed Tiberius had placed to check him.

strabo_geography.detail: He mentions the death of Juba II (AD 23/24, or 18 by an alternative date) and the transfer of Cappadocia; the work was probably drafted under Augustus and revised. Strabo had travelled from Armenia to Etruria and from the Black Sea to the borders of Ethiopia with Aelius Gallus. His geography is a political one, written for statesmen: it praises the unifying peace of Roman rule and preserves much from Eratosthenes, Polybius and Posidonius. His lost Historical Sketches continued Polybius.

artaxias_iii_crowned.detail: The appointment ended the Armenian dispute that followed the expulsion of Vonones (AD 16), whom Germanicus moved to Pompeiopolis in Cilicia; Vonones was killed while trying to escape in 19. Artaxias reigned peacefully until his death c. 34, after which Artabanus II installed his son Arsaces and provoked the crisis of 35.

death_of_germanicus.detail: Germanicus Caesar died at Epidaphne near Antioch on 10 October AD 19, aged 33, after an illness during which he became convinced that he had been poisoned by Gnaeus Calpurnius Piso, the legate of Syria, and his wife Plancina. He had been sent east in 17 with a maius imperium over all transmarine provinces, crowned Artaxias III in Armenia, organised Cappadocia and Commagene as provinces, and in 19 made an unauthorised tour of Egypt, entering the province without permission, opening granaries during a famine and sailing up the Nile to Elephantine, for which Tiberius rebuked him. Piso, an aristocrat of fierce independence, had obstructed his orders, cultivated the troops and reversed his arrangements; Germanicus renounced his friendship. Tacitus describes human remains, spells inscribed with Germanicus's name, lead tablets and charred ashes found under the floor of his room. On his deathbed he urged his friends to avenge him and asked Agrippina to put aside her pride. His body was displayed naked in the forum at Antioch, which some took as showing signs of poison, and cremated. Agrippina carried his ashes to Brundisium in a famous procession, met by grieving crowds, and the ashes were placed in the Mausoleum of Augustus. Rome mourned extravagantly; the people stoned temples and threw out their household gods, and barbarian kings were said to have suspended hostilities. The Senate voted honours known from the Tabula Siarensis and Tabula Hebana, including arches on the Rhine, in Syria and in Rome. Piso's attempt to return to Syria by force led to his trial and suicide in 20; the Senatus Consultum de Cn. Pisone patre (found in Spain in the 1980s) gives the official verdict, which accused him of disrupting military discipline and rejoicing at the death but did not confirm poisoning. Tacitus contrasts the charming, popular Germanicus with the dour Tiberius, implying that Tiberius was relieved; modern historians doubt any imperial involvement, and illness (perhaps malaria) is the likeliest cause. His death left the succession to Drusus the Younger and fuelled the rivalry between Agrippina's party and Sejanus.
death_of_germanicus.debate: Poisoning by Piso (popular belief) or natural illness; the SCPP does not confirm poison.

sources.a: Senatus Consultum de Cn. Pisone patre

tabula_siarensis.detail: The Tabula Hebana records the creation of five new 'centuries of Germanicus' in the destinatio assembly that pre-selected consuls and praetors, showing how electoral procedure had been engineered. The texts allow direct comparison with Tacitus's summary (Ann. 2.83), which proves accurate though selective. They also show the dissemination of senatorial decrees to provincial towns as part of dynastic loyalism.
scholarship: González, 'Tabula Siarensis, Fortunales Siarenses et municipia civium Romanorum', ZPE 55 (1984)
Crawford (ed.), Roman Statutes (1996) nos. 37-38

expulsion_of_jews_and_isiacs_19.detail: Josephus attributes the measures to two scandals: a noblewoman, Paulina, seduced in the temple of Isis by an equestrian posing as Anubis with the priests' connivance (the priests were crucified and the temple razed), and a convert, Fulvia, defrauded of gifts for the Jerusalem Temple. Tacitus remarks that if the conscripts died of the climate in Sardinia it would be 'a cheap loss'. The same year astrologers were again expelled.

rhescuporis_murders_cotys.detail: Cotys, a cultivated man praised by Ovid in letters from Tomis, had married Antonia Tryphaena of Pontus. Tiberius divided the kingdom again, giving Rhoemetalces II (son of Rhescuporis) the west and Cotys's children, under a Roman guardian Trebellenus Rufus, the east. The arrangement lasted until the annexation of 46.

fall_of_maroboduus.detail: Tiberius told the Senate that Maroboduus had been more dangerous than Philip to Athens or Pyrrhus and Antiochus to Rome (Tacitus 2.63). Catualda was soon expelled by the Hermunduri and settled at Forum Iulii. Their followers were settled beyond the Danube between the Marus and the Cusus under the Quadian king Vannius, whose client kingdom lasted until c. 50. Drusus the Younger, sent to Illyricum, earned an ovation for these diplomatic successes.

lex_junia_norbana.detail: Gaius (Institutes 1.22, 3.56) explains that such freedmen "live as free men and die as slaves". They could reach full citizenship by several routes, including marrying and producing a year-old child (anniculi probatio) under the Lex Aelia Sentia, or service in the vigiles. The date is disputed: some put the law in 17 BC under Augustus. The status was abolished by Justinian.
lex_junia_norbana.debate: Date: AD 19 (consuls Silanus and Norbanus) or 25/17 BC.

foundation_of_tiberias.detail: The city had a stadium, a palace decorated with animal images that was destroyed by rebels in 66, and a council (boule) on the Greek model. It replaced Sepphoris as capital of Galilee. After 70 and especially after the move of the Sanhedrin in the third century, Tiberias became a centre of rabbinic Judaism where the Jerusalem Talmud was compiled.

amphitheatre_of_the_three_gauls_19.detail: Rufus, a Santonian aristocrat whose family had received citizenship from Caesar, also built the arch at Mediolanum Santonum (Saintes) dedicated to Germanicus, Drusus and Tiberius in 18-19. The amphitheatre, enlarged under Hadrian, was where the Christian martyrs of Lyon, including Blandina, died in 177. Seats reserved for the delegations of individual civitates survive inscribed. The amphitheatre's dedication slab naming Rufus was found in 1958; the cited CIL text is the Saintes arch inscription.

trial_of_piso.detail: The decree, found near Seville in the late 1980s and published in 1996, condemns Piso's memory, confiscates part of his estate, orders his name erased from a statue of Germanicus, pardons his wife Plancina at Livia's request, and praises the loyalty of the soldiers and the restraint of the imperial family. It does not uphold the poisoning charge. It is the longest senatus consultum on record and confirms that Tacitus used senatorial records (acta senatus), though it shows he compressed and dramatised; the date of the decree also shows that Tacitus's sequence of events is slightly off.
scholarship: Eck, Caballos and Fernández, Das senatus consultum de Cn. Pisone patre (1996)
Griffin, 'The Senate's story', JRS 87 (1997)

apronius_decimation_20.detail: Tacitus says Apronius awarded Helvius the torques and spear himself and Tiberius added the civic crown, regretting that the proconsul had not given it under his own authority. Rufus is known from an inscription at Tibur as Marcus Helvius Rufus Civica, later primus pilus. Decimation was rarely used under the Principate; Galba applied it to the marines in 68.

battle_of_augustodunum.detail: Sacrovir's 40,000 men included a fifth equipped with legionary arms and a corps of crupellarii, slave gladiators encased in iron armour, whom the legionaries cut down with axes and picks 'as if demolishing a wall'. Sacrovir and his companions burned themselves in a villa. Tacitus ascribes the revolt to debts, tribute and the harshness of governors; Velleius blames Sacrovir alone. Tiberius did not leave Rome, a point of criticism.

death_of_arminius.detail: Tacitus's obituary calls him 'without doubt the liberator of Germany' and notes that he was still celebrated in German songs; he records that the Chattan chief Adgandestrius had offered to poison him, and that Tiberius proudly refused, preferring open arms. Maroboduus, overthrown by Catualda in 18-19, lived for 18 years at Ravenna. Arminius's son Thumelicus was raised at Ravenna and met an undisclosed fate.

ten_day_interval_21.detail: Tacitus says the measure gave Tiberius time to intervene but that he never softened a sentence. The case, in which Marcus Lepidus argued for exile against the consul designate's proposal of death, illustrates the elastic use of maiestas charges for words and writings under Tiberius. Dio (57.20.4) dates the measure to the same year.

blaesus_campaign_against_tacfarinas_22.detail: Blaesus offered amnesty to all except the leader and divided the theatre into three sectors. Tiberius granted him the triumphal ornaments and allowed his troops to hail him imperator, the last time a commander outside the imperial family received the acclamation. The legion IX Hispana, sent from Pannonia, was recalled in 23; Tacfarinas promptly reappeared and was finally killed by Dolabella in 24.

drusus_receives_tribunicia_potestas_22.detail: Tacitus says Marcus Silanus and Quintus Haterius proposed fawning honours that Tiberius rejected. The grant intensified the rivalry between Drusus and Sejanus, whom Drusus had struck; Drusus died in September 23, reputedly poisoned by Sejanus and Livilla, as Sejanus's divorced wife Apicata revealed in 31.

death_of_drusus_the_younger.detail: Tacitus presents the death as the turning point of the reign and accepts the poisoning story while rejecting a further rumour that Tiberius himself gave Drusus the cup. With Drusus dead, Tiberius commended Germanicus's sons Nero and Drusus to the Senate, setting Sejanus against Agrippina's family. Drusus's twin sons were born in 19; one, Tiberius Gemellus, survived.
death_of_drusus_the_younger.debate: The poison story rests on Apicata's testimony, given in grief after her children's execution, and on confessions under torture.

castra_praetoria.detail: The camp (about 440 by 380 m) on the Viminal had brick-faced concrete walls, one of the earliest large uses of brick facing in Rome; Aurelian later incorporated its north, east and south walls into the city wall, where they can still be seen. From here the praetorians would make and unmake emperors, beginning with Claudius in 41.

siege_of_auzea.detail: Tacfarinas's son was captured and his brother escaped. The Senate denied Dolabella triumphal ornaments to protect the reputation of Junius Blaesus, uncle of Sejanus; Tacitus regards this as discreditable. Ptolemy was rewarded with an ivory sceptre and embroidered toga, the old honours for a friend of the Roman people.

trial_of_cremutius_cordus.detail: Tacitus gives him a speech defending freedom of historical judgement and comments that the punishment of talent only increases its authority. His daughter Marcia preserved copies, and the work was republished under Caligula; Seneca's Consolation to Marcia praises her for it. The case is a landmark in the history of literary censorship.

thracian_revolt_26.detail: Tacitus's detailed account shows the role of client-kingdom levies in the Roman army and Roman tactics of circumvallation in mountainous country. Poppaeus Sabinus received triumphal ornaments. Thrace was annexed in 46.

tiberius_retires_to_capri.detail: At Spelunca (Sperlonga) the roof of a seaside grotto where he was dining collapsed, and Sejanus shielded him with his body, earning his total trust; the grotto, excavated in 1957, yielded the colossal Odysseus sculpture groups by Rhodian sculptors. On Capri Tiberius built or enlarged twelve villas, of which the Villa Jovis on the eastern cliffs survives. Suetonius's catalogue of his vices there derives from hostile gossip.

smyrna_wins_temple_of_tiberius_26.detail: Tacitus summarises the claims: Ilium for its Trojan origins, Halicarnassus for its freedom from earthquakes for 1,200 years, Pergamum because it already had the temple of Augustus, Sardis for kinship with the Etruscans. Smyrna pointed to its temple of Roma founded in 195 BC. Tiberius told the Senate that he was mortal and that the best temples were in their memory, rejecting worship in Spain.

pilate_standards_affair.detail: Josephus presents the incident as the first of several clashes. Earlier prefects had avoided bringing iconic standards into the city. Pilate's title is confirmed by the inscription found in the theatre at Caesarea in 1961, recording a Tiberieum dedicated by "[Pon]tius Pilatus [praef]ectus Iuda[ea]e". Philo, writing c. 41, describes him as inflexible, harsh and venal, but his ten-year tenure (26-36) was the second longest of any governor of Judaea, implying Tiberius found him satisfactory.

fidenae_amphitheatre_collapse.detail: The Senate responded with safety rules: no one with less than 400,000 sesterces could put on gladiatorial games, and amphitheatres were to be built only on ground tested for soundness. Atilius was exiled. Rich houses were opened to the injured, and Tacitus compares the scene to a battle.

fire_on_the_caelian_27.detail: Tacitus says people blamed the emperor's absence and the ill-omened year until his generosity changed their mood. Fires recurred on the Aventine and around the Circus in 36, when Tiberius paid out 100 million sesterces and four grandsons-in-law assessed the damage.

battle_of_baduhenna_wood.detail: A further 400 who had occupied the villa of a former auxiliary named Cruptorix killed one another rather than fall into Frisian hands. Tiberius concealed the losses to avoid entrusting a war to anyone, and the Frisii remained independent until Corbulo's operations of 47. Tacitus says their name then became famous among the Germans.

ministry_of_jesus.detail: Luke 3.1 dates John's appearance to the fifteenth year of Tiberius, which most reckon AD 28/29. The Synoptic gospels imply a single year with one Passover, John three Passovers. Jesus's preaching drew on Jewish apocalyptic expectation, and he avoided the Hellenised cities of Sepphoris and Tiberias. Josephus's Testimonium Flavianum (Antiquities 18.63-64) mentions him as a wise man and wonderworker crucified by Pilate; it has been interpolated by Christian copyists but most scholars think a core is authentic. The excavated first-century synagogue at Magdala and the boat from the Sea of Galilee illustrate the setting.
ministry_of_jesus.debate: Length of the ministry (one or three years) and authenticity of the Testimonium Flavianum.

death_of_livia.detail: Tacitus marks her death as removing the last restraint on Tiberius and Sejanus: 'from then on it was sheer, oppressive despotism'. The Senate voted an arch, which Tiberius promised to build himself and never did. Claudius deified her in 42. Her villa at Prima Porta, with its garden fresco room and the Augustus statue, survives.

fall_of_agrippina_and_her_sons.detail: Tacitus says Drusus was reduced to chewing the stuffing of his mattress and that Tiberius had the daily record of his words and sufferings, kept by a guard, read out in the Senate. Only the youngest son, Gaius, survived on Capri with Tiberius. Agrippina had lost an eye to a centurion's beating. Tiberius later boasted that he had not had her strangled.

pilate_aqueduct_riot.detail: Josephus gives the aqueduct's length as 200 or 400 stades; it is usually identified with part of the system bringing water from the Solomon's Pools area south of Bethlehem. The date within his prefecture is unknown. Luke 13.1 mentions "the Galileans whose blood Pilate mingled with their sacrifices", another unparalleled incident.

execution_of_john_the_baptist.detail: John baptised in the Jordan for the forgiveness of sins and preached imminent judgement; Jesus was among those he baptised. The gospels add the story of Salome's dance and the head on a platter (Mark 6.17-29). Josephus reports that when Antipas's army was destroyed by Aretas IV of Nabataea in 36, many Jews saw it as divine punishment for John's death, which is why his account appears in that context. John's followers persisted independently into the 50s (Acts 19.1-7).
execution_of_john_the_baptist.debate: Date uncertain (c. 28-30); the gospel motive and Josephus's political motive may both be true.

crucifixion_of_jesus.detail: Jesus of Nazareth was crucified outside Jerusalem by order of the prefect Pontius Pilate at Passover, on a Friday, during Pilate's prefecture (26-36). The execution is one of the best-attested facts about him: besides the four gospels and Paul's letters (1 Corinthians 15.3-8, written c. 54), it is recorded by Tacitus (Annals 15.44, "Christus, executed by the procurator Pontius Pilate in the reign of Tiberius") and in the core of Josephus's Testimonium (Antiquities 18.63-64). The gospels describe his entry into Jerusalem, a disturbance in the Temple, a last meal with his disciples, his arrest at night in Gethsemane by Temple police, a hearing before the High Priest Caiaphas and his council, and his transfer to Pilate on a political charge: the inscription on the cross, "King of the Jews", reflects Roman concern with royal claimants. Crucifixion was a Roman punishment for slaves, bandits and rebels, and the bones of a crucified man, Yehohanan, found in Jerusalem in 1968 with a nail through the heel bone, illustrate the method. The date is disputed. The Synoptics place the death on Passover day itself (15 Nisan), John on the eve, when the lambs were slaughtered (14 Nisan); astronomical calculation shows that 14 Nisan fell on a Friday in AD 30 (7 April) and AD 33 (3 April). AD 30 suits the reckoning from Luke's fifteenth year of Tiberius and a short ministry; AD 33 suits a three-year ministry and is favoured by some on the basis of the lunar eclipse visible from Jerusalem on 3 April 33, linked to Acts 2.20. Earlier dates (27, 29) and 36 have also been proposed. The gospel accounts of Pilate's reluctance and the crowd's responsibility are widely seen by historians as shaped by later apologetic aims, which minimised Roman guilt and blamed Jewish leaders, with terrible later consequences. The proclamation of the resurrection by Jesus's followers within days or weeks of his death was the origin of the Christian movement, and the execution site and tomb were venerated by the fourth century at the place later covered by the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.
crucifixion_of_jesus.debate: Date: Friday 7 April 30 or 3 April 33 (14 Nisan in John's chronology); Synoptic and Johannine chronologies differ by a day.
scholarship: Sanders, The Historical Figure of Jesus (1993)
Meier, A Marginal Jew I (1991)

velleius_history_30.detail: The second book becomes a detailed eyewitness account of Tiberius's campaigns and an unqualified panegyric of Tiberius and of Sejanus, whom Velleius calls "singularis principalium operum adiutor" a year before his fall. Despite its sycophancy it is the only contemporary narrative of the Illyrian revolt and the Varian disaster, and it contains early literary history, including essays on the clustering of genius in short periods.

arrest_of_asinius_gallus_30.detail: Gallus had spoken freely in the Senate since 14 and was one of the potential heirs Augustus was said to have named as "capable but unwilling" or "willing but unworthy". Dio (58.3) notes the cruelty of keeping him alive in isolation. His fall was part of the destruction of Agrippina's party that preceded Sejanus's own collapse.

fall_of_sejanus.detail: Lucius Aelius Sejanus, praetorian prefect from 14 (alone from c. 15), was arrested on 18 October 31 at a Senate meeting in the Temple of Apollo on the Palatine, condemned at a second session in the Temple of Concord beside the prison, and executed the same day. An equestrian from Volsinii, related by marriage to senatorial families, he had concentrated the nine praetorian cohorts in a single camp on the Viminal in 23, made himself indispensable to Tiberius, and after the death of Drusus the Younger (23), which his former wife Apicata later claimed he had arranged with Drusus's wife Livilla, systematically destroyed Agrippina the Elder and her elder sons Nero and Drusus. After Tiberius withdrew to Capri in 26, Sejanus controlled access to the emperor; statues of him were honoured, his birthday was celebrated and he held the consulship of 31 with Tiberius. He was betrothed to Livilla (or her daughter) and seems to have expected tribunician power. Tiberius, alerted, according to Josephus, by a letter from Antonia Minor, prepared his fall secretly. He appointed Macro as new prefect, who had the night watch (vigiles) replace the praetorians outside the Senate, and delivered a long, rambling letter from Capri that began with routine matters and ended by denouncing Sejanus. The Senate, which had come expecting to confer new honours, voted his arrest. He was strangled in the Tullianum, his body thrown down the Gemonian steps and torn by the crowd, and his statues smashed, a scene Juvenal (10.56-107) made the classic image of fallen greatness. His young children were executed, the daughter raped first by the executioner because a virgin could not be killed (Tacitus, 5.9). Apicata killed herself after revealing Drusus's murder, and Livilla was starved to death. A wave of trials of his associates followed (the "Sejanian" treason trials), which Tacitus describes in the darkest terms. Velleius's eulogy of Sejanus, published only a year before, shows how high he stood. Modern scholars debate whether he planned a coup or merely sought a regency over Tiberius's grandson Gemellus, and whether Tiberius struck from fear or genuine discovery of a plot.
fall_of_sejanus.debate: Whether Sejanus planned to seize power or to become regent; the significance of Antonia's warning.

valerius_maximus_memorable_deeds.detail: A passage (9.11.ext.4) denouncing an unnamed would-be parricide who planned to destroy the empire is generally taken as referring to Sejanus, which dates publication soon after October 31. Despised by modern critics for its style, the work was hugely popular in late antiquity and the Middle Ages, survives in many manuscripts and two ancient epitomes, and preserves much lost material, including from Livy.

temple_of_bel_palmyra_32.detail: Palmyra had come within the Roman orbit under Tiberius: a boundary marker set up by the legate Creticus Silanus (AD 11-17) fixes its territory, and a statue of Germanicus's agent Alexandros records his mission during Germanicus's eastern command. The temple combined a Hellenistic peristyle with Semitic-style crenellations and an off-centre entrance. It was demolished by Islamic State in 2015.

financial_crisis_of_33.detail: The Senate first gave lenders 18 months to comply and ordered two-thirds of loans to be invested in Italian land, but debtors had to sell to repay, flooding the market. The episode is an unusually detailed ancient account of credit contraction and a state bailout; it has attracted modern economic historians since Tenney Frank (1935).
scholarship: Frank, 'The financial crisis of 33 A.D.', AJP 56 (1935)
Rodewald, Money in the Age of Tiberius (1976)

phoenix_sighted_34.detail: Tacitus reports Egyptian and Greek opinion that earlier sightings fell under Sesosis, Amasis and Ptolemy III, and expresses doubt whether this bird was genuine. Pliny (10.5) records that a phoenix was exhibited in the Comitium under Claudius in AD 47, which nobody believed. Phoenix coin types later symbolised renewal of the age (saeculum aureum) under Hadrian and Antoninus Pius.

conversion_of_paul.detail: Paul's own account (Galatians 1.13-24) says he went to Arabia (Nabataea) and back to Damascus, visited Jerusalem three years later to meet Cephas (Peter) and James, then worked in Syria and Cilicia for some fourteen years. He escaped Damascus by being let down the wall in a basket when the ethnarch of king Aretas IV tried to seize him (2 Corinthians 11.32-33), which dates the episode before Aretas's death in 40. Acts gives three dramatised versions of the conversion.
conversion_of_paul.debate: Pauline chronology is built back from the Gallio inscription (51/52); dates of 31 to 36 have been proposed.

stoning_of_stephen.detail: Acts 6-7 describes the appointment of seven Hellenist deacons to oversee food distribution, Stephen's debates with diaspora synagogues and his trial before the council. The episode marks the first persecution and the scattering of the Hellenists to Samaria, Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, where the name "Christians" was first used. How a lynching could occur under Roman rule, which reserved capital jurisdiction, is debated.
stoning_of_stephen.debate: Historicity of the speech and date (c. 31-36).

armenian_crisis_35.detail: Tiridates was crowned at Ctesiphon in 36 by the Surena, but Artabanus returned with Dahae and Saka forces and recovered the throne. Tacitus (6.31-37, 6.41-44) gives a detailed account of the intrigues and the Iberian victory. The episode was Tiberius's classic use of diplomacy and client rulers instead of legions, and Mithridates held Armenia until Caligula recalled him.

fire_on_the_aventine_36.detail: Tacitus says the relief was the more welcome because Tiberius built little for himself. The episode is one of a series of great fires in Rome under the early Principate (6, 27, 36, 64) that shaped the vigiles and building regulations.

aretas_defeats_antipas_36.detail: Josephus says Antipas's army was defeated through the treachery of refugees from Philip's tetrarchy who had joined it, and that many Jews saw the defeat as punishment for the killing of John the Baptist. Vitellius marched two legions towards Petra but sent them around Judaea to avoid carrying images through the land, and himself sacrificed at Jerusalem.

pilate_recalled_36.detail: Pilate reached Rome after Tiberius's death (March 37) and disappears from reliable history; later Christian traditions variously made him a suicide, a martyr or a saint (in the Coptic and Ethiopian churches). Vitellius also deposed the High Priest Caiaphas, who had held office since c. 18, remitted market taxes in Jerusalem and restored the High Priest's vestments to Jewish custody.

death_of_tiberius.detail: Tiberius died on 16 March 37 at the villa of Lucullus at Misenum, aged 77, on his way back towards Rome, which he had not entered since 26 and approached several times without going in. He had held a dinner at Astura and fallen ill, but continued to attend banquets to hide his weakness; his physician Charicles, taking his pulse while pretending to kiss his hand, told Macro he would not last two days. Accounts of the end diverge. Tacitus says he seemed to have died and Gaius was being hailed as emperor when news came that he had recovered and asked for food; Macro calmly ordered him smothered with bedclothes. Suetonius gives versions in which Gaius poisoned him, starved him or smothered him with a pillow, and one in which, recovering from a faint, he called for his attendants and, finding no one, rose and collapsed. Dio says Gaius and Macro starved him or smothered him. Modern historians generally accept a natural death in extreme old age, the murder stories reflecting Gaius's later reputation. His will, made two years earlier, named Gaius and his grandson Tiberius Gemellus joint heirs; the Senate annulled it at Gaius's request, recognising Gaius as sole ruler, and Gemellus was killed within a year. The people greeted the news with joy, shouting "Tiberius to the Tiber!", and his body was escorted to Rome by soldiers and cremated, but the Senate did not deify him. Tacitus's famous obituary (Annals 6.51) divides his life into phases of progressive degeneration, from excellence while Augustus lived to unrestrained cruelty and lust after Sejanus's fall, a schema modern scholars criticise as literary. His reign left a full treasury of 2.7 billion sesterces, a stable frontier, competent provincial government and a demoralised Senate. The stories of debauchery on Capri retailed by Suetonius are widely discounted. Tiberius's refusal of honours, devotion to Augustan precedent and attempts to make the Senate share responsibility were sincere but failed, and his isolation on Capri set a precedent for government by an absent ruler through intermediaries.
death_of_tiberius.debate: Natural death or murder by Macro and Gaius.

accession_of_caligula.detail: Suetonius says more than 160,000 victims were sacrificed in thanksgiving in three months. Gaius brought back the ashes of his mother and brother from the islands, recalled exiles, published imperial accounts, restored elections to the people (briefly) and paid Tiberius's legacies. The one-day conferral of powers, rather than piecemeal grants as for Augustus and Tiberius, foreshadows the later lex de imperio.

caligulas_illness_and_purges.detail: Philo, writing a few years later, saw the illness as the turning point after seven months of exemplary government; modern scholars dispute whether it caused any mental change or simply freed him from his early backers. People who had vowed their lives for his recovery were held to their vows.

vitellius_artabanus_meeting_37.detail: Josephus dates the meeting to the end of Tiberius's reign and says Herod Antipas hosted a banquet in a pavilion on the bridge and sent the first report to Tiberius ahead of Vitellius, earning his enmity. Suetonius and Dio place it under Caligula. Darius walked in Caligula's procession over the bridge at Baiae in 39.

temple_of_divus_augustus_dedicated_37.detail: Its site is unknown, though it lay near the Palatine and is shown on Caligula's sestertii as a hexastyle Ionic temple with Caligula sacrificing. Domitian restored it after a fire and added a shrine of Minerva; Antoninus Pius rebuilt it again (his coins show an octastyle temple with statues of Augustus and Livia). A military diploma of AD 90 records that copies of discharge certificates were posted on the wall behind it.

agrippa_i_made_king_37.detail: Agrippa had spent his youth at Rome with Drusus the Younger and Claudius, and lived on loans from Antonia and Alexander the Alabarch. His arrival in Alexandria in 38 with royal display triggered the anti-Jewish riots there. In 39/40 he received Antipas's tetrarchy, and in 41, for his part in Claudius's accession, Judaea and Samaria, ruling a kingdom almost as large as Herod's until his death in 44.

vatican_obelisk_brought.detail: The ship, the largest ever seen according to Pliny, carried 120,000 modii of lentils as ballast and was later sunk by Claudius to form the base of the lighthouse at Portus; its hull was found in the 1950s during airport construction at Fiumicino. The obelisk, still bearing its dedication to Divus Augustus and Tiberius, is the only one in Rome never to have fallen; Sixtus V moved it to St Peter's Square in 1586. The circus, completed by Nero, was the traditional site of Peter's martyrdom.

death_of_drusilla.detail: A senator, Livius Geminius, swore he had seen her ascend to heaven and was paid a million sesterces. She had been named heir to Gaius's property and power in his illness of 37. Ancient allegations of incest between Gaius and his sisters are generally viewed with scepticism. Her cult as Panthea was short-lived.

alexandrian_pogrom_38.detail: Flaccus was arrested in October 38 and exiled to Andros, where he was later executed. Rival Jewish and Greek embassies, led by Philo and by Apion, went to Gaius in 39/40; Philo's Legatio ad Gaium describes a farcical audience in the gardens of Maecenas. Claudius's letter to the Alexandrians (41) settled the dispute. Philo's In Flaccum is our main source and is intensely partisan; the conflict turned on Jewish claims to civic rights in Alexandria.
scholarship: Gruen, Diaspora: Jews amidst Greeks and Romans (2002)
van der Horst, Philo's Flaccus (2003)

caligula_popular_measures_38.detail: He also enlarged the equestrian decuries and paid Tiberius's and Livia's legacies in full. The electoral reform failed because candidates would not compete and the assemblies were soon abandoned again. By 39 Caligula had exhausted Tiberius's reserve (reputedly 2.7 billion sesterces), reintroduced maiestas trials and imposed new taxes on lawsuits, porters and prostitutes, collected through posted notices in tiny letters.

caligula_client_kings_38.detail: Dio and Suetonius present the grants as the extravagance of a young emperor surrounded by eastern princes, but the policy of ruling marginal regions through client dynasts was Augustan. Caligula later deposed Antiochus and summoned Mithridates of Armenia to Rome, which let Parthia regain influence there.

conspiracy_of_gaetulicus.detail: The Arval Brethren recorded sacrifices on 27 October 39 'for the detection of the wicked plots of Gnaeus Lentulus Gaetulicus against Gaius Germanicus' (CIL VI 32346). Gaius had marched north with praetorians before the plot broke, and Servius Sulpicius Galba replaced Gaetulicus. Vespasian, as praetor, moved that the conspirators be denied burial.

caligulas_northern_expedition.detail: He built a lighthouse at Gesoriacum (the Tour d'Ordre, standing until 1644). The seashell story has been rationalised by modern scholars, who suggest that 'musculi' meant engineers' huts or that the troops refused to embark; preparations he made may have facilitated Claudius's invasion three years later. He celebrated an ovatio in Rome on his birthday, 31 August 40.
caligulas_northern_expedition.debate: The seashells: lunacy, mockery of mutinous troops, or misunderstanding of a technical term.
scholarship: Woods, 'Caligula's seashells', Greece and Rome 47 (2000)

exile_of_herod_antipas.detail: Josephus places the exile at Lugdunum, apparently Lugdunum Convenarum (Saint-Bertrand-de-Comminges) in the Pyrenees (War 2.183 says Spain). Herodias refused Caligula's offer to keep her property and followed her husband. Antipas had ruled Galilee and Peraea for 43 years.

embassy_of_philo.detail: Philo's Embassy to Gaius, written after Caligula's death, is a unique first-hand account of an imperial audience, and his Against Flaccus describes the pogrom and the downfall of the prefect Avillius Flaccus. During the embassy the envoys learned of the order to place Caligula's statue in the Temple. The dispute over Jewish civic status in Alexandria was settled only by Claudius's letter of 41.

caligulas_bridge_at_baiae.detail: Suetonius gives three explanations: to outdo Xerxes' Hellespont bridge, to frighten the Germans and Britons, or to refute Thrasyllus's prophecy that Gaius had no more chance of becoming emperor than of riding across the bay of Baiae. The requisition of grain ships was later blamed for a food shortage in Rome. The Parthian hostage Darius rode in the procession.

legate_of_numidia_39.detail: Tacitus (Histories 4.48) says the result was rivalry between proconsul and legate over the frontier; the legate became de facto governor of Numidia, which was formally separated as a province only under Septimius Severus. The legion's base moved from Ammaedara to Theveste and, under Trajan or Hadrian, to Lambaesis.

annexation_of_mauretania.detail: The revolt took two years to suppress (Suetonius Paullinus crossed the Atlas in 42; Hosidius Geta pursued the Moorish leader Salabus into the desert). Claudius divided the territory into two procuratorial provinces, Mauretania Caesariensis (capital Iol Caesarea) and Tingitana (capital Tingis). An inscription from Volubilis honours Marcus Valerius Severus, who commanded auxiliaries against Aedemon and obtained Roman citizenship and municipal status for the town.

caligula_temple_statue_crisis.detail: Josephus describes tens of thousands of Jews at Ptolemais and Tiberias who lay on the ground for forty days, abandoning the sowing, and declared they would die rather than see the Temple profaned. Gaius ordered Petronius to commit suicide, but the letter arrived after news of the emperor's assassination. Tacitus (Hist. 5.9) says the Jews took up arms rather than accept the order. The episode left a deep mark on Jewish and early Christian apocalyptic thought.

nemi_ships.detail: Dated by lead pipes stamped C CAESARIS AVG GERMANICI, the hulls were recovered by draining the lake in 1928-1932 and revealed ball-bearing rotating platforms, bilge pumps and anchors of advanced design. They were burned in 1944 when the museum built to house them was hit during fighting between German and Allied forces; only bronze fittings and models survive. Suetonius describes similar pleasure galleys with baths and vineyards.

assassination_of_caligula.detail: Gaius Caesar (Caligula) was murdered on 24 January 41, the last day of the Palatine Games in honour of Augustus, in a covered passage under the palace as he left the theatre for lunch. The conspiracy involved praetorian officers, senators and palace freedmen, including the praetorian prefect Arrecinus Clemens and the freedman Callistus. Its leading figure was the praetorian tribune Cassius Chaerea, a veteran of the German mutinies whom Gaius habitually humiliated with obscene watchwords such as "Priapus" and "Venus". Chaerea asked the watchword and struck first, cutting Gaius in the neck; another tribune, Cornelius Sabinus, stabbed him in the chest, and others joined, thirty wounds in all by Suetonius's count, some aimed at the genitals. His German bodyguard ran amok, killing several bystanders and senators, and a centurion killed his wife Milonia Caesonia and dashed their infant daughter Julia Drusilla against a wall. The motives were partly personal and partly political: after the conspiracy of Gaetulicus and Lepidus in 39, Gaius had turned against the Senate, demanded divine honours, threatened to move the capital to Alexandria and exhausted the treasury. Josephus (Antiquities 19.1-273), drawing on a detailed contemporary source, preserves the fullest narrative, with the senator Valerius Asiaticus telling the crowd he wished he had struck the blow himself. The Senate met on the Capitol, the consul Sentius Saturninus spoke of restoring liberty, and debate turned to abolishing the Principate or choosing a new princeps; candidates included Asiaticus and Marcus Vinicius. But the praetorians found Gaius's uncle Claudius hiding behind a curtain in the palace and carried him to their camp, and within a day the Senate had to accept their choice. The murder showed that the Principate could survive the death of a hated ruler without a designated heir, and that the praetorians, not the Senate, now decided the succession. Chaerea was executed by Claudius, while the other conspirators were largely spared.
scholarship: Barrett, Caligula: The Abuse of Power (2nd ed. 2015)
Wiseman, Death of an Emperor (1991)
