accession_of_claudius.detail: On 24-25 January 41, in the confusion after Caligula's murder, a praetorian named Gratus found the dead emperor's uncle Tiberius Claudius Germanicus, then fifty and long regarded as unfit for public life because of his limp, tremor and stammer, hiding behind a curtain in the palace. The soldiers carried him in a litter to the Castra Praetoria, where he spent the night. Meanwhile the consuls convened the Senate on the Capitol with the urban cohorts and debated restoring the Republic or electing a new emperor from among themselves. Herod Agrippa I, an old friend of Claudius, acted as go-between, encouraging Claudius to stand firm and advising the Senate to negotiate (Josephus). By the next day the urban cohorts had gone over to the praetorians and the Senate, abandoned, had to confer the powers of the Principate on Claudius. He promised each praetorian 15,000 sesterces, the first explicit donative paid for an accession, a precedent that Suetonius says made him the first emperor to buy the soldiers' loyalty. Coins of 41-42 show the praetorian camp with the legend IMPER RECEPT (the emperor received) and a praetorian clasping hands with Claudius (PRAETOR RECEPT). Claudius declared an amnesty for the senators, executed Cassius Chaerea and a few others for the murder, and recalled exiles, including his nieces Agrippina and Julia Livilla. His lack of senatorial support and his reliance on the army and on his freedmen (Narcissus, Pallas, Callistus, Polybius) shaped his whole reign, which saw the revolt of Scribonianus in 42 and recurrent conspiracies; Seneca's Apocolocyntosis claims that 35 senators and some 300 knights were executed. Modern historians (Levick, Osgood) suggest that the "accident" of his elevation may have been less spontaneous than the sources claim, with Claudius and his supporters among the praetorian officers acting quickly to secure the outcome. His scholarly background as a historian of the Etruscans and Carthaginians and his antiquarian interests left a strong mark on his policies.
accession_of_claudius.debate: Whether Claudius's accession was a chance event or a planned coup by his supporters in the guard.
scholarship: Levick, Claudius (1990)
Osgood, Claudius Caesar (2011)

claudius_letter_to_the_alexandrians.detail: Claudius threatens that if Jews persist he will proceed against them 'as fomenters of a general plague for the whole world', a phrase sometimes linked to early Christian missions, probably anachronistically. The document is one of the longest surviving texts in an emperor's own voice and shows the personal, reactive style of imperial government (Millar's 'petition and response').
scholarship: Millar, The Emperor in the Roman World (1977)

sources.w: Greek Papyri in the British Museum

seneca_exiled_to_corsica_41.detail: From exile Seneca wrote the Consolation to Helvia (his mother), which presents banishment as a Stoic indifferent, and the Consolation to Polybius, a fawning appeal to Claudius's freedman that he later preferred to forget. On his recall he was made praetor and, with Burrus, guided the first years of Nero's reign.

mauretanian_war_41.detail: Inscriptions from Volubilis honour the local notable Marcus Valerius Severus, who led auxiliaries against Aedemon and obtained for his town Roman citizenship, municipal status and tax remission (44). Gnaeus Hosidius Geta twice defeated the Moorish chief Salabus in 42, nearly dying of thirst until a native's rain-making ritual saved his army (Dio). The provinces were each governed by an equestrian procurator with auxiliary garrisons.

revolt_of_scribonianus.detail: Suetonius says Claudius was ready to comply. The loyal legions were rewarded with the titles Claudia Pia Fidelis. Among those condemned was Caecina Paetus; his wife Arria stabbed herself first and handed him the dagger with the words 'Paete, non dolet' ('It does not hurt, Paetus'). The revolt hardened Claudius's suspicion of senators and his dependence on freedmen.

portus_begun.detail: Canals linked the harbour to the Tiber, relieving Rome from floods as well, as an inscription of 46 records (ILS 207). The basin, about 200 hectares, proved too exposed: 200 ships sank inside it in a storm in 62. Nero completed it, celebrated on sestertii with the legend PORT(us) OST(iensis) AVGVSTI. Trajan added the hexagonal inner basin c. 110-112.
scholarship: Keay et al., Portus (2005)

paullinus_crosses_the_atlas_42.detail: Pliny the Elder, who read Paullinus's own account, preserves the details: snow on the summits even in summer, forests of unknown trees and the Canarii tribes who ate dog meat. Paullinus later commanded in Britain (58-61) and against Boudica, and fought for Otho in 69.

battle_of_the_medway.detail: On the second day Gnaeus Hosidius Geta, almost captured, won the battle and received triumphal ornaments though he had not been consul, a rare honour. The Britons fell back to the Thames, where Togodumnus died soon afterwards. Dio, our only source, names neither river.

claudius_in_britain.detail: His arch in Rome (dedicated 51/52) recorded that he received the surrender of eleven British kings 'without any loss' (CIL VI 920). He triumphed in 44, gave his son the name Britannicus, and placed a naval crown on the Palatine beside the civic crown, symbolising his conquest of the Ocean. Rome's first permanent fortress in Britain was built at Camulodunum.

invasion_of_britain_43.detail: In spring 43 Claudius launched the conquest of Britain that Caesar had begun and Caligula had abandoned. The pretext was an appeal from Verica, king of the Atrebates, driven out by the sons of Cunobelinus of the Catuvellauni, Togodumnus and Caratacus, whose expanding kingdom dominated the south-east. Claudius also needed military prestige to secure his position after the revolt of Scribonianus. Aulus Plautius, legate of Pannonia, commanded four legions, II Augusta (under the future emperor Vespasian), IX Hispana, XIV Gemina and XX Valeria, with a similar number of auxiliaries, some 40,000 men in all. The troops at Gesoriacum (Boulogne) at first refused to embark for "beyond the Ocean" until Claudius's freedman Narcissus addressed them from the tribunal and was mocked with cries of "Io Saturnalia", after which they sailed in three divisions. The landing place is debated: Richborough (Rutupiae), where a Claudian ditch system and later monumental arch have been excavated, is traditional, while some scholars argue for a landing near Chichester in Atrebatic territory. The Britons avoided battle at first, then fought a two-day battle at a river crossing (generally identified with the Medway), where Batavian auxiliaries swam across in armour and Hosidius Geta won triumphal ornaments. Togodumnus died soon after. Plautius halted at the Thames and summoned Claudius, who came with praetorians and elephants, spent sixteen days in Britain, took Camulodunum, received the surrender of eleven kings and returned to celebrate a triumph in 44. The client kingdoms of Togidubnus in the south and Prasutagus of the Iceni, and the treaty with Cartimandua of the Brigantes, allowed rapid progress; by 47 the frontier ran roughly along the Fosse Way from Exeter to Lincoln. Vespasian, according to Suetonius, fought thirty battles, subdued two peoples and took over twenty oppida, probably including Maiden Castle and Hod Hill. The conquest was costly and slow, requiring four legions for decades, and Appian and Strabo had already argued that Britain was not worth the expense.
invasion_of_britain_43.debate: Landing site (Richborough in Kent or the Chichester area) and the location of the river battle.

annexation_of_lycia.detail: The Stadiasmus Patarensis, a monumental pillar at Patara inscribed in 45/46, lists the roads built by the first governor Quintus Veranius with distances between Lycian cities, the most detailed road document of its kind. The League continued as a provincial assembly for the imperial cult.
scholarship: Şahin and Adak, Stadiasmus Patarensis (2007)

death_of_herod_agrippa_i.detail: Josephus says an owl appeared to him as an omen; Acts 12.23 says he was 'eaten by worms' because he did not give glory to God. He had begun a 'third wall' to enclose Jerusalem's northern suburb, halted on the orders of the Syrian legate Marsus. His son Agrippa II, aged 17, was considered too young to succeed and later received smaller territories.

siege_of_maiden_castle.detail: Wheeler's vivid narrative of a Roman assault and massacre became a classic of British archaeology. Re-analysis by Niall Sharples (1991) and Rebecca Redfern (2011) has shown that the burials span a longer period and that most injuries were not Roman; only a few can be tied to Roman weapons, and there is no destruction layer. Nearby Hod Hill, with ballista bolts concentrated on one hut and a Roman fort in its corner, gives clearer evidence of a Roman attack.
siege_of_maiden_castle.debate: Whether a Roman assault and massacre occurred at all.
scholarship: Wheeler, Maiden Castle, Dorset (1943)
Sharples, Maiden Castle (1991)
Redfern, 'A re-appraisal of the evidence for violence in the Late Iron Age human remains from Maiden Castle', OJA 30 (2011)

execution_of_james_son_of_zebedee.detail: Josephus and Acts both describe Agrippa dying after being hailed as a god at games in Caesarea, wearing a robe of silver that shone in the morning sun. Agrippa's attack on the Jerusalem church fits his cultivation of Jewish piety (Mishnah Sotah 7.8 remembers him weeping at the reading of the law). After 44 the leadership of the Jerusalem community passed to James the brother of Jesus.

claudius_british_triumph_44.detail: Governors who had won triumphal ornaments marched in the procession, and Messalina followed in a carriage. A naval crown was hung beside the civic crown on the Palatine to mark the conquest of the Ocean. The Arch of Claudius on the Via Flaminia, part of the Aqua Virgo, was dedicated in 51-52; its inscription records the surrender of eleven British kings "without any loss". Aulus Plautius received an ovation in 47, the last given to a non-imperial general.

eclipse_of_45.detail: Dio quotes the edict as explaining that the moon, passing under the sun, blocks its light. The annular eclipse of 1 August 45 was indeed visible in the Mediterranean. The episode reflects Claudius's scholarly bent and the political danger of portents, which had been used against emperors.

theudas_45.detail: Theudas is one of several "sign prophets" Josephus describes, who promised Exodus-style miracles; Acts 5.36 puts a Theudas before Judas the Galilean, a chronological error. Fadus's successor Tiberius Julius Alexander, an apostate Jew, crucified James and Simon, sons of Judas the Galilean.

annexation_of_thrace.detail: Thrace had been a client kingdom since Augustus, divided for a time between Rhoemetalces's heirs, with risings in 21 and 26 against levies. The annexation is dated by Eusebius's Chronicle and coins; the relevant books of Tacitus are lost. A senatorial legate governed Thrace from Trajan's time, and colonies were founded at Apri and Deultum.

famine_in_judaea_46.detail: The famine is one of several food crises under Claudius. Helena built a palace in Jerusalem and the monumental "Tomb of the Kings" north of the city, where a sarcophagus inscribed "Queen Sadan" has been identified as hers. The royal house of Adiabene, a Parthian vassal on the Tigris, sent soldiers to fight for the rebels in 66.

pauls_first_missionary_journey.detail: The journey (the "first journey" of Acts 13-14) is not mentioned explicitly in Paul's letters, which refer only to work in Syria and Cilicia. An inscription from Pisidian Antioch naming a Lucius Sergius Paullus and others from Cyprus support the plausibility of the proconsul. The admission of uncircumcised Gentiles provoked the dispute settled at Jerusalem.

corbulo_against_the_chauci.detail: Corbulo is said to have exclaimed 'Happy the Roman generals of old!' and set his troops to dig a 23-mile canal between the Rhine and the Meuse (fossa Corbulonis), whose timber revetments near Leiden have been dated by dendrochronology to 50. He received triumphal ornaments. The episode marks Claudius's decision that the lower Rhine would not be crossed again.

ludi_saeculares_47.detail: The Troy Game in the Circus featured Britannicus and the young Lucius Domitius (Nero), whose louder reception Tacitus treats as a sign of things to come. A phoenix was exhibited in the Comitium (Pliny). Claudius also extended the pomerium in 49 to include the Aventine, recorded on surviving cippi, justified by the conquest of Britain.

death_of_valerius_asiaticus_47.detail: Asiaticus, from Vienna in Narbonensis, was the first Gallic senator to hold two consulships; Claudius's Lyon speech the next year sneers at him as a "robber" from Vienna. Tacitus has him ask that his pyre be moved so as not to scorch his trees. The case is the classic example of Messalina's influence and Claudius's private trials (intra cubiculum).

first_iceni_revolt_47.detail: Tacitus says Ostorius used only auxiliaries. Prasutagus probably owed his client kingship to the aftermath. Ostorius then campaigned against the Deceangli and the Brigantes and turned against the Silures and Caratacus. The disarming policy, with its humiliation of a client people, prefigured the Boudican revolt of 60.

claudian_letters_47.detail: Tacitus (11.13-14) links the reform to Claudius's antiquarian learning. The letters appear on public inscriptions of his reign (the inverted digamma most often, as in AMPLIAVIT written with it) and were abandoned after his death, which makes them a precise dating criterion for epigraphers. Claudius had published a book on the subject before becoming emperor.

lyon_tablet_speech.detail: The original (CIL XIII 1668 = ILS 212) is digressive and antiquarian, recalling the Etruscan origins of king Servius Tullius (whom he identifies with Mastarna) and including a self-address ('it is time, Tiberius Caesar Germanicus, to reveal to the conscript fathers where your speech is going'). Tacitus (Ann. 11.24) turns it into a concise argument that Rome's strength lay in absorbing conquered peoples. The comparison is the classic test case for Tacitus's handling of documents. The census of 48 counted 5,984,072 citizens, nearly a million more than in AD 14, reflecting Claudius's liberal grants of citizenship.
scholarship: Griffin, 'The Lyons Tablet and Tacitean Hindsight', CQ 32 (1982)

fall_of_messalina.detail: Tacitus admits the story seems incredible but insists it is attested by older writers. Modern interpretations see a coup attempt aimed at replacing Claudius with Silius as guardian of Britannicus, rather than mere recklessness. Claudius, at dinner, asked why the empress had not come. The Senate ordered her name and images removed. Her fall opened the way for Agrippina.

claudius_marries_agrippina.detail: Agrippina became the most powerful woman of the Julio-Claudian age: she received the title Augusta in 50, sat on a tribunal to receive embassies, and had Seneca recalled from exile in Corsica (49) to tutor her son. The decree on uncle-niece marriage was so unusual that Tacitus says only one knight and one freedman followed the imperial example; it was repealed in 342.

expulsion_of_jews_from_rome_49.detail: Orosius dates the expulsion to 49, citing Josephus, though no such passage exists in Josephus's surviving works. Dio (60.6.6) says that in 41 Claudius did not expel the Jews but forbade them to assemble, leading some to place the measure in 41. Whether Chrestus was Christ, or a local agitator, remains debated. It is possibly the earliest pagan reference to Christianity.
expulsion_of_jews_from_rome_49.debate: Date (41 vs 49), extent, and identity of Chrestus.

colonia_camulodunum_founded.detail: Tacitus calls the temple 'a citadel of eternal domination' in British eyes, its priests 'pouring out whole fortunes under the pretext of religion'. The veterans' seizure of Trinovantian land was a main cause of the Boudican revolt. The podium of the temple survives beneath the Norman castle of Colchester.

council_of_jerusalem.detail: Paul's own account (Galatians 2.1-10) says only that he was asked to remember the poor, the origin of his later collection for Jerusalem. Acts 15 adds the "apostolic decree" requiring Gentiles to abstain from idol meat, blood, strangled animals and sexual immorality, which Paul never mentions. The subsequent "incident at Antioch", where Peter withdrew from table fellowship with Gentiles and Paul opposed him to his face, shows the question was not settled.
council_of_jerusalem.debate: Relationship between Galatians 2 and Acts 15 (and Acts 11.30) is disputed.

mithridates_bosporan_war_49.detail: Aulus Didius Gallus had installed Cotys c. 45-46. Tacitus describes the siege of Uspe with its wattle and earth walls and the slaughter that terrified the region. Mithridates was brought to Rome, where he addressed Claudius boldly ("I was not sent back, I came back"), and lived in Rome until Galba executed him in 68.

adoption_of_nero.detail: Nero assumed the toga virilis early, in 51, was designated consul for his twentieth year, received proconsular imperium outside Rome and the title princeps iuventutis, and married Claudius's daughter Octavia in 53. Agrippina gradually removed Britannicus's supporters, including his tutors and the praetorian prefects, replaced by her ally Afranius Burrus as sole prefect (51).

pauls_mission_to_macedonia_and_greece.detail: At Corinth Paul worked as a tentmaker with Aquila and Prisca, Jews recently expelled from Rome by Claudius. Acts 18.12-17 has the Jews bring him before the proconsul Gallio, whose term the Delphi inscription dates to 51/52, the fixed point of Pauline chronology. Gallio dismissed the charge as a dispute over words and names in Jewish law. The letters to the Corinthians, written from Ephesus soon after, reveal a fractious community divided over leaders, sex, food offered to idols and spiritual gifts.

battle_of_caer_caradoc.detail: Brought to Rome, Caratacus addressed Claudius and Agrippina so nobly (in Tacitus's version) that they pardoned him and his family; Dio has him remark, on seeing the city, 'Why do you, who have all this, covet our poor tents?' Tacitus compares his capture to those of Syphax and Perseus. The Silures fought on, defeating a legion under Manlius Valens, and Ostorius died worn out in 52.

radamistus_seizes_armenia_51.detail: Tacitus treats the episode as a scandal of Roman inaction. Vologases I exploited it to install his brother Tiridates in Armenia (52-54), opening the war Corbulo fought under Nero. Radamistus's pregnant wife Zenobia, abandoned in the Araxes during his flight, was rescued by shepherds and treated as royalty by Tiridates.

famine_of_51.detail: Suetonius (Claudius 18-19) lists the privileges: insurance against storm losses at state expense, exemption from the Papian-Poppaean marriage penalties for citizens, Latin rights to Latins and the ius trium liberorum to women who built ships of 10,000 modii capacity and carried grain to Rome for six years. The measures, together with the new harbour at Portus, show the state working through private shippers (navicularii).

caratacus_pardoned_in_rome.detail: Tacitus gives him a speech arguing that his resistance made Claudius's victory glorious and that mercy would be an eternal witness to his clemency. Dio adds that, seeing Rome, he asked why those who had such possessions coveted British huts. Tacitus notes the novelty of a woman presiding over Roman standards.

aqua_claudia_and_anio_novus_52.detail: Frontinus gives their deliveries as 4,607 and 4,738 quinariae, the two largest in the system, and the cost as 350 million sesterces. Their monumental double crossing of the Via Labicana and Praenestina is the Porta Maggiore, with inscriptions recording restorations by Vespasian (71) and Titus (81). Nero built a branch (Arcus Neroniani) to the Caelian to supply the Domus Aurea.

first_military_diplomas_52.detail: Diplomas were pairs of bronze tablets bound together, certified copies of a constitution posted in Rome (on the Capitol, later behind the temple of Divus Augustus). Over a thousand survive; their lists of units, governors and dates are a basic source for the provincial garrisons and fasti. Grants of citizenship to the children ended under Antoninus Pius c. 140, and diplomas faded out in the third century after the Constitutio Antoniniana.

gallio_inscription.detail: Gallio's proconsulship is usually placed in 51/52, putting Paul's eighteen-month stay in Corinth about 50-52. The letter itself concerns the depopulation of Delphi and invites new citizens to settle there. Gallio later fell victim to Nero after the Pisonian conspiracy.

fucine_lake_drainage.detail: The first opening failed because the channel was too shallow; at the second, the rush of water nearly swept away the banqueting stand, and Agrippina blamed Narcissus for profiteering. The tunnel silted up after Claudius's death; Trajan and Hadrian repaired it, and the lake was finally drained by Prince Alessandro Torlonia in 1875-78.

sc_claudianum_52.detail: Pallas was rewarded with the praetorian insignia and 15 million sesterces, which he refused, and the Senate inscribed its thanks on a bronze tablet beside the statue of Julius Caesar, an honour Pliny the Younger later found outrageous. The decree, aimed at protecting masters' property in slaves' offspring, remained law until Justinian repealed it.

silures_defeat_legion_52.detail: Ostorius had declared that the Silures' name must be blotted out like the Sugambri, which Tacitus says only made them fight harder. The Silures were finally subdued by Frontinus (74-77), who built the legionary fortress of Isca (Caerleon) in their territory.

honours_for_pallas_52.detail: Pallas, a freedman of Antonia Minor who allegedly carried her warning about Sejanus to Tiberius, backed Agrippina's marriage to Claudius and Nero's adoption. His brother Felix became procurator of Judaea. Nero dismissed him in 55 and had him killed in 62 for his wealth. Pliny the Younger, finding the inscription on his tomb on the Via Tiburtina, wrote two indignant letters about it.

edict_on_abandoned_slaves.detail: Suetonius and the jurist Modestinus record the measure. The Tiber island sanctuary of Aesculapius, founded in 291 BC, remained a place of healing; the hospital of San Giovanni Calibita stands there today. The edict is one of several early imperial interventions limiting masters' powers that culminated under Hadrian and Antoninus Pius.
edict_on_abandoned_slaves.debate: Exact date unknown within Claudius's reign.

pauls_ephesian_ministry.detail: The town clerk (grammateus) dispersed the crowd by warning of Roman action against an unlawful assembly, a detail consistent with Ephesian civic institutions known from inscriptions. Paul's letters mention "fighting with beasts at Ephesus" and an affliction in Asia so severe that he despaired of life, possibly imprisonment. The great theatre where the riot took place seated about 24,000.

apocolocyntosis.detail: The work mocks Claudius's limp, stammer, Gallic birth, passion for jurisdiction and execution of 35 senators and 221 knights. Dio mentions the title; the manuscripts call it Divi Claudii Apotheosis or Ludus de morte Claudii. It shows how quickly the new regime distanced itself from its predecessor even while maintaining his cult, which Nero soon neglected.

death_of_claudius.detail: Claudius died in the early hours of 13 October 54, aged 63, almost certainly poisoned on the orders of his wife Agrippina so that her son Nero, adopted in 50, would succeed before Claudius's own son Britannicus, then nearly fourteen, came of age. The ancient sources agree on poison but differ on details. Tacitus says the poisoner Locusta prepared the dose, the eunuch taster Halotus served it in a dish of mushrooms, Claudius's favourite food, and when he seemed to vomit it, the doctor Xenophon put a feather dipped in quick poison down his throat. Suetonius gives variants, including poisoning at a banquet of priests on the Capitol, and Dio adds Nero's later quip that mushrooms were "the food of the gods" since Claudius became a god by eating them. Josephus mentions the rumour more cautiously. Claudius's other protector, Narcissus, was conveniently away taking a cure in Campania. Agrippina concealed the death until the astrologically favourable hour; at noon the palace doors opened and Burrus presented the sixteen-year-old Nero to the praetorians, who hailed him after he promised a donative, and the Senate followed. Britannicus was kept in the palace. Claudius was deified, Nero delivering a laudation written by Seneca, which, Tacitus says, provoked laughter when it praised the dead emperor's foresight and wisdom. Seneca at the same time wrote the satirical Apocolocyntosis. Modern scholars have sometimes suggested natural causes, since Claudius was elderly and ill, but most accept murder; the timing, after Claudius showed signs of favouring Britannicus and was reported to have said that it was his fate to endure his wives' crimes and then punish them, points to a motive. Agrippina's temple to Divus Claudius on the Caelian was demolished by Nero, though Vespasian later completed it. Claudius's reign, despite the hostility of the senatorial tradition, saw major achievements: the conquest of Britain, the annexation of Mauretania, Thrace, Lycia and Judaea, the harbour at Portus, the Aqua Claudia, the extension of citizenship and the admission of Gallic senators.
death_of_claudius.debate: Murder by Agrippina (all main sources) or natural death of an elderly, ailing man.

accession_of_nero.detail: Nero, born Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus at Antium in December 37, son of Agrippina the Younger and Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus, was adopted by Claudius in 50 as Tiberius Claudius Nero Caesar, given the toga virilis early in 51 with the title princeps iuventutis, and married to Claudius's daughter Octavia in 53. On 13 October 54, when Claudius died, the praetorian prefect Burrus, Agrippina's appointee, presented him to the guard, which hailed him emperor after he promised a donative of 15,000 sesterces each, matching Claudius's; the Senate conferred his powers the same day. Aged sixteen, he was the youngest emperor yet. His accession speech to the Senate, written by Seneca, promised a return to Augustan principles: he would not judge all cases himself, his household would be kept separate from the state, and the Senate would retain its ancient functions. The first years, later called the quinquennium Neronis, were remembered as a period of good government directed by Seneca and Burrus; Trajan reportedly said that no emperor equalled Nero's first five years, though the phrase may refer to his building works. In practice power was disputed between Agrippina and the two advisers. Coins of 54 show Nero and Agrippina face to face, with her name in the place of honour, and she listened to Senate meetings behind a curtain; when she tried to join Nero on the tribunal to receive an Armenian embassy, Seneca directed him to step down to meet her. Her influence declined from 55, when Nero fell in love with the freedwoman Acte, removed Pallas, and poisoned Britannicus at a family dinner after Agrippina threatened to support his claim. The early Neronian period also saw the appointment of Corbulo to the eastern command, Seneca's De Clementia, and measures to restrict expenditure on games by governors. Modern historians (Griffin, Champlin) stress that the young emperor's dependence on advisers masked tensions that erupted after the murder of Agrippina in 59.
accession_of_nero.debate: Whether the 'quinquennium' refers to the first five years of the reign or to a later period, and whether Trajan's remark concerned building rather than government.

death_of_britannicus.detail: The poison was again supplied by Locusta. Agrippina, who had threatened to champion Britannicus against her son, and Octavia, Britannicus's sister, had to conceal their horror. Tacitus says Nero had earlier made the boy sing at a Saturnalia party, and he sang of his lost inheritance.

seneca_de_clementia.detail: The treatise opens with Nero imagined saying "I alone of mortals have been chosen to act as gods on earth", and holds up Augustus's pardon of Cinna. It is the first theoretical statement of the Principate as monarchy in Latin. Written soon after the murder of Britannicus, it has been read either as sincere programme or as an attempt to bind Nero to his own early promises in his accession speech.

arrest_of_paul_in_jerusalem_57.detail: Two Greek inscriptions found in Jerusalem warn foreigners not to pass the balustrade around the inner courts on pain of death, the charge against Paul. When Porcius Festus succeeded Felix (c. 59/60) and proposed trial in Jerusalem, Paul as a Roman citizen appealed to Caesar; Festus consulted Agrippa II and Berenice before sending him to Rome. The letter to the Romans, written from Corinth just before this journey, is Paul's most systematic theological statement.

capture_of_artaxata_58.detail: Tacitus records that a sudden brilliant light falling on the city was taken as a sign that the gods wished it destroyed. Nero was hailed imperator and the Senate voted extravagant honours. Corbulo then marched to Tigranocerta (59), which surrendered. Artaxata was later rebuilt by Tiridates as Neroneia.

nero_proposes_abolition_of_portoria_58.detail: Tacitus lists the reforms: claims older than a year lapsed, praetors and governors were to hear cases against publicani out of turn, soldiers kept their exemptions, and the 2.5% customs dues (quadragesima) and other duties stayed. The surviving customs law of Asia (Monumentum Ephesenum), revised in 62, reflects the same concern for published rules.

murder_of_agrippina.detail: In March 59, during the festival of Minerva (Quinquatria) at Baiae, Nero had his mother Agrippina murdered after the failure of an elaborate plot to make her death look like an accident. The freedman Anicetus, commander of the fleet at Misenum, devised a collapsible boat; after a dinner of reconciliation Agrippina embarked for her villa at Bauli, and the canopy loaded with lead fell, killing her companion Crepereius Gallus, while the boat failed to sink properly. Her maid Acerronia, who cried out that she was Agrippina hoping to be rescued, was clubbed to death by the rowers, while Agrippina, injured in the shoulder, swam to safety and was taken to her villa. She sent the freedman Agermus to tell Nero she had survived. Nero, panicking, consulted Seneca and Burrus; Burrus said the praetorians would not kill a daughter of Germanicus, and Anicetus volunteered. Agermus was accused of carrying a dagger to kill Nero, providing a pretext, and Anicetus with naval officers broke into Agrippina's villa. Tacitus reports her last words to the centurion as she offered her womb: "Strike here" (ventrem feri), where she had borne Nero. Nero sent the Senate a letter, drafted by Seneca, claiming she had plotted against him and killed herself on discovery, listing her past crimes. The Senate voted thanksgivings, and only Thrasea Paetus walked out. Agrippina was cremated on a dining couch and given a modest tomb. The sources differ on Nero's motives: his affair with Poppaea Sabina, whom Agrippina opposed, his resentment of her domination, and rumours of incest. Tacitus's account, the most dramatic, is regarded as substantially accurate in outline, though the collapsing boat has been questioned. The murder marks a turning point in Nero's reign: freed from his mother, he gave rein to his artistic ambitions (the Juvenalia of 59 and the Neronia of 60), and his reliance on Seneca and Burrus declined until Burrus died in 62. Suetonius says Nero was haunted by her ghost and the Furies and tried to summon her spirit through magi.

pompeii_amphitheatre_riot.detail: A fresco from a house in Pompeii (I.3.23), now in Naples, shows the fighting in and around the amphitheatre, with the awning (velarium) and stalls outside, one of the very few contemporary images of a historical event from a provincial town. Graffiti mocking Nucerians have also been found.

corbulo_takes_tigranocerta_59.detail: Tacitus describes the army living on meat and short of water, and the arrival at Tigranocerta of a Parthian noble's head catapulted into the camp of the defenders of Legerda. Tigranes, great-grandson of Herod and Archelaus of Cappadocia, proved reckless: his raid into Adiabene in 61 provoked Vologases to besiege him and reopen the war.

battle_of_mona.detail: The sacred groves, where Tacitus says altars were drenched with captives' blood, were cut down. As a garrison was being installed, news arrived of Boudica's revolt. Agricola, then a young tribune on Paullinus's staff, retook the island in 77/78.

sack_of_camulodunum.detail: Legio IX Hispana under Petillius Cerialis, marching to the rescue, lost its infantry; Cerialis escaped with the cavalry. The procurator Catus Decianus fled to Gaul. A thick burnt layer of 60/61 runs through Colchester, and a bronze head of Claudius found in the River Alde in Suffolk may be loot from the colony. Omens included the fall of the statue of Victory with its back turned 'as though fleeing the enemy'.

sack_of_londinium.detail: A red burnt horizon of the period is found across the early City of London. Dio describes atrocities against noblewomen in a grove of the goddess Andraste. The procurator who replaced Catus, Julius Classicianus, whose tombstone survives in the British Museum, later reported that reprisals were prolonging the war.

battle_of_watling_street.detail: In 60 or 61 the Iceni and Trinovantes under Boudica, having destroyed Camulodunum, Londinium and Verulamium and killed, according to Tacitus, some 70,000 Romans and allies (Dio says 80,000), faced the governor Gaius Suetonius Paullinus in a final battle somewhere in the Midlands. Paullinus had hurried back from his attack on Mona (Anglesey) with the XIV Gemina and detachments of XX Valeria and auxiliaries, around 10,000 men; II Augusta in the south-west failed to join him because its camp prefect Poenius Postumus refused to march, and he later fell on his sword. IX Hispana had already been mauled under Petillius Cerialis. Paullinus chose a narrow defile with a forest behind him and open plain in front, so that his flanks were protected and the Britons, numbering 230,000 in Dio's inflated figure, could attack only on a narrow front. The Britons brought their families in wagons at the rear to watch the victory. Tacitus gives Boudica a speech claiming to fight as a woman of the people avenging her lost liberty, her scourged body and the violation of her daughters, and Paullinus a brief order to keep the ranks, throw javelins, then advance with shields and swords. The legionaries threw their pila, then charged in wedge formation, followed by the auxiliaries and cavalry; the British host was driven back against its own wagons and slaughtered, women and animals included. Tacitus claims 80,000 Britons died against some 400 Romans killed. Boudica took poison (Tacitus) or fell ill and died (Dio). The site is unknown: candidates include Mancetter (Manduessedum) on Watling Street in Warwickshire, High Cross, Church Stowe and sites near Towcester, and the name "Battle of Watling Street" is modern. The victory was followed by a punitive campaign that devastated the territories of the rebels until the procurator Classicianus and Nero's freedman Polyclitus secured a more conciliatory policy. The revolt and its suppression nearly led Nero to consider abandoning Britain (Suetonius, Nero 18).
battle_of_watling_street.debate: Location (Mancetter, High Cross, Towcester area) and the reliability of the casualty figures.

neronia_60.detail: The Juvenalia of 59, held privately in his gardens to celebrate the first shaving of his beard, had already brought senators and noblewomen onto the stage. Nero was given the prize for Latin oratory and verse at the first Neronia without competing, and the prize for lyre by acclamation. Tacitus records traditionalist outrage at the Greek nudity of the gymnasium. The games lapsed after his death but prepared the way for Domitian's Capitoline Games.

comet_of_60.detail: Tacitus mentions the comet with lightning that struck Nero's table at Sublaqueum. Seneca's Natural Questions (7.17, 7.21) discusses a comet visible "in the principate of Nero, which has rescued comets from disrepute". Another comet in 64 and Halley's comet in 66 were followed by more executions, according to Suetonius, who says the astrologer Balbillus advised Nero to divert the omen onto noble victims.

laodicea_earthquake_60.detail: Tacitus contrasts Laodicea's self-sufficiency with the subsidies given to the Asian cities in 17. The city was a rich banking and textile centre; Revelation 3.17 has the church of Laodicea boasting "I am rich and need nothing". Colossae and Hierapolis nearby were probably also damaged.

periplus_maris_erythraei.detail: The author lists exports (pepper, malabathrum, pearls, ivory, silk, cotton, incense) and imports demanded in India (wine, coral, glass, Roman coin). He credits Hippalus with discovering the direct monsoon crossing. Allusions to the Nabataean king Malichus II (40-70) and the Kushana and Satavahana rulers give the date. Pliny says India drained 50 million sesterces a year from the empire. Excavations at Berenike, Myos Hormos and Arikamedu confirm the trade.

paul_shipwrecked_on_malta.detail: The "we" narrative of Acts 27 is one of the most detailed accounts of an ancient voyage, with its sounding of depths, the anchoring by the stern and the 276 people aboard; James Smith's classic study (1848) showed its nautical plausibility. Acts says nothing of Paul's trial or death, a silence variously explained. The Pastoral letters and 1 Clement 5 ("he reached the limits of the west") gave rise to the tradition of release and a mission to Spain.

murder_of_pedanius_secundus.detail: Tacitus gives the jurist Gaius Cassius Longinus a speech insisting that only fear could control households 'containing nations of slaves with foreign rites or none'. Soldiers lined the route to prevent the crowd rescuing the condemned. A proposal to deport Pedanius's freedmen too was vetoed by Nero. The episode is a key text for Roman slavery and its legal violence.

polyclitus_mission_to_britain_61.detail: Tacitus enjoys the Britons' astonishment that a general who had won such a war obeyed slaves. Classicianus died in office; his tombstone, set up by his wife Julia Pacata, daughter of the Treveran Indus, was found in London in 1852 and 1935 and is in the British Museum. The episode marks the end of the conquest phase and a shift to consolidation.

tigranocerta_besieged_61.detail: Corbulo advised Nero to appoint a separate commander for Armenia; Caesennius Paetus arrived in 62 boasting he would impose provincial taxes, and soon capitulated at Rhandeia. Tacitus suspects that Corbulo preferred a truce that preserved his own reputation.

campanian_earthquake_62.detail: A marble relief from the lararium of the banker Lucius Caecilius Iucundus at Pompeii shows the temple of Jupiter and the Vesuvius gate tilting in the quake. Seneca's Natural Questions (book 6) was prompted by it and dates it to 63; Tacitus places it in 62.

hero_of_alexandria_eclipse_62.detail: Otto Neugebauer's identification of the eclipse settled a dating controversy that had ranged from the third century BC to the third century AD. Hero's surviving works (Pneumatica, Automata, Mechanica, Metrica, Belopoeica, Dioptra) describe self-moving theatres, a programmable cart driven by a falling weight and string, a fire engine pump and surveying instruments, illustrating the sophistication and the limits of ancient mechanics.
hero_of_alexandria_eclipse_62.debate: Some still question the identification of the eclipse.

nile_expedition_of_nero.detail: Seneca heard the report from the centurions themselves; Pliny the Elder gives their measured distances from Syene to Meroë (871 miles) and observations on the decline of Meroë. The mission may have been reconnaissance for a planned Ethiopian war. It was the furthest documented Roman penetration into sub-Saharan Africa along the Nile.

plautius_silvanus_transdanubians.detail: These achievements are known only from his funerary elogium near Tibur (ILS 986), which also records that Vespasian granted him the triumphal ornaments that Nero had withheld. It is the earliest documented case of mass settlement of barbarians inside the empire, a practice that became routine under Marcus Aurelius and later emperors.

turning_point_of_62.detail: Burrus was replaced by Ofonius Tigellinus and Faenius Rufus. The same year the treason law was revived for the praetor Antistius Sosianus, who had recited satirical verses about Nero (Thrasea Paetus secured a lesser penalty), and the exiled Rubellius Plautus and Faustus Cornelius Sulla were murdered. Octavia's head was brought to Poppaea. The pseudo-Senecan tragedy Octavia dramatises her fate. Tacitus marks 62 as the decisive turn of the reign.

battle_of_rhandeia.detail: Rumour said the legions IV Scythica and XII Fulminata passed under the yoke. Paetus had earlier sent Nero dispatches announcing victory. Nero pardoned him with a joke that a man so prone to panic might fall ill from prolonged suspense. In Rome trophies for victory were already standing on the Capitol. The defeat led to the Rhandeia compromise of 63, negotiated on the same spot by Corbulo.

lex_portorii_asiae_62.detail: The text sets out the 2.5% duty (quadragesima) on goods entering or leaving the province, the list of customs stations, exemptions (for state property, soldiers' goods, items for religious use), the procedures for declaration and the rights of the publicani, with additions dated by consuls over 140 years. It is the most detailed document on Roman indirect taxation and illustrates the publication of tax rules Nero ordered in 58.

stoning_of_james_the_just_62.detail: Josephus's brief notice, generally accepted as authentic, says the fair-minded citizens strict in the law protested to Agrippa and to Albinus. James had led the Jerusalem church for nearly twenty years and was revered as "the Just" for his Torah piety; Hegesippus (in Eusebius) gives a legendary account of his being thrown from the Temple pinnacle. His death removed the main bridge between the Jesus movement and Jerusalem's Jewish establishment.

settlement_of_rhandeia_63.detail: The compromise accepted an Arsacid king of Armenia as a Roman client, an arrangement that kept peace between Rome and Parthia for half a century until Trajan broke it in 114. Corbulo gave Tiridates his son-in-law Annius Vinicianus as escort. Tiridates left his daughter as hostage and made his famous three-year journey to Rome, avoiding the sea for religious reasons, for the coronation of 66. Nero closed the temple of Janus.

annexation_of_the_cottian_alps_63.detail: The dynasty of Donnus and Cottius had ruled as Roman prefects and kings since Augustus; Cottius I's arch at Segusio (9-8 BC) lists the fourteen communities under his rule. Claudius had enlarged the kingdom and restored the royal title in 44. The Maritime Alps had already received Latin rights from Nero.

seneca_letters_to_lucilius.detail: The letters move from daily incidents (a trip in a tunnel at Naples, the noise above a bath-house, the treatment of slaves as "humble friends" in Letter 47) to ethical instruction. Letter 91 describes the fire that destroyed Lugdunum, and Letter 56 the din of a Baiae bath. The Natural Questions discuss the Campanian earthquake of 62, comets and the Nile. Seneca's apparent hypocrisy as a millionaire moralist, attacked by Suillius Rufus in 58, has shaped his reputation ever since.

great_fire_of_rome.detail: The Great Fire broke out on the night of 18-19 July 64 in shops around the Circus Maximus at the end facing the Palatine and Caelian, where flammable goods were stored, and spread with the wind through the valley and up the hills. It raged for six days, was checked at the foot of the Esquiline by demolishing buildings, then flared again from the estates of Tigellinus in the Aemilian quarter for three more days. Tacitus says that of the fourteen regions only four were untouched, three were razed to the ground and seven left with a few ruined buildings. Destroyed were the ancient temples of Jupiter Stator, Vesta with the penates, the shrine of Servius Tullius to Luna and the house of the Vestals, the Regia, Nero's own Domus Transitoria on the Palatine and countless works of art and libraries. Nero was at Antium and returned to organise relief: he opened the Campus Martius, the buildings of Agrippa and his own gardens to the homeless, built emergency shelters, brought furniture from Ostia and cut the price of grain to three sesterces a modius. Rumour nonetheless spread that he had sung of the fall of Troy on his private stage while the city burned (Tacitus reports it as hearsay; Suetonius and Dio say he did so from the tower of Maecenas or the palace roof) and that his agents had spread the flames to clear land for a new palace. Tacitus says some sources blamed accident and others the emperor. To deflect suspicion Nero blamed the Christians. The rebuilding introduced the first building code: streets were to be broad and straight, buildings limited in height, partly of fireproof Gabine or Alban stone, with porticoes paid for by the emperor, open courtyards and water supply for fire-fighting. Nero used the cleared land in the centre for the Domus Aurea, which provoked lasting resentment, and imposed levies on Italy and the provinces and despoiled temples for funds. The debasement and weight reduction of the coinage in 64 may also be linked to the costs. Modern estimates of damage vary; archaeologists have found burnt layers of 64 across the Palatine and Forum valley.
great_fire_of_rome.debate: Accident or arson; Nero's responsibility is doubted by most modern historians (he was at Antium, and his own palace burned).
scholarship: Champlin, Nero (2003)
Closs, Fire and Rebirth (2020)

annexation_of_pontus_polemoniacus.detail: Trapezus became the base of the Pontic fleet (classis Pontica), whose control of the eastern Black Sea was important in the Armenian wars. Polemon received compensation in Cilicia. The annexation continued the Julio-Claudian policy of absorbing client kingdoms when convenient.

neronian_persecution.detail: Tacitus provides the only detailed account of the first Roman persecution of Christians, in the aftermath of the Great Fire of 64. "To get rid of the rumour", Nero blamed "those whom the crowd called Chrestians, hated for their crimes". Tacitus explains that the name came from Christus, executed by Pontius Pilate under Tiberius, and that the "pernicious superstition", checked for a while, had broken out again not only in Judaea but in Rome, "where all things horrible and shameful flow together". Those who confessed were arrested first, and on their information "a huge multitude" was convicted, not so much of arson as of "hatred of the human race" (odium humani generis). They were mocked in their deaths: covered in animal skins and torn apart by dogs, crucified, or set alight as torches after dark. Nero offered his gardens on the Vatican for the spectacle and mingled with the crowd dressed as a charioteer, so that pity arose for the victims, "as if they were being destroyed not for the public good but for one man's cruelty". Suetonius mentions the punishment of Christians, "a race given to a new and harmful superstition", among Nero's police measures, without connecting it to the fire. 1 Clement (c. 96) alludes to "a great multitude of the elect" who suffered, including women forced to play roles as Dirce and the Danaids, and Christian tradition placed the deaths of Peter and Paul in this persecution. The episode raises several questions. Some scholars (Shaw, 2015) have argued that the link between the fire and the Christians is a later construction, and that the term "Christians" may be anachronistic for 64; most defend Tacitus. The legal basis is also debated: whether there was a specific Neronian law or edict (an "institutum Neronianum" mentioned by Tertullian) banning Christianity, or whether Christians were punished by magistrates' coercive powers. The persecution was confined to Rome but established a precedent that being a Christian was punishable. Revelation's image of the beast and Babylon drunk with the blood of the saints has been read as a reflection of it.
neronian_persecution.debate: Authenticity of the fire link (Shaw) and the legal basis for the persecution.
scholarship: Shaw, 'The Myth of the Neronian Persecution', JRS 105 (2015)
Jones, 'The historicity of the Neronian persecution', NTS 63 (2017)

domus_aurea.detail: The architects Severus and Celer built vaulted halls including the octagonal room on the Oppian hill, an early masterpiece of concrete architecture; Suetonius describes a main dining room that rotated day and night like the heavens. Its wall paintings, by Famulus, were rediscovered around 1480 by artists who lowered themselves into the buried rooms (the 'grottoes'), inspiring Raphael's grotesques. The Flavians gave the site back to the public: the Colosseum rose over the lake and Trajan's baths over the Oppian wing.

neronian_coinage_reform.detail: The reform may have been prompted by the cost of rebuilding after the fire, by shortages of bullion, or by a desire to align the gold-silver ratio; the reduced standards lasted until Trajan's further debasement. Pliny notes the reduction of the aureus. Neronian sestertii of the period are among the finest Roman coin dies.
scholarship: Butcher and Ponting, The Metallurgy of Roman Silver Coinage (2014)
MacDowall, The Western Coinages of Nero (1979)

lucan_pharsalia.detail: Suetonius's Life of Lucan says Nero walked out of a reading, and that Lucan recited a line of Nero's own in a latrine. Lucan reputedly recited verses on a dying soldier as he bled to death. The poem's hero is Cato, its verdict on the Republic's fall bleak ("victrix causa deis placuit sed victa Catoni"). Statius wrote a birthday poem for his widow Polla Argentaria.

martyrdom_of_peter_and_paul.detail: Around 200 the Roman presbyter Gaius pointed to the "trophies" of the apostles on the Vatican and on the road to Ostia (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 2.25). Excavations under St Peter's (1940-1949) found a small aedicula of c. 160 against the "red wall" in a pagan cemetery near Nero's circus, almost certainly Gaius's trophy; whether bones found nearby are Peter's is unprovable. Paul's execution is placed at Aquae Salviae (Tre Fontane), his tomb under San Paolo fuori le Mura. Dates of 64, 67 and 68 are all found.
martyrdom_of_peter_and_paul.debate: No contemporary evidence for the manner or date; Peter's presence in Rome was once doubted but is now widely accepted.

pisonian_conspiracy.detail: Nineteen were killed and thirteen exiled. The freedwoman Epicharis endured torture without naming anyone and strangled herself with her breast-band. The praetorian prefect Faenius Rufus, himself a conspirator, conducted interrogations until exposed. The tribune Subrius Flavus told Nero he hated him as a matricide, charioteer, actor and arsonist. Seneca was ordered to die and opened his veins in a slow, philosophical death; the poet Lucan recited his own verses as he bled. Petronius and Thrasea Paetus followed in 66 in the aftermath.

fire_of_lugdunum.detail: Tacitus records the gift under 65. The disaster made the city loyal to Nero in 68, when it refused to support Vindex and was besieged by the Viennenses. Seneca's Letter 91, consoling his friend Aebutius Liberalis, a native of the city, is the main description.

plague_of_65.detail: Tacitus lists the houses full of corpses and the streets full of funerals, with knights and senators dying alike. Suetonius gives the 30,000 figure in an autumn. The epidemic, of unknown nature, came in the year of the Pisonian purge, and Tacitus treats it as part of a catalogue of divine anger.

columella_de_re_rustica.detail: Book 10 on gardens is in hexameters, continuing Virgil's Georgics. Columella's model vineyard (3.3) with its cost of land, slaves and vines and expected return, has been central to debates about whether Roman landowners thought in terms of investment and profit. He discusses the vilicus and slave management in detail and describes his uncle's experiments breeding African rams with Spanish ewes.

outbreak_of_the_jewish_revolt.detail: The Jewish revolt broke out in Jerusalem in spring and summer 66 after years of tension under the procurators Albinus and Gessius Florus. At Caesarea, Greeks sacrificed birds at the entrance of a synagogue in a dispute over access, and the Jewish notables who complained to Florus were imprisoned. Florus then took seventeen talents from the Temple treasury "for Caesar's needs"; when Jerusalemites mocked him by passing round a basket for alms, he let his troops loose in the upper city, killing some 3,600 people, including Jews of equestrian rank whom he had scourged and crucified. Agrippa II and Berenice, who stood barefoot before Florus pleading, tried to calm the people; Agrippa's long speech in Josephus (War 2.345-401) lists the peoples Rome had subdued and the legions garrisoning them, a famous survey of imperial power. The crucial step came when Eleazar son of Ananias, captain of the Temple, persuaded the priests to stop the daily sacrifice for the emperor, effectively a declaration of independence. Fighting broke out between the peace party, backed by Agrippa's cavalry, and the rebels, who burned the High Priest's house, the palaces of Agrippa and Berenice and the archives containing debt records. Menahem, son of Judas the Galilean, seized Masada with its armoury, entered Jerusalem as a king and besieged the Roman garrison in Herod's palace; the high priest Ananias was killed, Menahem was then murdered by Eleazar's men, and the Roman cohort surrendered under an oath of safe conduct and was massacred. Violence spread across the region: at Caesarea 20,000 Jews were killed in a single hour according to Josephus, and Jews and Greeks fought in Scythopolis, Ascalon, Ptolemais and Alexandria, where Tiberius Julius Alexander's legions killed 50,000. In the autumn Cestius Gallus, legate of Syria, marched on Jerusalem with legio XII Fulminata and detachments, failed to take the Temple mount and was routed in the pass of Beth Horon, losing 6,000 men and the legion's eagle. That defeat committed Judaea to full-scale war and led Nero to appoint Vespasian.

battle_of_beth_horon_66.detail: Josephus gives Roman losses of 5,300 infantry and 480 cavalry; Suetonius says an eagle was lost. The rebels used the captured artillery in the defence of Jerusalem in 70. The victory convinced many waverers that God was with the revolt and led to the organisation of a rebel government with regional commanders, Josephus among them in Galilee. Nero then appointed Vespasian.

coronation_of_tiridates.detail: The nine-month journey cost the treasury 800,000 sesterces a day. The ceremony, staged at dawn with the Forum packed and the praetorians in arms, was followed by a gilded day at the theatre of Pompey (the 'Golden Day'). Pliny the Elder says Tiridates initiated Nero into magic banquets. The settlement kept peace on the eastern frontier until Trajan.

trial_of_thrasea_paetus_66.detail: The accuser Cossutianus Capito compared Thrasea's followers to the partisans of Cato; Soranus's daughter Servilia was charged with consulting magicians for her father. Thrasea's son-in-law Helvidius Priscus was exiled. The surviving text of the Annals breaks off in the middle of Thrasea's death scene. Thrasea had written a Life of Cato, and his circle became the core of the "Stoic opposition" persecuted again under Vespasian and Domitian.

nero_caspian_expedition_planned.detail: The objective was probably the Darial pass in the central Caucasus, which controlled the route of nomad raids into Armenia and Iberia, perhaps in cooperation with Parthia after the Rhandeia settlement. The Jewish revolt and the Vindex rising in 68 caused the plan to be dropped; detachments assembled for it were caught up in the civil war of 69.

siege_of_jotapata.detail: Josephus says 40,000 died (a figure inflated) and 1,200 were captured. His description of defensive devices (boiling oil, fenugreek poured on boarding planks, sacks to deaden ram blows) is vivid and self-serving. Brought before Vespasian, he predicted that Vespasian and Titus would become emperors; when this was fulfilled in 69 he was freed and took the name Flavius. The 'Josephus problem' in mathematics derives from his survival of the lots.
scholarship: Aviam, 'Yodefat-Jotapata: the archaeology of the first battle', in Berlin and Overman (eds), The First Jewish Revolt (2002)

siege_of_gamla.detail: Excavations since 1976 (Gutman, Syon) have revealed the breach in the wall, some 1,600 iron arrowheads, 2,000 ballista stones, and one of the oldest known synagogues, as well as coins struck by the rebels 'for the redemption of Jerusalem the holy'. Gamla is one of the best-preserved Roman siege sites anywhere.
scholarship: Syon, Gamla III: The Shmarya Gutmann Excavations (2014)

nero_liberates_greece.detail: His speech survives on an inscription from Acraephia in Boeotia (ILS 8794), deliberately echoing Flamininus's proclamation of Greek freedom in 196 BC. At Olympia he fell from a ten-horse chariot but was crowned anyway. The canal was dug by soldiers and 6,000 Jewish prisoners sent by Vespasian, but abandoned after his death; the modern canal (1881-1893) follows its line. Vespasian revoked Greek freedom.

death_of_corbulo.detail: Corbulo's son-in-law Annius Vinicianus had been implicated in a conspiracy at Beneventum in 66. The removal of the most prestigious commanders left the armies without loyalty to Nero, a factor in his fall a year later. Corbulo's daughter Domitia Longina married Domitian.

corinth_canal_begun_67.detail: Earlier schemes by Periander, Demetrius Poliorcetes and Caesar had been dropped. Nero's cuttings, about 2 km in all at both ends, were rediscovered when the modern canal (1881-1893) followed the same line. Egyptian engineers had reportedly warned that the Corinthian Gulf was higher than the Saronic and would flood Aegina. The diolkos tramway remained in use.

revolt_of_vindex.detail: Vindex had no legions but raised large Gallic levies (Plutarch says 100,000). His coins bore no emperor's portrait, with slogans such as SALVS GENERIS HVMANI and SIGNA P(opuli) R(omani). Nero reportedly cared most that Vindex had called him a bad lyre-player. Whether Vindex sought Gallic independence (as later Roman writers implied) or simply the overthrow of Nero is debated; most modern historians favour the latter.

galba_proclaimed.detail: Declared a public enemy by the Senate, he despaired after Vindex's defeat until news came that Nero was dead and he had been recognised. In Africa the legate Clodius Macer also revolted, cutting off grain to Rome and raising a legion (I Macriana), and was later killed on Galba's orders.

battle_of_vesontio.detail: The legions then offered Verginius the throne, which he refused, declaring that the Senate and people should choose. His epitaph, which he composed himself and Pliny quotes, claimed he had 'claimed the empire not for himself but for his country'. The battle showed that the Rhine armies, not Gallic levies, held the balance of power.

death_of_nero.detail: Nero died on 9 or 11 June 68 at the suburban villa of his freedman Phaon between the Via Salaria and the Via Nomentana, about four miles from Rome, the last of the Julio-Claudians. In March Gaius Julius Vindex, governor of Gallia Lugdunensis, had rebelled, and on 2 April Galba, governor of Hispania Tarraconensis, was proclaimed at Carthago Nova. Although Vindex was defeated by Verginius Rufus at Vesontio in May and killed himself, the Rhine legions offered the throne to Verginius, who refused; Clodius Macer rebelled in Africa, cutting the grain supply. Nero's response wavered between plans to march against the rebels with an army of concubines dressed as Amazons and fantasies of winning the troops back by weeping or retiring to Egypt to make a living as a lyre-player. The praetorian prefect Nymphidius Sabinus induced the guard to desert him by promising a donative in Galba's name, and the Senate declared Nero a public enemy (hostis). Abandoned by his guards and friends, Nero fled at night in disguise with four companions, including his freedmen Phaon, Epaphroditus and Sporus, hearing as he passed the praetorian camp the soldiers cheering Galba. At the villa, hiding in a cellar, he learned that the Senate had condemned him to be executed "in the ancestral fashion", stripped and beaten to death with rods. As horsemen approached he stabbed himself in the throat with the help of Epaphroditus, saying, in Suetonius's famous report, "qualis artifex pereo" ("what an artist dies in me"). A centurion who tried to staunch the wound heard his last words, "Too late. This is loyalty." He was buried in the family tomb of the Domitii on the Pincian by his nurses and Acte. Suetonius says that for years flowers were placed on his tomb, and edicts were issued as if he were alive, while false Neros appeared in the East in 69, c. 80 and c. 88. The date is either 9 June (Jerome and others) or 11 June (reckoning from Dio's length of reign). His death ended the dynasty and opened the civil wars of 68-69.

revolt_of_clodius_macer_68.detail: Macer's coins, with legends such as L CLODI MACRI LIBERA(TRIX) and the S C on silver, are among the rarest and most sought-after of the period and show a programme of senatorial "liberation" without claiming the purple. Plutarch says Calvia Crispinilla, Nero's former mistress of the wardrobe, urged him to starve Rome.

vitellius_proclaimed.detail: The Rhine legions resented Galba's failure to reward them for crushing Vindex and his dismissal of Verginius Rufus. Vitellius, a gourmand appointed by Galba as harmless, took the name Germanicus but refused that of Caesar at first. Two columns under Valens and Caecina marched on Italy while Vitellius followed with reserves.

murder_of_galba.detail: Galba had alienated the praetorians by refusing the donative promised in his name, declaring that he 'chose his soldiers, he did not buy them'. Tacitus's epitaph is famous: 'by universal consent capable of ruling, had he not ruled' (capax imperii nisi imperasset). Galba's adoption speech in Tacitus (Hist. 1.15-16), presenting adoption of the best man as a substitute for liberty, anticipates the ideology of the adoptive emperors under whom Tacitus wrote.

first_battle_of_bedriacum.detail: Otho remained at Brixellum with part of his forces, a decision Tacitus blames. The Danubian legions marching to Otho's aid had not arrived. The battle was fought among vines and ditches; legio I Adiutrix (Otho's marines) captured the eagle of XXI Rapax but was then routed. Many Othonian survivors were sent back to their Danube bases, where they soon declared for Vespasian.

death_of_otho.detail: Ancient writers who despised his life as Nero's companion admired his death: Martial (6.32) says Cato's death was less glorious than Otho's. Tacitus records that he had reigned 95 days. The episode became a classic exemplum of a noble end.

vespasian_proclaimed.detail: Titus Flavius Vespasianus, commander against the Jews since 67, was proclaimed emperor at Alexandria on 1 July 69 by the two legions of Egypt at the instance of the prefect Tiberius Julius Alexander, an apostate Jew; his own army in Judaea swore allegiance on 3 July, and the Syrian legions under Gaius Licinius Mucianus by mid-July. 1 July was later counted as his dies imperii. The move had been carefully prepared: after the death of Otho in April and Vitellius's victory, Vespasian, Mucianus and Titus, who had negotiated a reconciliation between the two generals, held meetings at Berytus and on Mount Carmel, where the priest Basilides gave a favourable oracle. Josephus, then a prisoner, claimed to have predicted Vespasian's rise at Jotapata in 67, and Tacitus and Suetonius record a widespread eastern prophecy that rulers would come from Judaea, which Jews applied to a messiah and the Romans to Vespasian. The plan was that Mucianus would march on Italy with a strong force while Vespasian held Egypt and its grain supply, threatening Rome with starvation. In practice the decisive action came from the Danube legions, who declared for Vespasian in August and under Marcus Antonius Primus invaded Italy without waiting for Mucianus, winning the second battle of Bedriacum in October and taking Rome in December. Vespasian's age (sixty), modest Sabine origins, military reputation and two adult sons, Titus and Domitian, made him an acceptable candidate offering dynastic stability after a year of chaos. The coalition behind him, the eastern legions, the Danube armies and client kings such as Agrippa II, Sohaemus of Emesa, Antiochus IV of Commagene and Vologases of Parthia, who offered 40,000 archers, gave him a strong base. Tacitus remarks that the secret of empire was out: an emperor could be made elsewhere than at Rome. Vespasian's stay at Alexandria, where he performed healing miracles, supplied the charisma his origins lacked.

second_battle_of_bedriacum.detail: Tacitus tells of a son who killed his father in the battle and recognised him while stripping the body. Some 40,000 soldiers and camp followers poured into Cremona, which was burned to the ground except for a temple of Mefitis; Dio gives 50,000 dead in the battle and sack. Augustus's colony took years to rebuild. The battle opened Italy to the Flavians.

burning_of_the_capitol_69.detail: Tacitus calls it the most lamentable and shameful crime in Rome's history: the temple founded under the kings, which neither Porsenna nor the Gauls had violated, destroyed by the madness of emperors. Domitian escaped disguised as an Isiac worshipper. Druids in Gaul, Tacitus says, saw in the burning a sign that world rule was passing to the peoples beyond the Alps. Vespasian began rebuilding in 70, personally carrying the first basket of rubble.

death_of_vitellius.detail: Tacitus describes the city as simultaneously given over to slaughter and to the Saturnalia. The praetorian camp fell after desperate resistance. Mucianus arrived soon after and took control, sidelining Primus; Domitian, as Caesar, represented the family until Vespasian reached Rome in October 70.

siege_of_vetera.detail: Civilis had siege towers built by Roman deserters and prisoners; the defenders burned them with fire-darts and grapnels. A relief by Dillius Vocula briefly broke the siege in late 69. Lupercus was sent as a gift to the seeress Veleda but was killed on the way. Tacitus highlights the shame of legions surrendering to auxiliaries trained in Roman ways.

first_false_nero_69.detail: Two further pretenders appeared: one under Titus (c. 80, Terentius Maximus, who found support in Parthia) and one c. 88, whom the Parthians nearly refused to surrender. The belief that Nero had not died or would return from the East (Nero redivivus) also shaped Jewish and Christian apocalyptic literature, including the Sibylline Oracles and possibly Revelation 13 and 17.

revolt_of_mariccus_69.detail: Tacitus treats the movement as a symptom of the disorder of 69, comparable to the Druidic prophecies that the burning of the Capitol foretold the transfer of empire to the Transalpine peoples. It foreshadows the Gallic risings around Civilis and Classicus in 70.

venutius_overthrows_cartimandua_69.detail: Cartimandua had ruled northern England as a Roman client since the 40s and had surrendered Caratacus. Roman troops had already intervened in the couple's quarrels under Didius Gallus (c. 57). The loss of the client kingdom forced conquest: Petillius Cerialis campaigned against the Brigantes from 71, and the great hillfort at Stanwick may have been Venutius's base.

siege_of_jerusalem_70.detail: Titus, left in command when his father went to Alexandria, began the siege of Jerusalem in April 70, shortly before Passover, with four legions (V Macedonica, X Fretensis, XII Fulminata and XV Apollinaris), detachments from Egypt and Syria and allied contingents, perhaps 60,000-70,000 men. The city was defended by three walls on the north and by rival rebel factions: John of Gischala held the Temple, Simon bar Giora the upper and lower city, and the Zealots under Eleazar ben Simon had been absorbed by John during Passover. Their internal war had destroyed food stores, and pilgrims swelled the population. Titus nearly lost his life on reconnaissance. The third wall (of Agrippa I) fell in May, the second wall after fierce fighting, and in June the Romans built a circumvallation wall of 39 stades in three days to starve the city. Josephus, who served as Titus's interpreter and pleaded with the defenders from outside the walls, describes the famine in harrowing detail, including the story of Mary of Bethezuba who ate her child; deserters who swallowed gold coins were cut open by Arab and Syrian auxiliaries. In July the Antonia fortress was taken and the daily sacrifice ceased. On the 10th of the month of Lous (Av), in late August, the Temple was set on fire. Josephus insists Titus wanted to spare it and a soldier threw a firebrand against orders, while Sulpicius Severus, probably drawing on Tacitus, says Titus decided to destroy it to eradicate the Jewish and Christian religions; modern scholars generally favour the latter. Soldiers sacrificed to their standards in the Temple court and hailed Titus imperator. The upper city fell in September. Josephus gives 1.1 million dead and 97,000 captives, figures widely regarded as exaggerated. John surrendered and was imprisoned for life; Simon was captured and executed in the triumph of 71. The city was razed except for three towers of Herod's palace and part of the western wall, and X Fretensis encamped on the ruins. The Temple treasures, including the menorah, were carried in the triumph and housed in the Temple of Peace.
siege_of_jerusalem_70.debate: Whether Titus ordered the burning of the Temple (Sulpicius Severus) or tried to save it (Josephus).
scholarship: Goodman, Rome and Jerusalem (2007)
Rajak, Josephus: The Historian and His Society (2nd ed. 2002)

lex_de_imperio_vespasiani.detail: The Lex de imperio Vespasiani is a bronze tablet, found in the Lateran in the fourteenth century and displayed by Cola di Rienzo in 1347 as proof of the sovereign rights of the Roman people, now in the Capitoline Museums. It preserves the final part of the law, or senatus consultum ratified by the people, conferring powers on Vespasian at the end of 69 or start of 70. Eight surviving clauses grant him: the right to make treaties with whomever he wished; to convene the Senate, propose and withdraw motions and pass decrees by relatio or written communication; to have candidates he recommended for office considered extra ordinem; to extend the pomerium; to do whatever he judged to be in the interests of the state, divine and human, public and private, "as was permitted to the deified Augustus, Tiberius and Claudius"; and exemption from laws from which earlier emperors had been released. A sanction clause frees from penalty anyone acting under it, and a retroactive clause validates everything Vespasian had done before the law was passed, from his proclamation on 1 July. The law is the clearest legal statement of imperial powers and has been central to debates about the constitutional nature of the Principate. Some scholars (Brunt) treat it as typical of the comprehensive grants given to every new emperor (Tacitus, Histories 4.3, mentions that the Senate voted Vespasian "all the usual powers"); others see it as unusual, formalising discretionary power (the "discretionary clause") for a new dynasty without Julio-Claudian lineage. The omission of Caligula and Nero from the list of precedents reflects their condemnation. The retroactive clause shows the legal difficulty of an emperor who had seized power by military proclamation. The text's survival in Rome made it a medieval and Renaissance icon of popular sovereignty and the "lex regia", by which jurists such as Ulpian held that the people had transferred their imperium to the emperor.
lex_de_imperio_vespasiani.debate: Whether the law was standard for all emperors or exceptional for the Flavians (Brunt versus Levick and others).
scholarship: Brunt, 'Lex de imperio Vespasiani', JRS 67 (1977)
Capogrossi Colognesi and Gabba (eds), Gli statuti municipali / La Lex de imperio Vespasiani (2009)

imperium_galliarum_proclaimed.detail: Sabinus, who claimed descent from Julius Caesar, was defeated by the Sequani, hid for nine years in a tomb with his wife Epponina, who bore two children there, and was executed in 79 despite her pleas, a story told by Plutarch and Dio. The episode showed the limits of Gallic separatism a century after the conquest: the provincial elites were too invested in Rome.

battle_of_rigodulum.detail: At Trier Cerialis addressed the Treveri and Lingones in a speech that Tacitus made into the classic Roman justification of empire: Gaul had always had kings and wars until it accepted Roman rule; peace requires armies, armies pay, pay requires tribute; if Rome were expelled, nothing would follow but wars among all nations. Days later Civilis and Classicus surprised Cerialis's camp at Trier; he rallied his troops, half-dressed, and won.

battle_of_vetera_70.detail: Civilis retreated to the Insula Batavorum, breaking Drusus's mole to flood the land. Cerialis negotiated, and Tacitus's account breaks off with Civilis addressing the Roman commander on a broken bridge over the Nabalia. The Batavi kept their privileged status and continued to supply elite cohorts, including those at Vindolanda a generation later.

vespasian_healing_miracles_alexandria.detail: Tacitus, Suetonius and Dio all report the miracles, which gave the new, low-born emperor the divine sanction he lacked. Tacitus says eyewitnesses still affirmed them when there was nothing to gain by lying. The Alexandrian crowd also hailed him as son of Ammon, as they had Alexander, and the Flavians promoted Egyptian cults at Rome (the Iseum Campense was rebuilt by Domitian).

yavneh_and_yohanan_ben_zakkai.detail: The story (Avot de-Rabbi Natan, Babylonian Talmud Gittin 56a-b, Lamentations Rabbah) has Yohanan predict Vespasian's accession, echoing Josephus's claim to have done the same. Yavneh, where the Romans had interned loyalist Jews, became the seat of a court under Gamaliel II, which standardised liturgy and the calendar and debated the canon. The later picture of a "Council of Jamnia" that fixed the Hebrew Bible and expelled Christians is now largely rejected.
yavneh_and_yohanan_ben_zakkai.debate: The escape story is legendary; the importance of Yavneh is historical but the notion of a canon-fixing "council" is doubted.

gospel_of_mark_composed.detail: Papias (c. 120, in Eusebius) says Mark had been Peter's interpreter and wrote down what he remembered "but not in order". Mark 13, with its "abomination of desolation" and warnings to flee to the mountains, is usually read as reflecting 66-70. Place of writing is disputed between Rome (patristic tradition, Latinisms, persecution theme) and Syria or Galilee. The original text ends abruptly at 16.8 with the women fleeing the empty tomb; longer endings were added later.
gospel_of_mark_composed.debate: Date (before or after 70) and place (Rome, Syria, Galilee).

flavian_triumph_71.detail: Josephus, an eyewitness, describes moving stages three or four storeys high depicting the war (BJ 7.123-157). The spoils were placed in the new Temple of Peace, the Law and the veils in the palace. The Arch of Titus on the Velia, erected after 81 by Domitian, shows the menorah carried in procession; a second arch in the Circus Maximus (81) claimed falsely that Titus was the first to capture Jerusalem. IVDAEA CAPTA coins circulated for a decade. The doors of Janus were closed.

fiscus_judaicus.detail: Ostraca receipts from Apollinopolis Magna (Edfu) in Egypt record payments by men, women and children. Domitian enforced it harshly, Suetonius recalling as a youth seeing a 90-year-old man stripped in court to see if he was circumcised. Nerva struck coins proclaiming FISCI IVDAICI CALVMNIA SVBLATA ('the false accusation of the Jewish treasury removed'), probably ending abuses rather than the tax. It identified Jews as a fiscal category and helped distinguish Christians from them.
scholarship: Heemstra, The Fiscus Judaicus and the Parting of the Ways (2010)

cerialis_and_the_brigantes.detail: Tacitus says Cerialis fought many battles, some bloody, and conquered or ravaged much of Brigantia. The great earthworks at Stanwick in North Yorkshire, once thought to be Venutius's final stronghold, are now seen as an earlier royal centre. His successor Julius Frontinus subdued the Silures (74-77), building the fortress of Isca (Caerleon).

emmaus_veteran_settlement_71.detail: Josephus says Lucilius Bassus received instructions to lease the land. The legion X Fretensis remained encamped on the ruins of Jerusalem, and the province was upgraded to a praetorian legateship with its own legion, governed from Caesarea, which became Colonia Prima Flavia Augusta. Flavia Neapolis was founded in Samaria in 72.

siege_of_machaerus.detail: Josephus says Machaerus was where John the Baptist was executed. Roman siege works (camps and a ramp) are still visible. Bassus also took Herodium and destroyed refugees in the forest of Jardes before dying in office; Flavius Silva succeeded him.

annexation_of_commagene.detail: Antiochus's sons fought a battle before fleeing to Parthia; the king retired to Sparta and then Rome, and his grandson Philopappus became an Athenian archon and Roman consul (his monument stands on the Mouseion hill in Athens). Legio XII Fulminata went to Melitene and XVI Flavia to Satala, creating for the first time a permanent legionary frontier facing Armenia. Emesa and other Syrian principalities were absorbed in the following years.

vespasian_urine_tax.detail: Suetonius and Dio report his reputation for avarice, including selling offices and buying goods to resell. He also reclaimed public land (subseciva) occupied illegally in Italy, a policy Domitian reversed. In French and Italian, public urinals are still called vespasiennes and vespasiani.
vespasian_urine_tax.debate: Date of the urine tax within the reign unknown.

censorship_of_vespasian_73.detail: Among those adlected to the patriciate were Agricola and the father of Trajan; Suetonius says Vespasian raised the orders to a thousand members from the best men of Italy and the provinces. The census returns gave Pliny the Elder his list of long-lived men in Region VIII. Pomerial cippi of 75 survive. This was the last formal censorship; Domitian took the title censor perpetuus in 85.

siege_of_masada.detail: Masada, Herod's palace-fortress on a 400 m high mesa above the Dead Sea, had been held since 66 by the sicarii under Eleazar ben Yair, a descendant of Judas the Galilean, who raided nearby villages such as Ein Gedi, where Josephus says they killed 700 women and children. After the fall of Jerusalem and the reduction of Herodium and Machaerus, the governor Lucius Flavius Silva marched against it with legio X Fretensis and auxiliaries, some 8,000 men, in the winter of 73/74 (the date is debated between 73 and 74).
