He surrounded the mountain with a circumvallation wall about 4 km long and eight camps, all still visible as the best-preserved Roman siege works anywhere. On the western side, Silva's men built a ramp on a natural spur of the White Promontory (Leuke), topped with a stone platform, up which they hauled a siege tower with a battering ram. When the ram breached the wall, the defenders built an inner wall of timber and earth, which the Romans set on fire. According to Josephus, Eleazar then persuaded the 960 men, women and children to kill themselves rather than face slavery: ten men chosen by lot killed the rest, then one killed the other nine and himself. Two women and five children who had hidden in a cistern survived to tell the story. The Romans found the dead the next morning, on the 15th of Xanthicus, around Passover. Yigael Yadin's excavations of 1963-1965 uncovered Herod's hanging palace, storerooms, a synagogue, ritual baths, scrolls including Ben Sira and the Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice, and a set of eleven ostraca with names, including "ben Yair", which Yadin connected with the lots. Modern scholars debate the historicity of Josephus's account: his speeches are literary, the number of skeletons found was small, and the ramp may have been only partly artificial. In twentieth-century Israel Masada became a national symbol of resistance ("Masada shall not fall again"), and its use as such has itself been studied critically.
siege_of_masada.debate: Date (73 or 74) and the historicity of the mass suicide as told by Josephus.
scholarship: Yadin, Masada (1966)
Ben-Yehuda, The Masada Myth (1995)
Eck, 'Die Eroberung von Masada und eine neue Inschrift des L. Flavius Silva Nonius Bassus', ZNW 60 (1969)

ius_latii_hispania.detail: Pliny says Vespasian 'tossed by the storms of the state' gave Latium to the whole of Spain. Bronze copies of the resulting municipal charter survive from Malaca and Salpensa (found 1851) and above all Irni (lex Irnitana, found in 1981 near El Saucejo, preserving about two-thirds of a standard Flavian municipal law in ten tablets), giving detailed rules on elections, councils, finance, manumission and civil jurisdiction. Over 350 Spanish communities may have benefited. The same censorship extended the pomerium (boundary stones of 75 survive) and adlected new senators, including provincials such as the father of Trajan.
scholarship: González and Crawford, 'The Lex Irnitana: a new copy of the Flavian municipal law', JRS 76 (1986)

frontinus_conquers_the_silures.detail: Tacitus (Agricola 17) says Frontinus "sustained the burden" worthily, overcoming the valour of the enemy and the difficulty of the ground. Frontinus later wrote the Strategemata and, as curator of the water supply, De Aquaeductu. The fortress at Caerleon, with its amphitheatre and baths, remained the base of II Augusta until the late third century.

execution_of_helvidius_priscus.detail: Helvidius refused to address Vespasian by any title but his private name and attacked hereditary succession. When the Cynic Demetrius insulted him, Vespasian is said to have replied that he did not kill a barking dog. The 'Stoic opposition', commemorated in Tacitus and Pliny, was less a philosophical programme than a code of senatorial independence. Helvidius's son was executed by Domitian in 93.

temple_of_peace.detail: Pliny counted it among the most beautiful buildings in the world. The Severan Marble Plan of Rome (Forma Urbis) later hung on one of its walls; fragments survive. The precinct burned in 192, destroying among much else the books of Galen, who lamented the loss in his recently discovered treatise On the Avoidance of Grief.

josephus_jewish_war.detail: The work presents the war as the fault of a small band of tyrants and brigands and of Roman procurators' misgovernment, exonerating the Flavians and the priestly aristocracy; Titus appears merciful. It is modelled on Thucydides and Polybius and uses Roman commentarii. Josephus later wrote the Jewish Antiquities (93/94), the Life and Against Apion. His works were preserved by Christians, partly because of the passages on Jesus, John the Baptist and James.

alan_invasion_of_75.detail: Josephus describes the Alan raid; Suetonius says Vespasian refused Vologases's request. Rome instead strengthened the Caucasus: a Latin inscription of 75 at Harmozica near Tbilisi records Roman fortification work for the Iberian king Mithridates. The episode explains the Flavian reorganisation of the eastern frontier and the Alan threat that Arrian faced in 135.

pliny_natural_history.detail: It covers cosmology, geography, anthropology, zoology, botany, medicine, metallurgy and art history, and is the main source for Greek painting and sculpture, Roman mining and countless technical details. His nephew describes his working method: read to while bathing and dining, taking notes always. The work circulated as an authority through the Middle Ages.

agricola_conquers_ordovices_and_mona.detail: Tacitus (Agricola 18) stresses that Agricola campaigned when the season was thought over. The completion of the conquest of Wales freed forces for the advance north. The date of Agricola's arrival (77 or 78) determines all later years of his governorship and the date of Mons Graupius (83 or 84).

death_of_vespasian.detail: He was the first emperor since Augustus to die naturally and be succeeded by his own son, Titus, who had been his colleague in tribunician power and censorship and praetorian prefect. His thrift (the tax on urine collected for fulling, 'money does not smell') restored finances drained by Nero and civil war; Suetonius says he estimated that 40,000 million sesterces were needed to set the state right.

eruption_of_vesuvius.detail: Vesuvius erupted in 79, destroying Pompeii, Herculaneum, Stabiae, Oplontis and the surrounding villas. The traditional date of 24 August comes from the manuscripts of Pliny the Younger's letter to Tacitus (Letters 6.16), but variant readings and archaeological evidence (autumn fruits such as pomegranates and walnuts, braziers in use, wine already fermenting in sealed jars, a coin of Titus with his fifteenth imperatorial acclamation, and in 2018 a charcoal inscription dated 17 October) have led many scholars to prefer 24 October. The eruption began around midday with a Plinian column of pumice and ash rising some 30 km, which the elder Pliny, commander of the fleet at Misenum, observed from across the bay. The ash fell south-east on Pompeii and Stabiae for about eighteen hours, collapsing roofs. During the night and next morning the column collapsed into pyroclastic surges and flows, superheated avalanches of gas and debris, which reached Herculaneum first, killing the hundreds of people who had sheltered in the boat houses on the shore (skeletons excavated since 1981), and later Pompeii, killing those still in the city, whose voids in the ash were cast in plaster by Giuseppe Fiorelli from 1863. Pliny the Elder, who had sailed to rescue friends at Stabiae, died on the beach, probably of a heart attack or asphyxiation. His nephew, who stayed at Misenum, describes in a second letter (6.20) the earthquakes, the darkness and the panic of the crowds. Titus came to Campania, appointed two consular curators to relieve the area and used the estates of victims without heirs for reconstruction. Some 1,150 bodies have been found at Pompeii, but most of its population of perhaps 10,000-12,000 seem to have escaped. Pompeii was rediscovered in 1748 and Herculaneum in 1738, where the Villa of the Papyri has yielded the only surviving ancient library of carbonised scrolls, now being read by imaging and machine learning. The two cities preserve the fullest record of everyday Roman life, from graffiti and election notices to bakeries and brothels.
eruption_of_vesuvius.debate: Date: 24 August (manuscript tradition) or 24 October (archaeological evidence and the 2018 charcoal inscription).
scholarship: Sigurdsson et al., 'The eruption of Vesuvius in A.D. 79', National Geographic Research 1 (1985)
Beard, Pompeii (2008)

agricola_civilizing_measures_79.detail: Agricola 21 is the classic text on "Romanisation". The forum at Verulamium, dedicated under Agricola in 79 according to a fragmentary inscription, and the early masonry phases of Fishbourne and other towns illustrate the building boom. Modern scholarship debates how far Roman officials drove such change rather than local elites seeking status.
agricola_civilizing_measures_79.debate: Romanisation as policy or as elite emulation (Haverfield, Millett, Woolf).

berenice_dismissed_79.detail: Two Cynic philosophers who denounced her in the theatre were punished, one by flogging and one by beheading (Dio). Berenice, born in 28, had been married to her uncle Herod of Chalcis and to Polemon of Cilicia, and had tried to calm the Jerusalem crowd barefoot in 66. The episode, with its echo of Antony and Cleopatra, inspired Racine's Berenice (1670).

inauguration_of_the_colosseum.detail: The Flavian Amphitheatre, begun by Vespasian around 70-72 on the site of the artificial lake of Nero's Golden House, was dedicated by Titus in 80 with games lasting a hundred days, though the topmost storey and possibly the hypogeum were finished by Domitian. An inscription reconstructed from peg holes, read by Géza Alföldy, records that Vespasian built it "ex manubiis", from the spoils of the Jewish war. The elliptical building (188 by 156 m, about 48 m high) had four storeys of travertine faced with Doric, Ionic and Corinthian half-columns and a top storey with pilasters, holding some 50,000 spectators, seated by rank, with senators at the front, women and slaves at the top. Eighty numbered entrances and a sophisticated system of stairs allowed rapid filling and emptying; awnings (velaria) operated by sailors from Misenum shaded the audience. Dio says the inaugural games included 9,000 animals killed, combats of cranes and elephants, women fighting beasts, and a naval battle staged after flooding the arena, probably before the hypogeum was built. Martial's Book of Spectacles celebrates the shows, including the execution of a criminal dressed as Orpheus mauled by a bear and the contest between the gladiators Priscus and Verus, who fought to a standstill and were both freed by Titus. The building became the symbol of Rome's spectacles. Gladiatorial games continued until the early fifth century (Honorius is said to have banned them after the monk Telemachus was killed in 404) and wild beast hunts until 523. Earthquakes in 847 and 1349 and centuries of quarrying stripped the southern side. The name "Colosseum", first attested in the eighth century, derives from the colossal statue of Nero, refashioned as the Sun, that stood nearby. Its use for executions of Christians is uncertain, though it was later consecrated to the martyrs. The building rewarded the people with the land Nero had taken, as Martial put it: "Rome has been restored to herself".
scholarship: Alföldy, 'Eine Bauinschrift aus dem Colosseum', ZPE 109 (1995)
Hopkins and Beard, The Colosseum (2005)

agricola_reaches_the_tay_80.detail: Tacitus says the garrisons were supplied for a year and could survive winter sieges. Dendrochronology and coin evidence support Flavian occupation of Scotland in this period, though many of the forts in Strathmore may belong to the following years.

fire_and_plague_of_80.detail: Titus stripped his own villas of decorations to restore public buildings and appointed two ex-consuls to relieve Campania, using the estates of those who died without heirs. Domitian rebuilt the Capitol on a lavish scale (gilding alone reputedly cost 12,000 talents) and restored the Pantheon. The fire and epidemic gave Titus's short reign its reputation for disaster borne with generosity.

death_of_titus.detail: Rumours accused Domitian of hastening his death. Domitian deified him and built the Arch of Titus on the Velia, its inscription reading simply 'The Senate and Roman people to the deified Titus, son of the deified Vespasian'. Rabbinic legend (Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 56b) says a gnat entered his brain as punishment for destroying the Temple. His affair with the Jewish queen Berenice, whom he sent away on becoming emperor, fascinated later dramatists (Racine).

agricola_forth_clyde_81.detail: Tacitus remarks that if the army's valour and Rome's glory had allowed, a frontier could have been found within Britain itself. The same isthmus was later chosen for the Antonine Wall (142).

arch_of_titus.detail: The vault shows Titus carried to heaven by an eagle, a key image of imperial apotheosis. A second, triple arch to Titus in the Circus Maximus (dedicated in 81 while he lived) claimed he had subdued the Jews and destroyed Jerusalem, "never before attacked", a falsehood. The surviving arch was built into the Frangipani fortress and restored by Valadier in 1821, who marked his additions in travertine. The menorah relief became a symbol of the Jewish diaspora.

agricola_southwest_scotland_82.detail: Tacitus says he often heard Agricola say this. No Roman conquest of Ireland followed; finds at Drumanagh north of Dublin and elsewhere attest trade rather than occupation. The passage is the earliest Roman reference to Irish harbours being known through merchants.

battle_of_mons_graupius.detail: Mons Graupius was the culmination of Agricola's campaigns in Scotland, fought in the late summer of 83 (or 84, depending on the date of his arrival in Britain). After his sixth season, in which the Caledonians attacked the IX legion's camp at night and nearly destroyed it, Agricola advanced north of the Tay with a fleet shadowing the army along the coast. The Caledonian confederacy, more than 30,000 strong according to Tacitus, under Calgacus, took up position on the slopes of a hill. Tacitus gives Calgacus the famous speech against Roman imperialism ("they make a desolation and call it peace") and Agricola a reply urging his men to end the war. Agricola kept his legions in reserve before the camp and placed 8,000 auxiliary infantry, Batavians and Tungrians, in the centre with 3,000 cavalry on the wings. The Britons, with chariots on the plain, held the high ground. The Batavian and Tungrian cohorts closed to sword range, where the Britons' long swords and small shields were ineffective, and pushed uphill. When the Britons tried to outflank the Roman line from the hilltop, Agricola sent four cavalry wings he had held back, which broke them and attacked from the rear. Tacitus reports 10,000 Caledonians killed and only 360 Romans, a lopsided figure; the next day the burned homesteads and silent hills showed the extent of the rout. Agricola then took hostages from the Boresti and sent his fleet round the north of Britain, which reached the Orkneys. The site is unknown: candidates include Bennachie in Aberdeenshire (near the Durno marching camp, which could hold the army), Raedykes, Megray Hill, the Gask Ridge region and Duncrub; the name, misread in Renaissance editions as "Grampius", gave the Grampian mountains their name. Domitian recalled Agricola in 84/85 and soon withdrew troops from Scotland for the Danube, abandoning the legionary fortress at Inchtuthil around 87, which Tacitus resentfully summarised as "Britain was conquered and immediately let go".
battle_of_mons_graupius.debate: Site (Bennachie, Raedykes, Megray, others) and date (83 or 84); the figures and speeches reflect Tacitus's artistry.
scholarship: Hanson, Agricola and the Conquest of the North (1987)
Maxwell, A Battle Lost: Romans and Caledonians at Mons Graupius (1990)

domitians_chattan_campaign.detail: Frontinus, a participant, records the use of cleared limites to deny the enemy cover and compensation for crops destroyed by forts. The new line of watchtowers and forts became the nucleus of the upper German limes. Germania Superior and Inferior became regular provinces in these years, replacing the military districts. Hostile authors (Tacitus, Pliny, Dio) mocked the triumph as a fraud; archaeology supports real gains.

domitian_army_pay_rise.detail: Suetonius says the pay rise and the cost of building and games drove him to confiscations. Metallurgical analyses (Walker, Butcher and Ponting) confirm the sharp rise in fineness in 82 and the partial return in 85 to near-Neronian standards. The pay increase, together with the expanding army, became a permanent structural burden on imperial finances.
domitian_army_pay_rise.debate: Whether the rise was in 83 or 84.
scholarship: Walker, The Metrology of the Roman Silver Coinage I (1976)
Speidel, 'Roman army pay scales', JRS 82 (1992)

mutiny_of_the_usipi.detail: Tacitus (Agricola 28) tells the story as an unintended circumnavigation that preceded Agricola's own fleet. Dio (66.20) has a garbled version making the mutineers prove Britain an island. The episode illustrates the risks of using newly levied German auxiliaries far from home.

agricolas_fleet_circumnavigates_britain.detail: The Usipi, killing a centurion and their instructors, drifted without pilots, were reduced to eating the weakest among them, were wrecked on the continent and sold as slaves by the Suebi and Frisii, some ending up on the Roman bank of the Rhine where their story became known. Tacitus presents the voyage as a final crowning of Agricola's governorship before his recall.

death_of_oppius_sabinus.detail: Domitian came to the Danube in person with the praetorian prefect Cornelius Fuscus, drove the invaders out and divided Moesia into Superior and Inferior (86). Jordanes, drawing on Dio, gives the Dacian perspective. The defeat began two decades of conflict culminating in Trajan's conquest.

domitian_censor_perpetuus_85.detail: The title appears on coins from 85 (CENS PER P). Dio says he was the first to hold it for life. His moral censorship included forbidding castration, enforcing the Lex Scantinia against homosexual acts among the elite and banning women of ill-repute from inheritances. The execution of the chief Vestal Cornelia (91) was its most notorious act.

germanic_provinces_and_limes_85.detail: Frontinus (Strategemata 1.3.10) describes Domitian driving roads 120 miles long through the forest to expose the enemy's hiding places. The Agri Decumates between upper Rhine and Danube were gradually occupied in the same period. Military diplomas from 90 first name Germania Superior. The palisade and later rampart and ditch that made the Upper German-Raetian limes a continuous barrier were added under Hadrian and the Antonines.

gospels_of_matthew_luke_and_john.detail: Matthew, possibly from Antioch, frames Jesus as interpreter of the Law and reflects a community in conflict with the emerging rabbinic leadership. Luke-Acts is addressed to the "most excellent Theophilus" and tells a story from Galilee to Rome. John speaks of believers being "put out of the synagogue". The Rylands papyrus P52, a fragment of John often dated c. 125-175, is among the earliest New Testament manuscripts.
gospels_of_matthew_luke_and_john.debate: Dates, places and the Q hypothesis (two-source theory versus Farrer-Goulder) are all debated.

defeat_of_cornelius_fuscus.detail: Juvenal mocks Fuscus as a man 'who studied war in his marble villa' and whose entrails were saved for Dacian vultures. Whether a legion (V Alaudae is the usual candidate) was destroyed is uncertain. The date may be 86 or 87. Decebalus, now king, emerged as a formidable opponent. The great funerary altar at Adamclisi, listing some 3,800 Roman dead, is sometimes attributed to this disaster rather than to Trajan's war.
defeat_of_cornelius_fuscus.debate: Date (86/87), site, and whether a legion was annihilated.

nasamones_revolt_86.detail: Dio says Domitian boasted to the Senate: "I have forbidden the Nasamones to exist." Inscriptions of Flaccus record a census of the Nybgenii and the measurement of lands in southern Tunisia. The episode shows the pressure of taxation on peripheral peoples and the brutality of frontier warfare.

agon_capitolinus_86.detail: For it he built the Stadium (whose outline survives as the Piazza Navona) and the Odeum. The poet Statius failed to win the crown in 90, a disappointment he lamented. The Capitoline Games, unlike Nero's Neronia, endured into the fourth century and became one of the most prestigious contests in the Greek athletic circuit; the eleven-year-old poet Quintus Sulpicius Maximus is commemorated on his tomb near the Porta Salaria for his Greek improvisation at the 94 games.

moesia_divided_86.detail: The two Germanies had been organised as formal provinces with civil governors around the same time (c. 83-85). The concentration of legions on the Danube, which rose from about seven under Vespasian to twelve under Trajan, reflected the end of expansion on the Rhine and the rise of Dacia.

julius_maternus_to_agisymba.detail: The expeditions are known only from Marinus of Tyre as cited and criticised by Ptolemy (Geography 1.8), who doubted the distances. Agisymba has been located anywhere from the Tibesti to Lake Chad. The journeys reflect good relations with the Garamantes after the punitive expedition of Valerius Festus in 69-70 and the trade route to the Fezzan.

dominus_et_deus.detail: The phrase never appears in official documents or on coins, and some scholars think the hostile tradition exaggerated a courtiers' flattery into imperial policy. Martial, after Domitian's death, declared (10.72) that under Trajan there would be no more "lord and god". Domitian's favouring of Minerva and the cult of the Flavian gens was nevertheless distinctive.
dominus_et_deus.debate: Whether Domitian demanded the title or flatterers used it.

martial_publishes_epigrams.detail: His 1,500 poems are a street-level chronicle of Rome: legacy hunters, dinner parties, bath-houses, booksellers in the Argiletum, the clients' morning salutation, gladiators and the poet's own poverty in a third-floor flat. They flatter Domitian lavishly; after 96 Martial courted Nerva and Trajan with less success and retired to Bilbilis in 98, where he died c. 102-104. Pliny paid his travel money and wrote his obituary.

inchtuthil_abandoned.detail: Excavated by Ian Richmond and J. K. St Joseph from 1952, Inchtuthil has the most complete plan of any legionary fortress: barracks, hospital, granaries, workshops, but no completed headquarters or commander's house. The latest coins are bronzes of 86. It is the archaeological counterpart of Tacitus's bitter phrase 'Britain was completely conquered and immediately let go' (Hist. 1.2).
scholarship: Pitts and St Joseph, Inchtuthil: The Roman Legionary Fortress (1985)

ludi_saeculares_88.detail: Tacitus mentions his role in passing (Ann. 11.11), one of the few autobiographical facts we have about him. The competing calculations (Augustan 110-year saecula, Claudian centenary of the city) show how the antiquarian calendar was manipulated for political ends.

battle_of_tapae_88.detail: Dio says Decebalus, fearing a Roman advance on his capital, had trees felled and dressed in armour so that the Romans would take them for soldiers. Julianus made his soldiers inscribe their own and their centurions' names on their shields to encourage bravery. The victory was not followed up because of the Saturninus revolt and war with the Suebi.

revolt_of_saturninus.detail: Lappius burned Saturninus's correspondence to prevent a witch-hunt, but Domitian's suspicion deepened. Trajan, then legate of legio VII Gemina in Spain, marched to the Rhine too late to fight. Domitian thereafter forbade two legions sharing a camp and limited soldiers' deposits to 1,000 sesterces. The episode marks the start of the 'terror' of Domitian's later years in the hostile tradition.

peace_with_decebalus_89.detail: Domitian then celebrated a double triumph over the Chatti and Dacians, which hostile writers mocked. Dio says Decebalus used Roman artisans to build up his fortifications in the Orăștie mountains, a grievance Trajan later exploited. Modern historians view the peace as a sensible arrangement that freed troops for the more urgent Suebic-Sarmatian front.

execution_of_vestal_cornelia.detail: Pliny the Younger describes her protesting her innocence as she was led to the underground chamber, adjusting her robe so as to descend with dignity. Earlier (c. 83) the Oculatae sisters and Varronilla had been allowed to choose their deaths. Domitian's revival of archaic religious penalties fits his self-image as restorer of morals and censor perpetuus (from 85).

lex_irnitana.detail: The law regulates the town council of 63 decurions, the annual magistrates (duoviri, aediles, quaestors) who gained Roman citizenship on taking office, elections, public finances, manumission, guardianship and civil jurisdiction, which followed Roman law and procedure even between Latin citizens. With the fragments from Malaca and Salpensa (found 1851) it shows how Rome built provincial self-government on a standard template.

vine_edict_92.detail: Modern interpretations range from protection of Italian wine producers to concern for grain supply. The measure was formally lifted only by Probus (c. 280). It is a rare example of an imperial attempt at agricultural regulation across the empire.

destruction_of_legio_xxi_rapax.detail: Suetonius mentions 'a legion slaughtered with its legate' in the Sarmatian war. Domitian celebrated only an ovatio in January 93, dedicating a laurel wreath to Capitoline Jupiter. Pannonia's garrison was reinforced, and Aquincum, Brigetio and Vindobona developed as legionary bases in the following years.

domus_flavia_dedicated.detail: Statius (Silvae 4.2) describes a banquet in the dining hall, where the emperor's presence is likened to Jupiter's. The palace remained the emperors' residence for three centuries and gave the word 'palace' (from Palatium) to European languages. Martial praises Rabirius's genius.

vindolanda_tablets.detail: Highlights include a strength report of the First Cohort of Tungrians showing 752 men on the books but only 296 present, the rest seconded elsewhere (Tab. Vindol. II 154); a birthday invitation from Claudia Severa to Sulpicia Lepidina, the wife of the Batavian prefect Flavius Cerialis, with a postscript in Severa's own hand, the earliest known Latin writing by a woman (II 291); a memorandum referring dismissively to 'Brittunculi', 'wretched little Britons' (II 164); and requests for socks, underpants and beer. They transformed knowledge of everyday military life, literacy and the Latin of the frontier.
scholarship: Bowman and Thomas, The Vindolanda Writing-Tablets (Tabulae Vindolandenses II, 1994)
Bowman, Life and Letters on the Roman Frontier (1994)

statius_thebaid_92.detail: The Thebaid ends by telling the poem not to rival "the divine Aeneid" but to follow it at a distance. Statius won the prize at Domitian's Alban games but lost at the Capitoline. Dante, who believed him a secret Christian, made him his guide in Purgatory. The Silvae include the poem on Domitian's colossal equestrian statue in the Forum and the poem to Sleep.

purge_of_93.detail: Tacitus, who was absent from Rome, opens the Agricola with the bitter claim that the Senate had given proof of extreme servitude and that Rome had lost even the memory of free speech. Pliny the Younger, praetor that year, claims (perhaps exaggerating) to have been in danger himself. Epictetus left for Nicopolis in Epirus, where his lectures were recorded by Arrian. The women Arria and Fannia were exiled.

epictetus_at_nicopolis.detail: Epictetus had been a slave of Nero's freedman Epaphroditus and was lame. His teaching centred on distinguishing what is "up to us" (judgements, desires) from what is not. Hadrian reportedly visited him, and Marcus Aurelius read the Discourses, lent to him by Junius Rusticus.

josephus_jewish_antiquities_94.detail: The Antiquities paraphrases the Bible and adds post-biblical sources (Nicolaus of Damascus, Hellenistic Jewish writers, Roman decrees). Book 18 contains the notices of John the Baptist, James and the much-debated Testimonium Flavianum on Jesus, which made Josephus a favourite of Christian copyists and ensured his survival. The patron was Epaphroditus, possibly not Nero's freedman of that name.

execution_of_flavius_clemens.detail: Eusebius makes Domitilla a Christian, exiled to Pontia; the Catacomb of Domitilla in Rome is on land associated with her family. Whether the charge reflects Judaising, Christianity or simply dynastic fear is disputed. The execution alarmed the palace staff; Domitilla's steward Stephanus was among Domitian's assassins months later.
execution_of_flavius_clemens.debate: Jewish or Christian sympathies of Clemens and Domitilla.

quintilian_institutio_oratoria.detail: Book 10 contains a reading list surveying Greek and Latin literature with famous verdicts ("satura quidem tota nostra est"). Quintilian taught Pliny the Younger and was tutor to Domitian's grand-nephews, the sons of Flavius Clemens, for which he received the consular insignia. The rediscovery of a complete manuscript by Poggio Bracciolini at St Gall in 1416 made him central to Renaissance humanist education.

book_of_revelation.detail: The number of the beast, 666 (616 in some manuscripts), is most commonly read as a gematria of "Nero Caesar" in Hebrew letters, and the wounded head that revives as a reflection of the Nero redivivus legend. The book's picture of Domitianic persecution is not confirmed by other evidence; it more likely reflects pressures of the imperial cult in Asia. It was admitted to the canon only after long dispute in the East.
book_of_revelation.debate: Date (Neronian or Domitianic) and the reality of a Domitianic persecution.

assassination_of_domitian.detail: Domitian was stabbed to death in his bedroom on the Palatine on 18 September 96, aged 44, by a conspiracy of palace staff, apparently with the knowledge of both praetorian prefects (Titus Petronius Secundus and Norbanus) and of his wife Domitia Longina. The immediate motive was fear: after the execution of his cousin Flavius Clemens in 95 and the exile of Clemens's wife Flavia Domitilla, and further executions of senators and courtiers, including his secretary Epaphroditus, members of the household believed they were next. Suetonius and Dio report that Domitian, who feared assassination and had lined his colonnades with reflective phengite stone, had been told by astrologers the day and hour of his death; he had executed the astrologer Ascletarion, whose prediction that he would be eaten by dogs was fulfilled when his pyre was overturned by rain. On the day, after asking the hour and being told the danger had passed, he received Stephanus, a steward of Domitilla accused of embezzlement, who had worn a bandage on his arm for days to conceal a dagger and claimed to bring news of a conspiracy. Stephanus stabbed him in the groin; Domitian fought back, trying to gouge his attacker's eyes and reaching for the dagger under his pillow, which had been removed. Other conspirators, Clodianus, a cornicularius, the freedman Maximus, Satur and a gladiator, joined in, inflicting seven wounds; Stephanus was killed in the struggle. The Senate rejoiced, decreed the erasure of his name from inscriptions and the destruction of his statues (damnatio memoriae), and the same day recognised the elderly senator Marcus Cocceius Nerva, who had been approached in advance, as emperor. The army, which loved Domitian for his pay rise, was angry; the praetorians forced Nerva in 97 to hand over the conspirators Petronius and Parthenius for execution. Domitian's nurse Phyllis secretly cremated him and mixed his ashes with those of Julia Titi in the Flavian temple. Pliny and Tacitus present the reign as a terror, but modern historians (Jones, Southern) credit Domitian with efficient administration, frontier consolidation and building.

accession_of_nerva.detail: Tacitus praised him for having joined two things once incompatible, principate and liberty. An agrarian law and 60 million sesterces were spent buying land for poor citizens; the abuses of the fiscus Judaicus were curbed. But the leniency led the consul Fronto to remark that it was bad to have an emperor under whom nobody was allowed to do anything, but worse to have one under whom everybody could do everything. At a dinner Junius Mauricus, asked what the dead informer Catullus Messalinus would be doing if alive, answered 'dining with us'.
scholarship: Grainger, Nerva and the Roman Succession Crisis of AD 96-99 (2003)

first_clement.detail: The letter apologises for delay caused by "sudden and repeated misfortunes", often taken as Domitianic pressure. It contains the first reference to the deaths of Peter and Paul and an early statement of apostolic succession of church officers. Later lists made Clement the third or fourth bishop of Rome, but the letter itself suggests government by a college of presbyters.

nerva_reforms_96.detail: His coins advertise FISCI IVDAICI CALVMNIA SVBLATA (the abuse of the Jewish tax removed), VEHICVLATIONE ITALIAE REMISSA and PLEBEI VRBANAE FRUMENTO CONSTITVTO. Economies included selling imperial property. The consul Fronto remarked that it was bad to have an emperor under whom nothing was allowed, but worse to have one under whom everything was. The alimentary schemes probably began under him.

adoption_of_trajan.detail: In October 97 Nerva, aged and childless, adopted Marcus Ulpius Traianus, governor of Upper Germany, announcing the adoption on the Capitol in front of the temple of Jupiter with the words "May it be good, fortunate and happy for the Senate and Roman people and myself: I adopt Marcus Ulpius Nerva Traianus." The adoption was a response to a crisis. In the summer the praetorians, led by the prefect Casperius Aelianus, had besieged the palace, demanding the punishment of Domitian's murderers; Nerva bared his throat to them but was forced to surrender Petronius Secundus and Parthenius, who were killed, and then to thank the soldiers publicly. His authority was broken, and there were rumours of a conspiracy by Calpurnius Crassus and of rivalry with the governor of Syria. By choosing Trajan, a respected general of senatorial family from Italica in Baetica, son of a distinguished Flavian consul, Nerva gained military backing from the powerful Rhine armies. The decision may have been brokered by senators such as Licinius Sura and Julius Frontinus, and the young Hadrian brought congratulations to Trajan from the Danube armies. Trajan received tribunician power and the title Caesar, and when Nerva died on 27 January 98, succeeded without difficulty, staying on the frontier for more than a year before entering Rome. Casperius and the guilty praetorians were summoned to him and executed. Pliny's Panegyricus presents the adoption as the choice of the best man (optimus), and the idea that selection by merit through adoption was superior to dynastic succession became a theme of second-century ideology, voiced in the speech Tacitus gives to Galba in the Histories (1.15-16). The so-called "adoptive emperors" from Nerva to Marcus Aurelius were, however, also linked by kinship and marriage, and adoption was a solution to the lack of sons rather than a principle. Trajan was the first emperor born outside Italy.
adoption_of_trajan.debate: Whether adoption was a principle of selection by merit or an expedient forced by childlessness and crisis.

forum_of_nerva_97.detail: The forum's frieze of the "Colonnacce" shows Minerva and scenes of women's work (the myth of Arachne). The temple survived largely intact until Pope Paul V dismantled it in 1606 for the Acqua Paola fountain. Domitian's name was erased and Nerva's substituted, a typical case of the appropriation of a condemned emperor's building.

frontinus_curator_aquarum_97.detail: He found that the official delivery figures underestimated actual intake and that much water was stolen by illegal pipes and wrongly sized nozzles (calices). He praises the aqueducts over "idle pyramids" and the "famous but useless works of the Greeks". Frontinus was consul for the third time in 100 with Trajan.

death_of_nerva.detail: Trajan had Casperius Aelianus and the mutinous praetorians summoned and executed. His entry into Rome on foot, embracing senators, is celebrated in the Panegyricus. He was the first emperor of provincial origin, from a colonist family of Italica in Baetica.

tacitus_writes_histories_and_annals.detail: Less than half survives: the Histories break off in 70 and the Annals lack books 7-10 and parts of 5, 6, 11 and 16, all depending on two Medicean manuscripts. Tacitus's compressed style, irony and psychological insight shaped the modern image of the Julio-Claudians. His sources include the acta senatus (confirmed by the SC de Pisone patre), memoirs (Agrippina, Corbulo), and earlier histories (Aufidius Bassus, Pliny the Elder, Cluvius Rufus, Fabius Rusticus). The Germania, rediscovered in the Codex Hersfeldensis and exploited by German nationalists and the Nazis, became, in Christopher Krebs's phrase, 'a most dangerous book'.
scholarship: Syme, Tacitus (1958)
Krebs, A Most Dangerous Book (2011)

tacitus_agricola_and_germania.detail: The Agricola's preface celebrates the return of liberty under Nerva and Trajan and contains Calgacus's speech at Mons Graupius ("they make a desert and call it peace"). The Germania, contrasting German virtue with Roman decadence, survived in a single manuscript found at Hersfeld and brought to Rome in 1455; it was later abused by German nationalists and the Nazis. Tacitus had been consul suffect in 97 and delivered the funeral oration for Verginius Rufus.

trajan_enters_rome_99.detail: Pliny's Panegyricus (22-24) describes the crowds on roofs and the emperor's accessibility. The staged modesty, contrasted with Domitian, set the tone of the "civil princeps" (civilis princeps) and Trajan's good relations with the Senate. He distributed a congiarium and paid soldiers only half the customary donative.

trial_of_marius_priscus_100.detail: Pliny's letter (2.11) describes speaking for nearly five hours, with Trajan concerned for his voice, and Tacitus replying "very eloquently and with the grandeur that marks his speaking". Repetundae trials before the Senate were a recurring check on provincial governors; Pliny also took part in the cases against Caecilius Classicus (Baetica) and Julius Bassus (Bithynia).

panegyricus_of_pliny_100.detail: It contrasts Trajan, optimus princeps, with Domitian point by point: modesty, accessibility, liberty of the Senate, end of informers, sound finances. It became the model for the late antique Panegyrici Latini, in whose manuscript it heads the collection. Pliny's ten books of letters, published in stages c. 100-109, with Book 10 containing his correspondence with Trajan from Bithynia, are the other great source for the period.

tabula_traiana_100.detail: The Tabula Traiana inscription records that Trajan "cut through mountains and removed projections" to make the road; when the Djerdap dam raised the river in 1972 the plaque was moved 21 m higher. A second inscription found in 1969 records the canal built "because of the danger of the cataracts" to make the Danube navigable. Holes for the beams of the cantilevered road are still visible.

battle_of_tapae_101.detail: Trajan's Column shows Jupiter hurling thunderbolts at the Dacians during the battle (scene XXIV). Before it, the Buri sent a message written in Latin on a giant mushroom urging Trajan to turn back (Dio 68.8.1). Despite victory the season was too far advanced to take Sarmizegetusa, and Trajan withdrew to winter quarters.

alimenta.detail: Two bronze tablets document it. The table of the Ligures Baebiani (101, CIL IX 1455) and the great table of Veleia near Piacenza (CIL XI 1147), the largest surviving Roman bronze inscription, record 1,044,000 sesterces lent to 52 landowners, supporting 263 boys at 16 sesterces a month, 35 girls at 12, and two illegitimate children. The arch of Beneventum and coins with ALIM(enta) ITAL(iae) celebrate it. Pliny implies a demographic and military purpose (future soldiers); others see charity or imperial display; the old theory of agricultural credit has been largely abandoned.
scholarship: Duncan-Jones, The Economy of the Roman Empire (2nd ed. 1982), ch. 7
Woolf, 'Food, poverty and patronage', PBSR 58 (1990)

battle_of_adamclisi.detail: Column scenes XXXI-XLVII show Sarmatian cataphracts drowning in the Danube and a night battle. Beside the Tropaeum stands a mausoleum and a funerary altar inscribed with the names of some 3,800 soldiers who fell 'fighting for the state', probably in this campaign, though some attribute it to Fuscus's defeat of 86/87. The 54 metopes of the Tropaeum, carved in a provincial style, depict Roman and barbarian soldiers with unusual realism.
battle_of_adamclisi.debate: Location of the battle (Adamclisi vs Nicopolis ad Istrum) and the date of the altar.
scholarship: Florescu, Das Siegesdenkmal von Adamklissi (1965)
Rossi, Trajan's Column and the Dacian Wars (1971)

peace_with_decebalus_102.detail: The standard lost by Fuscus was recovered. Trajan took the title Dacicus and triumphed in December 102. Decebalus's envoys addressed the Senate with chained hands. The southern Banat and Oltenia stayed under Roman occupation, preparing the ground for the next war.

trajans_bridge.detail: Dio describes piers 150 feet high and 60 wide set 170 feet apart, founded in a deep, fast river, and calls it the most magnificent of Trajan's works. It appears on Trajan's Column and on coins. Hadrian removed the superstructure to prevent barbarians using it. Stumps of the piers survive on both banks. Upstream in the Iron Gates gorge, the Tabula Traiana inscription (100) records the cutting of a towpath road into the cliff.

alcantara_bridge.detail: The inscriptions on the small temple at one end and on the triumphal arch at the centre name Trajan and the contributing towns. Its largest arches span almost 29 m. The bridge was broken in wars in 1214, 1760 and 1809 and repeatedly restored, and still carries traffic. Lacer was buried in the temple beside it.

capture_of_longinus_105.detail: Dio tells the story. Decebalus had also sent deserters to assassinate Trajan in Moesia. Decebalus offered to return Longinus's body and ten captives in exchange for the freedman, whom Trajan refused to surrender. The episode shows the desperate final phase of Dacian resistance.

plutarch_parallel_lives.detail: Plutarch was a Roman citizen (Lucius Mestrius Plutarchus) and, according to the Suda, received consular ornaments from Trajan and a procuratorship of Achaea from Hadrian, though these honours are doubted. He stressed that he wrote lives, not histories, revealing character in small things. Through Amyot's French and North's English translations the Lives became Shakespeare's main source for Julius Caesar, Antony and Cleopatra and Coriolanus.

annexation_of_arabia.detail: Coins proclaim ARABIA ADQVISITA ('acquired'), not 'captured'. The Via Nova Traiana from Bostra to Aila on the Red Sea, completed 111-114, carried milestones stating that Trajan 'reduced Arabia to the form of a province and opened and paved a new road from the borders of Syria to the Red Sea'. The Babatha archive from the Cave of Letters shows Roman law and administration operating in the new province within a generation. Petra continued to flourish.
scholarship: Bowersock, Roman Arabia (1983)

siege_of_sarmizegetusa.detail: The site, at 1,200 m in the Orăștie mountains, contains a fortified hill, a sacred precinct with circular and rectangular sanctuaries and an andesite 'sun disc'. After capture a legionary detachment was stationed there and the sanctuaries were dismantled. Decebalus escaped with a few followers.

death_of_decebalus.detail: Maximus's tombstone, found in 1965 at Grammeni near Philippi, narrates his career and shows him galloping towards the falling king, matching Column scene CXLV. The Dacian noble Bicilis betrayed the treasure Decebalus had buried under the diverted river Sargetia. The king became a Romanian national hero in the modern period.
scholarship: Speidel, 'The captor of Decebalus', JRS 60 (1970)

province_of_dacia_created.detail: Eutropius's phrase about the colonists, combined with claims that the Dacian population was annihilated, fed the modern controversy over Daco-Roman continuity and the origins of the Romanians. The gold mines of the Apuseni mountains were exploited by Illyrian (Pirustae) miners brought in for the purpose; the wax tablets from Alburnus Maior (Roșia Montană), dating from 131 to 167, preserve their labour contracts and sales. The province was abandoned by Aurelian around 271-275.
province_of_dacia_created.debate: Extent of depopulation and Daco-Roman continuity.
scholarship: Oltean, Dacia: Landscape, Colonisation and Romanisation (2007)

dacian_treasure_of_decebalus.detail: John Lydus, quoting Trajan's physician Crito, gives figures of five million pounds of gold and ten million of silver, almost certainly inflated by a factor of ten or more, plus 500,000 prisoners. Even reduced, the booty funded the games of 107 (123 days with 11,000 animals and 10,000 gladiators), the Forum of Trajan, the baths, the alimenta and an upturn in coin output. Dacia's gold mines at Alburnus Maior (Rosia Montana) were exploited by Illyrian miners brought in after the conquest.
dacian_treasure_of_decebalus.debate: Size of the booty: Crito's figures are generally reduced by Carcopino and others.

colonia_ulpia_traiana_sarmizegetusa.detail: The foundation inscription names Scaurianus. The colony, laid out on the site of a legionary camp, had a forum, amphitheatre and the seat of the provincial council of the three Dacias. Eutropius (8.6) says Trajan brought "infinite numbers of people from the whole Roman world" to repopulate Dacia, though the scale of Dacian depopulation is disputed.

dacian_triumph_107.detail: Dacian booty financed the Forum of Trajan, the baths on the Esquiline and other works; some scholars link a fall in the price of gold to the influx. The silver content of the denarius was reduced to around 89%. The Fasti Ostienses record further games and a naumachia in 109.

markets_of_trajan.detail: Brick stamps date the construction to the early Trajanic years; the work is attributed to Apollodorus or his circle. The complex was probably not a market in the modern sense but a mixture of shops, offices (perhaps of the procurators of the Forum and the annona) and storage. Its great hall, roofed with six cross vaults, anticipates later bath and basilica design. It was converted into a fortified convent and the Torre delle Milizie in the Middle Ages and is now a museum.
markets_of_trajan.debate: Function of the complex (market, offices or both) is debated.

trajan_recoinage_107.detail: The restored types reproduce some 50 Republican moneyers' designs and earlier emperors from Caesar to Titus. Hoard evidence shows the disappearance of heavier pre-Neronian denarii from circulation after this date, supporting the idea of a deliberate recall. The Dacian booty may have made the operation possible.

baths_of_trajan.detail: The complex covered about 10 hectares, three times the Baths of Titus next door. The Fasti Ostienses give the date, two days before the opening of the Aqua Traiana. Its plan set the model for the Baths of Caracalla and Diocletian. Building over the Domus Aurea preserved its rooms, whose rediscovery around 1480 inspired Renaissance "grotesque" decoration.

aqua_traiana.detail: Coins show a reclining river god in a grotto with the legend AQVA TRAIANA. The aqueduct drove mills on the Janiculum that ground the city's grain in late antiquity; when the Goths cut it in 537 Belisarius set up floating mills on the Tiber. Pope Paul V restored it as the Acqua Paola (1612). In 2009-2010 its source sanctuary (nymphaeum) was identified under a church near Manziana.

tropaeum_traiani_dedicated.detail: Its 54 metopes, carved in a vigorous provincial style, show Roman legionaries in segmented and mail armour fighting Dacians with the two-handed falx, Sarmatians and Germanic warriors; some legionaries wear greaves and arm guards, perhaps an adaptation to the falx. The town of Tropaeum Traiani grew beside it. The monument was reconstructed in concrete in 1977, with the originals in the site museum.

pliny_in_bithynia.detail: Pliny executed those who persisted after being asked three times if they were Christians, 'whatever it was they professed, their stubbornness deserved punishment', released those who sacrificed and cursed Christ, and tortured two slave women called deaconesses (ministrae), finding only 'a depraved, excessive superstition'. Trajan replied that Christians were not to be sought out, anonymous accusations were not to be admitted ('not in keeping with our age'), but those convicted who refused to sacrifice must be punished. The same correspondence shows Trajan refusing a fire brigade of 150 men at Nicomedia lest it become a political club.
pliny_in_bithynia.debate: Exact dates of the governorship (109-111 or 110-112).
scholarship: Sherwin-White, The Letters of Pliny: A Historical and Social Commentary (1966)

trajans_harbour_at_portus.detail: Each side of the basin was 358 m long, giving some 2 km of quays; the basin survives as a lake in the Torlonia estate near Fiumicino airport. Recent excavations (Portus Project) have found a huge shipshed or arsenal and the Palazzo Imperiale. Portus gradually supplanted Ostia, which saw a building boom under Trajan and Hadrian. Trajan also built harbours at Centumcellae (Civitavecchia) and Ancona.

martyrdom_of_ignatius.detail: The letters are the earliest witness to a single bishop (monepiskopos) presiding over presbyters and deacons in each church, attack docetists who denied Christ's physical suffering and Judaising Christians, and use the term "catholic church" for the first time. His letter to the Romans begs them not to intervene: "I am God's wheat, ground by the teeth of wild beasts." The authenticity of the "middle recension" of seven letters, established by Lightfoot and Zahn, is still occasionally challenged.
martyrdom_of_ignatius.debate: Date (often c. 110-117) and authenticity of the letters.

via_nova_traiana_built.detail: The road linked the legionary base of III Cyrenaica at Bostra with Philadelphia (Amman), Petra and the port of Aila, serving the incense and Red Sea trade as well as military movements; hundreds of milestones survive. Papyri from the Cave of Letters and the Babatha archive show the province's administration within a generation of annexation.

forum_of_trajan.detail: Building it required cutting away the saddle between the Capitoline and Quirinal; the Markets of Trajan on the Quirinal slope date from the same project. Ammianus records the awe of Constantius II on seeing it in 357, despairing of imitating anything but the horse. The Fasti Ostienses give the date of the Basilica Ulpia's dedication.
scholarship: Packer, The Forum of Trajan in Rome (1997)

trajans_column.detail: Trajan's Column was dedicated on 12 May 113 (Fasti Ostienses) in a small court between the two libraries of the Forum of Trajan, behind the Basilica Ulpia. Built of 17 drums of Luna marble, 29.8 m high (100 Roman feet) on a pedestal, about 38 m with the base, it carries a continuous spiral frieze about 200 m long, winding 23 times around the shaft, with some 2,600 figures in 155 scenes narrating the two Dacian wars (101-102 and 105-106), separated by a figure of Victory writing on a shield. The narrative begins with the crossing of the Danube on a pontoon bridge watched by the river god and continues with marching, building camps, roads and bridges, sacrifices, speeches (adlocutiones), battles, sieges, the submission of Dacian chiefs, Trajan's bridge at Drobeta, the storming of Sarmizegetusa, the Dacians' poisoning themselves and finally the suicide of Decebalus as Roman cavalrymen reach him, and the deportation of the Dacians. Trajan appears some 58 times. The frieze shows far more construction work than fighting, an image of the army as an instrument of order. The designer is often thought to be Apollodorus of Damascus. The column's height, according to the dedication inscription (whose letters became the model for Roman capitals), showed how deep the hill had been cut to make room for the forum, though this reading is debated. A spiral staircase of 185 steps inside, lit by small windows, leads to the top, where a bronze statue of Trajan stood (replaced by St Peter in 1587). Trajan's ashes and those of Plotina were placed in a golden urn in the pedestal, an exception to the ban on burial within the pomerium. The frieze is a key source for Roman military equipment, though its depiction of legionaries in segmented armour and auxiliaries in mail is partly conventional. Its sources may have been Trajan's lost commentaries on the war (Dacica). The relief could not have been read easily from the ground; it may have been viewed from the library terraces. It inspired the Column of Marcus Aurelius and, much later, Napoleon's column in the Place Vendome.
trajans_column.debate: Meaning of the inscription's statement about the height of the hill removed, and how the frieze was meant to be viewed.
scholarship: Lepper and Frere, Trajan's Column (1988)
Settis (ed.), La Colonna Traiana (1988)
Coarelli, The Column of Trajan (2000)

annexation_of_armenia_114.detail: The Senate voted Trajan the title Optimus, formalising an epithet used for years. Fronto and Dio criticised the treatment of Parthamasiris as a breach of faith. The annexation broke the Rhandeia compromise that had kept the peace for fifty years.

arch_of_trajan_beneventum.detail: The arch is the best-preserved of its type, with panels facing the city on domestic themes (the Senate and Capitoline gods welcoming Trajan, the alimenta, veterans' settlements) and those facing the country on provincial ones (the Danube frontier, Mesopotamia). Some reliefs may have been completed under Hadrian, who appears prominently.

antioch_earthquake_115.detail: Dio describes survivors buried for days living on milk from a mother's breast. Malalas gives the date. Trajan dedicated a temple to Zeus Kasios on Mount Casius in thanks. Reconstruction was ordered on a large scale.

diaspora_revolt_cyrene.detail: Inscriptions at Cyrene record Hadrianic restoration of the baths, temple of Apollo and roads 'torn up and destroyed in the Jewish tumult'. Papyri from Egypt include letters to the strategos Apollonios from his mother and wife fearing for his life. Quintus Marcius Turbo crushed the Egyptian and Cyrenaican risings; Jews were afterwards forbidden to set foot on Cyprus. The Alexandrian community, once the largest in the diaspora, never recovered.
scholarship: Pucci Ben Zeev, Diaspora Judaism in Turmoil, 116/117 CE (2005)

trajan_takes_nisibis_and_batnae_115.detail: Dio says Trajan was hailed imperator several times and the Senate voted him the right to celebrate as many triumphs as he wished. Mannus, the Arab dynast, and Sporaces of Anthemusia submitted or were deposed. In winter 115/116 Trajan was at Antioch when the earthquake struck.

capture_of_ctesiphon_116.detail: Osroes fled east. Trajan then sailed down to Charax and the Persian Gulf, where Dio says he watched a ship departing for India and lamented that he was too old to follow Alexander. The Fasti Ostienses date the announcement of the Parthicus title to February 116, which complicates the chronology of the campaigns.

provinces_of_mesopotamia_and_assyria.detail: Seleucia, Nisibis and Edessa rebelled; Maximus Santra was killed; Lusius Quietus retook Nisibis and Edessa and Erucius Clarus and Julius Alexander burned Seleucia. Coins show Trajan crowning Parthamaspates with the legend REX PARTHIS DATVS. Whether 'Assyria' was a real province (perhaps Adiabene) is disputed.
provinces_of_mesopotamia_and_assyria.debate: Existence and location of the province of Assyria.

trajan_at_the_persian_gulf_116.detail: The Persian Gulf expedition was the farthest point of Roman conquest. A Latin inscription from the Farasan islands in the southern Red Sea shows Roman presence in the region under the Antonines. While Trajan was in the south, the newly conquered lands revolted behind him.

mesopotamian_revolt_116.detail: Trajan then failed to take Hatra in 117, his army suffering from heat and flies, and fell ill. Quietus's brutal suppression of the Mesopotamian Jews led to his appointment as governor of Judaea. Hadrian abandoned Mesopotamia and Assyria on his accession, and Parthamaspates was soon driven out, becoming king of Osroene.

death_of_trajan.detail: After failing to take Hatra in 117 and with his eastern conquests in revolt, Trajan, now 63 and in poor health, left Antioch for Rome, leaving Hadrian in command of the army in Syria. He suffered a stroke that left him partly paralysed and developed oedema, and died at Selinus in Cilicia (renamed Traianopolis) on or about 8 August 117. Plotina, his niece Matidia, the praetorian prefect Attianus and the household were with him. The circumstances of Hadrian's succession were controversial from the start. Hadrian, Trajan's cousin once removed and husband of his grand-niece Sabina, had been consul in 108, governor of Syria and evidently favoured, but had not been formally adopted or given the title Caesar. On 9 August Hadrian at Antioch received letters announcing his adoption, and on 11 August news of Trajan's death, which he celebrated as his dies imperii. Dio, citing his father Apronianus, a later governor of Cilicia, reports that the adoption was a fiction arranged by Plotina, who concealed Trajan's death for several days and had someone impersonate his weak voice behind a curtain; the Historia Augusta repeats rumours that Trajan intended to leave the choice to the Senate or even to name Neratius Priscus. A recently noticed detail is that the letters announcing the adoption were signed by Plotina, not Trajan, and that Trajan's chamberlain Phaedimus died suddenly days later. Whatever the truth, the Syrian army acclaimed Hadrian, and the Senate accepted him. Trajan's ashes were taken to Rome by Plotina and Matidia and placed in his column; he was deified and celebrated with a posthumous Parthian triumph, his image carried in the procession. His reign was remembered as the empire's zenith: the Senate later wished new emperors to be "luckier than Augustus and better than Trajan" (felicior Augusto, melior Traiano). Hadrian immediately abandoned Mesopotamia and Assyria and executed four consular generals in 118, which poisoned his relations with the Senate.
death_of_trajan.debate: Whether Trajan really adopted Hadrian or Plotina staged the adoption after his death.

hadrian_abandons_eastern_conquests.detail: The Historia Augusta claims he justified this by Cato's dictum that Macedonia should be freed because it could not be held, and that he even considered abandoning Dacia, dissuaded by the fate of the colonists. The removal of the superstructure of Trajan's Danube bridge was ascribed to the same defensive policy. Hostile sources attribute the retreat to jealousy of Trajan's glory; strategically it recognised the impossibility of holding Babylonia.

siege_of_hatra_117.detail: Dio notes that the sun-god protected the city, and that Septimius Severus would fail there again (198-199). Hatra's great temple complex and Aramaic inscriptions survive, though damaged by the Islamic State in 2015.

lusius_quietus_in_judaea_117.detail: The Mishnah (Sotah 9.14) lists decrees issued "in the war of Qitos" banning bridal crowns and the teaching of Greek. Hadrian recalled and then executed Quietus in 118 with three other consulars. Legio II Traiana may have been stationed in Judaea at this time, giving the province a second legion before the Bar Kokhba war.

british_unrest_117.detail: The crisis is connected in modern discussion with the disappearance of legio IX Hispana, last attested at York in 108, though the legion's fate is debated (transfer to the Rhine at Nijmegen and loss in the East later are favoured). The unrest was a background to the decision to build Hadrian's Wall from 122.

execution_of_the_four_consulars.detail: All four were Trajanic marshals or potential rivals; Nigrinus may have been an alternative heir. The affair poisoned Hadrian's relations with the Senate for his whole reign. He tried to repair the damage with a donative, the remission of debts and gladiatorial shows.

debt_cancellation_118.detail: Coins proclaim RELIQVA VETERA HS NOVIES MILL(ies) ABOLITA, and an inscription of the Senate and people (ILS 309) thanks him as the first emperor to free citizens and their descendants from such debts. The reliefs known as the Anaglypha Traiani in the Curia, which show tablets being burned, may depict this or a similar act of Trajan. Hadrian also ordered periodic reviews of debts every fifteen years.

pantheon_rebuilt.detail: The Pantheon standing today was built under Hadrian, probably between about 114 and 125, on the site of Agrippa's temple of 25 BC, which had burned in 80, been restored by Domitian and burned again in 110. Brick stamps date most of the fabric to 115-125, suggesting the project may have been started under Trajan, perhaps by Apollodorus. Hadrian reinstated Agrippa's original inscription on the porch frieze (M AGRIPPA L F COS TERTIVM FECIT), in keeping with his policy of not putting his own name on buildings he restored, which led scholars until the nineteenth century to date the building to Agrippa. The building combines a pedimented porch of sixteen monolithic granite columns (the front eight of grey Mons Claudianus granite, each 11.8 m and weighing about 60 tonnes; the planned 50-foot columns apparently could not be obtained, so the porch is lower than the intermediate block, producing an awkward junction) with a rotunda whose interior diameter and height are both 43.3 m, so that a sphere would fit exactly inside. The unreinforced concrete dome, still the largest of its kind in the world, rests on walls 6 m thick and is lightened by graded aggregates: heavy travertine and tuff at the bottom, then brick, and light pumice and scoria near the top, with 140 coffers and an open oculus 8.9 m across. Hidden relieving arches in the drum distribute the load. The interior was paved and revetted with coloured marbles from Egypt, Numidia and Phrygia. Its function is debated: Dio says the name came from the statues of many gods or the resemblance of the dome to the heavens, and that Hadrian held court there; it may have been a dynastic shrine as much as a temple. The sun's disc entering through the oculus moves around the interior, and on 21 April, Rome's birthday, its noon beam strikes the entrance, possibly by design. Septimius Severus and Caracalla restored it in 202, and in 609 Pope Boniface IV consecrated it as the church of Santa Maria ad Martyres, which saved it. Its bronze roof tiles were stripped by Constans II in 663 and the porch bronzes by Urban VIII in 1625.
pantheon_rebuilt.debate: Whether begun under Trajan; function as temple, dynastic hall or audience hall.
scholarship: Hetland, 'Dating the Pantheon', JRA 20 (2007)
Wilson Jones, Principles of Roman Architecture (2000)

hadrians_villa.detail: Innovative domed and curvilinear spaces, such as the Maritime Theatre (an island retreat ringed by a moat) and the Piazza d'Oro, show architectural experimentation probably by the emperor himself. The villa's statuary, including copies of the Erechtheion caryatids around the Canopus pool and images of Antinous, has filled museums since the Renaissance. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
scholarship: MacDonald and Pinto, Hadrian's Villa and Its Legacy (1995)

roxolani_and_dacia_118.detail: Dio and Eutropius preserve a story that Hadrian considered giving up Dacia and was dissuaded by the presence of so many Roman colonists; he removed the superstructure of Trajan's Danube bridge to prevent its use by raiders. The Roxolanian king Rasparaganus later lived at Pola as a Roman citizen, Publius Aelius Rasparaganus.

juvenal_satires.detail: Book 1 refers to the trial of Marius Priscus (100); Satire 7 opens with hope in a new Caesar, probably Hadrian; Satire 15 mentions a consul of 127. Juvenal gave the world "panem et circenses" (10.81), "mens sana in corpore sano" (10.356) and "quis custodiet ipsos custodes?" (6.347-348, in the Oxford fragment). Almost nothing reliable is known of his life; a late tradition says he was exiled to Egypt in old age.

hadrians_first_journey.detail: Hadrian spent more than half his reign outside Italy, governing as a travelling emperor accompanied by architects, engineers and builders organised like a legion. Coin series celebrate provinces, armies (EXERCITVS) and his 'arrivals' (ADVENTVS). He enforced discipline personally, sleeping in the open and marching 20 miles in armour. A second journey (128-132) took him to Africa, Greece, Asia, Syria, Arabia, Judaea and Egypt.
scholarship: Birley, Hadrian: The Restless Emperor (1997)
Halfmann, Itinera principum (1986)

hadrian_in_germania_121.detail: The Historia Augusta describes stakes planted deep and fastened together; dendrochronology has dated felled timbers of the Upper German palisade to the winter of 119/120 and later, matching the account. Hadrian ate camp food (bacon, cheese, sour wine), marched 20 miles in full kit and examined arms and soldiers' ages personally.

plotina_epicurean_school_121.detail: The inscription (IG II2 1099) shows an empress acting as patron of a philosophical school and her personal adherence to Epicureanism. Marcus Aurelius later endowed chairs for all four major schools at Athens in 176.

suetonius_de_vita_caesarum.detail: An inscription from Hippo Regius records his career: in charge of the imperial libraries, of studies (a studiis) and of correspondence. His access to the palace archives shows in quotations from Augustus's letters in the early lives; the later lives are thinner, perhaps after he lost access. The thematic arrangement (family, career, public acts, private habits, death) and gossip made it the model for imperial biography from the Historia Augusta to Einhard.

hadrians_wall_begun.detail: Hadrian visited Britain in 122 and, according to the Historia Augusta, "was the first to build a wall 80 miles long to separate the Romans from the barbarians". The work was directed by the governor Aulus Platorius Nepos, who came from Lower Germany with legio VI Victrix, and carried out by the three British legions (II Augusta, VI Victrix and XX Valeria Victrix), whose building inscriptions survive. The original plan provided for a stone wall 10 Roman feet wide from Newcastle to the Irthing and a turf wall 20 feet wide from there to Bowness-on-Solway, with a ditch in front, small fortlets every Roman mile (milecastles) with gates, and two turrets between each. Before completion the plan changed: the stone wall was narrowed to 8 feet or less (the "narrow wall" on "broad foundations" seen at several sites), and some sixteen forts were added on the line itself, such as Housesteads, Chesters and Birdoswald, moving the garrison from the Stanegate road behind onto the wall. Behind the wall a great earthwork known as the Vallum, a flat-bottomed ditch with mounds on either side, marked the southern edge of the military zone. The wall was extended east to Wallsend and supplemented by forts and towers along the Cumbrian coast. The wall's purpose is debated: a military barrier against attack, a means of controlling movement and taxing trade through the milecastle gates, a statement of imperial power, or all of these; its forts housed auxiliary units, not legions, and it was not designed for fighting from the top. The Vindolanda tablets, written in the years just before the wall, mention the "Brittunculi" (wretched little Britons). Construction took about six years for the main elements. The Antonine Wall superseded it from 142, but it was recommissioned around 158-160 and remained the frontier, with modifications, until the end of Roman Britain. The Staffordshire Moorlands pan, a souvenir bronze vessel naming four western forts, and the Rudge cup show that it was perceived as a monument in antiquity. It became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1987.
hadrians_wall_begun.debate: Purpose: defensive barrier, customs and control line or symbolic statement.
scholarship: Breeze and Dobson, Hadrian's Wall (4th ed. 2000)
Hodgson, Hadrian's Wall: Archaeology and History at the Limit of Rome's Empire (2017)

hadrian_in_spain_122.detail: Hadrian never visited his ancestral town of Italica, though he gave it colonial status and lavish buildings. The Italicenses notoriously declined colonial status in favour of being a municipium, Hadrian's speech on which is preserved by Aulus Gellius. Recruitment resistance (the Italians mocked it as "Trebatian", the Spaniards objected strongly) suggests difficulty in filling the legions.

hadrian_euphrates_meeting_123.detail: The Historia Augusta credits Hadrian with resolving the crisis by conversation alone. Hadrian sent the daughter back in 129 and promised the golden throne taken at Ctesiphon, which Antoninus Pius later refused to return. The episode shows Hadrian's policy of securing the frontier by diplomacy after abandoning Trajan's conquests.

hadrian_in_bithynia_123.detail: Hadrian then toured the cities of Asia, founding Hadrianotherae where he had killed a bear, and Hadriani and Hadrianeia in Mysia. The cities competed for his benefactions, and the many places named Hadrianopolis or Hadriane date from these journeys. Antinous is first securely attested in Hadrian's company on the later journey of 128-130.

hadrian_eleusinian_initiation_124.detail: He returned to Eleusis for the higher grade (epopteia) in 128. The Athenian oil law, preserved in an inscription, required producers to sell a third of their oil to the city. Hadrian's identification with Athens culminated in the completion of the Olympieion and the founding of the Panhellenion in 131-132.

hadrian_climbs_etna_125.detail: The Historia Augusta preserves both anecdotes. Hadrian's curiosity (curiositas) and love of travel, satirised by the poet Florus ("I don't want to be Caesar, wandering among the Britons ... enduring Scythian frosts"), to which Hadrian replied with a jibe about Florus haunting taverns, were key traits of his self-presentation.

vipasca_tablets.detail: The procurator of the mines sold the right to work a shaft; the lessee had to begin work within 25 days and pay half the ore to the fiscus. Rules governed drainage galleries, timber supports and the sale of shares. The baths had to be heated daily and open for women from dawn to the seventh hour and men in the afternoon, and teachers were exempt from taxes.

lambaesis_address.detail: The emperor's remarks are specific and technical: he praises a cohort for building a wall in less time than usual, notes that the legion was understrength because a cohort had been sent to help another province and men transferred, criticises cavalry for chasing too fast, and commends the legate Quintus Fabius Catullinus. The inscriptions (CIL VIII 2532 and 18042) show Hadrian's hands-on style of command.
scholarship: Speidel, Emperor Hadrian's Speeches to the African Army: A New Text (2006)

hadrian_second_athens_stay_128.detail: Coins from 128 call him P P and Sabina appears as Augusta with a new hairstyle. Hadrian's building in Athens included a new quarter (the "city of Hadrian" marked by his arch, inscribed on one side "This is Athens, the old city of Theseus" and on the other "This is the city of Hadrian and not of Theseus"), an aqueduct finished under Antoninus, a gymnasium and the great library.

hadrian_in_asia_and_syria_129.detail: At the conference the Iberian king Pharasmanes II refused to come, while others received gifts. Hadrian quarrelled with Antioch, planning to split Syria, and favoured Damascus and Tyre. A Palmyrene inscription honours the local notable Males Agrippa for hosting Hadrian and his army. Petra became Hadriane Petra.

death_of_antinous.detail: Dio reports that Hadrian claimed it was an accident but others said Antinous sacrificed himself to prolong the emperor's life. Over a hundred portrait statues survive, more than of almost any other ancient figure apart from emperors, as well as coins struck by Greek cities, and Hadrian named a star after him. The obelisk now on the Pincian carries hieroglyphs describing his deification.
scholarship: Lambert, Beloved and God (1984)
Vout, Power and Eroticism in Imperial Rome (2007)

foundation_of_antinoopolis.detail: Antinoites enjoyed exemption from liturgies elsewhere, the right to intermarry with Egyptians and an alimentary fund for their children. The city was laid out on a Hippodamian grid with a theatre, hippodrome and colonnaded streets; the Via Hadriana (137) linked it with Berenice on the Red Sea. The cult of Antinous spread across the Greek East with games, temples and some 2,000 statues and coins. The Obelisk of Antinous now on the Pincian probably stood at his tomb, possibly at Hadrian's Villa.

colossus_of_memnon_visit_130.detail: The statue, cracked by an earthquake in 27 BC, emitted a sound at sunrise, probably caused by heating and evaporation of dew in the fissures; it fell silent after Septimius Severus repaired it c. 199. Some 107 Greek and Latin inscriptions by Roman visitors, including prefects of Egypt, cover its legs.

sources.w: Les inscriptions grecques et latines du Colosse de Memnon (Bernand)

foundation_of_aelia_capitolina.detail: Coins of Aelia showing the founding ritual of ploughing the boundary have been found in hoards together with Bar Kokhba coins, supporting a foundation before the revolt. The Historia Augusta gives a different cause, a ban on circumcision. After 135 Jews were forbidden to enter the city except, according to later tradition, on the 9th of Av. The city's Roman plan (the cardo, the Damascus Gate) underlies the Old City today.
foundation_of_aelia_capitolina.debate: Whether the colony was founded before or after the revolt; relative weight of the colony and the circumcision ban as causes.

edictum_perpetuum.detail: The 'perpetual edict' ended the praetor's creative role in Roman law, shifting legal innovation to imperial constitutions and juristic interpretation. Its text, lost as such, was reconstructed by Otto Lenel (1883) from commentaries quoted in Justinian's Digest. Julianus, a North African from Hadrumetum, held a double salary as quaestor for his learning and became one of the most cited jurists.
scholarship: Lenel, Das Edictum Perpetuum (1883; 3rd ed. 1927)

hadrian_in_judaea_and_arabia_130.detail: The triple Arch of Hadrian at Gerasa, dated 129/130, stands south of the city. Coins of 130-131 advertise his arrival (ADVENTVI AVG IVDAEAE). Whether the foundation of Aelia and the ban on circumcision provoked the Bar Kokhba revolt or followed it is one of the central debates of the period.
hadrian_in_judaea_and_arabia_130.debate: Whether Aelia Capitolina was founded before (Dio) or after (Eusebius) the revolt.

hadrian_in_egypt_130.detail: A papyrus fragment of Pancrates' poem describes the lion's wounding and the red lotus said to have sprung from its blood, which was named after Antinous. Hadrian's questions to the professors and his mockery of their pretensions became anecdotes in the Historia Augusta. From Alexandria the imperial party sailed up the Nile in the autumn.

hadrian_legal_reforms.detail: He also restricted the Silanian torture of slaves to those near enough to have heard, placed equestrians rather than freedmen in the palace secretariats, created the advocatus fisci, and gave his council (consilium) of jurists a formal role. The SC Tertullianum, passed under Hadrian, gave a mother with the ius liberorum the right to inherit from her children. The Italian consulars were abolished by Antoninus and revived as iuridici by Marcus.

panhellenion.detail: Member cities from Achaea, Macedonia, Thrace, Asia, Crete and Cyrene sent delegates; Hadrian was honoured as Panhellenios and Olympios. The Arch of Hadrian bears inscriptions on its two faces: 'This is Athens, the ancient city of Theseus' and 'This is the city of Hadrian and not of Theseus'. Pausanias describes the chryselephantine cult statue and the many statues of Hadrian dedicated by cities.
scholarship: Spawforth and Walker, 'The world of the Panhellenion', JRS 75-76 (1985-86)

arrian_periplus_131.detail: At Trapezus he found Hadrian's statue poorly made and asked for a better one; at Phasis he described the fort with its four hundred picked soldiers, artillery and ditches, and at Apsarus he paid five cohorts. He recorded the client kings of the Colchian peoples, appointed by Hadrian or Trajan. Arrian's other works include the Anabasis of Alexander, the Indike, the Tactica (136) and the Discourses of Epictetus.

lex_hadriana_de_rudibus_agris.detail: The law extended the earlier Lex Manciana (known from Henchir Mettich, 116/117), under which coloni paid a third of their crops to the estate. The Souk el-Khmis inscription of 180-183 records tenants of the saltus Burunitanus appealing to Commodus against excessive labour demands by the contractor. The texts show the expansion of olive culture that made Africa the empire's oil producer.

outbreak_of_the_bar_kokhba_revolt.detail: The second great Jewish revolt broke out in 132 in Judaea under Shimon bar Kosiba, whom followers called Bar Kokhba ("son of the star", after Numbers 24.17) and opponents later Bar Koziba ("son of the lie"). Its causes are debated. Dio says it was provoked by Hadrian's foundation of the colony of Aelia Capitolina on the ruins of Jerusalem with a temple of Jupiter on the site of the Temple; the Historia Augusta claims it was a ban on circumcision, which Hadrian may have extended to Jews as part of a general prohibition on castration and mutilation. Eusebius dates Aelia's foundation after the war. The revolt was well prepared: Dio says the Jews had deliberately made defective weapons for the Romans so that they would be rejected and kept, and had built a network of underground hideouts, many of which have been found in the Judaean foothills. The rebels controlled much of Judaea, though probably not Jerusalem itself, and issued coins overstruck on Roman denarii and tetradrachms with legends "Year one of the redemption of Israel", "For the freedom of Israel" and images of the Temple facade. Bar Kosiba bore the title "nasi (prince) of Israel", and the priest Eleazar appears beside him on coins. Rabbi Akiva reputedly hailed him as the messiah, to which Yohanan ben Torta replied "Akiva, grass will grow from your cheeks and the son of David will still not have come." Christians who refused to support him were persecuted, according to Justin Martyr. The governor Tineius Rufus and the legate of Syria, Publicius Marcellus, could not contain the rising; legio XXII Deiotariana may have been destroyed. Hadrian summoned Sextus Julius Severus from Britain and drew troops from at least a dozen legions; the war lasted until 135 or 136 and ended with the fall of Betar. Hadrian himself seems to have been present for a time and omitted the customary formula "I and the army are well" in his report to the Senate, a sign of heavy losses. Hadrian took a second imperatorial acclamation, and Severus and others received triumphal ornaments.
outbreak_of_the_bar_kokhba_revolt.debate: Cause (Aelia Capitolina or the circumcision ban) and whether the rebels held Jerusalem; the fate of XXII Deiotariana.
scholarship: Eshel, 'The Bar Kochba Revolt, 132-135', in Cambridge History of Judaism IV (2006)
Schäfer (ed.), The Bar Kokhba War Reconsidered (2003)
