library_of_hadrian_athens_132.detail: The east side contained the book rooms with niches for scrolls, flanked by reading halls. Damaged in the Herulian sack of 267 and restored c. 410, it later contained a tetraconch church and then the Byzantine Megali Panagia. Its west facade with Corinthian columns still stands on Areos Street.

bar_kokhba_letters.detail: The letters show Bar Kosiba demanding the gathering of the four species for Sukkot, threatening officers who neglect orders, and administering land leases dated by "year of the redemption of Israel". The Babatha papers (35 documents, 94-132) illustrate marriage contracts, guardianship, property disputes and Roman provincial courts in Arabia. Skeletons in the Cave of Letters attest the refugees' fate.

pons_aelius_134.detail: The dedication inscription, recorded in the Middle Ages, dates it to Hadrian's 18th tribunician year. The bridge survives as the Ponte Sant'Angelo; Bernini's workshop added the ten angels with the instruments of the Passion in 1669-1671. In 1450 a crowd of jubilee pilgrims crushed on it caused the collapse of its parapets.

mausoleum_of_hadrian.detail: A spiral ramp led to the central burial chamber. Hadrian, Sabina and Lucius Aelius were among the first interred; the inscriptions of the burials were recorded before they were lost. Incorporated in the Aurelian Wall, it became a fortress; its defenders hurled statues on the Goths in 537. The name Castel Sant'Angelo derives from Gregory the Great's vision of the archangel Michael ending a plague in 590.

arrian_and_the_alans.detail: Arrian's 'Order of Battle against the Alans' (Ektaxis kata Alanon) survives in part, describing marching order and a defensive formation of legionaries with long pikes in eight ranks, archers and artillery behind, designed to break a heavy cavalry charge. It is the only surviving battle plan by a Roman commander. Arrian also wrote a Periplus of the Black Sea for Hadrian, the Anabasis of Alexander, and recorded Epictetus's Discourses.
scholarship: Bosworth, 'Arrian and the Alani', HSCP 81 (1977)

siege_of_betar.detail: Eusebius says the defenders perished from hunger and thirst. Rabbinic tradition dates the fall to the 9th of Av, the same day as the destructions of both Temples, and tells of rivers of blood. Remains of the Roman siege wall and camps survive around Khirbet el-Yahud near Battir. Hadrian and his generals received triumphal honours but Hadrian did not celebrate a triumph.

temple_of_venus_and_roma.detail: Dio tells that Apollodorus criticised the design, saying the seated goddesses were too tall for their cellae and would hit their heads if they stood up, and that Hadrian, already offended by an earlier jibe ('go and draw your pumpkins'), exiled and later executed him. Many historians doubt the story. The temple's date (dedication in 135 or 136/137) is uncertain; the Natalis Urbis (21 April) was celebrated there as the Romaia.

hadrianic_decrees_135.detail: Dio says 580,000 men were killed and 985 villages destroyed, figures probably exaggerated but reflecting the devastation of Judaea, after which the Jewish centre shifted to Galilee. Antoninus Pius allowed Jews to circumcise their own sons (Modestinus, Digest 48.8.11). The extent and duration of the "persecution" (shmad) is debated.
hadrianic_decrees_135.debate: Whether the circumcision ban caused the revolt or was a punishment for it.

syria_palaestina_renamed.detail: The name first appears in a military diploma of 139. Rabbinic tradition remembers the 'decrees of persecution' (gezerot) against Torah study and circumcision, and the martyrdom of Rabbi Akiva and other sages; Antoninus Pius later exempted Jews from the ban on circumcision. The rabbinic centre moved to Galilee (Usha, later Sepphoris and Tiberias), where the Mishnah was compiled c. 200.

succession_of_136_138.detail: Servianus, before dying, prayed that Hadrian might long for death and be unable to die. The double adoption laid down the succession for two generations and reveals Hadrian's interest in Marcus, whom he nicknamed Verissimus. Some scholars think Antoninus was meant only as a placeholder for Marcus.

tariff_of_palmyra_137.detail: The tariff shows that taxes on goods consumed in the city were set locally but under Roman supervision, and preserves the rule that salt was to be measured in the Roman way. The stone, 5 m wide, was taken to St Petersburg in 1901 by Prince Abamelek-Lazarev and is in the Hermitage.

death_of_hadrian.detail: He was first buried at Puteoli; his ashes were moved to the great Mausoleum across the Tiber (now Castel Sant'Angelo), completed by Antoninus in 139. The Senate, resentful, was reluctant to deify him; Antoninus insisted, and received the name Pius, perhaps for this act of filial devotion. Marguerite Yourcenar's novel Memoirs of Hadrian (1951) shaped his modern image.

accession_of_antoninus_pius.detail: The Historia Augusta offers several explanations for 'Pius': his devotion to Hadrian, his support of his aged father-in-law in the Senate, or his saving of senators Hadrian had condemned. His reign, the longest since Augustus, is almost without narrative history: Dio's account is lost except for fragments and the Historia Augusta life is brief. Aelius Aristides's oration To Rome and the later image of the Antonine age as the happiest in human history (Gibbon) derive from it.

deification_of_hadrian_139.detail: Other explanations of the cognomen in the Historia Augusta include his supporting his aged father-in-law in the Senate, saving men Hadrian had condemned in his last illness, and his honours for Hadrian. Antoninus completed the Mausoleum, founded games at Puteoli where Hadrian was first buried, and dedicated a temple of Divus Hadrianus (145). The episode set the tone of a reign built on reconciliation and continuity.

lollius_urbicus_british_campaign.detail: Inscriptions from Corbridge (139 and 140) record building by II Augusta under Urbicus. Coins of 143-144 show Britannia seated on a rock. The motive for advancing beyond Hadrian's Wall is debated: genuine pressure from the Selgovae and others, or the new emperor's need for military prestige, as Fronto implied.

marcus_made_caesar_139.detail: Marcus was designated consul for 140 at eighteen. His education under Fronto (Latin rhetoric), Herodes Atticus (Greek) and the Stoic Junius Rusticus is recorded with gratitude in Meditations Book 1. Lucius, the other adoptee, was given no title until 161.

death_of_faustina_the_elder.detail: The Temple of Antoninus and Faustina survives as the church of San Lorenzo in Miranda, its porch columns still bearing grooves from failed medieval attempts to pull them down. Huge coin issues for DIVA FAVSTINA continued for years, among the most abundant of the period.

valentinus_in_rome.detail: Rome in the 140s was home to rival Christian teachers, including Marcion, Valentinus, Cerdo and Justin. The Gospel of Truth found at Nag Hammadi (1945) may be by Valentinus. Irenaeus's Against Heresies (c. 180) was written chiefly against the Valentinians, and the reaction to such teachers shaped the idea of orthodoxy, the canon and episcopal succession.

temple_of_antoninus_and_faustina_141.detail: The cipollino columns of the pronaos stand to their full height because the temple became the church of San Lorenzo in Miranda (by the 11th century); grooves cut high on the columns show where medieval builders tried to pull them down. The frieze shows griffins and candelabra.

rex_quadis_datus_141.detail: Antoninus's reign was the high point of Roman diplomatic prestige: the Historia Augusta says kings of the Bactrians, Indians and Hyrcanians sent envoys, that he deterred a Parthian invasion of Armenia by letter alone, and that Pharasmanes II of Iberia visited Rome and was allowed to sacrifice on the Capitol, his equestrian statue set up in the temple of Bellona.

antonine_wall.detail: Shortly after his accession Antoninus Pius ordered an advance into southern Scotland, and his governor Quintus Lollius Urbicus, after campaigns in 139-142, built a new frontier across the Forth-Clyde isthmus, about 160 km north of Hadrian's Wall. The Antonine Wall ran 37 Roman miles (about 60 km) from Bo'ness (Carriden) on the Forth to Old Kilpatrick on the Clyde. Unlike Hadrian's Wall it was built of turf on a stone foundation about 14 Roman feet wide, with a wide, deep ditch in front and a military road behind. The original plan seems to have had six large forts at roughly eight-mile intervals and fortlets every mile, but it was soon modified, with more forts added, giving some sixteen or seventeen at intervals of about two miles, such as Rough Castle, Bar Hill and Bearsden. Building was carried out by detachments of the three British legions, which recorded the lengths they completed on finely carved distance slabs, some twenty of which survive, showing victory scenes, sacrifices and bound captives. The Bridgeness slab depicts the suovetaurilia sacrifice. The wall was an expression of Antoninus's need for military prestige as much as of strategic necessity; he took his only imperatorial acclamation for the British victory, and Fronto compared the achievement to a triumph won by an emperor who stayed at home. Hadrian's Wall was partly decommissioned, its milecastle gates removed and the Vallum crossed. The occupation of the Antonine Wall was short. Much of the evidence once taken to indicate two periods of occupation with an interruption c. 155-158 has been reinterpreted, and the current view is that it was abandoned in the early 160s, at the start of Marcus Aurelius's reign, when Hadrian's Wall was restored. Septimius Severus reoccupied some of its forts during his Scottish campaigns (208-211). The name "Grim's Dyke" was used for it in the Middle Ages. It became part of the "Frontiers of the Roman Empire" World Heritage Site in 2008.
antonine_wall.debate: Date and sequence of abandonment; whether there were one or two periods of occupation.
scholarship: Breeze, The Antonine Wall (2006)
Hanson and Maxwell, Rome's North West Frontier (1983)

rhodes_earthquake_142.detail: Pausanias (8.43.4) and the Historia Augusta mention Antoninus's aid to Rhodes and the cities of Asia. Aelius Aristides' Rhodian oration describes the ruined city. The Opramoas inscription, with some seventy documents, is a key text for euergetism and imperial correspondence in the provinces.

fronto_correspondence.detail: They show the young Marcus's affection for his teacher, his daily life at Antoninus's villas (grape harvests, hunting, illness), and his turn from rhetoric to philosophy, which Fronto regretted. Fronto's archaising style (elocutio novella) favoured early Latin authors. The letters to Lucius include material on the Parthian war, and Fronto's Principia Historiae was meant to introduce a history of it.

marcion_excommunicated.detail: Tertullian dates the break 115 years and six and a half months after Christ's appearance under Tiberius. Marcionite churches spread across the empire and survived in the East for centuries. The challenge accelerated the formation of the orthodox New Testament canon and the Church's retention of the Old Testament.

aelius_aristides_roman_oration.detail: It is the fullest statement of the ideology of the Antonine peace from a provincial Greek perspective, praising the extension of citizenship and the security of travel. Aristides also wrote the Sacred Tales, an extraordinary record of his illnesses and dreams in the service of Asclepius at Pergamon. The date is probably 143 or 144, though 155 has been argued.
scholarship: Oliver, The Ruling Power (1953)

farasan_vexillation_144.detail: The inscriptions, published in 2004-2007, revealed a Roman naval and military presence at the mouth of the Red Sea far beyond the provincial frontiers, probably under the prefect of Mount Berenice and linked to protection of the Indian Ocean trade against piracy.

marriage_of_marcus_and_faustina_145.detail: The marriage produced at least fourteen children, including twins born in 161 (Commodus and Titus Aurelius Fulvus Antoninus); only Commodus among the sons survived to adulthood. Coins celebrate Faustina's fertility (FECVNDITAS, TEMPORVM FELICITAS). The hostile tradition that she was unfaithful with gladiators and sailors is generally dismissed.

mauretanian_war_of_antoninus.detail: Inscriptions of vexillations and the career of commanders such as Titus Varius Clemens, procurator of Mauretania Caesariensis, document the war; little narrative survives. Moorish incursions resumed into Baetica under Marcus Aurelius.

hadrianeum_dedicated_145.detail: Reliefs from its precinct, depicting personified provinces alternating with trophies, are now in the Capitoline Museums and Palazzo Massimo; they reflect Hadrian's ideology of an empire of partner provinces rather than conquered peoples.

rome_900th_anniversary_148.detail: The Aurelius Victor tradition says Antoninus celebrated the 900th year with splendour. The legend-types, unusually antiquarian, form a coherent series struck mostly in 140-144 and around 148. They fit his promotion of Lanuvium (his birthplace) and of Italian religion and Rome's Trojan heritage.

ptolemy_almagest.detail: Ptolemy's observations are dated between 127 and 141, and a 'Canobic inscription' of 147/148 recorded his parameters. The Almagest remained authoritative in the Islamic world and Europe until Copernicus; the Geography, rediscovered in the West around 1400, shaped Renaissance cartography and Columbus's underestimate of the globe. His Tetrabiblos systematised astrology, which was taken seriously at court.
scholarship: Toomer, Ptolemy's Almagest (1984)

disasters_under_antoninus.detail: The collapse in the Circus during games killed 1,112 people according to the Chronograph of 354. Antoninus is said to have relieved the famine by distributing wine, oil and wheat bought at his own expense. The forum of Carthage was rebuilt with his help; the Antonine Baths there were completed in 162.

muziris_papyrus.detail: The 25% customs duty (tetarte) payable at Alexandria on the cargo would alone have exceeded the annual pay of a legion. The text shows the immense scale of individual ventures in the Indian trade and the financing of merchants by lenders. Muziris itself is probably the site at Pattanam in Kerala.

antoninus_slave_rescripts.detail: Gaius (1.53) and the Digest (1.6.2) quote the rescript to the proconsul of Baetica Aelius Marcianus, which states that "it is in the master's interest that relief against cruelty, hunger or intolerable injury should not be denied to those who justly appeal". Antoninus also favoured the presumption in favour of liberty (favor libertatis) in manumission cases. The measures tempered but did not challenge slavery.

brigantian_revolt_154.detail: An inscription from the Tyne at Newcastle records the arrival of detachments from the three British legions from the two Germanies under Julius Verus. Earlier views of a major northern revolt that destroyed the Antonine Wall forts have been toned down; the Genounians may not even be British. The episode is linked to the reoccupation of Hadrian's Wall c. 158 and the abandonment of the Antonine Wall in the 160s.
brigantian_revolt_154.debate: Location of the Genounians and scale of the trouble.

polycarp_visits_anicetus.detail: Irenaeus recalled the meeting in a letter to Victor of Rome during the more bitter Quartodeciman controversy c. 190. Polycarp also met Marcion in Rome and called him "the firstborn of Satan". The visit shortly preceded Polycarp's martyrdom.

sources.w: Letter to Victor (in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 5.24.14-17)

justin_martyr_apology.detail: It contains the earliest detailed description of Christian worship: Sunday gatherings with readings from 'the memoirs of the apostles', prayers, and the eucharist of bread and wine mixed with water. Justin was beheaded around 165 under the city prefect Quintus Junius Rusticus, Marcus Aurelius's Stoic teacher; the trial record survives as the Acts of Justin.

outer_limes_advanced.detail: The advance added fertile land to the province and shortened communications to Raetia. Dendrochronology and building inscriptions date the new forts to c. 159-161. The palisade, ditch and bank (Pfahlgraben) and stone towers made this the classic image of the limes, now a UNESCO World Heritage site.

martyrdom_of_polycarp.detail: The Martyrdom of Polycarp, a letter of the church of Smyrna, is the earliest Christian martyr-act and establishes the cult of relics and the anniversary commemoration. Its date is disputed between about 155-156 and 167 (Eusebius). It shows persecution as local and crowd-driven, within the framework of Trajan's rescript.

rise_of_montanism.detail: Opponents in Asia held synods against it, among the earliest known. The movement demanded rigorous fasting, forbade second marriage and welcomed martyrdom. The site of Pepuza was identified in 2001 near Karayakuplu in western Turkey. Montanist communities survived in Phrygia until the sixth century.

apuleius_trial_at_sabratha.detail: The accusers, Pudentilla's relatives, cited his purchase of fish, a wooden statuette he worshipped and his handsomeness. The speech is a showpiece of learned wit and a unique document of a provincial elite feud. Apuleius later wrote the Metamorphoses (The Golden Ass), the only Latin novel to survive complete, with the tale of Cupid and Psyche and a final conversion to Isis, and became priest of the provincial cult at Carthage.

antonine_wall_abandoned.detail: Older views posited two Antonine occupations separated by a gap; most now favour a single occupation ending c. 158-165, perhaps when Marcus and Verus needed troops for the East. Building inscriptions of 158 on Hadrian's Wall attest refurbishment under the governor Julius Verus.
antonine_wall_abandoned.debate: Date and number of Antonine occupations.
scholarship: Hodgson, 'Were there two Antonine occupations of Scotland?', Britannia 26 (1995)

pausanias_description_of_greece.detail: Datable references include the Odeion of Herodes Atticus (after 161) and the Costoboci raid (170). Pausanias focuses on the ancient and sacred and largely ignores Roman buildings, reflecting the Second Sophistic's classicism. Excavations have repeatedly confirmed his accuracy, from the Olympia Heraion to the tombs at Mycenae.

appian_roman_history.detail: He had witnessed the Jewish revolt in Egypt in 116-117 and escaped by boat. His regional plan (Iberian, Hannibalic, Libyan, Syrian, Mithridatic) preserves sources otherwise lost. A letter of Fronto to Antoninus asking a procuratorship for the elderly Appian survives.

death_of_antoninus_pius.detail: He left a treasury surplus of 2,700 million sesterces, according to Dio. Marcus's long tribute to his adoptive father in the Meditations (1.16) describes his patience, courtesy and diligence. The column base of Antoninus, with its apotheosis relief, survives in the Vatican.

joint_accession_of_marcus_and_verus.detail: Antoninus Pius died on 7 March 161 at his villa at Lorium, having given the night watchword "aequanimitas" and ordered the golden statue of Fortuna, kept in the emperor's bedroom, to be moved to that of Marcus. Marcus Aurelius, Caesar since 139 and holder of tribunician power and proconsular imperium since 147, was the obvious successor and the Senate offered him sole rule. He insisted, however, that his adoptive brother Lucius, son of Hadrian's first intended heir Lucius Aelius, be made co-emperor with equal titles, Imperator Caesar Lucius Aurelius Verus Augustus, while Marcus took the name Antoninus. This was the first time the empire was formally ruled by two Augusti with equal powers, though Marcus alone was pontifex maximus and held seniority, having one more tribunician year. The arrangement honoured Hadrian's original plan of 138, under which Antoninus had adopted both young men. The two emperors went to the praetorian camp, where Lucius addressed the troops and they promised a donative of 20,000 sesterces each, a large sum. Lucius was betrothed to Marcus's daughter Lucilla. The motives for the collegiality are debated: loyalty to Hadrian's wishes, the need for a second emperor to command in war, as soon happened when Lucius went to the East in 162, and the desire to avoid a rival. Ancient writers contrasted Marcus's philosophical austerity with Lucius's love of pleasure, though the Historia Augusta's life of Verus is largely hostile invention. The joint rule set a precedent for collegial emperorship that became normal in the third and fourth centuries (Severus and Caracalla, Valerian and Gallienus, the Tetrarchy). The birth of twin sons to Faustina on 31 August 161, one of whom was Commodus, appeared to secure the dynasty. Within months the empire faced crisis: the Parthian invasion of Armenia and defeat at Elegeia, the Tiber flood and famine, and unrest in Britain and on the Rhine.
joint_accession_of_marcus_and_verus.debate: Motives for sharing power and the reliability of the Historia Augusta's portrait of Lucius.

gaius_institutes.detail: Barthold Georg Niebuhr discovered it in 1816 in the Chapter Library of Verona as a palimpsest beneath letters of Jerome; papyrus fragments from Oxyrhynchus and Antinoopolis have since filled gaps. Its scheme was adopted by Justinian's Institutes (533) and through them by modern civil codes. It preserves much on Republican procedure (legis actiones, formulary system) and Augustan status law.
scholarship: Honoré, Gaius (1962)

battle_of_elegeia.detail: Lucian says Severianus had been encouraged by the oracle of the false prophet Alexander of Abonuteichos, and mocks a historian who described his death absurdly. Dio's epitome confirms the destruction of a legion with its officers; whether it was IX Hispana, XXII Deiotariana or another is debated. A second Parthian army then defeated the governor of Syria.

tiber_flood_162.detail: The Historia Augusta lists it among the calamities of the opening years: war with Parthia, unrest in Britain, the Chatti invading Germany and Raetia. Marcus appointed curators for the affected communities. The disasters foreshadowed the plague that arrived four years later.

chatti_invade_upper_germany_162.detail: The attacks were early signs of pressure on the northern frontiers that culminated after 166. The Chatti appear again in 213 under Caracalla.

galen_arrives_in_rome_162.detail: He treated the philosopher Eudemus and the consul Flavius Boethus, for whom he wrote anatomical works. In 166, as the plague reached Rome, he left for Pergamum, claiming enemies; in 168-169 the emperors summoned him to Aquileia, and he became physician to the young Commodus. His some 150 surviving works, a tenth of ancient Greek literature, dominated medicine until the seventeenth century. The rediscovered treatise On Avoiding Distress (2005) describes his losses in the Palatine fire of 192.

capture_of_artaxata_163.detail: Sohaemus, a Roman senator of royal Emesene and Arsacid descent, was installed as king of Armenia (coins of 164: REX ARMENIIS DATVS). Kaine Polis is identified with Vagharshapat (Echmiadzin), later the seat of the Armenian church.

verus_marries_lucilla_164.detail: Marcus turned back to avoid seeming to seek a share in the glory of the war, and also, the Historia Augusta suggests, to keep an eye on rumours of Lucius's debaucheries at Antioch and Daphne. After Lucius's death in 169 Lucilla was married against her will to the older general Claudius Pompeianus; she later led the conspiracy of 182 against her brother.

sohaemus_restored_164.detail: Lucius took the title Armeniacus. Sohaemus, a member of the Emesene royal house, was later expelled by a pro-Parthian faction c. 172 and restored by Martius Verus. Kainepolis, garrisoned by Roman troops, became the nucleus of Etchmiadzin.

sack_of_seleucia_165.detail: Eutropius claims 400,000 inhabitants were captured. Roman sources blamed the city's alleged treachery; the Historia Augusta blames Cassius. Ammianus and the Historia Augusta tell that soldiers opening a gold chest (or crack) in the temple of Apollo released a pestilential vapour that spread plague across the empire, a moralising tale attached to the outbreak of the Antonine Plague among the returning army.

antonine_plague.detail: The Antonine Plague, which first appeared among Roman troops in Mesopotamia in 165-166, was the first known pandemic in the Roman empire. The ancient sources say that it broke out at Seleucia on the Tigris when soldiers opened a golden casket in a temple of Apollo, or in Babylonia, and it spread with the returning army through Syria and Asia Minor to Rome in 166, and to the armies on the Danube by 168-169, where it struck the forces gathered at Aquileia and carried off the praetorian prefect Furius Victorinus. Galen, who left Rome in 166 and was summoned to Aquileia in 168-169, describes symptoms of fever, vomiting, diarrhoea with black stools, and a black, dry rash that left scabs, which led most modern scholars to identify it as smallpox, though measles has been proposed. Outbreaks recurred over the next two decades; the worst attested was in 189, when Dio says 2,000 people often died in a day in Rome. Estimates of mortality vary enormously. Some historians (Gilliam, Bruun) have argued for limited effects; others, using papyri from Egyptian villages that show sudden declines in tax-payers (as at Soknopaiou Nesos, where the adult male population fell by a third or more), the fall in wages and land prices, the interruption of gold-mining tablets in Dacia, a gap in dated inscriptions and brick stamps, and the end of new building, argue for overall losses of 10% or more, possibly 20-25% in some places (Duncan-Jones, Harper). The plague contributed to the manpower crisis of the Marcomannic wars, when Marcus recruited slaves, gladiators and brigands, and to the settlement of barbarians on depopulated land. Lucian's Alexander shows the oracular verse inscribed on doors to ward it off, and inscriptions from Pergamum, Hierapolis and elsewhere record oracles of Apollo of Claros prescribing rituals. Some historians see it as the beginning of the end of the Roman "optimum" of demographic and economic growth, together with climate deterioration after the second century. Chinese sources record epidemics in the 160s and 170s, possibly related.
antonine_plague.debate: Disease identity (smallpox most likely) and mortality, from minor losses to 20-25%.
scholarship: Duncan-Jones, 'The impact of the Antonine plague', JRA 9 (1996)
Harper, The Fate of Rome (2017)
Elliott, Pox Romana (2024)

legiones_italicae_raised.detail: The foundation inscription of the fortress at Castra Regina (Regensburg), dated 179, survives. Raising legions in Italy, rather than in the provinces, was by then exceptional. Raetia and Noricum were upgraded to provinces governed by legionary legates of praetorian rank.

capture_of_edessa_and_dura_165.detail: Dura-Europos remained a Roman garrison town until its destruction by the Sasanians c. 256, preserving its synagogue, church house and military archives. Lucian mocks historians who invented bloody battles for the war, including one at Europos with 70,236 enemy dead. Coins of Mannus of Edessa carry Roman imperial portraits.

martyrdom_of_justin.detail: Justin, from Flavia Neapolis in Samaria, had taught in Rome "above the baths of Myrtinus". Eusebius reports that the Cynic Crescens, whom Justin had bested in debate, denounced him. The Acts are among the most reliable early martyr texts, showing the routine procedure under which confession of the name sufficed for death.

triumph_of_marcus_and_verus_166.detail: Lucian's How to Write History, written during the war, satirises the many historians who rushed to celebrate it with Thucydidean pastiche and absurd exaggeration. The returning troops brought the plague to Italy and the western provinces.

lucian_how_to_write_history.detail: The essay lays down principles still quoted: the historian should be fearless, incorruptible, "a stranger in his books and without a country". Lucian's other works, some 80 in all, include the True Histories (a parody travel tale reaching the moon), Alexander the False Prophet, The Passing of Peregrinus (on a Cynic who burned himself at Olympia in 165, with an early pagan comment on Christians) and dialogues of the gods and the dead.

avidius_cassius_invades_media_166.detail: The war ended with Roman control of north-western Mesopotamia (Dura, Carrhae, Edessa as client) and Cassius given a supra-provincial command in the East, the base of his usurpation in 175. Lucius returned to Rome for the joint triumph of October 166.

roman_embassy_to_china_166.detail: The Chinese account notes that the gifts were unremarkable, suspecting that the envoys were merchants who had acquired them on the way rather than official ambassadors. Earlier, the Han general Ban Chao's envoy Gan Ying had reached the Persian Gulf in 97 but turned back. Roman coins and glass found at Oc Eo in the Mekong delta attest the southern sea route.
roman_embassy_to_china_166.debate: Probably merchants claiming embassy status rather than an official mission.

plague_reaches_rome_166.detail: Galen left Rome that year. Later traditions blamed the soldiers who had opened a golden casket in the temple of Apollo at Seleucia. The disease, from Galen's description of fever, black rash and black stools, was probably smallpox. It returned in waves for some twenty years.

alexander_of_abonoteichus_oracle.detail: Lucian's Alexander the False Prophet is a hostile exposé; Alexander nevertheless won the patronage of the consular Rutilianus and sent an oracle to Marcus during the Marcomannic war advising him to throw two lions into the Danube, after which the Romans were defeated. Coins of Abonoteichus (renamed Ionopolis) and statuettes of Glykon confirm the cult's popularity.

langobardi_cross_the_danube.detail: This episode, preserved in a fragment of Dio, is usually taken as the opening of the Marcomannic Wars. Its significance lies in showing peoples from the lower Elbe on the Danube, a sign of pressure building in barbaricum, perhaps linked to Gothic movements towards the Black Sea.

expeditio_germanica_prima_168.detail: Galen, summoned to Aquileia, says the plague raged as never before and the emperors fled to Rome with a few soldiers, Lucius dying on the way early in 169. Marcus purified the city with every rite and recruited slaves, gladiators, Dalmatian brigands and German mercenaries to fill the ranks.

tres_daciae_168.detail: An inscription in the Forum of Trajan honours Fronto, who "fell fighting bravely for the state". Legio V Macedonica was moved to Potaissa to give Dacia a second legion. The province was briefly overrun by Iazyges and Astingi; the gold-mining tablets at Alburnus Maior stop in 167, perhaps from abandonment in the invasion.

denarius_debasement_antonine.detail: Metallurgical analyses (Walker, Butcher and Ponting) show stepwise reductions rather than collapse; the real crash came under Septimius Severus, when fineness fell to around 50%. Marcus's auction of palace treasures in 169 and his refusal of a donative after victories reflect the same pressures.
denarius_debasement_antonine.debate: Exact percentages vary with analytical method and sample.

death_of_lucius_verus.detail: Rumours accused Marcus, Faustina and Lucilla of poisoning him, which modern scholars dismiss. Marcus deified him. The Historia Augusta paints Verus as a pleasure-loving foil to Marcus, though the letters of Fronto show a cultured and affectionate younger brother.

auction_of_imperial_treasures.detail: Afterwards he offered to buy back items from purchasers who wished to return them. He also recruited slaves (voluntarii), gladiators (obsequentes), Dalmatian and Dardanian brigands and Greek police (diogmitae), and hired Germans to fight Germans, measures that show the manpower crisis caused by war and plague. The silver content of the denarius was cut to about 79%.

siege_of_aquileia_170.detail: In 170, when Marcus had launched an offensive across the Danube that seems to have ended in a serious defeat with the loss of up to 20,000 men (Lucian's Alexander mentions such a loss), a coalition of Marcomanni and Quadi under the Marcomannic king Ballomar broke through the Danube frontier, devastated Noricum and Pannonia, crossed the Julian Alps and besieged Aquileia, the great city at the head of the Adriatic, and destroyed Opitergium (Oderzo). It was the first invasion of Italy by a foreign enemy since the Cimbri and Teutones nearly three centuries earlier, and caused panic. The praetorian prefect Macrinius Vindex was killed in battle around the same time, and Marcus Claudius Fronto, commanding Dacia and Upper Moesia, fell fighting the Germans and Iazyges. At about the same time the Costoboci swept south through the Balkans to Greece, sacking the sanctuary of Eleusis, and Moors invaded Baetica. Aquileia held out. It had been fortified in haste in 168-169 under the praetorian prefects as part of a defence system in the Julian Alps, the praetentura Italiae et Alpium, commanded by Quintus Antistius Adventus, whose career inscription survives. The invaders were driven out of Italy in 171 by forces under Tiberius Claudius Pompeianus, Marcus's new son-in-law, and Publius Helvius Pertinax, who caught them as they recrossed the Danube with booty and prisoners. Marcus then moved his headquarters to Carnuntum and began the campaigns of 172-175. The chronology of 170 is uncertain, partly because the sources (Dio's epitome, the Historia Augusta, Ammianus Marcellinus 29.6.1) are fragmentary, and some scholars place the invasion in 167 or 169. The episode shook the confidence of the Antonine age and led to the creation of the Italian legions II and III Italica and a new defensive policy. It is regarded by many historians as the first sign of the barbarian pressure that dominated the third century.

costoboci_raid_greece.detail: Aelius Aristides lamented the burning of Eleusis in a speech; Pausanias records that at Elatea the Olympic victor Mnesibulus died fighting the raiders. In Spain, Baetica was temporarily transferred from senatorial to imperial control, displacing the young quaestor Septimius Severus to Sardinia. The simultaneous crises show how stretched imperial defences had become.

astingi_and_lacringi_171.detail: Dio's account is the earliest mention of Vandal groups in contact with Rome. The episode shows the divide-and-rule diplomacy that accompanied fighting in the Marcomannic wars, as migrating peoples pressed on the Danube from the north.

marcus_at_carnuntum_171.detail: Dio says some peoples were granted land in Dacia, Pannonia, Moesia and Germany or even Italy, and the Quadi made a separate peace, returning 13,000 prisoners. Book 2 of the Meditations is headed "at Carnuntum". Pertinax's success restored a career that had stalled.

bucoli_revolt.detail: Dio reports that some, disguised as women, lured a centurion into a trap, sacrificed his companion and ate his entrails. The marsh-dwelling Boukoloi were a literary topos in Greek novels (Achilles Tatius, Heliodorus), but the revolt appears real, perhaps fuelled by plague, tax burdens and depopulation in the Delta.

rain_miracle.detail: Dio's epitome attributes the miracle to the Egyptian priest Arnouphis invoking Hermes Aerios; Xiphilinus, the Byzantine epitomator, adds a Christian version: the prayers of Christian soldiers of legio XII Fulminata, a story told earlier by Apollinaris of Hierapolis and Tertullian, who cites a (spurious) letter of Marcus. Coins of 172-173 with Mercury may commemorate it. The date (172 or 174) and its relation to a separate 'lightning miracle' shown earlier on the Column are debated.
rain_miracle.debate: Date (172 or 174), agent (Egyptian magic, Jupiter, Christian prayer), and location.
scholarship: Kovács, Marcus Aurelius' Rain Miracle and the Marcomannic Wars (2009)

meditations_of_marcus_aurelius.detail: The work was apparently never meant for publication; it is first mentioned by Themistius in 364 and the Byzantine scholar Arethas around 900. The first printed edition (Zurich, 1558) was based on a now-lost manuscript. Its themes (the transience of life, duty, the cosmos as a city) made it among the most widely read ancient texts in modern times.
scholarship: Hadot, The Inner Citadel (1998)

marcomanni_defeated_172.detail: Roman camps at Musov (Burgstall) in Moravia, with legionary detachments and a forward command post, date from the Marcomannic wars. The Column of Marcus Aurelius shows the river crossing on a pontoon bridge at its base and divine interventions in the early scenes.

chauci_raid_belgica_172.detail: Coin hoards and burned villas in northern Gaul from the 170s have been connected with the raids, though their scale is uncertain. The episode foreshadows the seaborne Frankish and Saxon raids of the third century.

barbarian_settlements_ravenna.detail: Dio is the source. Such settlements (receptio) foreshadowed the late Roman practice of accepting barbarian groups as farmers and recruits. The Historia Augusta claims Marcus settled "infinite numbers" on Roman soil, filling lands depopulated by the plague.

battle_of_the_frozen_danube.detail: Dio's vivid account is one of the few tactical narratives of the Marcomannic Wars. The war against the Sarmatian Iazyges continued until 175, when Marcus, preoccupied by Cassius's revolt, made peace.

quadi_depose_furtius_174.detail: The Quadi had broken their peace by sheltering Marcomannic fugitives and refusing to return deserters. The Laugaricio inscription at Trencin records a legionary detachment wintering 120 km north of the Danube in 179-180. Book 1 of the Meditations ends "among the Quadi, on the Granua" (Hron).

revolt_of_avidius_cassius.detail: Dio reports a story that the empress Faustina, fearing for her son's future if Marcus died, had encouraged Cassius. Martius Verus held Cappadocia for Marcus. Marcus made peace with the Iazyges, travelled east, refused to see Cassius's head, burned his correspondence unread and pardoned most supporters. Faustina died at Halala in Cappadocia in the winter of 175/176; the village was refounded as Faustinopolis. Papyri dated by Cassius's regnal years show his recognition in Egypt. Thereafter no senator was allowed to govern his home province.

peace_with_the_iazyges_175.detail: Sarmatian cavalry are later attested at Bremetennacum (Ribchester) in Lancashire, where a unit of Sarmatians remained into the third century. Marcus took the title Sarmaticus. The figure of 100,000 captives, even if exaggerated, shows the scale of the raids.

death_of_faustina_the_younger_175.detail: Dio reports the rumour that she had encouraged Cassius, believing Marcus near death, and killed herself to avoid exposure; modern scholars are sceptical. Marcus had her deified, founded a second order of puellae Faustinianae, and placed silver statues of her and himself in the temple of Venus and Roma, where newly married couples sacrificed.

triumph_176_and_column_of_marcus.detail: The column's frieze is cruder and more emotional than Trajan's: barbarians are beheaded, women and children dragged off, villages burned, and the emperor appears as a remote, frontal figure. It includes the 'rain miracle' and 'lightning miracle' scenes. An inscription of the procurator Adrastus (193) records the completion. The statue of St Paul has stood on top since 1589, and the Piazza Colonna is named after it.
scholarship: Beckmann, The Column of Marcus Aurelius (2011)

marcus_at_athens_176.detail: Philostratus says Herodes Atticus was asked to choose the holders. The endowment institutionalised Athens as the empire's university city; the chairs survived in some form until Justinian's measures against pagan teachers in 529.

marcus_eastern_tour_176.detail: He also forbade anyone to govern his province of origin, because Cassius was a Syrian. Aristides made Marcus wait three days before speaking, according to Philostratus. The tour ended at Athens with the initiation and the endowment of the chairs.

commodus_made_augustus.detail: Marcus was the first emperor since Vespasian to have a surviving son, and there is no evidence he considered passing him over. Later writers, starting with Dio and the Historia Augusta, blamed Marcus for the choice; modern historians note that excluding a son would almost certainly have led to civil war.

martyrs_of_lyon.detail: The letter of the churches of Vienne and Lyon to those of Asia and Phrygia, preserved by Eusebius, is a key martyr text. The governor consulted Marcus, who ruled that Roman citizens should be beheaded and those who recanted released; the citizen Attalus was nonetheless thrown to the beasts. The executions took place at the annual festival of the Three Gauls in August, possibly linked to the senatorial decree of the same year allowing priests to buy condemned criminals cheaply for shows. Irenaeus became bishop afterwards.

sc_de_pretiis_gladiatorum.detail: The decree survives in a bronze tablet from Italica in Spain (Aes Italicense, CIL II 6278) and a marble fragment from Sardis. It includes the speech of a senator praising the emperors and a clause allowing Gallic priests to buy condemned criminals (trinqui) at six aurei each from procurators, a detail perhaps connected to the deaths of the Lyon martyrs.
scholarship: Oliver and Palmer, 'Minutes of an act of the Roman Senate', Hesperia 24 (1955)
Carter, 'Gladiatorial combat: the rules of engagement', CJ 102 (2006)

tabula_banasitana_177.detail: The documents include letters from the emperors to the governors of Tingitana and an extract from the imperial register (commentarius) of citizenship grants, with the signatures of twelve members of the emperor's council. The formula "salvo iure gentis" shows that holding citizenship did not cancel local obligations, which bears on the interpretation of the Constitutio Antoniniana of 212.

expeditio_germanica_secunda_178.detail: Dio reports the ritual. The expedition aimed at completing the subjugation of the Marcomanni and Quadi, possibly to create new provinces. Tarrutenius Paternus, praetorian prefect and a writer on military law, held field command.

celsus_true_doctrine.detail: The work survives only through Origen's point-by-point reply Contra Celsum (c. 248), which quotes perhaps 70% of it. Celsus knew the gospels, Jewish anti-Christian polemic (including the story that Jesus's father was a soldier named Panthera) and the variety of Christian sects. He closes by urging Christians to take part in civic life and fight for the emperor.

smyrna_earthquake_178.detail: Aristides' Smyrnaean Orations (18-21) lament and celebrate the city. The rebuilding, financed by the emperors and funded by remitted taxes, was celebrated by Aristides as Smyrna's rebirth; the excavated Agora of Smyrna (Izmir) belongs largely to this Marcan reconstruction, with a portrait of Faustina on its arch.

sc_orfitianum_178.detail: With the Hadrianic SC Tertullianum (mother inheriting from children), it marked a decisive step from the old agnatic family, based on descent through males under paternal power, towards a cognatic system based on blood relationship. Justinian's reforms of succession built on both decrees.

laugaricio_inscription.detail: It is the northernmost Roman inscription in central Europe and direct evidence of Roman garrisons deep in Quadi territory in Marcus's second expedition. Dio says 20,000 Roman soldiers were stationed in forts among the Marcomanni and Quadi. Maximianus's career inscription from Diana Veteranorum in Numidia records that he killed Valao, king of the Naristi, with his own hand.

battle_of_paternus_179.detail: Dio says the Quadi, unable to endure the garrisons of 20,000 men in forts among them with baths and every comfort, tried to migrate north to the Semnones, but Marcus blocked the roads. The battle is the last recorded engagement of Marcus's reign.

valerius_maximianus_kills_valao.detail: The career inscription is one of the most detailed for the Marcomannic wars: Maximianus brought grain down the Danube for the Pannonian armies, commanded Moorish horsemen against the Germans, led vexillations wintering at Laugaricio and rose to consul and legate of Numidia under Commodus.

planned_provinces_marcomannia_sarmatia.detail: The claim is debated: some see the occupation as a prelude to annexation, others as a security measure. Archaeology north of the Danube (Musov, Iza, Laugaricio) confirms large temporary installations. Commodus withdrew them under the peace of 180, a decision Dio and Herodian blame on his laziness but which many modern historians think prudent.

death_of_marcus_aurelius.detail: Marcus Aurelius died on 17 March 180, aged 58, at his headquarters on the Danube, at Vindobona (Vienna) according to Aurelius Victor or at Sirmium according to Tertullian, during his second German expedition. Dio says that his doctors, eager to please Commodus, hastened his death, a claim generally dismissed; the Historia Augusta describes a final illness, possibly the plague, during which he refused food and drink. On the sixth day, he summoned his friends and spoke of the vanity of things, and on the seventh, sending Commodus away for fear of infection, he gave the tribune the watchword "Go to the rising sun, for I am already setting." He had arranged the succession carefully: Commodus, aged eighteen, had been Caesar since 166 and co-Augustus since 177, the first emperor's son "born in the purple" to succeed his father since Titus. Marcus's choice of a biological heir over adoption has been criticised since antiquity, though no alternative was available without excluding his son. Marcus was deified at once; his ashes were placed in the Mausoleum of Hadrian. His reign had been dominated by war and disaster: the Parthian war (161-166), the plague, the Marcomannic wars, the revolt of Avidius Cassius and the death of Faustina. He nevertheless won a reputation as the ideal philosopher-king, sustained by his Meditations, twelve books of private Stoic reflections written in Greek during the campaigns, by his clemency to Cassius's supporters and by his endowment of philosophy chairs at Athens. Dio, who lived through the reign, said that with his death history descended "from a kingdom of gold to one of iron and rust". Modern historians acknowledge his conscientiousness while noting his persecution of Christians (Lyon, 177), his debasement of the coinage and his apparent intention to annex territory north of the Danube, abandoned by Commodus. The equestrian bronze statue on the Capitol, preserved because it was believed to represent Constantine, and the Column of Marcus Aurelius on the Campus Martius are the main monuments of his reign.
death_of_marcus_aurelius.debate: Place of death (Vindobona or Sirmium) and the wisdom of choosing Commodus.

scillitan_martyrs_180.detail: Asked what was in their case, the leader Speratus replied "books and the letters of Paul, a just man", showing that Latin scriptures existed. Saturninus offered them thirty days to reconsider. Tertullian says this proconsul was the first to use the sword against Christians in Africa.

peace_of_commodus_180.detail: Herodian portrays Commodus as eager to return to Rome's pleasures; Dio, more balanced, records the terms. Modern historians often consider the peace realistic given plague and exhaustion, and it held for decades. Marcus's intended provinces of Marcomannia and Sarmatia, if they were ever intended, were abandoned. Commodus triumphed on 22 October 180.

irenaeus_against_heresies.detail: His list of Roman bishops from Linus to Eleutherus (3.3.3) is the earliest such catalogue, and his insistence that there are exactly four gospels, "as there are four winds", is the first clear statement of the fourfold canon. A native of Asia, he had heard Polycarp in his youth. The full text survives in Latin translation.

lucilla_conspiracy.detail: Lucilla was exiled to Capri and executed; the praetorian prefect Tarrutenius Paternus was also killed, leaving Perennis in control. The episode, in which the attacker's words implicated the Senate, permanently soured Commodus towards the senatorial order and led to his withdrawal from government into the hands of favourites.

british_war_of_commodus.detail: Which wall is meant (Hadrian's or the Antonine) is uncertain; destruction layers at forts such as Halton Chesters and Rudchester have been linked to this invasion. Marcellus's severity provoked the army, which tried to proclaim a legate named Priscus emperor, and sent a delegation to Rome against Perennis.

saltus_burunitanus_petition.detail: The tenants describe themselves as "wretched peasants" and threaten to flee. The text shows the relationship between coloni, conductores and procurators on imperial estates, and the emperor's role as a court of appeal for humble petitioners.

execution_of_the_quintilii.detail: Their enormous villa on the Via Appia was confiscated and became an imperial residence that Commodus enjoyed. Dio says Condianus's son faked his death by drinking hare's blood and falling from a horse, and a ram was burned in his place, and that many impostors later claimed to be him. Saoterus, Commodus's chamberlain, was killed by the prefects around the same time.

dacian_war_under_commodus_183.detail: Dio records Sabinianus's settlement. The war shows the continued instability north of the Danube after the Marcomannic peace. Victories in Britain under Ulpius Marcellus brought Commodus the title Britannicus in 184.

fall_of_perennis.detail: Dio's account of a provincial army delegation reaching the emperor near Rome is unique. Herodian gives a different version, linked to coins found showing Perennis's son. The freedman chamberlain Cleander replaced Perennis as the power behind the throne.

pertinax_quells_british_mutiny_185.detail: The British army had already sent 1,500 men to Italy in 185 to denounce Perennis. Pertinax's severity in Britain prefigured his attempt to discipline the praetorians in 193, which cost him his life.

bellum_desertorum.detail: Herodian is the main source and presents a romanticised story; inscriptions mention operations against 'deserters' and the legio VIII Augusta's relief of Argentorate, earning it the title Pia Fidelis Constans Commoda. The episode reflects the social dislocation left by war and plague.

classis_africana_commodiana_186.detail: The Historia Augusta, hostile as always, mocks him for naming Carthage after himself (Alexandria Commodiana Togata) and calling the fleet Commodiana Herculea. The measure foreshadows the growing role of African grain, which became Rome's principal supply after Constantinople took the Egyptian annona in 330. Shortages in 189-190 nonetheless led to the riot that brought down Cleander.

plague_in_rome_189.detail: Dio also reports that criminals spread the disease by pricking people with needles smeared with poison, a typical plague panic. The outbreak combined with famine to produce the riot of 190 against Cleander. Herodian describes similar mortality among people and animals.

julius_alexander_of_emesa_189.detail: Dio tells the story as an example of Commodus's jealousy of anyone excelling in his own pursuits. The episode belongs to the last violent years of the reign; Commodus himself would display his skill as a beast-fighter in the arena in 192.

fall_of_cleander.detail: Dio, an eyewitness, says the shortage was deliberately engineered by the grain prefect Papirius Dionysius to bring down Cleander. The crisis followed a recurrence of plague in 189 that killed, Dio says, up to 2,000 people a day in Rome. Commodus formed an African grain fleet, the classis Commodiana Herculea, in 186 to secure supply.

marcia_frees_christians_sardinia.detail: The story comes from Hippolytus's hostile account of Callistus, a former slave of the imperial freedman Carpophorus, condemned for brawling in a synagogue. Marcia's Christian sympathies (Dio calls her favourable to Christians) illustrate the penetration of the faith into the imperial household by the late second century.

quartodeciman_controversy_190.detail: Eusebius reports synods in Palestine, Rome, Pontus, Gaul and Osrhoene that all supported Sunday observance. The episode is the first major assertion of Roman authority over other churches, and the first Latin-speaking bishop of Rome (Victor was African). The question was settled for most churches at Nicaea in 325.

assassination_of_commodus.detail: Commodus was murdered on the night of 31 December 192, aged 31, on the eve of the day when he planned to enter the consulship dressed as a gladiator from the gladiators' barracks, and, according to Herodian, to have the consuls designate killed. The conspirators were his mistress Marcia, the chamberlain (cubicularius) Eclectus and the new praetorian prefect Quintus Aemilius Laetus, all of whom feared for their lives; Herodian has the boy Philocommodus find a writing tablet listing them for execution. Marcia gave Commodus poisoned wine or beef after his bath; when he vomited and seemed likely to recover, they sent in the athlete Narcissus, his wrestling partner, who strangled him in his bath. The conspirators announced that he had died of apoplexy and went at once to the house of the urban prefect Publius Helvius Pertinax, who had probably been forewarned, and took him to the praetorian camp, where he was hailed emperor after promising a donative of 12,000 sesterces. The Senate, meeting before dawn, declared Commodus an enemy of the state and ordered his statues thrown down and his name erased, with ritual chants recorded by the Historia Augusta ("Let the enemy of the fatherland be dragged with the hook"); Pertinax had him buried quietly in the Mausoleum of Hadrian, and Septimius Severus later deified him to legitimise his own claim to be Marcus's son. Commodus's last years had been marked by his identification with Hercules, coins showing him in the lion skin, the renaming of the months with his titles and of Rome as Colonia Commodiana, his appearances in the arena in which he killed animals from a raised platform and fought gladiators with wooden weapons, and executions of senators. Dio, an eyewitness, records that senators in the Colosseum had to chew laurel leaves to stop themselves laughing when Commodus waved the severed head of an ostrich at them. His murder ended the Antonine dynasty and opened the civil wars of 193, the "year of the five emperors". Narcissus was executed by Severus; Laetus and Eclectus were killed with Pertinax in March 193.

commodus_as_hercules.detail: The month names were Lucius, Aelius, Aurelius, Commodus, Augustus, Herculeus, Romanus, Exsuperatorius, Amazonius, Invictus, Felix and Pius. Dio, as a senator in the audience, records chewing a laurel leaf to hide his laughter when Commodus advanced towards the senators brandishing the severed head of an ostrich. The famous Capitoline bust shows him with lion skin, club and the apples of the Hesperides. He replaced the head of Nero's Colossus with his own.

fire_of_192.detail: Galen lost books, drugs, instruments and recipes stored in a warehouse on the Via Sacra, including his own unpublished works and rare editions of earlier authors. He described the loss in De indolentia (On Avoiding Grief), rediscovered in 2005 in a manuscript at the Vlatadon monastery in Thessaloniki. Herodian took the fire as an omen of Commodus's fall.
scholarship: Rothschild and Thompson (eds), Galen's De indolentia (2014)

auction_of_the_empire_193.detail:
On 28 March 193 some 300 Praetorians, angered by Pertinax's discipline and his failure to pay the full donative, marched into the palace and killed him after only 87 days. With no obvious successor, the Guard shut itself in the Castra Praetoria. Inside, Pertinax's father-in-law Titus Flavius Sulpicianus, prefect of the city, began bargaining for the throne; outside the wall the wealthy senator Marcus Didius Julianus, a former governor of Germania Inferior and Africa, shouted counter-offers, reportedly holding up his fingers to show the sums. Cassius Dio, a senator in Rome at the time, says Sulpicianus had reached 20,000 sesterces per man when Julianus jumped to 25,000 (6,250 denarii) and warned the soldiers that Sulpicianus would avenge Pertinax. The gates opened, and the Guard escorted Julianus to the Senate under arms; the senators, Dio among them, ratified the choice out of fear.

The 'auction' became the classic image of imperial decadence, but its importance lay in what followed. The plebs jeered Julianus at the Circus, occupied it for a day and night and called on Pescennius Niger in Syria to save them. Within weeks three provincial armies had proclaimed their commanders: Severus on the Danube (9 April), Niger in Syria and, in effect, Clodius Albinus in Britain. Julianus tried to fortify the city, train elephants and marines, send assassins against Severus, and finally offered him a share of power. The Praetorians, softened by years in Rome, were useless, and the Senate deserted him once Severus reached Italy. On 1 June 193 the Senate condemned Julianus to death, and a soldier killed him in the palace; Dio reports his last words as 'What evil have I done? Whom have I killed?' He had reigned 66 days.

Herodian's version is more rhetorical and the Historia Augusta, more sympathetic, claims Julianus was pushed into the bid by his family. Modern historians (Birley, Hekster) stress that the episode exposed the Guard as a political liability and opened the door to a civil war decided by the frontier armies, ending the Antonine model of senatorial consensus.
auction_of_the_empire_193.debate: Herodian and Dio dramatise the 'auction'; the HA life is late and partly derivative, but the core sequence is accepted.
scholarship: Birley, Septimius Severus: The African Emperor (2nd ed., 1988)

pescennius_niger_proclaimed_193.detail: Niger controlled nine legions and Egypt's grain, and won the backing of Antioch and, crucially, Byzantium, which controlled the Bosporus crossing. Parthian and client rulers (Hatra, Osroene, Adiabene) offered or promised help, giving Severus his pretext for the eastern wars of 195 and 197-198.
pescennius_niger_proclaimed_193.debate: The HA life of Niger is among the most fictional in the collection (forged letters and documents).

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

septimius_severus_proclaimed_193.detail:
Lucius Septimius Severus, born at Lepcis Magna on 11 April 145 into a Punic-Italian family of equestrian and senatorial rank, had governed Gallia Lugdunensis and Sicily and in 191 was appointed legate of Pannonia Superior, with three legions at Carnuntum, Vindobona and Brigetio. His brother Geta governed Moesia Inferior, and friends held other Danube commands, so that when news of Pertinax's murder arrived the whole Danube army, sixteen legions from the Rhine to the Black Sea, could be swung behind him. On 9 April 193 the troops at Carnuntum hailed him Augustus; he took the name Pertinax and presented himself as avenger of the murdered emperor rather than as a rival of Julianus.

Severus acted with remarkable speed. To secure his rear he offered Clodius Albinus, governor of Britain with three legions, the rank of Caesar and implied succession, which Albinus accepted. He then marched on Italy with a picked force, covering some 800 miles in about two months; Ravenna and its fleet were taken, the Julian Alps were left undefended, and Julianus' envoys and assassins either failed or changed sides. Severus ordered the Praetorians to hand over Pertinax's killers, which they did. On 1 June the Senate deposed Julianus, and Severus entered Rome in early June, staying about a month before marching east against Pescennius Niger, who had been proclaimed by the Syrian legions at about the same time.

Dio, who knew Severus, records dreams and omens that the emperor himself publicised in his autobiography, including a vision of being carried on a horse to the Forum. Herodian contrasts Severus' cunning with the slowness of Niger. The proclamation inaugurated a dynasty that lasted, with the interruption of Macrinus, until 235 and reoriented the empire around the army, the African and Syrian connections of Severus and his wife Julia Domna, and a much more openly military monarchy.
scholarship: Birley, Septimius Severus: The African Emperor (1988)

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

severus_disbands_praetorian_guard_193.detail:
After Julianus' death the Senate sent a delegation of a hundred senators to meet Severus at Interamna, where they were searched for daggers before admission. Before entering Rome Severus ordered the Praetorians to parade outside the city unarmed, in ceremonial dress, as if to swear the oath. Surrounded by his Illyrian legionaries, they were harangued for the murder of Pertinax and the sale of the empire, stripped of their military belts, daggers and insignia, and dismissed in disgrace, with orders not to come within a hundred miles of Rome on pain of death. Their horses were taken; Dio reports that one horse followed its rider and both were killed.

Severus then entered the city on foot in civilian dress, though his army followed in arms and camped in temples and porticoes, a scene Dio, an eyewitness, describes as the most brilliant he had seen and yet alarming. Severus swore before the Senate that he would put no senator to death without trial, an oath he soon broke. A new Guard was formed, ten cohorts probably of a thousand men each (perhaps 1,500), recruited not from Italy, Spain, Macedonia and Noricum as before but from the best soldiers of all the legions, overwhelmingly Danubians. Severus also enlarged the urban cohorts and vigiles and later stationed II Parthica at Albanum.

Dio complained that the change filled Rome with uncouth soldiers terrifying to hear and see, and drove the young men of Italy into banditry or gladiatorial schools, since a career in the Guard was closed to them. Modern scholarship (Campbell, Speidel) sees the reform as a turning point: the Guard became a corps of elite legionaries and a military reserve that fought in the Parthian and British wars, and the legions gained a channel of promotion into Rome. It survived until Constantine abolished it after the Milvian Bridge in 312.
scholarship: Campbell, The Emperor and the Roman Army (1984)

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

clodius_albinus_made_caesar_193.detail: Albinus, an aristocrat from Hadrumetum, struck coins as Caesar at Rome and held the consulship of 194 with Severus. The arrangement implied succession, a promise Severus cancelled in 195 when he made his elder son Caesar.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

battle_of_cyzicus_193.detail: Niger had crossed into Europe and occupied Byzantium and Perinthus, but Severus' troops, crossing the Propontis elsewhere, caught Aemilianus, proconsul of Asia, near Cyzicus. Aemilianus was killed (Dio says while fleeing; Herodian hints he was already disloyal to Niger).
battle_of_cyzicus_193.debate: Exact date (late 193 or early 194) uncertain; commander on the Severan side probably Ti. Claudius Candidus.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

siege_of_byzantium_193.detail: Dio gives a vivid account of the city's walls of squared stone bound with bronze plates, the engines of the engineer Priscus of Nicaea, and the citizens reduced to eating hides and finally each other. Severus executed the magistrates and soldiers, razed the walls, and subordinated the city to Perinthus as a village; it was soon rebuilt, reportedly at Caracalla's request.
siege_of_byzantium_193.debate: Marius Maximus, later biographer of emperors and a lost source of the HA, commanded Moesian forces in the siege according to his career inscription.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus
History of the Empire after Marcus

battle_of_issus_194.detail: Niger's army held a strong position in the pass, but a cavalry force under Valerianus outflanked it through the woods while a thunderstorm, beating into the faces of Niger's men and at the backs of the Severans, was read as divine favour. Dio claims 20,000 of Niger's men died. Niger fled toward the Euphrates hoping to reach Parthia but was caught and beheaded near Antioch; his head was displayed before Byzantium to break its resistance.
battle_of_issus_194.debate: Date usually spring 194; Dio's casualty figure is a round literary number. Both authors stress the Alexandrian echo.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

battle_of_nicaea_194.detail: Dio describes a battle fought partly on the plain and partly in the narrows and on the lake of Ascania, with Niger's appearance briefly rallying his men. Candidus' victory exposed Bithynia and led cities such as Nicaea and Nicomedia to declare for opposite sides, a vivid sign of civic rivalry exploited in civil wars.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

division_of_syria_194.detail: The division continued the Hadrianic and Antonine practice of reducing the number of legions under any single governor; Britain was likewise split into Superior and Inferior, probably early in the third century. Antioch was made a village of Laodicea and its Olympic games transferred, while Laodicea, Tyre and other loyal cities received colonial or metropolitan titles. Antioch's status was restored under Caracalla.
division_of_syria_194.debate: Date of the British division (197, c. 213 or later) disputed; Herodian 3.8.2 places it under Severus.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

severus_first_parthian_campaign_195.detail: Using the pretext of the clients' support for Niger, Severus based himself at Nisibis and sent columns across northern Mesopotamia. Much of Osroene was annexed, leaving the Abgarid king at Edessa with a rump. The campaign laid the groundwork for the province of Mesopotamia and was cut short by news of Albinus' defection. Severus refused the title Parthicus to avoid provoking Vologaeses.

severus_self_adoption_195.detail: The fiction, ridiculed by a senator who congratulated Severus on finding a father, gave the new dynasty Antonine legitimacy and allowed the rehabilitation of Commodus, deified as Severus' 'brother' in 197. Inscriptions trace Severus' lineage back to Nerva. The making of Caracalla Caesar, probably at Viminacium in 195 or 196, converted the agreement with Albinus into war.

clodius_albinus_proclaimed_augustus_196.detail: Albinus had senatorial sympathy at Rome, where crowds at the Circus chanted against a new civil war. In Gaul he defeated the governor of Germania Inferior, Virius Lupus, but failed to win over the Rhine legions, which remained loyal to Severus.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus
History of the Empire after Marcus

battle_of_lugdunum_197.detail:
The rupture between Severus and Albinus came after Severus, having defeated Niger, declared his elder son Caracalla Caesar in 195-196, effectively disinheriting Albinus, who then took the title Augustus and crossed to Gaul with the British legions. Albinus based himself at Lugdunum and defeated Severus' general Virius Lupus; a mint at Lugdunum struck his coins. Severus came west through Pannonia and Noricum, and after a preliminary victory at Tinurtium (Tournus) on the Saône the decisive battle was fought near Lugdunum on 19 February 197.

Dio, whose figure of 150,000 men on each side is certainly inflated, describes a long and evenly matched struggle. Albinus' left wing was routed and fled to its camp, but on the right his men dug concealed pits and trenches in front of their line, lured the Severan troops forward with a feigned retreat and inflicted heavy losses. Severus brought up the Praetorians, was nearly killed, lost his horse and in one version tore off his imperial cloak and drew his sword to rally the fugitives. The cavalry under Julius Laetus then arrived and decided the day; Dio claims Laetus had deliberately held back to see which side would win, and Severus later executed him. Albinus fled to a house by the Rhône and killed himself or was killed; his head was sent to Rome, and Severus rode his horse over the naked body before it was thrown into the river with those of his wife and sons.

Lugdunum, capital of the Three Gauls, was sacked and burned and never fully regained its pre-eminence, while Trier rose. In Rome Severus read to the Senate a eulogy of the severity of Sulla, Marius and Augustus and executed 29 senators, and confiscations of the property of Albinus' partisans in Gaul and Spain enriched the res privata. Herodian and the Historia Augusta offer different details; the exact site, perhaps on the plateau north of the city around Trévoux, remains unknown.
battle_of_lugdunum_197.debate: Size of the armies (Dio: 150,000 each) and exact site disputed; role of Laetus contested.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

severan_purge_197.detail: Severus deified Commodus as his adoptive brother, a deliberate insult to senators who had hated him. The confiscations, together with those of Niger's partisans, filled the treasury and enabled the first pay rise for soldiers since Domitian.
severan_purge_197.debate: The HA lists 41 names, many probably invented.

severan_army_reforms_197.detail:
Severus owed his throne to the army and is remembered, by Dio and Herodian alike, for binding it to the dynasty with money and privileges. Legionary pay, unchanged since Domitian at 300 denarii a year, was raised, probably to 400 or 450 denarii (Caracalla raised it again by half, perhaps to 675); donatives grew, and a regular allowance in kind (later the annona militaris) became a burden on the provinces. Herodian says Severus allowed soldiers to live with their wives, effectively lifting the Augustan ban on marriage for serving men, legalising families that already existed around the forts. He also granted soldiers the right to wear the gold ring of the equestrian order, opened promotion from the centurionate into equestrian posts, and ordered the collegia of principales and junior officers formed at Lambaesis and elsewhere.

Three new legions, I, II and III Parthica, were raised for the eastern war and commanded by equestrian prefects rather than senatorial legates, a pattern that pointed towards Gallienus' later exclusion of senators. I and III Parthica garrisoned the new province of Mesopotamia at Singara and Rhesaina, while II Parthica was stationed at Albanum near Rome. With the doubled Praetorian Guard, the enlarged urban cohorts and vigiles, and the equites singulares, the emperor kept roughly 30,000 troops at the capital.

Dio quotes Severus' dying advice to his sons to 'enrich the soldiers and scorn all others', and Gibbon called him the principal author of the decline of the empire. Modern scholars are more cautious. Brian Campbell and Michael Speidel point out that pay had lost value through inflation and that the reforms professionalised rather than barbarised the army; the debate concerns how heavily the rising wage bill drove the debasement of the denarius and later the antoninianus, and whether Severus' openness to promotion from the ranks created the soldier-emperors of the following decades.
severan_army_reforms_197.debate: The size of the pay increase is reconstructed from papyri and Speidel's calculations; dates for the marriage concession range 197-200.
scholarship: Speidel, "Roman Army Pay Scales", JRS 82 (1992)
Campbell, The Emperor and the Roman Army (1984)

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus
History of the Empire after Marcus

sack_of_ctesiphon_198.detail:
While Severus was fighting Albinus, the Parthian king Vologaeses V attacked Roman Mesopotamia and besieged Nisibis. Severus returned east in the summer of 197, relieved Nisibis and, at the Euphrates, built a river fleet. The army sailed and marched downstream past Dura, found Seleucia and Babylon abandoned, and reached Ctesiphon, the Parthian winter capital on the Tigris, which was stormed in late 197 or January 198. Vologaeses escaped with a few horsemen, but the city was given over to plunder; Dio says the soldiers killed all the adult males and took about 100,000 captives, along with the royal treasure.

On 28 January 198, the hundredth anniversary of Trajan's accession, Severus took the title Parthicus Maximus, raised the ten-year-old Caracalla to Augustus and made Geta Caesar, a choreographed link with Trajan, the last emperor to take Ctesiphon. The army, short of supplies, then withdrew up the Tigris, the Euphrates route having been stripped of forage, and Severus twice failed to take the desert city of Hatra in 198 and 199, the second time, Dio says, because he called off an assault that had breached the walls in the hope of saving the temple treasures, by which time his European troops refused to attack again.

The campaign is commemorated on the Arch of Septimius Severus in the Forum (203), whose four large panels depict the sieges of Nisibis, Edessa or Carrhae, Seleucia and Ctesiphon in the style of campaign paintings. Its long-term significance was greater than its immediate gains: the humiliation of the Arsacid house, the third Roman sack of Ctesiphon in eighty years, contributed to the internal discredit that allowed Ardashir to overthrow the dynasty in 224. Dio judged the annexations that followed costly and provocative, a view many modern historians share.
sack_of_ctesiphon_198.debate: Date of the capture (late 197 or January 198) disputed.

siege_of_hatra_198.debate: Herodian telescopes the two sieges into one; Dio distinguishes them.
