province_of_mesopotamia_198.detail:
Roman Mesopotamia began with Severus' first eastern campaign of 195, when he punished Osroene, Adiabene and Arab allies of Niger and restored Roman control over the territory between the Euphrates and the Khabur. After the sack of Ctesiphon and the failures at Hatra, the land was organised as a province under an equestrian prefect on the Egyptian model, so that no senator could command its legions. I Parthica was based at Singara and III Parthica at Rhesaina, and Nisibis, the key fortress city controlling the road from the Tigris to the Euphrates, became the colonia Septimia Nisibis and seat of the governor. The client kingdom of Osroene, ruled from Edessa by Abgar VIII 'the Great', who had visited Rome, was reduced to a small territory around the city; Caracalla deposed its dynasty and made Edessa a colonia in 213-214.

Cassius Dio, who opposed the annexation, wrote that Severus claimed it as a bulwark for Syria, but that it was a constant source of wars and expense, since it lay near the Medes and Parthians and Rome was always fighting for those who lived there. Modern historians have often agreed that the forward position committed Rome to a frontier on the Khabur and the Jebel Sinjar that a revived Persia could not accept. Nisibis and Carrhae changed hands repeatedly in the third century (lost c. 235-238, regained by Timesitheus in 243, lost and regained in the 250s and 260s), and in the fourth Nisibis held off Shapur II three times (338, 346, 350) before Jovian surrendered it in 363.

The province thus defined the Roman-Persian frontier for 165 years and was the scene of the most important sieges of late antiquity. Inscriptions and the Dura parchments show prefects, legionary vexillations and a dense network of forts linking the Euphrates and Tigris.
scholarship: Millar, The Roman Near East 31 BC-AD 337 (1993)
Edwell, Between Rome and Persia (2008)

numidia_made_province.debate: The precise date of the formal separation (between 197 and 208) is disputed.

siege_of_hatra_199.detail: Dio records that the Syrian troops ordered to attack were slaughtered and that Severus could not get his men to try again. The failure marked the limit of Severan expansion; Hatra later became a Roman ally with an attested Roman garrison (cohors IX Maurorum) in the 230s.

severus_in_egypt_200.detail: The grant of councils, completed in 200/201, aligned Egypt with the civic organisation of the rest of the East and made councillors liable for tax collection. Severus is said to have repaired the Memnon colossus, after which it ceased to sing at dawn. He also issued responses to petitions (apokrimata) preserved on papyrus, a rare direct view of the emperor's justice.

severus_in_africa_202.debate: Whether Severus visited Africa in 202/203 is inferred from coins and the HA; Gholaia's foundation is dated 201 by inscription.

alexandrian_persecution_202.debate: Whether an empire-wide Severan ban on conversion existed is disputed; the persecution may have been local.

martyrdom_of_perpetua_and_felicity_203.detail: The Passio Perpetuae records her dreams of a ladder to heaven and of fighting an Egyptian as a man, and her refusal of her pagan father's pleas. The text, possibly edited by a Montanist (Tertullian has been suggested), is a central document for women, martyrdom and North African Christianity. The HA claims Severus banned conversion to Judaism and Christianity, a statement most scholars doubt.
martyrdom_of_perpetua_and_felicity_203.debate: Whether there was a general Severan persecution is rejected by most; prosecutions were local.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

fall_of_plautianus_205.detail: Plautianus had accumulated statues, wealth and influence beyond any prefect since Sejanus; Dio says he castrated a hundred free Romans to attend his daughter. The plot charge was probably fabricated by Caracalla, who loathed his wife. Plautilla was exiled to Lipara and killed in 212. Papinian and Maecius Laetus replaced Plautianus, inaugurating the age of jurist-prefects.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Carettoni et al., La pianta marmorea di Roma antica (1960)
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project

bulla_felix_brigandage_206.detail: Dio attributes to Bulla a Robin Hood maxim to the praetorian prefect Papinian, telling him to 'feed your slaves, so they won't turn bandit'. The episode, whatever its embellishment, reflects rural insecurity and the absorption of runaway and underpaid imperial slaves.

severus_british_expedition_208.detail:
In 207 the governor of Britain reported that the Caledonii and Maeatae were overrunning the province and asked for troops or the emperor himself. Severus, now over sixty and crippled by gout, came in 208 with Julia Domna, both sons and much of the court. Herodian adds the motive of removing his quarrelling sons from the luxuries of Rome. Eboracum became the seat of government, and Geta was left to administer the province while Severus and Caracalla advanced north in 209, building roads through forests and causeways across marshes. A new legionary base at Carpow on the Tay and the refurbished harbour at South Shields and the fort at Cramond supported the campaign, which may have reached the Moray Firth.

The Caledonians avoided pitched battle, using ambush, bogs and lures of cattle, and Dio claims, implausibly, that the Romans lost 50,000 men. Severus nevertheless forced a treaty by which the enemy ceded territory, and in 210 he and his sons took the title Britannicus. When the Maeatae and Caledonii rose again, Severus ordered a war of extermination, quoting Agamemnon in Homer that no one should escape, not even the child in its mother's womb; Caracalla led the 210 campaign because his father was ill. The Hadrian's Wall system was heavily rebuilt in these years, so that medieval and early modern writers credited Severus with building the Wall itself.

Severus died at York on 4 February 211. Caracalla immediately made peace, withdrew from the newly occupied territory and returned with Geta to Rome, abandoning Carpow. The Severan settlement nonetheless brought nearly a century of relative peace to the northern frontier, perhaps through treaties and subsidies with the northern peoples, and the division of Britain into two provinces followed. Scholars debate whether Severus aimed at the conquest of the whole island or a punitive war followed by a strengthened frontier.
severus_british_expedition_208.debate: Whether Severus intended permanent conquest of all Scotland or a punitive war is debated; the Carpow fortress (with stamps of II Augusta and VI Victrix) argues for occupation.
scholarship: Birley, The Roman Government of Britain (2005)
Hodgson, Hadrian's Wall (2017)

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

death_of_septimius_severus_211.detail:
Severus died at Eboracum on 4 February 211, aged 65, after nearly eighteen years of rule. Gout had disabled him for years, and the Caledonian campaign of 210 had to be led by Caracalla. Dio reports that Caracalla had tried to kill his father on horseback in front of the army during a parley with the Caledonians and that Severus, though aware, had pardoned him; Herodian says Caracalla tried to persuade the doctors to hasten his death. The dying emperor's words to his sons, as reported by Dio, were 'Be harmonious, enrich the soldiers and scorn all others'; his last watchword to the tribune was 'Laboremus' ('Let us work'). He is also said to have remarked, 'I took over a state in turmoil everywhere and leave it at peace even in Britain'.

His body was cremated at York, apparently in the presence of the army, and his ashes taken by his sons in an urn of purple stone, or gold, to the Mausoleum of Hadrian. He was promptly deified. The succession passed jointly to Caracalla, Augustus since 198, and Geta, Augustus since 209/210, an arrangement that collapsed within ten months in fratricide.

Severus' reign transformed the monarchy. He fought three civil wars, doubled the troops near Rome, raised the army's pay and status, created Mesopotamia, divided large provinces to prevent rebellion, and favoured equestrians and jurists such as Papinian, Ulpian and Paul in the administration. He lavished buildings on Rome and his native Lepcis. Gibbon blamed him for the military despotism of the following century; modern biographers such as Anthony Birley present an able, ruthless provincial who completed the integration of Africa and the east into the governing class, while acknowledging that the costs of his army policy weighed on his successors.
scholarship: Birley, Septimius Severus: The African Emperor (1988)

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus
History of the Empire after Marcus

murder_of_geta_211.detail:
Caracalla (born 188) and Geta (born 7 March 189) had hated each other since childhood, competing in quail-fighting and chariot racing, and their father's attempt to bind them by naming both Augustus failed. After returning from Britain they lived in the imperial palace in Rome with the connecting passages walled up and separate guards; each feared poisoning. Herodian reports a plan to divide the empire, with Geta taking the east from Asia, ruling from Antioch or Alexandria, and Caracalla Europe and Africa, the Senate and armies split along the Propontis, until Julia Domna asked how they proposed to divide their mother.

In late December 211, under the pretext of a reconciliation meeting arranged by their mother in her apartments, Caracalla had centurions burst in and stab Geta, who died in Julia Domna's arms; she was wounded in the hand by his blood-soaked attackers and was forbidden to mourn. Caracalla rushed to the Praetorian camp, claimed he had escaped a plot, and secured the soldiers with a donative of 2,500 denarii each and a pay rise of fifty per cent. The legion at Albanum at first shut its gates, saying it had sworn to both sons.

A purge followed in which, Dio says, 20,000 people died, including Geta's freedmen and soldiers, the jurist and prefect Papinian, Pertinax's son, and Cornificia, daughter of Marcus Aurelius. Geta suffered damnatio memoriae on an unparalleled scale: his name was chiselled from inscriptions across the empire, his portraits defaced, his face scraped from the Severan family tondo now in Berlin and his figure removed from the Arch of the Argentarii in Rome; papyri show his name deleted in Egypt. The date is usually given as 26 December 211, though some scholars prefer 19 December or early 212. The murder poisoned Caracalla's reign and made him, in the hostile tradition, the archetypal tyrant.
murder_of_geta_211.debate: Date (19 or 26 December 211, or early 212) and the historicity of the partition plan disputed.

purge_after_geta_212.debate: The famous retort of Papinian is from the Historia Augusta and may be invented.

constitutio_antoniniana_212.detail:
The Constitutio Antoniniana, issued by Caracalla probably in 212 (some argue 213 or 214), granted Roman citizenship to all free inhabitants of the empire except, apparently, the dediticii. It ended the distinction between citizens and peregrines that had structured Roman society since the Republic. Our knowledge depends on a brief notice in Cassius Dio, a sentence of Ulpian in the Digest ('those who are in the Roman world have been made Roman citizens by a constitution of the emperor Antoninus') and a damaged Greek papyrus in Giessen (P.Giss. 40, col. I), which presents the grant as a thank-offering to the gods for the emperor's preservation, probably from Geta's alleged plot.

Dio, hostile to Caracalla, claimed the real motive was fiscal: new citizens became liable to the 5 per cent inheritance and manumission taxes, which Caracalla doubled to 10 per cent, payable to the military treasury. Others stress ideology: Caracalla's universalism, the religious language of the papyrus, and the culmination of a long process of enfranchisement. The meaning of the excluded dediticii is the most debated question: surrendered barbarians, Egyptian villagers, freedmen of the lowest category, or a narrow technical group.

The effects were visible at once in nomenclature. Millions of new citizens took the emperor's family name, so that 'Marcus Aurelius' became the most common name in the eastern papyri. Roman law spread, at least in principle, to all, though local law persisted in practice. The legal line of privilege shifted from citizen versus foreigner to the honestiores versus humiliores, the latter liable to torture and degrading penalties. Later writers such as Augustine and Justinian attributed the measure to Antoninus Pius, showing how its author had faded from memory. Recent studies (Lavan, Ando, Buraselis) emphasise that it extended a Roman identity across the empire just as the third-century crisis began.
constitutio_antoniniana_212.debate: Date (212 vs 213/214), motive (fiscal, religious, ideological) and the meaning of the dediticii are debated.
scholarship: Buraselis, Theia Dorea (1989/2007)
Ando, Imperial Rome AD 193 to 284 (2012)
Besson, Constitutio Antoniniana (2020)
Sherwin-White, The Roman Citizenship (2nd ed., 1973)
Ando (ed.), Citizenship and Empire in Europe 200-1900: The Antonine Constitution after 1800 Years (2016)

caracalla_alamannic_campaign_213.detail: The Acta of the Arval Brethren record sacrifices on 11 August 213 for Caracalla's entry into barbarian territory through Raetia. The victory was followed by payments to tribes, which Dio criticises. Whether the name Alamanni in Dio's text is original or inserted by the Byzantine excerptor Xiphilinus is a well-known controversy; Drinkwater argues the Alamanni as a people coalesced only in the later third century.
scholarship: Drinkwater, The Alamanni and Rome 213-496 (2007)

division_of_britain_severan.debate: Herodian dates it 197, epigraphy suggests c. 211-216.

antoninianus_introduced_215.detail:
In 215, while preparing his Parthian war, Caracalla introduced a new silver coin, called by modern numismatists the antoninianus after a phrase in the Historia Augusta. It is identified by the radiate crown worn by the emperor, while empresses appear on a crescent moon, signs that it was a double denomination. Weighing about 5.1 grams against the contemporary denarius of about 3.2 grams, and of similar silver fineness, around 50 per cent, it contained the silver of about 1.5 denarii while presumably being tariffed at two, a disguised devaluation that let the treasury stretch its bullion to pay the army whose wages Caracalla had just raised by half.

Macrinus and Elagabalus continued it briefly, but it was dropped around 219, and Severus Alexander struck none, perhaps because it was distrusted. It was revived in 238 by Balbinus and Pupienus and under Gordian III became the main silver coin, driving the denarius out of production by the 240s. From then on its weight and fineness fell rapidly: by the reign of Gallienus and in the issues of Claudius II and the Gallic emperors of the late 260s the silver content had fallen to around 2-3 per cent and sometimes below, the coins being little more than bronze with a silver wash. Hoards of thousands of these 'radiates' from the period 260-274 are among the commonest finds in Britain and Gaul, including barbarous imitations.

Aurelian's reform of 274 restored a heavier radiate with a fixed 5 per cent silver content marked XXI, and Diocletian replaced the system in 294. The antoninianus is thus the clearest physical index of the third-century fiscal crisis. Debate continues about its official name (argenteus antoninianus, radiatus or simply argenteus) and its exact value, which has been inferred mainly from weights and from the parallel double sestertius.
antoninianus_introduced_215.debate: The face value of the antoninianus (two denarii is the usual but unproven assumption) is disputed.
scholarship: Walker, The Metrology of the Roman Silver Coinage III (1978)
Estiot, in Metcalf (ed.), Oxford Handbook of Greek and Roman Coinage (2012)
Harl, Coinage in the Roman Economy, 300 BC to AD 700 (1996)

massacre_at_alexandria_215.detail: Dio and Herodian both describe thousands killed. A papyrus (P.Giss. 40 col. II) preserves Caracalla's order expelling Egyptian peasants from Alexandria, except those engaged in trade or worship, with the line that true Egyptians can be recognised by their speech and manners. The Museum's scholars lost their privileges.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

baths_of_caracalla_216.detail: The complex contained libraries, a natatio, and colossal sculptures such as the Farnese Bull and Farnese Hercules. Its frigidarium vaults and brick-faced concrete remained the model for later imperial baths, including those of Diocletian.

caracalla_parthian_campaign_216.detail: Herodian's tale of Caracalla massacring Parthian wedding guests is probably invented; Dio's version has Artabanus refusing outright. Caracalla advanced from Edessa, where he wintered, and planned a new campaign for 217 when he was murdered.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

assassination_of_caracalla_217.detail:
Caracalla wintered at Edessa in 216-217 after his first invasion of Parthia, during which, according to Herodian, he had tricked Artabanus IV with a marriage proposal and massacred Parthian nobles at a wedding feast, though Dio says only that Artabanus refused the match. On 8 April 217, travelling with a small escort from Edessa to the temple of the Moon god Sin at Carrhae, he dismounted to relieve himself and was stabbed by Julius Martialis, an evocatus who resented being refused promotion to centurion (Herodian adds that his brother had been executed). Martialis was killed at once by a Scythian archer of the bodyguard. Caracalla was 29 and had reigned six years since his father's death.

The plot was organised by the praetorian prefect Marcus Opellius Macrinus, a Mauretanian equestrian lawyer, who had learned that letters from Rome were warning the emperor that an astrologer had predicted Macrinus would reign; since Macrinus handled the emperor's correspondence, he intercepted one and acted before he could be denounced. Two tribunes of the Guard, the Aurelii Nemesianus and Apollinaris, were involved. For three days the army had no emperor; on 11 April the soldiers proclaimed Macrinus, who professed grief, had Caracalla's ashes sent to Julia Domna at Antioch and allowed his deification to placate the troops, who idolised the dead emperor.

Macrinus was the first emperor who was not a senator. He had to fight Artabanus at Nisibis, bought peace for 200 million sesterces, and tried to cut the soldiers' pay rises, which proved fatal: in May 218 the Syrian legions declared for Caracalla's supposed son Elagabalus, promoted by Julia Maesa. Julia Domna, ill with breast cancer and fearful of being reduced to private status, starved herself to death at Antioch. Dio, then in Pergamum as Macrinus' appointee, is the main and well-informed source.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

battle_of_nisibis_217.detail: Herodian says the Parthian cataphracts and camel-riders were hampered by caltrops strewn by the Romans, and that the field was so heaped with bodies the armies could not see each other. The payment, presented as gifts, was the last major Roman-Arsacid settlement: within seven years Artabanus was dead and the Sasanians ruled Iran.
battle_of_nisibis_217.debate: Some (on Herodian's account) count it a Parthian victory.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

revolt_of_elagabalus_218.detail: Maesa's wealth (distributed freely), the boy's resemblance to Caracalla and dissatisfaction with Macrinus' pay cuts for new recruits all played a part. The eunuch Gannys organised the coup.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus
History of the Empire after Marcus

battle_of_antioch_218.detail: Dio describes Julia Maesa and Julia Soaemias leaping from their chariots to rally the wavering Elagabalan troops and the boy emperor charging with drawn sword. Macrinus fled disguised, shaved his head and beard, and got as far as Chalcedon.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus
History of the Empire after Marcus

elagabal_cult_in_rome_220.detail: Elagabalus also 'married' the god to Urania of Carthage, whose cult image was brought to Rome, and moved the Palladium and Vesta's fire into the new temple. Midsummer processions saw the emperor running backwards before the god's chariot. Dio and Herodian present the reign as a catalogue of sexual and religious outrages, and the HA life adds much fiction; modern work (Icks, 2011) sees a real religious programme alienating the Roman elite and army. Coins with the legend SANCT DEO SOLI ELAGABAL confirm the cult.
elagabal_cult_in_rome_220.debate: The HA life is largely invented; Herodian moralising; the god's Syrian character is overplayed in sources.
scholarship: Icks, The Crimes of Elagabalus (2011)

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus
History of the Empire after Marcus

assassination_of_elagabalus_222.detail: The Emesene god was sent home and Jupiter restored. Real power passed to Julia Maesa (died c. 224) and then to Alexander's mother Julia Mamaea, governing with a council of senators and jurists including Ulpian.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

murder_of_ulpian_223.detail: Ulpian had reportedly executed his predecessors Flavianus and Chrestus. His writings supplied about a third of Justinian's Digest, making him perhaps the single most influential legal author in European history. Dio, then governor of Pannonia, was himself threatened by the Guard for disciplining soldiers and spent his second consulship (229) outside Rome for safety.
murder_of_ulpian_223.debate: Traditional date 228 has given way to 223 on the basis of P.Oxy. 2565 and Dio's sequence; still disputed.

battle_of_hormozgan_224.detail:
Ardashir, son (or adopted son) of Papak and grandson of Sasan, priest of the temple of Anahid at Istakhr, began as a local ruler in Persis and in the 210s-220s conquered the neighbouring kingdoms of Kerman, Isfahan and Mesene, exploiting the Parthian civil war between Artabanus IV and his brother Vologaeses VI. When Artabanus finally marched against him, the armies met on the plain of Hormozgan, whose location is unknown, perhaps near Ram Hormoz in Khuzestan. Arabic and Persian tradition (Tabari, drawing on the Sasanian Book of Kings) dates the battle to 28 April 224 and says Ardashir killed Artabanus with his own hands, while his son Shapur killed the Parthian secretary Dadbundad. The great rock relief at Firuzabad shows three equestrian duels: Ardashir unhorsing Artabanus, Shapur his opponent and a page another Parthian noble.

Ardashir spent two more years subduing Media and the rest of the Parthian realm and was crowned King of Kings of Eran at Ctesiphon, probably in 226. He took the title 'King of Kings of the Iranians whose lineage is from the gods' and founded cities such as Ardashir-Khwarrah (Firuzabad) and Veh-Ardashir opposite Ctesiphon. Branches of the Arsacid family survived in Armenia, which became a long-term point of conflict.

For Rome the change was momentous. Dio, writing in 229, already warned that Ardashir was a fearful threat; Herodian states that he claimed all lands once held by the Achaemenids up to the Aegean, though modern scholars such as Kettenhofen and Potter doubt whether such irredentism was real Sasanian policy or Roman projection. In any case the new dynasty was more centralised, militarily aggressive and ideologically Zoroastrian, and within twenty years its kings had raided Mesopotamia, killed one Roman emperor (Gordian III) and would soon capture another.
battle_of_hormozgan_224.debate: Date (224 or 227) and location of the battle; reality of Sasanian Achaemenid claims.
scholarship: Daryaee, Sasanian Persia (2009)
Wiesehöfer, Ancient Persia (1996)
Frye, The History of Ancient Iran (1984)

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

coronation_of_ardashir_226.detail: Ardashir's coins show the fire altar on the reverse and call him 'Mazda-worshipping divine Ardashir, King of Kings of Iran, whose lineage is from the gods'. Roman authors (Herodian, Dio) report that he claimed all lands once ruled by Darius as far as Ionia and Caria, though this may be a Roman projection.

cassius_dio_second_consulship_229.detail: Dio spent ten years collecting material and twelve writing. Books 36-60 survive largely intact; the books for 193-229, our best source for the Severans, survive only in Byzantine epitomes (Xiphilinus, Zonaras) and excerpts, apart from parts of books 78-79. As a senator and eyewitness of Commodus, Pertinax and the Severans, he is invaluable but hostile to soldiers and to upstarts like Macrinus.

ardashir_invades_mesopotamia_230.detail: An embassy from Alexander urging Ardashir to be content with his own borders was answered (Herodian) with 400 tall Persian horsemen demanding Roman withdrawal from Syria and Asia. Mutinies in the Roman eastern army, including the murder of the governor of Mesopotamia Flavius Heracleo, show the weakness of the Roman position.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

severus_alexander_persian_campaign_232.detail: Herodian presents the campaign as a humiliating failure caused by Alexander's timidity and Mamaea's influence; Alexander's own coinage and triumph of 233 claimed victory, and the HA invents a great battle. Modern scholarship (e.g. Edwell) sees a costly stalemate that preserved Mesopotamia. The dangerous Germanic incursions on the Rhine and Danube in 233-234 forced the field army to the West.
severus_alexander_persian_campaign_232.debate: Outcome disputed: Herodian (defeat) vs HA and coins (victory).
scholarship: Edwell, Between Rome and Persia (2008)

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Kraeling, The Christian Building (Excavations at Dura-Europos, Final Report VIII.2, 1967)
Peppard, The World's Oldest Church (2016)

alamannic_invasion_233.debate: The identification of the invaders as Alamanni is anachronistic for 233; the name is first secure in 289.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

assassination_of_severus_alexander_235.detail:
After an indecisive Persian campaign in 232, Severus Alexander and his mother Julia Mamaea were called west by Germanic attacks on the Rhine and Danube. In 234 he assembled an army at Mogontiacum, including eastern archers and Osrhoene troops, and built a pontoon bridge across the Rhine. Instead of fighting, however, he opened negotiations and offered money for peace, a policy the soldiers saw as cowardly and as diverting to barbarians funds that should have been theirs. Mamaea's dominance and reputed avarice deepened the resentment.

In March 235 recruits from Pannonia, being trained by the gigantic Thracian equestrian officer Gaius Julius Verus Maximinus, proclaimed their commander emperor. When the news reached the imperial camp at Vicus Britannicus (probably Bretzenheim near Mainz), Alexander's own troops deserted; he was found clinging to his mother in his tent, and both were killed together with their advisers. He was 26 and had reigned thirteen years. Herodian, the only contemporary narrative, describes the scene; the Historia Augusta places it in Britain or Gaul, confusingly. Alexander was later deified, and a tradition associates the Monte del Grano tomb outside Rome, where the Portland Vase was reputedly found, with him and his mother.

The murder ended the Severan dynasty and is conventionally taken as the start of the so-called crisis of the third century, the half-century of short-lived soldier emperors that followed. Maximinus, the first emperor to rise from the ranks and never to visit Rome, symbolised the new dominance of the Danubian army. Modern historians debate how far Alexander's reign really was the peaceful, Senate-friendly regime portrayed by the Historia Augusta, which idealises him, and stress the strain of fighting on two frontiers at once that Herodian's narrative reveals.
assassination_of_severus_alexander_235.debate: Vicus Britannicus is often identified with Bretzenheim near Mainz.
scholarship: Potter, The Roman Empire at Bay AD 180-395 (2nd ed., 2014)

History of the Empire after Marcus

battle_of_harzhorn.detail: Over 2,700 artefacts include catapult bolts, hipposandals, a dolabra stamped for Legio IIII Severiana Alexandriana, and coins down to Severus Alexander, which together date the battle to the campaign of Maximinus in 235/236. Bolt patterns show Roman artillery clearing the ridge and infantry storming it. Herodian had reported Maximinus marching 300-400 stades into Germany and fighting a battle in a swamp, long dismissed as rhetoric; the Harzhorn confirms large-scale operations near the Elbe-Weser region.
battle_of_harzhorn.debate: Identification with Maximinus' campaign is very probable but not explicit in the sources.
scholarship: Pöppelmann, Deppmeyer and Steinmetz (eds.), Roms vergessener Feldzug (2013)
Geschwinde and others, 'Roms vergessener Feldzug', Germania (2009)

crisis_of_the_third_century.detail:
The 'crisis of the third century' is a modern label, popularised in German scholarship (Reichskrise) and by Rostovtzeff and Alföldy, for the half-century between the murder of Severus Alexander (235) and the accession of Diocletian (284). In those 49 years some 26 emperors were recognised in Rome, almost all of them killed by their own troops or in battle, alongside dozens of regional usurpers. At the worst moment, after Valerian's capture in 260, the empire split into three: the Gallic Empire in the west (260-274), the Palmyrene sphere in the east, and Gallienus' central rump.

The pressures were simultaneous. In the east the new Sasanian dynasty killed or captured two emperors (Gordian III at Misiche, Valerian at Edessa) and sacked Antioch. On the Danube Gothic, Carpic and Herul invasions culminated in the death of Decius at Abritus (251) and the seaborne raids that burned Ephesus and Athens; on the Rhine the Franks and Alamanni broke through, and the Agri Decumates were lost around 260. A great pandemic, the Plague of Cyprian, raged from about 249 to the 260s. The silver content of the antoninianus fell from about 50 per cent to under 5, and prices in Egypt rose many times over, especially after Aurelian's reform. Cities in Gaul built tight walled circuits; Rome itself was given walls in 271. The habit of setting up inscriptions collapsed, which partly explains the poverty of our evidence: no contemporary narrative survives beyond fragments of Dexippus, and later sources (Zosimus, Zonaras, the Latin epitomes and the unreliable Historia Augusta) are thin.

Recovery came from Gallienus' reforms (mobile cavalry, equestrian commanders), the Illyrian soldier emperors Claudius II, Aurelian and Probus, and above all Diocletian's restructuring. Historians now debate the very concept. Christian Witschel and others stress regional variation: Africa and parts of the east prospered, and urban life continued in many places. Kyle Harper adds climate change and pandemic as drivers; MacMullen and Potter emphasise the government's responses. Most still see a real systemic crisis, but one that produced the transformed late Roman state rather than collapse.
crisis_of_the_third_century.debate: Whether 'crisis' is an apt term at all; whether it was general or regional; whether its causes were external pressure (Persia, Goths), internal politics (the army and usurpation), economics, or epidemic and climate.

Witschel, Krise, Rezession, Stagnation? (1999)
Potter, The Roman Empire at Bay AD 180-395 (2004, 2nd ed. 2014)
Drinkwater, 'Maximinus to Diocletian and the crisis', CAH XII (2005)
Hekster, Rome and its Empire AD 193-284 (2008)
Liebeschuetz, 'Was there a crisis of the third century?', in Hekster et al. (eds.), Crises and the Roman Empire (2007)
Harper, The Fate of Rome (2017)

revolt_of_the_gordians_238.detail:
Maximinus' fiscal pressure fell heavily on the rich of the provinces. In early 238 a procurator in Africa Proconsularis pressed landowners around Thysdrus (El Djem) with demands for arrears; young men of the local aristocracy armed their rural workers, killed him at a meeting and went to the proconsul, Marcus Antonius Gordianus Sempronianus Romanus, a wealthy senator of about eighty from an old family, and proclaimed him emperor. He accepted, reluctantly according to Herodian, and took his son Gordian II, his legate, as co-Augustus. They moved to Carthage and wrote to Rome, where the Senate, delighted, recognised them, declared Maximinus a public enemy, killed his supporters including the prefect of the city, and appointed a board of twenty consulars (vigintiviri) to defend Italy. Provinces across the empire followed.

The revolt was crushed within about three weeks. Capelianus, governor of Numidia and a personal enemy of the elder Gordian, marched on Carthage with legio III Augusta and Moorish auxiliaries. Gordian II led out a large but untrained militia and was killed in battle; his father hanged himself with his belt. The chronology is much disputed: Herodian implies a reign of 22 days, the Historia Augusta 36, and modern reconstructions place it anywhere from January to April 238.

The consequences went far beyond Africa. Having broken with Maximinus, the Senate could not turn back, and elected two of the vigintiviri, Pupienus and Balbinus, as emperors, adding the boy Gordian III, grandson of Gordian I, as Caesar to satisfy the urban mob. Maximinus' invasion stalled before Aquileia, where his soldiers killed him; the Praetorians then murdered Pupienus and Balbinus, leaving Gordian III. Legio III Augusta was disbanded in punishment. The great amphitheatre of Thysdrus, one of the largest in the empire, dates roughly from this period and was never completely finished.
revolt_of_the_gordians_238.debate: Chronology of 238 (length of the Gordians' reign; dates of Aquileia) intensely debated (Peachin, Drinkwater).

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus
History of the Empire after Marcus

battle_of_carthage_238.detail: Gordian III later cashiered III Augusta for its role, and its name was erased from inscriptions until the legion was reconstituted in 253.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

pupienus_and_balbinus_elected_238.detail: The collegiate emperorship with two equal Augusti, without a senior partner, was unprecedented. Street fighting broke out between the plebs and the Praetorians, and parts of the city burned.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

siege_of_aquileia_238.detail: Herodian describes the Aquileians melting down statues for missiles and women giving their hair for bowstrings (a topos also attached to Carthage). The local god Belenus was said to have appeared on the walls. The heads of Maximinus and Maximus were sent to Rome.
siege_of_aquileia_238.debate: Date of Maximinus' death (April to June 238) disputed.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus
History of the Empire after Marcus

sack_of_histria_238.detail: The Historia Augusta's 'excidium Histriae' is corroborated by a destruction layer at the site. Menophilus' subsidies to the Goths and refusal to pay the Carpi, reported by the fragment of Petrus Patricius (from Dexippus), illustrate the developing system of tribute and divide-and-rule on the lower Danube.
scholarship: Heather, Goths and Romans 332-489 (1991)
Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)

accession_of_shapur_i_240.detail: Shapur's own trilingual (Middle Persian, Parthian, Greek) inscription on the Ka'ba-ye Zartosht at Naqsh-e Rustam (ŠKZ) narrates his three Roman wars, listing defeated emperors and captured cities and recording the deportation of Roman prisoners to build cities such as Gundeshapur (Weh-Andiok-Shabuhr, 'better than Antioch, Shapur built this') and Bishapur.
accession_of_shapur_i_240.debate: The date 12 April 240 derives from Manichaean sources; sole rule 241 or 242.

siege_of_hatra_240.detail: The Cologne Mani Codex dates the fall to the year Mani received his second revelation (240/241). Arabic legend tells of the king's daughter al-Nadira betraying the city for love of Shapur. Persian pressure also took Nisibis and Carrhae around this time, prompting Gordian III's expedition.
siege_of_hatra_240.debate: King's identity in 240 uncertain (Sanatruq II is the last securely attested king).

battle_of_rhesaina_243.detail: Gordian had opened the temple of Janus before leaving Rome, an antiquarian gesture. The victory was followed by Timesitheus' death from illness, possibly helped along by his successor Philip.

battle_of_misiche_244.detail:
In 243 Gordian III's army, directed by his father-in-law Timesitheus, drove the Persians out of Roman Mesopotamia, defeating Shapur near Rhesaina and recovering Carrhae and Nisibis. After Timesitheus died of illness, his successor as prefect, the Arabian equestrian Marcus Julius Philippus, advanced with the young emperor down the Euphrates towards Ctesiphon. Early in 244 the armies met at Misiche (Mesiche, probably near modern Fallujah) where, according to the trilingual inscription of Shapur I at Naqsh-e Rostam (ŠKZ), 'Gordian Caesar raised a force from the whole Roman empire, from the Goths and Germans, and marched on Assyria against Eranshahr and against us. On the border of Assyria at Misiche a great frontal battle took place. Gordian Caesar was killed and the Roman force destroyed. And the Romans made Philip Caesar.' Shapur renamed the town Peroz-Shapur, 'Victorious is Shapur'.

Roman sources tell a different story. They never admit a defeat. Zosimus and the Historia Augusta say Philip engineered a supply shortage, stirred the soldiers against the 19-year-old emperor and had him killed; others say he died of illness or a fall from his horse. The soldiers built him a cenotaph at Zaitha near Circesium, which Ammianus saw in 363. Some scholars think Gordian died of wounds from the battle, as the Persian relief at Bishapur implies by showing him lying under Shapur's horse.

Philip, proclaimed emperor, quickly made peace: according to the ŠKZ he paid 500,000 denarii as ransom and became tributary, and he apparently abandoned support for Armenia, though he kept Mesopotamia. He then hurried to Rome. The episode illustrates the difficulty of writing third-century history: the Persian royal propaganda and the Roman literary tradition must be read against each other (Kettenhofen; Dodgeon and Lieu).
battle_of_misiche_244.debate: Whether Gordian died in or after the battle, by wounds, illness or murder by Philip.
scholarship: Dodgeon and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars AD 226-363 (1991)
Potter, The Roman Empire at Bay (2004/2014)

peace_of_philip_244.detail: The ŠKZ calls Philip a tributary. Roman writers say he later reneged on the Armenian clause. Philip also founded Philippopolis (Shahba) in his native Trachonitis and deified his father Marinus.

scholarship: Kraeling, The Synagogue (Dura Final Report VIII.1, 1956)

millennium_of_rome_248.detail: Coins carry SAECULUM NOVUM. The celebration coincided with Gothic and Carpic invasions and military revolts, an irony later Christian tradition, which also made Philip the first Christian emperor (Eusebius, HE 6.34), exploited. The Christian claim is generally rejected.
millennium_of_rome_248.debate: Philip's Christianity is a later legend; the animal list in the HA is suspect.

revolts_of_pacatianus_and_jotapianus_248.detail: Philip's offer to resign was answered by the senator Decius, who predicted the usurpers would fall; Philip then sent Decius to the Danube, where the troops proclaimed him instead. Pacatianus' coins, minted at Viminacium, are dated 'year 1001 of Rome'.

battle_of_verona_249.debate: Location (Verona vs Beroea in Macedonia, a scribal confusion) and date (September or October 249) debated.

plague_of_cyprian.detail:
The pandemic known after Bishop Cyprian of Carthage broke out, according to later chroniclers, in Ethiopia and reached Egypt around 249, spreading westward to Italy and Africa by 251-252 and recurring in waves for perhaps fifteen to twenty years. Cyprian's sermon De Mortalitate (c. 252) describes diarrhoea that drained the body's strength, fever in the marrow causing sores in the throat, constant vomiting, bloodshot eyes, gangrene of the feet and other extremities, and loss of hearing or sight among survivors. Bishop Dionysius of Alexandria wrote that the city's population had fallen so far that the number of people aged 14 to 80 receiving the grain dole now equalled those formerly aged 40 to 70. The Historia Augusta claims 5,000 deaths a day at Rome.

The disease killed the emperor Hostilian in 251 and was blamed for the death of Claudius II in 270; it disrupted recruitment and armies, contributed to the perception that the gods were angry (one motive suggested for the Decian and Valerian edicts) and depopulated cities and countryside. At Thebes in Egypt Italian excavators found a mass burial in the funerary complex of Harwa and Akhimenru, with bodies covered in lime and kilns for producing it, dated to the mid-third century and linked to this plague.

The pathogen is unknown. Smallpox, measles, influenza and, recently, a viral haemorrhagic fever such as a filovirus (Kyle Harper) have been proposed; no ancient DNA has yet been recovered. Christian writers stressed the contrast between pagans who abandoned the sick and Christians who nursed them; Pontius says Cyprian organised care for all, and Rodney Stark argued that such care raised Christian survival rates and boosted conversion. The plague's demographic and fiscal effects are central to modern arguments that disease, as much as war, drove the crisis of the third century.
plague_of_cyprian.debate: Pathogen unknown (smallpox, measles, filovirus proposed); scale contested.
scholarship: Harper, The Fate of Rome (2017)
Harper, 'Pandemics and passages to late antiquity', JRA 28 (2015)
Huebner, 'The Plague of Cyprian: A revised view', Klio (2021)
Harper, "Pandemics and Passages to Late Antiquity", JRA 28 (2015)
Tiradritti, "Of Kilns and Corpses", Egyptian Archaeology 44 (2014)

decian_persecution_250.detail:
Soon after his accession late in 249, Decius ordered all inhabitants of the empire to sacrifice to the gods, pour a libation and taste the sacrificial meat in the presence of local commissioners, by a set deadline, and to receive a signed certificate. Some 46 such libelli survive on papyrus from Egypt, dated June to July 250, including one for a priestess of the crocodile god Petesouchos, which show that the measure applied to everyone, not only Christians. James Rives has interpreted the edict as an attempt to create a unified religion of empire, a collective act of piety to secure the gods' favour at the millennium's turn and in a time of war and plague, rather than a targeted persecution. For Christians, however, the effect was the first empire-wide test.

The bishop of Rome, Fabian, was executed on 20 January 250, Babylas of Antioch and Alexander of Jerusalem died in prison, and Origen was tortured at Caesarea. Pionius of Smyrna was burned on 12 March 250; Dionysius of Alexandria escaped arrest by accident; Cyprian of Carthage went into hiding and governed his church by letter, which later cost him authority. Large numbers complied: the sacrificati who sacrificed, the thurificati who offered incense, the libellatici who bribed officials for certificates. Others, the confessors, endured prison and torture, and claimed the right to forgive the lapsed.

The persecution faded after Decius' death at Abritus in June 251, but its aftermath split the church. Rigorists rallied around Novatian in Rome and laxists around Felicissimus in Carthage, while Cornelius and Cyprian forged a middle way through councils that imposed graded penance. The number of executions was probably modest, but the experience of mass apostasy shaped ecclesiology, the sacrament of penance and, ultimately, the Donatist controversy of the next century.
decian_persecution_250.debate: Whether Decius intended to target Christians is debated; Rives argues for a universalising religious policy.
scholarship: Rives, 'The Decree of Decius and the Religion of Empire', JRS 89 (1999)
Knipfing, 'The Libelli of the Decian Persecution', HTR 16 (1923)
Rives, "The Decree of Decius and the Religion of Empire", JRS 89 (1999)
Clarke, The Letters of St. Cyprian I-IV (1984-89)

sources.w: Libelli of 250 (over 40 surviving papyri from Egypt)

siege_of_philippopolis_250.detail: A Vienna palimpsest (the 'Scythica Vindobonensia', identified in 2014) preserves fragments of Dexippus describing this campaign in Thrace, including speeches by Decius. Priscus was declared a public enemy and soon disappeared.
scholarship: Martin and Grusková, 'Scythica Vindobonensia', WS 127 (2014)
Knipfing, "The Libelli of the Decian Persecution", HTR 16 (1923)
Rives, "The Decree of Decius and the Religion of Empire", JRS 89 (1999)

battle_of_abritus.detail:
In 250 a great Gothic coalition under King Cniva crossed the Danube. One force besieged Novae and was driven off by Trebonianus Gallus, governor of Moesia; Cniva moved to Nicopolis, where Decius defeated him, then crossed the Haemus. At Beroe (Augusta Traiana) the Goths surprised and routed Decius' army, and they went on to take Philippopolis, where the governor Lucius Priscus proclaimed himself emperor with Gothic support; the city was sacked and Ammianus later claims 100,000 died. In the spring of 251 Decius, with his son Herennius Etruscus, now Augustus, tried to cut off the Goths as they withdrew north with their booty and captives.

The armies met near Abritus (modern Razgrad in north-east Bulgaria) in June 251. According to Jordanes, drawing on Dexippus, Cniva drew up his men in three lines, the third concealed behind a marsh. Herennius was killed early by an arrow; Decius declared that the loss of one soldier mattered little and pressed on. The Romans broke the first two lines but, pursuing into the swamp, were trapped in the mud and annihilated by missiles. Decius' body was never found. Zosimus and Zonaras accuse Gallus, who commanded part of the army and became emperor, of treacherously advising the attack across the marsh, a charge modern historians treat with caution.

Decius was the first Roman emperor killed by a foreign enemy in battle, and the shock was profound: Christian writers such as Lactantius saw it as divine punishment for the persecution. Gallus made a humiliating treaty allowing the Goths to leave with their prisoners and promising annual payments. Hoards buried around Abritus and coin finds in the area testify to the disaster, and excavations at Hisarlaka near Razgrad have explored the later fortress of Abritus.
battle_of_abritus.debate: Exact site and the role of Trebonianus Gallus.
scholarship: Bursche, 'The battle of Abritus, the imperial treasury and aurei in Barbaricum', NC 173 (2013)
Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)
Bursche, "The Battle of Abritus, the Imperial Treasury and Aurei in Barbaricum", NC 173 (2013)

novatian_schism_251.detail: Cyprian at Carthage backed Cornelius after hesitation and held councils on the lapsed. The Novatianists ('Cathari') spread across the empire; Constantine later tolerated them, and their bishops attended Nicaea. Novatian's De Trinitate is the first major Latin Trinitarian treatise from Rome.

battle_of_barbalissos_252.detail:
Shapur I's second great campaign against Rome is known mainly from his own trilingual inscription at the Ka'ba-ye Zartosht (ŠKZ). After the treaty with Philip in 244, Shapur says, 'Caesar lied again and did wrong to Armenia', probably by supporting the Armenian Arsacids against Persia; Armenian tradition remembers the murder of King Khosrov, instigated by Persia, and the flight of his son Tiridates to the Romans. Shapur first invaded Armenia, then turned on Roman Syria. 'At Barbalissos we annihilated a Roman force of 60,000', the inscription continues, 'and Syria and the surroundings of Syria we burned, ruined and pillaged'. It then lists 37 cities captured in this campaign, from Anatha on the Euphrates to Antioch, Hierapolis, Beroea, Chalcis, Apamea, Raphanaea, Zeugma, Cyrrhus, Seleucia, Samosata and others in Syria, Commagene and Cappadocia.

Barbalissos (Balis, near Meskene) lay on the right bank of the Euphrates where the river turns east, a natural invasion route from Mesopotamia into northern Syria. The Roman sources say nothing about the battle, and the figure of 60,000 is a round number of royal propaganda; but the subsequent capture of Antioch shows that the Roman field army in Syria had been destroyed. The emperor Trebonianus Gallus was occupied with the Goths and the plague, and only the local initiative of Uranius Antoninus at Emesa checked the invaders.

The date is debated: most scholars place it in 252 or 253, connected with the sack of Antioch in 253, though some prefer 256 for parts of the campaign. Either way it inaugurated the most catastrophic decade in Rome's eastern history, ending with Valerian's capture in 260. The episode is a reminder that much third-century history must be reconstructed from Persian royal inscriptions, Syriac and Armenian traditions and archaeology rather than Greco-Roman narratives.
scholarship: Dodgeon and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars AD 226-363 (1991)
Kettenhofen, Die römisch-persischen Kriege des 3. Jahrhunderts n. Chr. (1982)

sack_of_antioch_253.detail:
Antioch on the Orontes, with perhaps 200,000-300,000 inhabitants the greatest city of the Roman east, fell to Shapur I during his second campaign, most probably in 253 (some scholars date it 256 or posit two captures). Ammianus Marcellinus, himself an Antiochene, preserves a story that the city was taken by surprise while the people sat in the theatre: an actor and his wife were performing a scene when she cried, 'Is it a dream or are the Persians here?', and the audience turned to see archers on the hill above. The Thirteenth Sibylline Oracle and later chroniclers (Malalas, Syncellus) name a renegade, Mariades or Cyriades, a member of the city council expelled for embezzlement, who led the Persians to his native city; the Historia Augusta turns him into a usurper. Shapur reportedly had him executed afterwards.

The Persians plundered the city and deported a large part of the population, including craftsmen and the bishop Demetrianus, to Persia. Shapur resettled them in new foundations such as Veh-Andiyok-Shabuhr ('Shapur's better Antioch', Gundeshapur) in Khuzestan and Bishapur in Fars, where Roman prisoners worked on buildings and mosaics; their descendants contributed to the textile, engineering and medical traditions of Sasanian Iran and formed the nucleus of the Christian church in Persia, with Greek-speaking and Syriac-speaking communities.

The sack demonstrated that the Roman east lay open. Uranius Antoninus defended Emesa and struck his own coins; Valerian, proclaimed later in 253, came east and restored Antioch's mint and defences, but Dura-Europos fell in 256 and Valerian himself was captured in 260. Antioch recovered quickly enough to become a Tetrarchic residence under Diocletian.
sack_of_antioch_253.debate: Date 253 or 256; possibility of two captures.
scholarship: Downey, A History of Antioch in Syria (1961)
Potter, Prophecy and History in the Crisis of the Roman Empire (1990)

uranius_antoninus_253.detail: Malalas records a priest of Aphrodite (Sampsigeramus) driving off Shapur from Emesa with slingers; the identification with Uranius is widely accepted. His local defence anticipates the larger role of Odaenathus of Palmyra.

aemilianus_and_valerian_253.detail: Valerian, a senior senator in his sixties, made his son Gallienus co-Augustus, dividing responsibility between East (Valerian) and West (Gallienus), a pattern for later joint rule.

siege_of_dura_europos_256.detail:
Dura-Europos, founded by the Seleucids on a cliff above the Euphrates and Roman since 165, was in the 250s a frontier fortress garrisoned by cohors XX Palmyrenorum and legionary vexillations, with a mixed population of Greeks, Semites, Iranians, Jews and Christians. Anticipating the Persian attack, the defenders built huge embankments of earth and mud brick against the inside of the western desert wall and filled the street behind it, burying houses including the synagogue, the Christian house church and the Mithraeum, which is why their paintings survive.

Shapur's army besieged the city around 256 (some argue 257). The Persians built a siege ramp at the south-west corner and dug mines under the wall at Tower 19 and the Palmyrene Gate. The Romans countermined, and in the tunnel under Tower 19 excavators in the 1930s found the bodies of some 19-20 Roman soldiers in arms and mail, together with one Persian. Simon James has argued (2011) that the Persians, hearing the Roman countermine approach, set a fire of bitumen and sulphur crystals and pumped the toxic smoke into the Roman gallery, killing the defenders in minutes before collapsing the tunnel with the Persian soldier caught inside: perhaps the earliest archaeological evidence of chemical warfare. The city fell, its inhabitants were killed or deported, and it was never reoccupied; Ammianus' army passed its empty ruins in 363.

Excavated by Yale and the French Academy in 1928-1937 (Cumont, Rostovtzeff), Dura became one of the most important sites in the ancient world, yielding papyri and parchments including the military records of the cohort, painted shields, horse armour, the synagogue and church paintings and the 'Pompeii of the desert'. During the Syrian civil war after 2011 the site was extensively looted, satellite images showing thousands of pits.
scholarship: James, 'Stratagems, Combat, and Chemical Warfare in the Siege Mines of Dura-Europos', AJA 115 (2011)
James, The Roman Military Base at Dura-Europos (2019)
James, "Stratagems, Combat, and 'Chemical Warfare' in the Siege Mines of Dura-Europos", AJA 115 (2011)
Baird, Dura-Europos (2018)

gothic_raid_on_trapezus_257.detail: Zosimus describes the raiders climbing the walls with tree trunks against the hillside and carrying off immense booty and captives. Gregory Thaumaturgus' Canonical Epistle deals with Christian captives and collaborators after these raids in Pontus. In 258 another fleet raided the Propontis and sacked Chalcedon, Nicomedia and Nicaea.

valerian_persecution_257.detail: Victims included Pope Sixtus II, beheaded with deacons in the catacomb of Callixtus on 6 August 258, the deacon Lawrence (later legend: the gridiron), and Cyprian of Carthage. Unlike Decius, Valerian targeted the Church's leadership and property, implying awareness of its institutional strength.

martyrdom_of_sixtus_ii_and_lawrence_258.debate: Lawrence was probably beheaded like Sixtus; the gridiron is late legend.

martyrdom_of_cyprian_258.detail: The Acta Proconsularia record his reply 'Deo gratias' to the sentence. His letters and treatises (De Unitate Ecclesiae, De Lapsis) are the most important sources for third-century church organisation and the plague and persecutions.

battle_of_mediolanum_259.detail: The invasion forced Gallienus to concentrate cavalry in northern Italy, often seen (with caution) as the origin of a mobile cavalry reserve under Aureolus based at Milan.

battle_of_augusta_vindelicum_260.detail: The altar is dated by the consuls of 260 'Postumus Augustus and Honoratianus', showing that Raetia had joined Postumus' Gallic Empire. It is a rare contemporary document of the invasions and of a provincial army acting without the emperor.
scholarship: Bakker, 'Raetien unter Postumus', Germania 71 (1993)
Drinkwater, The Alamanni and Rome (2007)

revolts_of_ingenuus_and_regalianus_260.detail: Regalianus' coins, crude overstrikes on older denarii, include issues for his wife Sulpicia Dryantilla. Both revolts reflect frontier armies' demand for an emperor on the spot.

battle_of_edessa_260.detail:
In 259-260, during Shapur I's third campaign, the Persians besieged Edessa and Carrhae in Osroene. Valerian, about seventy and ruling the east while his son Gallienus held the west, marched to relieve them with an army weakened by plague. What happened next is told differently by the two sides. Shapur's inscription (ŠKZ) says: 'Valerian Caesar came against us with 70,000 men from Germania, Raetia, Noricum, Dacia, Pannonia, Moesia, Istria, Spain, Africa, Thrace, Bithynia, Asia, Pamphylia, Isauria, Lycaonia, Galatia, Lycia, Cilicia, Cappadocia, Phrygia, Syria, Phoenicia, Judaea, Arabia, Mauretania, Germania, Lydia, Asia and Mesopotamia. Beyond Carrhae and Edessa a great battle took place, and we captured Valerian Caesar with our own hands, and the others, the praetorian prefect, senators and officers, all these we made prisoner and deported to Persis.' Zosimus and Zonaras instead say that Valerian, unable to break through, went to negotiate with Shapur in person with a small escort and was seized by treachery.

Valerian is the only Roman emperor ever captured by a foreign enemy. Shapur commemorated the event in rock reliefs at Naqsh-e Rostam, Bishapur and Darabgird, showing the kneeling Philip and Valerian held by the wrist. Christian writers relished his fate: Lactantius says Shapur used him as a mounting block and after his death had him flayed, his skin dyed red and hung in a temple. Roman captives were settled in Khuzestan and Fars, and a persistent tradition credits them with building the bridge-dam of Band-e Kaisar at Shushtar.

The consequences were dramatic. Gallienus did not ransom his father; the eastern army proclaimed the Macriani, Odaenathus of Palmyra emerged as Rome's champion, Postumus founded the Gallic Empire and Gallienus revoked the persecution of Christians. The battle's exact site and date (spring or summer 260; some argue 259) are uncertain.
battle_of_edessa_260.debate: Battle or treacherous capture during negotiations; date 260 or 259.
scholarship: Dodgeon and Lieu (1991)
Potter, The Roman Empire at Bay (2014)
Canepa, The Two Eyes of the Earth (2009)
Dodgeon and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars (1991)

postumus_founds_gallic_empire_260.detail:
When news of Valerian's capture arrived, Gallienus was on the Danube facing Ingenuus and Regalianus, leaving his young son Saloninus at Colonia Agrippina under the guardianship of the praetorian prefect Silvanus, with Marcus Cassianius Latinius Postumus, a Batavian or Gallic general, in command of the Rhine. When Postumus' troops, after defeating a band of raiders, divided the booty among themselves, Silvanus demanded it be handed over. The soldiers proclaimed Postumus emperor and besieged Cologne; the citizens surrendered Saloninus, who had hastily been made Augustus, and Silvanus, and both were killed.

Postumus' regime, the Imperium Galliarum, controlled the German and Gallic provinces, Britain, Spain and, briefly, Raetia: the Augsburg victory altar, found in 1992, records a victory on 24-25 April 260 over the Semnones or Juthungi by the governor Simplicinius Genialis, dated by the consuls Postumus and Honoratianus. Its capitals were Cologne and later Trier. Postumus had a senate, consuls, a praetorian guard and good-quality coinage with types of Hercules Deusoniensis and Magusanus, and his gold is among the finest of the century. Crucially, he never tried to take Rome, presenting himself as defender of the Rhine against the Franks and Alamanni. Gallienus' campaigns against him around 265 failed, and Gallienus was wounded by an arrow.

In 269 Postumus suppressed the usurper Laelianus at Mogontiacum but refused to let his men sack the city, and they killed him. His successors Marius, Victorinus and the Tetrici lasted until Aurelian's victory at Châlons in 274. John Drinkwater's study argues that the Gallic Empire was not separatist but a Roman regime meeting regional needs that the central government could not, a view now widely accepted; the episode nonetheless foreshadowed the later regional emperors of the west.
scholarship: Drinkwater, The Gallic Empire (1987)
Bakker, "Raetien unter Postumus", Germania 71 (1993)

gallienus_edict_of_toleration_260.detail: Eusebius quotes Gallienus' rescript to Bishop Dionysius of Alexandria and others. The forty years of peace saw large churches built in cities like Nicomedia, opposite the imperial palace.

frankish_raid_on_tarraco_260.debate: Dates range 256-262; Orosius claims Tarraco was still in ruins in his day.

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

agri_decumates_abandoned_260.debate: Gradual erosion from 233 versus a single collapse in 259/60; some forts were possibly retained into the 270s.
scholarship: Nuber, "Das Ende des Obergermanisch-Raetischen Limes", in Ausgewählte Aspekte (1990)
Drinkwater, The Alamanni and Rome 213-496 (2007)

revolt_of_mussius_aemilianus_261.debate: Whether he claimed the title Augustus is uncertain; no coins.

odaenathus_persian_campaigns_262.detail:
Septimius Odaenathus belonged to a leading family of Palmyra that had held Roman citizenship since the Severans; by the 250s he was a senator of consular rank and 'exarch' (ras) of Tadmor. Inscriptions show him already prominent before Valerian's capture. When Shapur's army withdrew from Cilicia and Syria in 260, Odaenathus attacked its rear on the Euphrates, seizing booty and part of the royal harem. In 261 he destroyed the last of the Macriani, Quietus, at Emesa, and Gallienus, unable to come east, made him his commander there, with titles later attested for him and his son as dux Romanorum and corrector (or restitutor) totius Orientis.

In 262 Odaenathus, with Palmyrene cataphracts, mounted archers and the remains of the Roman eastern army, crossed into Mesopotamia, retook Carrhae and Nisibis (whose inhabitants, according to the Historia Augusta, had sided with Persia), and advanced down the Euphrates to Ctesiphon, which he besieged without taking. A second expedition followed around 266-267, again reaching the Persian capital. He took the title King of Kings, crowning his eldest son Herodes (Hairan) as co-king, in deliberate rivalry with Shapur, while Gallienus celebrated the victories on his own coins and took the title Persicus Maximus.

Odaenathus was murdered with Herodes in 267 or 268, at Emesa or Heraclea Pontica, by a relative named Maeonius, in circumstances later blamed on Zenobia or on Gallienus. Historians debate his status: was he a loyal Roman official who saved the east for Gallienus (as Zosimus, Festus and Zonaras suggest), a client king, or an independent ruler laying the foundation of the Palmyrene empire of Zenobia? Udo Hartmann's study stresses the ambiguity of a man who was simultaneously Roman senator, governor and an Oriental 'King of Kings'. Persian sources are silent, and Shapur's later inscriptions do not mention him.
odaenathus_persian_campaigns_262.debate: Number and dates of expeditions to Ctesiphon disputed; the official meaning of corrector totius Orientis is uncertain.
scholarship: Hartmann, Das palmyrenische Teilreich (2001)
Andrade, Zenobia: Shooting Star of Palmyra (2018)

gallienus_excludes_senators_262.detail: Epigraphy shows senatorial legionary legates disappearing in the 260s, confirming a real shift, though Victor's language of an edict may oversimplify a gradual process. Combined with the Danubian origins of the officer corps, this produced the soldier-emperors Claudius, Aurelian, Probus and Diocletian, and separated civil and military careers, a separation Diocletian and Constantine made systematic.
gallienus_excludes_senators_262.debate: Whether there was a formal edict (Victor) or a de facto trend is disputed.
scholarship: De Blois, The Policy of the Emperor Gallienus (1976)
Christol, Essai sur l'évolution des carrières sénatoriales (1986)

earthquake_of_262.debate: Only the Historia Augusta reports it in these terms; details may be exaggerated or invented.

siege_of_athens_267.detail:
In 267 or 268 a great coalition of Heruli and Goths from the Sea of Azov built a fleet, said by Syncellus to number 500 ships, sailed through the Bosporus, failed before Byzantium, where the Roman fleet won a skirmish, and broke into the Aegean. They plundered Cyzicus, Lemnos and Scyros and landed in Greece, sacking Corinth, Argos and Sparta and attacking Athens. The city's old walls had been repaired under Valerian, but the Heruli took and burned it, devastating the Agora, the Library of Pantainos and much of the lower city; destruction layers and coin hoards in the American Agora excavations are dramatic.

The Athenian historian Publius Herennius Dexippus, a former archon, rallied 2,000 Athenians in the woods outside the city and harassed the raiders. A fragment of his Scythica preserves the speech he claims to have made to them, in the style of Thucydides, and an inscription honours him. With the help of a Roman fleet under Cleodamus and Athenaeus, the Athenians forced the Heruli to withdraw. In 2014 newly deciphered palimpsest fragments of Dexippus in Vienna (the Scythica Vindobonensia) revealed further fighting at Thermopylae and in Thessaly and Boeotia. The invaders moved north, where Gallienus defeated them on the Nestus in 268 and won over the Herul chief Naulobatus.

Afterwards the Athenians built the so-called post-Herulian wall, enclosing only a small area north of the Acropolis with rubble from destroyed buildings, a vivid image of the shrinkage of classical cities. Later legend, reported by Zonaras and others, has the Goths about to burn Athens' libraries until one argued that they should leave the Greeks their books to keep them unwarlike. Date (267 or 268) and sequence remain disputed.
siege_of_athens_267.debate: Date 267 or 268; Dexippus' own role probably self-glorifying.
scholarship: Frantz, The Athenian Agora XXIV: Late Antiquity (1988)
Mallan and Davenport, 'Dexippus and the Gothic invasions', JRS 105 (2015)
Millar, "P. Herennius Dexippus: The Greek World and the Third-Century Invasions", JRS 59 (1969)
Martin et al., "Scythica Vindobonensia", Wiener Studien 127 (2014)

murder_of_odaenathus_267.debate: Year 267 or 268; Zenobia or Gallienus were suspected of instigating it.

murder_of_gallienus_268.detail:
Early in 268 Aureolus, commander of Gallienus' new mobile cavalry force based at Milan and a former shepherd from the Danube, rebelled, perhaps first declaring for Postumus and then claiming the throne himself. Gallienus hurried back from the Balkans, defeated him at a bridge over the Adda later called Pons Aureoli (Pontirolo) and shut him up in Milan. During the siege a conspiracy formed among the senior officers: the praetorian prefect Aurelius Heraclianus, the general Marcianus, the commander of the Dalmatian cavalry Cecropius and, according to Aurelius Victor and Zosimus, the future emperors Claudius and Aurelian. One night Cecropius brought news that Aureolus was making a sortie; Gallienus rushed out with only a few guards and was run through by a spear or javelin. He died in late summer, probably August or September 268, after fifteen years of rule.

The army, devoted to Gallienus, mutinied and had to be calmed with a donative of 20 aurei per man. Claudius, proclaimed emperor, asked the Senate to deify Gallienus and halted a massacre of Gallienus' relatives and supporters that the Senate had begun in Rome, where his brother and surviving son were killed. Aureolus surrendered and was killed. The Historia Augusta, written in a later Constantinian climate that claimed Claudius as Constantine's ancestor, takes pains to exonerate him.

The Latin tradition, shaped by senators bitter at Gallienus' exclusion of senators from command, portrays him as a frivolous voluptuary. Modern scholars (de Blois, Geiger) emphasise instead his achievements: survival through usurpations, plague and invasion, creation of a central cavalry reserve, promotion of professional officers, toleration of Christians, and patronage of Plotinus. His murder by the 'Illyrian' officers he had promoted opened the line of soldier emperors who completed the recovery.
scholarship: de Blois, The Policy of the Emperor Gallienus (1976)
Geiger, Gallienus (2013)

battle_of_naissus.detail:
The invasion of 268-269 was the largest Gothic incursion of the century. Zosimus' figures of 320,000 warriors and 6,000 ships, and the Historia Augusta's 2,000 ships, are absurd, but the coalition of Goths, Heruli, Peucini and others was clearly vast. After failing before Tomis and Marcianopolis and losing ships in the Bosporus, they besieged Cassandreia and Thessalonica, then moved north up the Axius when Claudius approached. Near Naissus in Moesia Superior Claudius brought them to battle. Zosimus says the Romans were at first pressed hard, but that a flanking movement by troops on an unexpected route turned the tide and 50,000 barbarians were killed.

The survivors, fortified behind their wagons, retreated into the Haemus mountains, where Roman cavalry under Aurelian harassed them; cut off from supplies in winter and ravaged by the plague, they dissolved. Many surrendered and, as the Historia Augusta says, the provinces filled with Gothic slaves and farmers, and Goths were enrolled in the army. A naval detachment that raided Crete, Rhodes and Cyprus was destroyed. Claudius took the title Gothicus Maximus, but died of the plague at Sirmium early in 270.

The victory became central to Constantinian propaganda after 310, when Constantine claimed descent from Claudius, and the Historia Augusta inflates it into a Roman Salamis. Modern debate concerns chronology and credit: some scholars (notably Bray and others) argue that the decisive battle was fought by Gallienus in 268 (identified with or following the Nestus victory) and later transferred to Claudius by the Constantinian tradition. Most accept a Claudian victory in 269. Either way, the Gothic threat on the Danube was broken for a generation, enabling Aurelian's campaigns in the east and west.
battle_of_naissus.debate: Whether Naissus was won by Gallienus (268) or Claudius (269).
scholarship: Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)
Mallan and Davenport, JRS 105 (2015)
Bray, Gallienus (1997)
Wolfram, History of the Goths (1988)

palmyrene_conquest_of_egypt_270.detail:
After Odaenathus' murder his widow Septimia Zenobia ruled in the name of their son Vaballathus, who inherited his father's titles of King of Kings and corrector of the east. In 270, after Claudius' death, Palmyra moved decisively. The general Septimius Zabdas, reportedly with 70,000 men, invaded Egypt with the help of an Egyptian collaborator, Timagenes. The prefect Tenagino Probus, returning from operations against pirates, recovered Alexandria and drove out the Palmyrene garrison, but was outmanoeuvred near Babylon (Old Cairo) by Timagenes, who knew the terrain, and killed himself. Egypt, the empire's granary, passed under Palmyrene control, while other forces occupied Arabia, destroying the temple of Jupiter Hammon at Bostra, garrisoned by legio III Cyrenaica, and pushed through Asia Minor to Ancyra, attempting Chalcedon.

Zenobia did not at first claim independence. Coins at Antioch and Alexandria in 270-272 paired Aurelian (as Augustus) on the obverse with Vaballathus as 'vir clarissimus, rex, imperator, dux Romanorum' on the reverse, and papyri date documents by both rulers. Only in 272, as Aurelian approached, did Vaballathus take the title Augustus and Zenobia that of Augusta. Her court included the philosopher Cassius Longinus, and later sources depict her as learned, chaste and ambitious, claiming descent from Cleopatra.

Historians debate her aims. Some see a bid for independent eastern empire; others (Andrade, Hartmann) see an attempt to secure for her son the eastern command and perhaps the imperial title within a Roman framework at a moment when the central regime was weak. Whatever the intention, control of Egypt and Asia Minor threatened Rome's grain supply and could not be tolerated, and Aurelian launched his eastern campaign in 272.
scholarship: Andrade, Zenobia (2018)
Hartmann, Das palmyrenische Teilreich (2001)
Southern, Empress Zenobia (2008)

death_of_claudius_gothicus_270.detail: Claudius' reputation was later inflated by Constantinian propaganda, which invented his descent from Constantius I, and the HA life is a panegyric. Quintillus' reign may have lasted 17 days or several months.

porphyry_against_the_christians.debate: Date c. 270-300; whether the fragments of Macarius Magnes' pagan are Porphyry is disputed.

battle_of_placentia_271.detail: The defeat prompted the consultation of the Sibylline Books and the decision to wall Rome. Dexippus' fragment preserves negotiations in which Juthungian envoys demanded the subsidies they had formerly received.
battle_of_placentia_271.debate: Identity of invaders (Juthungi, Alamanni, Marcomanni) and the date (270 or 271) debated.

revolt_of_the_mint_workers_271.detail: The scale suggests that senatorial opponents and the urban plebs joined the moneyers. Aurelian closed the Rome mint temporarily and executed several senators. The episode was linked to the deeply debased antoninianus, which Aurelian set out to reform.

aurelian_walls_271.detail:
The Juthungian invasion of Italy in 270-271, which defeated Aurelian at Placentia and caused panic in Rome, prompted the emperor to give the capital its first new wall since the Republic. Begun in 271, the circuit ran about 19 km, enclosing roughly 13.7 square kilometres including the Campus Martius and Trastevere. The original wall was a concrete core faced with brick, about 3.5 m thick and 6-8 m high, with a square tower every hundred Roman feet (about 29.6 m), giving 381 towers and around 18 main gates, plus posterns. To save time and money it incorporated existing structures: the Castra Praetoria, the Amphitheatrum Castrense, the Pyramid of Gaius Cestius, the arches of aqueducts at Porta Maggiore, and stretches of tombs and houses. Malalas says the citizens themselves were drafted to build it, and the guilds probably supplied labour. It was completed under Probus by about 279.

The wall was designed against raiding war bands without siege equipment, not regular armies. Maxentius raised and improved parts of it in preparation for war with Constantine, and under Honorius in 401-403, with Stilicho, it was doubled in height, with a covered gallery and rebuilt gates, the form in which the Visigoths found it in 408-410. Belisarius defended it during the Gothic siege of 537-538. It remained the city's defence until Italian troops breached it at Porta Pia on 20 September 1870, and long stretches survive.

The wall marks a symbolic turn: the capital of the empire, which had trusted to the frontier armies for 300 years, now needed physical protection, as did dozens of Gallic and Italian towns whose late Roman walls are smaller still. Hendrik Dey argues that it also reshaped the city's identity and later Christian topography.
scholarship: Todd, The Walls of Rome (1978)
Dey, The Aurelian Wall and the Refashioning of Imperial Rome (2011)
Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Dey, The Aurelian Wall and the Refashioning of Imperial Rome, AD 271-855 (2011)

aurelian_defeats_goths_271.debate: Cannabaudes known only from the HA; some identify him with Cniva.

abandonment_of_dacia.detail:
Trajan's Dacia, the only Roman province north of the lower Danube, had been under pressure from the Carpi, Goths and other peoples since the 240s. Coin circulation and inscriptions in the province end around 256-260, and many scholars think that Roman control had already effectively collapsed under Gallienus. The formal decision came under Aurelian, probably in 271 after his Gothic victory, or perhaps in 272-275. Eutropius writes that Aurelian, despairing of keeping Dacia since Illyricum and Moesia had been devastated, withdrew the Romans from its cities and fields and settled them in the middle of Moesia, calling it Dacia, so that it now divided the two Moesias.

The new Dacia, carved from Moesia Superior and Inferior, was soon divided into Dacia Ripensis on the Danube, with its capital at Ratiaria where legio XIII Gemina was transferred and V Macedonica at Oescus, and Dacia Mediterranea inland around Serdica and Naissus. The surrendered territory came under the control of the Tervingian Goths, Taifali and Carpi, though Constantine later built a bridge across the Danube at Oescus-Sucidava (328) and held bridgeheads on the north bank.

The question of what happened to the Latin-speaking population has been politically charged since the eighteenth century. The Romanian 'continuity theory' holds that a Daco-Roman population remained and became the ancestors of the Romanians; the 'immigration theory' of Robert Roesler (1871) argues that Romance speakers moved north of the Danube in the Middle Ages. Archaeology shows some continuity of Roman-style material culture and early Christian objects, such as the fourth-century Biertan donarium with its chi-rho, but no proof either way. The withdrawal was a rational shortening of the frontier and showed Aurelian's readiness to abandon a symbolically important conquest.
abandonment_of_dacia.debate: Date (271, 272-275, or gradually from Gallienus), the extent of evacuation and Daco-Roman continuity are disputed.
scholarship: Bichir, Archaeology and History of the Carpi (1976)
Ellis, 'Dacians, Sarmatians and Goths', in Shepherd and Mattingly (eds.) (1996)
Opreanu, "The North-Danube Regions from the Roman Province of Dacia to the Emergence of the Romanian Language", in History of Romania: Compendium (2006)
Ellis, "Dacia Terra Deserta", Dacia 42 (1998)
Abdy, "The Domitian II coin from Chalgrove", Numismatic Chronicle 164 (2004)

siege_of_tyana_272.detail: The HA adds that the ghost of Apollonius of Tyana appeared to Aurelian to plead for his city, a story revealing the HA's interest in Apollonius. Aurelian executed the traitor.

battle_of_immae.detail: Zabdas retreated into Antioch and then slipped away by night after parading a lookalike of Aurelian in chains. Aurelian entered Antioch and won over the population with an amnesty.

battle_of_emesa_272.detail: Aurelian attributed the victory to the sun god of Emesa, whom he believed had appeared to rally his troops, an episode tied to his later promotion of Sol Invictus in Rome.

siege_of_palmyra_272.detail:
After defeating the Palmyrene army under Zabdas at Immae near Antioch and again at Emesa in 272, Aurelian marched across about 150 km of desert to Palmyra, harassed by Bedouin raiders but supplied, Zosimus says, by the cities of Syria. Zenobia had refused his terms; the Historia Augusta gives an exchange of letters in which she cites Cleopatra's choice of death over submission, almost certainly an invention. Aurelian surrounded the oasis city, whose walls had been strengthened, and starved it while bringing in supplies by caravan from the conquered regions.

Realising that Persian help, promised or hoped for, would not arrive (Shapur I had just died or was dying), Zenobia slipped out of the city on a female camel to seek aid from Persia, but was caught by Roman horsemen as she was about to cross the Euphrates. Palmyra then surrendered, in the summer of 272. Aurelian spared the city but took its treasure and left a garrison under Sandarion. At Emesa Zenobia was tried before a tribunal; according to Zosimus she blamed her advisers, and the philosopher Cassius Longinus was executed, meeting his death calmly.

Zenobia's fate is reported differently: Zosimus says she died, by illness or hunger strike, on the way to Rome; the Historia Augusta and other Latin sources say she was led in gold chains in Aurelian's triumph of 274 and then given a villa at Tibur, where she lived as a Roman matron and married into the aristocracy.
