In 273 Palmyra revolted again under Septimius Antiochus and Apsaeus, killing the garrison; Aurelian returned and sacked the city, which never recovered its commercial importance, though it later became a Diocletianic legionary fortress. The campaign reunited the east and Egypt with the empire.
siege_of_palmyra_272.debate: HA letters between Aurelian and Zenobia are fabrications.
scholarship: Andrade, Zenobia: Shooting Star of Palmyra (2018)
Watson, Aurelian and the Third Century (1999)

paul_of_samosata_case_272.detail: The first known case of an emperor arbitrating a church dispute, a precedent for Constantine. Paul was accused of behaving like a ducenarius procurator, with a throne and choir of women singing his praises.

destruction_of_the_bruchion_272.debate: Date 272 or 273 (connected with the revolt of Firmus); the fate of the Library is one of antiquity's most contested questions.

sack_of_palmyra_273.detail: Diocletian later built a legionary camp (Legio I Illyricorum) on the site of the Temple of Allat. Aurelian restored the Temple of Bel, damaged in the sack, and used Palmyrene treasure for his temple of Sol.
sack_of_palmyra_273.debate: Firmus is known chiefly from the HA and his significance may be exaggerated.

temple_of_sol_invictus_274.detail: Whether Aurelian himself fixed the festival on 25 December, and whether the Christian Christmas borrowed it or vice versa, is debated (Hijmans argues the 25 December Sol festival is not attested before 354). The Sol cult provided a unifying imperial religion that Constantine's early coinage continued until about 325.
temple_of_sol_invictus_274.debate: Date of the dedication and the relationship to Christmas are disputed.
scholarship: Hijmans, Sol: The Sun in the Art and Religions of Rome (2009)
Berrens, Sonnenkult und Kaisertum (2004)

battle_of_chalons_274.detail:
The Gallic Empire had been weakened by the murders of Postumus (269), Marius and Victorinus (271), the secession of Spain and Narbonensis, and Germanic raids. Its last emperor, Gaius Pius Esuvius Tetricus, a senator and governor of Aquitania, proclaimed at Burdigala in 271, made his son Tetricus II Caesar and moved the court to Trier. After returning from the east, Aurelian invaded Gaul early in 274 and met the Gallic army on the Catalaunian Fields near Durocortorum and Châlons-en-Champagne.

The Latin tradition (Eutropius, Aurelius Victor, the Historia Augusta) claims that Tetricus, tired of his mutinous troops, had secretly offered to surrender, quoting Virgil to Aurelian ('Eripe me his, invicte, malis', 'snatch me from these evils, unconquered one'), and deserted his army during the battle. The Gallic soldiers fought on with great loss of life before surrendering. The story may well be propaganda that excused Tetricus, who was spared and later given an administrative post as corrector Lucaniae (or of part of Italy), where, the Historia Augusta says, Aurelian addressed him as colleague. Tetricus and his son were displayed in Aurelian's triumph in 274 alongside Zenobia.

The battle reunited Britain, Gaul and Spain with the central empire after fourteen years, and Aurelian took the title Restitutor Orbis. The bloodshed, however, weakened the Rhine defences, and in 275-276 Franks and Alamanni ravaged Gaul so badly that the Historia Augusta speaks of 60 or 70 cities taken, which Probus had to recover. Aurelius Victor also mentions a short-lived revolt of a certain Faustinus at Trier around this time. The battlefield's exact location is unknown.
battle_of_chalons_274.debate: Truth of Tetricus' betrayal; exact site and date (early 274).
scholarship: Drinkwater, The Gallic Empire (1987)
Watson, Aurelian and the Third Century (1999)

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

aurelian_triumph_274.detail: The HA's description (elephants, tigers, Goths, Alans, Franks, captured Amazons, Zenobia in golden chains) is embroidered but probably reflects a real show. Aurelian's coinage also introduced the title deus et dominus natus, a step toward the openly sacral monarchy of the Tetrarchs.

aurelian_coin_reform_274.detail:
By 270 the radiate coins that made up the bulk of the money supply contained around 2 per cent silver or less, often struck on crude, light flans; forgeries and barbarous imitations circulated widely, and in 271 the mint workers of Rome, implicated in fraud, rose under their chief Felicissimus and were suppressed with thousands of deaths. After reuniting the empire, Aurelian reorganised the coinage in 274. He closed the Rome mint temporarily, opened or reorganised others (Lugdunum, Ticinum, Siscia, Serdica, Cyzicus, Antioch, Tripolis, Alexandria), and issued a new, heavier radiate of about 3.9-4 g with a guaranteed silver content of about 5 per cent, carefully struck with a silver surface. Its reverse bears the mark XXI or, in Greek mints, KA.

The meaning of XXI is the most disputed question in late Roman numismatics. The most widely accepted explanation is a ratio of twenty parts copper to one of silver (5 per cent fineness); alternatives read it as 'twenty units (nummi or sestertii) equal one' denomination, or as a value of 20 asses or 2.5 denarii. Aurelian also struck a heavier aureus at 50 to the pound and introduced a laureate denarius and bronze fractions. Zosimus says he distributed the new silver and called in the debased coin.

The immediate effect was paradoxical. In Egypt prices recorded on papyri jumped roughly tenfold soon after 274, suggesting that the new coin was overvalued by decree or that the old coin was retariffed downward, triggering a surge of inflation that continued to Diocletian's reforms. The reform's coin types, showing Sol and the legend 'Deus et dominus natus' at Serdica, also expressed Aurelian's theology of power. Diocletian replaced the system in 294, but Aurelian's centralised mint network and marked fineness laid its foundations.
aurelian_coin_reform_274.debate: Meaning of XXI/KA: 20:1 alloy ratio versus a tariff of value.
scholarship: Estiot, Ripostiglio della Venèra III (1995)
Harl, Coinage in the Roman Economy 300 BC to AD 700 (1996)
Rathbone, 'Monetisation, not price-inflation, in third-century AD Egypt?' (1996)
Estiot, Monnaies de l'Empire romain XII.1: D'Aurélien à Florien (2004)
Harl, Coinage in the Roman Economy (1996)

assassination_of_aurelian_275.detail: An interregnum of several weeks followed (exaggerated by the HA into six months), after which the elderly Marcus Claudius Tacitus was chosen. The HA's story that the army deferred to the Senate is a senatorial fantasy.
assassination_of_aurelian_275.debate: The HA's long interregnum is fictional.

mani_executed.detail: Manichaeism, a dualist synthesis of Christian, Zoroastrian and Buddhist elements, spread to Roman Egypt, Syria and North Africa (where Augustine was a hearer for nine years) and along the Silk Road to China. Kartir's inscriptions boast of persecuting Jews, Buddhists, Christians, Manichaeans and others. Diocletian's edict against the Manichaeans followed in 297 or 302.

probus_gallic_campaign_277.detail: Zosimus tells of Frankish prisoners settled on the Black Sea who seized ships, raided Greece, Sicily (sacking Syracuse) and Africa, and sailed home through the Strait of Gibraltar. Probus is also credited with allowing vines to be planted in Gaul, Pannonia and Moesia, and using soldiers to plant vineyards near Sirmium.
probus_gallic_campaign_277.debate: The campaign is not really part of the Gallic Empire war; listed here for the Rhine context. Numbers of cities are rhetorical.

scholarship: Mitchell, Cremna in Pisidia (1995)

usurpers_against_probus_280.debate: The HA lives of these men are almost wholly fictional.

probus_permits_viticulture_280.debate: How far the Domitianic vine edict was ever enforced, and therefore how much Probus' grant changed, is debated; viticulture was already spreading in the Moselle and Rhône valleys.

kartir_inscriptions.debate: Date c. 280-293; the scale of persecution claimed is debated.

carus_persian_campaign_283.detail: The lightning story was taken as a divine warning that no emperor should pass Ctesiphon, a superstition still current in Julian's time. Carus never consulted the Senate on his accession, a sign of the Senate's irrelevance; his sons Carinus (West) and Numerian (East) succeeded.
carus_persian_campaign_283.debate: Whether Carus died of illness, lightning or murder by the prefect Aper is uncertain.

accession_of_diocletian_284.detail:
Carus' Persian expedition ended in 283 with his death near Ctesiphon, by lightning according to the official story. His younger son Numerian led the army back west, travelling in a closed litter because of an eye infection. Near Nicomedia, in November 284, the soldiers noticed the smell of decay and found him dead; suspicion fell on his father-in-law, the praetorian prefect Arrius Aper, who had concealed the death. On 20 November 284 an assembly of the army outside Nicomedia chose as emperor Diocles, commander of the imperial bodyguard (protectores domestici), a Dalmatian of humble origin, possibly the son of a scribe or freedman, born around 244 near Salona.

Standing on a tribunal before the troops, Diocles swore by the sun that he had no part in Numerian's death, accused Aper and ran him through with his own sword. The Historia Augusta adds that a Druidess in Gaul had once told him he would be emperor when he had killed a boar (aper), and that he had hunted boars in vain until this moment. He took the name Gaius Aurelius Valerius Diocletianus and the consulship. Carus' elder son Carinus, ruling the west, defeated the usurper Sabinus Julianus and marched against Diocletian, winning the battle of the Margus in 285 before being killed by his own officers. Diocletian notably kept Carinus' prefect Aristobulus in office and avoided purges.

The accession marks the conventional end of the third-century crisis and the beginning of 'late antiquity' in many textbooks. Diocletian reigned for over twenty years, the longest since Antoninus Pius, and created the Tetrarchy, the enlarged provincial system, new taxation and coinage, and the last great persecution of Christians, before abdicating in 305. Modern biographies (Kolb, Leadbetter, Roberto) emphasise his pragmatism and experimentation rather than a master plan.
scholarship: Barnes, The New Empire of Diocletian and Constantine (1982)
Williams, Diocletian and the Roman Recovery (1985)
Rees, Diocletian and the Tetrarchy (2004)
Leadbetter, Galerius and the Will of Diocletian (2009)

battle_of_margus_285.detail: Diocletian retained Carinus' praetorian prefect Aristobulus and most officials, a conciliatory move that contrasted with earlier purges and helped consolidate the regime.

antony_withdraws_to_the_desert_285.debate: Chronology rests on the Life of Antony; Antony's seven Coptic letters show a more learned figure than Athanasius portrays.

maximian_made_augustus_286.detail:
Marcus Aurelius Valerius Maximianus, born around 250 near Sirmium to shopkeeper parents, was a veteran officer of Aurelian and Probus and an old comrade of Diocletian. After the defeat of Carinus, Diocletian, facing simultaneous threats in the east and the west, made him Caesar in July 285, probably at Milan, and sent him to Gaul against the Bagaudae, rural rebels led by Amandus and Aelianus, whom he quickly suppressed. Maximian was then raised to Augustus, probably on 1 April 286 (some scholars date the promotion later in 286 or even to 287), becoming Diocletian's colleague rather than his heir; Diocletian had no son, and Maximian's son Maxentius was a child.

By 287 the two rulers had adopted the signa Jovius and Herculius: Diocletian was protected by Jupiter, ruler of the gods, and Maximian by Hercules, his helper and son, a theology that expressed both partnership and hierarchy. Maximian ruled the west from Milan and Trier, campaigning against Alamanni, Burgundians, Heruli and Franks, while losing Britain to Carausius (286) and failing in a naval expedition against him (289). The panegyrics of 289 and 291 celebrate the harmony of the two Augusti, whose meeting at Milan in the winter of 290-291 is staged as an epiphany.

The dyarchy was the first step towards the Tetrarchy of 293. It embodied the idea that the empire was too large and too threatened for one ruler, and established the pattern of regional imperial courts that lasted until 476. Maximian remained, as Lactantius complains, the rougher partner, but was loyal to Diocletian until his reluctant abdication in 305; his later attempts to regain power (306-310) ended in his death at Massilia. The precise chronology of 285-286 depends on papyri, coins and the panegyrics and is still debated.
maximian_made_augustus_286.debate: Date of elevation to Augustus (1 April 286 or later).
scholarship: Kolb, Diocletian und die Erste Tetrarchie (1987)
Rees, Layers of Loyalty in Latin Panegyric AD 289-307 (2002)

bagaudae_suppressed_286.detail: The Bagaudae reappear in Gaul and Spain in the fifth century. Older Marxist scholarship saw a peasant revolution; more recent work (Drinkwater) stresses local self-help, banditry and aristocratic leadership. Later tradition placed their stronghold at Saint-Maur-des-Fossés near Paris.
scholarship: Drinkwater, 'Patronage in Roman Gaul and the problem of the Bagaudae', in Wallace-Hadrill (ed.), Patronage in Ancient Society (1989)

revolt_of_carausius_286.detail: Carausius' coinage was of unusually good silver and full of Virgilian allusions: RSR (Redeunt Saturnia Regna) and INPCDA (Iam nova progenies caelo demittitur alto), the most literary legends in Roman coinage. He also struck coins of 'Carausius et fratres sui', claiming collegiality with Diocletian and Maximian.
scholarship: Casey, Carausius and Allectus: The British Usurpers (1994)
de la Bédoyère, 'Carausius and the marks RSR and I.N.P.C.D.A.', NC 158 (1998)

codex_gregorianus_291.detail: These private but semi-official codes were the models for the Theodosian Code (438) and Justinian's Codex (529/534), into which much of their content passed. Diocletian's reign is the best-documented in rescripts of any emperor, over 1,200 surviving, reflecting the emperor's role as dispenser of law to ordinary petitioners, including women and slaves.
scholarship: Corcoran, The Empire of the Tetrarchs (1996, rev. 2000)
Connolly, Lives Behind the Laws (2010)

formation_of_the_tetrarchy_293.detail:
On 1 March 293 the two Augusti each appointed a Caesar: Maximian chose Flavius Valerius Constantius, his praetorian prefect, at Milan, and Diocletian chose Gaius Galerius Valerius Maximianus, a former herdsman from Dacia Ripensis, probably at Sirmium (Lactantius implies Nicomedia). Both Caesars were adopted into the families of their Augusti and married to their daughters or stepdaughters: Constantius had already put aside Helena, mother of Constantine, to marry Maximian's stepdaughter Theodora, and Galerius married Diocletian's daughter Valeria. The Caesars received the signa Herculius and Jovius respectively.

The four rulers shared the empire's wars while governing it as a single college: laws and coins were issued in all four names, and statues showed them as interchangeable, as in the porphyry group now at San Marco in Venice, brought from the Philadelphion in Constantinople, with its embracing pairs. Each had a regional sphere and residences: Constantius in Trier fighting Carausius and the Franks, Maximian in Milan and Aquileia, Galerius in Sirmium and later Thessalonica, Diocletian in Nicomedia and Antioch. The panegyric of 297 compares the four rulers to the elements, seasons and other natural fours.

The term 'Tetrarchy' is modern; contemporaries spoke of Augusti and Caesars. Historians debate whether Diocletian intended a system of succession by merit and adoption, as the abdication of 305 suggests (Kolb), or improvised a structure in response to military needs (Barnes, Leadbetter). It was effective in war, winning back Britain (296), Egypt (297-298) and victory over Persia (298), but it ignored dynastic loyalty: in 306 the armies proclaimed the sons of Constantius and Maximian, and the second Tetrarchy dissolved into civil war.
formation_of_the_tetrarchy_293.debate: Planned system or improvisation; place of Galerius' proclamation; whether the Caesars were appointed in 293 or earlier (Galerius possibly in 287 per some).
scholarship: Kolb, Diocletian und die Erste Tetrarchie (1987)
Barnes, The New Empire of Diocletian and Constantine (1982)
Rees, Diocletian and the Tetrarchy (2004)
Leadbetter, Galerius and the Will of Diocletian (2009)

diocletian_provincial_reorganisation.detail:
Over the decades after 293 the roughly 50 provinces of the Severan empire were divided into about 100 smaller units. The Laterculus Veronensis, a list of provinces preserved in a seventh-century manuscript at Verona and dated to around 314, gives twelve dioceses with their provinces: Oriens, Pontica, Asiana, Thraciae, Moesiae, Pannoniae, Britanniae, Galliae, Viennensis, Italia, Hispaniae and Africa. Each diocese was supervised by a vicarius ('deputy of the praetorian prefects'), forming a new tier between the governors and the prefects. Italy lost its privileged status: it was divided into districts under correctores and subjected to the land tax, with a distinction between Italia annonaria in the north, which fed the court and army, and Italia suburbicaria, which supplied Rome. Egypt was split into several provinces (Aegyptus Iovia, Herculia, Thebais), and Asia, Syria and Africa into smaller units.

The purpose was to bring government closer to the taxpayers, to make the new tax system workable, and to reduce the power of individual governors to rebel. Gradually, and not fully until Constantine, civil governors (praesides, consulares, correctores) were separated from the military commanders (duces) of frontier districts. The number of officials rose sharply: Lactantius, hostile, complains that the provinces were chopped into fragments and that there were more people receiving salaries than paying taxes.

The chronology is uncertain. Barnes and others place most divisions under Diocletian between 293 and 305; Constantin Zuckerman and others argue that the dioceses were created only around 313-314 under Constantine and Licinius. The system lasted, with modifications, until the seventh century, and the dioceses later shaped ecclesiastical geography, since metropolitan sees and patriarchates largely followed provinces and dioceses.
diocletian_provincial_reorganisation.debate: Dioceses created c. 297 (Diocletian) or c. 313-314 (Constantine and Licinius).
scholarship: Barnes, The New Empire of Diocletian and Constantine (1982), ch. 12-13
Zuckerman, 'Sur la liste de Vérone et la province de Grande Arménie', TravMém 14 (2002)
Jones, The Later Roman Empire (1964)
Barnes, The New Empire of Diocletian and Constantine (1982)
Zuckerman, "Sur la liste de Vérone et la province de Grande Arménie", Travaux et Mémoires 14 (2002)
Jones, The Later Roman Empire 284-602 (1964)

strata_diocletiana.detail: The programme, along with new legions (by now smaller units of perhaps 1,000-2,000 men) and quadriburgia, reflects the tetrarchic investment in frontier defence that Zosimus contrasts with Constantine's withdrawal of troops into cities.
scholarship: Bowersock, Roman Arabia (1983)
Parker, Romans and Saracens (1986)

revolt_in_upper_egypt_293.debate: Jerome dates the destruction of Busiris and Coptos to 293; some link it to Domitianus' revolt of 297.

diocletian_currency_reform_294.detail:
Around 294 Diocletian replaced the remnants of the third-century coinage with a uniform imperial system struck to the same standards and types in a network of mints that eventually numbered about fifteen, each marked on the coins: Londinium, Treveri, Lugdunum, Ticinum, Aquileia, Roma, Carthago, Siscia, Serdica, Thessalonica, Heraclea, Nicomedia, Cyzicus, Antiochia and Alexandria. The gold aureus was set at 60 to the pound (about 5.4 g); a new silver coin, the argenteus, of almost pure silver at 96 to the pound (about 3.4 g), revived the standard of Nero's denarius; and a large bronze coin of about 10 g with a small silver content, the nummus (called follis by modern collectors), carried the reverse GENIO POPVLI ROMANI. Smaller radiate and laureate bronze fractions completed the system.

The local civic and provincial coinages of the east, including the billon tetradrachms of Alexandria, came to an end (the last Alexandrian tetradrachms date to 296/297), so that a single Roman currency now circulated across the empire for the first time. The reform was accompanied by the tax reform and, in 301, by a currency edict known from an inscription at Aphrodisias that doubled the face value of the coins, and by the Price Edict.

The nominal values of the coins in denarii (the unit of account) are uncertain, and the reform did not stop inflation: the nummus soon shrank, falling to about 1/96 pound by 318 under Constantine and his rivals. Gold, however, became the anchor of the late Roman monetary system, especially after Constantine's solidus. Numismatists (Sutherland, Hendy, Harl) see 294 as the creation of the late Roman coinage; debates concern the tariffs of the coins and how far the state deliberately used retariffing to manage its finances.
diocletian_currency_reform_294.debate: Exact date (293-296) and denominational values debated.
scholarship: Sutherland, RIC VI (1967)
Harl, Coinage in the Roman Economy (1996)
Corcoran, The Empire of the Tetrarchs (2000)
Hendy, Studies in the Byzantine Monetary Economy c. 300-1450 (1985)

carpi_resettled_295.debate: Dates of the Carpic victories range 295-297 (Diocletian took Carpicus Maximus several times).

diocletians_palace_split.detail: The peristyle with its arcuated colonnades and the palace's courtly architecture influenced late antique and Renaissance taste (Robert Adam's 1764 publication). Comparable tetrarchic palace-mausolea are Galerius' Felix Romuliana (Gamzigrad) and the Thessalonica complex.
scholarship: Wilkes, Diocletian's Palace, Split (1986)

recovery_of_britain_296.detail: The famous gold medallion from the Arras (Beaurains) hoard shows Constantius on horseback before a kneeling Londinium with the legend REDDITOR LVCIS AETERNAE ('restorer of the eternal light').

battle_of_callinicum_296.detail: Ammianus and others tell that Diocletian, in his carriage at Antioch, made Galerius walk a mile in front of it in his purple, a humiliation that Galerius turned into a determination to win; the story's meaning (punishment or ceremonial) is debated.

diocletian_tax_reform_297.detail:
The Roman state of the third century had come to rely on ad hoc requisitions in kind (indictiones) to feed the army as the coinage collapsed. Diocletian systematised them. An edict of Aristius Optatus, prefect of Egypt, dated 16 March 297 and preserved on a papyrus from Karanis (P.Cair.Isid. 1), announces that the emperors have fixed a just assessment so that each person may know what he owes, according to the quality of land and the number of people (capita) on it. Land was measured in units (iuga) adjusted for productivity: the Syro-Roman lawbook gives, for Syria, 5 iugera of vineyard, 20 of first-class arable, 40 of second-class or 60 of third-class land as one iugum, with olive trees counted by number. People and animals were counted as capita. A census, at first every five years and from 312 in a fifteen-year cycle, the indiction, determined each province's liability, and each year the government published the rate per unit needed to meet the budget.

The system made state revenues predictable and spread the burden more systematically, and the indiction became a standard way of dating documents into the Middle Ages. But it also tied people to the land and to their occupations: to keep the tax base fixed, laws bound coloni to estates, decurions to city councils and members of essential guilds to their trades. Lactantius describes the census-takers torturing people to make them declare more than they owned and taxing even the dead. Over the fourth century much of the tax in kind was commuted into gold (adaeratio).

Modern scholars (Jones, Carrié, Bransbourg) debate whether iugatio and capitatio were a single system or two separate taxes, and how uniform it was across the empire; Egypt, Syria, Asia and Gaul show different practices.
diocletian_tax_reform_297.debate: Whether capitatio and iugatio were separate or merged taxes, and how uniform the system was, remain debated.
scholarship: Carrié, 'Dioclétien et la fiscalité', AnTard 2 (1994)
Jones, The Later Roman Empire 284-602 (1964)
Carrié and Rousselle, L'Empire romain en mutation (1999)

siege_of_alexandria_297.detail: According to the legend, his horse stumbled at the city gate, staining its knees, and the grateful Alexandrians set up a statue of the horse. The tall column known as 'Pompey's Pillar' was erected in honour of Diocletian around 298, probably for his provision of grain to the city. Busiris and Coptos, which had joined the revolt, were razed.
siege_of_alexandria_297.debate: Relationship of Domitianus and Achilleus (same revolt, successive leaders) and chronology (297-298) disputed.

maximian_african_campaign_297.debate: The date of Maximian's adventus at Carthage (10 March 298) comes from a single papyrus/calendar tradition.

dodecaschoenus_abandoned_298.detail: Procopius records the arrangement, including shared temples at Philae for the Isis cult, which continued until Justinian closed them c. 537.

battle_of_satala_298.detail:
In 296 Narseh, son of Shapur I and King of Kings since 293, invaded Roman Armenia and Mesopotamia. Galerius, sent against him, was defeated between Callinicum and Carrhae in 296 or 297. According to Eutropius, Festus and Ammianus, Diocletian then humiliated his Caesar by making him run a mile in front of his carriage in his purple robes, although some modern historians read the scene as a misunderstood ceremonial. Galerius raised a new army of veterans and recruits from Illyricum and Moesia, perhaps 25,000 strong, and in 298 attacked through Armenia, where the terrain favoured infantry and the population was friendly.

According to Festus and Eutropius, Galerius personally reconnoitred the Persian camp with two companions and then fell on it by surprise, perhaps at night or at dawn. Narseh, wounded, fled; his camp was taken with his treasury, his harem, his wife Arsane, his sisters and children and many nobles. The site is usually located near Satala in Armenia Minor, though the evidence for the name is weak and some prefer a location in Greater Armenia. Galerius then advanced into Media and Adiabene and probably reached Ctesiphon, though it is unclear whether he took it.

The victory was celebrated on the Arch of Galerius at Thessalonica, where Galerius is shown on horseback fighting Narseh and the Persian royal women are captured. Petrus Patricius preserves the scene in which Narseh's envoy Apharban appealed to Galerius to remember that Rome and Persia were the two eyes of the world, and Galerius angrily reminded him of the treatment of Valerian. The battle led directly to the Peace of Nisibis and was the greatest Roman victory over the Sasanians, restoring Roman prestige in the east for a generation and boosting Galerius' standing within the Tetrarchy.
battle_of_satala_298.debate: Location of the battle (Satala or elsewhere in Armenia) and whether Galerius took Ctesiphon.
scholarship: Leadbetter, Galerius and the Will of Diocletian (2009)
Dodgeon and Lieu (1991)
Dodgeon and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars (1991)

peace_of_nisibis_299.detail:
After his defeat in 298 Narseh sought peace to recover his family. Diocletian and Galerius met at Nisibis and sent the magister memoriae Sicorius Probus to Narseh in Media, where, according to Petrus Patricius, he was kept waiting until the Persian king had gathered his forces before being received on the river Asprudis. The terms, as preserved by Petrus, were: the cession to Rome of five regions east of the Tigris (listed by Petrus as Intelene, Sophene, Arzanene, Corduene and Zabdicene, while Ammianus, recording their loss in 363, names Arzanena, Moxoena, Zabdicena, Rehimena and Corduena); the Tigris to form the boundary; the frontier of Armenia to be at the fortress of Zintha on the border of Media; Rome to appoint the king of Iberia; and Nisibis to be the sole place of trade between the empires. Narseh accepted all the terms except the trade clause, according to Petrus, but was forced to yield. His family was returned.

The treaty, usually dated to 299 (some argue 298), marked the high point of Roman power in the east. It placed Roman garrisons beyond the Tigris, secured Armenia under Tiridates III, whose conversion to Christianity followed in the early fourth century, and brought Iberia into the Roman orbit. Diocletian strengthened the frontier with the Strata Diocletiana and new forts.

The peace held for almost forty years. Shapur II, who had come of age by the 330s, refused to accept it, and war resumed at Constantine's death in 337. The Transtigritane regions became the main prize of the long war that culminated in Jovian's surrender of them, with Nisibis, in 363. Modern scholars (Blockley, Winter) debate the exact list of regions and whether the trade clause was designed to control commerce or to channel customs revenue.
scholarship: Blockley, 'The Romano-Persian peace treaties of AD 299 and 363', Florilegium 6 (1984)
Winter, Die sasanidisch-römischen Friedensverträge des 3. Jahrhunderts n. Chr. (1988)
Blockley, East Roman Foreign Policy (1992)
Winter, "On the Regulation of Trade in the Treaty of 298", in Studies in Roman Warfare (1990)

arch_of_galerius_thessalonica.debate: The arch is dated c. 298-305; the purpose of the Rotunda (temple, mausoleum or throne hall) is debated.
scholarship: Laubscher, Der Reliefschmuck des Galeriusbogens in Thessaloniki (1975)
Jones and McFadden (eds), Art of Empire: The Roman Frescoes and Imperial Cult Chamber in Luxor Temple (2015)

currency_edict_of_301.debate: Exact values in the damaged text are disputed.

edict_on_maximum_prices_301.detail:
Issued at the end of 301 in the names of the four rulers, the Edict on Maximum Prices is known from over 40 inscriptions and fragments, mostly from the Greek-speaking eastern provinces (Aphrodisias, Stratonicea, Aezani, Corinth, Egypt and elsewhere), Latin and Greek, which together preserve most of its text. Its long preamble, in convoluted official rhetoric, blames the 'raging avarice' of profiteers who exploit soldiers on the march by charging four or eight times the fair price, so that a soldier loses his donative and pay in a single purchase. It fixed maximum prices and wages in denarii for more than a thousand items, with death as the penalty for selling above them, for hoarding, or for buying at higher prices.

The list ranges from foodstuffs and wine to textiles, leather, timber, animals and services, with sea freight rates between named ports. A military modius of wheat was set at 100 denarii; the daily wage of a farm labourer at 25 denarii with food, of a carpenter or baker at 50; a teacher of rhetoric could charge 250 denarii per pupil per month. Wines were graded: ordinary wine was capped at 8 denarii per Italian sextarius, while the finest Italian wines, Falernian and others, and Maeonian from Lydia could fetch up to 30, and Pannonian and Gallic beer 4. A pound of purple-dyed silk cost 150,000 denarii.

Lactantius, a witness in Nicomedia, says the edict caused much bloodshed over trivial goods, that goods vanished from the market, and that it was eventually abandoned. Its economic logic is still debated. Some see it as an attempt to make the new currency work after the doubling of its face value earlier in 301; others as a policy aimed mainly at army supply. For historians it is an unparalleled source for relative prices, wages and the regional economy of the late Roman world.
edict_on_maximum_prices_301.debate: Whether the edict was ever seriously enforced, and whether it was applied in the West, are disputed; Lactantius is hostile.
scholarship: Lauffer, Diokletians Preisedikt (1971)
Corcoran, The Empire of the Tetrarchs (2000)
Crawford and Reynolds, 'The Aphrodisias copy of Diocletian's Edict on Maximum Prices', ZPE 26 (1977)
Corcoran, The Empire of the Tetrarchs (2nd ed., 2000)

sources.w: Edictum Diocletiani de pretiis rerum venalium
Edictum de pretiis (ed. Lauffer 1971, with later Aphrodisias fragments)

christianisation_of_armenia.detail: Armenian tradition (Agathangelos) dates the conversion to 301, after Gregory's thirteen years in a pit at Khor Virap and the king's transformation into a boar. Most modern scholars prefer c. 314, after the Edict of Milan and Galerius' and Maximinus' persecutions, which Eusebius says included a war by Maximinus against Christian Armenians.
scholarship: Garsoïan, in Hovannisian (ed.), The Armenian People from Ancient to Modern Times I (1997)

edict_against_the_manichaeans.debate: Date 297 or 302 depends on the identification of the proconsul Julianus and Diocletian's itinerary.

great_persecution_303.detail:
By 303 Christians held offices in the palace, the army and the provinces, and a large church stood in Nicomedia opposite the imperial palace. Lactantius blames Galerius and his mother Romula for urging Diocletian to persecute; Diocletian consulted his council and the oracle of Apollo at Didyma, which complained that 'the just on earth' prevented it from speaking truly. Intellectual attacks on Christianity accompanied the campaign: Sossianus Hierocles, governor of Bithynia, wrote the Philalethes comparing Christ unfavourably with Apollonius of Tyana.

On 23 February 303, the feast of the Terminalia, soldiers demolished the Nicomedia church. The first edict, published the next day, ordered churches destroyed and scriptures surrendered and burned, banned Christian assemblies, deprived Christians of high rank of their privileges and the right to appear in court, and reduced imperial freedmen to slavery. After two fires in the palace were blamed on Christians, a second edict ordered the arrest of the clergy, a third (for the vicennalia in November 303) released those who sacrificed, and a fourth, in early 304, required everyone to sacrifice. Enforcement varied: in the west Constantius, Lactantius says, only pulled down churches, while Maximian enforced the edicts in Italy and Africa; in Galerius' and Maximinus' east the persecution continued with interruptions until 311 and, under Maximinus, until 313. Eusebius describes the burning of the church at Nicomedia with its congregation, mass executions in the Thebaid and martyrdoms in Palestine.

Geoffrey de Ste Croix estimated some 3,000-3,500 executions; others suggest fewer. The crisis created the problem of the traditores who had handed over scriptures, the root of the Donatist and Melitian schisms, and a cult of martyrs that shaped Christian identity. It was the last and most severe attempt by the Roman state to suppress Christianity.
great_persecution_303.debate: Lactantius and Eusebius are partisan Christian sources writing after the persecutors' defeat; Galerius' role may be exaggerated to exculpate Diocletian or vice versa. Numbers of martyrs are uncertain.
scholarship: de Ste. Croix, 'Aspects of the Great Persecution', HTR 47 (1954)
Barnes, Constantine and Eusebius (1981)
Corcoran, 'Before Constantine', in Lenski (ed.), Cambridge Companion to the Age of Constantine (2006/2012)
de Ste Croix, "Aspects of the Great Persecution", HTR 47 (1954)
Frend, Martyrdom and Persecution in the Early Church (1965)

martyrdom_of_agnes_304.debate: Date (304 or under Valerian) and age are from later tradition.

fourth_edict_304.debate: Whether the fourth edict was promulgated in the west is disputed.

abdication_of_diocletian_305.detail:
Diocletian fell gravely ill after his vicennalia in Rome in late 303; Lactantius says he collapsed in December 304 and was believed dead, appearing in public again in March 305 so changed as to be scarcely recognisable. According to Lactantius, Galerius pressed him to retire, threatening civil war, and to appoint Caesars of Galerius' choosing. A panegyric of 307 adds that Maximian had sworn an oath in the Capitoline temple during the vicennalia that he would abdicate with Diocletian.

On 1 May 305, on a hill three miles outside Nicomedia where Galerius had been made Caesar, with a statue of Jupiter on a column, Diocletian addressed the troops in tears, saying he was old and needed rest. The soldiers expected Constantine, who was standing on the platform, and Maxentius to be named; instead Diocletian announced Severus, a heavy-drinking officer and friend of Galerius, and Maximinus Daia, Galerius' nephew. Galerius brought Maximinus forward, removed his private dress and Diocletian put his own purple cloak on him. Diocletian then rode in a carriage through the city to his native Dalmatia and the palace he had built at Split. On the same day Maximian abdicated at Milan in favour of Severus. Constantius and Galerius became Augusti.

It was the first voluntary abdication by a reigning Roman emperor. When in 308 Galerius asked him to return to power at the conference of Carnuntum, Diocletian replied, according to the Epitome, that if they could see the cabbages he grew with his own hands at Salona, they would never ask him to exchange that happiness for power. The succession of 305, which excluded the sons of emperors, soon collapsed with the proclamations of Constantine and Maxentius in 306, and Diocletian lived to see his system destroyed and his wife and daughter murdered.
scholarship: Barnes, Constantine and Eusebius (1981)
Leadbetter, Galerius and the Will of Diocletian (2009)

synod_of_elvira.debate: Date anywhere from c. 295 to 314; the canon collection may be a later compilation (Meigne, Vilella).

sources.w: Canons of the Council of Elvira

constantines_flight_to_constantius_305.debate: The dramatic escape is a pro-Constantinian story; Galerius probably had little choice but to let him go.

constantine_proclaimed_306.detail:
Constantine, born at Naissus on 27 February around 272-273 to Constantius and Helena, spent his youth at Diocletian's court, serving in the Persian and Danubian wars and witnessing the outbreak of the persecution at Nicomedia. Passed over in 305, he obtained permission to join his father, who was preparing an expedition against the Picts, and reached him at Gesoriacum. Father and son campaigned north of Hadrian's Wall in 305-306. Constantius died at Eboracum on 25 July 306. His army, at the instigation of the Alamannic king Crocus, who commanded auxiliaries, at once proclaimed Constantine Augustus.

The circumstances were later shaped by propaganda. Lactantius and Eusebius have the dying Constantius designating his son and the army fulfilling his will; the panegyric of 310 claims Constantine resisted the soldiers and spurred his horse to escape the purple. In reality the proclamation broke the Tetrarchic rules of 305, under which Severus should have become Augustus in the west. Galerius, receiving Constantine's laureled portrait, wanted to burn it but, to avoid war, recognised him only as Caesar and promoted Severus to Augustus; Constantine accepted the lower rank. He ruled Britain, Gaul and Spain from Trier, fought the Franks and Bructeri, built the Cologne bridge and, in 307, married Maximian's daughter Fausta and accepted the title Augustus from Maximian.

The proclamation at York was the first step in a career that ended with Constantine as sole emperor (324) and the transformation of the empire into a Christian state. A modern bronze statue outside York Minster commemorates it. Historians debate whether Constantius had deliberately planned the succession by summoning his son, as Barnes thinks, or whether the army acted on its own; either way it reasserted the dynastic principle that the Tetrarchy had sought to suppress.
scholarship: Barnes, Constantine: Dynasty, Religion and Power in the Later Roman Empire (2011)
Potter, Constantine the Emperor (2013)

maxentius_usurpation_306.detail:
Marcus Aurelius Valerius Maxentius, son of Maximian and the Syrian Eutropia, son-in-law of Galerius through his marriage to Valeria Maximilla, had been passed over in 305 and was living as a private citizen on an estate on the Via Labicana outside Rome. In 306 Galerius planned to extend the census and taxation to the people of the city of Rome, hitherto exempt, and to abolish the remaining Praetorian cohorts. On 28 October 306 the Praetorians, a few tribunes (Marcellianus, Marcellus) and Lucianus, who controlled the free distribution of pork, proclaimed Maxentius; the vicar of the prefect who resisted was killed. Maxentius at first styled himself princeps, not Augustus, perhaps hoping for recognition, and called his father out of retirement; Maximian resumed the purple.

Italy and Africa recognised the new regime. When Severus invaded Italy in early 307, his troops, many of them Maximian's veterans, deserted, and Severus surrendered at Ravenna and was later killed. Galerius invaded in the summer of 307 but found Rome's walls too large to besiege and withdrew, his troops plundering on the way. In 308 Maximian tried to depose his son and fled to Constantine. Africa revolted under Domitius Alexander (308-309/310), cutting Rome's grain supply and causing famine until Maxentius' prefect Volusianus crushed the revolt.

Maxentius presented himself as conservator urbis suae, the champion of Rome and its traditions, and built lavishly: the Basilica Nova, the restored Temple of Venus and Roma, a villa, circus and mausoleum on the Via Appia. He ended the persecution in his territories and restored Christian property in 311. The Constantinian tradition made him a tyrant, oppressive and debauched; modern scholarship (Cullhed) presents a more traditional Roman ruler whose regime collapsed at the Milvian Bridge in 312.
scholarship: Cullhed, Conservator Urbis Suae: Studies in the Politics and Propaganda of the Emperor Maxentius (1994)
Sutherland, RIC VI (1967)
Bruun, RIC VII (1966)

conference_of_carnuntum_308.detail: Diocletian refused to resume power, replying that if Maximian could see the cabbages he grew at Salona he would never urge it. An altar to Mithras 'fautor imperii sui' dedicated by the emperors at Carnuntum survives. The settlement failed at once: Maximinus Daia and Constantine both claimed the Augustan title in 309-310.

revolt_of_domitius_alexander_308.detail: Cirta was rebuilt by Constantine and renamed Constantina (Constantine, Algeria). The famine in Rome during the revolt weakened Maxentius' popularity.

hilarion_in_gaza.debate: Jerome's Life is partly romance; dates approximate.

introduction_of_the_solidus.detail:
Diocletian had struck the aureus at 60 to the pound. Around 309-310, at the Trier mint, Constantine began striking a lighter gold coin at 72 to the Roman pound, about 4.5 g, which came to be called the solidus ('solid' or 'whole'). The term appears in laws by 325, and the 72 solidi to the pound also fixed the late Roman reckoning of gold by weight: a solidus equalled 24 siliquae (carats, from the carob seed), the origin of the modern carat. Constantine's solidus circulated first in his western territories; after the defeat of Licinius in 324 it became standard empire-wide, and the eastern aureus at 60 to the pound disappeared.

Constantine's ability to maintain the solidus rested on large stocks of gold: Anonymous De Rebus Bellicis and Eusebius link it to the confiscation of temple treasures after 324, and taxes such as the chrysargyron (collatio lustralis) and senatorial levies were paid in gold or silver. Gold coins were used for state payments to soldiers and officials, and much taxation in kind was progressively commuted into gold. Valentinian I's reforms of 366-368 refined the metal (marked OB) and centralised its minting at the imperial court.

The solidus was the most successful coin in history in terms of stability: it kept its weight and nearly pure fineness in the Byzantine empire (as the nomisma) until debasement began in the 1030s-1040s, and it served as an international currency from Britain to India; Indian and Chinese finds attest its reach. The flip side was that bronze coinage for everyday use continued to inflate against gold. Jairus Banaji argues that the gold economy created a new aristocracy of service; others stress continuity. The date is debated (309 or 310, some say 312), but Trier is certain as the first mint.
introduction_of_the_solidus.debate: Date (309 or 310) and whether introduced initially only in Constantine's territories (extended east after 324).
scholarship: Banaji, Agrarian Change in Late Antiquity (2001)
Harl, Coinage in the Roman Economy (1996)
Bruun, RIC VII (1966)
Banaji, Agrarian Change in Late Antiquity: Gold, Labour and Aristocratic Dominance (2001)
Hendy, Studies in the Byzantine Monetary Economy (1985)

death_of_maximian_310.detail: Lactantius adds a second plot in which Maximian tried to murder Constantine in bed and killed a eunuch substitute. Constantine then abandoned his Herculian descent and claimed descent from Claudius II, announced in the panegyric of 310.

constantine_vision_of_apollo_310.detail: Peter Weiss argued that what Constantine actually saw was a solar halo phenomenon, later reinterpreted as the Christian vision reported by Eusebius; others keep the 310 and 312 visions distinct. Constantine's coinage honoured Sol Invictus as 'comes' until the early 320s.
constantine_vision_of_apollo_310.debate: Identification of the temple; relation to the later Christian vision.
scholarship: Weiss, 'The vision of Constantine', JRA 16 (2003)
Barnes, Constantine: Dynasty, Religion and Power (2011)

edict_of_serdica_311.detail:
By 311 the persecution had lasted eight years and had failed to suppress Christianity. Galerius, senior Augustus, fell ill with what Lactantius describes in gruesome detail as a cancer of the genitals, an abscess that rotted and swarmed with worms, with an unbearable stench reaching the whole palace at Serdica. Lactantius and Eusebius present his illness as divine punishment. On 30 April 311 an edict issued in the names of Galerius, Licinius and Constantine (Maximinus' name is missing from Eusebius' Greek version, and he only grudgingly complied) was posted at Nicomedia.

The text, preserved in Latin by Lactantius and in Greek by Eusebius, is remarkably candid. It explains that the emperors had wanted to bring the Christians, who had abandoned the religion of their ancestors, back to a good disposition; that many had been punished, but most persisted and neither worshipped the gods nor their own God. 'Therefore, in view of our most mild clemency', the emperors permitted that 'Christians may exist again and set up the houses in which they used to meet', so long as they did nothing contrary to good order, and asked them to pray to their God for the emperors' safety and their own. A letter to the governors was to set out the details.

Galerius died a few days later, early in May 311, and was buried at Felix Romuliana. The edict was the first legal recognition of Christianity as a permitted religion (religio licita) and ended the persecution in the Balkans and the west, though Maximinus Daia, after initially complying through a circular of his prefect Sabinus, resumed persecution in his eastern territories in the autumn of 311. Compared with the 'Edict of Milan' of 313, which proclaimed religious freedom for all and ordered restitution of property, Galerius' text grants toleration grudgingly; but it was the decisive admission that the persecution had failed.
edict_of_serdica_311.debate: Lactantius' gloating account of Galerius' illness is a stock 'death of the persecutor' motif.
scholarship: Corcoran, The Empire of the Tetrarchs (2000)
Barnes, Constantine and Eusebius (1981)

donatist_schism.detail:
When Mensurius, bishop of Carthage, died around 311 (some date it 307), his archdeacon Caecilian was quickly consecrated by local bishops including Felix of Abthugni, who was accused of having been a traditor, one who surrendered scriptures in the persecution. Caecilian had made enemies by restricting the veneration of martyrs not officially recognised, including that of a wealthy woman, Lucilla, who was accused of kissing a dubious martyr's bone before communion. A council of some 70 Numidian bishops under Secundus of Tigisis, primate of Numidia, declared Caecilian's consecration invalid and elected the lector Majorinus, who was succeeded around 313 by Donatus of Casae Nigrae, after whom the movement was named.

The Donatists held that sacraments administered by traditores were invalid, so that those baptised by them had to be rebaptised: a continuation of Cyprian's insistence on a pure church. They appealed to Constantine, who referred the case to the council of Rome under Miltiades (313) and the council of Arles (314), which both found for Caecilian. An inquiry cleared Felix in 315, and in 316 Constantine judged in person at Milan. He then tried coercion (317-321), which produced Donatist martyrs, before tolerating them. Under Constans the mission of Paul and Macarius (347) brought violence and the exile of Donatus; Julian allowed the exiles to return in 362, and under Parmenian the Donatists became the majority church in Numidia and much of Africa.

Augustine's writings, the conference of Carthage in 411 and imperial laws of 405 and 412 finally suppressed the Donatist church, though it survived into the sixth century. W. H. C. Frend saw it as a Numidian, rural and Berber protest against Roman Carthage; later scholars (Brown, Shaw, Tilley) stress theology, martyr cult and local identity rather than nationalism. The schism was the first case of a Roman emperor intervening to decide a church dispute.
donatist_schism.debate: Date of Caecilian's consecration (307 or 311/312); social versus theological explanations.
scholarship: Frend, The Donatist Church (1952)
Shaw, Sacred Violence (2011)
Shaw, Sacred Violence: African Christians and Sectarian Hatred in the Age of Augustine (2011)

death_of_diocletian.debate: Date disputed: 3 December 311 (Barnes), 312 or 313; older views 316.

vision_of_constantine_312.detail:
Two versions of Constantine's conversion experience survive. Lactantius, writing about 314-315 in De Mortibus Persecutorum, says that on the night before the battle at the Milvian Bridge Constantine was told in a dream to mark 'the heavenly sign of God' on his soldiers' shields, and did so by drawing 'the letter X turned, with its top bent around', most likely a staurogram or a chi-rho. Eusebius of Caesarea, in the Life of Constantine written after the emperor's death in 337, tells a different story that he claims to have heard from Constantine himself on oath: while marching with his army earlier in the campaign, at midday, Constantine and all his soldiers saw a cross of light above the sun with the words 'By this conquer' (Greek touto nika; Latin in hoc signo vinces). That night Christ appeared to him in a dream with the same sign and told him to make a likeness of it as a protection in battle. Eusebius then describes the labarum, a tall gilded spear with a crossbar and a wreath enclosing the chi-rho, from which hung a square banner with portraits of the emperor and his sons.

Earlier, in 310, a panegyrist reported that Constantine had seen Apollo with Victory at a shrine in Gaul (probably Grand), offering him laurel wreaths with the numeral XXX. Peter Weiss proposed that Constantine saw a solar halo phenomenon in 310, interpreted first in pagan and later in Christian terms. The chi-rho appears on a silver medallion of Ticinum around 315 on Constantine's helmet, while Sol Invictus remained on his coins until about 322.

The debate is endless: was the conversion a sudden experience (Barnes), a gradual shift from solar monotheism (Bleckmann, Van Dam), or political calculation? What is clear is that from 312 Constantine identified his victories with the Christian God and lavished favours on the church.
vision_of_constantine_312.debate: Lactantius and Eusebius are partisan; their versions are inconsistent. The sincerity and timing of Constantine's conversion are among the most contested questions in Roman history.
scholarship: Barnes, Constantine: Dynasty, Religion and Power (2011)
Weiss, JRA 16 (2003)
Van Dam, Remembering Constantine at the Milvian Bridge (2011)
Lenski (ed.), Cambridge Companion to the Age of Constantine (2006/2012)
Weiss, "The Vision of Constantine", JRA 16 (2003)
Barnes, Constantine (2011)
Bleckmann, Konstantin der Grosse (1996)

battle_of_the_milvian_bridge.detail:
In the spring of 312 Constantine crossed the Alps by the Mont Genèvre or Mont Cenis with perhaps 40,000 men, a quarter of his army, leaving the rest to guard the Rhine. He stormed Segusio, defeated Maxentius' heavy cavalry (clibanarii) near Turin by letting their charge pass through opened ranks and clubbing the armoured riders from their horses, entered Milan, won at Brescia, besieged and took Verona after killing Maxentius' praetorian prefect Ruricius Pompeianus in a hard battle, and then marched on Rome. Zosimus gives Maxentius 188,000 men, wildly inflated, but he certainly outnumbered Constantine and could have sat out a siege behind the Aurelian Walls, which he had raised and supplied.

Instead, Lactantius says, after riots in the Circus in which the crowd chanted that Constantine was invincible, Maxentius consulted the Sibylline Books, which declared that 'on this day the enemy of the Romans will perish'. On 28 October 312, the sixth anniversary of his accession, he crossed the Tiber on a bridge of boats beside the partly demolished Milvian Bridge and drew up on the plain near Saxa Rubra with the river behind him. Constantine's Gallic cavalry broke Maxentius' horse on the wings; the Praetorians fought and died where they stood; the rest fled back to the bridge of boats, which collapsed under them. Maxentius drowned in the Tiber with many of his men. His body was recovered and his head carried on a spear into Rome the next day, then sent to Africa.

Constantine entered Rome on 29 October, disbanded the Praetorian Guard and its horse guard, the equites singulares, and was hailed by the Senate as senior Augustus. Eusebius compared the drowning to Pharaoh's army in the Red Sea. The battle made Constantine master of the west and, through the vision that preceded it and the Christian sign on his soldiers' shields, became the founding moment of the Christian empire. The Arch of Constantine (315) shows the battle with Maxentius' men drowning.
battle_of_the_milvian_bridge.debate: Zosimus' numbers are fantastical; the precise topography (Saxa Rubra vs the bridge itself) and the Sibylline story are uncertain. Eusebius compares the drowning to Pharaoh in the Red Sea.
scholarship: Van Dam, Remembering Constantine at the Milvian Bridge (2011)
Barnes, Constantine (2011)
Potter, Constantine the Emperor (2013)

siege_of_verona_312.detail: The panegyrist of 313 records that Constantine fought in person and was rebuked by his officers for risking himself, and that the captured Maxentian soldiers were chained with fetters made from their own swords.

praetorian_guard_abolished_312.detail: The equites singulares' cemetery on the Via Labicana was built over by the basilica of Saints Marcellinus and Peter and the mausoleum of Helena, and their barracks on the Caelian by the Lateran basilica, a pointed reuse of the losers' property for Christian building.

lateran_basilica_founded.detail: The Liber Pontificalis lists its endowments of gold and silver fittings and estates. Constantine's churches in Rome were placed mostly on imperial land at the edges of the city (Lateran, St Peter's on the Vatican, St Paul's, the cemetery basilicas), leaving the monumental core to its traditional cults.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City (1980)
Krautheimer, Three Christian Capitals (1983)

constantine_army_reforms.detail:
The late Roman army differed sharply from that of the Principate, and ancient and modern writers credit Constantine with key steps. After 312 he abolished the Praetorian Guard and the equites singulares and relied on new mounted guard units, the scholae palatinae, under the master of offices. He built up a large mobile army attached to the emperor's person, the comitatus, whose soldiers (comitatenses) enjoyed better pay and privileges than the frontier troops, known first as ripenses and later limitanei; a law of 325 (CTh 7.20.4) already distinguishes comitatenses, ripenses and auxiliaries. New infantry units, the auxilia palatina such as the Cornuti and Brachiati, many recruited among Germans, became the elite of the field army, while the legions were reduced to units of about 1,000 men.

Command was reorganised. Constantine created the posts of magister peditum and magister equitum, the masters of foot and horse, who took over the military functions of the praetorian prefects; the prefects became purely civil officials in charge of supply, finance and justice in regional prefectures. Frontier troops were placed under duces in each sector. Germanic officers rose to the top: Bonitus, father of Silvanus, under Constantine, then Magnentius, Silvanus and many others.

Zosimus, a hostile pagan writing c. 500, accused Constantine of ruining the empire by withdrawing troops from the frontiers into cities where they grew soft, leaving the borders exposed. Modern debate concerns whether Diocletian or Constantine created the field army: Jones and van Berchem stressed Diocletian's increase of the frontier forces and the comitatus, while others (Nicasie, Southern and Dixon) see a gradual evolution from Gallienus' cavalry to Constantine's comitatenses. The system was later formalised into regional field armies, as shown in the Notitia Dignitatum around 400.
constantine_army_reforms.debate: Dating of the comitatenses/limitanei division and Zosimus' hostile interpretation.
scholarship: Jones, The Later Roman Empire (1964)
Elton, Warfare in Roman Europe AD 350-425 (1996)
Southern and Dixon, The Late Roman Army (1996)
Jones, The Later Roman Empire 284-602 (1964)
Nicasie, Twilight of Empire: The Roman Army from the Reign of Diocletian until the Battle of Adrianople (1998)

edict_of_milan_313.detail:
In February 313 Constantine and Licinius met at Milan, where Licinius married Constantine's half-sister Constantia. They agreed a common religious policy. No edict as such survives, and the familiar title is a modern convention criticised since Otto Seeck. What we have is a letter issued by Licinius after his victory over Maximinus Daia at Tzirallum (30 April 313), posted at Nicomedia on 13 June 313 and preserved in Latin by Lactantius, and a Greek version addressed to the governor of Palestine in Eusebius' Ecclesiastical History.

The text states that 'when I, Constantine Augustus, and I, Licinius Augustus, met happily at Milan', they decided to grant 'both to Christians and to all others free power to follow the religion each wished', so that 'whatever divinity there is in heaven may be favourable to us and all under our rule'. All restrictions on Christians were removed; meeting places and other property confiscated from Christians, including those belonging to the Christian community as a corporate body, were to be returned at once without payment, and those who had bought or received them as gifts could seek compensation from the treasury.

In the west Constantine had already, after the Milvian Bridge, ordered restitution of church property in Africa and exempted clergy from civic duties (letters to Anullinus). The Milan agreement extended these measures to the east once Licinius defeated Maximinus. Its importance lies in the principle of religious liberty for all and the recognition of the church as a legal body able to own property, which made possible the church's growth into a wealthy institution. Modern scholars stress that it was not the establishment of Christianity as the state religion, which took decades, and that Licinius soon turned against the church.
edict_of_milan_313.debate: Its legal form (edict, rescript, letter) and whether Constantine had already issued a similar measure in the West are debated.
scholarship: Seeck, "Das sogenannte Edikt von Mailand", ZKG 12 (1891)
Corcoran, The Empire of the Tetrarchs (2000)

battle_of_tzirallum.debate: Lactantius' numbers and angelic prayer are part of his providential narrative.

eusebius_ecclesiastical_history.debate: Number and dates of editions (Schwartz, Barnes, Burgess) disputed.

council_of_arles_314.detail: The first council called by an emperor, it set the pattern for Nicaea. The British bishops' signatures are the earliest firm evidence for an organised church in Britain.

sources.w: Canons of the Council of Arles (314)

arch_of_constantine.detail: Its inscription attributes the victory to 'instinctu divinitatis' (by the prompting of the divinity), a famously ambiguous phrase acceptable to pagans and Christians. The stylistic contrast between the second-century spolia and the squat Constantinian frieze is a textbook case in debates about 'decline' versus deliberate late antique aesthetics.
scholarship: Elsner, 'From the culture of spolia to the cult of relics', PBSR 68 (2000)

battle_of_cibalae.detail: The war began after a failed plan to make Bassianus, husband of Constantine's half-sister Anastasia, Caesar of a buffer zone in Italy and Illyricum. Licinius raised his officer Valens as co-Augustus.

battle_of_mardia.detail: Licinius' co-emperor Valens was deposed and executed as part of the settlement.

arian_controversy_begins.detail:
Arius, a Libyan-born ascetic presbyter in charge of the church of Baucalis in Alexandria, taught around 318 (the date is disputed, some prefer 320-322) that God the Father alone was without beginning and that the Son, though created before all ages and through him all things, was created out of nothing by the Father's will. 'There was when he was not', 'before he was begotten, he was not', and the Son was 'not equal to the Father' became the slogans of his opponents' summaries. He drew on a subordinationist reading of Origen and on biblical texts such as Proverbs 8:22 ('the Lord created me at the beginning of his ways'). His Thalia, a work partly in verse, was popular; Philostorgius says he wrote songs for sailors, millers and travellers.

Bishop Alexander of Alexandria, insisting on the Son's eternal generation, condemned Arius at a synod of about a hundred Egyptian and Libyan bishops and excommunicated him with several presbyters and deacons. Arius found support from his fellow pupils of Lucian of Antioch, the 'Collucianists', especially the powerful Eusebius of Nicomedia, and from Eusebius of Caesarea; synods in Bithynia and Palestine backed him. A war of encyclical letters followed, which Alexander circulated widely. After defeating Licinius in 324, Constantine sent Ossius of Cordoba with a letter describing the dispute as a trivial question of words, but reconciliation failed; a synod at Antioch early in 325 condemned Arius' supporters, and the emperor called the council of Nicaea.

Modern scholars (Hanson, Rowan Williams, Gwynn) emphasise that 'Arianism' as a coherent heresy is largely a construct of Athanasius' polemic; the following decades saw a spectrum of positions (homoians, homoiousians, anomoeans) rather than an Arian party loyal to Arius. The controversy dominated church politics for sixty years until the council of Constantinople in 381, and among the Goths and other Germanic peoples into the sixth century.
scholarship: Hanson, The Search for the Christian Doctrine of God (1988)
Williams, Arius: Heresy and Tradition (1987/2001)
Ayres, Nicaea and its Legacy (2004)
Williams, Arius: Heresy and Tradition (2nd ed., 2001)
Gwynn, The Eusebians (2007)

old_st_peters_basilica.detail: Excavations under the Vatican in 1940-1949 exposed the necropolis and the 'Tropaion of Gaius'. The basilica, about 120 m long, was a funerary hall and martyrium rather than a cathedral and stood until its demolition from 1506.

forty_martyrs_of_sebaste_320.debate: Date 320 or 316; details are hagiographical but the core is accepted.

piazza_armerina_villa.debate: Ownership hotly debated (Maximian, a Nicomachus, Proculus Populonius or other senator).
scholarship: Wilson, Piazza Armerina (1983)

sunday_law_321.detail: The religiously neutral language (Sun, not Lord's day) suited both Christians and solar worshippers, and the law founded the Western legal tradition of Sunday rest.

battle_of_the_hellespont_324.detail: The victory broke the blockade of the straits and allowed Constantine to supply the siege of Byzantium and ferry his army to Asia. It was the last major naval battle in the Mediterranean between Roman fleets until the fifth century.

battle_of_adrianople_324.detail: Zosimus gives Licinius 150,000 foot and 15,000 horse against Constantine's 120,000 foot and 10,000 horse, figures much inflated. Constantine was wounded in the thigh. Eusebius presents the war as a crusade against Licinius' renewed harassment of Christians.

battle_of_chrysopolis.detail:
The final war between Constantine and Licinius began in 324 after years of tension, Constantine's incursion into Licinius' Thrace while pursuing Goths in 323, and Licinius' restrictions on Christians. On 3 July 324 Constantine defeated Licinius at Adrianople, and his son Crispus destroyed Licinius' fleet under Abantus (Amandus) at the Hellespont, opening the straits. Licinius abandoned Byzantium, crossed to Asia and proclaimed his master of offices Martinianus as co-Augustus.

Constantine ferried his army across the Bosporus in light vessels and on 18 September 324 attacked Licinius' army near Chrysopolis (Üsküdar), on the Asian shore opposite Byzantium. Licinius' forces included Gothic auxiliaries under their chief Alica. Eusebius emphasises the protective power of the labarum, carried by a picked guard to wherever the line wavered. The battle was a crushing victory: Zosimus speaks of some 25,000 Licinian dead and the rest scattering. Licinius fled to Nicomedia with about 30,000 survivors and, after his wife Constantia interceded with her brother, surrendered on the promise of his life. He was sent to live as a private citizen at Thessalonica with Martinianus, but both were executed in 325 on the charge, perhaps fabricated, of plotting with the Goths.

Chrysopolis left Constantine the sole ruler of the empire, the first since 285 (and the last until Theodosius briefly in 394-395). Within weeks he founded Constantinople on the site of Byzantium as a victory city, raised his son Constantius to Caesar (8 November 324) and extended his pro-Christian policies to the east, summoning the council of Nicaea for 325. Christian writers presented the war as a crusade; modern historians see it as a power struggle in which religion was an instrument of propaganda.
scholarship: Odahl, Constantine and the Christian Empire (2004)
Barnes, Constantine (2011)

foundation_of_constantinople_324.detail:
Immediately after Chrysopolis, on 8 November 324, Constantine marked out the boundaries of a new city on the site of Byzantium, the Greek colony on the promontory between the Golden Horn, the Bosporus and the Sea of Marmara, which Septimius Severus had punished in 196 and then rebuilt. Philostorgius tells that the emperor walked the line on foot, spear in hand, and when his companions asked how far he would go, replied, 'Until he who walks before me stops'. The new land wall ran about 2.8 km west of the Severan wall, roughly quadrupling the area of the city to about six square kilometres. On the same day he made his son Constantius Caesar.

The city was built rapidly. Its main features were the Mese (main street), the round Forum of Constantine with a porphyry column topped by a statue of the emperor as Apollo-Helios, the enlarged Hippodrome linked to the Great Palace, the Augustaion, a Senate house, the baths of Zeuxippus and the church of the Holy Apostles, designed as Constantine's mausoleum. Statues were taken from all over the eastern Mediterranean, including the Serpent Column from Delphi, set up on the spina of the Hippodrome; Jerome remarked that Constantinople was dedicated by stripping nearly every other city bare. Settlers were attracted by the grant of houses and from 332 by a free bread dole on the Roman model, said to be 80,000 rations. A senate was created, initially of lower rank than Rome's.

Why Constantine chose Byzantium remains debated: strategic location between the Danube and Euphrates fronts and at a nodal point of land and sea routes, a victory monument, and a Christian capital free of Rome's pagan traditions have all been proposed. Gilbert Dagron's Naissance d'une capitale argues that it became 'New Rome' only gradually, under Constantius II and Theodosius I, from one imperial residence among several to the capital of the east.
foundation_of_constantinople_324.debate: Date of foundation 324 (standard) and the city's original character (Christian or not) disputed.
scholarship: Dagron, Naissance d'une capitale (1974)
Krautheimer, Three Christian Capitals (1983)
Bassett, The Urban Image of Late Antique Constantinople (2004)
Dagron, Naissance d'une capitale: Constantinople et ses institutions de 330 à 451 (1974)
Mango, Le développement urbain de Constantinople (1985)

optatian_figured_poems_324.debate: Dates of the collection (c. 324-326) and exile debated.

council_of_nicaea.detail:
Constantine originally summoned the council to Ancyra but moved it to Nicaea in Bithynia, closer to his residence at Nicomedia, offering bishops free use of the imperial post. It opened around 20 May 325 (some sources give 19 June) in the imperial palace, with between 250 and 300 bishops; later tradition fixed the number at 318, the servants of Abraham. Almost all came from the eastern provinces; the west was represented by Ossius of Cordoba, two Roman presbyters (Vitus and Vincentius) for the aged Pope Silvester, Caecilian of Carthage and a handful of others. Constantine entered in purple and gold, addressed the bishops in Latin and took part in the debates.

No minutes survive. From Eusebius' letter to his church, Athanasius' On the Decrees of Nicaea and the church historians, we know that the council condemned Arius and adopted a creed declaring the Son 'begotten, not made, of one substance (homoousios) with the Father', with anathemas against those who said 'there was when he was not' or that the Son was of another hypostasis or ousia. The term homoousios, possibly suggested by Constantine or Ossius, was accepted by Eusebius of Caesarea with reservations. Arius and two Libyan bishops who refused to sign were exiled to Illyricum, and Eusebius of Nicomedia and Theognis of Nicaea soon after. The council also settled the Melitian schism, agreed that Easter should be celebrated on the same Sunday everywhere without reference to Jewish calculations, and issued twenty canons, including canon 6 recognising the authority of Alexandria over Egypt, Libya and the Pentapolis on the model of Rome, and canon 7 honouring Jerusalem. The council closed with a banquet for Constantine's vicennalia in late July.

Nicaea became the first 'ecumenical council', but its creed only achieved its central place after 350 thanks to Athanasius and the Cappadocians; for decades many bishops preferred other formulas. It established the model of the emperor convening and enforcing church councils.
council_of_nicaea.debate: Number of bishops, president, and the significance of homoousios at the time are debated; Athanasius' later accounts are partisan.
scholarship: Ayres, Nicaea and its Legacy (2004)
Hanson, The Search for the Christian Doctrine of God (1988)
Barnes, Constantine and Eusebius (1981)
Ayres, Nicaea and Its Legacy (2004)
Kim (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to the Council of Nicaea (2021)

council_of_antioch_325.debate: Authenticity of the Syriac letter was doubted but is now generally accepted.

siliqua_and_miliarense_introduced.debate: Names attested later; how they were tariffed against the solidus is debated.

execution_of_crispus_and_fausta_326.detail: No contemporary source explains why. Later writers (Zosimus, Zonaras) tell of Fausta falsely accusing Crispus of seducing her, a Phaedra story; others suggest adultery between them, or Fausta's attempt to secure the succession for her own sons. Both were subjected to damnatio memoriae. Zosimus claims Constantine's guilt drove him to Christianity, a pagan polemic Sozomen explicitly refutes.
execution_of_crispus_and_fausta_326.debate: Motive unknown; Woods suggests Fausta died from a botched abortion in a hot bath.
scholarship: Woods, 'On the death of the empress Fausta', G&R 45 (1998)
Barnes, Constantine (2011)

helenas_pilgrimage_and_holy_sepulchre.detail:
Shortly after Nicaea Constantine wrote to Macarius, bishop of Jerusalem, ordering the demolition of the temple of Venus that Hadrian had built over the site venerated by local Christians as Christ's tomb, and the construction of a basilica 'more beautiful than any in the world', funded by the imperial treasury and supplied with columns and marble by the governor of Palestine. Excavation uncovered a rock-cut tomb, which Eusebius describes as resurrection after burial. The complex, dedicated in 335, comprised the Anastasis rotunda over the tomb (completed later), a courtyard with the rock of Golgotha, and the five-aisled basilica of the Martyrium.

Constantine's mother Helena, now Augusta and nearly eighty, travelled through the eastern provinces to the Holy Land, probably in 326-328, a year after the executions of Crispus and Fausta in which she may have had a part. Eusebius says she prayed at the holy places, gave money to soldiers, cities and the poor, freed prisoners and founded churches at the cave of the Nativity in Bethlehem and on the Mount of Olives (the Eleona) over the cave associated with the Ascension. She died soon after, probably in 329, and was buried in a porphyry sarcophagus (now in the Vatican Museums) in a mausoleum on the Via Labicana beside the church of Saints Marcellinus and Peter. Drepanum in Bithynia, her birthplace, was renamed Helenopolis.

Eusebius says nothing about the True Cross. The story of Helena discovering it, identified by a miracle, appears first in Ambrose's funeral oration for Theodosius in 395 and in Rufinus, and developed into one of the most influential legends of the Middle Ages. Modern scholars (Hunt, Drijvers) see Helena's journey as an imperial progress combining piety and politics, and the Holy Sepulchre as the beginning of the Christian 'holy land' and mass pilgrimage.
scholarship: Hunt, Holy Land Pilgrimage in the Later Roman Empire (1982)
Drijvers, Helena Augusta (1992)

temple_treasures_and_chrysargyron.detail: The anonymous author of De Rebus Bellicis links the temple gold to the debasement of social values, saying it swelled the houses of the powerful while the poor suffered. Libanius and Zosimus attack the chrysargyron as falling cruelly on the poor; it was abolished by Anastasius in 498.

dedication_of_constantinople_330.detail:
On Monday 11 May 330 Constantine formally dedicated his new city, which bore his name. The Chronicon Paschale describes forty days of celebrations, races in the Hippodrome and distributions to the people. A gilded wooden statue of Constantine holding a small figure of the Tyche of the city was carried in procession into the Hippodrome, escorted by soldiers in white with candles, and the reigning emperor was to rise and bow to it each year on the city's birthday, a ceremony performed into the sixth century. The city's Tyche bore the name Anthousa ('flourishing'), possibly a Greek translation of the secret name of Rome, Flora.

Special coins were struck in all mints: CONSTANTINOPOLIS, with a helmeted personification and Victory on a ship's prow, and URBS ROMA, with the wolf and twins, presenting the two capitals as equals. Later Byzantine tradition claimed that pagan rites accompanied the foundation: that the philosopher Sopater, later executed, assisted, that the astrologer Vettius Valens cast its horoscope, and that the Palladium of Troy and Rome was buried under the porphyry column of Constantine's forum, along with Christian relics. Zosimus says Constantine built temples to Rhea and to the Tyche of Rome. Eusebius, in contrast, presents it as a Christian city free of idols, with fountains decorated with the Good Shepherd and Daniel.

The population grew fast; by the end of the century the city needed extensions and in the early fifth century Theodosius II built the great land walls further west. The dedication date became the anniversary of the empire that lasted until 1453, and 11 May was celebrated in the church calendar as the birthday of the city. Historians debate how far Constantine intended a new capital rather than a monumental imperial residence like Nicomedia or Trier.
scholarship: Dagron, Naissance d'une capitale (1974)
Bassett, The Urban Image of Late Antique Constantinople (2004)

constantine_destroys_temples_330.debate: Scale disputed: Eusebius cites a few spectacular cases, and most temples stayed open.

constantine_divorce_law_331.debate: Christian versus traditional moral motives for Constantine's family legislation are debated (Evans Grubbs).

gothic_treaty_332.detail: The treaty, whose exact terms are disputed (whether the Goths became foederati in the later sense), kept the lower Danube quiet for a generation and fostered Gothic Christianisation and Romanisation; the son of the Gothic king Ariaric was sent as a hostage to Constantinople.
gothic_treaty_332.debate: Nature of the foedus of 332 (equal alliance or subjection) is debated.
scholarship: Heather, Goths and Romans 332-489 (1991)
Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)

law_binding_coloni_332.detail: Older scholarship saw the beginning of serfdom here. Since the 1980s (Carrié, Sirks, Grey) the colonate has been reinterpreted as a fiscal device for registering tax liability rather than a uniform legal status binding peasants to the soil.
law_binding_coloni_332.debate: Meaning of the colonate (proto-serfdom vs fiscal registration).
scholarship: Carrié, 'Le colonat du Bas-Empire: un mythe historiographique?', Opus 1 (1982)
Grey, 'Contextualizing colonatus', JRS 97 (2007)
Sirks, 'The colonate in Justinian's reign', JRS 98 (2008)

council_of_tyre_335.detail: Athanasius would be exiled five times under four emperors (335-337, 339-346, 356-362, 362-363, 365-366), and his polemical writings shaped the later picture of an 'Arian' conspiracy.
scholarship: Barnes, Athanasius and Constantius (1993)

death_of_arius_336.debate: Poisoning has been suspected; the account is polemical.

sources.w: Epistula ad Serapionem de morte Arii

death_of_constantine_337.detail:
In 336-337 Shapur II intervened in Armenia and Constantine prepared a great expedition against Persia, planning to be baptised in the Jordan and taking with him bishops and a tent-church. Around Easter 337 he fell ill in Constantinople. He went to the hot baths of Helenopolis in Bithynia and then to a villa called Achyron near Nicomedia, where, realising he was dying, he asked for baptism, which he had deferred, as was common, until the end of his life. Eusebius of Nicomedia, the leader of the anti-Athanasian bishops, baptised him; he then refused to wear the purple again, dressing only in white baptismal robes. He died at noon on the feast of Pentecost, 22 May 337, aged about 65, after nearly 31 years of rule.
