Arce, Bárbaros y romanos en Hispania (2005)

siege_of_rome_409.detail: Attalus, a pagan baptised by an Arian bishop, failed to secure Africa, whose comes Heraclian stayed loyal to Honorius and cut the grain. Alaric deposed him near Ariminum in summer 410. Honorius had been about to flee to Constantinople when 4,000 eastern troops arrived at Ravenna.

sack_of_rome_410.detail: After two blockades in 408 and 409, and the brief elevation of the senator Priscus Attalus as his puppet emperor, Alaric was negotiating with Honorius near Ravenna in summer 410 when he was attacked by the Goth Sarus, a personal enemy in Roman service. Taking this as proof of bad faith, he marched on Rome. On the night of 24 August 410 the Goths entered by the Salarian Gate, according to Procopius through treachery: either slaves opened it or the noblewoman Proba, pitying the starving people, ordered it opened. The sack lasted three days. Alaric, an Arian Christian, ordered the churches of Peter and Paul respected as sanctuaries, and Orosius tells of a Goth who found a consecrated virgin guarding the sacred vessels of St Peter and escorted her and them in procession to the basilica. But the city was plundered, the Gardens of Sallust burned, houses of the aristocracy on the Aventine and Caelian looted, and many were killed or carried off, among them Honorius's sister Galla Placidia. Wealthy refugees fled to Sicily, Africa and the Holy Land, where Jerome wrote 'the city which had taken the whole world was itself taken'. The physical damage was limited compared with the psychological shock. Pagans blamed the abandonment of the old gods, and Augustine began the City of God in 413 to answer them, arguing that no earthly city was eternal. Orosius minimised the event as less destructive than the fire of Nero. Archaeology confirms burning in the Basilica Aemilia, where coins melted into the floor, and in parts of the Forum. Alaric left after three days, marched south intending to cross to Sicily and Africa, lost his fleet in a storm at the Straits and died near Consentia before the end of 410.
sack_of_rome_410.debate: Procopius's tale of a treacherous gate opening by Proba's slaves or by a Gothic 'gift' of youths is legendary. Ward-Perkins uses 410 and its aftermath as evidence of real violence; Goffart and Halsall stress its limited material impact.
scholarship: Lipps, Machado & von Rummel (eds.), The Sack of Rome in 410 AD (2013)
Ward-Perkins, The Fall of Rome and the End of Civilization (2005)
Lipps, Machado and von Rummel (eds.), The Sack of Rome in 410 AD (2013)
Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)
Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)

britain_abandoned_410.detail: Zosimus, drawing on Olympiodorus, says that around 409 the Britons, harried by Saxon raids and abandoned by Constantine III, took up arms, freed their cities from barbarian attack, expelled the Roman officials and set up their own administration, and that the Armoricans followed their example. Elsewhere he says that in 410 Honorius wrote letters to the cities of Britain telling them to look to their own defence. The second passage has been doubted: some scholars, following a suggestion first made in the nineteenth century, argue that Zosimus wrote of Bruttium in southern Italy, which fits the surrounding narrative of Alaric's movements, and that the letter has nothing to do with Britain. Either way, no Roman official is attested in Britain after 409, no field army returned and imported coin ceased to arrive: the latest substantial hoards, such as Hoxne, end with issues of Constantine III and Honorius. The Groans of the Britons, an appeal to Aetius in his third consulship (446), shows that some Britons still thought of Rome as their protector a generation later. Gildas's narrative in the sixth century and Bede's in the eighth are later constructions. Archaeology shows the rapid collapse of the Roman economy in Britain in the early fifth century: towns, villas, coin use and pottery industries disappeared within a generation, a more drastic break than in any other western province. The end of Roman Britain is therefore less a single event than a process, but 409-410 marks the point at which the island ceased to be part of the empire's administration. Its subsequent history, the rule of tyranni such as Vortigern and the settlement of Angles and Saxons, belongs to a different world.
britain_abandoned_410.debate: Whether Honorius's letter of 410 (Zosimus 6.10.2) was addressed to Britain or Bruttium is disputed.
scholarship: Esmonde Cleary, The Ending of Roman Britain (1989)
Halsall, Worlds of Arthur (2013)
Thompson, 'Britain AD 406-410', Britannia 8 (1977)
Birley, The Roman Government of Britain (2005)

sources.w: Ecclesiastical History of the English People

death_of_alaric_410.debate: The burial story comes only from Jordanes, who drew on Cassiodorus's lost Gothic History and wrote 140 years later; treasure hunters still dig at Cosenza.

theodosian_walls_413.detail: The land walls that protected Constantinople for a thousand years were built under the regency of Anthemius, praetorian prefect of the East from 405 to 414, during the minority of Theodosius II. A law of 4 April 413 in the Theodosian Code refers to the new wall as complete and assigns the towers to the use of the landowners on whose land they stood. The new line ran some 1.5 km west of Constantine's wall, from the Sea of Marmara near the Golden Gate to the Golden Horn near Blachernae, about 5.7 km long, enclosing much new land for the growing city. The first phase consisted of the great inner wall, about 5 m thick and 12 m high, with 96 towers. After the earthquake of 447 the prefect Constantinus rebuilt the damaged sections in sixty days and added an outer wall with its own towers and a moat some 20 m wide, creating a triple line of defence across the peninsula; inscriptions on the Mevlevihane gate commemorate the feat. The Golden Gate, a triumphal arch of marble, was incorporated into the wall as a ceremonial entrance. The sea walls along the Marmara and the Golden Horn were added and strengthened in the following decades, and in the 620s the Blachernae area was enclosed after the Avar siege. The walls were decisive in the survival of the eastern empire: they withstood the Huns in 447 by deterrence, Vitalian in 515, the Kutrigurs in 559, the Avars and Persians in 626, the Arabs in 674-678 and 717-718, and fell to an assault only in 1204 and 1453. Their construction reflects the confidence and resources of the eastern state in the decade after the sack of Rome.
theodosian_walls_413.debate: Some scholars think the walls were begun before 405, under Arcadius, and only completed under Anthemius.
scholarship: Van Millingen, Byzantine Constantinople: The Walls of the City (1899)
Crow, 'The infrastructure of a great city', in Lavan et al. (eds.), Technology in Transition (2007)
Meyer-Plath and Schneider, Die Landmauer von Konstantinopel (1943)

burgundians_on_the_rhine_413.debate: Worms as the Burgundian centre rests on the Nibelung tradition; the location is uncertain.

athaulf_marries_galla_placidia_414.detail: Orosius reports that a Narbonne citizen heard Athaulf say at Bethlehem that he had once wanted to turn Romania into Gothia, but had decided to use Gothic strength to restore the Roman name, since Goths could not obey laws. Whether authentic or Orosian invention, it is the clearest ancient statement of a barbarian king's aspiration to Roman legitimacy.

scholarship: Holum, Theodosian Empresses (1982)

murder_of_hypatia_415.debate: Socrates, a moderate Christian, condemns the murder as shaming Cyril; John of Nikiu, centuries later, celebrates it. The modern image of Hypatia as a young martyr of science owes much to Gibbon and Kingsley; she was probably about 60.
scholarship: Dzielska, Hypatia of Alexandria (1995)
Watts, Hypatia (2017)
Van Nuffelen, Orosius and the Rhetoric of History (2012)
Brown, Augustine of Hippo (1967, rev. 2000)

visigothic_settlement_aquitaine_418.detail: After Athaulf's death in 415 and Sigeric's brief reign, the new Gothic king Wallia, starving and blockaded by the Roman fleet, made a treaty with Constantius in 416: in return for 600,000 measures of grain he returned Galla Placidia and fought the Rhine invaders in Spain as a Roman federate. In 416-418 his Goths annihilated the Siling Vandals in Baetica and so mauled the Alans that they joined the Hasdings. In 418 Constantius recalled them and settled them in Aquitania Secunda, with some adjacent cities of Novempopulana and Narbonensis, between Toulouse and the Atlantic. The terms are much debated. Older scholarship, following later Burgundian and Visigothic law codes, assumed the Goths received a share, two-thirds or one-third, of the land of Roman estates under the system of hospitalitas. Walter Goffart argued instead that they were assigned shares of tax revenue, not land; most scholars now see a combination of land grants and tax assignments varying from place to place. Why the Goths were settled in prosperous south-western Gaul, rather than on a frontier, is also disputed: suggested reasons include protecting Aquitaine against Bacaudae and Saxon raiders, keeping the Goths away from the Mediterranean and Italy, and rewarding them near the Atlantic grain lands. In the same year Honorius re-established the council of the Seven Provinces at Arles, giving the Gallo-Roman aristocracy a forum. The settlement was meant to create a dependent federate force. Wallia died in 418 and was succeeded by Theodoric I, under whom the Goths fought both for and against Rome. From this base grew the Visigothic kingdom of Toulouse, which by 475 covered most of Gaul south of the Loire and much of Spain.
visigothic_settlement_aquitaine_418.debate: Land versus tax shares, and the date (418 or 419; Prosper and Hydatius differ), are disputed.
scholarship: Goffart, Barbarians and Romans AD 418-584: The Techniques of Accommodation (1980)
Heather, Goths and Romans (1991)

notitia_dignitatum.detail: The Notitia Dignitatum, 'list of offices', survives only in Renaissance copies of a lost Carolingian manuscript from Speyer. It lists every senior civil and military post of the two halves of the empire with their staffs and, for military commanders, the units under them and their stations, with painted illustrations of insignia, shield patterns of the regiments, and personifications of provinces. The eastern section appears to reflect conditions around 395-400 and was not updated. The western section was revised piecemeal into the 420s: it includes units raised by Honorius and Constantius III and reflects the losses of the 410s, but entries for Britain and the Rhine may be fossilised. It was evidently a working document of the primicerius notariorum, who issued letters of appointment, and was probably copied for the western court around 425-430. The Notitia is the fundamental source for the late Roman army. It shows the division into mobile field armies (comitatenses and palatini) under magistri militum and frontier troops (limitanei) under duces and comites, the proliferation of small units, the names of new regiments such as the Honoriani and Theodosiani, and in the West the transfer of frontier units into field armies (pseudocomitatenses). It also lists the arms factories (fabricae), mints, weaving mills and treasuries. Its figures, if all units were at full strength, would give an army of 500,000 to 600,000, but scholars regard many units as under strength or existing only on paper. The British chapters, including the dux Britanniarum and the count of the Saxon Shore with its forts from Brancaster to Portchester, are the main evidence for the last Roman garrison of the island. The date, purpose and reliability of each chapter remain subjects of intensive debate.
notitia_dignitatum.debate: Whether the western Notitia was systematically updated or only patchily revised is debated.
scholarship: Jones, The Later Roman Empire 284-602 (1964), app. II
Kulikowski, 'The Notitia Dignitatum as a historical source', Historia 49 (2000)
Jones, The Later Roman Empire 284-602 (1964), ch. 17
Brennan, 'The Notitia Dignitatum', in Les littératures techniques dans l'Antiquité (1996)

marriage_of_theodosius_ii_421.debate: Malalas's romantic bride-show tale is late and embroidered.
scholarship: Holum, Theodosian Empresses (1982)

roman_sasanian_war_421_peace_422.debate: The treaty is reconstructed from later references (Procopius, Malchus); the claim of a '100-year peace' is modern shorthand.
scholarship: Greatrex & Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars, Part II (2002)

university_of_constantinople_425.debate: Calling it a 'university' is anachronistic, but it was the first state-funded teaching body of its kind.

accession_of_valentinian_iii_425.detail: When Honorius died of dropsy at Ravenna on 15 August 423, the eastern court hesitated to recognise anyone, and a western official, the primicerius notariorum Joannes, was proclaimed at Rome with the backing of the general Castinus. Galla Placidia and her children, Justa Grata Honoria and Valentinian, had fled to Constantinople in 423 after quarrelling with Honorius. Theodosius II decided to restore his cousin's line. Valentinian was named Caesar at Thessalonica in October 424 and betrothed to Theodosius's infant daughter Licinia Eudoxia. In 425 an eastern expedition under Ardabur, his son Aspar and the magister Candidianus invaded Italy; Ardabur was captured at sea and held in Ravenna, but Aspar, guided by a shepherd through the marshes, entered the city, and Joannes was captured, paraded on a donkey in the hippodrome at Aquileia and beheaded. Three days later the young Aetius arrived with a Hunnic army said to be 60,000 strong, too late to help Joannes; he was bought off with the command in Gaul. On 23 October 425 the master of offices Helion invested the six-year-old Valentinian as Augustus in Rome. Galla Placidia governed as regent for twelve years, balancing the generals Felix, Bonifatius and Aetius, whose rivalry brought civil war in 432 and contributed to the loss of Africa. In 437 Valentinian went to Constantinople to marry Licinia Eudoxia, and the eastern court received western Illyricum, perhaps including Sirmium, as the price of its support. His reign of thirty years was the longest of any western emperor of the fifth century, but power lay with Aetius until Valentinian killed him in 454.
scholarship: Oost, Galla Placidia Augusta (1968)
Salisbury, Rome's Christian Empress (2015)
McEvoy, Child Emperor Rule in the Late Roman West (2013)

city_of_god_426.detail: The sack of 410 brought refugees to Africa and renewed pagan arguments that Rome had fallen because it abandoned its gods. Prompted by the tribune Marcellus, Augustine began De Civitate Dei in 413 and worked on it for thirteen years, publishing it in instalments until about 426-427. The first ten books are polemical. Books 1-5 argue that the gods never protected Rome, citing Roman history from Varro, Sallust and Livy: the Gauls took the city, Cannae was lost, and civil wars raged while the old cults flourished. Rome's empire was granted by the true God as a reward for the Romans' love of glory, a lesser virtue. Books 6-10 attack pagan theology, Varro's antiquarianism, and the Neoplatonists, whom Augustine admired but faulted for refusing the Incarnation. Books 11-22 present the positive doctrine of two cities, formed by two loves, love of self to the contempt of God and love of God to the contempt of self, intermingled in this world until the Last Judgement: the heavenly city, a pilgrim on earth, and the earthly city, whose highest good is peace. Augustine traced them from the fall of the angels through Cain and Abel, Babylon and Rome, to the end of time, and concluded with the resurrection and eternal rest. The work refuses to identify the Roman empire with God's purpose, against the triumphalist history of Eusebius and Orosius, Augustine's own pupil. Its definition of a people as a multitude bound by common objects of love, and its claim that a kingdom without justice is a great robbery, deeply influenced medieval political thought. The City of God, written as Vandals approached Hippo, is the most important intellectual response to the crisis of the western empire.
scholarship: Markus, Saeculum: History and Society in the Theology of St Augustine (1970)
O'Donnell, Augustine: A New Biography (2005)
Brown, Augustine of Hippo (1967, 2000)
O'Daly, Augustine's City of God: A Reader's Guide (1999)

vandal_crossing_to_africa_429.detail: In May 429 Gaiseric, king of the Vandals and Alans since 428, led his people from southern Spain across the Straits of Gibraltar, probably from Iulia Traducta (Tarifa) to Tingitana. Victor of Vita says he ordered a count of the whole people, including old men, children and slaves, and found 80,000; Procopius, using the same figure, says Gaiseric organised them into 80 units of 'thousands' to make his army seem larger. The transport of such numbers across 15 km of sea required ships, possibly provided by the Spanish coastal cities or seized in earlier raids on the Balearics. Procopius tells that Bonifatius, comes Africae and at odds with the court of Galla Placidia, invited the Vandals in as allies; most modern historians regard the story as a later invention, since Bonifatius fought them from the start. The Vandals' motives were probably a search for a secure and rich base away from Gothic and Roman pressure in Spain. Advancing east along the coast, they defeated Bonifatius in 430 and besieged Hippo, where Augustine died. In 432 an eastern army under Aspar arrived and was beaten. The treaty of 435 gave the Vandals parts of Mauretania and Numidia as federates; in 439 Gaiseric seized Carthage. The loss of Africa, the West's richest source of tax revenue, grain and olive oil, was the most damaging single blow to the western empire. Heather calculates that Africa provided a major share of western revenues; without it the government could no longer pay for a large army. Gaiseric's fleet also made the western Mediterranean insecure for decades, culminating in the sack of Rome in 455.
vandal_crossing_to_africa_429.debate: The figure of 80,000 is suspiciously round; Bonifatius's invitation is probably legend.
scholarship: Merrills & Miles, The Vandals (2010)
Wijnendaele, The Last of the Romans: Bonifatius (2015)
Courtois, Les Vandales et l'Afrique (1955)
Merrills and Miles, The Vandals (2010)
Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)

siege_of_hippo_regius_430.detail: After defeating Bonifatius, the comes Africae, in the field in 430, Gaiseric besieged him in the walled port of Hippo Regius, the second city of Numidia, from about June 430. The siege lasted fourteen months. Inside the city were refugees from the surrounding countryside and many clergy, among them the bishop Augustine, aged 75, and his biographer Possidius, bishop of Calama, who describes the misery of the province: churches burned, clergy killed or tortured, consecrated virgins scattered, and the survivors hiding in mountains and caves. In the third month of the siege, on 28 August 430, Augustine died of fever after asking for the penitential psalms to be written on the wall facing his bed; Possidius says he left no will because he had no property, but bequeathed his library to the church. The library survived the siege, which is how his enormous oeuvre reached posterity. The Vandals, with little siege equipment and suffering from hunger, raised the siege in July 431. Bonifatius, reinforced by an eastern army under Aspar, then offered battle and was defeated again, after which he was recalled to Italy and the Vandals took Hippo, which was largely abandoned by its inhabitants. Gaiseric made it his first capital in Africa, and the treaty of 435 left him in control of much of Numidia. Archaeology at Hippo has revealed the cathedral complex, the so-called Basilica Pacis, possibly Augustine's church. The siege shows the Vandals' limited capacity in siege warfare at this stage, which made them reliant on treaties and surprise, as at Carthage in 439, rather than assault.
scholarship: Brown, Augustine of Hippo (1967, 2000)
Merrills and Miles, The Vandals (2010)

council_of_ephesus_431.detail: The controversy began in 428 when Nestorius, the new patriarch of Constantinople, a monk from Antioch, objected to the title Theotokos, 'bearer of God', for Mary, preferring Christotokos, and emphasised the distinction of Christ's divine and human natures. Cyril of Alexandria attacked him as dividing Christ into two persons, won the support of Pope Celestine, who condemned Nestorius at a Roman synod in August 430, and sent him twelve anathemas. Theodosius II summoned a general council to Ephesus for Pentecost 431. Cyril arrived with some 50 Egyptian bishops and allies among the Asian bishops led by Memnon of Ephesus, and opened the council on 22 June, before John of Antioch and the Syrian bishops arrived, and despite the protest of the imperial commissioner Candidian. In a single session the 150 or more bishops present deposed Nestorius, who refused to attend, and the city celebrated with a torchlight procession in honour of the Theotokos. When John arrived four days later, his 43 bishops held a rival council and deposed Cyril and Memnon. The papal legates then arrived and joined Cyril. Theodosius at first confirmed both depositions and detained Cyril, Memnon and Nestorius, but under pressure from Cyril's gifts to the court and monastic demonstrations in Constantinople he released Cyril and sent Nestorius back to his monastery near Antioch; he was later exiled to the Great Oasis in Egypt, where he wrote the Book of Heracleides. In 433 Cyril and John reconciled in the Formula of Reunion, which accepted Theotokos and two natures in one person. The council, later counted as the Third Ecumenical, left the Church of the East, which honoured Nestorius's teacher Theodore of Mopsuestia, outside imperial communion.
council_of_ephesus_431.debate: The role of Pulcheria, whom Nestorius had offended, is emphasised by Holum and doubted by others. Whether Nestorius actually held the 'two sons' heresy he was condemned for is a long-running question.
scholarship: McGuckin, St Cyril of Alexandria: The Christological Controversy (1994)
Holum, Theodosian Empresses (1982)
Wessel, Cyril of Alexandria and the Nestorian Controversy (2004)

mission_of_palladius_and_patrick.debate: Patrick's dates are uncertain; some place his mission later in the fifth century.

battle_of_rimini_432.debate: Later tradition says Aetius had a longer spear prepared for a duel with Bonifatius; this is likely legend.

treaty_of_margus_435.debate: Date is 435 or 439; Priscus survives only in Constantinian excerpts.

destruction_of_the_burgundians_436.debate: The Worms location is from the medieval epic; the kingdom's centre in the 430s is uncertain (perhaps the middle Rhine or Main valley).

publication_of_theodosian_code_438.detail: In March 429 Theodosius II ordered a commission to collect all general imperial constitutions issued since Constantine, arranged by subject under titles and in chronological order within each, as a first stage towards a fuller code combining laws and juristic opinion. The second stage was abandoned; in 435 a new commission of sixteen under the former prefect Antiochus was empowered to edit the texts, removing preambles and redundant words and adapting them to make them clear. The result, the Codex Theodosianus in sixteen books with some 2,500 constitutions, was promulgated in Constantinople on 15 February 438 and took effect on 1 January 439 for both halves of the empire. In the West it was presented to the Senate of Rome on 25 December 438 by the praetorian prefect Anicius Acilius Glabrio Faustus, who had brought it from Constantinople after Valentinian III's wedding; the minutes of that session, the Gesta Senatus, survive with the senators' acclamations, repeated dozens of times. The code replaced all earlier collections of constitutions, including the private Gregorian and Hermogenian codes, and later laws, the Novels, were exchanged between the two courts. Books 1-5 cover public offices and private law, 6-8 the civil service, 9 criminal law, 10-11 finance, 12-15 cities and public works, and 16 religion, with laws on heresy, Jews and pagans. The Code is the fundamental source for the institutions of the fourth and early fifth century. In the West it survived through the Visigothic Breviary of Alaric (506), from which the first five books are mainly known, while in the East it was superseded by Justinian's Code (529-534), which drew on it extensively.
scholarship: Matthews, Laying Down the Law: A Study of the Theodosian Code (2000)
Harries & Wood (eds.), The Theodosian Code (1993)
Honoré, Law in the Crisis of Empire 379-455 AD (1998)
Harries and Wood (eds.), The Theodosian Code (1993)
Sirks, The Theodosian Code: A Study (2007)

vandal_capture_of_carthage_439.detail: Under the treaty of 435 the Vandals held parts of Mauretania and Numidia as federates, and Gaiseric's son Huneric was sent to Italy as a hostage. In 439, while Aetius and Litorius were fighting the Goths in Gaul, Gaiseric broke the treaty and on 19 October seized Carthage, the second city of the western empire, apparently by surprise and with little fighting. Prosper says he confiscated the property of the nobles and clergy and subjected the people to slavery; many senators and the bishop Quodvultdeus were put on unseaworthy ships and drifted to Naples. Gaiseric dated his reign from this event. With Carthage came its harbour and fleet, and the Vandals soon raided Sicily (440) and besieged Panormus. In 441 a combined eastern and western expedition assembled in Sicily, but the eastern contingent was recalled when the Huns and Persians attacked the eastern frontier. In 442 Valentinian III made a treaty recognising Vandal possession of Proconsularis, Byzacena and eastern Numidia in exchange for the Mauretanias and western Numidia. Carthage became the Vandal capital and Gaiseric's kingdom the first independent barbarian kingdom on Roman soil, with its own royal dating and coinage. The fiscal consequences for the West were severe: a law of 440 granting tax relief to refugees, and another of 445 reducing the taxes of Numidia and Mauretania to one-eighth, show the loss. Vandal confiscations created a lasting religious conflict between Arian rulers and Catholic subjects, described by Victor of Vita. Control of Carthage gave Gaiseric naval power that made him master of the western Mediterranean for forty years.
scholarship: Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)
Merrills & Miles, The Vandals (2010)
Merrills and Miles, The Vandals (2010)
Conant, Staying Roman (2012)
Courtois, Les Vandales et l'Afrique (1955)

aborted_sicily_expedition_441.debate: Heather suggests the Huns deliberately attacked to wreck the expedition, perhaps in concert with Gaiseric; there is no direct evidence of collusion.

adventus_saxonum_441.debate: The Gallic chronicler's view from southern Gaul may exaggerate; archaeology shows Anglo-Saxon cemeteries from the 420s-430s in eastern England and a slow, regionally varied process. Halsall and others stress small elite migration and acculturation; genetic studies (Gretzinger et al. 2022) suggest substantial migration in the east.

peace_of_anatolius_443.debate: 2,100 lbs a year was perhaps 2-3% of eastern revenue; Priscus's complaint reflects the burden on the senatorial class rather than imperial insolvency.

groans_of_the_britons_446.debate: The identification of Agitius with Aetius rests on the 'thrice consul' title, which dates the letter to 446-454; some suggest Aegidius. Whether the barbarians were Picts and Irish or Saxons is unclear.

earthquake_and_rebuilding_walls_447.detail: On 26 January 447 a series of severe earthquakes struck Constantinople and the surrounding region, throwing down large sections of the land walls, including 57 towers, while the people took refuge outside the city and processed barefoot with the emperor to the Hebdomon, chanting the Trisagion. The timing was disastrous: Attila was moving against the eastern empire with his largest army, and the plague had broken out. The praetorian prefect Flavius Constantinus organised the reconstruction, mobilising the members of the circus factions, the Blues and the Greens, as labour gangs, each responsible for a section. The work was completed, according to the inscriptions, in sixty days. The inscriptions on the Mevlevihane gate (the Rhegium gate) say in Greek that 'by the emperor's command Constantinus built this strong wall in sixty days', and in Latin that 'by the orders of Theodosius, Constantinus built these strong walls in less than two months; even Pallas could hardly have built so stout a citadel so quickly'. Constantinus also added the outer wall and the moat that made the Theodosian Walls a triple defence. Attila, who defeated the eastern field army at the Utus and raided to Thermopylae, did not attack the city. In the Peace of Anatolius later that year the East agreed to pay arrears of 6,000 lb of gold and an annual tribute of 2,100 lb, and to evacuate a strip of land south of the Danube five days' journey wide. The episode shows the importance of the walls to eastern survival and the organisation of urban manpower through the factions.
scholarship: Croke, 'The date and circumstances of Marcian's decree', Byzantion 48 (1978)
Crow, 'The infrastructures of a great city' (2007)

embassy_of_maximinus_449.detail: In 449 Theodosius II sent the senior officer Maximinus as envoy to Attila, accompanied by his friend the historian Priscus of Panium, whose account is the most vivid description of the Hunnic court to survive. Unknown to Maximinus, the eunuch Chrysaphius had bribed Attila's envoy Edeco, with the interpreter Vigilas as go-between, to assassinate Attila. Edeco revealed the plot to his master. The embassy travelled through the ruins of Naissus, still strewn with bones after the sack of 442, crossed the Danube and followed Attila north to his residence on the Hungarian plain, a complex of wooden buildings and palisades, with a bath built of stone brought from Pannonia by a Roman captive architect. Priscus describes Attila's banquets, where he ate from a wooden plate while his guests had silver, the singers who celebrated his victories, a Moorish dwarf jester named Zercon, and Attila's wife Kreka. He records a famous conversation with a Greek merchant from Viminacium who had been captured, won his freedom fighting for the Huns, and now preferred life among them to the injustice, taxation and corrupt courts of the empire; Priscus answers with a defence of Roman law. Vigilas, returning with 50 lb of gold for the assassination, was seized, and Attila sent envoys to Constantinople with the moneybag hanging round Vigilas's neck, demanding Chrysaphius's head. Theodosius sent the patricians Anatolius and Nomus, who bought peace with gifts and secured the return of prisoners and land. The episode illustrates Roman diplomacy, the intelligence networks of the Hunnic court, and the presence of Romans in Hunnic service, among them Attila's secretary Orestes, the father of Romulus Augustulus.
embassy_of_maximinus_449.debate: Priscus survives only in Constantine VII's Excerpta de legationibus and in Jordanes's paraphrase; the location of Attila's court (somewhere on the Tisza plain) is unknown.
scholarship: Blockley, The Fragmentary Classicising Historians of the Later Roman Empire (1981-83)
Maenchen-Helfen, The World of the Huns (1973)
Kelly, Attila the Hun: Barbarian Terror and the Fall of the Roman Empire (2008)
Blockley, The Fragmentary Classicising Historians of the Later Roman Empire II (1983)
Kelly, Attila the Hun (2008)

death_of_theodosius_ii_450.detail: Theodosius II, emperor since 402 and sole eastern ruler since 408, died on 28 July 450 at the age of 49 after a fall from his horse while hunting near the Lycus river. His reign, the longest of any Roman emperor, had seen the building of the land walls, the Theodosian Code, the foundation of the school at the Capitol (425), the Councils of Ephesus (431 and 449), and the costly appeasement of Attila. He left no son: his daughter Licinia Eudoxia was married to Valentinian III, and the western emperor might have claimed the eastern throne. Instead power was settled by his sister Pulcheria, Augusta since 414 and a consecrated virgin, who had been eclipsed in the 440s by the eunuch Chrysaphius. With the support of the magister militum Aspar, she chose Marcian, a retired officer from Thrace who had served under Aspar, and married him on the condition that she keep her vow of virginity. Marcian was proclaimed on 25 August 450 at the Hebdomon, perhaps crowned by the patriarch Anatolius, although the role of the patriarch in coronations is debated for this date. The new regime reversed Theodosius's last policies at once: Chrysaphius was executed, tribute to Attila was stopped, and a new council was summoned that met at Chalcedon in 451 and overturned the Robber Synod. The western court did not recognise Marcian until 452. Theodosius was later remembered as a pious and learned but weak ruler, dominated by his sister, his wife Eudocia and his eunuchs, an image modern historians have partly revised to stress the effectiveness of his government.
death_of_theodosius_ii_450.debate: Aspar, Marcian's patron, was the real kingmaker. Marcian's halt to tribute redirected Attila westward.
scholarship: Holum, Theodosian Empresses (1982)
Millar, A Greek Roman Empire: Power and Belief under Theodosius II (2006)
Burgess, 'The accession of Marcian', BZ 86/87 (1993/4)

honoria_affair_450.debate: Some scholars doubt the story entirely as court gossip; Jordanes dates the affair to 434 and has Honoria pregnant and sent to Constantinople.

battle_of_avarayr.debate: Armenian sources are hagiographic; numbers unreliable. The date (26 May or 2 June 451) depends on the Armenian church calendar.

sources.w: History of Vardan and the Armenian War

battle_of_the_catalaunian_plains.detail: In 451 Attila turned west, claiming that Valentinian's sister Honoria had offered herself to him in marriage and that half the western empire was her dowry; he may also have intended to attack the Visigoths. His army of Huns and subject peoples, Ostrogoths, Gepids, Rugi, Sciri, Heruli, Thuringians and others, crossed the Rhine, sacked Metz on 7 April and besieged Orléans, which the bishop Anianus held until Aetius arrived in June with a coalition of the Roman army, the Visigoths of Theodoric I, the Alans of Sangiban, Franks, Burgundians, Saxons, Armorican and other groups. Attila retreated to the Campus Mauriacus, apparently in Champagne between Troyes and Châlons. The battle, around 20 June 451, began with a struggle for a ridge, which the Romans and Visigoths won. In the main fighting Theodoric was killed, trampled by his own men or struck by an Ostrogothic javelin, and his son Thorismund led a charge that broke the Hunnic line. Attila retreated into his wagon laager and had a pyre built of saddles to burn himself if the camp were stormed. Jordanes, following Cassiodorus and probably Priscus, gives the impossible figure of 165,000 dead. Aetius did not press the siege; he persuaded Thorismund to return to Toulouse to secure his throne, perhaps to avoid strengthening the Goths too much. Attila withdrew across the Rhine and invaded Italy in 452. The battle has been called one of the decisive battles of world history, but modern scholars stress that Attila's power was not broken by it: it was rather an inconclusive defence that demonstrated Aetius's diplomacy and the dependence of the western empire on its federates.
battle_of_the_catalaunian_plains.debate: The site is unknown; candidates include Montgueux near Troyes and Châlons-en-Champagne. The date of 20 June is not certain.
scholarship: Maenchen-Helfen, The World of the Huns (1973)
Kelly, Attila the Hun (2008)
Kim, The Huns (2016)
Hughes, Patricius: The Life and Times of Flavius Aetius (2012)
Bury, History of the Later Roman Empire I (1923)

council_of_chalcedon_451.detail: The Second Council of Ephesus of 449, dominated by Dioscorus of Alexandria, had restored Eutyches, deposed Flavian of Constantinople, who died after rough treatment, and refused to read the Tome of Leo; Leo called it a latrocinium, a robbery. After Theodosius's death, Marcian and Pulcheria summoned a new council, first to Nicaea and then to Chalcedon, close enough for imperial control. It met in the church of St Euphemia from 8 October to 1 November 451, with some 500 bishops, nearly all eastern, under the presidency of imperial commissioners; papal legates attended. In the first session the acts of Ephesus II were read and Dioscorus was condemned, and in the third he was deposed for disobedience. The Tome of Leo was read and acclaimed with the cry 'Peter has spoken through Leo; Cyril taught thus'. Under imperial pressure the bishops agreed in the fifth session on a definition of faith confessing one and the same Christ 'in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation', the distinction of natures not being removed by the union, with each nature preserving its property and coming together in one person and one hypostasis. The council also passed canons, among them canon 28, which gave Constantinople privileges equal to Rome's as the New Rome and jurisdiction over the dioceses of Pontus, Asia and Thrace; Leo's legates protested and the pope refused to ratify it. Chalcedon, counted as the Fourth Ecumenical Council, became the touchstone of orthodoxy in Rome and Constantinople, but Egypt, much of Syria and Armenia rejected it as Nestorian. The resulting division into Chalcedonian and anti-Chalcedonian (Miaphysite) churches dominated imperial religious politics for two centuries, through the Henotikon, the Three Chapters and monoenergism.
scholarship: Price & Gaddis, The Acts of the Council of Chalcedon (2005)
Gray, The Defense of Chalcedon in the East 451-553 (1979)
Frend, The Rise of the Monophysite Movement (1972)
Price and Gaddis, The Acts of the Council of Chalcedon (2005)
Grillmeier, Christ in Christian Tradition II.1 (1987)

siege_of_aquileia_452.detail: In spring 452 Attila, frustrated in Gaul, crossed the Julian Alps into Italy, which Aetius had left undefended. The first target was Aquileia, the great port and fortress at the head of the Adriatic, one of the largest cities of Italy with a mint and the seat of a bishop. The Huns besieged it for about three months. Jordanes and Procopius tell that Attila was about to abandon the siege when he saw storks carrying their young away from the city, interpreted it as an omen that the city was doomed, and ordered a final assault, which succeeded. Aquileia was destroyed so thoroughly, Jordanes says, that hardly a trace of it remained; this is an exaggeration, since the city continued as a bishopric, but it never recovered its earlier importance. Later Venetian legend made refugees from Aquileia and other mainland cities the founders of settlements in the lagoons, such as Grado and Torcello, where the patriarch of Aquileia later took refuge from the Lombards. After Aquileia the Huns took Concordia, Altinum, Patavium, Vicetia, Verona, Brixia, Bergamum, Mediolanum and Ticinum; at Milan, the Suda says, Attila saw a painting of Roman emperors with Scythians at their feet and had a painter show himself with the emperors pouring out gold at his feet. Famine and disease weakened his army, Marcian sent troops across the Danube to attack the Hunnic homeland, and an eastern army under another Aetius reached Italy. These factors, as much as the embassy of Pope Leo, explain Attila's withdrawal. The destruction of Aquileia marked the end of its role as the principal city of north-eastern Italy, a role inherited by Cividale and later Venice.
scholarship: Kelly, Attila the Hun (2008)
Maenchen-Helfen, The World of the Huns (1973)

meeting_of_leo_and_attila_452.detail: After the sack of the cities of the Po valley in summer 452, the western court sent an embassy to Attila, encamped near the Mincio close to Mantua: the former consul and prefect Gennadius Avienus, the former prefect Trygetius, an experienced negotiator who had made the treaty of 435 with the Vandals, and Pope Leo I. The embassy secured Attila's withdrawal from Italy. Prosper, a member of Leo's household, gives the credit to the pope: Attila received the envoys and was so pleased by the presence of the high priest that he promised peace and withdrew beyond the Danube. Jordanes, following Priscus, adds that Attila's advisers warned him of the fate of Alaric, who had died soon after taking Rome. Later hagiography, embodied in Raphael's fresco in the Vatican, has the apostles Peter and Paul appear in the sky with swords threatening Attila. Hydatius, a contemporary in Spain, gives a different account: famine and plague were destroying the Huns, and auxiliaries sent by Marcian under a general named Aetius had attacked them in Italy and their homeland, forcing withdrawal. Modern historians combine the factors: the Hunnic army, unable to besiege Rome after a long campaign, was suffering from disease and lack of supplies in a land that had suffered famine in 451, and the eastern counter-offensive threatened its base, so the embassy offered a face-saving agreement, probably with payments. The episode became central to papal prestige: Leo's intervention, with his reported negotiation with Gaiseric in 455, established the bishop of Rome as the city's defender, a role later claimed by Gregory the Great.
meeting_of_leo_and_attila_452.debate: Classic case of competing explanations: papal prestige (Prosper), logistics and disease (Hydatius), and Attila's fear of Alaric's fate after taking Rome (Jordanes).
scholarship: Kelly, Attila the Hun (2008)
Wessel, Leo the Great and the Spiritual Rebuilding of a Universal Rome (2008)

death_of_attila_453.detail: Attila died in early 453, probably in his residence in the Hungarian plain, after a feast celebrating his marriage to a young woman named Ildico, one of many wives. Jordanes, quoting Priscus, says that he drank heavily, lay down on his back, and suffered a haemorrhage from the nose that choked him in his sleep; in the morning his attendants broke down the door and found him dead and the bride weeping beneath her veil. Marcellinus Comes, writing in the sixth century, records a rumour that Ildico stabbed him; the later Germanic legend of Kriemhild or Gudrun avenging her kin on Atli developed from this. The funeral described by Jordanes followed steppe custom: horsemen rode around his body lying in state in a silk tent, singing a funeral song which Jordanes paraphrases; the warriors cut their hair and slashed their faces so that the greatest of warriors should be mourned not with women's tears but with men's blood. He was buried at night in three coffins of gold, silver and iron, with weapons and treasure, and the workers who dug the grave were killed so that it would never be found. Priscus also reports that Marcian dreamed on the same night of a broken bow. Attila's death led quickly to the break-up of his empire. His sons Ellac, Dengizich and Ernak quarrelled over the inheritance, and the subject peoples led by Ardaric of the Gepids rebelled and defeated them at the Nedao in 454. Within twenty years the Hunnic empire had disappeared, and the peoples it had ruled, Ostrogoths, Gepids, Rugi, Sciri and Heruli, became the new powers of the Danube and Italy.
death_of_attila_453.debate: Marcellinus Comes records a rumour that Ildico stabbed him; the strava funeral chant in Jordanes is often taken as authentic Priscan material.
scholarship: Kelly, Attila the Hun (2008)
Maenchen-Helfen, The World of the Huns (1973)
Kim, The Huns (2016)

murder_of_aetius_454.detail: Flavius Aetius had dominated the western empire for twenty years, as magister militum and patricius, holding three consulships (432, 437, 446) and defending Gaul with Hunnic and federate troops. By 454 his position seemed secure: he had persuaded Valentinian III to betroth his younger daughter Placidia to Aetius's son Gaudentius, linking the general's family to the dynasty. This alarmed the court, especially the senator Petronius Maximus and the eunuch primicerius sacri cubiculi Heraclius, who persuaded Valentinian that Aetius intended to kill him. On 21 or 22 September 454, during a meeting in the palace at Rome to discuss finances, Valentinian, aged 35, accused Aetius of treason, drew his sword, and with Heraclius cut him down. The praetorian prefect Boethius, a friend of Aetius, was killed at the same time. Sidonius Apollinaris, Prosper and Procopius tell the story with variations; Procopius has a courtier tell Valentinian afterwards that he had cut off his right hand with his left. The murder deprived the West of its most capable general and its links to the federate peoples. It brought about Valentinian's own death six months later, when two of Aetius's bucellarii, Optila and Thraustila, killed him on the Campus Martius at Petronius Maximus's instigation. With the end of the Theodosian dynasty in 455 the western empire entered its final phase of short-lived emperors controlled by generals such as Ricimer. The Vandals, whose treaty of 442 depended on the betrothal of Huneric to Eudocia, felt released from their obligations and sacked Rome in 455.
murder_of_aetius_454.debate: The trigger was Aetius's push to marry his son Gaudentius to Valentinian's daughter Placidia. Petronius Maximus and Heraclius are said to have stoked the emperor's fear.
scholarship: Stickler, Aëtius (2002)
Hughes, Aetius: Attila's Nemesis (2012)

battle_of_nedao.detail: After Attila's death, his sons, whom Jordanes describes as dividing the peoples among themselves like household slaves, fought over the succession. Ardaric, king of the Gepids and one of Attila's most trusted subordinates, led a revolt of the subject peoples. The decisive battle was fought in 454 at the river Nedao in Pannonia, whose location is unknown. Jordanes describes a remarkable spectacle: Goths fighting with pikes, Gepids with swords, Rugi breaking spears in their wounds, Suebi on foot, Huns with bows, Alans with heavy armour, Heruli with light weapons. The Gepids and their allies won; Attila's eldest son Ellac was killed with some 30,000 Huns and their allies. The battle broke Hunnic power in central Europe. The Gepids took over the Hungarian plain east of the Danube and Dacia, with their centre at Sirmium in the sixth century. The Ostrogoths, whose participation in the battle is unclear, received land as federates in Pannonia from Marcian, under the brothers Valamir, Thiudimir and Vidimir. Other groups, Sciri, Rugi, Heruli and Alans, were settled in the Danube provinces or moved into Roman service. The surviving Huns under Dengizich and Ernak retreated east towards the Black Sea steppe, where Dengizich was killed in 469. The Nedao thus marks the transition from the Hunnic empire to the successor kingdoms of the Danube, from which Theodoric's Ostrogoths and Odoacer's following would emerge to rule Italy. The Gepids, as the winners, remained a significant power until they were destroyed by the Lombards and Avars in 567. Jordanes, himself of Gothic-Alan descent, is the only narrative source.
battle_of_nedao.debate: Location (perhaps a tributary of the Sava in Pannonia) and exact date (454 or 455) are uncertain; the Ostrogoths may have fought on either side.
scholarship: Heather, Empires and Barbarians (2009)
Kim, The Huns (2016)
Wolfram, History of the Goths (1988)

assassination_of_valentinian_iii_455.detail: Petronius Maximus, a senator of great wealth who had held two consulships and the urban and praetorian prefectures, had helped persuade Valentinian III to murder Aetius in 454. Disappointed of the position of patricius that he hoped to inherit, Maximus approached two of Aetius's former bodyguards, the Huns or Goths Optila and Thraustila, now in the emperor's guard, and encouraged them to avenge their master. On 16 March 455, as Valentinian rode to the Campus Martius to watch athletic exercises near the Two Laurels, Optila struck him on the temple and Thraustila killed the eunuch Heraclius; the emperor's guards did not intervene, and the killers took the imperial diadem and robe to Maximus. The assassination ended the Theodosian dynasty in the West after 76 years. Valentinian was 35 and left two daughters, Eudocia, betrothed to Huneric, and Placidia, married to the senator Olybrius. The next day, the army and Senate proclaimed Petronius Maximus emperor. He forced Valentinian's widow Licinia Eudoxia to marry him and married his son Palladius to Eudocia, breaking the Vandal engagement. Procopius says that Eudoxia, outraged, appealed to Gaiseric for help. Whether or not this is true, Gaiseric seized the pretext and his fleet appeared at Portus at the end of May 455. Maximus, who had reigned less than three months, fled and was killed by the crowd or by soldiers on 31 May. The assassination of Valentinian and the Vandal sack together mark the beginning of the end for the western empire: the following twenty-one years saw nine emperors, mostly puppets of generals, and the shrinking of the western state to Italy.
scholarship: Mathisen, 'Petronius Maximus', De Imperatoribus Romanis (online)
Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)

vandal_sack_of_rome_455.detail: Gaiseric's fleet landed at Portus at the end of May 455, using as a pretext the breaking of the engagement between his son Huneric and Valentinian's daughter Eudocia, and perhaps responding to an appeal from Licinia Eudoxia. The emperor Petronius Maximus panicked and fled, and was killed on 31 May by a mob or by imperial servants who stoned him or tore him apart. On 2 June the Vandals entered Rome without resistance. According to Prosper, Pope Leo I met Gaiseric outside the gates and persuaded him to refrain from burning, torture and murder; the account may be an embellishment parallel to Leo's meeting with Attila. The sack lasted fourteen days, much longer than Alaric's three days in 410, and was systematic. The Vandals removed the treasures of the imperial palace, half the gilded bronze roof tiles of the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus, statues, and, according to Procopius, the treasures of the Temple of Jerusalem brought to Rome by Titus, which Belisarius later recovered at Carthage and Justinian returned to Jerusalem. They took thousands of captives to Africa, among them Licinia Eudoxia and her daughters Eudocia and Placidia; Eudocia married Huneric and became mother of Hilderic. Bishop Deogratias of Carthage sold church plate to ransom captives and housed them in two basilicas. The term vandalism, coined by the Abbé Grégoire in 1794, has unfairly fixed the Vandals' reputation: the sack was a plunder for wealth, not a wanton destruction. Politically, it destroyed what remained of western prestige, gave Gaiseric hostages from the imperial family, and led to the Visigothic-backed proclamation of Avitus in Gaul in July 455.
vandal_sack_of_rome_455.debate: Procopius's claim that Eudoxia invited Gaiseric to avenge her husband is likely gossip. The Temple spoils' later fate is legendary.
scholarship: Merrills and Miles, The Vandals (2010)
Steinacher, Die Vandalen (2016)

accession_of_leo_i_457.debate: Whether Leo's was the first patriarchal coronation is disputed; De Ceremoniis describes a military raising on the shield with the patriarch present.

destruction_of_majorians_fleet_460.debate: Procopius's tale that Majorian dyed his hair and visited Carthage in disguise as his own envoy is folklore.

battle_of_cape_bon.detail: In 468 Leo I and the western emperor Anthemius, whom Leo had sent to Italy in 467, launched a combined assault on the Vandal kingdom, the most ambitious military undertaking of the fifth century. Three forces converged on Africa: Marcellinus, the independent ruler of Dalmatia, cleared Sardinia of Vandals; Heraclius of Edessa landed in Tripolitania and advanced overland; and the main fleet under Leo's brother-in-law Basiliscus sailed from Constantinople. John Lydus, a well-placed official, says the expedition cost 65,000 lb of gold and 700,000 lb of silver, an amount that crippled the eastern treasury for years; Procopius speaks of 100,000 men and over 1,100 ships, figures that should not be taken literally. Basiliscus anchored off Promunturium Mercurii (Cape Bon), some 60 km from Carthage, and instead of attacking at once granted Gaiseric's request for a five-day truce to consider terms. Gaiseric used the time to prepare fireships and wait for a favourable wind. When it came, the Vandals towed burning hulks into the crowded Roman fleet at night, and in the confusion attacked with their warships. Much of the fleet was burned or sunk; the general John, rather than be captured by Gaiseric's son Genso, leapt into the sea in full armour. Basiliscus fled to Sicily and returned to Constantinople, where he took sanctuary in Hagia Sophia; Procopius alleges that Aspar had bribed him to fail, so that Leo's power would not be strengthened. Marcellinus was murdered in Sicily soon afterwards, possibly at Ricimer's instigation. The disaster ended the last realistic chance of recovering Africa for the West and with it the fiscal base on which a revived western empire might have rested. In 474 Zeno concluded the 'endless peace' with Gaiseric.
battle_of_cape_bon.debate: Procopius's figures for the fleet are exaggerated; John Lydus's cost figures, though precise, may also be inflated. Aspar's alleged sabotage is uncertain.
scholarship: Merrills and Miles, The Vandals (2010)
Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)
Courtois, Les Vandales et l'Afrique (1955)

battle_of_deols_469.debate: Whether Riothamus's Britons came from Britain or from Armorica is debated; his identification with a historical Arthur (Ashe) has little support.

scholarship: MacGeorge, Late Roman Warlords (2002)
Anders, Flavius Ricimer (2010)

usurpation_of_basiliscus_475.detail: A great fire in 475 destroyed the Basilica library (said to have held 120,000 books, including a 120-foot dragon-gut copy of Homer) and the Lauseion palace with its famous collection of Greek statues.

battle_of_placentia_476.detail: In 475 the patrician Orestes, a Roman from Pannonia who had been Attila's secretary and then a general in Italy, drove the emperor Julius Nepos from Ravenna to Dalmatia and on 31 October proclaimed his own young son Romulus emperor. Orestes's power rested on the federate troops of the Italian army, Heruli, Sciri, Rugi and Turcilingi, many of whom had come from the former Hunnic empire. In 476 they demanded land, a third of the estates of Italy according to Procopius, under the system that had been applied to federates in Gaul. Orestes refused. The soldiers turned to Odoacer, son of Edeco (perhaps the Edeco of the embassy of 449) and a former officer of Anthemius's guard, who promised them what they asked. Proclaimed king by the troops on 23 August 476, Odoacer marched against Orestes, who took refuge in Ticinum (Pavia); the city was taken and sacked, and Orestes fled to Placentia, where he was captured and executed on 28 August 476. His brother Paulus was killed at Ravenna, in the Pineta near Classe, on 4 September. Odoacer then entered Ravenna and deposed Romulus. The episode was thus a mutiny of the federate army over the terms of its maintenance, not a barbarian invasion. Odoacer's settlement of his followers, apparently by allocating a third of land or of tax revenues, was carried out by the Roman praetorian prefect Liberius's predecessors and continued by Theodoric. The battle and its aftermath are recorded mostly in brief annals, the Fasti Vindobonenses and the Anonymus Valesianus, which give precise dates; later narrative sources such as Procopius and Jordanes provide the land claim and the background.
scholarship: MacGeorge, Late Roman Warlords (2002)
Halsall, Barbarian Migrations and the Roman West (2007)
Goffart, Barbarians and Romans (1980)

deposition_of_romulus_augustulus_476.detail: After defeating Orestes, Odoacer entered Ravenna on 4 September 476 and deposed his son Romulus, whom contemporaries mockingly called Augustulus, the little Augustus. The Anonymus Valesianus says Odoacer spared him because of his youth and beauty, gave him an annual pension of 6,000 solidi, and sent him to live with his relatives in Campania, at the Castellum Lucullanum on the bay of Naples, where a letter of Cassiodorus may show him alive in 507-511. Odoacer did not take the imperial title. Malchus records that the Roman Senate sent an embassy to Zeno saying that one emperor was enough for both parts and that Odoacer, a man of political and military skill, should govern Italy with the title of patricius; the imperial insignia were returned to Constantinople. At the same time Julius Nepos, deposed in 475 but still recognised by Zeno, sent his own envoys from Dalmatia; Zeno told the senators that they should take back Nepos, and Odoacer struck coins in Nepos's name until his murder in 480. Marcellinus Comes, writing in Constantinople around 518, made 476 the end of the western empire: 'the western empire of the Roman people, which Octavian Augustus first began to rule in the 709th year from the foundation of the city, perished with this Augustulus'. Jordanes and later Procopius echoed this. For contemporaries in Italy the change was less dramatic: the Senate, the consulship, the prefecture and the Roman administration continued under Odoacer and Theodoric. Modern historians debate whether 476 marks a real break, as Heather and Ward-Perkins argue in terms of the end of the western state, or merely a symbolic one in a long transformation, as the 'late antiquity' school maintains.
deposition_of_romulus_augustulus_476.debate: Whether the 'Romulus' of Cassiodorus Variae 3.35 is the former emperor is uncertain.
scholarship: Croke, 'AD 476: the manufacture of a turning point', Chiron 13 (1983)
Ward-Perkins, The Fall of Rome and the End of Civilization (2005)
Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)
Halsall, Barbarian Migrations and the Roman West (2007)
Goffart, Barbarian Tides (2006)
Kaldellis, The New Roman Empire (2023)

murder_of_julius_nepos_480.debate: For legitimists, Nepos's death, not 476, ended the line of western emperors.

hunerics_persecution_484.debate: Victor is a partisan exile writing to rouse Constantinople; the Notitia provinciarum et civitatum Africae lists 466 bishops summoned in 484.

revolt_of_illus_484.debate: Illus courted pagan intellectuals like the philosopher Pamprepius, whose oracles promised a pagan restoration; Pamprepius was executed in 488.

battle_of_soissons_486.detail: After the death of Aegidius in 465, his son Syagrius ruled a remnant of Roman Gaul between the Somme and the Loire from Soissons, styled by Gregory of Tours 'king of the Romans', a title probably given to him by the Franks. Clovis, who had succeeded his father Childeric as king of the Salian Franks of Tournai in 481 or 482, challenged him in 486 or 487, together with his relative Ragnachar of Cambrai. Gregory, writing a century later, says simply that Clovis defeated Syagrius in battle and that Syagrius fled to Alaric II at Toulouse; Clovis demanded his surrender, and the Visigoths, fearing the Franks, handed him over in chains. Clovis had him secretly killed. The famous story of the vase of Soissons belongs to the aftermath: Clovis asked his warriors to give him a precious vessel from a church, which he had promised to return to the bishop, Remigius; one warrior struck it with his axe, saying the king should only receive his share by lot. A year later Clovis split the man's skull at a review with the words 'thus you did to the vase at Soissons'. The battle gave Clovis control of northern Gaul as far as the Seine and later the Loire, with its Roman administrative structures and the cities of Soissons, Reims and Paris, which became his capital. The extent and nature of Syagrius's realm are debated: some see it as a substantial Roman state, others as a modest local lordship magnified by Gregory. Clovis's expansion from Tournai into the Roman heartland of northern Gaul made the Franks heirs to the provincial administration and the Gallo-Roman church, paving the way for his conversion and the battle of Vouillé.
battle_of_soissons_486.debate: Gregory's date (Clovis's fifth year, 486 or 487) depends on an uncertain chronology; the 'kingdom of Soissons' may be largely a literary construct.
scholarship: James, The Franks (1988)
Wood, The Merovingian Kingdoms 450-751 (1994)
MacGeorge, Late Roman Warlords (2002)

evacuation_of_noricum_488.debate: Eugippius's Life is a vivid picture of a frontier province fending for itself, but archaeology shows continuing Romance-speaking populations in Noricum afterward.
scholarship: Thompson, Romans and Barbarians: The Decline of the Western Empire (1982)

battle_of_the_isonzo_489.debate: The size of Theodoric's following is guesswork; Procopius gives no number.

sources.w: Cause of the Foundation of the Schools

siege_of_ravenna_490.detail: Theodoric entered Italy in 489 as Zeno's agent against Odoacer and won battles on the Isonzo and at Verona. In 490 Odoacer's general Tufa defected and then returned to him; Odoacer retook Milan and besieged Theodoric in Pavia, but with Visigothic help Theodoric won on the Adda on 11 August 490 and blockaded Odoacer in Ravenna. The city, protected by marshes and lagoons, was nearly impregnable from land. A night sortie by Odoacer's Heruli on 10 July 491 against Theodoric's camp in the Pineta, the pine woods near Classe, was repulsed with heavy losses. From August 492 Theodoric used ships from Rimini to blockade the port of Classe, cutting supplies, and famine struck the city, where a modius of wheat cost six solidi. On 25 February 493, through the mediation of Bishop John of Ravenna, the two kings agreed to share rule over Italy; Odoacer handed over his son Thela as a hostage, and Theodoric entered Ravenna on 5 March. Ten days later, on 15 March, Theodoric killed Odoacer with his own hands at a banquet in the palace of the Laurel, cutting him from collarbone to hip, and said, according to John of Antioch, 'there was not a bone in this wretched man'. Theodoric justified the act by claiming that Odoacer had plotted against him. Odoacer's brother, wife and son were also killed, and his soldiers massacred throughout Italy. Theodoric then took the title of king (rex) and ruled Italy for 33 years, nominally as Zeno's representative. The siege established the Ostrogothic kingdom and made Ravenna the Gothic capital, the setting of Theodoric's great building programme.
scholarship: Moorhead, Theoderic in Italy (1992)
Wolfram, History of the Goths (1988)
Arnold, Theoderic and the Roman Imperial Restoration (2014)

accession_of_anastasius_i_491.detail: Zeno died on 9 April 491 without a son, his only son Leo II having died in 474 and his other son Zeno before him. His brother Longinus, consul in 486 and 490, hoped to succeed. The ceremony book of Constantine VII preserves, from the sixth-century official Peter the Patrician, a detailed account of the selection. The high officials and the Senate, meeting in the palace, agreed with the patriarch Euphemius to let the empress Ariadne choose. The people in the Hippodrome chanted 'an orthodox emperor for the world' and 'a Roman emperor', a rejection of another Isaurian. Ariadne chose Anastasius, a silentiarius of about sixty from Dyrrachium, known for his piety and his miaphysite sympathies, whom she married on 20 May. Before his coronation on 11 April, Euphemius made him sign a written promise not to alter the faith of Chalcedon. Anastasius was crowned in the Hippodrome, appearing in the kathisma, raised on a shield, crowned with a torque by a military officer, then given the diadem by the patriarch. Anastasius's reign of 27 years was one of the most successful in eastern Roman history. He expelled the Isaurians from the capital and fought the Isaurian war of 492-497, reformed the copper coinage (498), abolished the chrysargyron tax on trade, replaced compulsory deliveries with cash payment (coemptio), and left a reserve of 320,000 lb of gold in the treasury. But his miaphysite sympathies caused riots in Constantinople (512) and the revolt of Vitalian (513-515). His accession ceremony is the first for which a detailed protocol survives.
scholarship: Haarer, Anastasius I: Politics and Empire in the Late Roman World (2006)
Meier, Anastasios I (2009)

baptism_of_clovis.detail: Clovis, king of the Franks, had married around 493 the Burgundian princess Clotilde, a Catholic, while most Germanic rulers, including her own uncle Gundobad, were Arians. Gregory of Tours tells that Clotilde urged him to convert and that their first son, baptised, died, confirming Clovis's suspicion of her god. During a battle against the Alamanni, traditionally at Tolbiac (Zülpich), facing defeat, Clovis prayed to the god of Clotilde and promised to be baptised if he won. He won, and was instructed by Bishop Remigius of Reims and baptised with more than 3,000 of his warriors on a Christmas Day; Remigius told him 'bow your head, proud Sicambrian; adore what you have burned and burn what you have adored'. Gregory places the baptism in 496, after Clovis's fifth year, but the chronology is uncertain. A letter from Avitus of Vienne congratulating Clovis, which mentions his sister's conversion from Arianism, has led many scholars to place the baptism around 508, after Vouillé, and possibly at Tours. Others argue for c. 500 or 503. There is also debate whether Clovis was first attracted to Arianism, as his sister Lantechild had been. Whatever the date, the choice of Catholic over Arian Christianity was momentous. It allied the Franks with the Gallo-Roman bishops and aristocracy, who controlled the cities, and set them apart from the Arian Goths and Burgundians. Gregory presents Clovis as a new Constantine, and the Vouillé campaign as a crusade against heretics. The Franks became the main Catholic power of the West and later allies of the papacy. Later tradition invented the Holy Ampulla brought by a dove for the anointing, used at French coronations until 1825.
baptism_of_clovis.debate: Date debated: 496 (Gregory), c. 500, or 508 (from Avitus's letter).
scholarship: Wood, The Merovingian Kingdoms 450-751 (1994)
Shanzer, 'Dating the baptism of Clovis', Early Medieval Europe 7 (1998)
Wood, 'Gregory of Tours and Clovis', Revue belge de philologie et d'histoire 63 (1985)
Wood, The Merovingian Kingdoms (1994)

battle_of_tolbiac.debate: Gregory does not name Tolbiac in 2.30 (the name comes from 2.37 on Sigibert the Lame); there may have been two Alamannic wars (c. 496 and 506), and the conversion parallel with Constantine is a literary construct.

theodoric_recognized_497.debate: How far Theodoric was a Roman magistrate, a client king or a sovereign is the key question in modern accounts (Moorhead, Heather, Arnold).
scholarship: Moorhead, Theoderic in Italy (1992)
Arnold, Theoderic and the Roman Imperial Restoration (2014)

follis_reform_498.debate: A heavier follis followed in 512; the reform may have imitated coinage already struck in Ostrogothic Italy and Vandal Africa.
scholarship: Grierson, Byzantine Coins (1982)
Hendy, Studies in the Byzantine Monetary Economy c.300-1450 (1985)

battle_of_mount_badon.debate: Date (c. 480-520), site and the participants are all uncertain; Arthur's association is not contemporary. Included for completeness of sub-Roman Britain.

sources.w: Ecclesiastical History of the English People

edictum_theoderici.debate: Piero Rasi argued in 1953 that it was issued by the Visigothic king Theoderic II in Gaul; the question is unresolved.

scholarship: Greatrex, Rome and Persia at War 502-532 (1998)

anastasian_wall.debate: Date uncertain (c. 497-507); some argue for an earlier Theodosian or Leonine origin.
scholarship: Crow, 'The Anastasian Wall and the Lower Danube frontier', in Poulter (ed.), The Transition to Late Antiquity (2007)

breviary_of_alaric_506.debate: Issued months before Vouillé, perhaps to win Roman and Catholic loyalty against Clovis.

battle_of_vouille.detail: By 506 Clovis, ruler of northern Gaul, and Alaric II, king of the Visigoths of Toulouse, faced each other across the Loire. Theodoric, who was married to Clovis's sister Audofleda and whose daughter Theodegotha was Alaric's wife, wrote letters, preserved in Cassiodorus's Variae, urging both to keep the peace and appealing to the kings of the Burgundians, Heruli, Warni and Thuringians to join a coalition against aggression. Alaric tried to win his Catholic subjects with the Breviary (506) and the Council of Agde. In 507 Clovis, with the support of the Burgundians under Gundobad's son Sigismund and of Anastasius, who sent a fleet to raid southern Italy and prevent Theodoric's intervention, attacked. Gregory of Tours presents the campaign as a holy war against Arian heretics: Clovis said 'it grieves me that these Arians hold part of Gaul'. The armies met at the Campus Vogladensis, ten miles from Poitiers, in spring or summer 507. The Visigoths were defeated and Clovis killed Alaric with his own hand; Gregory adds that Clovis was saved from two Gothic spearmen by his armour and his horse. The Arvernian contingent, led by Sidonius Apollinaris's son Apollinaris, fought on the Visigothic side. Clovis wintered in Bordeaux and took the treasure at Toulouse in 508. The Visigoths lost all of Gaul except Septimania, which Theodoric's army saved in 508 by relieving Arles, and the Visigothic kingdom moved its centre to Spain, eventually at Toledo. The site of the battle is debated, with candidates including Vouillé and Voulon. In 508 Clovis received from Anastasius an honorary consulship at Tours. The victory made the Franks the dominant power in Gaul.
battle_of_vouille.debate: The site (Vouillé or Voulon) and the role of Byzantine diplomacy are debated.
scholarship: Mathisen & Shanzer (eds.), The Battle of Vouillé, 507 CE (2012)
Mathisen and Shanzer (eds.), The Battle of Vouillé, 507 CE (2012)
Wood, The Merovingian Kingdoms (1994)

consulship_of_clovis_508.debate: What exact title Anastasius granted is unclear: honorary consul, patricius, or something else; Clovis does not appear in the consular fasti.

scholarship: Wood, The Merovingian Kingdoms (1994)

naval_battle_of_constantinople_515.debate: Not Greek fire, which appeared c. 672; the Proclus here is a different man from the Neoplatonist (d. 485). Malalas's account mixes the miraculous with the technical.

accession_of_justin_i_518.detail: Anastasius died on the night of 9-10 July 518, aged about 88, without having designated a successor, although his nephews Hypatius, Pompeius and Probus were well placed. The account in Constantine VII's De Ceremoniis, derived from Peter the Patrician, describes the confusion of the following day. In the Hippodrome the people waited while the senators and officials deliberated in the palace. The excubitors proposed a tribune named John, who was rejected by the Blues; the scholarians proposed the general Patricius, who was nearly killed by the excubitors. Justin, commander of the excubitors, an elderly illiterate Thracian peasant from Bederiana near Naissus who had come to Constantinople as a young man and risen through the guard, was finally accepted by the Senate and the army. Evagrius and Procopius allege that the grand chamberlain Amantius gave Justin money to buy the votes of the guards for his own candidate, Theocritus, and that Justin used it for himself. Justin was crowned in the Hippodrome, raised on a shield and crowned with a torque before the patriarch John placed the diadem on his head. His reign marked a decisive change in religious policy: within days crowds in Hagia Sophia demanded the proclamation of Chalcedon, and in 519 Justin ended the Acacian schism with Rome on the terms of Pope Hormisdas. Amantius and Theocritus were executed. Vitalian was recalled and made consul, then murdered in 520, probably on the orders of Justin's nephew Justinian, who became the real power in government. Procopius's Secret History mocks Justin as illiterate, signing documents with a stencil, a story often doubted.
accession_of_justin_i_518.debate: Procopius's Secret History says Justin was illiterate and signed with a stencil; this is hostile caricature but possibly rooted in fact. Anastasius left 320,000 lbs of gold in the treasury (Procopius, Secret History 19.7).
scholarship: Vasiliev, Justin the First (1950)
Croke, 'Justinian under Justin', BZ 100 (2007)

execution_of_boethius_524.debate: Was there a real senatorial conspiracy, or did Theodoric's growing paranoia, sharpened by Justin's anti-Arian measures, drive the trials? Cassiodorus, Boethius's successor as magister officiorum, stayed silent.
scholarship: Moorhead, Theoderic in Italy (1992)
Chadwick, Boethius (1981)
Harrison, A Temple for Byzantium (1989)
Bardill, 'A new temple for Byzantium', in Bowden et al. (eds.), Social and Political Life in Late Antiquity (2006)

massacre_of_najran_and_aksumite_invasion.debate: Dates of the Najran massacre (518 or 523) and the invasion (525 or later) are debated.
scholarship: Bowersock, The Throne of Adulis (2013)

earthquake_of_antioch_526.debate: Malalas's death toll is surely exaggerated, but the disaster was real and contributed to Antioch's sixth-century decline alongside 540 and the plague.

death_of_theodoric_526.detail: Theodoric died at Ravenna on 30 August 526, after a reign of 33 years in Italy, the last few marked by crisis. The end of the Acacian schism in 519 removed the religious barrier between the Roman Senate and Constantinople and weakened the Arian king's position; the accusations of treasonable correspondence with the eastern court led to the executions of Boethius in 524 and Symmachus in 525. In 523 the Vandal king Hilderic had broken with Theodoric's sister Amalafrida and killed her Gothic guard, and in 525-526 Justin's anti-Arian measures in the East led Theodoric to send Pope John I to Constantinople, who died in prison on his return. The Anonymus Valesianus says that Theodoric had just ordered that Arians should take over Catholic churches when he died of dysentery, a divine judgement in the Catholic author's view; Procopius tells that he was served a large fish head at dinner, which he saw as the face of Symmachus threatening him, and died of the shock and grief. The succession was difficult. His only son-in-law and intended heir, Eutharic, had died in 522 or 523, and the throne passed to his ten-year-old grandson Athalaric under the regency of Theodoric's daughter Amalasuntha. Theodoric was buried in the mausoleum he had built outside the walls of Ravenna, with its 230-tonne monolithic dome; his remains were later removed, perhaps after the Byzantine reconquest. In Germanic legend he became Dietrich von Bern (Verona). Historians see his reign as a successful attempt to preserve Roman government and culture in Italy alongside a Gothic army, a balance that his death dissolved.
scholarship: Moorhead, Theoderic in Italy (1992)
Arnold, Theoderic and the Roman Imperial Restoration (2014)
Wiemer, Theoderich der Grosse (2018)

accession_of_justinian_527.detail: Justinian, born Petrus Sabbatius around 482 at Tauresium near Bederiana in Dardania, was the nephew of Justin I, who brought him to Constantinople and had him educated. During his uncle's reign he held the posts of comes domesticorum and magister militum praesentalis, was consul in 521, when he gave spectacular games, and was made nobilissimus and Caesar. He married Theodora, a former actress, around 525, after Justin changed the law forbidding senators to marry actresses. On 1 April 527 the aged and sick Justin crowned him co-emperor, and Theodora Augusta, in the palace; when Justin died on 1 August 527 Justinian became sole ruler. His reign of 38 years transformed the empire. In law, he commissioned the Code (529, 534), the Digest and Institutes (533) and issued the Novels. In war, his generals Belisarius and Narses reconquered Africa from the Vandals (533-534), Italy from the Ostrogoths (535-554) and part of southern Spain (552), while the Persian wars (527-532, 540-562) and Balkan invasions strained resources. In building, he rebuilt Hagia Sophia after the Nika riots, and Procopius's Buildings lists hundreds of churches, forts and aqueducts. In religion, he sought to unify Chalcedonians and Miaphysites, condemning the Three Chapters in 553, and persecuted pagans, heretics and Samaritans. His administration, through ministers such as John the Cappadocian and Tribonian, increased tax efficiency at the cost of popular hatred. The plague of 541-542 struck in the middle of his reign. Historians differ in assessing whether his reconquests overextended the empire, leaving his successors with an impossible burden, or represented a feasible restoration of Roman power.
scholarship: Maas (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to the Age of Justinian (2005)
Moorhead, Justinian (1994)
Sarris, Economy and Society in the Age of Justinian (2006)
Meier, Justinian (2004)
Sarris, Justinian: Emperor, Soldier, Saint (2023)

battle_of_mindouos_528.debate: Mindouos and Thannuris may be the same or neighbouring sites.

massacre_of_the_mazdakites_528.debate: Dates range from 524 to 531; much of the story is romance.
