closure_of_the_academy_529.debate: Whether the Academy was formally closed, or starved by confiscation of its endowment, and where the philosophers settled afterward (Harran?) is disputed; the image of 529 as 'the end of ancient philosophy' is exaggerated.
scholarship: Cameron, 'The last days of the Academy at Athens', PCPS 15 (1969)
Watts, City and School in Late Antique Athens and Alexandria (2006)

founding_of_monte_cassino_529.debate: The date 529 is traditional and the only source, Gregory's Dialogues (593/594), is hagiography; some historians question how much of the Rule is Benedict's own.

battle_of_dara.detail: The Iberian war began in 526 over the Persian attempt to impose Zoroastrian practices on Iberia and the construction of Roman forts on the frontier. In June 530 a Persian army under Perozes (Firuz), the mirranes, marched on Dara, the fortress built by Anastasius in 505 near Nisibis. Belisarius, newly appointed magister militum per Orientem, and Hermogenes, magister officiorum, had some 25,000 men; the Persians had about 40,000, later reinforced to 50,000. Belisarius dug a complex system of trenches in front of the city walls, in the shape of a broken line with a recessed centre, with gaps for counter-attacks, positioning his infantry behind the central trench and cavalry on the wings, with Hunnic cavalry under Sunicas and Aigan at the angles, and a detachment of Heruli under Pharas hidden behind a hill on the left. On the first day there were skirmishes and single combats, including one in which the bath attendant Andreas killed two Persian champions. After an exchange of letters, the battle took place on the second day. The Persian right attacked the Roman left and was taken in the flank and rear by Pharas's Heruli; the Persian left, with the elite Immortals, pressed the Roman right but was cut in two by the Hunnic cavalry of Sunicas, who killed the Persian standard-bearer and commander Baresmanas. Some 5,000 Persians died. Procopius, who was present as Belisarius's secretary, gives the most detailed account of the battle in his Wars. Dara was the first major Roman victory over the Persians in generations, and showed the combination of fieldworks, missile cavalry and mobile reserves that characterised the sixth-century Roman army.
scholarship: Greatrex, Rome and Persia at War 502-532 (1998)
Whately, Battles and Generals: Combat, Culture, and Didacticism in Procopius' Wars (2016)
Haldon, The Byzantine Wars (2001)
Syvänne, Military History of Late Rome 518-565 (2021)

battle_of_callinicum.detail: In spring 531 a Persian army of about 15,000 cavalry under Azarethes, with the Lakhmid king al-Mundhir III, crossed the Euphrates at Circesium and advanced northward through Commagene, avoiding the fortified cities of Mesopotamia, to strike at Antioch. Belisarius, with some 20,000 men including the Ghassanid al-Harith and his Arabs, followed and forced them to retreat without battle. The Romans pursued them along the Euphrates. On 19 April 531, Easter Saturday, near Callinicum, Belisarius's troops, impatient for battle, forced their general to attack the Persians against his advice; Procopius says they insulted him, and that fasting soldiers were exhausted. Belisarius drew up his infantry on the left, near the river, with the Arabs on the right. The Persians, concentrating their best troops against the Arabs, broke the Roman right, the Arabs fleeing or, according to Procopius, betraying the Romans. The Roman cavalry fled, and Belisarius dismounted to join the infantry, which formed a shield wall with its back to the river and held until nightfall, when the survivors escaped across the Euphrates to an island and then to Callinicum. Malalas, who had access to the official report, gives a different version, less favourable to Belisarius, in which he fled across the river with his standard while the infantry fought on. A commission of inquiry under the magister militum Constantiolus found Belisarius at fault and he was recalled. Persian losses were also heavy, and Azarethes was disgraced by Kavad for failing to take any city. The battle led to peace negotiations, which were accelerated by Kavad's death later in 531 and concluded with the Eternal Peace in 532.
battle_of_callinicum.debate: Procopius's account exculpates Belisarius; Malalas, using the official report, is more critical.
scholarship: Greatrex, Rome and Persia at War 502-532 (1998)
Shahid, Byzantium and the Arabs in the Sixth Century (1995)
Greatrex and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars II (2002)
Rubin, 'The reforms of Khusro Anushirwan', in Cameron (ed.), The Byzantine and Early Islamic Near East III (1995)

nika_riots_532.detail: The circus factions, the Blues and the Greens, were organisations of fans and performers that had become powerful forces in urban politics across the empire. In January 532, after a riot, the urban prefect Eudaemon condemned several men to death; at the execution on 10 January the scaffold broke twice and two of the condemned, one Blue and one Green, survived and were taken by monks to sanctuary in the church of St Laurentius. At the races of 13 January, the factions asked Justinian for mercy, and when he did not respond, they united with the cry 'Nika' (conquer) and attacked the prefect's praetorium, freeing prisoners and setting fires. Over the following days the rioters burned the Chalke gate of the palace, the Senate house, the church of Hagia Sophia, the baths of Zeuxippus and much of the city centre, demanding the dismissal of John the Cappadocian, the praetorian prefect, Tribonian, the quaestor, and Eudaemon. Justinian dismissed them, but the rioters continued and on 18 January proclaimed Hypatius, nephew of Anastasius, emperor in the Hippodrome. Justinian considered fleeing by sea. Procopius puts into Theodora's mouth a speech arguing that 'royalty is a good burial shroud'. Belisarius and Mundus, with their bucellarii and Herul troops, entered the Hippodrome from two sides while the eunuch Narses bribed the Blues, and massacred the crowd: Procopius says over 30,000 were killed. Hypatius and his brother Pompeius were executed and their bodies thrown into the sea. The riots allowed Justinian to rebuild the city centre and Hagia Sophia, and strengthened his autocracy, as the factions and senatorial opposition were crushed. The ministers he had dismissed were reinstated.
nika_riots_532.debate: Theodora's speech is a Procopian literary construction; the death toll of 30,000-35,000 is a round figure.
scholarship: Greatrex, 'The Nika riot: a reappraisal', JHS 117 (1997)
Cameron, Circus Factions (1976)
Meier, 'Die Inszenierung einer Katastrophe: Justinian und der Nika-Aufstand', ZPE 142 (2003)

hagia_sophia_construction_532.detail: The second church of Hagia Sophia, built by Theodosius II and dedicated in 415, was burned in the Nika riot on 14 January 532. Forty days later, on 23 February 532, Justinian began the construction of a new church on an unprecedented scale. Its designers were Anthemius of Tralles, a mathematician and author of a treatise on burning mirrors, and Isidore of Miletus, a geometer who edited Archimedes; they were not builders in the conventional sense, but theorists of geometry and mechanics. The church combined the longitudinal basilica with a centralised domed structure: a dome of about 31 m in diameter, rising some 55 m above the floor, rested on four massive piers and pendentives, buttressed by two semi-domes to east and west and by smaller exedrae, creating a nave of about 70 by 75 m. A ring of forty windows at the base of the dome made it seem, in Procopius's words, to be suspended from heaven by a golden chain. Some 10,000 workmen are said to have been employed; materials included green marble from Thessaly, porphyry from Egypt, and columns from older buildings. The church was dedicated on 27 December 537, after less than six years, and Justinian is said to have exclaimed, according to a later legend, 'Solomon, I have outdone you'. The dome, too shallow, collapsed partly after earthquakes in 557, on 7 May 558, and was rebuilt higher by Isidore the Younger, the church being rededicated in 562, the occasion of Paul the Silentiary's Ekphrasis. Hagia Sophia remained the largest church in Christendom for nearly a thousand years and served as the model for Ottoman imperial mosques.
scholarship: Mainstone, Hagia Sophia: Architecture, Structure and Liturgy of Justinian's Great Church (1988)
Mark & Çakmak (eds.), Hagia Sophia from the Age of Justinian to the Present (1992)
Mark and Çakmak (eds.), Hagia Sophia from the Age of Justinian to the Present (1992)
Krautheimer, Early Christian and Byzantine Architecture (1986)

sources.w: Narratio de aedificatione templi S. Sophiae

vandal_war_begins_533.detail: After the Eternal Peace of 532 freed the eastern army, Justinian decided to intervene in Africa, where Gelimer had deposed the pro-Roman Hilderic in 530. Procopius reports that the praetorian prefect John the Cappadocian opposed the expedition, recalling the disaster of 468 and the cost and risk of a sea campaign far from home, and that the generals feared it; a bishop's dream promising victory and the prospect of restoring Catholics' rights persuaded the emperor. Revolts in the Vandal provinces helped: Godas, governor of Sardinia, rebelled and asked for Roman support, and Pudentius led a rising in Tripolitania. Gelimer sent his brother Tzazon with 5,000 men and 120 ships to Sardinia, weakening his forces in Africa. Belisarius sailed from Constantinople around the summer solstice of 533 with 10,000 infantry, 5,000 cavalry including his bucellarii, 400 Heruli and 600 Hunnic horse archers, in 500 transport ships with 30,000 sailors and 92 warships, accompanied by his wife Antonina and by Procopius. The voyage was difficult: bread baked insufficiently on John the Cappadocian's orders went mouldy and killed 500 men, and Belisarius executed two Huns for murder at Abydos. The fleet stopped in Sicily, where Amalasuntha's government provided supplies and a market, and where Procopius learned in Syracuse that the Vandals were unaware of the expedition and that Gelimer was away at Hermione. The fleet landed at Caput Vada, about 200 km south of Carthage, in early September. Belisarius insisted on strict discipline toward the inhabitants, presenting the Romans as liberators. The campaign ended Vandal rule in less than a year.
vandal_war_begins_533.debate: Procopius reports mouldy bread from John the Cappadocian's money-saving double-baking, killing 500 men; a hostile anecdote about a man he loathed.
scholarship: Merrills and Miles, The Vandals (2010)
Hughes, Belisarius: The Last Roman General (2009)

battle_of_ad_decimum.detail: After landing at Caput Vada in early September 533, Belisarius marched north along the coast with the fleet following, reaching the tenth milestone from Carthage, Ad Decimum, on 13 September. Gelimer, who had executed Hilderic and his family on hearing of the landing, planned a three-pronged ambush: his brother Ammatas would attack from Carthage, his nephew Gibamund with 2,000 men from the west, and Gelimer himself from the rear. The plan failed through bad coordination. Ammatas, arriving early with a small force, ran into the Roman vanguard under John the Armenian, killed twelve of the best Romans, but was killed in turn, and his men fled. Gibamund's force was destroyed by the Hunnic horse archers on the left flank. Gelimer, advancing between the Roman columns, routed the Roman advance cavalry and was in a position to win, but on finding his brother's body he stopped to mourn and bury him, losing the moment. Belisarius rallied his troops and drove off the Vandals, who fled west toward Numidia. Procopius says that if Gelimer had pressed on, he would have destroyed the Roman army or seized Carthage and the fleet. On 15 September 533 Belisarius entered Carthage unopposed, ate the banquet that had been prepared for Gelimer in the palace, and ensured that the soldiers bought what they needed instead of looting. The Catholic clergy took over the churches of the city, and the fleet entered the harbour of Mandracium. The battle was won with Belisarius's cavalry and bucellarii alone, in confused fighting, and showed the importance of Hunnic horse archers in sixth-century warfare.
battle_of_ad_decimum.debate: Procopius admits Gelimer could have won had he pressed on; Vandal numbers are unknown and modern estimates of the whole Vandal army range from 20,000 to 30,000.
scholarship: Merrills and Miles, The Vandals (2010)
Hughes, Belisarius (2009)
Syvänne, Military History of Late Rome 518-565 (2021)

battle_of_tricamarum.detail: After the defeat at Ad Decimum, Gelimer retired to Bulla Regia in Numidia, bribed Moorish and Punic peasants to kill Romans, and recalled his brother Tzazon, who had recovered Sardinia. Reinforced, the Vandals advanced on Carthage, cutting the aqueduct, and tried to suborn Belisarius's Hunnic allies. In mid-December 533 Belisarius marched out and met them at Tricamarum, about 30 km west of Carthage. Procopius's figures suggest the Vandals outnumbered the Romans; the Romans' infantry arrived late, and the battle was fought by cavalry alone. Gelimer ordered his men to fight only with swords. The Romans under John the Armenian crossed a stream that separated the armies and made three charges against the Vandal centre, where Tzazon was killed. The Vandal army broke; some 800 Vandals and fewer than 50 Romans died. In the evening the Roman infantry attacked the Vandal camp, and Gelimer fled on horseback toward Numidia without warning his men, who abandoned the camp with its women, children and treasure. The Roman soldiers spent the night plundering, and Belisarius feared that a counter-attack would destroy his scattered army. Gelimer took refuge on Mount Papua among the Moors, where he was besieged by the Herul Pharas, and surrendered in March 534, reportedly asking for a lyre to accompany a song on his misfortune, a sponge to wipe his eyes and a loaf of bread. The Vandal treasure, including the vessels of the Temple of Jerusalem taken from Rome in 455, was seized at Hippo. Tricamarum completed the destruction of the Vandal kingdom after only three months, an extraordinary success that encouraged Justinian's further ambitions in Italy.
battle_of_tricamarum.debate: The very low casualty figures suggest the Vandals broke early; Procopius's date ('about three months' after Carthage) gives mid-December.
scholarship: Merrills and Miles, The Vandals (2010)
Hughes, Belisarius (2009)

digest_and_institutes_533.detail: After the first edition of the Code in 529, Justinian ordered on 15 December 530, by the constitution Deo auctore, a commission of sixteen under Tribonian, the quaestor, to compile an anthology of the writings of the classical jurists who had the ius respondendi, from the late Republic to the third century. The commission, which included the law professors Theophilus and Dorotheus, read some 2,000 books of 3 million lines and condensed them into 50 books with 9,123 excerpts and about 150,000 lines, an operation completed in three years. The Digest (Greek: Pandects) was published on 16 December 533 by the constitution Tanta (in Greek, Dedoken), and entered into force on 30 December. Ulpian provides about 40 per cent of the text, Paul 17 per cent, with Papinian, Gaius, Modestinus and others. The compilers were authorised to alter texts (interpolations) to bring them into line with current law, and modern scholarship has long debated the extent of these changes. In parallel, Tribonian, Theophilus and Dorotheus compiled the Institutes, an elementary textbook in four books based on the Institutes of Gaius, promulgated on 21 November 533 by the constitution Imperatoriam, and given the force of law. The constitution Omnem reorganised legal education in a five-year course based on the new texts. The Digest is the main source for classical Roman law, which would otherwise be largely lost. Rediscovered in Italy in the eleventh century through the Florentine manuscript (Littera Florentina), copied in the sixth century, it became the basis of legal education in the universities of medieval Europe and of the civil law systems of continental Europe and beyond.
scholarship: Honoré, Tribonian (1978)
Watson (ed.), The Digest of Justinian (1985)
Humfress, 'Law and legal practice in the age of Justinian', in Maas (ed.), Cambridge Companion to the Age of Justinian (2005)
Humfress, 'Law and legal practice in the age of Justinian', in Maas (ed.), Cambridge Companion (2005)

murder_of_amalasuntha_535.detail: Amalasuntha, Theodoric's daughter, educated in Latin and Greek, governed Italy as regent for her son Athalaric from 526. Her Roman-style education of her son and her pro-imperial policy, including support for Belisarius's Vandal expedition in 533, alienated the Gothic nobles, who took Athalaric from her tutors and encouraged him in drinking; three leaders of the opposition were killed on her orders, and she secretly negotiated with Justinian for asylum in Constantinople, sending treasure to Dyrrachium. Athalaric died on 2 October 534, aged about 18. Amalasuntha made her cousin Theodahad, a wealthy landowner in Tuscia with philosophical interests, co-ruler, having him swear to leave government to her. Theodahad allied with the relatives of the murdered Gothic nobles, confined Amalasuntha on the island of Martana in Lake Bolsena and, in late April or early May 535, she was strangled in her bath. Procopius in the Wars attributes the murder to the relatives of the executed nobles with Theodahad's consent; in the Secret History he adds that Theodora, jealous of Amalasuntha's beauty and influence, had secretly instructed the imperial envoy Peter the Patrician to encourage the murder, a claim most scholars doubt. Justinian, whose envoy had promised protection, used the murder as a pretext for war. Belisarius occupied Sicily in late 535 and Mundus invaded Dalmatia, opening the Gothic war. Amalasuntha's letters in Cassiodorus's Variae show a ruler of great intelligence, whose fate illustrates the difficulty of maintaining the balance between Gothic military elite and Roman administration that Theodoric had achieved, and her murder gave Constantinople the moral pretext it had been waiting for.
murder_of_amalasuntha_535.debate: Theodora's involvement (Secret History 16) is generally doubted.
scholarship: Moorhead, Theoderic in Italy (1992)
Vitiello, Amalasuintha: The Transformation of Queenship in the Post-Roman World (2017)

volcanic_winter_536.detail: Procopius, in Africa or Italy, wrote that in 536 'the sun gave forth its light without brightness, like the moon, during this whole year, and it seemed exceedingly like the sun in eclipse'. Cassiodorus, praetorian prefect in Italy, described a bluish sun, moonlight without lustre, a summer without heat, and frosts during harvest, and ordered the distribution of reserves. John Lydus in Constantinople reported a dimmed sun for almost a year; Michael the Syrian, drawing on John of Ephesus, says the sun was darkened for eighteen months, appearing for only four hours a day. Chinese chronicles record yellow dust and summer snow. Tree-ring evidence from Europe, Siberia and North America shows the coldest decade of the last two thousand years beginning in 536, with summer temperatures in the northern hemisphere 1.5-2.5 °C lower than average. Ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica reveal sulphate deposits, and a study published in 2018 by McCormick and others identified volcanic glass in a Swiss glacier core pointing to an Icelandic eruption in early 536, followed by another major eruption in 539-540, perhaps in the tropics (Ilopango in El Salvador has been proposed). The resulting cooling, sometimes called the Late Antique Little Ice Age (536-660), coincided with crop failures and famines, and some historians link it to the spread of the Justinianic plague from 541 and to migrations in Eurasia. The causal connections remain debated; the volcanic dimming of 536 is, however, one of the best-documented climatic events of antiquity, and it illustrates the use of written sources with natural science data.
volcanic_winter_536.debate: The identification of the eruptions and the extent of their social consequences are debated.
scholarship: Sigl et al., 'Timing and climate forcing of volcanic eruptions for the past 2,500 years', Nature 523 (2015)
Büntgen et al., 'Cooling and societal change during the Late Antique Little Ice Age', Nature Geoscience 9 (2016)
Harper, The Fate of Rome (2017)
Loveluck, McCormick et al., Antiquity 92 (2018)

siege_of_rome_537.detail: Belisarius entered Rome on 9 December 536 with only some 5,000 men, as the Gothic garrison withdrew. In February or March 537 Witiges arrived with an army that Procopius puts at 150,000, certainly greatly exaggerated, and established seven fortified camps around the city, six on the left bank and one on the Campus Neronis. The Goths cut all fourteen aqueducts, ending the use of the baths and forcing Belisarius to install floating mills on the Tiber, driven by the river current, to grind grain. The siege lasted a year and nine days. The Goths launched a major assault on the eighteenth day with siege towers drawn by oxen, which Belisarius stopped by shooting the oxen; the most dangerous attacks came at the Praenestine gate (Vivarium) and the Mausoleum of Hadrian, where the defenders broke up the statues and threw them at the Goths. Belisarius used sorties of mounted archers to inflict losses on the Goths, who lacked horse archers, a tactical analysis Procopius explains. Hunger and plague afflicted both sides. Pope Silverius was deposed in March 537, accused of plotting to open the Asinarian gate. Reinforcements arrived in November 537, and the Roman cavalry under John, nephew of Vitalian, raided Picenum, threatening the Gothic families. A three-month truce in December 537 allowed the Romans to occupy Portus, Ostia and Albanum, and in March 538 Witiges, hearing that John had taken Ariminum, raised the siege and retreated, burning his camps; Belisarius attacked his troops crossing the Milvian bridge. The siege was the longest of the Gothic war and showed the decisive importance of the Aurelian Walls and Belisarius's leadership.
siege_of_rome_537.debate: The size of the Gothic army is greatly exaggerated by Procopius.
scholarship: Wolfram, History of the Goths (1988)
Heather, Rome Resurgent (2018)
Hughes, Belisarius (2009)
Heather, Rome Resurgent: War and Empire in the Age of Justinian (2018)

siege_of_milan_538.debate: Procopius's 300,000 is impossible; it likely reflects the whole adult male population as a rhetorical figure.

scholarship: Bjornlie, Politics and Tradition between Rome, Ravenna and Constantinople: A Study of Cassiodorus and the Variae (2013)

siege_of_ravenna_539.detail: After the siege of Rome, the Romans divided their command between Belisarius and Narses, and the Goths took and destroyed Milan in 539 because of these quarrels. Narses was recalled and Belisarius took Fiesole and Auximum in 539, while the Frankish invasion of Theudebert ravaged Liguria. In late 539 Belisarius blockaded Witiges in Ravenna, the strongest city of Italy, protected by marshes, and sent troops to the Po to cut off grain supplies; a fire, perhaps caused by Roman agents and Witiges's own wife Matasuntha, destroyed the Gothic grain stores. Justinian, threatened by Persia, sent envoys offering generous terms: Witiges would keep Italy north of the Po and half the royal treasure. Belisarius refused to sign the treaty. The Goths, admiring Belisarius, then offered to make him emperor of the West if he would rule them; Belisarius pretended to accept, and in May 540 entered Ravenna with his army. Procopius, who entered with him, says that the Gothic women spat in their husbands' faces at the sight of the small Roman army. Belisarius took Witiges, Matasuntha, the Gothic nobles and the royal treasure to Constantinople, where Justinian displayed the treasure to the senators in the palace but refused Belisarius a triumph. The Goths north of the Po, who had not surrendered, chose Ildibad, nephew of the Visigothic king Theudis, as king, then Eraric, and in 541 Totila, who reconquered almost all Italy. The fall of Ravenna appeared to end the war, but the departure of Belisarius and the financial demands of the imperial administration under the logothete Alexander, known as 'Snips' (Psalidios), alienated the Italians and gave the Goths a second chance.
siege_of_ravenna_539.debate: Justinian had offered terms leaving the Goths north of the Po; Belisarius refused to sign them, preferring total victory. Whether he was ever tempted by the crown is unknowable.
scholarship: Hughes, Belisarius (2009)
Heather, Rome Resurgent (2018)
Wolfram, History of the Goths (1988)

sack_of_antioch_540.detail: Khosrow I, who had agreed to the Eternal Peace in 532, was alarmed by Justinian's successes in Africa and Italy and received envoys from Witiges and the Armenians urging war. In spring 540 he crossed the Euphrates with a large army, taking advantage of the absence of Belisarius in Italy. He burned Sura, whose bishop's appeal he rejected, extorted ransoms from Hierapolis (2,000 lb of silver) and Beroea (Aleppo), where the people took refuge in the citadel, and arrived at Antioch in June. The patriarch Ephraim and the governor fled, and Justinian's cousin Germanus, sent with a small force, retreated after deciding the walls were not defensible. The city's young men and Blues and Greens fought bravely, but the Persians broke in through a weak point near the citadel on the hills. Antioch, the third city of the empire, was sacked and burned, except for the great church; its inhabitants were deported to Mesopotamia, where Khosrow founded a new city near Ctesiphon called Weh Antiok Khosrow, 'Khosrow's better Antioch', with a hippodrome and baths, known to the Arabs as al-Rumiya. Khosrow bathed in the Mediterranean at Seleucia Pieria and watched chariot races at Apamea, where he favoured the Greens because Justinian favoured the Blues. On his return he extorted money from Edessa and other cities, and broke the treaty again by besieging Dara. Justinian agreed to pay 5,000 lb of gold immediately and 500 lb a year. The sack ended the Eternal Peace, opened twenty years of war in Mesopotamia and Lazica, and was a severe blow to Justinian's prestige.
scholarship: Greatrex and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars II (2002)
Börm, Prokop und die Perser (2007)
Downey, A History of Antioch in Syria (1961)

gildas_de_excidio.debate: Datings range from the 480s to the 540s.

justinianic_plague_541.detail: The plague first appeared at Pelusium on the eastern edge of the Nile Delta in July 541, apparently arriving from the Red Sea, and spread west to Alexandria and east to Gaza and Palestine. It reached Constantinople in spring 542 and raged for four months. Procopius, an eyewitness, describes the symptoms: sudden fever, buboes in the groin and armpits, delirium, coma and death within a few days, with black pustules in some cases; he says the death toll rose to 5,000 and then 10,000 a day, and the bodies were piled in the towers of the walls of Sycae across the Golden Horn and in ships. John of Ephesus, who travelled through Asia Minor during the epidemic, describes deserted villages and fields and officials counting 230,000 dead in the capital before giving up. Evagrius, who caught the disease as a child at Antioch, says it recurred in cycles, killing his wife, children and grandchildren. The emperor himself fell ill and recovered. The plague spread to Italy, Gaul, Spain, Britain and Ireland and to Persia, recurring about every 10-15 years until 749. DNA analysis of skeletons from Aschheim in Bavaria and other sites, published from 2013, confirmed that the disease was caused by Yersinia pestis, a strain distinct from that of the Black Death, originating in central Asia. Mortality is debated: older estimates of a quarter to a half of the Mediterranean population have been challenged by Mordechai, Eisenberg and others, who argue for a less catastrophic impact; others, like Harper and Sarris, maintain the plague was a demographic disaster that undermined Justinian's reconquests and the late Roman economy.
justinianic_plague_541.debate: The scale of mortality and economic consequences are vigorously debated.
scholarship: Little (ed.), Plague and the End of Antiquity (2007)

election_of_totila_541.debate: Whether Totila pursued a deliberate 'social revolution' (older Marxist readings) or simply exploited Roman fiscal oppression is debated.

jacob_baradaeus_ordinations_542.debate: The numbers are hagiographical; the date of his consecration is 542 or 544.

siege_of_edessa_544.debate: A classic example of later legend (the Mandylion, or 'image not made by hands') growing onto a sober contemporary account.

totila_takes_rome_546.debate: The '40 days with no living creature in Rome' (Marcellinus Comes, continuator) is rhetorical.

death_of_theodora_548.debate: Victor of Tunnuna's 'cancer' (cancri plaga) may be literal or metaphorical.

secret_history_550.detail: Procopius of Caesarea, legal adviser to Belisarius and author of the official History of the Wars, wrote around 550, after Theodora's death in 548, a work he did not publish: the Anekdota (unpublished things), known as the Secret History. In it he says he would now tell the truth he could not write while those responsible were alive. It is a savage attack on Justinian and Theodora, as well as on Belisarius and his wife Antonina. Justinian is portrayed as a demon in human form, who walked at night without a head, and whose policies destroyed the population and wealth of the empire, through endless wars, confiscations, the debasement of laws and the persecution of heretics and pagans. Theodora is portrayed as a former actress and prostitute of insatiable sexual appetite, with lurid scenes of her theatrical performances, who manipulated her husband and persecuted her enemies. Belisarius is a cuckold dominated by Antonina. The work survived in a single family of manuscripts and was known in the tenth century to the Suda; it was first published in 1623 from a manuscript in the Vatican library and was long considered a forgery. Its relationship with the Wars and the Buildings, a panegyric of Justinian's construction works, poses the problem of Procopius's real view: modern scholars debate whether he was a classical, traditionalist opponent of the regime (Kaldellis), a man with a complex view (Cameron), or whether the work served a specific political purpose. Its precise factual details on the tax system and administration often confirm other sources, while its personal invective draws on the conventions of classical invective.
secret_history_550.debate: The date (550 or 558-559) and purpose of the work are debated.
scholarship: Cameron, Procopius and the Sixth Century (1985)
Kaldellis, Procopius of Caesarea: Tyranny, History and Philosophy at the End of Antiquity (2004)
Greatrex, 'The dates of Procopius' works', BMGS 18 (1994)
Kaldellis, Procopius of Caesarea: Tyranny, History and Philosophy (2004)
Kaldellis, Prokopios: The Secret History with Related Texts (2010)

jordanes_getica_551.debate: How much is Cassiodorus, how much Jordanes, and how much invention is endlessly debated. Goffart sees a pro-imperial work with a political agenda; Heather and Wolfram trust some oral Gothic traditions in it; Christensen doubts nearly all of the early migration story.
scholarship: Goffart, The Narrators of Barbarian History (1988)
Christensen, Cassiodorus, Jordanes and the History of the Goths (2002)
Heather, Goths and Romans (1991)

battle_of_taginae.detail: After years of reverses in Italy under Totila, Justinian assembled a new army under the eunuch Narses, who was given lavish funds and recruited a large force including Lombards (5,500 sent by Audoin), Heruli, Gepids and Huns as well as Roman regiments, perhaps 20,000-30,000 men in all. Narses marched along the Adriatic coast, bypassing Gothic positions at Verona, reached Ravenna in June 552 and advanced along the Via Flaminia. Totila, waiting for reinforcements under Teia, met him at Busta Gallorum near Taginae (Gualdo Tadino) in the Apennines in late June or early July 552. Narses placed his dismounted Lombards and Heruli in the centre, with Roman infantry and 8,000 archers on foot on the wings, slightly advanced in a crescent, and cavalry in reserve, while a hill on his left flank was occupied by fifty men. Totila delayed the battle until his 2,000 reinforcements arrived, performing equestrian exercises with his weapons in front of the armies, dressed in gold-decorated armour. In the afternoon the Gothic cavalry charged the Roman centre, where it was caught by the archers on the wings and broke, and the fleeing horsemen threw the infantry into disorder. Some 6,000 Goths were killed. Totila was mortally wounded in the flight and died at Caprae; Procopius gives two versions of his death. His bloodstained clothes and jewelled hat were sent to Constantinople and laid at Justinian's feet. Narses then sent the unruly Lombards home and marched on Rome, which he took, the fifth capture of the city in the war. The Goths elected Teia, who made a last stand at Mons Lactarius.
battle_of_taginae.debate: The location of Busta Gallorum and the date (late June or July 552) are debated.
scholarship: Rance, 'Narses and the Battle of Taginae (Busta Gallorum) 552', Historia 54 (2005)
Hughes, Narses (2017)
Heather, Rome Resurgent (2018)
Rance, 'Narses and the battle of Taginae', Historia 54 (2005)

battle_of_mons_lactarius.detail: After Totila's death at Taginae, the surviving Goths gathered at Pavia and elected Teia king. He massacred Roman senators and 300 child hostages, and tried to obtain help from the Franks. Learning that Narses was besieging his brother Aligern, who guarded the Gothic treasure at Cumae, Teia marched south, avoiding Roman forces by following the Adriatic coast, and crossed into Campania. Narses blockaded him on the river Draco (the Sarno), near Nuceria, where the two armies faced each other for two months, the Goths supplied by their fleet. When the Romans captured the fleet through the treachery of its commander, the Goths, short of supplies, retreated to Mons Lactarius (the Monti Lattari, near Vesuvius) and then attacked the Roman army in desperation in late October 552 (or early 553). The battle lasted two days. The Goths fought on foot in a deep phalanx. Teia fought in the front line, holding off the Romans with his shield, which he exchanged for a new one when it was full of javelins; at the twelfth exchange, as his chest was exposed for a moment, he was struck by a javelin and killed. The Romans displayed his head on a pole, but the Goths fought on until the next evening, when they negotiated to leave Italy with their property and to live in freedom under no Roman command. About 1,000 Goths under Indulf withdrew to Pavia; others submitted. Procopius closes his History of the Wars with this battle; Agathias takes up the story. Gothic resistance continued in a few northern cities until 562, and Aligern surrendered Cumae in 553, joining Narses against the Franks.
battle_of_mons_lactarius.debate: Date (October 552 or early 553) is uncertain; Procopius's account of Teia's last fight is literary.
scholarship: Hughes, Narses (2017)
Heather, Rome Resurgent (2018)

silkworms_smuggled_552.debate: Date c. 552-553; Serinda's identification is uncertain.

spania_founded_552.debate: Spania's extent is debated; Corduba and the interior may never have been Roman. An inscription of 589/590 at Cartagena names the magister Comentiolus.
scholarship: Collins, Visigothic Spain 409-711 (2004)
Wood, 'Defending Byzantine Spain', Early Medieval Europe 18 (2010)

second_council_of_constantinople_553.debate: The council failed to win the miaphysites and caused a schism with Aquileia and Milan (the Schism of the Three Chapters) lasting until 698. Whether the anathemas against Origen belong to this council is disputed.
scholarship: Price, The Acts of the Council of Constantinople of 553 (2009)

battle_of_the_volturnus_554.detail: In 553, after the defeat of the Goths, an army of Franks and Alamanni under two Alamannic brothers, Butilinus and Leutharis, dukes in the service of the Frankish king Theudebald, invaded Italy, claiming to support the Goths; Agathias gives a figure of 75,000, obviously inflated. They ravaged central Italy and divided at Samnium: Leutharis marched along the Adriatic and into Apulia and Calabria; Butilinus marched along the Tyrrhenian coast as far as the Straits of Messina, sacking churches. Leutharis decided to return home with his booty, but his army was defeated near Fanum by the Armenian Artabanes, lost much of the plunder, and was decimated by plague in Venetia, where Leutharis died. Butilinus, whose men were dying of dysentery from eating unripe grapes, decided to fight Narses, and fortified a camp near Casilinum on the Volturnus in autumn 554. Narses, with some 18,000 men, drew up his infantry in the centre with the Heruli, and cavalry on the wings. The Franks, fighting on foot with throwing axes (francisca) and barbed spears (angons), attacked in a wedge, broke through the Roman centre where the Heruli were absent after a dispute, but were then caught by the Roman cavalry on both flanks, who shot them with arrows from horseback without engaging in close combat. Agathias claims only five of the Franks survived while the Romans lost 80 men. The victory, described by Agathias in detail, secured Italy against the Franks and allowed Narses to celebrate a triumph in Rome. It is a classic example of the effectiveness of mounted archers against heavy infantry, and Agathias's description of Frankish weapons is valuable for archaeology.
battle_of_the_volturnus_554.debate: Agathias's casualty figures are impossible; the role of the Heruli is disputed.
scholarship: Hughes, Narses (2017)
Bachrach, Merovingian Military Organization (1972)
Cameron, Agathias (1970)
Pohl, The Avars: A Steppe Empire in Central Europe 567-822 (2018)

fifty_years_peace_562.debate: Menander preserves the treaty's thirteen clauses in remarkable detail, one of the most complete Roman treaties to survive. It lasted only ten years.
scholarship: Greatrex & Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars, Part II (2002)

death_of_justinian_565.detail: Justinian died in the night of 14 to 15 November 565, aged about 83, after a reign of 38 years. In his last years he had devoted himself to theology, and his last edict, on the incorruptibility of the body of Christ (aphthartodocetism), had led to the deposition of the patriarch Eutychius in January 565 and resistance from the bishops; he died, Evagrius says, before it could be enforced. He had outlived Theodora (d. 548), Belisarius (d. March 565), Tribonian and John the Cappadocian, and he did not designate a successor. His nephew Justin, the curopalates, married to Theodora's niece Sophia, was in the palace and was informed by the praepositus Callinicus, who said the dying emperor had named him; with the support of the Senate and the excubitors under Tiberius, Justin was crowned on 15 November before his cousin Justin, son of Germanus, commanding on the Danube, could intervene. The poet Corippus, in his panegyric In laudem Iustini, describes Justinian's funeral: the emperor's body laid out on a golden bed in the palace, covered with a shroud embroidered by Sophia showing the victories of his reign, including the defeated Gelimer, and the procession to the church of the Holy Apostles, where he was buried in a porphyry sarcophagus in the mausoleum of Constantine. His legacy was mixed: he had reconquered Africa, Italy and part of Spain, codified Roman law and built Hagia Sophia, but left an exhausted treasury, an empire weakened by plague, the Balkans exposed to Avars and Slavs, and an unresolved religious division. Justin II's refusal to pay subsidies reflected this situation.
death_of_justinian_565.debate: The balance of his reign is contested: an empire enlarged by a third, a legal and architectural legacy without equal, against an overextended army, fiscal exhaustion, plague and unsolved religious division that his successors inherited.
scholarship: Cameron, Flavius Cresconius Corippus: In laudem Iustini Augusti minoris (1976)
Moorhead, Justinian (1994)
Meier, Justinian (2004)
Cameron (ed.), Corippus: In laudem Iustini Augusti minoris (1976)

murder_of_justin_son_of_germanus_566.debate: Evagrius is hostile to Justin II; the head-kicking detail may be rhetorical.

lombard_invasion_568.detail: The Lombards had settled in Pannonia under Justinian as federates against the Gepids, and 5,500 of them fought for Narses at Taginae. In 567 their king Alboin, allied with the Avars of Bayan, destroyed the Gepid kingdom, killed the Gepid king Cunimund, made a drinking cup of his skull and married his daughter Rosamund. Facing the powerful Avars as neighbours, Alboin led his people into Italy, leaving Pannonia to the Avars by a treaty that Paul the Deacon says reserved the Lombards' right to return within 200 years. On Easter Monday, 2 April 568 (Paul's date, often corrected to 569 from Marius of Avenches), a mixed host of Lombards, Saxons (20,000 according to Paul), Gepids, Bulgars, Sarmatians, Pannonians, Suebi and Noricans crossed the Julian Alps into Friuli. Paul records the legend that Narses, dismissed by Justin II and insulted by Sophia, who sent him a spindle, had invited them. Italy, exhausted by the Gothic war and plague, offered little resistance: Forum Iulii (Cividale) became the first Lombard duchy under Alboin's nephew Gisulf, Milan fell in September 569, and Pavia after a three-year siege in 572. The Roman administration under the prefect Longinus held only fortified coastal cities, Ravenna, Rome and Naples. Alboin was murdered in 572 by Rosamund and her lover Helmichis, and after the brief reign of Cleph the Lombards were ruled by dukes for ten years. The invasion ended the political unity of Italy, which would not be restored until 1861, and created a lasting division between Lombard and Byzantine territories, including the exarchate of Ravenna, the duchy of Rome and the southern duchies, that shaped Italian history for centuries.
lombard_invasion_568.debate: Date (568 or 569) and the story of Narses's invitation are disputed.
scholarship: Christie, The Lombards (1995)
Wickham, Early Medieval Italy (1981)
Pohl & Erhart (eds.), Die Langobarden (2005)

tiberius_defeated_by_the_avars_570.debate: Date (570 or 571) and location are uncertain; Menander's fragments give the diplomatic context.

year_of_the_elephant_570.debate: Many scholars date the expedition c. 552 or the 560s and doubt the synchronism with Muhammad's birth, which may be a later symbolic construction.

sasanian_conquest_of_yemen_570.debate: Dated anywhere from c. 570 to 575; the story of the prisoner army is Arabic tradition.

lombard_duchies_spoleto_benevento.debate: Foundation dates are inferred; Paul gives Zotto a twenty-year reign ending c. 591, suggesting 571, but some prefer 576.

assassination_of_alboin_572.debate: Paul writes two centuries later with saga elements; the involvement of the exarch Longinus is plausible.

outbreak_of_persian_war_572.detail: The Fifty Years' Peace of 562 obliged Rome to pay Persia 30,000 solidi a year, with the first seven and then three years paid in advance. Justin II, who had refused the Avar subsidies on his accession, regarded these payments as humiliating tribute. Several developments made war attractive. The Western Turks, who had destroyed the Hephthalites with Persia and then quarrelled with Khosrow over the silk trade, sent an embassy under the Sogdian Maniakh to Constantinople in 568, and Justin sent Zemarchus in 569 to the court of Istämi, creating an alliance to encircle Persia. In Persarmenia, the Armenian prince Vardan Mamikonian led a revolt and killed the Persian governor Chihor-Vishnasp (Suren) at Dvin in February 572, appealing to Justin for help as a fellow Christian. Iberia was also restive. Justin refused to pay the annual sum due in 572 and declared his support for the Armenians, despite the treaty's prohibition on receiving subjects of the other. The Roman general Marcian, Justin's cousin, raided Arzanene in 572 and besieged Nisibis in 573, while the Persians under Khosrow I counter-attacked, taking Dara and raiding Syria under Adarmahan. The war of 572-591 thus began with an act of aggression by Justin, contrary to the advice of his ministers, and turned out disastrously: the Turkish alliance collapsed after Justin's ambassadors were humiliated in 576, the loss of Dara drove the emperor mad, and the war lasted almost twenty years, ending only when the Persian civil war gave Maurice the chance to restore Khosrow II in 591. Evagrius and John of Ephesus blame Justin's arrogance, while Theophylact presents the war as a Roman defence of Christian Armenians.
scholarship: Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and his Historian (1988)
Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and His Historian (1988)
Greatrex and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars II (2002)

leovigild_takes_cordoba_572.debate: Whether Córdoba was under Roman control or an autonomous Hispano-Roman city is debated.

siege_of_dara_573.detail: Dara, the fortress built by Anastasius in 505 at Anastasiopolis to face Nisibis, was the keystone of the Roman defence of Mesopotamia; its walls, cisterns and dams had been rebuilt by Justinian, and its existence had been a grievance of the Persians since its foundation. After the panic and collapse of the Roman siege of Nisibis in spring 573, Khosrow I, aged over seventy, led his army in person to Dara, while his general Adarmahan raided Syria. The siege lasted about six months. Khosrow diverted the river that supplied the city and built siege mounds; the defenders were hampered by the weakness of the imperial response, as Justin had recalled Marcian and no relief army came. The city fell in November 573, betrayed according to some sources, after the Persians took a section of the wall on the mound. The Persians massacred many of the inhabitants and deported the rest; John of Ephesus claims that among the deportees were girls whom Khosrow sent to the Turks, and who drowned themselves in a river rather than suffer. The loss of Dara was a catastrophe: it was the first major Roman city in Mesopotamia captured permanently since Amida in 503, and it opened Roman territory to further raids. When Justin II heard the news, Evagrius says, he went mad; his wife Sophia took power and bought a truce. The return of Dara became the key demand of Roman negotiators, and it was finally obtained only in 591 when Maurice restored Khosrow II, who ceded Dara and Martyropolis. Khosrow II took Dara again in 604.
scholarship: Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and His Historian (1988)
Greatrex and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars II (2002)
Croke and Crow, 'Procopius and Dara', JRS 73 (1983)

sack_of_apamea_573.debate: John of Ephesus's figures for the captives are enormous and untrustworthy.

rule_of_the_dukes_574.debate: The 'thirds' passage (PD 2.32) is central to the debate on Lombard settlement: expropriation versus tax-sharing.

battle_of_melitene_576.debate: Date 575 or 576; the sources' accounts of the battle differ substantially.

lombards_sack_monte_cassino.debate: The date is given variously as 577, 581, 584 or 589.

revolt_of_hermenegild_579.debate: Spanish sources (John of Biclaro, Isidore) treat him as a rebel and say nothing of religion; the martyr image comes from Gregory.

slav_settlement_in_greece_580s.detail: Slavs (Sclaveni and Antes) had raided south of the Danube since Justinian's early years, but in the 570s and 580s, while Roman armies were fighting the Persians, they began to settle permanently. John of Ephesus, writing around 584, says that in the third year of Tiberius (581) the 'accursed people of the Slavs' overran all Greece, Thessaly and Thrace, taking many cities and forts, devastating, burning and enslaving, and that they now lived in Roman territory without fear, as in their own land, had grown rich in gold and silver, horses and weapons, and had learned to fight better than the Romans. Evagrius records that the Avars, with Slavs, reached the Long Walls and took Singidunum, Anchialus and the whole of Greece. The Chronicle of Monemvasia, a later and controversial text, records that the Avars and Slavs conquered the Peloponnese in the sixth year of Maurice (587-588) and held it for 218 years, the inhabitants of Patras fleeing to Rhegium and those of Lacedaemon to Sicily or to Monemvasia, the 'single entrance' rock. Archaeology shows the abandonment of many settlements and the appearance of Slavic-style handmade pottery and cremation burials at Olympia and elsewhere, though the dating and interpretation are disputed. The Miracles of St Demetrius describe Slavic sieges of Thessalonica and settled Slavic tribes around the city. The scale of the settlement was debated in the nineteenth century by Fallmerayer, who claimed the Greeks had been replaced by Slavs. Modern scholarship accepts large-scale Slavic settlement in the Balkans and parts of Greece from the 580s, with Roman control limited to coastal cities until the Byzantine reconquest in the late eighth and ninth centuries.
slav_settlement_in_greece_580s.debate: The Chronicle of Monemvasia's reliability and the date and scale of Slav settlement in the Peloponnese are disputed.
scholarship: Curta, The Making of the Slavs (2001)
Curta, Southeastern Europe in the Middle Ages 500-1250 (2006)
Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and His Historian (1988)
Avramea, Le Péloponnèse du IVe au VIIIe siècle (1997)

fall_of_sirmium_582.detail: Sirmium, once one of the imperial capitals of the tetrarchy and the seat of the prefecture of Illyricum, had been held by the Gepids until 567, when, after their destruction by the Lombards and Avars, the Romans recovered it. Bayan, the Avar khagan, claimed it as part of the Gepid inheritance. In 579 the Avars, with the help of Roman craftsmen requisitioned on the pretext of building baths, built two bridges across the Sava, one above and one below the city, and blockaded it. Menander, the main source, describes the long negotiations: Tiberius II, whose armies were committed to the Persian war, sent envoys and offered subsidies; Bayan swore on a sword and on the Gospels that he did not intend to attack Roman territory. The garrison and people suffered from hunger. Tiberius tried to send troops under Theognis, but they were too few. In 582 Tiberius agreed to surrender the city; the inhabitants were allowed to leave with nothing but their clothes, and the Avars received the arrears of their annual subsidy of 80,000 solidi for three years. Sirmium was abandoned; excavations show a sharp break at the end of the sixth century. A brick from Sirmium bears a scratched inscription in Greek: 'Lord, help the city and stop the Avars, and protect Romania and the writer. Amen.' The fall of Sirmium gave the Avars a base on the Danube frontier and opened the way for their attacks on Singidunum, Viminacium and the Balkan interior in the following years, and is often seen as the beginning of the collapse of the Roman Danube frontier.
fall_of_sirmium_582.debate: The famous brick inscription's date and authenticity have been questioned but are generally accepted.
scholarship: Pohl, The Avars: A Steppe Empire in Central Europe 567-822 (2018)
Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and His Historian (1988)
Curta, The Making of the Slavs (2001)

pontificate_of_gregory_590.detail: Gregory, born around 540 into a senatorial family of Rome that had produced Pope Felix III, was urban prefect around 573, then gave away his property, founded monasteries in Sicily and on his family estate on the Caelian hill (St Andrew's) and became a monk. Pope Pelagius II made him deacon and sent him to Constantinople as apocrisiarius (579-586), where he debated with the patriarch Eutychius and began his Moralia on Job. Elected pope after Pelagius died of plague in February 590, he hesitated, reportedly wrote to Maurice asking him to refuse confirmation, and was consecrated on 3 September 590. His fourteen-year pontificate shaped the medieval papacy. With Rome threatened by the Lombards and the exarch in Ravenna unable to defend it, Gregory organised the defence of the city, paid troops, negotiated with Agilulf in 593 and 598, and managed the vast estates of the Roman church in Sicily, southern Italy, Dalmatia, Gaul and Africa, the patrimony of St Peter, which supplied grain to Rome. His 850 surviving letters show him intervening in the affairs of churches from Spain to Constantinople, protesting against the patriarch John the Faster's title of ecumenical patriarch and calling himself servant of the servants of God. He sent Augustine and forty monks to convert the English in 596-597. He wrote the Pastoral Rule (591), a handbook for bishops, the Dialogues (593-594), homilies on the Gospels and Ezekiel, and was later credited with the reform of liturgical chant. He died on 12 March 604 and became one of the four Latin Doctors of the Church.
scholarship: Markus, Gregory the Great and His World (1997)
Richards, Consul of God (1980)
Straw, Gregory the Great: Perfection in Imperfection (1988)

sources.w: Ecclesiastical History of the English People

battle_of_blarathon.detail: In 590 the Persian general Bahram Chobin, humiliated by Hormizd IV after a defeat by the Romans in the Caucasus, rebelled and marched on Ctesiphon. A palace coup overthrew Hormizd and placed his son Khosrow II on the throne, but Bahram defeated Khosrow on the Nahrawan canal and seized the throne himself as Bahram VI, the first non-Sasanian king. Khosrow fled with a few followers to Roman territory at Circesium and appealed to Maurice, offering Dara, Martyropolis and much of Armenia in return for help. Against the advice of his senators, who argued that letting the Persians fight each other was better, Maurice agreed, perhaps seeing the chance of peace on the eastern frontier after twenty years of war, and Khosrow was given an army. In 591 a Roman army under Narses, magister militum per Orientem, and the Armenian John Mystacon, with Armenian troops under Mushegh Mamikonian and Persian loyalists led by Khosrow's uncles Vistahm and Vinduyih, invaded Persia through Armenia and Atropatene. They met Bahram on the river Blarathon near Ganzak in Atropatene in late summer 591. Bahram's forces, including elephants, were defeated after a hard fight; Theophylact says the Romans captured his elephants and that Bahram fled to the Turks in Central Asia, where he was assassinated in 592 at Khosrow's instigation. Khosrow was restored to the throne and, in the peace of 591, ceded Dara, Martyropolis, much of Persarmenia including Dvin, and Iberia up to Tiflis to the Romans, without annual payments. It was the most favourable treaty Rome had ever made with Persia, but Khosrow II's debt to Maurice became the pretext for the devastating war of 603-628.
scholarship: Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and His Historian (1988)
Howard-Johnston, Witnesses to a World Crisis (2010)
Pourshariati, Decline and Fall of the Sasanian Empire (2008)

gregory_dialogues_593.debate: Francis Clark argued the Dialogues were a later forgery; most scholars reject this.

captives_massacre_599.debate: Theophanes, drawing on a source hostile to Maurice, gives the ransom detail; Theophylact suggests Comentiolus betrayed the army deliberately on Maurice's orders to punish it, which most doubt.

battle_of_viminacium_599.detail: In 598 Maurice and the khagan Bayan concluded a peace that allowed the Romans to cross the Danube to fight the Slavs. In 599 Maurice broke it, perhaps after Bayan's demands, and ordered Priscus, magister militum per Thracias, to cross the Danube into Avar territory at Viminacium, while Comentiolus led a second army. Theophylact describes a campaign of several battles on the Pannonian plain north of the river. Priscus's army, transported across the Danube on boats, won a series of victories over the Avars near Viminacium; in the first, the khagan's four sons were killed, according to Theophylact, and the Avars lost 4,000 men. Priscus then won two further battles and pursued the khagan towards the Tisza, where in a fifth engagement 3,000 Avars, 8,000 Slavs and 6,200 other barbarians were captured and some 30,000 enemies killed. Gepid villages were destroyed. The prisoners were sent to Tomis, but Maurice ordered them returned to the khagan as part of a settlement, a decision that angered the army. Theophylact's figures are exaggerated, but the campaign showed that the Roman army under competent leadership could defeat the Avars in their own territory and was the high point of Maurice's Balkan war. In 600 Bayan's counter-offensive in Dalmatia and the plague in his army weakened the Avars further. However, the army's exhaustion and resentment at Maurice's economy measures, including orders to winter north of the Danube, led to the mutiny of 602, the overthrow of Maurice and the end of the Roman offensive. Within two decades the Avars were besieging Constantinople.
battle_of_viminacium_599.debate: Theophylact's casualty figures are untrustworthy; Whitby dates the campaign to 599.
scholarship: Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and His Historian (1988)
Pohl, The Avars (2018)
Curta, The Making of the Slavs (2001)

strategikon_c600.detail: The Strategikon is a military manual in twelve books written in Greek around 592-610, traditionally attributed to Maurice, who may have commissioned or contributed to it, although some manuscripts name an Urbicius and others attribute it to Maurice's brother-in-law Philippicus. It is the most important source on the late Roman army. Books 1-3 deal with the organisation and training of the cavalry, by then the main striking force: the army is divided into moirai and banda of 200-400 men, armed with bow and lance, wearing mail and helmets, using stirrups (first mentioned in Byzantine sources), and drilling with Latin commands such as 'cede', 'iunge', 'deus adiuta'. Books 4-10 cover ambushes, baggage, marches, camps, sieges and the general's conduct, with maxims. Book 11 describes the characteristics and tactics of the enemies of the Romans: Persians, 'Scythians' (Avars and Turks), 'light-haired peoples' (Franks and Lombards), and Slavs and Antes, who live in forests and marshes, are disorderly, hospitable to strangers, and should be attacked in winter when the trees are bare and the rivers frozen. Book 12 covers infantry formations, drill and camps, including a Latin and Greek vocabulary of commands. The Strategikon shows a professional army adapted to fight steppe nomads by adopting their methods, with emphasis on careful planning, intelligence, deception and avoidance of risky pitched battles. It was the basis of later Byzantine military manuals such as the Taktika of Leo VI. Its Latin commands show that Latin remained the language of the army a century after it had disappeared as the administrative language of the eastern empire.
strategikon_c600.debate: Authorship (Maurice, Philippicus or an anonymous officer) and the date (590s or early seventh century) are debated.
scholarship: Dennis (trans.), Maurice's Strategikon (1984)
Rance, 'The date of the military compendium of Syrianus Magister', BZ 100 (2007)

revolt_of_phocas_602.detail: Maurice's Balkan campaigns had restored Roman control of the Danube by 600, but at great cost, and his attempts to reduce military expenditure had already caused a mutiny in the eastern army in 588 and unrest in the Balkans. In autumn 602 he ordered the army under his brother Peter to winter north of the Danube in Slav territory, to save money and to feed off the enemy's land. The soldiers, exhausted and fearing the cold, mutinied; they raised on a shield the centurion Phocas, a junior officer of Thracian origin who had previously been part of a delegation of soldiers to Maurice, when he was humiliated by the patrician Comentiolus. The army marched on Constantinople. Maurice tried to defend the city with the circus factions, but the Greens turned against him; on the night of 22 November he fled by boat with his family to Asia, sending his son Theodosius to Persia to seek help from Khosrow II. The army and the Greens first offered the throne to Germanus, Theodosius's father-in-law, who refused, and then Phocas, who was crowned in the church of St John the Baptist at the Hebdomon by the patriarch Cyriacus on 23 November and entered the capital the next day. Phocas ordered the execution of Maurice and his sons. His eight-year reign was remembered by later sources, partly written under Heraclius, as a tyranny of terror, executions and military disaster, as the Persians invaded the East and the Avars and Slavs overran the Balkans. Modern historians see the revolt of 602 as a turning point: the first violent overthrow of an emperor in Constantinople since its foundation, it opened a period of civil war and external invasion that nearly destroyed the empire.
scholarship: Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and his Historian (1988)
Olster, The Politics of Usurpation in the Seventh Century (1993)
Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and His Historian (1988)
Kaegi, Byzantine Military Unrest 471-843 (1981)

execution_of_maurice_602.detail: After his flight across the Bosporus on 22 November 602, Maurice, suffering from gout, stopped at the church of St Autonomus near Praenetus (or at Chalcedon) with his wife Constantina and their children; his eldest son and co-emperor Theodosius had been sent towards Persia. Phocas, crowned on 23 November, sent the officer Lilius with soldiers to seize them. On 27 November 602, at the harbour of Eutropius at Chalcedon, they executed his five younger sons, Tiberius, Petrus, Paulus, Justinus and Justinianus, one after another before his eyes, and then Maurice himself. Theophylact records that Maurice repeated the verse of Psalm 119 'Righteous art thou, O Lord, and upright are thy judgements', and that when a nurse tried to substitute her own child for one of his sons, Maurice refused to allow it and handed over his own son. The heads were displayed on the Tribunal at the Hebdomon until they began to rot, and the bodies were thrown into the sea; Theodosius was captured and executed near Nicaea, as were Maurice's brother Peter and the general Comentiolus. Constantina and her daughters were confined in a monastery and executed some years later. The murder of a legitimate emperor and his family shocked contemporaries; Khosrow II, who owed his throne to Maurice, used it as the pretext for war and sponsored a pretender claiming to be Theodosius. Later Byzantine sources, written under Heraclius, portrayed Maurice as a pious martyr and Phocas as a monster, and Maurice was venerated as a saint in the Orthodox church. The details of the execution are in Theophylact and the Chronicon Paschale.
scholarship: Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and His Historian (1988)
Olster, The Politics of Usurpation in the Seventh Century (1993)

outbreak_of_persian_war_603.detail: Khosrow II, restored to power by Maurice in 591, had maintained peace for a decade, keeping good relations with the emperor, whom he called his father. When news of Maurice's execution arrived, Khosrow imprisoned Phocas's envoy Lilius and declared war in 603, presenting himself as avenger of his benefactor. He sponsored a man claiming to be Maurice's son Theodosius, who had supposedly escaped to Persia, and had him crowned by the catholicos. At the same time Narses, the Roman magister militum per Orientem and an old friend of Khosrow, refused to recognise Phocas, seized Edessa and appealed to Khosrow for help. Khosrow led his army in person, relieved Edessa, defeated the Roman general Germanus near Constantina (Germanus died of his wounds), defeated another Roman army at Arxamoun, and besieged Dara, which fell after nine months in 604. The war that followed lasted twenty-six years, the longest and most destructive of all Roman-Persian wars. In its first phase (603-610) the Persians conquered Roman Mesopotamia and Armenia; in the second (610-619) they took Syria, Palestine with Jerusalem (614), Egypt (619) and much of Anatolia, reaching Chalcedon. Historians debate Khosrow's aims: revenge for Maurice was a pretext, but the ambition of restoring the Achaemenid empire, or simply exploiting Roman weakness, explains the escalation. The war exhausted both empires and left them vulnerable to the Arab conquests of the 630s. The near-contemporary sources are the Armenian history attributed to Sebeos, the Chronicle of Khuzistan and the Chronicon Paschale; Theophanes, writing two centuries later, supplies much of the year-by-year chronology, not always reliably.
scholarship: Howard-Johnston, Witnesses to a World Crisis (2010)
Howard-Johnston, The Last Great War of Antiquity (2021)
Greatrex & Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars, Part II (2002)
Greatrex and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars II (2002)
Kaegi, Heraclius, Emperor of Byzantium (2003)

execution_of_empress_constantina_605.debate: The Chronicon Paschale dates the conspiracy to 605; Theophanes's chronology places the executions c. 607.

heraclian_revolt_608.detail: By 608 Phocas's regime was failing: the Persians were advancing in Mesopotamia and Armenia, his executions had alienated the aristocracy, and the circus factions, especially the Greens, were rioting in many cities. The revolt began in Africa, the richest and most secure province in the West. Heraclius the Elder, the exarch of Carthage, a veteran general of Maurice's Persian war of Armenian origin, and his brother Gregory, encouraged, according to some sources, by Priscus, Phocas's son-in-law and comes excubitorum, rebelled in 608, stopped the grain shipments to Constantinople, and struck coins showing himself and his son as consuls, without imperial insignia, a carefully ambiguous claim. Two expeditions were organised: Gregory's son Nicetas marched overland with an army of Moors and Romans to Egypt, the other granary of the capital, where he won the support of the population and the Greens and defeated Phocas's general Bonosus in 609-610, taking Alexandria. The younger Heraclius, the exarch's son, sailed with a fleet in 610, stopping at Thessalonica, the Aegean islands and Abydos, where he gathered supporters; his fleet carried icons of the Virgin on the masts. As he approached Constantinople, the excubitors under Priscus and the Greens deserted Phocas. On 5 October 610 Heraclius was crowned emperor and married Fabia-Eudokia; Phocas was executed after a famous exchange in which Heraclius asked him whether he had governed better, and he answered: 'will you do better?'. The revolt was the first time a provincial governor from the West overthrew an emperor in Constantinople, and it founded the Heraclian dynasty, which ruled until 711.
scholarship: Kaegi, Heraclius: Emperor of Byzantium (2003)
Olster, The Politics of Usurpation in the Seventh Century (1993)
Kaegi, Heraclius, Emperor of Byzantium (2003)
Grierson, 'The consular coinage of Heraclius and the revolt against Phocas', DOP 6 (1950)

sources.w: Ecclesiastical History of the English People

riots_of_antioch_609.debate: Modern scholars doubt a specifically Jewish uprising and see circus-faction and anti-Phocas violence.

accession_of_heraclius_610.detail: Heraclius's fleet reached the Hebdomon on 3 October 610 after a voyage through the Aegean. Constantinople was ready to change sides: the Greens, whom Phocas had alienated by executions, burned parts of the city, and the comes excubitorum Priscus, Phocas's son-in-law, who had been in secret contact with the rebels, withdrew his support. Phocas's brother Domentziolus, guarding the Long Walls, fled. Phocas was seized by senators and by the Greens, stripped of the purple and brought to Heraclius on his ship. According to John of Antioch, Heraclius asked him 'Is this how you governed the state?' and Phocas replied 'Will you govern it better?'. Phocas was beheaded and his body mutilated; his head was paraded through the city, and his statue in the Hippodrome burned. His brother Domentziolus, the comes Orientis Bonosus and others were killed. On 5 October 610 the patriarch Sergius crowned Heraclius in the palace chapel of St Stephen, and on the same day married him to Fabia, renamed Eudokia, who was crowned Augusta. Heraclius, aged about 35, inherited a disastrous situation: the Persians had taken Mesopotamia and Armenia and were crossing the Euphrates into Syria and Anatolia, the Avars and Slavs were overrunning the Balkans, the army was demoralised and the treasury empty. Phocas's brother Comentiolus held out in Anatolia until 611. Heraclius's early years saw new defeats, including Antioch (613), Jerusalem (614) and Egypt (619). But his reign of 31 years would see the defeat of Persia (622-628) and then the loss of Syria, Palestine and Egypt to the Arabs (634-641). His accession marks the beginning of the Heraclian dynasty and is often taken as the beginning of the Byzantine empire proper.
scholarship: Kaegi, Heraclius, Emperor of Byzantium (2003)
Reinink and Stolte (eds.), The Reign of Heraclius (2002)
Haldon, Byzantium in the Seventh Century (1990)

battle_of_antioch_613.detail: After the Persian capture of Caesarea in Cappadocia (611) and its recovery in 612, the Persians under Shahrbaraz attacked Syria, taking Apamea and Emesa in 611-612. In 613 Heraclius took the field in person, the first reigning emperor in two centuries to lead an army into battle, together with his brother Theodore and his cousin Nicetas, who brought troops from Egypt. The armies met near Antioch. The Romans had some initial success, but were then defeated by Shahrbaraz and Shahin; the Persians pursued them, and in a second battle in the Cilician Gates the Romans under Theodore were again defeated, though they inflicted heavy losses. Sebeos is the main source; Theophanes adds a few details. The defeat had serious consequences. It split the Roman East in two: the Persians took Antioch, cut off Syria and Palestine from Anatolia, captured Damascus and Tarsus, and opened the way to Jerusalem (614) and Egypt (618-619). When Shahin reached Chalcedon in 615, the Senate sent envoys to Khosrow with a letter, preserved by the Chronicon Paschale, which recognised Khosrow as the 'supreme emperor' and asked for peace; Khosrow had the envoys imprisoned and said he would not make peace until the Romans renounced Christ and worshipped the sun. For the next nine years Heraclius concentrated on reorganising the army and finances. The defeat at Antioch is significant as evidence of the military weakness of the empire after the revolt of Phocas, when the Roman field army had been greatly reduced by civil war, and as a lesson Heraclius learned for his later campaigns.
scholarship: Kaegi, Heraclius, Emperor of Byzantium (2003)
Howard-Johnston, The Last Great War of Antiquity (2021)
Greatrex and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars II (2002)

heraclius_marries_martina.debate: Nikephoros implies c. 613-614; some scholars prefer c. 622-623.

siege_of_jerusalem_614.detail: After the Roman defeat at Antioch in 613, the Persian army under Shahrbaraz marched south through Syria and Palestine, taking Caesarea Maritima, the provincial capital, without resistance. Jerusalem first agreed to submit, but an uprising killed the Persian officials left in the city. Shahrbaraz returned and besieged the city for about twenty days in April and May 614; according to the monk Antiochus Strategos, an eyewitness, the Persians undermined the walls with siege engines, broke in, and massacred the inhabitants, the dead being counted at 66,509 (later versions give other numbers) in the lists of the burial party led by one Thomas; Sebeos gives 57,000 dead and 35,000 captives. The patriarch Zacharias and many survivors were deported to Persia, with the relic of the True Cross, which was taken to Ctesiphon and given to the Christian queen Shirin. The churches of the Holy Sepulchre and others were burned. Christian sources accuse the Jews of helping the Persians and of massacring Christians at the Mamilla pool, but these claims, coloured by anti-Jewish polemic, have been questioned; excavations at Mamilla have found a mass grave with a chapel, consistent with the event. The Persians first entrusted Jerusalem to the Jews, then around 617 reversed this policy and allowed the abbot Modestus to restore the churches. The capture of the holy city and the loss of the True Cross shocked the Christian world and gave the war a religious character: Heraclius's campaigns from 622 were presented as a holy war, and the restoration of the Cross in 630 was its climax. The fall of Jerusalem is a central episode of apocalyptic literature, Christian and Jewish.
siege_of_jerusalem_614.debate: Casualty figures and Jewish participation are disputed; archaeology suggests less destruction than the literary sources claim.
scholarship: Avni, 'The Persian conquest of Jerusalem (614 CE): an archaeological assessment', BASOR 357 (2010)
Howard-Johnston, Witnesses to a World Crisis (2010)

Flusin, Saint Anastase le Perse et l'histoire de la Palestine (1992)

persian_conquest_of_egypt_619.detail: Egypt was the richest province of the empire and the source of the grain that fed Constantinople. After the fall of Jerusalem, Shahrbaraz invaded Egypt in 618, taking Pelusium and advancing into the Delta. Alexandria was besieged; the Roman governor Nicetas, Heraclius's cousin, and the Chalcedonian patriarch John the Almsgiver fled to Cyprus. The city fell in 619, according to the History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria because a student named Peter showed the Persians a way in through the canal at the gate of the Sun, or because a defector opened a gate. The Persians massacred monks in the monasteries around Alexandria, according to Coptic sources, then advanced up the Nile, taking Upper Egypt by 621. Egypt remained under Persian rule for about ten years. Papyri in Pahlavi and Greek from Egypt show that the Persians maintained the existing tax administration, with Persian officials collecting the revenues and requisitioning supplies; the Coptic patriarch Andronicus remained in Alexandria, and the Persians appear to have favoured the Miaphysite majority over the Chalcedonians. The loss of Egypt had immediate consequences in Constantinople: the free bread distribution, introduced by Constantine in 332, was suspended in 618 and never restored, and Heraclius considered moving the capital to Carthage. Persian rule ended after the peace of 628-629, when Shahrbaraz withdrew under the agreement at Arabissus. The episode showed the vulnerability of Egypt, which would be conquered permanently by the Arabs barely ten years later, in 639-642, partly with the same Miaphysite resentment against Constantinople. The Persian occupation is thus a rehearsal for the Arab one.
persian_conquest_of_egypt_619.debate: The date of the fall of Alexandria (618 or 619) is debated.
scholarship: Sänger, 'The administration of Sasanian Egypt', GRBS 51 (2011)

heraclius_campaign_622.detail: After twelve years of defeats, with the Persians in control of Syria, Palestine and Egypt and raiding in Anatolia, and the Avars threatening the capital, Heraclius decided to take the offensive in person. He made peace with the Avars, paying a large subsidy, and financed the campaign with the treasures of the churches lent by the patriarch Sergius and by halving official salaries. On Easter Monday, 5 April 622, he left Constantinople, carrying an icon of Christ 'not made by human hands' (acheiropoietos), and crossed to Bithynia. He spent the summer training his army in the region of Pylae and in Cappadocia, according to George of Pisidia, whose poem Expeditio Persica describes the campaign: he held drills, mock battles and exercises, and improved discipline. In the autumn he marched east into Armenia or Pontus, threatening Persian communications, and drew Shahrbaraz into a battle in which the Persians were defeated, perhaps in the region of Cappadocia; George of Pisidia describes a solar eclipse and a ruse by which Heraclius lured the Persians out of an ambush position. The campaign is reconstructed differently by historians: Howard-Johnston places it in Pontus and Armenia, Kaegi in Cappadocia, and Zuckerman argues for a different chronology. In winter Heraclius returned to Constantinople because of an Avar threat. The campaign of 622 was the first victory of Heraclius over Persia and restored the morale of his army; it was presented as a holy war for the recovery of the True Cross. It also marked a change in imperial conduct, with the emperor commanding in person for years far from the capital.
heraclius_campaign_622.debate: The route and location of the 622 victory are debated.
scholarship: Howard-Johnston, 'Heraclius' Persian campaigns and the revival of the East Roman Empire', War in History 6 (1999)
Kaegi, Heraclius, Emperor of Byzantium (2003)
Zuckerman, 'Heraclius in 625', REB 60 (2002)

hijra_622.detail: According to the Muslim tradition, Muhammad, who had preached in Mecca since about 610, faced increasing hostility from the Quraysh after the deaths of his uncle and protector Abu Talib and his wife Khadija in 619. He sought support from other towns and tribes, and in 621 and 622, at Aqaba near Mecca, he made agreements with members of the Aws and Khazraj tribes from Yathrib, an oasis some 350 km to the north divided by long feuds, who invited him to come as arbiter. His followers emigrated in small groups during the summer of 622, and Muhammad himself, with Abu Bakr, left Mecca secretly, hiding in a cave on Mount Thawr to escape his pursuers, and arrived at Quba near Yathrib, traditionally on 24 September 622 (12 Rabi I). Yathrib became Madinat al-Nabi, the city of the Prophet, or simply Medina. There Muhammad organised the community (umma), building a mosque and agreeing a document, the so-called Constitution of Medina, preserved by Ibn Ishaq, which defined the rights and obligations of the emigrants (Muhajirun), the Medinan helpers (Ansar) and the Jewish tribes as a single community. The Hijra marked the transition of Muhammad from a persecuted preacher to the leader of a political community and military power. Under the caliph Umar, around 638, the year of the Hijra was adopted as the beginning of the Islamic calendar, its first day being 16 July 622. The traditional narrative depends on sources written more than a century later; non-Muslim contemporary sources say little about Muhammad before the conquests, and some revisionist historians have questioned the chronology.
hijra_622.debate: Islamic sources are later than the events by 150 years or more and were shaped by later concerns; revisionist scholarship (Crone, Cook) once questioned much of the traditional narrative, while Donner and Hoyland reconstruct a core supported by early non-Muslim sources.
scholarship: Donner, Muhammad and the Believers (2010)
Hoyland, Seeing Islam as Others Saw It (1997)
Watt, Muhammad at Medina (1956)
Lecker, The Constitution of Medina (2004)

avar_surprise_623.debate: Date disputed: 617 (Theophanes, Nikephoros) or 623 (Chronicon Paschale); Howard-Johnston and Whitby favour 623. The captives figure is surely inflated.
