destruction_of_adur_gushnasp_624.detail: After a winter in Constantinople, Heraclius left on 25 March 624 with his wife Martina and marched through Cappadocia and Armenia to Theodosiopolis, then crossed into Persian Armenia, taking Dvin and Nakhchivan, and invaded Atropatene (Azerbaijan), the heartland of Persian religion. Khosrow II, who was at Ganzak with 40,000 men, fled before him. Heraclius took Ganzak and destroyed the city. He then advanced to the great fire temple of Adur Gushnasp, one of the three most sacred fires of Zoroastrianism, associated with the king and the warrior class, at Takht-i Suleiman (ancient Shiz, 'Thebarmais' in Greek sources), beside a volcanic lake; Theophanes says Heraclius extinguished the fire and destroyed the temple in revenge for Jerusalem, and that the treasures of Croesus were found there, a legend. Archaeological excavations at Takht-i Suleiman show a destruction layer of this period, although the sanctuary was later restored. Heraclius then turned north into Caucasian Albania for the winter, rather than returning to Roman territory, freeing, according to Theophanes, 50,000 prisoners, and recruited allies among the Lazi, Abasgians and Iberians. The campaign of 624 was a bold strategic innovation: instead of trying to recover Roman territory directly, Heraclius struck at the heart of the Persian empire, forcing Khosrow to withdraw his armies from Anatolia and Syria to defend Persia. It was also a religious war: the destruction of the fire temple answered the capture of the Cross in 614. Movses Daskhurantsi's history of the Albanians describes the arrival of Heraclius's army and its effect on the region.
destruction_of_adur_gushnasp_624.debate: Whether the fire temple destroyed was at Takht-i Suleiman or elsewhere in Atropatene is debated.
scholarship: Kaegi, Heraclius (2003)
Howard-Johnston, Witnesses to a World Crisis (2010)
Kaegi, Heraclius, Emperor of Byzantium (2003)
Naumann, Die Ruinen von Tacht-e Suleiman und Zendan-e Suleiman (1977)

visigoths_conquer_spania_624.debate: Whether the Balearics stayed Roman (likely) and when exactly the last town fell are debated.

siege_of_constantinople_626.detail: In 626, while Heraclius was in the Caucasus, Khosrow II and the Avar khagan agreed to attack Constantinople at the same time. Shahrbaraz marched across Anatolia and camped at Chalcedon opposite the capital, while the khagan advanced from the Balkans with an army of Avars, Slavs, Bulgars and Gepids, perhaps 80,000 strong. The defence was led by the patriarch Sergius and the patrician Bonus, magister officiorum, in the name of the young Constantine III; Heraclius sent 12,000 soldiers as reinforcement and remained in the East, sending his brother Theodore against Shahin. The siege began on 29 July 626. The Avars attacked the land walls with siege towers and catapults, particularly in the section near the gate of St Romanus. The defenders replied with artillery, and Sergius carried icons of the Virgin along the walls. On 7 August the Slavs, in monoxyla (dugout boats), tried to cross the Golden Horn to join the attack on the Blachernae area and to ferry Persian troops across the Bosporus; the Roman fleet destroyed them, and the sea was filled with corpses. The khagan, discouraged, burned his siege engines and withdrew on 8 August. Shahrbaraz withdrew to Syria. The defenders attributed the victory to the Virgin; the Akathistos hymn was later associated with this deliverance, and Theodore Syncellus preached a homily on the anniversary. The siege was a turning point: the failure weakened the Avars, whose subject peoples, Slavs and Bulgars, soon rebelled, and freed Heraclius to strike at the heart of Persia in 627. The Chronicon Paschale provides a day-by-day account.
scholarship: Howard-Johnston, 'The siege of Constantinople in 626', in Mango & Dagron (eds.), Constantinople and its Hinterland (1995)
Pohl, The Avars (2018)
Howard-Johnston, 'The siege of Constantinople in 626', in Mango and Dagron (eds.), Constantinople and Its Hinterland (1995)
Kaegi, Heraclius (2003)

sources.w: Homily on the Siege of Constantinople

battle_of_nineveh.detail: In 627 Heraclius made an alliance with the Western Turks, whose army under Tong Yabghu's commander (called Ziebel in Byzantine sources) joined him at the siege of Tiflis. When the Turks withdrew in the autumn, Heraclius, with perhaps 25,000-50,000 men, including some Turks, marched south from the Caucasus in September 627 into Atropatene and then across the Zagros into Assyria, the heartland of the Persian empire, where no Roman army had been since Julian. Khosrow II sent an army under the general Rhahzadh (Roch Vehan), which followed the Romans. On 12 December 627, near the ruins of Nineveh, opposite Mosul, Heraclius turned and gave battle in the morning fog, which hid the Roman advance and neutralised the Persian archers. The battle lasted eleven hours. Heraclius, mounted on his horse Dorkon, fought in person, killing Rhahzadh in single combat, according to Theophanes, and two other Persian champions, and being wounded in the lip. The Persians lost 6,000 men and all their commanders, but did not flee, remaining near the battlefield overnight. The Romans captured 28 standards. Heraclius did not pursue but marched on toward Ctesiphon, plundering the royal palaces, including Dastagird, which Khosrow had abandoned, recovering 300 Roman standards. Khosrow fled to Ctesiphon, where he was overthrown by his son Kavad II in February 628. The battle of Nineveh, though not a crushing victory, destroyed the last Persian field army and Khosrow's prestige, and decided the war. Heraclius's own dispatch, read in Hagia Sophia, survives in the Chronicon Paschale, a rare first-person report of a Roman emperor on his campaign.
scholarship: Kaegi, Heraclius (2003)
Howard-Johnston, Witnesses to a World Crisis (2010)
Haldon, The Byzantine Wars (2001)

siege_of_tbilisi_627.debate: The identity of Ziebel (Tong Yabghu or a Khazar/Turkic subordinate) is debated.

fall_of_khosrow_ii_628.detail: After the defeat at Nineveh and the sack of Dastagird, Khosrow II retreated to Ctesiphon, refusing Heraclius's peace offers. His authority collapsed: he had alienated the nobility with executions and heavy taxes to finance the war, imprisoned many officials, and planned, according to some sources, to execute Shahrbaraz, who was still in Egypt and Syria. A conspiracy of nobles, including Shahrbaraz's son, the general Gurdanaspa and the sons of the executed Yazdin, freed prisoners and proclaimed Khosrow's son Kavad (Sheroe), born of the Christian Maria, king. Khosrow was arrested around 23-25 February 628, imprisoned in the 'House of Darkness' (or the house of a certain Maraspand), and executed a few days later, according to Tabari after being shown the corpses of his children; Kavad II also killed seventeen of his brothers. Heraclius learned of the coup in March near Ganzak, and Kavad II sent envoys to make peace. The terms, settled in April 628, were the return of all occupied Roman territory, the release of prisoners, and the return of the True Cross; Heraclius's dispatch from his camp, read in Hagia Sophia on 15 May 628, rejoiced that 'the arrogant Khosrow, enemy of God, has fallen'. The evacuation of Persian troops was slow, since Shahrbaraz refused to obey Kavad, and it was only in July 629 at Arabissus that Heraclius and Shahrbaraz agreed. Kavad II died of plague in September 628, and Persia fell into four years of civil war. Khosrow II, who had come closest of any Sasanian king to restoring the Achaemenid empire, ended in disaster.
fall_of_khosrow_ii_628.debate: Kavad II died of plague within months; Shahrbaraz agreed at Arabissos in July 629 to evacuate Egypt and Syria, then seized the Persian throne in 630 and was murdered after 40 days.
scholarship: Howard-Johnston, The Last Great War of Antiquity (2021)
Pourshariati, Decline and Fall of the Sasanian Empire (2008)
Kaegi, Heraclius (2003)

heraclius_title_basileus_629.debate: A classic marker in narratives of 'Byzantinisation'. Kaldellis argues the term 'Byzantine' is a post-1550 invention and that the subjects of Heraclius called themselves Romans and their state Romanía; title changes reflect usage, not a new state. Shahid connected the title with the Persian victory over a 'king of kings'.
scholarship: Shahid, 'The Iranian factor in Byzantium during the reign of Heraclius', DOP 26 (1972)
Kaldellis, Romanland: Ethnicity and Empire in Byzantium (2019)
Chrysos, 'The title basileus in early Byzantine international relations', DOP 32 (1978)

restoration_of_the_true_cross_630.detail: The True Cross, taken from Jerusalem in 614 and kept at Ctesiphon, was returned by Shahrbaraz as part of the agreements of 629, possibly in exchange for Roman support for his usurpation. Heraclius took the relic in its case, with the seals still intact, and entered Jerusalem in a solemn procession on 21 March 630, through the Golden Gate, with his wife Martina, and restored it to the patriarch Modestus at the Holy Sepulchre. The date of 21 March 630 is given by Sebeos and Strategius; some historians, following a different reading of the sources, argue for 629. Later legend, celebrated in the liturgical feast of the Exaltation of the Cross on 14 September, claims that Heraclius was unable to pass through the gate until he had removed his royal clothes and walked barefoot, in humility, like Christ. The restoration was the high point of Heraclius's reign: he had defeated Persia, recovered the eastern provinces and the most sacred relic of Christendom, and in 629 had taken the title of basileus. At the same time, he ordered the Jews expelled from Jerusalem and its surroundings and, according to later sources, the forced baptism of Jews throughout the empire, in revenge for their alleged collaboration with the Persians. Within seven years, however, Jerusalem would surrender to the Arabs, and the Cross was taken to Constantinople in 636. The event became one of the most celebrated in medieval art and legend, and a model for crusading imagery; Piero della Francesca's frescoes in Arezzo show Heraclius defeating Khosrow and returning the Cross.
scholarship: Drijvers, 'Heraclius and the restitutio crucis', in Reinink & Stolte (eds.), The Reign of Heraclius (2002)
Zuckerman, 'Heraclius and the return of the Holy Cross', Travaux et Mémoires 17 (2013)
Drijvers, 'Heraclius and the restitutio crucis', in Reinink and Stolte (eds.), The Reign of Heraclius (2002)
Zuckerman, 'Heraclius and the return of the Holy Cross', in Zuckerman (ed.), Constructing the Seventh Century (2013)
Kaegi, Heraclius (2003)

sources.a: History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria

death_of_muhammad_632.detail: According to the Muslim tradition, Muhammad, after leading the Farewell Pilgrimage to Mecca in March 632, fell ill with fever and headaches at Medina in the house of his wife Aisha, and died there on 8 June 632 (12 Rabi I 11 AH), aged about 62; he was buried in Aisha's room, now within the Mosque of the Prophet. At his death most of Arabia acknowledged his authority, through treaties with tribes and the conquest of Mecca in 630, and an expedition under the young Usama ibn Zayd was preparing to march to the Syrian frontier. He left no son and no clear provision for the succession. At a meeting in the hall (saqifa) of the Banu Sa'ida, the Medinan Ansar proposed one of their own leaders, but Umar and Abu Ubayda persuaded them to accept Abu Bakr, Muhammad's father-in-law and earliest supporter, as successor (khalifa). Ali, Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, and his supporters later contested this choice, the origin of the Sunni-Shia split. Many tribes considered their allegiance to have been personal to Muhammad and refused to pay the alms tax, while others followed rival prophets. Abu Bakr's response, the Ridda wars of 632-633, unified Arabia by force and created the army that invaded Syria and Iraq in 633-634. Some revisionist scholars point to the Doctrina Jacobi, a Greek text written in 634, which speaks of a prophet appearing among the Saracens, and to Christian sources implying that Muhammad led the first invasions, to question the traditional date; most historians accept 632.
death_of_muhammad_632.debate: Shoemaker argues from non-Muslim sources that Muhammad may have been alive at the start of the conquest of Palestine.
scholarship: Watt, Muhammad at Medina (1956)
Donner, Muhammad and the Believers (2010)
Shoemaker, The Death of a Prophet (2012)

battle_of_walaja_633.debate: Tactical details are literary and may be modelled on later practice.

scholarship: Booth, Crisis of Empire: Doctrine and Dissent at the End of Late Antiquity (2014)
Allen (ed.), Sophronius of Jerusalem and Seventh-Century Heresy (2009)

sources.w: ACO ser. 2, II (Acts of the Sixth Council)

scholarship: Hoyland, In God's Path (2015)
Kaegi, Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests (1992)

khalids_desert_march_634.detail: In 633 Abu Bakr sent four armies under Amr ibn al-As, Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan, Shurahbil ibn Hasana and Abu Ubayda to Syria, where they met growing Roman resistance. Khalid ibn al-Walid, who had conquered al-Hira and the lower Euphrates in Iraq in 633, was ordered to reinforce them. To arrive quickly and by surprise, he chose the most direct route across the desert from Iraq to Syria. The tradition, preserved in Tabari, Baladhuri and others, describes the march: Khalid, with perhaps 500 to 800 picked men (later traditions say up to 9,000), crossed from Qurraqir to Suwa, a five-day march without water, guided by Rafi ibn Umayra of the Tayy tribe; the camels were made to drink large amounts before setting off, and some were slaughtered on the way so that the water in their stomachs could be given to the horses. When the guide, nearly blind, found the hidden spring at Suwa by the smell of a boxthorn, the army survived. Khalid emerged near Palmyra, which surrendered, raided the Ghassanids at Marj Rahit on Easter Sunday, and joined the Muslim armies near Bostra, which he helped take. The route is debated: a northern route through the Euphrates valley and Palmyra, a central route through the desert, and a southern route via Dumat al-Jandal have been proposed. The march, which probably took place in spring 634, is famous as a feat of endurance, but it was also strategically important: it brought the most experienced Muslim commander to Syria before the decisive battles of Ajnadayn, Fahl and the Yarmuk, and surprised the Romans, who did not expect an army from the desert.
khalids_desert_march_634.debate: The route, date and size of the force are disputed.
scholarship: Donner, The Early Islamic Conquests (1981)
Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007)
Kaegi, Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests (1992)

battle_of_ajnadayn.detail: The first major battle between the Arabs and a Roman field army took place at Ajnadayn, between Ramla and Beit Guvrin (Eleutheropolis) in southern Palestine, traditionally on 30 July 634 (28 Jumada I 13 AH). After the Arab victory at Dathin near Gaza in February 634, in which the Roman commander Sergius was killed, Heraclius, then at Emesa, sent an army under his brother Theodore (or under a commander named in Arabic sources as Wardan) to Palestine. The Arab armies in Syria, under Amr ibn al-As, Yazid, Shurahbil and Abu Ubayda, combined with the forces of Khalid ibn al-Walid, who had just arrived from Iraq, and gave battle. The Muslim tradition reports heavy fighting, a Roman defeat and the flight of the Roman army to Jerusalem, Gaza, Caesarea and Damascus, with Arab losses including several notable Companions. Numbers are uncertain: later traditions give 100,000 Romans, an impossible figure; modern estimates are of the order of 10,000-20,000 on each side. Christian sources say little about the battle; the Chronicle of 640 by Thomas the Presbyter records a battle between the Romans and the 'Arabs of Muhammad' in February 634 near Gaza (Dathin), and Theophanes mentions the defeat of Theodore. The victory opened Palestine to the Arabs, who besieged its cities, and led Heraclius to send another army, defeated at Fahl in early 635. The exact location and the identity of the Roman commander are debated; some scholars have suggested that Ajnadayn and the Yarmuk have been confused in the tradition. The battle marks the beginning of the Arab conquest of Roman Syria.
battle_of_ajnadayn.debate: Date, location and Roman command are disputed; the date of 30 July 634 is traditional.
scholarship: Donner, The Early Islamic Conquests (1981)
Kaegi, Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests (1992)
Hoyland, In God's Path (2015)

siege_of_damascus_635.detail: After their victories at Ajnadayn (634) and Marj al-Saffar, the Arab armies blockaded Damascus, the main city of Phoenicia Libanensis, from about March 635. The siege lasted about six months. The city, with strong walls and a garrison, was cut off from outside help after the Roman relief army was defeated at Fahl (Pella) in January 635. According to the Muslim tradition, the city surrendered in September 635 under negotiations conducted by the bishop or the fiscal official Mansur ibn Sarjun, grandfather of John of Damascus, with Khalid ibn al-Walid, who agreed to spare the lives and property of the inhabitants, their churches and their walls in return for the payment of tribute (jizya), at one dinar and a measure of wheat per head. Another tradition says that Khalid entered the eastern gate by assault at night while Abu Ubayda accepted the surrender at the western gate, leading to a dispute over whether the city had been taken by force or by treaty, which affected the legal status of its property; the jurists settled that it was by treaty. As the Roman counter-offensive that ended at the Yarmuk approached in 636, the Arabs temporarily evacuated Damascus, returning after the victory. Damascus became the capital of the Umayyad caliphate under Mu'awiya, governor of Syria from 639 and caliph from 661. Its Christian population remained in the majority for a long time; the cathedral of St John was shared, according to tradition, until the caliph al-Walid I built the Great Mosque in 705-715. The surrender of Damascus is a classic example of the negotiated capitulations that marked the conquest of Syria.
siege_of_damascus_635.debate: Whether Damascus was taken by treaty or force, and the date (635 or 636), are debated in the Arabic sources.
scholarship: Donner, The Early Islamic Conquests (1981)
Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007)
Kaegi, Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests (1992)

battle_of_the_yarmuk.detail: After the fall of Damascus and Emesa in 635-636, Heraclius, based in Antioch, assembled the largest army he could raise to recover Syria: regular troops, Armenians under Vahan (the commander-in-chief), troops under the sakellarios Theodore Trithyrios, Christian Arabs of the Ghassanid king Jabala ibn al-Ayham, and Slavs. Numbers are uncertain; Arab sources speak of 200,000 or more, modern estimates range from 15,000-20,000 to 40,000-50,000. The Arab armies, perhaps 20,000-30,000, evacuated Emesa and Damascus and concentrated south of the Golan, near the Yarmuk river and its tributary the Wadi al-Ruqqad. After weeks of manoeuvres and skirmishes in which the Romans were weakened by quarrels between Vahan and Theodore, a mutiny of the Armenians who proclaimed Vahan emperor according to Theophanes, and the desertion of Christian Arabs, the decisive battle took place over several days, ending on 20 August 636 (12 Rajab 15 AH). The Arab tradition describes a series of attacks in which the Muslim women at the rear drove back fleeing men, and a final cavalry charge by Khalid that separated the Roman cavalry from the infantry; the Roman infantry was driven into the ravines of the Wadi al-Ruqqad, where many died. A dust storm blowing in the faces of the Romans is also mentioned. Vahan and Theodore were killed. The defeat was decisive: Heraclius abandoned Syria, the Roman army never again faced the Arabs in a pitched battle in Syria, and Jerusalem, Antioch, Aleppo and Caesarea fell within four years. Theophanes and the Arabic sources agree on the outcome, if on little else, and the battle was remembered on both sides as the moment Syria was lost.
battle_of_the_yarmuk.debate: Numbers, the command structure and the exact sequence of the battle are debated.
scholarship: Kaegi, Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests (1992)
Donner, The Early Islamic Conquests (1981)
Hoyland, In God's Path (2015)
Jandora, 'The battle of the Yarmuk: a reconstruction', Journal of Asian History 19 (1985)
Nicolle, Yarmuk 636 AD (1994)

heraclius_leaves_syria_636.debate: The farewell is a literary topos; Kaegi notes that Heraclius continued to direct defence from Anatolia.
scholarship: Kaegi, Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests (1992)

surrender_of_emesa_636.debate: The returned tribute story may be idealising; it illustrates the conquerors' wish to present themselves as protectors.

battle_of_qadisiyya.debate: Dated 636 by most, but 637 or 638 in some traditions; numbers and the day-by-day narrative are heavily literary. Sa'd was said to have directed the battle from a castle roof because of boils.

siege_of_jerusalem_637.detail: Jerusalem, whose patriarch Sophronius had lamented in his Christmas sermon of 634 that the Saracens prevented Christians from going to Bethlehem, was blockaded by the Arabs under Amr ibn al-As or Abu Ubayda from 636, after the Yarmuk. Its garrison and people held out, apparently for several months, until Sophronius agreed to surrender on condition that the caliph Umar come in person to accept it, according to the Muslim tradition and Theophanes. Umar travelled from Medina to al-Jabiya in the Golan, where he organised the administration of Syria, and then entered Jerusalem in 637 or 638, dressed in a simple camel-hair garment, according to Theophanes, who calls his appearance 'diabolical pretence'. The terms, known in a later version as the Covenant of Umar, guaranteed the lives, property and churches of the inhabitants in return for the jizya, and, according to Tabari's version, excluded Jews from residing in the city; some versions of the tradition say Jews were allowed to return, which they had been forbidden since Hadrian, with limited exceptions. Sophronius showed Umar the Holy Sepulchre, where, according to a later legend, Umar refused to pray to prevent the church being turned into a mosque. Umar visited the Temple Mount, then a rubbish dump, and ordered it cleared; a simple mosque was built there, which the Gallic pilgrim Arculf described around 680, and which was replaced by the Dome of the Rock in 691-692. Sophronius died soon after the surrender, in 638 or 639. The capture of Jerusalem gave the new Muslim community control of a city sacred to Jews, Christians and Muslims.
siege_of_jerusalem_637.debate: Date (637 or 638) and the authenticity of the terms are debated.
scholarship: Kaegi, Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests (1992)
Gil, A History of Palestine 634-1099 (1992)
Levy-Rubin, Non-Muslims in the Early Islamic Empire (2011)
Conrad, 'Umar at Sargh: the evolution of an Umayyad tradition on flight from the plague', in Leder (ed.), Story-telling in the Framework of Non-fictional Arabic Literature (1998)
Booth, Crisis of Empire (2014)

sources.w: ACO ser. 2, I (Lateran Council of 649), text of the Ecthesis

arab_invasion_of_egypt_639.detail: After the conquest of Syria and Palestine, Amr ibn al-As, who had traded in Egypt before Islam according to the tradition, persuaded the caliph Umar, who was meeting the commanders at al-Jabiya, to allow him to invade Egypt; Umar, the tradition says, sent a letter ordering him to turn back if he had not yet crossed the border, which Amr opened only after entering Egypt. Amr left Caesarea or Gaza in December 639 with perhaps 3,500-4,000 men, mostly from the tribes of Akk and Ghafiq, crossed Sinai and celebrated the Feast of the Sacrifice at al-Arish. He besieged Pelusium (al-Farama) for about a month, taking it in early 640, and advanced through the eastern Delta to Bilbeis, which fell after a month, and then to the fortress of Babylon near Memphis at the head of the Delta, where he camped in spring 640. Egypt was defended by a considerable Roman army under the commander Theodore and the governor of Arcadia and others, but divided by rivalries and by the hostility of the Coptic population toward the Chalcedonian patriarch Cyrus (al-Muqawqis), who had persecuted the Miaphysites since 631. John of Nikiu, a Coptic bishop writing at the end of the seventh century, is the principal non-Arab source, describing in vivid detail the indecision of the Roman commanders, the atrocities of the conquerors, and the collaboration of some Egyptians. Arab sources, especially Ibn Abd al-Hakam's Futuh Misr, are much later and contain legendary elements. The conquest of Egypt, completed with the capitulation of Alexandria in 641-642, deprived the empire of its richest province and its grain supply, and gave the Arabs a base for the conquest of North Africa and a fleet.
scholarship: Butler, The Arab Conquest of Egypt (1902; 2nd ed. Fraser, 1978)
Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007)
Butler, The Arab Conquest of Egypt (1902; 2nd ed. 1978)
Booth, 'The Muslim conquest of Egypt reconsidered', Travaux et Mémoires 17 (2013)

battle_of_heliopolis_640.detail: In spring 640 Amr ibn al-As, with perhaps 4,000 men, was encamped near the fortress of Babylon, unable to take it, and asked the caliph Umar for reinforcements. Umar sent some 4,000 men under al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, a cousin of Muhammad, which arrived in June 640, bringing the Arab army to about 12,000-15,000. The Roman army of Egypt under Theodore, supreme commander, which had concentrated at Babylon, came out to give battle near Heliopolis (Ayn Shams), north of Babylon, in July 640. According to the Arab tradition, Amr divided his army into three: the main force faced the Romans, while two detachments, one hidden at Umm Dunayn on the Nile and another in the hills to the east, attacked the Romans from behind during the battle. The Romans broke and fled, some to Babylon and others to Nikiu downstream. John of Nikiu reports the battle as a Roman defeat caused by the indecision of the commanders, and describes the subsequent capture of the fort of Umm Dunayn and of Fayyum. The victory gave the Arabs control of the region around Babylon and Memphis and allowed them to begin a regular siege of the fortress, which surrendered in April 641. Heliopolis was the decisive field battle of the conquest of Egypt: after it, the Roman army did not again risk a pitched battle in Egypt and confined itself to defending fortified cities, especially Alexandria, while divisions within the Roman leadership deepened after the death of Heraclius in February 641. The tactical model of the hidden detachments resembles accounts of other battles in the conquest literature and may be partly literary.
scholarship: Butler, The Arab Conquest of Egypt (1978)
Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007)

umars_diwan.debate: Tradition dates it to 15 or 20 AH (636 or 641).

death_of_heraclius_641.detail: Heraclius died in Constantinople on 11 February 641, aged about 66, after a reign of over thirty years. In his last years, after the loss of Syria, he lived mostly in the palace of Hieria on the Asian shore, suffering, according to Nikephoros, from a fear of water (he crossed the Bosporus on a bridge of boats screened with branches so as not to see the sea) and from a disease, perhaps dropsy, in which his genitals turned back on themselves so that his urine sprayed his face, a punishment, according to contemporaries, for his incestuous marriage to his niece Martina. His last years were dominated by the Arab conquests, the failure of his religious policy (the Ekthesis of 638, which Pope John IV condemned), conspiracies, including one in 637 led by his illegitimate son Athalarichos, who was mutilated and exiled, and the struggle for succession between Constantine III, his son by Eudokia, and Heraclonas, his son by Martina. His will named Constantine III and Heraclonas co-emperors with equal rights, with Martina as their mother and empress, a solution which led to a crisis: Constantine III died in May 641, perhaps poisoned, and Heraclonas and Martina were overthrown in September-October 641 in favour of Constantine III's son Constans II. Heraclius was buried in the church of the Holy Apostles. His reign is one of the most paradoxical in Roman history: he saved the empire from Persia in a brilliant war and restored the True Cross, but lost the eastern provinces to the Arabs within a decade. Historians also attribute to his reign the beginning of administrative changes, such as the use of Greek as the language of government and the title of basileus.
scholarship: Kaegi, Heraclius: Emperor of Byzantium (2003)
Reinink & Stolte (eds.), The Reign of Heraclius (610-641): Crisis and Confrontation (2002)
Haldon, The Empire That Would Not Die (2016)
Kaegi, Heraclius, Emperor of Byzantium (2003)
Reinink and Stolte (eds.), The Reign of Heraclius (2002)
Haldon, Byzantium in the Seventh Century (1990)

surrender_of_babylon_fortress_641.detail: The fortress of Babylon, a Roman stronghold built under Trajan and rebuilt under Diocletian on the right bank of the Nile, at the point where the river divides into the Delta (in present-day Old Cairo), controlled river traffic between Upper and Lower Egypt. Its massive walls and towers, parts of which survive under the Hanging Church and the Coptic Museum, were defended by a large garrison. After the battle of Heliopolis in July 640, Amr ibn al-As besieged it from September 640. According to the tradition, the Roman patriarch and governor Cyrus negotiated with Amr, agreeing to pay tribute, but Heraclius rejected the agreement and recalled Cyrus to Constantinople, where he was accused of treason. The siege lasted seven months. The defenders were weakened by disease and by news of the death of Heraclius in February 641, which removed hope of reinforcements. The Arabs finally stormed or forced the surrender of the fortress on Easter Monday, 9 April 641 (or Good Friday, 6 April), al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam leading an assault over the walls, according to some traditions. The garrison was allowed to leave by river for Nikiu and Alexandria. Amr's camp near the fortress became the garrison city of Fustat, the new capital of Egypt and later the core of Cairo, where Amr built the first mosque in Africa in 641-642. The fall of Babylon opened the Delta and the way to Alexandria. John of Nikiu describes the fall and the atrocities that followed in the towns of the Delta, including Nikiu, where the inhabitants were massacred in May 641.
surrender_of_babylon_fortress_641.debate: The date (Good Friday or Easter Monday 641) and whether it was taken by storm or treaty are debated.
scholarship: Butler, The Arab Conquest of Egypt (2nd ed. 1978)
Butler, The Arab Conquest of Egypt (1978)
Sheehan, Babylon of Egypt: The Archaeology of Old Cairo (2010)
Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007)

treaty_of_alexandria_641.detail: After the death of Heraclius in February 641, a power struggle in Constantinople between Constantine III, Heraclonas and Martina paralysed imperial policy. Martina's regime, seeking peace on the eastern front, restored Cyrus, the former Chalcedonian patriarch, who had negotiated with Amr in 640 and had been exiled by Heraclius, and sent him back to Alexandria in September 641 with full powers to make peace. Cyrus travelled to Babylon, where he met Amr, and signed a treaty on 8 November 641. According to John of Nikiu, the principal source, the terms were: an armistice of eleven months to allow the Roman troops to evacuate Alexandria by sea with their property; payment of a tribute (poll tax) of two dinars per adult male, plus a land tax; the delivery of 150 soldiers and 50 civilians as hostages; the Arabs undertaking not to seize churches or interfere with Christians; and the Jews allowed to remain in Alexandria. When the Alexandrians learned of the treaty they rioted against Cyrus, who persuaded them that it was the best option. The Roman garrison left Alexandria on 17 September 642, and Amr entered the city. Cyrus had died in March 642. The treaty marked the end of nearly a thousand years of Greek and Roman rule in Egypt since Alexander. In 645-646 a Roman fleet under Manuel briefly recovered Alexandria, but Amr retook it in 646. The well-known story that Amr burned the Library of Alexandria on Umar's orders appears only in thirteenth-century sources and is generally considered a legend. The treaty's terms, known mainly from John of Nikiu, became a model for later conquests.
treaty_of_alexandria_641.debate: The famous story of Amr burning the Library of Alexandria on Umar's orders first appears in thirteenth-century writers (Abd al-Latif al-Baghdadi, Ibn al-Qifti) and is rejected by historians; the library had long since ceased to exist in its Ptolemaic form. A Roman fleet briefly retook Alexandria in 645-646.
scholarship: Butler, The Arab Conquest of Egypt (2nd ed. 1978)
Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007)
Butler, The Arab Conquest of Egypt (1978)
Booth, 'The Muslim conquest of Egypt reconsidered', Travaux et Mémoires 17 (2013)

succession_crisis_641.debate: Exact dates in 641 are uncertain; Constantine III's death is placed between April and May, Martina's fall in September-November.

romulus.detail: The twins legend is attested in Greek sources from the 4th-3rd century and monumentalised at Rome by the Ogulnii in 296. Romulus' 'institutions' (Senate of 100, curiae, the asylum, the rape of the Sabines, joint rule with Titus Tatius) are etiological reconstructions. Wiseman argues Remus was added in the 4th century to reflect patrician-plebeian power-sharing.
scholarship: Wiseman, Remus: A Roman Myth (1995)
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 57-80

numa_pompilius.detail: The Calpurnii, Pomponii, Pinarii and Aemilii later claimed descent from his sons. The supposed 'books of Numa' discovered in 181 BC were burned as subversive.

servius_tullius.detail: Murdered at the instigation of his daughter Tullia and her husband Tarquinius Superbus; Tullia drove her carriage over his body in the Vicus Sceleratus. The 'Servian' constitution as described by Livy is a 4th-3rd century system projected back. His patronage of Fortuna and Mater Matuta at the Forum Boarium (Sant'Omobono temples, 6th century) is archaeologically plausible.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 130-141, 173-197

tarquinius_superbus.detail:
Lucius Tarquinius, called Superbus ('the Proud'), was by tradition the seventh and last king of Rome (534-509), son or grandson of Tarquinius Priscus. He came to power through crime: married to Tullia, daughter of King Servius Tullius, after each had murdered their first spouses, he seized the throne, had Servius killed in the street, and Tullia drove her carriage over her father's body in the street thereafter called the Vicus Sceleratus. He ruled without consulting the Senate, executed his opponents, and forced the plebs to labour on the Capitoline temple and the Cloaca Maxima.

He was also the most powerful of the kings. He presided over the Latin council at the spring of Ferentina and had its rebellious spokesman Turnus Herdonius of Aricia drowned; he took Suessa Pometia, captured Gabii through his son Sextus' treachery (signalling with the famous lopping of the tallest poppies, a motif borrowed from Herodotus' story of Thrasybulus and Periander), concluded the treaty with Gabii kept in the temple of Dius Fidius, and planted colonies at Signia and Circeii. Legend made him buy the Sibylline Books from an old woman who burned six of the nine before he paid her full price for the last three. The first treaty with Carthage, which assumes Roman hegemony over the coastal Latin cities, reflects his dominion.

Expelled in 509 after his son's rape of Lucretia, he spent fourteen years trying to return, with Veii and Tarquinii at the Silva Arsia, with Porsenna, and with the Latins at Lake Regillus, before dying in exile at Cumae in 495, the guest of the tyrant Aristodemus. Modern historians see the Superbus portrait as a Greek tyrant stereotype grafted on to a real ruler, possibly of the Etruscan Tarchna family; the archaeology of late 6th-century Rome, a city of some 285 hectares with monumental temples and drains, fits a strong monarchy. The François Tomb at Vulci, showing the killing of a 'Cneve Tarchunies Rumach', preserves an Etruscan memory of the Tarquins in internecine wars.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 215-239

lucretia.detail:
Lucretia, daughter of Sp. Lucretius Tricipitinus and wife of L. Tarquinius Collatinus, is the central figure of the foundation legend of the Republic. When the young princes at the siege of Ardea wagered on their wives' virtue and rode home by night, they found the king's daughters-in-law feasting, and Lucretia late at night spinning wool among her maids. Her beauty and chastity inflamed Sextus Tarquinius, who returned days later as a guest and, threatening to kill her and lay a dead slave beside her to make it appear she had been caught in adultery, raped her. She sent for her father and husband, each to come with a trusted friend; they came with P. Valerius and L. Junius Brutus. She told them what had happened, made them swear to avenge her, declared that though she absolved herself of guilt she would not be freed from punishment, so that no unchaste woman should live by her example, and stabbed herself. Her body, displayed in the forum of Collatia and in Rome, roused the people against the Tarquins.

For Livy and Ovid she was the supreme exemplum of pudicitia, the Roman matron's chastity, whose violation by a tyrant justified revolution, as the Verginia story would justify the fall of the decemvirs. Augustine, in the City of God, challenged the Roman admiration: if she was innocent, her suicide was the killing of an innocent woman; if she consented, she was not admirable. The story mirrors Greek tales in which sexual outrage triggers the fall of tyranny, notably the Athenian tyrannicides.

Lucretia became one of the most represented women of antiquity in later culture: Shakespeare's narrative poem The Rape of Lucrece (1594), paintings by Botticelli, Titian, Cranach, Artemisia Gentileschi and Rembrandt, and Benjamin Britten's opera The Rape of Lucretia (1946). Modern scholarship (Donaldson, Joshel) reads the legend as a meditation on the female body as the site of political order.

lucius_junius_brutus.detail:
L. Junius Brutus was, according to tradition, the son of Tarquinius Superbus' sister, who survived his uncle's murder of his father and brother by pretending to be dim-witted, earning the name brutus ('dullard'). Sent to Delphi with the king's sons, he carried a gold rod hidden in a hollow staff as his offering, and when the oracle said the first to kiss his mother would rule Rome, he pretended to stumble and kissed the earth, mother of all. When Lucretia killed herself he drew the knife from her body and swore the oath that began the revolution, harangued the people in the Forum, won over the army at Ardea, and was elected consul with Collatinus in 509.

As consul he made the people swear never to allow a king, enlarged the Senate to 300 by enrolling equestrian leaders (conscripti), and persuaded Collatinus to resign. He presided over the trial of the royalist conspirators, among them his own sons Titus and Tiberius, and watched unmoved as they were scourged and beheaded. In the battle at the Silva Arsia against Veii and Tarquinii, Brutus and Arruns, son of Tarquin, charged each other and fell together; the matrons mourned him for a year as the avenger of chastity. A bronze statue of him with drawn sword stood on the Capitol among the statues of the kings.

Brutus is the founding hero of Republican liberty, but his historicity is doubtful. The plebeian Junii Bruti of the later Republic claimed descent from him, which the tradition that he executed his only sons made awkward; Posidonius invented a third son to save the claim. His most famous descendant, M. Junius Brutus, put the first consul's head on his coins (54 BC, with the legend BRVTVS and the image of Servilius Ahala) and was urged by anonymous graffiti at the statue on the Capitol to live up to his ancestor before the Ides of March 44.

lucius_tarquinius_collatinus.detail: His expulsion illustrates the archaic idea of a whole gens tainted by the regnum; Sp. Lucretius and then Publicola replaced him.

publius_valerius_publicola.detail:
P. Valerius, later called Publicola or Poplicola ('friend of the people'), belonged to a gens said to descend from the Sabine Volesus who came to Rome with Titus Tatius. He was one of the witnesses of Lucretia's death and the oath, was elected suffect consul after Collatinus' resignation in 509, and was consul again in 508, 507 and 504 by the traditional count. After Brutus' death he governed alone for a time, and suspicion that he aimed at kingship was dispelled by his demolition of his house on the Velia and by lowering the fasces before the people.

A cluster of measures is credited to him: the first law granting citizens a right of appeal (provocatio) against capital sentences by magistrates, a law making anyone who aspired to kingship sacer, so that he could be killed without trial, the appointment of quaestors to administer the treasury in the temple of Saturn, and a rule that magistrates' fasces carry no axes in the city. He triumphed over Veii after the Silva Arsia, fought Porsenna, and in 504 celebrated a triumph over the Sabines in the year Attus Clausus migrated to Rome. He died in 503 so poor that the state paid for his funeral, the women mourned him for a year, and his family received the right of burial inside the city.

Plutarch paired Publicola's Life with that of Solon, as the lawgiver of a free state. Modern scholars attribute much of his image to the Valerian family tradition, transmitted by the 1st-century annalist Valerius Antias, who credited Valerii with every popular law (509, 449, 300). The Lapis Satricanus, a dedication of c. 500 to Mars by the 'companions of Poplios Valesios', has been tentatively linked to him, though the identification is disputed. If accepted, it shows a Valerius leading a private war band, a world of aristocratic warlords far from the civic hero of tradition.
scholarship: Broughton, MRR I 1-7

lars_porsenna.detail:
Lars Porsenna (Lars is an Etruscan praenomen or title; the name may render Etruscan Purthna) was king of Clusium, the inland Etruscan city on the Chiana valley route from Etruria to Latium. Roman tradition says he besieged Rome in 508 to restore Tarquinius Superbus, occupied the Janiculum, and blockaded the city until the heroism of Horatius Cocles, Mucius Scaevola and Cloelia convinced him to make peace, receiving hostages and the return of the Veientine land. He then sent his son Arruns against Aricia, where the Latins and Aristodemus of Cumae defeated and killed him in 504, and returned the hostages, after which Rome gave him an ivory throne, sceptre, golden crown and triumphal robe.

The other evidence suggests he took Rome. Tacitus speaks of the city's surrender (dedita urbe) to Porsenna; Pliny quotes the treaty forbidding the Romans the use of iron except for farming; and the gifts sent to him are insignia of submission. He may have expelled Tarquin himself, as some modern historians suggest, before his power in Latium collapsed after Aricia. The surviving Etruscan fugitives were settled at Rome in the Vicus Tuscus, and Roman auctions kept a ritual phrase, 'the goods of King Porsenna are for sale'.

Etruscan memory made him a figure of legend. Varro, quoted by Pliny, describes his tomb at Clusium as a square base 300 feet each side containing an inextricable labyrinth, crowned by five pyramids and a bronze disc hung with bells, and above that further tiers of pyramids. Pliny called the description 'fabulous'. Attempts to identify the tomb in the tunnels under Chiusi or at the Poggio Gaiella tumulus have not succeeded. Pliny also reports that Porsenna called down lightning to kill a monster, a sign of the Etruscan reputation for controlling heavenly signs.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 215-218

horatius_cocles.detail: Polybius (6.55) tells a version in which he drowns, as an example of Roman self-sacrifice. A statue in the Comitium, probably of Vulcan or an unrelated lame figure, was explained by his story. Rewarded with as much land as he could plough in a day.

gaius_mucius_scaevola.detail: The legend explained the cognomen of the plebeian Mucii Scaevolae, a great jurist family of the late Republic, and the 'Prata Mucia' across the Tiber.

cloelia.detail: An equestrian statue of her stood at the top of the Sacra Via, a rare honour for a woman; it may originally have represented a goddess (Venus Equestris).

aristodemus_of_cumae.detail: Nicknamed Malakos ('the effeminate', or 'the soft'), he allegedly raised boys as girls to prevent a new aristocracy. He seized Roman grain ships in 492 as Tarquin's heir. Overthrown and killed by the sons of the exiles he had murdered. Dionysius' detailed narrative is thought to derive from a local Cumaean chronicle.
scholarship: Alföldi, Early Rome and the Latins (1965) 56-72

aulus_postumius_albus_regillensis.detail: His son dedicated the temple of Castor in 484. The Postumii were one of the great patrician houses of the early Republic.
scholarship: Broughton, MRR I 10-11

octavius_mamilius.detail: The Mamilii of Tusculum later became Roman citizens and reached the consulship (from 265). Their family legend traced them to Telegonus, son of Odysseus and Circe.

spurius_cassius_vecellinus.detail:
Sp. Cassius Vecellinus was the dominant statesman of the first generation of the Republic. Tradition makes him consul three times: in 502, when he triumphed over the Sabines; in 493, when he concluded the treaty with the Latins that bears his name and dedicated the temple of Ceres, Liber and Libera; and in 486, when he made a treaty with the Hernici admitting them to the Latin alliance. He is also listed as the first master of horse, under the dictator T. Larcius in 501.

In his third consulship he proposed the first agrarian law, distributing land taken from the Hernici and public land occupied by patricians among the plebs and the Latins. His colleague Proculus Verginius and the Senate opposed him, accusing him of buying popularity to make himself king. In 485, after his term, he was condemned and executed. Livy gives two versions: that his own father tried him in a domestic court and had him scourged and killed, dedicating his property to Ceres in a statue inscribed 'given from the Cassian family'; or that the quaestors Caeso Fabius and L. Valerius accused him before the people, who condemned him. His house was razed, and the site, an open space before the later temple of Tellus, remained a warning.

Cassius is the first of the three men of the early Republic, with Sp. Maelius (439) and M. Manlius Capitolinus (384), killed for 'aiming at kingship' (adfectatio regni), a charge that late Republican writers used against the Gracchi and others. His agrarian law is widely seen as a retrojection of Gracchan controversies. But his career is plausible in outline, and his treaties are well attested: Cicero saw the text of the Foedus Cassianum on a bronze column. The later Cassii, including Caesar's assassin, were plebeian, and later writers struggled to connect them with him.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 269-270, 299-301

coriolanus.detail:
Cn. Marcius Coriolanus is the most famous early Roman whose existence is doubtful. According to Livy, Dionysius and Plutarch, he was a young patrician of the Marcian gens, raised by his widowed mother, who won a civic crown at Lake Regillus and in 493, as a junior officer, captured the Volscian town of Corioli almost single-handed, earning his cognomen. Proud and contemptuous of the plebs, he proposed during the famine of 491 that the grain sent from Sicily be withheld unless the plebs gave up the tribunate. Summoned to trial by the tribunes, he refused to appear, was condemned in absence, and went into exile to the Volscian leader Attius Tullius at Antium.

In 488 he led a Volscian army against Rome, taking Circeii, Satricum, Longula, Polusca, Corioli, Lavinium and other Latin towns, and camped at the Fossae Cluiliae, five miles from the city. He sent back delegations of senators and of priests in their robes. Only when his mother Veturia, his wife Volumnia and their children came at the head of the Roman matrons did he yield, saying (in Livy's version) that his mother had saved Rome and ruined her son. The temple of Fortuna Muliebris marked the spot. His end is uncertain: Dionysius and Plutarch say the Volsci killed him as a traitor; Livy reports Fabius Pictor's version that he lived to old age in exile, lamenting that exile is bitterer for an old man.

Modern scholars note that no Marcius appears in the early Fasti and that cognomina derived from conquered towns are otherwise later. The story may combine a genuine memory of Volscian advances into Latium in the 480s, possibly under a Latin or Roman renegade, with a moral tale about pride, family and the limits of personal glory. Plutarch paired him with Alcibiades, and Shakespeare's tragedy (c. 1608), based on North's Plutarch, made him a lasting figure of political drama.
scholarship: Cornell, 'Coriolanus: myth, history and performance', in Braund & Gill (eds.), Myth, History and Culture in Republican Rome (2003)

menenius_agrippa.detail: The fable has Greek and Near Eastern parallels (Aesop, an Egyptian papyrus) and was probably attached to him later. He died so poor that the plebs paid for his funeral.

appius_claudius_sabinus.detail: The archetype of Claudian arrogance (superbia) in Livy's portrayal of the family. His descendants include the decemvir (451), Caecus (312) and, through adoption and marriage, the emperors Tiberius and Claudius.

cincinnatus.detail:
L. Quinctius Cincinnatus ('the curly-haired') is the archetype of the citizen-farmer called to save the state. A patrician of an established family, he was impoverished after his son Caeso jumped bail in 461 and the sureties' pledges had to be paid; he retired to a farm of four iugera across the Tiber, later called the Prata Quinctia. In 460, after the consul P. Valerius fell retaking the Capitol from Appius Herdonius, he was elected suffect consul and spoke harshly against the tribunes.

In 458 the Aequi under Gracchus Cloelius trapped the consul L. Minucius and his army on Mount Algidus. Envoys of the Senate found Cincinnatus ploughing, or digging a ditch, and asked him to put on his toga to hear their message; his wife Racilia fetched it from the cottage, and he was hailed as dictator. He chose L. Tarquitius as master of horse, closed the courts, ordered every man of military age to report with five days' food and twelve stakes, marched by night, and enclosed the Aequi with a ditch and palisade. Caught between two Roman armies, they surrendered and passed under the yoke. Cincinnatus triumphed and laid down the dictatorship after sixteen days. In 439, aged about eighty, he was named dictator again to deal with Sp. Maelius, whom his master of horse C. Servilius Ahala killed in the Forum.

The details are legendary, and the four-iugera farm sits oddly with a wealthy patrician house; the episode may also be a doublet of other rescues of trapped armies. But its moral power proved enormous. Livy uses it to show contempt for wealth in early Rome, and it became a model for Republican virtue in the modern world: George Washington was hailed as the American Cincinnatus when he resigned his command in 1783, officers of the Continental Army founded the Society of the Cincinnati, and the city of Cincinnati in Ohio was named after it.
scholarship: Broughton, MRR I 39, 56

appius_herdonius.detail: An example of the archaic condottiere with a personal war band, like Attus Clausus or the Fabii.

appius_claudius_decemvir.detail:
Ap. Claudius, called Crassus Inregillensis Sabinus in the Fasti, probably a son or grandson of Attus Clausus, was consul-designate for 451 when the consulship was suspended and the first board of decemvirs was elected to write the laws. He was its leading member and, in Livy's narrative, a skilled populist who courted the plebs. When a second board was elected for 450, he manipulated the elections to secure his own re-election alongside compliant colleagues, including men of plebeian names, and the board ruled as a tyranny: 120 lictors with axes, executions without appeal, refusal to lay down office at the end of the year.

His downfall came through his lust for Verginia, the plebeian centurion's daughter whom he tried to claim as a slave through his client M. Claudius. After Verginius killed her in the Forum and the armies seceded, the decemvirs were forced to abdicate. Verginius, as tribune, prosecuted Appius, who invoked the appeal he had denied others; he was imprisoned and killed himself before trial, or was killed on the tribunes' order.

Livy's Appius is the culmination of a recurring type: the arrogant Claudian patrician who despises the plebs, like his grandfather the consul of 495 and his father the consul of 471. T. P. Wiseman and others have argued that this hostile image of the Claudii was shaped by late Republican annalists, especially Licinius Macer, and by the political quarrels of Clodius' time, and that Appius may have been a reforming figure, author of a law code that many plebeians wanted. Some scholars also suspect that the image of a tyrannical second decemvirate was constructed to explain the unpopular clauses of the last two tables.
scholarship: Broughton, MRR I 45-48

verginia.detail: A conscious doublet of Lucretia, her story ends the decemvirate as Lucretia's ended the monarchy.

gaius_canuleius.detail: Livy's speech for him (4.3-5) is one of the great set pieces on the equality of citizens, appealing to Rome's history of admitting outsiders (Numa, Tarquinius Priscus, Servius).

spurius_maelius.detail: His razed house site, the Aequimaelium, remained an open space below the Capitol used as a livestock market. Cicero repeatedly cites his death as just tyrannicide.

gaius_servilius_ahala.detail: His dagger became a symbol of tyrannicide: Marcus Brutus, Caesar's assassin, displayed Ahala's portrait alongside L. Brutus' on his coins (c. 54 BC) through his Servilian mother.

aulus_cornelius_cossus.detail: Augustus' claim to have read 'consul' on Cossus' linen corslet served to deny the honour to M. Licinius Crassus in 29-27 BC.
scholarship: Rich, 'Augustus and the spolia opima', Chiron 26 (1996)

lars_tolumnius.detail: A Tolumnius family is attested in Etruscan inscriptions at Veii (a 6th-century dedication by Karcuna Tulumnes in the Portonaccio sanctuary), which lends the name authenticity.

marcus_furius_camillus.detail:
M. Furius Camillus dominated Rome in the generation of Veii and the Gallic sack, and Livy called him a second founder of the city. He was censor in 403, consular tribune six times (401, 398, 394, 386, 384, 381) and dictator five times (396, 390, 389, 368, 367). As dictator in 396 he took Veii by tunnelling into its citadel, summoned Juno Regina to Rome by evocatio, and triumphed with four white horses, a sacrilegious imitation of Jupiter that alienated the plebs. In 394 he besieged Falerii; when a schoolmaster led the sons of the leading Faliscans into the Roman camp, Camillus had him stripped and driven back by the boys with rods, and the Faliscans, moved by his good faith, surrendered.

In 391, accused over the Veientine booty, he went into exile at Ardea, praying that Rome would need him. In 390, recalled by a decree carried by messengers through the Gallic lines, he was named dictator, arrived as the ransom was being weighed, declared that Rome would be ransomed with iron, not gold, and destroyed the Gauls. He then persuaded the people not to abandon the ruined city for Veii, in a speech Livy makes a meditation on Rome's sacred places. In the following years he defeated the Volsci at Maecium (389), the Etruscans at Sutrium, the Volsci and Praenestines at Satricum (381), arranged Tusculum's incorporation, and in 367 defeated a Gallic raid near Alba and presided over the Licinio-Sextian compromise, vowing a temple of Concord. He died of plague in 365.

Polybius does not mention him, and the hero of 390 is almost certainly a later elaboration; the miraculous rescue contradicts the versions in which the Gauls left with the gold. Momigliano showed that the Concord vow and much of Camillus' role as reconciler reflect later political ideology. Ancient writers read him as a model for later saviours and Augustus' propaganda drew on him as a refounder. Plutarch wrote his Life, without a Greek pair surviving.
scholarship: Momigliano, 'Camillus and Concord', CQ 36 (1942)
Bruun, 'What every man in the street used to know: M. Furius Camillus, Italic legends and Roman historiography', in Bruun (ed.), The Roman Middle Republic (2000)

brennus.detail:
Brennus is the name Roman tradition gave to the leader of the Senonian Gauls who defeated Rome at the Allia and sacked the city in 390 (387/386). Polybius does not name the commander. Livy, Plutarch and Diodorus make him the chieftain who besieged Clusium, demanded the surrender of the Fabian envoys who had violated the law of nations, led the army to the Allia, took the city, and besieged the Capitol for seven months. When the Romans complained that the weights for the ransom of 1,000 pounds of gold were false, he threw his sword onto the scales and said 'vae victis', woe to the vanquished, the phrase by which he is remembered.

In Livy's patriotic version Camillus arrived at that moment and destroyed the Gauls in two battles, killing Brennus' army to a man. Other traditions, preserved by Polybius, Diodorus and Strabo, have the Gauls depart with the gold because the Veneti were raiding their new lands in the Po valley, or be ambushed by the Caeretans on the way home. Justin says the Gauls who sacked Rome then sought alliance with Dionysius of Syracuse, and some may have marched south as mercenaries.

The same name was borne by the leader of the Celtic army that attacked Delphi in 279, which has led some scholars to suggest that 'brennos' was a title or that the Roman tradition borrowed the name from the Greek story. The Senones had settled the Adriatic coast south of Ariminum shortly before, and their grave goods at Montefortino and Filottrano show warriors with Etruscan bronzes and Greek wine services. Brennus became a symbol of barbarian violence in Roman memory, while in 19th-century France he was celebrated as a national hero of Gallic resistance.

marcus_manlius_capitolinus.detail:
M. Manlius, consul in 392, was the hero of the defence of the Capitol in 390: woken by the cackling of Juno's sacred geese as Gauls climbed the cliff at night, he rushed to the edge, struck the first Gaul down, and rallied the defenders. He was rewarded with gifts of grain and wine from each soldier, and Roman tradition derived his cognomen Capitolinus from the exploit, though it probably came from the family's residence on the Capitol. His house stood on the Arx.

After the sack, jealous of Camillus' fame and moved, says Livy, by the misery of debtors, he became the plebs' champion. In 385 he paid from his own purse the debt of a decorated centurion being led away in bondage, sold his estate at Veii to free 400 debtors, and accused the patricians of hiding the gold intended for the Gallic ransom. The Senate appointed a dictator, A. Cornelius Cossus, who imprisoned him; the plebs' outcry forced his release. In 384 he was tried for aiming at kingship. In the Campus Martius, where he could point to the Capitol he had saved and display the spoils of 30 enemies, the people would not condemn him; the trial was moved to the Peteline grove, out of sight of the citadel, and he was condemned and thrown from the Tarpeian Rock, the place of his triumph. His house was razed, the site later given to the temple of Juno Moneta, and the Manlian gens resolved that no patrician Manlius would again bear the praenomen Marcus.

Manlius completes the trio of early 'tyrants' with Sp. Cassius and Sp. Maelius. Livy's account echoes the Catilinarian and Gracchan crises, but the debt problem of the 380s was real, and the political use of debt relief by an ambitious aristocrat is plausible. The paradox of the saviour of the Capitol thrown from it fascinated ancient writers.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. I (1997) 476-567

titus_manlius_torquatus.detail:
T. Manlius Imperiosus Torquatus embodied the severity of the 4th-century Roman aristocracy. As a slow-spoken youth he was banished to the family's farm by his harsh father, L. Manlius Imperiosus; when a tribune prosecuted the father in 362 the son forced him at knifepoint to drop the case. Elected a military tribune, in 361 he answered the challenge of a huge Gaul at the bridge over the Anio and killed him, taking his torque (torques) and placing it, bloodstained, around his own neck; the soldiers' jesting cognomen Torquatus passed to his descendants. The annalist Claudius Quadrigarius' vivid description of the duel, quoted by Gellius, is one of the finest surviving passages of early Latin prose.

He was dictator in 353 against Caere, in 349 to hold elections and in 320, and consul in 347, 344 and 340. In the Latin War of 340, having ordered that no one should fight outside the ranks, he learned that his son had accepted a challenge from the Tusculan cavalry commander Geminus Maecius and killed him. He had his son bound to the stake and beheaded before the army; 'Manlian commands' (imperia Manliana) became proverbial, and the young men of Rome refused to go out to meet him when he returned in triumph. He led the Roman army at the battle of Vesuvius, where his colleague Decius devoted himself, and won again at Trifanum.

The Manlii Torquati kept his memory alive: a moneyer of the 60s BC put a torque border on his coins, and Cicero's friend L. Manlius Torquatus is the Epicurean spokesman in De finibus. The duel and the execution, whether or not exact, defined for later Romans the subordination of family to discipline.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998)

marcus_valerius_corvus.detail:
M. Valerius Corvus (or Corvinus) had perhaps the longest career in Roman history. Pliny says he lived to 100 and that 46 years separated his first and sixth consulships. As a military tribune in 349 he accepted the challenge of a gigantic Gaul in the Pomptine territory; a raven landed on his helmet and attacked the Gaul's face with beak and claws, and Valerius killed him, taking the name Corvus. Augustus placed his statue among the great men in his Forum with a raven on its helmet.

He was elected consul at the age of 23 in 348, and again in 346, 343, 335, 300 and 299 (as suffect), dictator in 342 and 302 or 301, and held 21 curule offices in all. In 346 he defeated the Volsci and burned Satricum; in 343 he won the first great Roman victory over the Samnites at Mount Gaurus in Campania; in 342, as dictator, he calmed the mutiny of the Campanian garrison, granting amnesty and protection from arbitrary discharge; in 335 he took Cales, where a Latin colony followed; and as consul in 300 he carried the third lex Valeria on appeal, the first that most scholars accept as genuine, which made it a crime for a magistrate to scourge or execute a citizen who had appealed to the people. In 302 or 301 as dictator he campaigned against the Marsi and Etruscans and restored the Cilnii at Arretium.

Livy portrays him as an affable commander who shared the soldiers' games, the opposite of the stern Manlius. His career spans the critical half-century from the Gallic raids to the Third Samnite War, and its length, plausible in principle, may also have attracted episodes from homonymous Valerii.
scholarship: Broughton, MRR I

gaius_licinius_stolo.detail:
C. Licinius Stolo was the plebeian tribune who, with L. Sextius Lateranus, led the decade-long campaign that ended in the laws of 367. Varro explains his cognomen: he was so careful a farmer that he dug out the useless suckers (stolones) from the roots of his trees and vines. Livy introduces him through his wife Fabia, younger daughter of the patrician M. Fabius Ambustus, whose envy of her sister, wife of a consular tribune, prompted her father to help his plebeian son-in-law win the consulship for men of his order.

Elected tribune from 376, Licinius and Sextius proposed three laws: relief of debt by deducting interest already paid, a ceiling of 500 iugera on holdings of public land, and the replacement of consular tribunes by consuls, one of whom must or might be plebeian. Re-elected year after year, they vetoed the election of curule magistrates and faced vetoes from colleagues won over by the patricians. They also carried the reform of the priestly board for the Sibylline Books, making it ten men, half plebeian. The laws passed in 367, and Sextius became the first plebeian consul in 366. Licinius was consul in 364 and 361, though the Fasti call the consul C. Licinius Calvus, and the identity of Stolo and Calvus is debated.

In 357 he was prosecuted by the plebeian aedile M. Popillius Laenas under his own law and fined 10,000 asses, because he and his emancipated son held 1,000 iugera of public land between them. The irony delighted ancient writers. Modern historians see Licinius as the leader of a wealthy plebeian elite seeking office, using the grievances of debtors and land-hungry farmers to build support, whose success created the patricio-plebeian nobility of the Middle Republic. The 500-iugera limit was revived, or invented in Livy's sources, by Ti. Gracchus in 133.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. I (1997)

lucius_sextius_lateranus.detail: His consulship marks the formal admission of plebeians to supreme magistracy, though plebeian tenure was not continuous until 342.

gaius_marcius_rutilus.detail: His son C. Marcius Rutilus Censorinus, censor twice (294, 265), carried the law against iterating the censorship.

publius_decius_mus_cos340.detail:
P. Decius Mus was a plebeian whose family became the type of self-sacrifice for the state. As a military tribune in 343, during the First Samnite War, he saved the army of the consul A. Cornelius Cossus, trapped in a valley near Saticula, by seizing a hill above the Samnites with a detachment, drawing their attack, and breaking out at night through their sleeping camp. The army awarded him the grass crown (corona graminea or obsidionalis), the highest Roman military decoration, given by soldiers to the man who saved them from a siege, together with a golden crown, 100 oxen and a white bull with gilded horns.

As consul in 340 with T. Manlius Torquatus he commanded against the Latins and Campanians. Both consuls dreamed that one side's general and the other side's army were owed to the Earth and the gods of the dead. At the battle near Vesuvius, when the Roman left under his command gave way, he called the pontifex M. Valerius, who dictated to him the formula of devotio, offering himself together with the enemy's army to the Di Manes and Tellus. Wearing the toga in the Gabine manner and standing on a spear, he recited the prayer, then rode into the enemy and was killed. His body was found the next day buried under enemy corpses, and his colleague gave him a splendid funeral.

Livy's text of the devotio is the most important document of the ritual, though its authenticity and that of the act itself are debated. His son devoted himself at Sentinum (295), and his grandson was said to have done so at Ausculum (279). Cicero repeatedly cites the three Decii as the supreme example of patriotic death, and the family's glory showed that plebeian virtus could match patrician nobility.

publius_decius_mus_cos295.detail: His devotio is attested in Livy, Polybius' contemporary-era chronology and was celebrated by the dramatist Accius in a praetexta, 'Decius'.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005)

quintus_publilius_philo.detail:
Q. Publilius Philo was the most important plebeian statesman of the generation after the Licinio-Sextian laws. As consul in 339 he defeated the Latins on the Fenectane plains and triumphed. Named dictator the same year, he carried three laws that Livy calls 'most favourable to the plebs and most damaging to the nobility': that plebiscites should bind all citizens; that the patrician senators should give their approval (auctoritas patrum) to laws proposed in the centuriate assembly in advance, before the vote, so that the patricians could no longer annul legislation after the event; and that one of the two censors must be a plebeian. In 336 he became the first plebeian praetor, despite the presiding consul's objection, and in 332 he was censor.

In his second consulship (327) he besieged Neapolis and Palaepolis, and when his year ended the people voted to extend his command 'in place of a consul' (pro consule) until the siege was finished: the first prorogation of imperium, the device that later made possible Rome's overseas commands. He captured the city in 326, after which Neapolis received a favourable treaty, and celebrated the first triumph by a proconsul. He was consul again in 320 and 315, serving with Papirius Cursor in the years after the Caudine Forks.

Philo's career shows how quickly the plebeian elite integrated into the leadership of the state after 367. His laws of 339 are part of the series (449, 339, 287) that gradually made the plebeian assembly sovereign; modern scholars debate what each added. His prorogation transformed the annual magistracy into a flexible instrument for long wars.

lucius_papirius_cursor.detail:
L. Papirius Cursor was the Roman general most admired by the annalists for the Second Samnite War. He was consul five times (326, 320, 319, 315, 313) and dictator twice (325 and 309). His cognomen 'the runner' was said to come from his speed of foot; he was also known for an enormous appetite, physical strength and an iron discipline that made him feared by his soldiers. Livy tells that he once ordered his lictor to prepare the axe for a Praenestine praetor who had been slow, then had him merely cut a tree root before dismissing him.

As dictator in 325 he left his master of horse Q. Fabius Rullianus in command with orders not to engage; Fabius fought and won at Imbrinium, and Papirius demanded his execution for disobedience. Fabius fled to Rome, and only the pleas of his father, the Senate and the people persuaded Papirius to pardon him, while insisting that military authority had been upheld. After the Caudine Forks, as consul in 320 and 319, he was credited with retaking Luceria, recovering the 600 hostages and sending 7,000 Samnites under the yoke, a story many modern historians reject. As dictator in 309 he won the battle in which the Samnites fought with gilded and silvered shields, and he triumphed.

Livy uses Papirius in his famous digression on Alexander the Great, arguing that had Alexander invaded Italy he would have met generals like Papirius, Fabius, Valerius Corvus and Manlius, and been defeated. His son of the same name, consul in 293 and 272, won at Aquilonia and took Tarentum. The Papirii were a patrician house whose prestige rested heavily on these two men.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005) 184-261

lucius_papirius_cursor_cos293.detail: His Aquilonia triumph brought vast bronze and silver into the treasury; the spoils decorated the temple of Quirinus and the Forum.

quintus_fabius_maximus_rullianus.detail:
Q. Fabius Maximus Rullianus (or Rullus) was the greatest Roman commander of the Samnite wars and the founder of the Fabii Maximi. As master of horse in 325 he fought and won at Imbrinium against the dictator Papirius Cursor's orders, and was nearly executed. He was consul five times (322, 310, 308, 297, 295), dictator in 315, when he was defeated by the Samnites at Lautulae, and censor in 304, and was princeps senatus.

His campaign of 310 made his name. With Sutrium besieged by the Etruscans, he sent his brother, raised at Caere and fluent in Etruscan, disguised as a peasant through the dense Ciminian forest, then marched his army through it into central Etruria, where no Roman army had been, ravaged the land and won at Perusia, provoking the Senate's alarm and then its admiration. In 308 he defeated the Umbrians at Mevania. As censor in 304 he undid Appius Claudius' distribution of humble citizens and freedmen among all the tribes, confining them to the four urban tribes, which earned him the cognomen Maximus, and he instituted the annual parade of the equites on 15 July. In 295, at nearly 70, he commanded with Decius Mus at Sentinum, where his patience and use of reserves won the battle after his colleague's death, and vowed a temple to Jupiter Victor. In 292 he served as legate to his son, Q. Fabius Gurges, and shared in the capture of Gavius Pontius.

Livy's account of him is shaped by the family historian Fabius Pictor, and Diodorus sometimes contradicts the Fabian victories. The Esquiline painting naming a Q. Fabius may show him. His great-grandson Q. Fabius Maximus Cunctator, the opponent of Hannibal, inherited his cognomen and a family tradition of cautious generalship.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vols. II-IV

spurius_postumius_albinus_cos321.detail: The cognomen Caudinus appears in some sources. The handing-over (deditio noxae) was repeated with Mancinus in Spain in 137.

gavius_pontius.detail:
Gavius Pontius, son of Herennius, commanded the Samnite army in 321 and inflicted on Rome its most humiliating defeat before Cannae. Learning that the Roman consuls were camped near Calatia, he sent soldiers disguised as shepherds to tell them that the Samnites were besieging Luceria, lured them through the Caudine pass and trapped them between blocked defiles. Livy gives him eloquent speeches: before the war, protesting that the Samnites had offered every satisfaction and that the gods would favour the side wronged; at Caudium, consulting his aged father, who advised him either to free the Romans without humiliation or to kill them all. Pontius chose the middle course, making the consuls and the army pass under the yoke and taking 600 equites as hostages.

When Rome repudiated the agreement and handed over the consul Sp. Postumius and the other guarantors, Pontius refused to accept them, denouncing the Romans for mocking the gods with legal tricks and offering to return the army to the pass if they wished to cancel the peace. Livy then makes him suffer defeat and the yoke at Luceria, which modern scholars largely reject.

A Gavius Pontius commanded the Samnites again in 292 against Q. Fabius Gurges; captured, he was led in Fabius' triumph in 291 and executed, a breach of the usual Roman custom of sparing kings that later writers condemned. Whether this was the same man, thirty years after Caudium, or a son is uncertain. Cicero quotes a saying attributed to Pontius that he wished he had been born when the Romans accepted bribes, for then he would not have let them rule. In Samnite memory he remained the national hero; the Pontii of the late Republic, such as Pontius Telesinus who fought Sulla at the Colline Gate in 82, claimed his tradition.

appius_claudius_caecus.detail:
Ap. Claudius Caecus ('the Blind') was the most original Roman statesman before the Punic wars. His career, recorded in an elogium set up in the Forum of Augustus, included three military tribunates, the quaestorship, two curule aedileships, two praetorships, the censorship (312), two consulships (307 and 296), a dictatorship and three interregna. As censor with C. Plautius he built the Via Appia to Capua and the Aqua Appia, Rome's first aqueduct, carrying water 16.4 km, mostly underground, from springs near the Via Praenestina to the Forum Boarium; he enrolled sons of freedmen in the Senate and distributed the landless and freedmen among all the tribes, increasing their voting weight; he transferred the cult of Hercules at the Ara Maxima from the Potitii to public slaves; and he refused to resign after eighteen months, holding office, by some accounts, for nearly five years until his roads and aqueduct were finished.

As consul in 296 he fought in Etruria and Samnium and vowed the temple of Bellona, in front of which stood the column from which the fetials threw a spear to declare war. His scribe Gnaeus Flavius published the legal formulas and the calendar of court days. Blind in old age, he had himself carried into the Senate in 280 when it was inclined to accept Pyrrhus' peace offer through Cineas, and delivered a speech that persuaded it to refuse while Pyrrhus remained in Italy; Cicero knew the speech in writing. He is the first Roman author whose works were known later: a collection of moral maxims in verse ('every man is the maker of his own fortune' is attributed to him), a legal treatise, and spelling reforms, including the rhotacism that turned intervocalic s into r (Valesii into Valerii) and the removal of the letter z.

Mommsen saw him as a democratic reformer; others see a Hellenising aristocrat who built a personal clientele among the urban population. The contradictions of his censorship, combining public works on an unprecedented scale with the defiance of convention, anticipate later popular politicians.
scholarship: Humm, Appius Claudius Caecus: la République accomplie (2005)
Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005)

gnaeus_flavius.detail: He dedicated a bronze shrine to Concord in the Graecostasis, vowed without the Senate's approval; the episode produced a law requiring Senate or tribune consent for dedications. Livy draws on the annalist Licinius Macer and on Piso for his story.

quintus_ogulnius_gallus.detail: A neat example of a plebeian noble whose career spans religious reform, monument-building and Hellenistic diplomacy in the generation before the Punic Wars.

gellius_egnatius.detail: The Egnatii were a prominent Samnite family; Marius Egnatius led the Samnites in the Social War (90-89).

lucius_cornelius_scipio_barbatus.detail:
L. Cornelius Scipio Barbatus ('the Bearded'), consul in 298, censor perhaps in 280, and great-grandfather of Scipio Africanus, is the earliest Roman whose own funerary monument survives. His peperino sarcophagus, the oldest burial in the Tomb of the Scipios on the Via Appia, was found in 1780 and is now in the Vatican Museums. Its form, with a Doric frieze of triglyphs and rosettes and Ionic volutes on the lid, is a Roman adaptation of Greek altar design. The inscription, in Saturnian verse, reads in archaic Latin: 'Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus, offspring of his father Gnaeus, a brave and wise man, whose appearance was most equal to his virtue, who was consul, censor and aedile among you; he took Taurasia and Cisauna in Samnium, subdued all Lucania and led away hostages.'

Livy tells a different story for 298: that Barbatus campaigned in Etruria, fighting an indecisive battle near Volaterrae, while his colleague Cn. Fulvius fought in Samnium. Livy also places Barbatus as a legate in the campaigns of 297 and 295.
