Jerome's chronicle says he was born in 94, wrote in intervals of madness caused by a love potion, killed himself at forty-four, and that Cicero edited the poem; Donatus' life of Virgil places his death in 55 on the day Virgil assumed the toga virilis. The love potion story is generally rejected as Christian polemic, and the dates are inconsistent.

The poem explains that the universe consists of atoms moving in an infinite void, that the world arose by chance and will perish, that the soul is made of atoms and dies with the body, and that the gods exist but take no interest in the world. Its purpose is to free humanity from fear of death and of the gods, which Lucretius blames for crimes such as Agamemnon's sacrifice of Iphigenia. Book 5 traces the history of civilisation; Book 6 ends with the plague of Athens, perhaps unfinished.

The poem's power lies in its imagery and argument, combining Ennian epic style with philosophical precision; Virgil's Georgics echo it ('felix qui potuit rerum cognoscere causas'), and Ovid predicted its immortality. A fragment from the Villa of the Papyri at Herculaneum appears to contain lines from it.

Lost in the Middle Ages, the poem survived in a few Carolingian manuscripts; Poggio Bracciolini's discovery in 1417 made it a key text for Renaissance and Enlightenment thought, influencing Montaigne, Gassendi and modern atomism.
lucretius.debate: Dates of birth and death and the circumstances of death are uncertain.
scholarship: Sedley, Lucretius and the Transformation of Greek Wisdom (1998)
Gale (ed.), Oxford Readings in Lucretius (2007)
Greenblatt, The Swerve (2011)

augustus.detail: Born Gaius Octavius on 23 September 63 BC in Rome, son of a new man from Velitrae and of Atia, Julius Caesar's niece, Octavian was adopted in Caesar's will in 44 BC and, at nineteen, raised a private army, fought Antony at Mutina, formed the triumvirate with Antony and Lepidus, proscribed his enemies, defeated the Liberators at Philippi, besieged Perusia, crushed Sextus Pompey and finally defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium (31 BC). The settlements of 27 and 23 BC turned his military supremacy into a lasting constitutional form: a provincial command over most legions, tribunician power and maius imperium, dressed in the language of a restored Republic and the informal title princeps. Over a 41-year reign he created the standing army with fixed terms and a military treasury, the praetorian guard, urban cohorts and vigiles, a provincial administration of legates and equestrian prefects and procurators, the cura annonae, the regions and vici of Rome and the imperial cult. He transformed the city, claiming to have found it brick and left it marble, and promoted a programme of moral and religious renewal through the marriage laws, the Secular Games of 17 BC and the restoration of 82 temples. His wars added Egypt, north-west Spain, the Alps, Noricum, Raetia, Pannonia, Galatia, Moesia and Judaea, but the Illyrian revolt and the loss of Varus's legions ended expansion in Germany. His great weakness was the succession: Marcellus, Agrippa, Gaius and Lucius died before him, and he was forced to adopt Tiberius. His private life was simple: he lived in a modest house on the Palatine, wore clothes woven by his household, suffered chronic illness and gambled at dice. The ancient verdict was divided: Tacitus (Annals 1.9-10) sets the praise of admirers against the critics who saw only deceit, cruelty and a lust for power. Modern interpretations range from Syme's cold revolutionary to Galinsky's cultural visionary. He died at Nola on 19 August AD 14 and was deified.

livia.detail: Livia Drusilla, born on 30 January 58 BC, daughter of Marcus Livius Drusus Claudianus, who killed himself after Philippi, married her cousin Tiberius Claudius Nero and bore him Tiberius (42 BC). After fleeing with him through Sicily and Greece in the civil wars, she was divorced in 39 BC and married Octavian on 17 January 38 BC while six months pregnant with Drusus, a union that brought Octavian the prestige of the Claudii and lasted 52 years without children. She played the role of the virtuous Roman matron and was the first woman to receive the sacrosanctity of a tribune (35 BC), statues and, in 9 BC after Drusus's death, the ius trium liberorum. She owned vast estates and workshops across the empire, managed a household of over a thousand slaves and freedmen known from the columbarium of her familia, and acted as patron to client kings, Herod's family, provincial cities and senatorial families, including Otho's grandfather and Galba. Her villa at Prima Porta, ad gallinas albas, with its painted garden room and the statue of Augustus, and her house on the Palatine survive. Augustus consulted her on policy and Dio credits her with persuading him to pardon Cinna. By his will she was adopted into the Julian family as Julia Augusta. Under Tiberius, her influence and her claims to share in decisions created tension; Tiberius refused the Senate's proposals to call him "son of Julia" or give her the title mater patriae. She died in 29 aged 86, and Tiberius did not attend her funeral or execute her will; Caligula, who called her "Ulysses in a stola", delivered the eulogy. Claudius deified her in 42. The hostile tradition, especially Tacitus and Dio, accused her of poisoning Marcellus, Gaius, Lucius, Agrippa Postumus, Germanicus and even Augustus to advance Tiberius, charges with no solid basis that reflect hostility to female power. Modern biographers (Barrett) stress her political skill and her model of the imperial woman as dynastic mediator.

agrippa.detail: Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa, born c. 63 BC of obscure family, studied with Octavian at Apollonia and was with him when news of Caesar's murder arrived; he remained his closest collaborator for thirty years. He prosecuted Cassius in absentia, commanded at Perusia, as governor of Gaul crossed the Rhine (39-38 BC) and resettled the Ubii, and as consul in 37 BC built the Portus Julius in the Lucrine lake to train a fleet with which he defeated Sextus Pompey at Mylae and Naulochus (36 BC), earning the naval crown. His command of the left wing at Actium won the decisive battle. As aedile in 33 BC, after holding the consulship, he renovated Rome's water supply and sewers, distributing oil and salt and providing free baths and barbers. He was consul again in 28 and 27 BC with Octavian and conducted the census. After 23 BC he received a maius imperium in the East and tribunician power in 18 BC, renewed in 13, and married Julia (21 BC), siring Gaius, Lucius, Julia, Agrippina and Agrippa Postumus. He completed the Cantabrian war in 19 BC with severe measures against his own mutinous troops, settled the Bosporus in 14 BC, befriended Herod, and was commissioned to pacify Pannonia shortly before his death in 12 BC. His buildings included the Pantheon, the Baths of Agrippa, the Saepta Julia, the Aqua Virgo and Aqua Julia, and his geographical commentaries underpinned the map displayed in the Porticus Vipsania. He refused triumphs offered to him, setting a precedent that later restricted triumphs to the imperial family. Seneca the Elder reports that aristocrats despised his origins, and Agrippa himself suppressed his gentile name Vipsanius. Pliny records he suffered painful gout in his last years. His grandchildren included Caligula and Agrippina the Younger, and his great-grandson was Nero. Tacitus and Dio portray him as the indispensable loyal partner, and modern historians agree that the Principate would hardly have been possible without him.

julia_the_elder.detail: Julia, born in 39 BC, was Augustus's only child, by his second wife Scribonia, whom he divorced on the day of her birth. Raised strictly under Livia's supervision, taught to spin and weave and forbidden to speak to anyone without permission, she became the key instrument of her father's dynastic policy. She married her cousin Marcellus (25 BC), then Agrippa (21 BC), with whom she had five children, travelled with him in the East, where cities honoured her as a goddess, and after his death was married to Tiberius (11 BC), who had to divorce Vipsania. The marriage failed, and their only child died in infancy. Julia was intelligent, witty and popular; Macrobius preserves her sayings, such as her retort, when asked how her children resembled Agrippa despite her affairs, that she only took on passengers when the ship was full. In 2 BC, the year of the Forum of Augustus and the title pater patriae, Augustus learned of her adulteries and, without consulting her, denounced her in a letter to the Senate, banishing her to the island of Pandateria. Her lovers allegedly included Iullus Antonius, son of Mark Antony, who was executed or committed suicide, and other nobles such as Sempronius Gracchus and Quinctius Crispinus, who were exiled. Augustus refused all appeals, saying that she should have such a daughter and wife, and after five years allowed her to move to Rhegium, but she was never permitted wine, luxuries or visitors without his inspection. When Tiberius became emperor he cut her allowance, and she died of starvation or despair in 14. Augustus excluded her from his Mausoleum. Ancient writers saw a moral scandal; many modern historians suspect that the affair concealed a political conspiracy around Iullus Antonius and her son-in-law Paullus Aemilius, perhaps aimed at Tiberius or at securing power for her sons, as the severity of the punishment suggests.
julia_the_elder.debate: Moral scandal or political conspiracy behind her exile.

maecenas.detail: Gaius Maecenas, born c. 70 BC at Arretium of an Etruscan royal line (Horace calls him "descended from kings"), remained an equestrian all his life and never held a magistracy, yet was Octavian's chief political agent in the triumviral years. He negotiated the marriage of Octavian and Scribonia (40 BC), helped broker the treaties of Brundisium (40 BC) and Tarentum (37 BC) with Antony, and governed Rome and Italy informally during Octavian's absences, notably during the Actium campaign, when he suppressed the conspiracy of the younger Lepidus (30 BC). His greatest legacy was cultural patronage: from about 39 BC he supported Virgil, who dedicated the Georgics to him, Horace, to whom he gave the Sabine farm, Propertius and Varius, so that his name became the generic word for a patron of the arts. Through his circle the poets helped articulate the ideology of the new regime without crude propaganda. Maecenas was famous for luxury and effeminacy: he wore loose tunics, loved gems and silks, was the first to build a heated swimming pool in Rome, and wrote mannered prose and verse that Augustus parodied and Seneca condemned. His gardens on the Esquiline, built over a paupers' cemetery, were famous. His influence waned after 23 BC, when his wife Terentia's brother Licinius Murena was implicated in a conspiracy and Maecenas warned her, angering Augustus; there were also rumours of Augustus's affair with Terentia. Seneca, who disliked him, reports that he suffered from insomnia and listened to distant music to fall asleep, and quotes his verses expressing a desperate wish to live even maimed. He died in 8 BC, leaving his estate to Augustus and asking him to "remember Horace as you would myself". Dio gives him a long speech advising Octavian to establish a monarchy (52.14-40), a third-century composition. Modern scholars debate how far Maecenas directed the poets as opposed to providing a framework of patronage.

drusus_the_elder.detail: Nero Claudius Drusus, born in January 38 BC, three months after Livia married Octavian, was raised in Augustus's household with his elder brother Tiberius and became the most popular member of the family. With Tiberius he conquered the Raeti and Vindelici in 15 BC, crossing the Alps from Italy while Tiberius advanced from Gaul. As governor of the Three Gauls from 13 BC he dedicated the Altar of Rome and Augustus at Lugdunum on 1 August 12 BC, the day Claudius was born there. In four campaigns from 12 to 9 BC he invaded Germany: he dug the canal from the Rhine to the IJssel, sailed along the North Sea coast and won over the Frisii, defeated the Sugambri, Usipetes and Bructeri, fought the Chatti and Cherusci, nearly lost his army in an ambush at Arbalo (11 BC), built forts at Aliso and on the Taunus, and in 9 BC reached the Elbe, where, Dio says, a giant barbarian woman appeared and warned him to turn back. On the return march he fell from his horse and broke his leg, dying after thirty days of gangrene in his summer camp; Tiberius rode 200 miles in a day and night to reach his deathbed. His body was carried to Rome, the soldiers erected a cenotaph at Mogontiacum, where an annual festival was held, and he was given the posthumous name Germanicus, inherited by his son. Augustus delivered a eulogy and composed his epitaph. Suetonius and Tacitus report that Drusus favoured restoring the Republic and had written to Tiberius suggesting they force Augustus to do so, which later fuelled rumours that Augustus poisoned him, which modern scholars reject. He married Antonia Minor, by whom he had Germanicus, Livilla and Claudius. The Consolatio ad Liviam, a poem on his death attributed to Ovid, and the Tropaeum in Mainz (the Drususstein) commemorate him. His campaigns brought Germany between Rhine and Elbe under Roman control for nearly two decades.

tiberius.detail: Tiberius Claudius Nero, born on 16 November 42 BC, son of Tiberius Claudius Nero and Livia, became Augustus's stepson when his mother remarried in 38 BC. As a teenager he delivered his father's eulogy, rode in the Actium triumph and served in the Cantabrian war. In 20 BC he received the Parthian standards and crowned Tigranes in Armenia; with Drusus he conquered the Alpine peoples (15 BC); he subdued Pannonia (12-9 BC) and, after Drusus's death, Germany, deporting 40,000 Sugambri. Forced to divorce Vipsania and marry Julia, and overshadowed by Gaius and Lucius, he withdrew to Rhodes in 6 BC for seven years. Recalled and adopted in AD 4, he campaigned in Germany, crushed the Illyrian revolt (6-9) and stabilised the Rhine after Varus. Emperor at 55 in 14, he ruled conscientiously for 23 years: he refused divine honours and titles, deferred to the Senate, kept provincial governors in post for long periods ("a good shepherd shears his flock, does not flay it"), avoided wars and new conquests, balanced the budget and left a surplus of 2.7 billion sesterces. But his reserve and dissimulation alienated the aristocracy; the death of Germanicus, the destruction of Agrippina's family and the expanding use of maiestas trials created a climate of fear. From 26 he lived on Capri and let Sejanus rule Rome until his fall in 31, after which the treason trials intensified. Suetonius's stories of depravity on Capri, with swimming boys called his "minnows", are generally discounted as hostile gossip. He died at Misenum in 37, possibly hastened by Macro, and was not deified. Tacitus's portrait of a hypocrite whose true nature was gradually revealed is a literary masterpiece but has been challenged by modern historians (Levick, Seager), who see a capable but awkward aristocrat ill-suited to the role of popular princeps, whose administration was among the most competent of the period. Velleius's panegyric offers the contemporary official view.

germanicus.detail: Germanicus Julius Caesar, born on 24 May 15 BC as son of Drusus the Elder and Antonia Minor, took his father's posthumous cognomen and was adopted by Tiberius in AD 4 at Augustus's command, marrying Augustus's granddaughter Agrippina the Elder, by whom he had nine children, including Caligula and Agrippina the Younger. He served in the Illyrian war and on the Rhine, was consul in 12 and in 13 received command of the eight legions on the Rhine. When the legions mutinied on Augustus's death in 14 and offered him the throne, he refused, threatening to kill himself, and restored order by sending away his wife and infant son Gaius ("Little Boots"), the soldiers' favourite. In three campaigns (14-16) he attacked the Marsi, Chatti, Bructeri and Cherusci, buried the remains of Varus's legions, recovered two eagles and defeated Arminius at Idistaviso and the Angrivarian wall, but suffered heavy losses, including the shipwreck of 16. Tiberius recalled him, granted him a triumph (26 May 17) and sent him east with maius imperium, where he settled Armenia, Cappadocia and Commagene. His unauthorised visit to Egypt, Tiberius's private domain, and his quarrels with Piso preceded his death near Antioch in October 19. He was a talented orator and wrote Greek comedies and a Latin translation of Aratus's astronomical poem Phaenomena, which survives. Tacitus presents him as the ideal Roman prince, a contrast to Tiberius and a lost hope of a gentler principate, comparing him to Alexander the Great, but also notes his rashness and theatricality. Modern historians are more critical of his German campaigns, which achieved little at great cost, and his flamboyance. His popularity made his family the focus of opposition to Tiberius and Sejanus and later secured the throne for his son Caligula, his brother Claudius and his grandson Nero. The honours voted after his death, known from the Tabula Siarensis and Hebana, show the cult of his memory.

agrippina_the_elder.detail: Vipsania Agrippina, born c. 14 BC, daughter of Agrippa and Julia and granddaughter of Augustus, married Germanicus in AD 5 and accompanied him on campaign, which was itself unconventional. During the Rhine mutiny of 14 she left the camp with the infant Gaius, shaming the soldiers; in 15 she stood at the Rhine bridge to prevent its destruction and welcomed the retreating troops with clothes and bandages, which Tiberius resented as usurping a commander's role. She went east with Germanicus in 17 and, after his death in 19, carried his ashes from Antioch to Brundisium and Rome, a procession that made her a symbol of loyalty. Convinced that Tiberius and Livia had caused her husband's death, she became the centre of a political faction promoting her sons Nero and Drusus as heirs. Her pride and temper, which Tacitus repeatedly notes, made her an easy target for Sejanus: in 26 she asked Tiberius for permission to remarry, which he refused, and at a dinner she refused to eat fruit he offered, fearing poison. After Livia's death in 29 Tiberius denounced her and Nero to the Senate. She was exiled to Pandateria, where a centurion beat her so badly that she lost an eye, and she starved herself to death on 18 October 33, the second anniversary of Sejanus's fall; Tiberius boasted that he had not strangled her. Nero had died on Pontia in 31 and Drusus was starved in a palace dungeon in 33. Caligula, her third son, brought her ashes and those of Nero to the Mausoleum of Augustus in 37; the inscribed urn base survives in the Capitoline Museums. Her daughter Agrippina the Younger became empress and mother of Nero. Tacitus's portrait, sympathetic but critical, emphasises her chastity, fertility and ambition. Modern scholars see her as an early example of a woman wielding influence through dynastic legitimacy and popular sympathy rather than formal position.

sejanus.detail: Lucius Aelius Sejanus was born at Volsinii in Etruria c. 20 BC, son of Lucius Seius Strabo, praetorian prefect under Augustus, and of a woman of senatorial family; he was adopted into the gens Aelia. He accompanied Gaius Caesar to the East and became joint prefect with his father in 14, sole prefect when Strabo became prefect of Egypt. Tacitus's famous portrait (Annals 4.1) describes him as physically tough, bold, secretive, a mixture of servility and arrogance, his ambition aimed at supreme power. In 23 he concentrated the praetorian cohorts in the Castra Praetoria on the Viminal, creating a formidable instrument. He won Tiberius's trust, especially after saving him in 26 when a grotto collapsed at Sperlonga. In 23, Drusus the Younger, who had struck him, died, poisoned according to later testimony by Sejanus and Drusus's wife Livilla, whom he had seduced. In 25 he asked to marry Livilla and Tiberius refused, warning of senatorial resentment. After Tiberius withdrew to Capri in 26, Sejanus controlled access and correspondence, and engineered the prosecution of the friends of Agrippina and the exile of Agrippina and her son Nero (29) and imprisonment of Drusus (30). Statues of him were set up beside the emperor's, his birthday was celebrated, and he held the consulship of 31 with Tiberius. He received proconsular imperium and seemed about to receive tribunician power when Tiberius, warned (according to Josephus) by Antonia, turned on him. On 18 October 31 he was arrested in the Senate on the reading of Tiberius's letter and executed the same day. His body was abused for three days and thrown into the Tiber, and his children were executed. Juvenal used his fall as the classic example of the vanity of ambition. Modern historians debate whether he plotted a coup or was simply destroyed by Tiberius's suspicion; his career demonstrated the potential of the praetorian prefecture, which several later prefects exploited.

caligula.detail: Gaius Julius Caesar Germanicus, born on 31 August 12 at Antium, son of Germanicus and Agrippina the Elder, grew up in military camps on the Rhine, where soldiers nicknamed him Caligula ("Little Boot") for his miniature uniform. He survived the destruction of his mother and brothers by obsequiousness, lived on Capri with Tiberius from 31 and was named co-heir with Tiberius Gemellus. Acclaimed emperor in March 37 aged 24, he was hugely popular at first: he burned the records of treason trials, recalled exiles, published the imperial accounts and restored elections. In October 37 he fell gravely ill, and afterwards, according to the sources, his behaviour changed. He had Gemellus and Macro killed, lived openly with his sisters (with whom incest was alleged), deified Drusilla on her death in 38, and squandered Tiberius's surplus on spectacles, building projects such as the bridge at Baiae, the Nemi ships, the Vatican circus and the aqueducts. In 39 he revived treason trials, broke with the Senate, and after uncovering the conspiracy of Gaetulicus and Lepidus, exiled his sisters Agrippina and Julia Livilla. His northern expedition of 39-40 ended with soldiers collecting seashells on the Channel coast as "spoils of the Ocean". He demanded worship as a living god, ordered his statue placed in the Jerusalem Temple, had Ptolemy of Mauretania killed and annexed his kingdom. He was murdered by praetorian officers on 24 January 41. The extreme anecdotes of the sources, including the plan to make his horse Incitatus consul, are now often read as distortions of a young autocrat's sarcasm and contempt for the Senate (Barrett, Winterling) rather than evidence of insanity, although Suetonius and Philo describe mental instability. Philo, who met him, offers an eyewitness view of his mockery. Seneca, who survived his hostility, depicts him as the archetype of cruelty. His reign showed how completely the Principate depended on the character of its holder.
caligula.debate: Madness (ancient tradition) or rational if brutal autocracy distorted by hostile sources (Winterling).

claudius.detail: Tiberius Claudius Nero Germanicus, born at Lugdunum on 1 August 10 BC, son of Drusus the Elder and Antonia, suffered from a physical disability, possibly cerebral palsy, that caused a limp, tremor and stammer, and was kept from public life by Augustus and Tiberius; his mother called him a "monster of a man". He devoted himself to scholarship, writing histories of the Etruscans (20 books) and Carthaginians (8 books) in Greek and a history of Rome from 44 BC, encouraged by Livy, and a defence of Cicero. Caligula made him consul in 37 but treated him with contempt. Made emperor by the praetorians in 41, he proved an active and innovative ruler. He conquered southern Britain (43), annexed Mauretania, Lycia, Thrace and Judaea, built the harbour at Portus, the Aqua Claudia and Anio Novus and the drainage tunnel of the Fucine Lake, revived the censorship (47-48) and admitted Gallic nobles to the Senate, defending the decision in a speech preserved on the Lyon tablet. He extended citizenship generously, regulated the treatment of slaves, devoted enormous time to judging cases in person, and developed the central bureaucracy staffed by freedmen such as Narcissus, Pallas, Callistus and Polybius. These features, together with his reliance on his wives, made him the butt of senatorial hostility: Seneca's Apocolocyntosis, Suetonius and Tacitus depict him as absent-minded, pedantic and dominated by women and freedmen. His third wife Messalina was executed in 48 after her bigamous marriage to Gaius Silius, and his fourth, his niece Agrippina, induced him to adopt her son Nero in preference to Britannicus. He executed 35 senators and over 300 knights. He died in October 54, probably poisoned by Agrippina, and was deified. Modern historians (Momigliano, Levick, Osgood) have rehabilitated him as a capable administrator whose reign consolidated the imperial system, and Robert Graves's novels made him a popular figure.

messalina.detail: Valeria Messalina, born c. 17-20, great-granddaughter of Octavia through both parents, married her cousin Claudius around 38 and bore him Claudia Octavia and Britannicus (41). As empress she was immensely influential, controlling access to Claudius together with the freedmen, and she used that power to eliminate rivals: Julia Livilla and Seneca (41), Appius Silanus (42), Julia daughter of Drusus (43), Poppaea Sabina the Elder and Valerius Asiaticus (47), the last of whom she reputedly destroyed to get his gardens. Ancient writers, above all Juvenal (Satire 6), Pliny the Elder, Tacitus and Dio, portray her as insatiable: Juvenal has her slipping out of the palace at night to work in a brothel under the name Lycisca, Pliny claims she competed with a prostitute to see who could have more partners in a night. In 48, while Claudius was at Ostia, she went through a formal marriage ceremony with the consul designate Gaius Silius, with witnesses, a dowry and a feast. The freedman Narcissus, fearing a coup, persuaded Claudius through his concubines that Silius aimed at the throne; Silius and many others were executed. Messalina, waiting in the Gardens of Lucullus, was killed on Narcissus's orders before Claudius, who was said to be softening, could see her; told of her death at dinner, he asked for more wine. The Senate ordered her name removed from monuments. The marriage to Silius remains puzzling: modern historians suggest it was a genuine conspiracy to replace Claudius with Silius as regent for Britannicus, either initiated by Messalina to protect her position as Claudius aged and Agrippina rose, or a plot by Narcissus to destroy her. Her sexual reputation, magnified by later satirists, is regarded with scepticism, as political charges against women typically took sexual form. Her fall opened the way for Agrippina's marriage to Claudius and Nero's succession.
messalina.debate: Whether the marriage to Silius was a coup attempt, a plot by Narcissus or a reckless affair.

agrippina_the_younger.detail: Julia Agrippina, born on 6 November 15 at Ara Ubiorum (later named Colonia Agrippinensis in her honour), daughter of Germanicus and Agrippina the Elder, married Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus in 28 and bore Lucius Domitius, the future Nero, in December 37. Under her brother Caligula she was honoured with her sisters, then exiled in 39 for involvement in the Lepidus conspiracy, and recalled by Claudius in 41. After Messalina's fall she married her uncle Claudius in 49, the Senate having changed the law forbidding marriage with a brother's daughter. She secured Nero's adoption (50) and marriage to Octavia (53), had Seneca recalled as his tutor and Burrus appointed praetorian prefect, and became the first living wife of an emperor to receive the title Augusta and to appear on coins. She received foreign envoys, sat on a tribunal before the standards when Caratacus was paraded, and had a colony founded in her name. She is accused of poisoning Claudius in 54 to secure Nero's succession. In the first year of Nero's reign she appeared on coins facing him, but her domination provoked resistance from Seneca, Burrus and Nero himself; the murder of Britannicus in 55 and her removal from the palace marked her decline. She was murdered on Nero's orders in 59 after the failed attempt with the collapsing boat. She wrote memoirs (commentarii), used by Tacitus and Pliny, which recounted her family's misfortunes. Tacitus describes her as possessing "masculine domination", seeking power for herself through men. Modern historians (Barrett, Ginsburg) emphasise that the hostile portrait reflects senatorial anxiety about female power, while acknowledging her skill and ruthlessness. She was the only woman to be daughter, sister, wife and mother of emperors. Her temple to Divus Claudius on the Caelian was completed later by Vespasian.

nero.detail: Nero Claudius Caesar Augustus Germanicus, born Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus on 15 December 37 at Antium, became emperor at sixteen in October 54. The early reign, guided by Seneca and Burrus, was well regarded: the Senate's role was respected, Corbulo restored the position in Armenia and the treasury was managed carefully. After murdering Britannicus (55) and his mother Agrippina (59), Nero turned to his passions for the lyre, poetry, chariot racing and Greek culture, founding the Juvenalia and Neronia and performing in public, scandalising the aristocracy. Burrus's death in 62, Seneca's retirement and the rise of Tigellinus brought a harsher regime: he divorced and executed Octavia and married Poppaea Sabina, who died in 65, reportedly after he kicked her while pregnant. The Boudican revolt (60-61) and the defeat at Rhandeia (62) were followed by the compromise with Parthia that brought Tiridates to Rome for coronation (66). The Great Fire of 64, for which rumour blamed him and he blamed the Christians, was followed by his rebuilding of Rome with a new building code and the vast Domus Aurea, and by a coinage reform. The Pisonian conspiracy of 65 led to the deaths of Seneca, Lucan, Petronius and many others, and Corbulo was forced to suicide in 67. His tour of Greece (66-67), in which he competed in all the festivals and won 1,808 prizes, ended with the proclamation of Greek freedom at Corinth and the start of the Corinth canal. The revolts of Vindex and Galba in 68 found him unable to act, and he killed himself on 9 or 11 June 68. The senatorial tradition (Tacitus, Suetonius, Dio) made him the archetypal tyrant, and Christians identified him with the Antichrist, but his popularity with the urban plebs and in the Greek East lasted, as false Neros show. Modern scholars (Griffin, Champlin, Drinkwater) analyse him as a performer emperor whose behaviour, though often brutal, was more rational and populist than the sources admit.

seneca.detail: Lucius Annaeus Seneca was born at Corduba c. 4 BC, son of the elder Seneca, the rhetorician, and brother of Gallio and of Mela, father of Lucan. Brought to Rome as a child, he studied rhetoric and Stoic and Pythagorean philosophy (with Attalus and Sotion), spent time in Egypt for his health and entered the Senate under Tiberius. A brilliant orator, he aroused Caligula's jealousy and in 41 was exiled to Corsica on Messalina's charge of adultery with Julia Livilla. Recalled in 49 by Agrippina to tutor her son, he became, with the prefect Burrus, the guiding minister of Nero's early reign, writing his speeches, including the accession speech and the eulogy of Claudius, while privately composing the satire Apocolocyntosis and the treatise De Clementia. He was implicated, at least in the cover-up, in the murder of Agrippina in 59. After Burrus's death in 62 he tried to retire and offered Nero his fortune, estimated at 300 million sesterces, much of it from loans that Dio blamed for provoking the Boudican revolt. In retirement he wrote the Natural Questions and the Moral Letters to Lucilius. Accused of involvement in the Pisonian conspiracy in 65, he was ordered to die; Tacitus describes his long death, in which he opened his veins, took hemlock and finally suffocated in a hot bath, dictating to secretaries and comforting his wife Paulina, who tried to die with him. His works include dialogues on anger, the brevity of life, providence, tranquillity and constancy, consolations, De Beneficiis and nine tragedies (Medea, Phaedra, Thyestes, Oedipus and others) that shaped Renaissance drama. The contrast between his teaching and his wealth and complicity was attacked in his lifetime by Suillius Rufus and has shaped his reputation since. Medieval Christians even forged a correspondence between him and Paul.

corbulo.detail: Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo, son of a senator of the same name, was consul suffect probably in 39; his half-sister Milonia Caesonia was Caligula's wife. Appointed by Claudius to Lower Germany in 47, he defeated the Chaucian pirate leader Gannascus, settled the Frisii and enforced strict discipline, making his soldiers dig a canal between the Rhine and the Meuse, but Claudius ordered him to withdraw behind the Rhine, prompting his remark "how fortunate the Roman generals of old were". After governing Asia, he was sent by Nero in 54 to command in Cappadocia and Galatia against Parthian control of Armenia. He spent years retraining the softened Syrian legions, wintering them in tents in the Armenian highlands with severe punishments, then in 58 took and burned Artaxata and in 59 Tigranocerta, installing Tigranes VI. When his successor Caesennius Paetus capitulated at Rhandeia (62), Corbulo, now governor of Syria, was given an extraordinary maius imperium over the East, invaded Armenia again and in 63 negotiated the settlement of Rhandeia, by which Tiridates received the Armenian crown from Nero in Rome in 66. Corbulo was the most famous general of his age, a tall, imposing figure who wrote memoirs used by Tacitus and Pliny. In 67 Nero summoned him to Greece, and at Cenchreae, on landing, he received the order to die. He stabbed himself, saying "I deserved it" (axios). The reason is unclear: his son-in-law Annius Vinicianus had been involved in a conspiracy at Beneventum in 66. His daughter Domitia Longina married Domitian, and the Flavians honoured his memory. Tacitus admires his discipline but notes his vanity and his manipulation of reports to enhance his reputation at others' expense, especially Paetus's. Modern historians see his career as an example of the limits imposed on great generals by imperial suspicion.

publius_quinctilius_varus.detail: Velleius calls him a man of mild character, more suited to camp leisure than war, who 'came poor to rich Syria and left rich Syria poor'. Modern scholars see him more as the victim of an unworkable policy and of Arminius's betrayal.

arminius.detail: Arminius, born c. 18 or 17 BC, son of the Cheruscan noble Segimer, served with his brother Flavus as an officer of Cheruscan auxiliaries in the Roman army, probably in the Illyrian war, and received citizenship and equestrian rank; his Germanic name is unknown (the identification with "Hermann" is a sixteenth-century invention). Trusted by Varus, he organised a coalition of the Cherusci, Bructeri, Marsi and Chatti, and in September AD 9 lured Varus's army into an ambush and destroyed three legions. He sent Varus's head to Maroboduus of the Marcomanni, inviting him to join the war, but Maroboduus sent it on to Augustus. He had abducted and married Thusnelda, daughter of the pro-Roman Segestes, who opposed him; in 15 Segestes handed her over to Germanicus while she was pregnant, and she and her son Thumelicus walked in Germanicus's triumph in 17. Arminius fought Germanicus in 15-16, nearly destroying Caecina's army at the pontes longi and fighting at Idistaviso and the Angrivarian wall, where he was defeated but escaped, his face smeared with his own blood to avoid recognition. Tacitus records a dialogue across the Weser between Arminius and his loyal brother Flavus, each denouncing the other in Latin and German. In 17 he defeated Maroboduus, whose kingdom collapsed, but his own growing power provoked fears that he aimed at kingship, and in 21 he was murdered by his relatives. Tacitus (Annals 2.88) gives him an epitaph as "undoubtedly the liberator of Germany", who challenged Rome at the height of its power, undefeated in war, still sung of among the Germans. The Chattan chief Adgandestrius had offered to poison him, but Tiberius refused, saying Rome took vengeance openly. In the nineteenth century Arminius became the national hero of Germany, commemorated by the Hermannsdenkmal near Detmold (1875), and his symbolism was later exploited by German nationalism.

herod_the_great.detail: Herod, born c. 73 BC, son of the Idumaean Antipater, who served the Hasmonean Hyrcanus II and Caesar, and the Nabataean Cypros, was appointed governor of Galilee in 47 BC, where he executed the bandit leader Hezekiah, and was declared king of Judaea by the Senate in 40 BC on Antony's and Octavian's initiative after the Parthian invasion installed Antigonus. He took Jerusalem with Roman help in 37 BC and ruled until his death in 4 BC. He married the Hasmonean princess Mariamme, whom he executed in 29 BC, and successfully switched allegiance from Antony to Octavian after Actium, receiving back territory Cleopatra had taken and more. He became one of the greatest builders of antiquity: the rebuilt Temple in Jerusalem with its vast platform (begun c. 20 BC), the fortress palaces of Masada, Herodium (where his tomb was found in 2007), Machaerus and the Antonia, the port city of Caesarea with its harbour Sebastos, Sebaste (Samaria) and benefactions abroad, including endowments for the Olympic Games. He promoted Hellenistic culture and the imperial cult in his Gentile cities while respecting Jewish law in Jerusalem, a balancing act that earned suspicion from both sides. He maintained an efficient administration, relieved a famine in 25 BC with his own wealth, and protected diaspora Jews through his friendship with Agrippa. His later years were dominated by intrigue in his large family: he married ten wives and executed three of his sons, Alexander and Aristobulus (7 BC) and Antipater (4 BC), with Augustus's permission. His death, after a painful illness (possibly chronic kidney disease with Fournier's gangrene), was followed by revolt and the division of his kingdom among Archelaus, Antipas and Philip. Matthew's story of the massacre of the innocents at Bethlehem is not found in Josephus and is generally regarded as legendary. Josephus, drawing on Nicolaus of Damascus, is the main source. Modern historians stress his effectiveness as a Roman client king.

jesus_of_nazareth.detail: Jesus (Yeshua) of Nazareth was born c. 6-4 BC, probably in Nazareth in Galilee (the gospels of Matthew and Luke set his birth at Bethlehem), to Mary and Joseph, a craftsman (tekton); he had brothers, including James, and sisters. Around 28 he was baptised by John the Baptist and, after John's arrest, began preaching the imminent kingdom of God in Galilee, especially around Capernaum and the Sea of Galilee, gathering disciples, including an inner circle of twelve, symbolising the restoration of Israel, among them Peter, Andrew, James and John. He acquired fame as a healer and exorcist, taught in parables, shared meals with tax collectors and sinners, emphasised love of God and neighbour, forgiveness and the reversal of status, and debated the interpretation of the Torah with Pharisees and scribes. He went to Jerusalem for Passover around 30 or 33, where his entry and action in the Temple, overturning the tables of money changers, alarmed the priestly authorities. After a final meal with his disciples, he was arrested at night, examined by the High Priest Caiaphas and handed to the prefect Pontius Pilate, who had him crucified as "King of the Jews". His followers soon proclaimed that God had raised him from the dead and that he would return as messiah and Lord. The main sources are the four gospels (c. 70-100) and Paul's letters (c. 50-60), with references in Josephus (Antiquities 18.63-64, 20.200) and Tacitus (Annals 15.44); later rabbinic and pagan references are polemical. The "quest for the historical Jesus" since Reimarus and Schweitzer has produced varying portraits: apocalyptic prophet (Schweitzer, Sanders, Ehrman), Jewish sage or Cynic-like teacher (Crossan), social reformer or charismatic healer (Vermes). Almost all historians accept that he existed, was baptised by John, preached in Galilee and was crucified under Pilate. The movement he founded spread rapidly through the eastern Mediterranean and reached Rome by the 40s.
jesus_of_nazareth.debate: Reconstructions of the historical Jesus: apocalyptic prophet, sage, reformer or healer.

paul_of_tarsus.detail: Paul (Saul), born c. 5 in Tarsus in Cilicia to a Jewish family of the tribe of Benjamin, was, according to Acts, a Roman citizen by birth, trained as a Pharisee in Jerusalem under Gamaliel, and worked as a tentmaker. He persecuted the followers of Jesus until a vision of the risen Christ near Damascus c. 33-36 made him an apostle to the Gentiles. After time in Arabia (Nabataea), Damascus and a first visit to Peter and James in Jerusalem, he worked for about fourteen years in Syria and Cilicia, then with Barnabas in Cyprus and southern Galatia. At the Jerusalem council (c. 48-49) he won recognition that Gentile converts need not be circumcised, and he confronted Peter at Antioch over table fellowship. In the years c. 49-57 he founded churches in Galatia, Macedonia (Philippi, Thessalonica), Achaea (Corinth, where he appeared before Gallio c. 51-52) and Asia (Ephesus), and organised a collection for the poor of Jerusalem. His seven undisputed letters (1 Thessalonians, Galatians, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Philippians, Philemon, Romans) are the earliest Christian writings and set out his theology: justification by faith in Christ rather than by works of the Law, the inclusion of Gentiles in Israel's promises, the church as the body of Christ, and the imminent return of the Lord. Arrested in the Temple in Jerusalem c. 57, held for two years at Caesarea under Felix, he appealed to Caesar before Festus and was sent to Rome, shipwrecked on Malta on the way, and lived under house arrest in Rome for two years. Christian tradition says he was beheaded on the Via Ostia under Nero, c. 62-67. Colossians, Ephesians, 2 Thessalonians and the Pastorals are widely considered later works in his name. His interpretation has been central to Christian theology (Augustine, Luther) and to modern debates (the "New Perspective" of Sanders, Dunn and Wright) about his relationship to Judaism.

boudica.detail: Boudica, wife of Prasutagus, client king of the Iceni of East Anglia, led the most dangerous revolt against Roman rule in Britain. When Prasutagus died around 60, leaving half his kingdom to Nero and half to his two daughters, in hope of protecting his family, the procurator Catus Decianus and centurions seized the kingdom, flogged Boudica and raped her daughters; Iceni nobles were stripped of their estates. Roman financiers, including Seneca according to Dio, called in loans, and the veterans of the colony at Camulodunum had driven the Trinovantes from their land and built a temple to Claudius regarded as a citadel of oppression. While the governor Suetonius Paullinus was attacking the Druid stronghold of Mona, the Iceni and Trinovantes rose, destroyed Camulodunum, where the last defenders held out in the temple for two days, defeated part of IX Hispana under Petillius Cerialis, and burned Londinium and Verulamium, killing according to Tacitus 70,000 people with torture and impalement. Destruction layers of burnt red clay and ash dated to this time have been found in all three towns. Paullinus, having abandoned Londinium as indefensible, defeated her army in a battle somewhere in the Midlands, and Boudica died by poison or illness. Dio describes her as very tall, with a harsh voice, a mass of tawny hair to her hips, a great golden torque and a multicoloured tunic and cloak, holding a spear, and gives her a speech invoking the goddess Andraste and releasing a hare for divination. Tacitus has her declare that it was customary for Britons to fight under women's leadership. The spelling Boudica (from a Celtic word for victory) is now preferred to the Renaissance form Boadicea. She became a national heroine in Victorian Britain, symbolised by Thomas Thornycroft's bronze group by Westminster Bridge (1902), and her story continues to be debated in terms of colonial exploitation and resistance.

virgil.detail: Publius Vergilius Maro was born on 15 October 70 BC near Mantua in Cisalpine Gaul to a landowning family, educated at Cremona, Milan and Rome, and studied Epicurean philosophy with Siro at Naples. His first work, the Eclogues (c. 42-38 BC), ten pastoral poems modelled on Theocritus, reflected the land confiscations for veterans after Philippi (the first eclogue alludes to the loss and recovery of land) and included the "messianic" fourth eclogue prophesying the birth of a child who would bring a golden age, later read by Christians as a prophecy of Christ. Through Asinius Pollio and Maecenas he entered Octavian's circle and introduced Horace to Maecenas. The Georgics (c. 29 BC), four books on farming, bees and the story of Orpheus, dedicated to Maecenas, were read to Octavian on his return from the East. He then spent eleven years on the Aeneid, the national epic of Rome in twelve books, telling of Aeneas's flight from Troy, his love affair with Dido at Carthage, his descent to the underworld, where he sees the future heroes of Rome, and his war in Latium against Turnus. The poem combines Homeric models with Roman history and Augustan ideology, while expressing the suffering and cost of empire. Virgil went to Greece in 19 BC to revise it, met Augustus at Athens, fell ill at Megara and died at Brundisium on 21 September 19 BC; he asked for the unfinished poem to be burned, but Augustus had it published by Varius and Tucca. He was buried near Naples. Shy, unmarried and reputedly called "Parthenias" (the virgin), he became the central author of Latin education; the Aeneid was quoted on Pompeian walls and studied for centuries, and in the Middle Ages he was seen as a sage and magician, Dante's guide through Hell and Purgatory. Modern criticism debates the "two voices" of the Aeneid, celebration and pessimism.

ovid.detail: Publius Ovidius Naso was born on 20 March 43 BC at Sulmo in the Paelignian country to an old equestrian family; he studied rhetoric in Rome under Arellius Fuscus and Porcius Latro, toured Greece and Asia Minor, held minor judicial posts and abandoned a senatorial career for poetry. Patronised by Messalla Corvinus, he became the leading poet of Rome after the deaths of Virgil, Tibullus and Propertius. His elegiac works include the Amores (love poems to "Corinna"), the Heroides (letters from mythological heroines to absent lovers), the Ars Amatoria (a mock-didactic manual of seduction, c. 2 BC-AD 2), the Remedia Amoris and the Medicamina Faciei Femineae (on cosmetics). His masterpiece, the Metamorphoses, fifteen books of hexameter tales of transformation from the creation of the world to the apotheosis of Julius Caesar and the reign of Augustus, was completed by AD 8, as was half of the Fasti, a poetic calendar of Roman festivals. In AD 8 Augustus suddenly relegated him (keeping his property and citizenship) to Tomis on the Black Sea, citing "a poem and a mistake" (carmen et error): the poem was the Ars Amatoria, while the mistake remains a mystery, often linked to the adultery scandal of Augustus's granddaughter Julia the Younger, exiled the same year. In exile he wrote the Tristia and the Epistulae ex Ponto, laments and appeals to friends and to Augustus and Tiberius, describing the cold, the Getae, the dangers of raids and his learning of the Getic language, in which he claimed to have written a poem. He was never recalled and died at Tomis in AD 17 or 18. His influence on European literature and art, through the Metamorphoses as a source for mythology, has been immense, from Chaucer and Shakespeare to Titian and Bernini. Some scholars have even questioned whether the exile was real, a minority view.

vespasian.detail: Titus Flavius Vespasianus was born on 17 November 9 at Falacrinae near Reate in Sabine country, son of a tax collector and banker of equestrian rank; his mother's family had senatorial connections. He rose slowly through the senatorial career with help from Antonia's freedwoman Caenis, his lifelong companion, and Claudius's freedman Narcissus, and won fame as legate of II Augusta in the conquest of Britain (43-47), fighting thirty battles and taking the Isle of Wight and over twenty hillforts, for which he received triumphal ornaments and the consulship of 51. He governed Africa, where he was pelted with turnips and became so poor he traded mules, accompanied Nero to Greece in 66 and fell from favour for dozing during the emperor's recitals, but was appointed in 67 to suppress the Jewish revolt, perhaps because his humble origins made him no threat. He reduced Galilee and most of Judaea by 68. Proclaimed emperor at Alexandria on 1 July 69, he won the civil war through the Danube legions and Mucianus and reached Rome in 70. As emperor (69-79) he restored order and finances, raising taxes vigorously (hence the urine tax), reorganised the eastern frontier and annexed Commagene, granted Latin rights to Spain, held the censorship (73-74), enrolled new senators from Italy and the provinces, and built the Temple of Peace and the Colosseum, restored the Capitol and completed the temple of Claudius. He established a new dynasty, insisting "either my sons will succeed me or no one will", and associated Titus closely in power. His humour was earthy and his manner affable; his last words were reportedly "Alas, I think I am becoming a god", and, trying to rise, "an emperor should die standing". He died of fever and diarrhoea at Aquae Cutiliae on 23 June 79. The sources are generally favourable, and modern historians (Levick) regard him as one of the most effective emperors, the restorer of the Principate after 68-69.

titus.detail: Titus Flavius Vespasianus, Vespasian's elder son, born on 30 December 39, was educated at court with Britannicus, beside whom he was dining when Britannicus was poisoned. He served as military tribune in Germany and Britain and commanded XV Apollinaris under his father in Judaea, taking Tarichaeae, Gamala and Gischala. He brokered the alliance of Vespasian and Mucianus in 69 and was left to finish the Jewish war, capturing Jerusalem in 70 after a five-month siege and destroying the Temple. He celebrated the triumph with his father in 71 and became his colleague in power, holding tribunician power, seven consulships, the censorship and the praetorian prefecture, in which role he gained a reputation for ruthlessness, killing the consular Caecina Alienus at dinner on suspicion of conspiracy. His affair with the Jewish queen Berenice, who lived with him on the Palatine, caused scandal, and he sent her away. Becoming emperor on 24 June 79, he reinvented himself as the "delight and darling of the human race" (amor ac deliciae generis humani), refusing to sign death warrants and expelling informers. His brief reign was marked by disasters: the eruption of Vesuvius (79), a three-day fire in Rome and an epidemic (80), to which he responded with generous relief. He inaugurated the Colosseum with a hundred days of games and built the Baths of Titus. Suetonius records his saying, on a day when he had given no gift, "friends, I have lost a day". He died of fever on 13 September 81 at the family villa near Reate, aged 41, reportedly saying that he had only one regret; rumours accused Domitian of hastening his death. Rabbinic legend attributed it to a gnat that entered his brain as punishment for destroying the Temple. He was deified, and the Arch of Titus commemorates his apotheosis and triumph. Modern historians note that his popularity owed much to the brevity of his reign and the contrast with Domitian.

domitian.detail: Titus Flavius Domitianus, younger son of Vespasian, born on 24 October 51, was in Rome during the civil war of 69, escaped the burning of the Capitol disguised as a follower of Isis, and was briefly acting ruler before Mucianus arrived. Under his father and brother he was kept in honorific roles and devoted himself to poetry. Emperor from 81 to 96, he ruled with great energy and personal control. He campaigned against the Chatti (83), annexing the Taunus and building the Upper German limes; organised the provinces of Upper and Lower Germany; fought the Dacians after their invasion of Moesia (85-89), losing Oppius Sabinus and Cornelius Fuscus but winning at Tapae (88) and making a peace in 89 that paid Decebalus subsidies; and fought the Suebi and Sarmatians (89-92). He crushed the revolt of Antonius Saturninus (89). He raised army pay by a third, improved the silver content of the coinage (82) before reducing it (85), held the censorship for life, enforced moral legislation, executed Vestals, rebuilt the Capitol and built a huge palace on the Palatine, the Stadium, the Odeum, the Forum Transitorium and a villa at Alba. Administration in the provinces was strict and effective; Suetonius admits that governors had never been more honest. His relations with the Senate were poor: he was suspicious, autocratic and sarcastic, styled "lord and god" by flatterers, and after 93 executed many senators, including the Stoic circle around Helvidius Priscus the Younger and Arulenus Rusticus, and expelled philosophers. He was murdered by his court on 18 September 96. The Senate condemned his memory, and the writers of the next generation, Tacitus, Pliny and Juvenal, painted him as a tyrant, but the army mourned him. Modern historians (Jones, Southern) present him as a capable, hardworking ruler whose autocratic style alienated the elite.

josephus.detail: Yosef ben Matityahu, born in Jerusalem in 37/38 to a priestly family related through his mother to the Hasmoneans, studied with the Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and the hermit Bannus, and in 64 went to Rome to secure the release of priests sent there by Felix, gaining access to Poppaea. In 66 the revolutionary government appointed him general in Galilee, where he fortified towns, clashed with John of Gischala and was besieged at Jotapata by Vespasian in 67. After the fall of the town he hid in a cave with forty men who agreed to kill each other by lot; Josephus survived, by luck or manipulation, surrendered and predicted that Vespasian would become emperor. Freed in 69, he took the name Titus Flavius Josephus, served Titus as interpreter during the siege of Jerusalem and pleaded with the defenders to surrender, earning the hatred of both sides. After the war he lived in Rome on a pension in Vespasian's former house, with Roman citizenship and estates in Judaea. He wrote the Jewish War (seven books, c. 75-79, first in Aramaic then Greek), the Jewish Antiquities (twenty books, 93/94), an autobiography (Life) defending his conduct in Galilee against Justus of Tiberias, and Against Apion, a defence of Judaism. His works are the main source for Jewish history from the Maccabees to 74, Herod, the procurators, the revolt and Masada, and contain the notices of John the Baptist, James and Jesus. He married four times. Jews long regarded him as a traitor, while Christians preserved his works for their testimony to Christ and to the punishment of Jerusalem. Modern scholarship (Rajak, Mason) reads him as a sophisticated author with his own apologetic agenda, defending both the Flavians and the Jewish people, and blaming the revolt on a small group of brigands and tyrants. He died around 100.

gnaeus_julius_agricola.detail: Gnaeus Julius Agricola was born on 13 June 40 at Forum Julii (Fréjus) in Narbonensis, into a family of senatorial rank; his father Julius Graecinus was executed by Caligula. Educated at Massilia, he served as military tribune in Britain under Suetonius Paullinus during the Boudican revolt, was quaestor in Asia, tribune and praetor under Nero, and in 69 lost his mother to Othonian marines who plundered the family estates in Liguria. He joined Vespasian early and commanded XX Valeria Victrix in Britain (70-73) under Petillius Cerialis. He was adlected to the patriciate, governed Aquitania (74-76), and was consul in 76 or 77, when he betrothed his daughter to Tacitus. As governor of Britain for an unusually long term (77/78 to 83/84), he completed the conquest of Wales, encouraged towns, baths and Roman education among the British elite, advanced through northern England into Scotland, reaching the Tay, consolidating the Forth-Clyde line, considering an invasion of Ireland, and defeated the Caledonians at Mons Graupius in 83 or 84. His fleet sailed round the north of Britain. Domitian recalled him, granting triumphal ornaments and a statue but no further appointment, and he declined to draw lots for Asia or Africa. He died on 23 August 93, with rumours of poison that Tacitus reports but does not endorse. Almost everything known about him comes from Tacitus's biography (98), an encomium which presents him as a model of the good man under a bad emperor, quietly serving the state without seeking glory or provoking martyrdom. Archaeology (the forts and marching camps of Scotland, the Verulamium forum inscription and inscribed lead water pipes from Chester naming him) confirms the broad outline, but scholars debate how much of the Flavian advance should be credited to his predecessors Cerialis and Frontinus. A fragmentary inscription from Verulamium (79) bears his name.

tacitus.detail: Publius (or Gaius) Cornelius Tacitus was born c. 56, probably in Narbonensis or northern Italy, perhaps son of an equestrian procurator of Belgica mentioned by Pliny. Trained in oratory in Rome, he married Agricola's daughter in 77 and began a senatorial career under Vespasian, advanced by Titus and Domitian; he was praetor and quindecimvir in 88, served in the provinces from 89 to 93, and was in Rome during the terror of Domitian's last years, which he describes with personal shame. He was consul suffect in 97 under Nerva, delivering the funeral oration for Verginius Rufus, prosecuted Marius Priscus with Pliny in 100, and was proconsul of Asia c. 112-113, according to an inscription from Mylasa. His works are the Agricola and the Germania (98), the Dialogue on Orators (c. 102), the Histories (covering 69-96, of which Books 1-4 and part of 5 survive, ending in 70) and the Annals (from the death of Augustus to Nero, of which Books 1-6, partly, and 11-16, partly, survive). He promised to write "sine ira et studio" (without anger or partisanship) but his narrative is shaped by a bleak view of the Principate, a fascination with the corruption of power and the moral compromises of the aristocracy, and a style of extreme concision, variation and innuendo. He used senatorial records (acta senatus), memoirs (of Agrippina, Corbulo, Suetonius Paullinus) and earlier historians such as Pliny the Elder, Cluvius Rufus and Fabius Rusticus. His accuracy has been confirmed in many details by documents such as the Lyon tablet and the SC de Cn. Pisone patre, though the latter also shows his selective emphasis. Almost forgotten in late antiquity, his works survived in two Monte Cassino and Fulda manuscripts. He influenced Machiavelli, Montaigne and political thought of the early modern period and remains the greatest Roman historian in the judgement of many, including Syme, who wrote his monumental biography (1958).

pliny_the_younger.detail: Gaius Plinius Caecilius Secundus was born at Comum (Como) in 61/62, son of Lucius Caecilius Cilo and nephew of Pliny the Elder, who adopted him in his will after dying at Vesuvius in 79, an event the 17-year-old witnessed from Misenum and later described for Tacitus. He studied rhetoric with Quintilian and became a leading advocate in the centumviral court, where he pleaded inheritance cases. His senatorial career, under Domitian, Nerva and Trajan, included the prefecture of the military treasury (94-96) and of the treasury of Saturn (98-100), the consulship (suffect, September 100), when he delivered the Panegyricus to Trajan, the augurate and the curatorship of the Tiber (104-106). He prosecuted provincial governors for extortion, including Marius Priscus with Tacitus. Around 110 Trajan sent him as legate with consular power to Bithynia and Pontus to sort out municipal finances; he died there c. 112-113. His nine books of literary letters, published in stages, offer a portrait of the senatorial elite of the period: villas at Laurentum and in Tuscany, literary recitations, patronage, legacies, his three marriages and his affection for his young wife Calpurnia, the ghost of Athens, the dolphin of Hippo, and the eruption of Vesuvius. The tenth book contains his official correspondence with Trajan, including requests for advice on a fire brigade for Nicomedia, aqueducts, a canal and the treatment of Christians (Letter 10.96), with Trajan's replies. An inscription from Comum lists his career and his benefactions, including a library, an alimentary fund for children and baths, totalling over five million sesterces. He has been criticised for vanity and complacency, but his letters are an incomparable source for social history and for the relationship between emperor and governor.

decebalus.detail: Decebalus, king of the Dacians from c. 87, possibly the successor of Duras, was the most capable enemy Rome faced on the Danube in the first century. In 85-86 the Dacians invaded Moesia and killed the governor Oppius Sabinus, and in 86 or 87 destroyed the army of the praetorian prefect Cornelius Fuscus. Defeated by Tettius Julianus at Tapae (88), Decebalus negotiated a peace in 89 with Domitian, who needed his troops against the Marcomanni and Quadi. Under its terms Decebalus became a client king, receiving an annual subsidy, Roman engineers and craftsmen, which he used to strengthen his fortresses in the Orastie mountains around Sarmizegetusa Regia. Dio describes him as shrewd in war, skilled in ambushes and in knowing when to retreat. Trajan regarded the treaty as humiliating and in 101 invaded Dacia. In the first war (101-102) the Romans won a hard battle at Tapae and Decebalus's counter-offensive into Moesia was defeated at Adamclisi; he accepted harsh terms, giving up territory, engineers, deserters and weapons, and his sister was captured. He soon rearmed, attacked the Iazyges and in 105 captured the Roman commander Pompeius Longinus, sent assassins against Trajan and attacked Roman garrisons. In the second war (105-106) Trajan, crossing on the new bridge at Drobeta, took Sarmizegetusa; Decebalus fled north and, when a Roman cavalry patrol led by Tiberius Claudius Maximus overtook him, cut his own throat. Maximus carried his head and right hand to Trajan at Ranisstorum, and they were displayed on the Gemonian steps in Rome. Maximus's tombstone found at Grammeni in Macedonia (1965) shows the scene, as does Trajan's Column. His treasure, hidden in the river Sargetia, was revealed by his companion Bicilis. In modern Romanian national tradition Decebalus is a hero of resistance, commemorated by a 40 m rock carving of his face on the Danube at the Iron Gates (1994-2004).

trajan.detail: Marcus Ulpius Traianus was born on 18 September 53 at Italica in Baetica, son of a distinguished general of the same name who commanded X Fretensis in the Jewish war, was consul under Vespasian, governor of Syria and patrician. The younger Trajan served for ten years as military tribune, commanded VII Gemina in Spain, marched it to the Rhine against Saturninus in 89, was consul in 91 and governor of Upper Germany when Nerva adopted him in October 97. Emperor from January 98, he stayed on the frontier until 99 and won a reputation as the "best princeps" (optimus, officially part of his titulature from 114) through his respect for the Senate, accessibility and modest lifestyle, while firmly holding power. He conquered Dacia in two wars (101-102, 105-106), creating a province rich in gold, and annexed the Nabataean kingdom as the province of Arabia (106). The Dacian spoils financed his Forum, Column, Markets and Baths, the harbour at Portus, the Via Traiana and the alimenta for poor Italian children. His correspondence with Pliny shows a careful administrator. In 113 he launched a war against Parthia, annexing Armenia (114), Mesopotamia (115) and reaching the Persian Gulf after taking Ctesiphon (116), but revolts in the new territories and among the Jewish diaspora in Cyrenaica, Egypt, Cyprus and Mesopotamia forced a retreat. He died at Selinus in Cilicia in August 117, and Hadrian, whose adoption was disputed, succeeded and gave up the eastern conquests. Dio notes his fondness for wine and boys, but considered them harmless. Late antique senators acclaimed new emperors with the wish that they be "luckier than Augustus, better than Trajan", and a medieval legend held that Pope Gregory's prayers saved his soul. Modern historians debate his motives for the Parthian war, from glory-seeking (Dio's view) to strategic or commercial aims.

hadrian.detail: Publius Aelius Hadrianus, born on 24 January 76, probably in Rome, to a family from Italica related to Trajan, was orphaned at ten and became the ward of Trajan and Acilius Attianus. His love of Greek culture earned him the nickname "Graeculus". He served as military tribune in three legions, carried the news of Nerva's death to Trajan, married Trajan's grand-niece Vibia Sabina in 100 with Plotina's support, commanded I Minervia in the Second Dacian War, was archon at Athens (112) and governor of Syria when Trajan died. Emperor from August 117, he abandoned Trajan's eastern conquests and spent more than half his reign travelling through the provinces (121-125 and 128-132), inspecting armies, building frontier works including the Wall in Britain and the palisade in Germany, founding cities (Antinoopolis, Hadrianopolis) and showering benefactions, especially on Athens, where he completed the Olympieion and founded the Panhellenion. He reformed administration, placing equestrians in the palace bureaus, codified the praetor's edict through Salvius Julianus, extended the consilium and protected slaves from abuse. In Rome he built the Pantheon, the Temple of Venus and Roma (to his own design, which Apollodorus mocked, allegedly at the cost of his life), his Mausoleum and the Villa at Tibur. His beloved Antinous drowned in the Nile in 130 and was deified. The Bar Kokhba revolt (132-136), provoked by his foundation of Aelia Capitolina or a ban on circumcision, was suppressed with great loss. His relations with the Senate were tense from the execution of four consulars in 118 to the forced suicide of his brother-in-law Servianus and his grand-nephew Fuscus in 136. Ill in his last years, he adopted Lucius Aelius Caesar (136) and after his death Antoninus (138), who was to adopt Marcus and Lucius. He died at Baiae on 10 July 138, composing the poem "animula vagula blandula". Modern biographers (Birley) stress his restlessness, intellect, curiosity and capacity for cruelty.

antoninus_pius.detail: Titus Aurelius Fulvus Boionius Arrius Antoninus was born on 19 September 86 at Lanuvium, from a wealthy senatorial family of Nemausus in Narbonensis. He was consul in 120, one of the four consulars appointed by Hadrian to administer justice in Italy, and proconsul of Asia (c. 134-135), where he was known for fairness. In February 138, after the death of Lucius Aelius, Hadrian adopted him on condition that he in turn adopt Marcus Annius Verus (Marcus Aurelius) and Lucius Ceionius Commodus (Lucius Verus). Emperor from July 138 to March 161, he forced the reluctant Senate to deify Hadrian and received the name Pius. His 23-year reign, the most peaceful in Roman history, was marked by careful finance, respect for the Senate, mild justice and the absence of major wars, apart from the advance in Britain to the Antonine Wall (142), a war in Mauretania (145-152) and minor troubles in Dacia, Egypt and among the Brigantes. He never left Italy during his reign, governing from Rome and his villa at Lorium, and relied on long-serving governors and friends. He left a surplus of 2.7 billion sesterces. He named his daughter Faustina's husband, Marcus, as heir, granting him tribunician power in 147. His wife Faustina the Elder died in 140, and he founded the alimentary scheme of the puellae Faustinianae in her honour. Legal measures of his reign favoured slaves and the presumption of liberty, and jurists such as Volusius Maecianus and Gaius were active. He celebrated Rome's 900th anniversary in 148. Aelius Aristides delivered his Roman Oration under him, praising the empire as a world city. He died at Lorium on 7 March 161 after eating Alpine cheese, giving the watchword "aequanimitas". Marcus Aurelius's tribute in Meditations 1.16 is the fullest portrait of a good ruler in ancient literature. The scarcity of narrative sources (Dio's account is lost) makes the reign appear uneventful, which modern historians see as both a reality and an illusion.

marcus_aurelius.detail: Marcus Annius Verus, born in Rome on 26 April 121 to a rich Spanish family, grandson of the three-times consul Annius Verus, was noticed by Hadrian, who called him "Verissimus". In 138, aged seventeen, he was adopted by Antoninus at Hadrian's command, becoming Marcus Aelius Aurelius Verus, was made Caesar in 139, married Antoninus's daughter Faustina in 145, received tribunician power in 147, and was trained in government for over twenty years. His teachers included Fronto in Latin rhetoric, Herodes Atticus in Greek and the Stoics Junius Rusticus and Apollonius of Chalcedon; at about 25 he turned decisively to philosophy. On succeeding in 161 he made Lucius Verus co-emperor. His reign was dominated by crises: the Parthian invasion of Armenia and Syria, the Roman counter-offensive (162-166), the Antonine Plague brought back by the army, the invasion of Italy by Marcomanni and Quadi (170), the long Marcomannic wars along the Danube (166-180) that kept him at the front for most of his last fourteen years, the revolt of Avidius Cassius (175) and the death of Faustina. He financed the wars by auctioning palace treasures rather than raising taxes, recruited slaves and gladiators, settled barbarians within the empire and debased the coinage. He was conscientious in jurisdiction, generous to the Senate and patron of Athens' philosophical schools. Christians suffered in local persecutions, including the martyrs of Lyon (177), though there was no imperial persecution policy. He made his son Commodus co-Augustus in 177 and died on the Danube front on 17 March 180, possibly of plague. His Meditations, written in Greek as private notes for self-examination, are the last great work of Stoicism and present the struggle of a ruler to live by reason, duty and acceptance of mortality. The Column of Marcus Aurelius and the Capitoline equestrian statue survive. Dio and Herodian celebrate him as the best emperor; his choice of Commodus as successor has been criticised since antiquity.

lucius_verus.detail: Lucius Ceionius Commodus, born on 15 December 130, son of Hadrian's first chosen heir Lucius Aelius Caesar, was adopted by Antoninus in 138 according to Hadrian's plan, together with Marcus Aurelius, but was given no title as Caesar and held a single consulship (154) before his elevation. On Antoninus's death in 161, Marcus insisted that Lucius be made co-emperor with equal titles as Lucius Aurelius Verus Augustus, the first formal joint rule. When the Parthian king Vologases IV invaded Armenia and destroyed a Roman army at Elegeia (161) and defeated the governor of Syria, Lucius was sent east in 162 as commander, travelling slowly and enjoying himself at Corinth, Athens and Antioch, and at the resort of Daphne, where he was accused of debauchery. The campaigns were directed by his generals, Statius Priscus, who took Artaxata (163), Avidius Cassius, who captured Seleucia and Ctesiphon (165) and invaded Media (166), and Martius Verus. Lucius took the titles Armeniacus, Parthicus Maximus and Medicus and celebrated a triumph with Marcus in October 166. He married Marcus's daughter Lucilla at Ephesus in 164. His army brought back the plague. He then went with Marcus to the northern front in 168, and on the return to Rome early in 169 he died of a stroke (apoplexy) near Altinum, aged 38; he was deified. The Historia Augusta portrays him as a pleasure-loving playboy who turned his house into a tavern, kept a golden statue of his favourite horse Volucer and fed it raisins and nuts; this portrait is coloured by the biographer's fictions, though Fronto's letters show genuine affection between Lucius, his tutor and Marcus. Rumours that Marcus or Faustina poisoned him have no basis. Modern historians (Birley) present him as a loyal, if lightweight, colleague who did what was required of him as figurehead commander.

commodus.detail: Lucius Aurelius Commodus, born at Lanuvium on 31 August 161 with a twin brother who died at four, was the first emperor born to a reigning emperor since Titus. Made Caesar in 166, he accompanied his father to the Danube, received the toga virilis in 175, tribunician power and the title Augustus in 177 and married Bruttia Crispina in 178. On Marcus's death in March 180 he became sole emperor at eighteen, and against the advice of his father's generals quickly made peace with the Marcomanni and Quadi, returning to Rome, a decision the sources blame on his laziness but which may have been prudent. The conspiracy of his sister Lucilla in 182, in which an assassin cried "the Senate sends you this" as he struck, poisoned his relations with the Senate. He left government to favourites: the praetorian prefect Perennis, who dominated until 185 when soldiers from Britain secured his execution, then the freedman Cleander, who sold offices and was sacrificed to the mob during a grain riot in 190. Commodus's reign saw wars in Britain and Dacia, the "War of the Deserters" led by Maternus in Gaul and Spain, a plot that nearly killed him at the Megalensia (187), the return of the plague (189) and fires. In his last years he identified himself with Hercules, renamed the months after his twelve names, called Rome Colonia Commodiana, and fought in the arena as a secutor, killing animals and gladiators; Dio was an eyewitness. He was strangled in his bath on 31 December 192 by the athlete Narcissus in a plot organised by his mistress Marcia, the chamberlain Eclectus and the prefect Laetus. The Senate condemned his memory, but Septimius Severus deified him in 195 to legitimise his own claimed descent from Marcus. Dio's judgement that his accession marked the descent from an age of gold to one of iron set the tradition. Modern historians (Hekster) see his self-presentation as a deliberate, if extreme, strategy to appeal to the people and the army over the Senate.

avidius_cassius.detail: Gaius Avidius Cassius was born c. 130 at Cyrrhus in Syria, son of Gaius Avidius Heliodorus, an orator from Egypt who became Hadrian's secretary for Greek correspondence and prefect of Egypt; he claimed descent from the Seleucids. Entering the Senate, he made his name as legate of III Gallica in the Parthian war under Lucius Verus, leading the advance down the Euphrates, winning a battle at Dura-Europos, and capturing Seleucia and Ctesiphon in 165, where Seleucia was sacked despite opening its gates, and invading Media in 166. He became consul (166) and governor of Syria and received a special command over the whole East, known from inscriptions, which made him the most powerful man after the emperors. He suppressed the Bucoli revolt in Egypt (172). Dio describes him as a stern disciplinarian, who crucified deserters and cut off the hands of soldiers who attacked the enemy without orders. In April 175, apparently having received false news of Marcus's death on the Danube, and according to rumour encouraged by Faustina, who feared for her son Commodus's succession if Marcus died, he proclaimed himself emperor. He was recognised in Syria, Egypt and much of the East, though not in Cappadocia, held by Martius Verus. When it became clear that Marcus was alive and marching east, his support collapsed; after three months and six days he was killed by a centurion and a decurion, who sent his head to Marcus. Marcus refused to see it, burned Cassius's correspondence unread and pardoned most of his supporters, though the Senate punished some. Dio's sympathetic picture of Marcus's clemency contrasts with the Historia Augusta's life, which contains forged letters. Modern historians debate whether Faustina was involved and whether the revolt was an honest mistake or a long-planned attempt to secure power against the young Commodus.
avidius_cassius.debate: Whether the revolt arose from a false report of Marcus's death, and whether Faustina encouraged it.

galen.detail: Aelius (or Claudius) Galenus was born in Pergamum in 129, son of a wealthy architect, Nicon, who directed him to medicine after a dream. He studied philosophy and medicine in Pergamum, Smyrna, Corinth and Alexandria, where he learned anatomy from skeletons, then served as physician to the gladiators of the high priest of Asia at Pergamum (157-161), gaining experience of wounds and diet. In 162 he went to Rome, where his public anatomical dissections and vivisections, his cures of aristocrats such as the philosopher Eudemus and the consul Flavius Boethus, and his polemics with rival medical sects made him famous and controversial. He left Rome in 166 as the plague arrived, but was summoned by Marcus and Lucius to Aquileia in 168-169 and became court physician, looking after the young Commodus and preparing the theriac antidote for Marcus. He spent the rest of his life in Rome, surviving into the reign of Septimius Severus and possibly Caracalla, dying c. 216, though some sources say later. His output was enormous, around 500 works, of which some 150 survive in Greek, Arabic or Latin, about 3 million words, covering anatomy, physiology, pathology, pharmacology, diagnosis, prognosis, hygiene, and philosophy (logic, ethics and the soul). He combined Hippocratic humoral theory with Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy and his own experimental work, demonstrating that arteries carry blood, not air, the functions of the recurrent laryngeal nerve and spinal cord, and the role of the kidneys. His descriptions of the Antonine Plague are the main medical source for it. The rediscovered treatise On Avoiding Distress (found in Thessaloniki in 2005) describes his losses of books, drugs and instruments in the fire of 192. Translated into Syriac and Arabic by Hunayn ibn Ishaq and others, and then into Latin, his works dominated medicine in Europe and the Islamic world until Vesalius and Harvey.

pertinax.detail:
Pertinax tried to restore Antonine austerity: he sold Commodus's luxuries at auction, cut court spending and promised the Praetorians less than they expected. On 28 March 193 some 200 to 300 guardsmen stormed the palace and killed him; the guard then sold the throne to Didius Julianus.
