After her father's death, according to Procopius, the Greens refused to help her mother, but the Blues took the family in, which explains her later support of the Blues. She became an actress and courtesan, and the Secret History describes her performances in lurid detail. She became the mistress of Hecebolus, governor of Libya Pentapolis, was abandoned, and on her way back through Alexandria and Antioch came into contact with miaphysite leaders, notably Timothy III and Severus of Antioch. In Constantinople she met Justinian, who married her around 525 after his uncle changed the law forbidding senators to marry actresses. She was crowned Augusta on 1 April 527. Theodora had considerable influence. Procopius credits her with a speech during the Nika riot (532) urging Justinian not to flee, with the line 'royalty is a good burial shroud'. She protected the miaphysites, sheltering hundreds of monks and bishops in the palace of Hormisdas and supporting the missions of Jacob Baradaeus and the Nubian mission of Julian; she promoted the deposition of Pope Silverius and the election of Vigilius. She was credited with laws protecting women, against forced prostitution and on dowries, and with a convent for former prostitutes, the Metanoia. She led the intrigue against John the Cappadocian in 541. She died of cancer, perhaps, on 28 June 548. Her portrait in the mosaics of San Vitale in Ravenna is one of the most famous images of late antiquity. Modern historians consider Procopius's account largely as invective.
scholarship: Garland, Byzantine Empresses (1999)
Potter, Theodora (2015)
Potter, Theodora: Actress, Empress, Saint (2015)
Cameron, Procopius and the Sixth Century (1985)
Watts, Hypatia: The Life and Legend of an Ancient Philosopher (2017)

stilicho.detail: Flavius Stilicho, born around 359, son of a Vandal cavalry officer and a Roman mother, rose under Theodosius I, who sent him as envoy to Persia around 383 and married him to his niece and adopted daughter Serena. He commanded at the Frigidus (394) and on Theodosius's death in 395 claimed to be guardian of both sons, effectively ruling the West for Honorius, whom he married to his daughters Maria and later Thermantia. His thirteen years in power were spent in constant crisis: he fought Alaric in Greece (395, 397), crushed the revolt of Gildo in Africa (398), defeated Alaric at Pollentia and Verona (402) and destroyed Radagaisus at Faesulae (406). He was in permanent conflict with the eastern court over Illyricum, being declared a public enemy in Constantinople (397), and sought to use Alaric to seize eastern Illyricum (407). His critics accused him of letting the barbarians in, of withdrawing troops from the Rhine and Britain, and of favouring barbarians; Rutilius claims he burned the Sibylline books and Orosius accuses him of plotting to put his son Eucherius on the throne. When the Rhine was breached (406), Constantine III took Gaul, and Alaric demanded 4,000 lb of gold, which Stilicho forced the Senate to pay, his position weakened. A court conspiracy led by Olympius provoked a mutiny at Ticinum in August 408, and Stilicho, refusing to let his barbarian troops fight the Roman soldiers, was executed at Ravenna on 22 August 408. His death led to the massacre of barbarian soldiers' families and their desertion to Alaric. Claudian's poems are his main propaganda.
scholarship: Hughes, Stilicho (2010)
Cameron, Claudian (1970)
Hughes, Stilicho: The Vandal Who Saved Rome (2010)
Matthews, Western Aristocracies and Imperial Court (1975)

aetius.detail: Flavius Aetius, born around 391 at Durostorum in Moesia, son of the magister equitum Gaudentius and an Italian noblewoman, spent his youth as a hostage with Alaric's Goths (405-408) and then with the Huns of Uldin and Rua, whose friendship became the basis of his career. In 425 he arrived in Italy with a Hunnic army, said to be 60,000 strong, to support the usurper Joannes, too late; Galla Placidia bought him off with the command in Gaul. There he fought the Visigoths at Arles (426, 430), the Franks, the Juthungi and Norici (430-431). He eliminated his rivals: the general Felix, killed in 430, and Bonifatius, who defeated him at Rimini in 432 but died of his wounds. Restored with Hunnic help, Aetius became magister militum, patricius and the real ruler of the West from 433 to 454, consul three times (432, 437, 446). He used the Huns to destroy the Burgundians (436), defeated the Visigoths at Narbonne (436-437) and the Bacaudae of Armorica, and settled Alans and Burgundians as federates in Gaul (440-443). He failed to stop the Vandals taking Africa. In 446 the Britons appealed to him in vain. In 451 he assembled the coalition of Romans, Visigoths, Franks, Burgundians and Alans that stopped Attila at the Catalaunian Plains, but he could not prevent the invasion of Italy in 452. His plan to marry his son Gaudentius to Valentinian's daughter Placidia alarmed the court, and on 21 or 22 September 454 Valentinian III killed him with his own hands. Procopius calls him, with Bonifatius, the last of the Romans.
scholarship: Stickler, Aëtius (2002)
Hughes, Patricius (2012)
Hughes, Aetius: Attila's Nemesis (2012)
Zecchini, Aezio: l'ultima difesa dell'Occidente romano (1983)

sources.a: Renatus Profuturus Frigeridus (in Gregory of Tours)

scholarship: Wijnendaele, The Last of the Romans: Bonifatius (2015)

ricimer.detail: Flavius Ricimer, born around 418, was the son of a Suebian prince and a daughter of the Visigothic king Wallia; his sister married the Burgundian king Gundioc. He served under Aetius with the future emperor Majorian. After Aetius's murder he became the dominant figure in the western empire. In 456 he defeated the Vandals at Agrigentum and in a naval battle off Corsica, and then, with Majorian, overthrew the emperor Avitus at Placentia. He installed Majorian as emperor (457), becoming patricius and magister militum, but after the failure of Majorian's expedition against the Vandals in 460, he had him arrested and executed (461). He then installed a series of puppet emperors: Libius Severus (461-465), after whose death he ruled Italy without an emperor for eighteen months; Anthemius, imposed by Leo I in 467, whose daughter Alypia he married; and finally Olybrius (472). As an Arian of barbarian descent, he could not take the throne himself, but he controlled the army in Italy, issued coins with his monogram and commissioned mosaics in the Gothic church of Sant'Agata dei Goti in Rome. He faced rivals: Aegidius in Gaul and Marcellinus in Dalmatia, who refused to recognise his emperors. His relationship with Anthemius broke down in civil war (470-472); in 472 he besieged Rome, where Anthemius was killed in July. Ricimer died of a haemorrhage on 18 August 472, weeks later. His nephew Gundobad succeeded him as patricius. Older historians saw him as a barbarian destroyer of the empire; modern scholars such as MacGeorge regard him as a Roman general defending Italy with limited resources.
scholarship: MacGeorge, Late Roman Warlords (2002)
Anders, Flavius Ricimer (2010)

belisarius.detail: Flavius Belisarius, born around 500 at Germania in Thrace or Illyricum, served in Justinian's bodyguard and commanded in the Persian frontier from 527. As magister militum per Orientem, he won the battle of Dara (530) and was defeated at Callinicum (531). In January 532 he helped suppress the Nika riot with his bucellarii, massacring the rebels in the Hippodrome. In 533-534 he conquered the Vandal kingdom in a brilliant campaign (Ad Decimum, Tricamarum), bringing Gelimer to Constantinople, where he celebrated a triumph in the Hippodrome, the first by a non-emperor in centuries, and was consul in 535. He then conquered Sicily (535), Naples (536), defended Rome against Witiges (537-538) and took Ravenna (540) after the Goths offered him the western throne, which he pretended to accept. Returning to the East, he fought Khosrow I (541-542). Suspected of disloyalty during Justinian's illness in 542, he was recalled and stripped of his wealth. In 544-549 he returned to Italy with insufficient resources against Totila, recovering Rome but failing to defeat the Goths. In 559 he came out of retirement with 300 veterans and peasants to defeat the Kutrigur Huns at Melantias near the capital. In 562 he was accused of conspiracy, disgraced and restored in 563, and died in March 565. His wife Antonina, a friend of Theodora, accompanied him on campaign. Procopius, his secretary, praises him in the Wars and denigrates him in the Secret History. The medieval legend that he was blinded and reduced to begging is first found in the eleventh century. He used heavily armed horse archers and bucellarii as the core of his armies.
scholarship: Hughes, Belisarius: The Last Roman General (2009)
Whately, Battles and Generals (2016)
Cameron, Procopius and the Sixth Century (1985)

narses.detail: Narses, an Armenian eunuch born around 478-480, rose in the imperial household to become cubicularius and sakellarios, treasurer of the privy purse, and praepositus sacri cubiculi. During the Nika riot (532) he bribed the Blues to abandon the rebels. In 535 he was sent to Alexandria to restore the miaphysite patriarch Theodosius, supported by Theodora. In 538 he was sent to Italy with reinforcements, where he insisted on relieving Ariminum against Belisarius's advice, creating a division in command that led to the loss of Milan (539), and was recalled. In 551, aged over seventy, he was appointed commander-in-chief for Italy with large funds and a big army of Lombards, Heruli, Huns and Gepids. He marched along the Adriatic coast and in 552 defeated Totila at Busta Gallorum (Taginae), took Rome, and defeated Teia at Mons Lactarius. He then defeated the Franks and Alamanni at the Volturnus (554), and reduced the last Gothic strongholds, including Verona and Brixia in 562. He governed Italy as supreme commander, implementing the Pragmatic Sanction (554) and rebuilding cities and bridges, such as the Ponte Salario in Rome. Unpopular with the Romans for his taxation, he was recalled by Justin II around 567. Paul the Deacon reports the legend that Sophia sent him a spindle, saying he should spin with the women, and that he replied he would spin a thread she could not unravel, inviting the Lombards into Italy. He died in Rome around 573-574, aged about 95, and his body was taken to Constantinople. He was pious and devoted to the Virgin, who was said to tell him when to attack.
scholarship: Hughes, Narses (2017)
Fauber, Narses: Hammer of the Goths (1990)

john_the_cappadocian.detail: John, born around 490 at Caesarea in Cappadocia, of modest origins, began as a clerk (scriniarius) in the office of a magister militum, and rose through his financial ability to become praetorian prefect of the East in 531, a post he held, apart from a few months in 532, until 541. He was Justinian's leading fiscal minister. He reformed the administration to increase revenue: he reduced the number of officials, abolished the public post on certain routes, simplified the procedures of the prefecture by replacing Latin with Greek, introduced new taxes such as the aerikon (air tax), and aggressively collected arrears. These measures made him hugely unpopular, and John Lydus, an official in the prefecture, describes his corruption, cruelty, torture of debtors, and gluttony. During the Nika riot (532), the crowd demanded his dismissal along with Tribonian, and Justinian complied, only to reappoint him months later. He opposed the Vandal expedition in 533, warning of the risks. He was hated by Theodora, who feared his influence over Justinian. In 541 Theodora and Antonina laid a trap: Antonina persuaded John's daughter Euphemia that Belisarius was planning a coup and arranged a secret meeting between John and Antonina, where imperial agents caught him discussing conspiracy. John was dismissed, his property confiscated, and he was forcibly ordained priest at Cyzicus. Accused of complicity in the murder of the bishop of Cyzicus, he was flogged and exiled to Egypt. After Theodora's death in 548, he was recalled to Constantinople, but not to office, and died as a priest. Procopius calls him the worst of men but recognises his extraordinary ability.
scholarship: Maas, John Lydus and the Roman Past (1992)
Kelly, Ruling the Later Roman Empire (2004)
Jones, The Later Roman Empire (1964)
Honoré, Tribonian (1978)

alaric_i.detail: Alaric, born around 370 in the region of the Danube delta, of the Balti family according to Jordanes, led Gothic federates in Theodosius's army at the Frigidus (394). Disappointed of a command and of rewards, he rebelled in 395 and ravaged Thrace, Macedonia and Greece (396), escaping Stilicho at Pholoe (397). The eastern court made him magister militum per Illyricum (397). In 401 he invaded Italy, besieged Milan, and was defeated by Stilicho at Pollentia and Verona (402), withdrawing to Illyricum. Stilicho then made him an ally, planning to use him to seize eastern Illyricum (407); after the plan failed, Alaric demanded 4,000 lb of gold, which the Senate paid. After Stilicho's execution in 408, he invaded Italy, joined by deserting federates, and besieged Rome three times: in 408, receiving a huge ransom; in 409, when he had the Senate proclaim Priscus Attalus emperor, with Alaric as magister militum; and in 410, when, after negotiations with Honorius failed and he was attacked by Sarus, he sacked Rome on 24 August 410. He then marched to southern Italy, planning to cross to Africa, but his fleet was destroyed by a storm, and he died of illness at Consentia (Cosenza) at the end of 410. Jordanes records that his followers diverted the river Busento, buried him with treasure in its bed and restored the river, killing the slaves who had done the work. His brother-in-law Athaulf succeeded him. Modern historians see his aim as gaining for his followers a recognised place within the empire, land and supplies, and for himself a high Roman military command, rather than destroying Rome.
scholarship: Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)
Burns, Barbarians within the Gates of Rome (1994)
Heather, Goths and Romans 332-489 (1991)

gaiseric.detail: Gaiseric (Geiseric, Genseric), born around 389, illegitimate son of the Vandal king Godegisel, who was killed fighting the Franks during the Rhine crossing of 406, became king of the Vandals and Alans in Spain in 428 after his brother Gunderic. Jordanes describes him as short, lame from a fall from his horse, of few words, despising luxury, furious in anger, greedy and skilled at sowing discord. In May 429 he led his people, said to number 80,000, across to Africa, besieged Hippo (430-431), and defeated Bonifatius and an eastern army. He made a treaty with Rome in 435 and broke it by seizing Carthage on 19 October 439, from which he dated his reign. The treaty of 442 recognised his kingdom in Proconsularis, Byzacena and eastern Numidia. He was an Arian and persecuted the Catholic clergy, exiling bishops and confiscating churches, as described by Victor of Vita. He built a fleet that dominated the western Mediterranean, raiding Sicily, Sardinia, Corsica, the Balearics and the coasts of Italy and Greece, and in June 455 sacked Rome for two weeks, taking the empress Licinia Eudoxia and her daughters. He defeated Majorian's expedition (460) by burning his fleet in Spain, and Leo I's great expedition at Cape Bon (468) with fireships. In 474 Zeno concluded an 'eternal peace' with him recognising Vandal rule in Africa, Sicily (which he partly ceded to Odoacer), Sardinia, Corsica and the Balearics. He established a law of succession by seniority among his descendants. He died on 25 January 477, after a reign of 49 years, the most successful barbarian king of his century.
scholarship: Merrills & Miles, The Vandals (2010)
Merrills and Miles, The Vandals (2010)
Steinacher, Die Vandalen (2016)
Courtois, Les Vandales et l'Afrique (1955)

attila.detail: Attila, born around 406, son of Mundzuk, nephew of the Hunnic kings Rua and Octar, became joint ruler with his brother Bleda on Rua's death in 434 or 435. The brothers renegotiated the treaty of Margus (435), doubling the annual tribute from the eastern empire to 700 lb of gold, and in 441-442 invaded the Balkans, taking Viminacium, Margus, Singidunum, Sirmium and Naissus. Around 445 Attila killed Bleda and became sole ruler of a vast empire stretching from the Rhine to the Black Sea steppe, including Germanic peoples such as the Ostrogoths and Gepids. In 447 he invaded the eastern empire again, defeated the Roman army on the Utus and reached Thermopylae; the Peace of Anatolius tripled the tribute to 2,100 lb of gold a year. Priscus, who accompanied the embassy of 449, describes his wooden palace, his modest table, his stern judgements and his court with Roman secretaries such as Orestes. In 450, after Honoria's appeal and Marcian's refusal to pay tribute, he turned west. In 451 he invaded Gaul, sacking Metz and besieging Orléans, but was stopped by Aetius and the Visigoths at the Catalaunian Plains. In 452 he invaded Italy, destroying Aquileia and sacking the Po valley cities, but withdrew after the embassy of Pope Leo, with famine, disease and an eastern counter-attack contributing. He died in early 453 on the night of his wedding to Ildico. His empire dissolved within a year. In medieval legend he became the Scourge of God (flagellum Dei) and Etzel or Atli in Germanic epic.
scholarship: Maenchen-Helfen, The World of the Huns (1973)
Kelly, Attila the Hun (2008)
Kim, The Huns (2016)
Thompson, The Huns (1948, rev. Heather 1996)

theodoric_the_great.detail: Theodoric, born around 454 in Pannonia, son of the Ostrogothic king Theodemir of the Amal family, spent ten years as a hostage at Constantinople (c. 461-471), where he received a Roman education. Becoming king around 474, he led his people in the Balkans, alternately serving and fighting Zeno and competing with Theodoric Strabo, whose followers he absorbed after 481-484; he was consul in 484. In 488 Zeno sent him to Italy against Odoacer. After defeating Odoacer on the Isonzo, at Verona and on the Adda (489-490), he besieged him in Ravenna for three years, made an agreement to share power in 493 and then killed him with his own hands. He ruled Italy as king until 526, recognised by Anastasius in 497. His rule combined a Gothic army, Arian in religion, settled in northern Italy, with a Roman civil administration staffed by senators such as Cassiodorus, Boethius, Liberius and Symmachus. He maintained the Senate, the consulship and Roman law, restored buildings in Rome and Ravenna, and built the palace and churches of Ravenna and his mausoleum. Through marriage alliances, his sister to the Vandal Thrasamund, daughters to the Visigothic Alaric II and the Burgundian Sigismund, himself to Clovis's sister, he created a network of kingdoms; after Vouillé he saved the Visigoths and annexed Provence (508), ruling Spain as regent (511-526). His last years were darkened by the executions of Boethius (524) and Symmachus (525), and the imprisonment of Pope John I (526). He died on 30 August 526. In Germanic legend he became Dietrich von Bern.
scholarship: Moorhead, Theoderic in Italy (1992)
Arnold, Theoderic and the Roman Imperial Restoration (2014)
Wiemer, Theoderich der Große (2018)
Wiemer, Theoderich der Grosse (2018)
Heather, 'Theoderic, king of the Goths', Early Medieval Europe 4 (1995)

clovis_i.detail: Clovis (Chlodovechus), born around 466, son of Childeric I and the Thuringian Basina, succeeded his father as king of the Salian Franks of Tournai around 481. Bishop Remigius of Reims wrote to him at his accession advising him to work with the bishops. In 486 or 487 he defeated Syagrius at Soissons, taking northern Gaul. He married the Burgundian Catholic princess Clotilde around 493. He fought the Thuringians, the Alamanni (battle of Tolbiac, traditionally 496) and the Burgundians (battle of Dijon, 500). His conversion to Catholic Christianity, baptised by Remigius at Reims with 3,000 warriors, is dated by Gregory of Tours to 496, but possibly to 508. In 507, with Burgundian support and imperial encouragement, he defeated and killed the Visigothic king Alaric II at Vouillé and conquered Aquitaine, although Theodoric prevented him from reaching the Mediterranean. In 508 at Tours he received from Anastasius an honorary consulship or patriciate, and appeared in the basilica of St Martin in a purple tunic and chlamys, wearing a diadem, and distributing coins to the people. He made Paris his capital, building the church of the Holy Apostles (later Sainte-Geneviève), where he was buried. In his last years he eliminated other Frankish kings, including Sigibert of Cologne, Chararic and Ragnachar, unifying the Franks under his rule. He issued the Pactus Legis Salicae and called the Council of Orléans (511). He died on 27 November 511, and his kingdom was divided among his four sons. Gregory of Tours, a century later, portrayed him as a new Constantine, despite his violence.
scholarship: Wood, The Merovingian Kingdoms (1994)
Wood, The Merovingian Kingdoms 450-751 (1994)
James, The Franks (1988)
Becher, Chlodwig I. (2011)
Pohl, The Avars (2018)

khosrow_i.detail: Khosrow I Anushirvan ('of the immortal soul'), born around 501, the favourite son of Kavad I, was designated heir despite having older brothers, and in 525 Kavad asked Justin I to adopt him, a request rejected. As crown prince he directed the suppression of the Mazdakite movement around 528. He succeeded on Kavad's death in September 531, eliminating his brothers, and in 532 concluded the Eternal Peace with Justinian, receiving 11,000 lb of gold. Alarmed by Justinian's conquests, he broke the peace in 540, sacking Antioch and deporting its people to a new city near Ctesiphon, and fought in Mesopotamia and in Lazica (541-562), until the Fifty Years' Peace of 562, which gave him annual payments of 30,000 solidi. In the east, around 560 he allied with the Turks to destroy the Hephthalites, and around 570 he conquered Yemen. Internally, he reformed the empire after the Mazdakite upheavals: he introduced a fixed land tax based on a cadastral survey, divided the military command into four regions under spahbeds, created a class of small landholding cavalry (dehqans), and strengthened royal authority over the nobility. He was a patron of learning; he welcomed the Athenian philosophers who fled after 529, had Greek and Indian works translated into Pahlavi, including the Panchatantra (Kalila wa-Dimna), and a medical school flourished at Gundeshapur. In 572 the war with Rome resumed; he took Dara (573), but was defeated at Melitene (576). He died in early 579. Persian and Arabic tradition made him the model of the just king, while Procopius portrays him as cunning and faithless.
scholarship: Rubin, 'The reforms of Khusro Anushirwan', in Cameron (ed.), The Byzantine and Early Islamic Near East III (1995)
Börm, Prokop und die Perser (2007)
Daryaee, Sasanian Persia (2009)

khosrow_ii.detail: Khosrow II Parviz ('the victorious'), born around 570, son of Hormizd IV, was proclaimed king in February 590 after a palace coup against his father, who was killed. Defeated by the usurper Bahram Chobin, he fled to Roman territory and appealed to Maurice, who restored him with a Roman army at the battle of the Blarathon (591), in return for Dara, Martyropolis and much of Armenia. He maintained peace with Maurice, whom he called his father, and favoured his Christian subjects, with his Christian wives Shirin and, according to tradition, Maria, a daughter of Maurice. He also sent gifts to the shrine of St Sergius at Resafa. After Maurice's murder in 602, he declared war to avenge him, beginning a war of 26 years in which his generals Shahrbaraz and Shahin conquered Mesopotamia, Armenia, Syria, Jerusalem (614), from which the True Cross was taken to Ctesiphon, Egypt (619) and parts of Anatolia, reaching Chalcedon in 615 and 626. It was the greatest extent of the Sasanian empire, almost restoring the Achaemenid frontiers. But Heraclius's counter-offensives from 622, the failure of the siege of Constantinople in 626, and the defeat at Nineveh (627) brought collapse. Khosrow also destroyed the Lakhmid buffer state (c. 602), exposing the Arab frontier. His heavy taxation, his executions and his treatment of the nobility led to his overthrow by his son Kavad II in February 628; he was imprisoned and executed. He was remembered in Persian tradition for the splendour of his court, his palaces, his horse Shabdiz, and his love for Shirin, celebrated by Nizami.
scholarship: Howard-Johnston, The Last Great War of Antiquity (2021)
Pourshariati, Decline and Fall of the Sasanian Empire (2008)
Daryaee, Sasanian Persia (2009)

odoacer.detail: Odoacer (Odovacar), born around 433, son of Edeco, perhaps the Hunnic envoy of 449, of the Sciri or Rugi or Thuringians according to different sources, served in Italy in the guard of the emperor Anthemius and supported Ricimer in 472. Eugippius's Life of Severinus says that as a young man on his way to Italy he visited the holy man Severinus in Noricum, who predicted his greatness. In 476, when the federate troops in Italy demanded land and Orestes refused, they proclaimed Odoacer king on 23 August; he defeated and killed Orestes at Placentia and deposed Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna on 4 September 476, sending the imperial insignia to Constantinople. He ruled Italy as king (rex) and patricius, nominally under Zeno, minting coins in the name of the eastern emperor and of Julius Nepos until 480. He settled his soldiers, probably giving them a third of the land or of its tax revenue, maintained the Senate, the consulship and the Roman administration, and recovered Sicily from the Vandals (476-477) and Dalmatia after Nepos's murder (481-482). In 487 he destroyed the Rugian kingdom on the Danube, and in 488 ordered the evacuation of Noricum. Zeno, alarmed at his growing power and wishing to remove the Ostrogoths from the Balkans, sent Theodoric against him. Defeated on the Isonzo (489), at Verona (489) and on the Adda (490), Odoacer held out in Ravenna for three years. Under the agreement of February 493 he was to share rule with Theodoric, but on 15 March Theodoric killed him at a banquet. Historians see his reign as a continuation of late Roman government in Italy rather than a barbarian conquest.
scholarship: MacGeorge, Late Roman Warlords (2002)
Moorhead, Theoderic in Italy (1992)
Jones, 'The constitutional position of Odoacer and Theoderic', JRS 52 (1962)

augustine_of_hippo.detail: Aurelius Augustinus, born on 13 November 354 at Thagaste in Numidia, son of the pagan Patricius and the Christian Monica, studied at Madauros and Carthage, where reading Cicero's Hortensius turned him to philosophy. For nine years he was a Manichaean hearer. He taught rhetoric at Carthage and Rome and in 384 obtained, with the support of Symmachus, the chair of rhetoric at Milan, where he heard the sermons of Ambrose and read the Neoplatonists. In 386 he was converted, as he recounts in the Confessions, in a garden in Milan on hearing a child's voice say 'take up and read', and was baptised by Ambrose at Easter 387. After the death of Monica at Ostia he returned to Africa, founded a community at Thagaste, and in 391 was ordained priest at Hippo Regius, becoming bishop in 395 or 396 and remaining there until his death. He wrote over 100 books, 300 letters and 400 sermons, including the Confessions (397-401), On the Trinity, On Christian Doctrine, and the City of God (413-426). He fought three great controversies: against the Manichaeans; against the Donatists, culminating in the Conference of Carthage (411) and his justification of coercion; and against Pelagius and his followers on grace and free will, original sin and predestination, leading to their condemnation in 418. He died on 28 August 430 during the Vandal siege of Hippo. His influence on Western Christianity is unrivalled: on the doctrine of grace, the theology of the sacraments, political thought, and the theory of history. Peter Brown's biography is the standard modern account.
scholarship: Brown, Augustine of Hippo (1967, rev. 2000)
Brown, Augustine of Hippo: A Biography (1967, 2000)
Lancel, Saint Augustin (1999)
O'Donnell, Augustine: A New Biography (2005)
Kelly, Jerome (1975)
Kelly, Golden Mouth (1995)

sources.w: Dialogue on the Life of John Chrysostom

cyril_of_alexandria.detail: Cyril, born around 376, nephew of the patriarch Theophilus of Alexandria, whom he accompanied to the Synod of the Oak (403), succeeded his uncle as patriarch in October 412 after a disputed election. His early years were marked by violence in Alexandria: conflicts with the Novatians, whose churches he closed, with the Jews, whom he expelled from the city in 414 after riots, and with the prefect Orestes. In March 415 a mob led by the reader Peter murdered the philosopher Hypatia, a friend of Orestes; Socrates blames the climate created by Cyril, although his direct responsibility is unproven. From 428 he led the attack on Nestorius, patriarch of Constantinople, who rejected the title Theotokos, accusing him of dividing Christ into two persons. He wrote his Twelve Anathemas, won the support of Pope Celestine, and presided over the Council of Ephesus (431), which deposed Nestorius before the Syrian bishops arrived. After a period of detention, he used generous gifts to the court to win Theodosius II's support, and in 433 reconciled with John of Antioch in the Formula of Reunion, which accepted two natures in one person. His Christology, centred on the 'one incarnate nature of God the Word', which he believed came from Athanasius but was actually Apollinarian, was later claimed both by the Chalcedonians and by the miaphysites. He wrote extensive commentaries on Scripture, the treatise Against Julian in reply to the emperor's work against the Galileans, and Festal Letters. He died on 27 June 444. He is honoured as a saint and Doctor of the Church.
scholarship: McGuckin, St Cyril of Alexandria (1994)
Wessel, Cyril of Alexandria and the Nestorian Controversy (2004)
Russell, Cyril of Alexandria (2000)

pope_leo_i.detail: Leo, born around 400 probably in Tuscia, was a deacon of the Roman church under Celestine I and Sixtus III and was influential enough for Cassian to dedicate his treatise against Nestorius to him. He was on a diplomatic mission in Gaul, reconciling Aetius and the prefect Albinus, when he was elected pope in 440, consecrated on 29 September. His pontificate of 21 years was decisive for the development of papal authority. He developed the theory of the pope as the heir of Peter, exercising his authority in the church, against the claims of Hilary of Arles, obtaining from Valentinian III the Novel 17 of 445 confirming his jurisdiction over Gaul. He fought the Manichaeans in Rome, Pelagians and Priscillianists. In 449 he sent his Tome to Flavian of Constantinople defining the two natures of Christ; rejected at the Second Council of Ephesus (449), which he called a 'robber synod', it was acclaimed at the Council of Chalcedon in 451. He refused to accept canon 28 of Chalcedon, which gave Constantinople equal privileges to Rome. In 452 he took part in the embassy to Attila on the Mincio, and in 455 he met Gaiseric outside Rome, obtaining, according to Prosper, a promise that the city would not be burned and its people not massacred. His 96 sermons and 143 letters are models of Latin style and doctrinal clarity. He died on 10 November 461 and was the first pope buried in St Peter's. He was later called 'the Great' and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1754. He is regarded as the founder of the medieval papacy.
scholarship: Wessel, Leo the Great and the Spiritual Rebuilding of a Universal Rome (2008)
Neil, Leo the Great (2009)
Ullmann, 'Leo I and the theme of papal primacy', JTS 11 (1960)

gregory_the_great.detail: Gregory, born around 540 into a wealthy senatorial family in Rome, great-grandson of Pope Felix III, was praetor or urban prefect around 573. After his father's death he converted his family house on the Caelian into the monastery of St Andrew, founded six monasteries in Sicily and became a monk. Pope Pelagius II made him deacon and sent him as apocrisiarius to Constantinople (579-586), where he formed friendships with Leander of Seville and the imperial family, and debated with the patriarch Eutychius. Elected pope during the plague of 590, he was consecrated on 3 September 590 and reigned until 12 March 604. He governed Rome in place of the absent imperial authorities: he organised the food supply from the papal estates in Sicily and elsewhere, which he managed with meticulous attention, paid troops, ransomed captives, and negotiated with the Lombard king Agilulf in 593 and 598, despite Maurice's disapproval. He corresponded with Theodelinda, encouraging the conversion of the Lombards, with Brunhild and the Frankish kings, with Reccared, and with the emperor and patriarchs, protesting against the title 'ecumenical patriarch' of John the Faster. In 596 he sent Augustine with forty monks to convert the English. His writings, the Pastoral Rule (591), the Moralia on Job, the Dialogues (593-594), the homilies on the Gospels and Ezekiel, and a Register of over 850 letters, made him one of the four Latin Doctors of the Church and a central figure of medieval spirituality. He called himself 'servant of the servants of God'. His epitaph calls him 'consul of God'.
scholarship: Markus, Gregory the Great and His World (1997)
Richards, Consul of God (1980)
Straw, Gregory the Great (1988)
Neil and Dal Santo (eds.), A Companion to Gregory the Great (2013)

sources.w: Ecclesiastical History of the English People

scholarship: Booth, Crisis of Empire (2014)

sources.a: History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria

procopius.detail: Procopius, born around 500 at Caesarea in Palestine, trained in rhetoric and law, became in 527 legal adviser (assessor) and secretary to Belisarius, accompanying him on the Persian frontier (527-531), in the Vandal war (533-536), where he was left in Carthage and witnessed the military mutiny, and in Italy (536-540), where he took part in the siege of Rome and the capture of Ravenna. He was in Constantinople during the plague of 542, which he describes as an eyewitness. He wrote three works. The History of the Wars, in eight books, books 1-7 published around 550-551 and book 8 around 553-554, narrates the Persian, Vandal and Gothic wars in the classical style of Thucydides and Herodotus, with speeches, ethnographic digressions and moral reflections. The Secret History (Anekdota), written around 550 and not published, attacks Justinian, Theodora, Belisarius and Antonina with extreme violence. The Buildings, a panegyric of Justinian's construction works, probably from around 554 or 560, describes Hagia Sophia, fortifications in the Balkans and the East and churches throughout the empire, but was apparently left unfinished. His views are difficult to reconcile: the Wars are critical but balanced, the Buildings flattering, the Secret History savage. Some identify him with the Procopius who was urban prefect of Constantinople in 562, though this is uncertain. He probably died in the 560s. He is the principal source for the reign of Justinian and the last great historian of classical antiquity. Modern scholarship debates whether he was a Christian, a classicising traditionalist opposed to the regime, or a complex writer adapting to different genres.
scholarship: Cameron, Procopius and the Sixth Century (1985)
Kaldellis, Procopius of Caesarea (2004)
Greatrex, 'Perceptions of Procopius in recent scholarship', Histos 8 (2014)
Paschoud (ed.), Zosime: Histoire nouvelle (1971-89)
Blockley, The Fragmentary Classicising Historians of the Later Roman Empire (1981-83)
Blockley, The Fragmentary Classicising Historians (1981-83)
Given (trans.), The Fragmentary History of Priscus (2014)
Cameron, Agathias (1970)
Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and his Historian (1988)
Whitby & Whitby (trans.), The History of Theophylact Simocatta (1986)
Goffart, The Narrators of Barbarian History (1988)
Christensen, Cassiodorus, Jordanes and the History of the Goths (2002)
Harries, Sidonius Apollinaris and the Fall of Rome (1994)
Chadwick, Boethius: The Consolations of Music, Logic, Theology and Philosophy (1981)
O'Donnell, Cassiodorus (1979)
Cameron, Claudian: Poetry and Propaganda at the Court of Honorius (1970)
Jeffreys, Jeffreys & Scott (trans.), The Chronicle of John Malalas (1986)
Heinzelmann, Gregory of Tours: History and Society in the Sixth Century (2001)
Goffart, The Narrators of Barbarian History (1988)
Blockley (ed.), The History of Menander the Guardsman (1985)
Whitby, 'George of Pisidia's presentation of the emperor Heraclius', in Dabrowa (ed.), The Roman and Byzantine Army in the East (1994)
Whitby (trans.), The Ecclesiastical History of Evagrius Scholasticus (2000)
Burgess (ed.), The Chronicle of Hydatius (1993)
Moorhead (trans.), Victor of Vita: History of the Vandal Persecution (1992)

muhammad.detail: Muhammad ibn Abd Allah, born in Mecca, traditionally in 570, the Year of the Elephant, into the Hashim clan of the Quraysh, was orphaned young and raised by his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib and his uncle Abu Talib. He worked as a merchant, travelling, according to tradition, to Syria, and married a wealthy widow, Khadija. Around 610, at about forty, he began to receive revelations in a cave on Mount Hira, which he preached in Mecca, calling for the worship of one God and warning of the Last Judgement. Persecuted by the Quraysh, some of his followers emigrated to Aksum around 615; in 622 he emigrated to Yathrib (Medina), the Hijra, where he became the leader of a community of believers. In Medina he fought the Meccans at Badr (624), Uhud (625) and the Trench (627), expelled or destroyed the Jewish tribes of the city, made the truce of Hudaybiyya (628), conquered Khaybar (628), and in January 630 took Mecca almost without fighting, destroying the idols of the Kaaba. After the battle of Hunayn, tribes from across Arabia sent delegations to submit; the expedition to Tabuk (630) brought agreements with communities on the Roman frontier, after the Muslim defeat at Mu'ta (629). He died on 8 June 632 at Medina, leaving most of Arabia united. The Qur'an, the record of his revelations, was compiled after his death. The biography of Muhammad depends mainly on Muslim sources written in the eighth and ninth centuries, notably Ibn Ishaq via Ibn Hisham; contemporary non-Muslim references, such as the Doctrina Jacobi (634), are few.
scholarship: Donner, Muhammad and the Believers (2010)
Hoyland, Seeing Islam as Others Saw It (1997)
Watt, Muhammad at Mecca (1953) and Muhammad at Medina (1956)
Shoemaker, The Death of a Prophet (2012)
Anthony, Muhammad and the Empires of Faith (2020)

umar.detail: Umar ibn al-Khattab, born around 584 in Mecca into the Adi clan of the Quraysh, was at first a fierce opponent of Muhammad but converted around 616, an event that, according to tradition, allowed the Muslims to pray openly at the Kaaba. He emigrated to Medina, fought at Badr and Uhud, and became one of Muhammad's closest advisers; his daughter Hafsa married the Prophet. On Muhammad's death in 632 he secured the election of Abu Bakr, and on Abu Bakr's death in August 634 succeeded him as caliph, taking the title amir al-mu'minin (Commander of the Faithful). His ten-year caliphate saw the most rapid expansion of the Islamic state. His armies conquered Syria, with the victories of Fahl, Damascus and the Yarmuk (636); Iraq, with Qadisiyya (636), Ctesiphon and Jalula (637); Mesopotamia; Egypt (639-642); and western Iran, with Nahavand (642). He went in person to Syria, holding a council at al-Jabiya (638) and accepting the surrender of Jerusalem. He organised the conquered territories: he founded the garrison cities (amsar) of Basra, Kufa and Fustat, where the Arab troops lived apart from the conquered population; he created the diwan, a register of soldiers and their pensions; he adopted the Hijra calendar; and he left the existing Roman and Persian administrations in place, imposing tribute and land tax on non-Muslims. He dismissed Khalid ibn al-Walid in 634 and again in 638. He was known for his austerity and harsh justice. He was stabbed in the mosque of Medina by a Persian slave named Abu Lu'lu'a in November 644 and died soon after.
scholarship: Donner, The Early Islamic Conquests (1981)
Madelung, The Succession to Muhammad (1997)
Kennedy, The Prophet and the Age of the Caliphates (1986, 3rd ed. 2016)
Donner, The Early Islamic Conquests (1981)

titus_larcius_flavus.detail: Livy admits his sources disagreed on whether Larcius or M'. Valerius was the first dictator. Dionysius gives a long account of a census held under his dictatorship. The Larcii were an Etruscan-named gens that vanished from the Fasti after the early 5th century.

manius_valerius_maximus_dict494.detail: He is presented as a Valerian friend of the people, part of the family tradition that runs from Publicola to the consuls of 449 and 300. The title Maximus was said to have been granted for his conduct.

attius_tullius.detail: Livy makes him engineer the expulsion of Volscians from the Roman games of 490 to provoke war. After Coriolanus withdrew, the Volsci quarrelled with the Aequi and Attius disappears from the record.

anaxilas_of_rhegium.detail: His coins show a hare and a mule-car commemorating his Olympic mule-cart victory. He blocked the Strait against Etruscan shipping. His sons were displaced by his regent Micythus, who led the Rhegines in the disaster against the Iapygians in 473.

theron_of_acragas.detail: Pindar celebrated his Olympic chariot victory of 476 (Olympian 2 and 3), with its unusual eschatology of the Isles of the Blest. His son Thrasydaeus lost power soon after his death.

kaeso_fabius_vibulanus.detail: Livy places Caeso at the head of the clan's march out through the right arch of the Porta Carmentalis, ever after ill-omened. Dionysius makes him prosecutor of Sp. Cassius.

marcus_fabius_vibulanus.detail: His care for wounded soldiers in patrician houses is Livy's turning point in Fabian popularity.

veturia.detail: Livy gives her one of the great speeches of his first decade: 'Am I in your camp as a mother or a prisoner?'. Her deed was commemorated in the temple of Fortuna Muliebris. She is the model of the Roman mother whose authority over an adult son outweighs his military command.

volumnia.detail: The naming differs between Livy (wife Volumnia) and Plutarch (mother Volumnia, wife Vergilia), and Shakespeare followed Plutarch.

valeria_sister_of_publicola.detail: Her role belongs to the Valerian family tradition, which inserted Valerii into the key moments of early Republican history.

gnaeus_genucius_tr473.detail: The Genucii were a leading plebeian family: L. Genucius was the first plebeian consul to lead an army under his own auspices (362), and a tribune Genucius carried the laws of 342.

caeso_quinctius.detail: His case gives the first recorded use of sureties (vades) for a defendant's appearance. The witness against him, M. Volscius Fictor, was later convicted of perjury.

ducetius.detail: His career, known from Diodorus, is the most ambitious native response to Greek colonisation in Sicily.

lucius_siccius_dentatus.detail: Tribune of the plebs in 454 in some accounts, he was a symbol of plebeian service to the state. His catalogue of dona militaria is the classic list for Roman military decorations.

lucius_icilius.detail: The Icilii appear as hereditary champions of the plebs in Livy's narrative.

mamercus_aemilius_mamercinus.detail: He took Fidenae in 426 by mining under its citadel, according to Livy. His dignity under the censors' punishment became exemplary.

hermocrates.detail: Thucydides gives him two major speeches. His daughter married Dionysius I, who exploited his memory.

velthur_spurinna.detail: The elogia were set up in the 1st century AD by his descendants; the haruspex Spurinna who warned Caesar about the Ides of March may belong to the same family.

hannibal_mago_409.detail: He sacrificed 3,000 Himeraean prisoners to the shade of his grandfather Hamilcar, killed at Himera in 480. Not to be confused with the Hannibal son of Gisco of the First Punic War.

dionysius_ii.detail: Anecdotes made him a schoolmaster or begging priest at Corinth, a proverbial example of fallen fortune.

marcus_popillius_laenas.detail: As consul in 359 he was also flamen Carmentalis and, by tradition, came straight from a sacrifice in his priestly robe to calm a riot.

gaius_junius_bubulcus_brutus.detail: As censor with M. Valerius Maximus he built roads through the countryside at public expense.

herennius_pontius.detail: Cicero says he conversed with Archytas of Tarentum and Plato, an anecdote showing Samnite elites in the Italiote intellectual world.

lucius_albinius.detail: Valerius Maximus and Livy make him an exemplum of religious piety; Aristotle's 'Lucius' who saved Rome may be him.

catulus_cos78.detail: Catulus was the model of the upright Sullan noble: he refused bribes, defended the Senate's authority and was widely respected even by opponents. When he asked the people in 67 whom they would turn to if Pompey died, they shouted 'You!'. His humiliation by the young Caesar in the pontifical election, despite offering Caesar a bribe to withdraw, marked the arrival of a new generation.

atticus.detail: Atticus is the great example of a Roman who prospered by staying out of politics: he lent money to Marius' son and to Brutus, protected Fulvia when Antony was outlawed, and was spared in the proscriptions because of it. His Liber Annalis, a chronological table of Roman history, was used by Cicero and Nepos. His slaves copied and distributed Cicero's works. Nepos' Life of him is an admiring portrait by a friend.

munatius_plancus.detail: Velleius calls him a 'morbid traitor'. He was said to have performed in Alexandria as the sea god Glaucus, painted blue and naked, crawling on his knees at a banquet of Antony and Cleopatra. Yet he was among the most successful survivors of the age, rebuilt the Temple of Saturn, and Horace addressed an ode to him.

asinius_pollio.detail: Pollio cultivated independence: he refused to join Octavian at Actium, saying he would be the prize of the victor, and as a critic he called Caesar's commentaries careless and Livy's style provincial ('Patavinitas'). Horace's Ode 2.1 warns him that writing the history of the civil wars was walking on fire hidden under ash.

juba_ii.detail: He wrote in Greek on Libya, Arabia (for Gaius Caesar's eastern expedition), Roman antiquities, the theatre and painting, works much cited by Pliny the Elder. He sent expeditions to the Canary Islands (the Fortunate Isles) and to the Purple Islands off Mogador, and named the euphorbia plant after his physician Euphorbus. His coins carry Latin legends for himself and Greek for his queen. He served in the Cantabrian war and on Gaius's eastern staff.

cleopatra_selene.detail: Her coins bear Greek legends (BASILISSA KLEOPATRA) with crocodile and Isis symbols, asserting her Ptolemaic descent. Her death is placed c. 5 BC, linked by some to an epigram of Crinagoras on a lunar eclipse. Her son Ptolemy succeeded Juba.

livy.detail: Livy held no public office and seems to have lived at Rome on private means, on friendly terms with Augustus, who called him a Pompeian, and encouraging the young Claudius to write history. Asinius Pollio sneered at his "Patavinity". A man from Gades travelled to Rome only to see him (Pliny, Letters 2.3). He returned to Patavium and died there in AD 17.

vitruvius.detail: He built the basilica at Fanum Fortunae and received a pension through Octavia. His treatise covers urban planning, materials, temple design, acoustics of theatres, aqueducts, sundials and machines. Rediscovered at St Gall in 1416, it shaped Renaissance architecture from Alberti to Palladio.

strabo.detail: From a family that had served Mithridates VI and then gone over to Lucullus, Strabo studied at Nysa and Rome, travelled with Aelius Gallus in Egypt (25-24 BC) and wrote a lost history continuing Polybius. He was a Stoic and admirer of Augustan peace.

nicolaus_of_damascus.detail: He tutored the children of Antony and Cleopatra, then served Herod, defending the Jews of Ionia before Agrippa (14 BC), reconciling Herod with Augustus (8-7 BC) and pleading for Archelaus at Rome in 4 BC. His Life of Augustus is the earliest biography of the princeps, covering his youth and Caesar's assassination in vivid detail.

antonius_musa.detail: Horace (Epistles 1.15) took a cold-water cure on his advice. His brother Euphorbus was physician to Juba II. Several pharmacological works were attributed to him later.

vipsania_agrippina.detail: She then married Gaius Asinius Gallus, bearing him at least five sons. Tacitus says she alone of Agrippa's children died naturally, in AD 20. Tiberius never forgave Gallus for marrying her.

lucius_domitius_ahenobarbus_cos16.detail: Suetonius describes him as arrogant, extravagant and cruel, a keen charioteer who staged gladiatorial shows so bloody that Augustus had to restrain him. Augustus named him in his will. His son Gnaeus married Agrippina the Younger and fathered Nero.

cossus_cornelius_lentulus.detail: Seneca (Epistles 83.15) records that Cossus came drunk to the Senate and had to be carried home, yet Tiberius confided matters to him that he would tell no one else. His son Cn. Lentulus Gaetulicus commanded Upper Germany for ten years until Caligula executed him in 39.

lucius_calpurnius_piso_pontifex.detail: Velleius praises his combination of vigilance and apparent indolence. Like Cossus he was said to have earned Tiberius's confidence during long drinking sessions. Tacitus records his state funeral in 32.

marcus_antistius_labeo.detail: His father was among Caesar's assassins and died at Philippi. He divided his year between teaching in Rome and writing in the country. Innovative in method, he drew on grammar and dialectic. Gellius and Pomponius record his frank opposition to Augustus, who mocked him in the Senate.

gaius_ateius_capito.detail: Tacitus contrasts him with the independent Labeo: Capito's obsequiousness was rewarded with a consulship. In 15 he chaired the commission on the Tiber floods. He wrote on pontifical law and on the duties of senators; Suetonius records him flattering Tiberius that he could grant citizenship to words.

masurius_sabinus.detail: He lived on fees from his pupils and reached the equestrian order only around fifty. The Sabinian school took its name from him. Ulpian, Paul and Pomponius wrote huge commentaries following his order.

judas_the_galilean.detail: His sons James and Simon were crucified c. 46-48; Menahem, son or grandson, led a faction in 66; Eleazar ben Yair, commander at Masada, was a descendant. Acts 5.37 says he perished and his followers were scattered.

herod_antipas.detail: His divorce of Aretas IV's daughter to marry his niece Herodias led to war with Nabataea and a disastrous defeat c. 36. Jesus called him "that fox" (Luke 13.32). He enjoyed Tiberius's favour and hosted the meeting of Vitellius and Artabanus.

herodias.detail: Her daughter by her first marriage is the Salome of later tradition, named by Josephus. Ambitious for royal title, she pushed Antipas to seek it from Caligula, which led to his exile; she chose to share it.

john_the_baptist.detail: Luke makes him a kinsman of Jesus born to the priest Zechariah. His movement survived his death, with disciples at Ephesus in the 50s and the later Mandaeans claiming descent from it.

caiaphas.detail: His long tenure suggests close cooperation with Pilate; both were removed by Lucius Vitellius in 36-37. An ossuary inscribed "Joseph son of Caiaphas" found in a Jerusalem tomb in 1990 may be his.

james_the_just.detail: Paul lists him as a witness of the risen Jesus (1 Corinthians 15.7). Josephus records his execution. The epistle of James is attributed to him. Later tradition, through Hegesippus, made him a Nazirite who prayed in the Temple until his knees were like a camel's.

stephen_protomartyr.detail: His relics were "discovered" at Kfar Gamla in 415, an event that spread his cult across the Mediterranean, including to Augustine's Hippo.

barnabas.detail: He sided with Peter at the Antioch incident (Galatians 2.13). The Epistle of Barnabas (c. 130) is wrongly attributed to him. The church of Cyprus claims him as founder.

aretas_iv.detail: Augustus was angry that he took the throne without permission but recognised him. His daughter's divorce by Antipas caused the war. His coins call him "lover of his people". His reign is the most prolifically attested in Nabataean inscriptions.

artabanus_ii.detail: Tacitus says he wrote to Tiberius demanding Augustus's treasure and threatening to reclaim the lands of Cyrus and Alexander. He was briefly driven out by Tiridates III in 36 but returned. His sons Vardanes and Gotarzes fought for the succession.

pharasmanes_i.detail: Tacitus portrays him as ambitious and ruthless; he eventually executed Radamistus for treason to win Roman favour (58). The Harmozica inscription of 75 shows Roman support for his successor Mithridates.

mithridates_of_armenia.detail: His fate exposed the weakness of the Roman garrison commanders in Armenia and opened the way for the Parthian candidate Tiridates.

radamistus.detail: His flight from Armenia with his pregnant wife Zenobia, whom he stabbed and threw into the Araxes rather than leave her to the enemy, became a famous scene (and the subject of Handel's opera Radamisto, 1720).

lucius_vitellius_censor.detail: Tacitus and Suetonius present him as a model of courtly flattery: he worshipped Caligula as a god, carried Messalina's slipper inside his toga and kissed it, and urged the Senate to approve Claudius's marriage to his niece Agrippina. Yet his eastern governorship was capable and humane toward the Jews.

marcus_furius_camillus_cos8.detail: His son Furius Camillus Scribonianus led the failed revolt in Dalmatia against Claudius in 42. His daughter Livia Medullina was engaged to the young Claudius but died on the wedding day.

vannius.detail: Claudius refused to intervene militarily but gave him refuge in Pannonia. The kingdom lay between the rivers Marus (Morava) and Cusus.

rhescuporis_ii.detail: His son Rhoemetalces II kept the western kingdom after his fall.

artaxias_iii.detail: A rare Roman coin of Germanicus shows him crowning Artaxias with the legend ARTAXIAS GERMANICVS.

polemon_ii.detail: His coins carry his own and the emperors' portraits; for Berenice he underwent circumcision.

gaius_asinius_gallus.detail: Augustus reputedly named him among men "eager but unequal" to the principate. He wrote a comparison of his father and Cicero, to which Claudius replied. Five of his sons reached the consulship.

valerius_maximus.detail: His work, despised for its rhetoric, was enormously read in late antiquity and the Middle Ages.

apion.detail: He lectured in Rome under Tiberius and Claudius; Tiberius called him "the cymbal of the world". Aulus Gellius preserves his story of Androcles and the lion, which he claimed to have witnessed in the Circus Maximus.

julia_livilla.detail: Her fall and Seneca's exile illustrate the struggle for influence at Claudius's court.

pallas.detail: His brother Antonius Felix was procurator of Judaea. The Senate's honours for him in 52 were Pliny's symbol of the shame of the Claudian court.

aulus_didius_gallus.detail: An inscription from Olympia lists his long career, including curator aquarum and proconsul of Asia.

mithridates_of_bosporus.detail: His defiant words to Claudius impressed the emperor. His coins carry Claudius's portrait.

helena_of_adiabene.detail: Rabbinic sources remember her golden lamp over the Temple entrance and her Nazirite vows. Pausanias admired her tomb's mechanical door.

antonius_felix.detail: Tacitus says he "exercised royal power with the mind of a slave". The sicarii first appeared under him, assassinating the former High Priest Jonathan.

porcius_festus.detail: Josephus describes his campaigns against sicarii and a dispute over a wall built by the priests to block Agrippa's view of the Temple.

venutius.detail: Tacitus calls him second only to Caratacus in military skill. His end is unknown.

lucius_clodius_macer.detail: His denarii, with legends such as L CLODI MACRI and a portrait of Libertas, are prized rarities.

yohanan_ben_zakkai.detail: He issued ordinances (taqqanot) adapting Temple rituals such as the shofar on the Sabbath and the lulav to synagogue practice. His pupils included Eliezer ben Hyrcanus and Joshua ben Hananiah.

columella.detail: He owned estates near Rome at Ardea, Carseoli and Alba, and served as a military tribune in Syria (inscription from Tarentum).

hero_of_alexandria.detail: His date rests on the lunar eclipse of 62 AD in the Dioptra. He probably taught at the Museum of Alexandria.

quintilian.detail: Brought to Rome by Galba in 68, he taught for twenty years (Pliny the Younger was a pupil), retired c. 90 and was given consular ornaments for tutoring the sons of Flavius Clemens. He lost his young wife and two sons, grief he records in the preface to Book 6.

statius.detail: His father was a famous teacher and poet at Naples. Statius won at Domitian's Alban games but lost at the Capitoline, and retired to Naples. Dante made him a guide in Purgatorio.

juvenal.detail: Martial addresses him as a friend toiling through the clients' round. An inscription from Aquinum may name him as a militia officer, and the ancient Lives claim he was exiled to Egypt for mocking an actor, details of doubtful value.

suetonius.detail: Pliny obtained for him the ius trium liberorum. An inscription from Hippo Regius lists his court posts. His lost works included treatises on games, courtesans, Greek insults and the Roman year.

plutarch.detail: He studied at Athens under Ammonius, visited Rome and Alexandria and lectured in Rome under Vespasian or Domitian. His Roman citizenship came through Lucius Mestrius Florus. His works, some 78 essays and 50 lives surviving, shaped the European image of antiquity.

clement_of_rome.detail: Later legend identified him with the consul Flavius Clemens and made him a martyr in the Crimea; a mass of pseudo-Clementine literature (Homilies, Recognitions) grew up around his name. The basilica of San Clemente in Rome is built over a house and mithraeum associated with him.

ignatius_of_antioch.detail: He met Polycarp at Smyrna; his letter to the Romans begs them not to save him. Origen and Eusebius say he was Peter's second successor at Antioch.

polycarp.detail: He visited Anicetus of Rome to discuss the Easter date. The Martyrdom of Polycarp, a letter of the Smyrnaean church, is the oldest martyr narrative outside the New Testament; he told the proconsul "86 years I have served him and he has done me no wrong".

marcion.detail: He returned a donation of 200,000 sesterces on his expulsion. His church spread widely and survived in Syria into the fifth century. Tertullian's five books Against Marcion preserve much of his Antitheses.

valentinus_gnostic.detail: Educated in Alexandria, he reportedly claimed instruction from Theudas, a disciple of Paul. Tertullian says he expected to be bishop. Fragments survive in Clement of Alexandria, and the Gospel of Truth may be his.

irenaeus.detail: He carried the Lyon confessors' letter to Rome and mediated in the Easter controversy. His Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching survives in Armenian. Later tradition, not early, makes him a martyr.

montanus.detail: Opponents claimed he had been a priest of Cybele and that he and Maximilla hanged themselves, hostile stories. His movement attracted Tertullian and persisted for centuries.

victor_bishop.detail: Jerome credits him with the first Latin theological works. He excommunicated the adoptionist Theodotus the Cobbler.

callistus.detail: Hippolytus, his rival, accuses him of banking fraud and laxity in readmitting sinners. He may have died in a riot in Trastevere.

marcus_cornelius_fronto.detail: His letters, recovered from palimpsests in the nineteenth century, reveal court life and his disappointment at Marcus's turn to philosophy. He was in poor health with gout for most of his life and seems to have died of the plague c. 167.

apuleius.detail: Educated at Carthage, Athens and Rome, initiated into several mystery cults, he became a celebrated lecturer at Carthage. Augustine, also from Madauros, discussed his demonology.

lucian.detail: He gave up a career as a sculptor for rhetoric, toured Ionia, Italy and Gaul, settled at Athens and late in life took a salaried post in the prefect of Egypt's administration.

pausanias_periegetes.detail: He mentions Herodes Atticus's Odeion and the Costoboci raid of 170. Little else is known of him.

appian.detail: He experienced the Jewish revolt in Egypt (116-117) and narrowly escaped. His Civil Wars is the main continuous narrative of 133-35 BC.

celsus_philosopher.detail: Origen confused him with an Epicurean of the same name; his identity and place are unknown.

alexander_of_abonoteichus.detail: He persuaded the emperor to rename his town Ionopolis and married his daughter to the consular Rutilianus. Statues and coins of Glykon show the cult's reach from the Danube to Athens.

julia_balbilla.detail: Her brother was Philopappus, whose monument stands on the Hill of the Muses at Athens. The epigrams are among the very few surviving poems by Roman women.

sources.w: Les inscriptions grecques et latines du Colosse de Memnon (Bernand)

tarrutenius_paternus.detail: Dio says he negotiated with the Cotini during the war. Fragments of his military law survive in the Digest.

quintus_junius_rusticus.detail: Marcus thanks him in Meditations 1.7 for showing him the need to correct his character and for lending him his copy of Epictetus. He was consul a second time in 162, a rare honour.

sohaemus_of_armenia.detail: The novelist Iamblichus claimed he knew him. Coins of Verus show the investiture with the legend REX ARMENIIS DATVS.

ariogaesus.detail: His case shows Rome claiming the right to approve the rulers of the Quadi, as Antoninus's REX QVADIS DATVS coins advertised.

gaius_aufidius_victorinus.detail: Dio says he faced down Perennis and died, possibly by suicide, around 185.

quintus_pompeius_falco.detail: He married the granddaughter of Sosius Senecio and is said to have shown Fronto his vine-grafting experiments.

gnaeus_julius_verus.detail: He was designated for a second consulship c. 180 but died before holding it.

decimus_terentius_scaurianus.detail: He had commanded in the Second Dacian War; military diplomas of 109-110 name him.

abgar_vii.detail: After his death Osroene was briefly administered directly, then given to the Parthian prince Parthamaspates.

decimus_valerius_asiaticus.detail: He had accompanied Claudius to Britain. After Caligula's murder he told the crowd he wished he had done it.

opramoas.detail: The dossier is a key document of provincial euergetism and of the way imperial honours were negotiated through letters.

ummidius_quadratus.detail: His career inscription from Casinum records service under Tiberius. He died in office.

gaius_septicius_clarus.detail: The Historia Augusta says the cause was their behaviour toward Sabina without the emperor's permission.

bruttia_crispina.detail: Her coins show Venus, Juno Lucina and Concordia. Her disgrace has been placed in 182 after the Lucilla conspiracy or as late as 187-188.

milonia_caesonia.detail: Suetonius reports he displayed her naked to friends and rode with her in military cloak; rumour said she drove him mad with a love potion.

statilia_messalina.detail: Inscriptions record her at the Vatican and among the Arval Brethren's honours. Otho's last letters were addressed to her.

salonia_matidia.detail: Fragments of Hadrian's laudatio survive on an inscription from Tibur. She accompanied Trajan to the East and returned with his ashes.

ulpia_marciana.detail: Trajan named the colony Marcianopolis in Moesia and the Thamugadi foundation (Colonia Marciana Traiana Thamugadi) after her.

domitia_lucilla.detail: The Domitian brickyards she owned passed to Marcus and became imperial property, their stamps a dating tool for Roman buildings. Fronto's letters show the young Marcus chatting with her at Antoninus's villas.

julia_flavia.detail: Her portraits with towering curls are a hallmark of Flavian female fashion; she appears on coins as DIVA IVLIA.

titus_furius_victorinus.detail: His death is recorded by the Historia Augusta. He was succeeded by Macrinius Vindex, killed in battle with the Marcomanni in 170.

gaius_claudius_severus.detail: His family produced Marcus Aurelius's Peripatetic friend Claudius Severus Arabianus and Commodus's brother-in-law.

anicetus_bishop.detail: Hegesippus visited Rome in his time and compiled a succession list of Roman bishops.

sources.w: Life of Paul the First Hermit
History of Vardan and the Armenian War

scholarship: Shahid, Byzantium and the Arabs in the Sixth Century (1995-2010)

sources.a: History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria

porsenna_war.detail:
The first years of the Republic were spent fighting off the exiled Tarquins and their Etruscan allies. In 509 Veii and Tarquinii marched on Rome; in the battle at the Silva Arsia the consul Brutus and Arruns, son of Tarquin, killed each other in single combat, the battle was drawn, and in the night a voice from the forest, attributed to Silvanus, proclaimed that the Etruscans had lost one man more. P. Valerius triumphed. In 508 Lars Porsenna of Clusium, the most powerful Etruscan king of the day, attacked: Roman legend tells of Horatius at the bridge, Mucius Scaevola's burned hand and Cloelia's escape, after which Porsenna made peace in admiration, taking hostages and the land Rome had taken from Veii.

Non-Roman evidence suggests the reality was harsher. Tacitus speaks of the city's surrender to Porsenna, and Pliny quotes a treaty forbidding the Romans iron except for agriculture. Porsenna's power in Latium collapsed when his son Arruns besieged Aricia (504 in the traditional chronology) and was defeated and killed by the Latins and the Cumaean army of Aristodemus. Dionysius' account of this battle comes from a Cumaean chronicle independent of Roman tradition, and confirms the broad outline. Etruscan survivors who fled to Rome were settled in the Vicus Tuscus below the Palatine. Tarquin then moved to Tusculum, where his son-in-law Octavius Mamilius was building the Latin coalition that fought at Lake Regillus.

Modern historians read the war as part of the collapse of Etruscan hegemony in Latium and Campania at the end of the 6th century: Etruscan defeat at Aricia (504) was followed by the naval defeat at Cumae (474). Rome emerged independent, but weaker than under the kings, and needed a generation to rebuild its position among the Latins. Some scholars think Porsenna, not the Roman aristocracy, removed Tarquin, and that the Republic was born under Clusine supervision.

first_latin_war.detail:
After the fall of the monarchy Rome lost the hegemony over Latium that the first treaty with Carthage assumes. The Latin cities met in council at the grove and spring of Ferentina near Aricia, and Dionysius preserves a list of about thirty Latin peoples who swore alliance against Rome, among them Ardea, Aricia, Lanuvium, Lavinium, Tibur, Tusculum, Praeneste, Gabii, Velitrae, Norba, Circeii, Cora, Satricum and Corioli. Their leader was Octavius Mamilius of Tusculum, son-in-law of Tarquinius Superbus, who sheltered the old king. Cato's fragment on the dedication of the grove of Diana at Aricia by a Tusculan 'Latin dictator' may belong to this coalition.

Rome's response included the first dictatorship (501 or 498), the capture of Crustumerium and the defection of Praeneste to Rome (499). The decisive battle was fought at Lake Regillus in Tusculan territory, in 499 or 496, under the dictator A. Postumius Albus. Mamilius was killed, the Tarquins' last army destroyed, and the old king fled to Cumae, where he died in 495; legend added the epiphany of Castor and Pollux, whose temple in the Forum was dedicated in 484.

The war did not end in Roman domination. The rise of the Volsci and Aequi, who were pressing into the Pontine plain and the Alban hills, gave both sides reasons to reconcile, and in 493 Sp. Cassius concluded the Foedus Cassianum, a treaty of perpetual peace and mutual defence between Rome and the Latins on equal terms, with shared booty and joint colonies. The Hernici joined in 486. The alliance, renewed in 358, lasted until the Latin revolt of 340. Historians debate how equal it really was, but the first Latin war established the framework of Roman-Latin relations that underpinned Rome's survival in the 5th century.

volscian_wars.detail:
The Volsci, an Oscan-Umbrian people whose language is known from the 3rd-century Tabula Veliterna, descended from the uplands of the Liris and Sacco valleys around 500 and took over much of southern Latium: Antium, Satricum, Velitrae, Suessa Pometia, Anxur (Tarracina), Privernum, Circeii, Ecetra and Corioli. Their arrival, part of the wider movement of Sabellian peoples out of the Apennines that also brought Samnites into Campania and Lucanians into the south, threatened Rome and the Latins equally, and was a main reason for the Foedus Cassianum.

The wars fall into phases. From 495 to the 460s Rome and the Latins fought for the Pontine plain: Suessa Pometia (502, 495), Corioli (493), Coriolanus' march on Rome (488), the capture of Antium (468) and the colony there (467). Through the mid-5th century the Volsci and their Aequian allies raided Latium almost yearly by the Algidus pass, and Livy's narrative of these 'Volscian and Aequian' campaigns is repetitive and partly fictitious. The tide turned with Rome's victory on the Algidus (431), and in 406 Rome took Anxur. After the Gallic sack the Volsci revived, with Latin cities such as Velitrae and Circeii joining them; Camillus fought them at Maecium (389) and Satricum (386, 381), the colonies at Satricum, Setia, Sutrium and Nepet secured the frontier, and the Pomptine tribe was created on Volscian land in 358. Valerius Corvus burned Satricum in 346, and the Volsci joined the Latin revolt of 340.

The end came in 338, when Antium's fleet was destroyed and its beaks fixed to the Rostra, and in 329, when Privernum fell after a siege; its envoys' famous reply, that they would keep faithfully a good peace but not a bad one, won them citizenship. The Volscian country became Roman territory, with citizen colonies at Antium and Tarracina and the Oufentina tribe (318). A century and a half of warfare had turned the southern edge of Latium into the base for Rome's advance into Campania.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 304-309

aequian_wars.detail:
The Aequi inhabited the valleys of the upper Anio and Turano and the highlands around Carseoli and the Fucine lake, east of Tibur and Praeneste. Their raids came down through the Algidus pass between the Alban hills and the Praenestine mountains, threatening Tusculum, Labici and the approaches to Rome, often in concert with the Volsci. For most of the 5th century the Aequian war was a seasonal struggle for the Algidus.

Livy's narrative records repeated crises: in 465 and 464 consular armies were nearly trapped; in 458 the Aequi under Gracchus Cloelius surrounded the consul L. Minucius on the Algidus, and Cincinnatus, called from his plough, relieved him and sent the Aequi under the yoke; in 449 the decemvirs' army was beaten; in 446 the Aequi and Volsci raided up to the Esquiline Gate. The decisive victory came in 431, when the dictator A. Postumius Tubertus defeated a combined Aequian and Volscian army on the Algidus, after which Rome took the offensive, planting a colony at Labici (418) and fighting for Bolae (415-414). After the Gallic sack the Aequi were a lesser threat.

The end was brutal. After the Second Samnite War, in 304, the consuls P. Sempronius Sophus and P. Sulpicius Saverrio invaded Aequian territory and, according to Livy, stormed 31 towns in 50 days, most of which were burned; 'the name of the Aequi was nearly annihilated'. Latin colonies were planted at Alba Fucens (303, with 6,000 settlers) and Carseoli (298), and the road later known as the Via Valeria secured the route through their land to the Marsi and the Adriatic. The neighbouring Marsi, Paeligni, Marrucini and Frentani, watching, sought treaties with Rome. A remnant, the Aequiculi, survived around Nersae. The fate of the Aequi became a lesson in what awaited peoples who resisted Rome to the end.

first_veientine_war.detail:
Veii, the great Etruscan city 15 km north of Rome, controlled the right bank of the lower Tiber, the salt pans at its mouth, and the bridgehead of Fidenae on the left bank. The first war of the Republic with Veii (483-474) was fought over these routes. After years of raids, in 480 the consuls M. Fabius and Cn. Manlius fought a costly battle before Veii in which the former consul Q. Fabius and the consul Manlius were killed. The Fabii then made the war their own: in 479, according to Livy, 306 men of the Fabian gens, with their clients (4,000 according to Dionysius), marched out through the right-hand arch of the Porta Carmentalis and built a fort on the Cremera, a tributary of the Tiber below Veii, from which they raided Veientine territory for two years. In 477 they were lured into an ambush and annihilated; only one boy, left at home, survived to continue the family. Ovid dates the disaster to 13 February, Livy to 18 July, the day of the Allia.

The Veientes exploited the disaster, occupied the Janiculum and crossed the Tiber; fighting at the temple of Spes and the Colline Gate and a grain shortage followed, until in 476 they were dislodged. The tribunes prosecuted the consul T. Menenius for failing to relieve the Fabii. In 474, after a further Roman victory, Veii obtained a forty-year truce.

The Cremera story is surely embellished. The figure of 306 Fabii echoes the 300 Spartans at Thermopylae, fought in the same years, and the family tradition was transmitted by Fabius Pictor. But a private war fought by an aristocratic clan with its retainers fits the world of the Lapis Satricanus, where a Valerius' 'companions' dedicate to Mars, and many historians accept that the early Republic's wars were partly conducted by gentilicial war bands. The truce of 474 coincided with Syracuse's naval victory over the Etruscans at Cumae, a sign of declining Etruscan power.

second_veientine_war.detail:
The second war with Veii (438-425) began with the defection of Fidenae, the Tiber-crossing town 8 km north of Rome, which had received Roman colonists, to Lars Tolumnius, king of Veii. The Fidenates killed four Roman envoys at Tolumnius' prompting, an outrage commemorated by their statues on the Rostra. In 437 the dictator Mam. Aemilius and his master of horse fought the Veientes, Fidenates and Faliscans below Fidenae, and A. Cornelius Cossus, then a military tribune, killed Tolumnius in single combat and dedicated his armour to Jupiter Feretrius: the spolia opima, won only three times in Roman history (Romulus, Cossus and Marcellus in 222).

Cossus' rank became a political issue under Augustus. Livy reports that Augustus, restoring the temple of Jupiter Feretrius, saw Cossus' linen corslet inscribed with the title of consul, which implied the spolia were won in his consulship of 428, not as a tribune in 437. The point mattered because in 29 BC M. Licinius Crassus, proconsul of Macedonia, claimed the spolia opima for killing a Bastarnian king, and Augustus, by insisting that only a commander fighting under his own auspices could dedicate them, blocked the claim.

Plague slowed the war in the 430s, while the Etruscan council at the Fanum Voltumnae refused Veii help (434). In 426 Fidenae revolted again and massacred its Roman colonists; the dictator Mam. Aemilius took it, Livy says by driving a tunnel into its citadel, sold the inhabitants and destroyed the town. In 425 Veii accepted a twenty-year truce. The war gave Rome the whole left bank of the lower Tiber and its crossing points, preparing the final war with Veii twenty years later.

third_veientine_war.detail:
When the truce of 425 expired, Veii refused Rome's demands for redress, and in 406 the war began that ended with the city's destruction. It was a different kind of war from the seasonal raids of the 5th century. Pay for soldiers, funded by a property tax, was introduced in 406; the army wintered before Veii for the first time in 403; citizens of equestrian rank volunteered to serve on their own horses. The siege lines, as Livy describes them, included camps, ramparts and siege works. Veii's allies, Capena and the Faliscans, attacked the lines in 402, exploiting the quarrel of the consular tribunes M'. Sergius and L. Verginius, and the camp was lost. The Etruscan league at the Fanum Voltumnae refused to help, partly because Veii had chosen a king whom the other cities disliked.

The religious narrative dominates the last years: the rising of the Alban Lake (398), the oracle from Delphi and a Veientine prophecy that the city would fall when the lake was drained, the drainage tunnel, and the dictatorship of M. Furius Camillus in 396, who took the city by mining under its citadel and called out its goddess Juno Regina. The population was sold, the booty divided, a tenth vowed to Apollo, and a golden bowl sent to Delphi, which was intercepted by pirates from Lipara and restored by their magistrate Timasitheus, honoured by Rome with hospitium.

Capena surrendered in 395 and Falerii in 394. The Veientine territory was distributed in seven-iugera plots and organised in four new tribes in 387, raising Rome's territory from about 820 to some 1,500 km2 by Beloch's estimate. Rome had destroyed a major Etruscan city for the first time, and its manpower and land were now greater than any Latin or Etruscan rival's. The victory was nearly lost six years later when the Gauls sacked Rome, and there was serious debate about moving the whole people to Veii.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 309-313

gallic_war_390.detail:
Celtic peoples had been crossing the Alps into the Po valley for generations; Livy dates the first migration to the reign of Tarquinius Priscus, Polybius describes the settlement of the Insubres, Boii, Lingones and finally the Senones on the Adriatic coast. Early in the 4th century they overwhelmed the Etruscan cities north of the Apennines (Melpum fell in 396, in the same year as Veii according to Nepos). In 391 a band of Senones under Brennus crossed into Etruria and besieged Clusium; Livy repeats a story that a Clusine noble, Arruns, had invited them in revenge on a seducer, luring them with wine.

Rome sent three envoys, sons of M. Fabius Ambustus, to mediate. When they fought in the Clusine ranks and one killed a Gallic chief, the Gauls demanded their surrender; the Roman people instead elected them consular tribunes. The Gauls marched south, routed the Roman army at the Allia on 18 July, and entered the undefended city three days later. They plundered and burned it but failed to take the Capitol, which held out for seven months until the defenders, starving, paid 1,000 pounds of gold. Livy has Camillus arrive at that moment and destroy the Gauls; Polybius says they left because the Veneti were attacking their homeland, and Diodorus and Strabo that the Caeretans defeated them on the way back.
