The Lusitanian War (155-139) was a long war against the Lusitanians, a people of the western Iberian Peninsula between the Tagus and the Douro (central Portugal and western Spain), who raided the Roman province of Hispania Ulterior and its allies. In 155 the Lusitanians under Punicus defeated the praetors Manius Manilius and Lucius Calpurnius Piso; in 153 Punicus' successor Caesarus defeated the praetor Lucius Mummius. In 151-150 the praetor Servius Sulpicius Galba and the consul Lucius Licinius Lucullus ravaged Lusitania; in 150 Galba, offering land to the Lusitanians, massacred those who laid down their arms, an act that provoked outrage and the trial of 149.

In 147 Viriathus, a survivor of the massacre, took command and began an eight-year campaign of guerrilla warfare, defeating the praetor Gaius Vetilius at Tribola (147), Gaius Plautius (146), Claudius Unimanus and Gaius Nigidius (145). Quintus Fabius Maximus Aemilianus (145-144) checked him, but Viriathus incited the Celtiberians to rise (143), beginning the Numantine War. In 141-140, Quintus Fabius Maximus Servilianus won some successes but was trapped by Viriathus near Erisane; Viriathus spared the army in exchange for a treaty that recognised him as a friend of the Roman people, ratified in Rome.

In 140/139 Servilianus' brother Quintus Servilius Caepio, with the Senate's connivance, broke the treaty and bribed three of Viriathus' companions to murder him. His successor Tautalus surrendered, and the Lusitanians were settled at Valentia (138) by Decimus Junius Brutus, who campaigned north to Gallaecia (137-136), crossing the Douro and the Limia (Lethe). The war was marked by Roman bad faith and brutality and by the military skill of Viriathus. Appian (Iberica 56-75), based on Polybius and Posidonius, and Diodorus (33) are the main sources. Modern historians debate the social character of Lusitanian resistance (poverty driving raids, as Appian suggests) and the role of Viriathus as a national hero in Portuguese tradition.
scholarship: Simon, Roms Kriege in Spanien 154-133 v. Chr. (1962)
Richardson, Hispaniae (1986)
Pastor Muñoz, Viriato: la lucha por la libertad (2000)
Alarcão, Roman Portugal (1988)

fourth_macedonian_war.detail:
The Fourth Macedonian War (150-148) was the revolt of Andriscus, a man of humble origin from Adramyttium in Mysia who claimed to be Philip, a son of Perseus who had died in Italy. Andriscus first sought support from Demetrius I of Syria, who handed him over to Rome; he escaped from custody in Italy, raised support among the Thracians, and in 149 invaded Macedonia, defeated the forces of the merides and proclaimed himself king as Philip VI. The four republics established in 167, weak and divided, collapsed quickly, and Andriscus reunited Macedonia, revealing the strength of Macedonian monarchist sentiment.

Andriscus invaded Thessaly in 149. Rome, occupied with Carthage and Spain, sent the praetor Publius Juventius Thalna with a single legion, which was destroyed, Juventius himself being killed, the only time in this period that a Roman army was destroyed in the Greek East. Scipio Nasica Corculum had earlier helped the Thessalians with Achaean troops. In 148 Rome sent the praetor Quintus Caecilius Metellus with two legions, supported by the fleet of Attalus II of Pergamon. Metellus defeated Andriscus near Pydna, the site of Aemilius Paullus' victory twenty years earlier. Andriscus fled to Thrace, where a Thracian chief, Byzes, handed him over; he was led in Metellus' triumph (146) and executed.

In 148 or 146 Rome made Macedonia a permanent province, abandoning the system of four republics, with a governor responsible for defending the northern frontier and supervising Greece; the Via Egnatia was built soon afterwards. Further pretenders appeared in 143 and 142 (a pseudo-Alexander and a pseudo-Philip), easily suppressed. The war marked the shift from indirect hegemony to direct rule in the Greek East, closely connected with the Achaean War (146). The sources are fragmentary: the Livian Periochae (49-50), Diodorus (32), Florus, Velleius, Zonaras and Polybius (36.10, 36.17), who expressed astonishment that such a man could succeed.
scholarship: Kallet-Marx, Hegemony to Empire (1995)
Morgan, Metellus Macedonicus and the Province Macedonia, Historia 18 (1969)
Hammond and Walbank, A History of Macedonia III (1988)

third_punic_war.detail:
The Third Punic War (149-146) resulted in the destruction of Carthage. After 201, Carthage had recovered economically, paying off its indemnity and offering to pay it early in 191. Masinissa, protected by the vague clause of the treaty of 201 allowing him to recover his ancestral lands, seized Carthaginian territory, notably the Emporia (161) and the Great Plains (c. 152), with Roman acquiescence. Cato, after an embassy in 153, demanded the destruction of Carthage, opposed by Scipio Nasica Corculum. In 150 Carthage, provoked, fought Masinissa and was defeated near Oroscopa; this breach of the treaty gave Rome its pretext.

In 149 Rome declared war; Utica surrendered to Rome, and the consuls Manius Manilius and Lucius Marcius Censorinus crossed with 80,000 infantry and 4,000 cavalry. Carthage surrendered by deditio, handed over 300 hostages and 200,000 sets of armour and 2,000 catapults, but when the consuls demanded that the city be abandoned and rebuilt inland, the Carthaginians resisted. The siege lasted three years: the consuls of 149 and 148 failed; Manilius was beaten at Nepheris, where the military tribune Scipio Aemilianus distinguished himself. In 147 the people elected Aemilianus consul, though below the legal age. He restored discipline, took the suburb of Megara, cut the city off by a siege wall across the isthmus and a mole across the harbour, defeated the Carthaginian fleet that broke out through a new channel, and destroyed the field army at Nepheris. In spring 146 he stormed the city; after six days of street fighting, 50,000 survivors surrendered and were enslaved, and the city was razed.

Carthaginian territory became the province of Africa, governed from Utica. Polybius, an eyewitness, saw Scipio weep over Carthage, quoting Homer. The war is a classic case in debates on Roman imperialism: ancient writers (Sallust, Posidonius) saw the removal of the 'fear of the enemy' (metus hostilis) as the start of Roman moral decline. Appian (Punica 67-135), based on Polybius, is the main source.
third_punic_war.debate: Motives: fear of a recovering Carthage (metus Punicus), Cato's influence, greed for land, or the wish to prevent Masinissa from taking Carthage; Polybius 36.9 records Greek debates on the war's justice.
scholarship: Astin, Scipio Aemilianus (1967)
Harris, War and Imperialism in Republican Rome (1979)
Miles, Carthage Must Be Destroyed (2010)
Ridley, 'To Be Taken with a Pinch of Salt', CPh 81 (1986)
Lancel, Carthage (1995)
Le Bohec, Histoire militaire des guerres puniques (1996)

achaean_war.detail:
The Achaean War (146) ended the independence of the Achaean League and of Greece. Its origins lay in the long dispute over Sparta, which had been forced into the Achaean League in 192 and repeatedly appealed to Rome against Achaean interference, and in the return in 150 of the Achaean exiles deported in 167, among whom were bitter enemies of Rome. In 149-148 Sparta, encouraged by Roman non-intervention, seceded from the League; the Achaean general Damocritus and then Diaeus attacked it. In 147 the Roman envoy Lucius Aurelius Orestes announced at Corinth that Sparta, Corinth, Argos, Heraclea and Orchomenus should be detached from the League. Riots broke out, and Spartans and perhaps Roman envoys were insulted.

The radical leaders Critolaus and Diaeus led the League to war in 146, appealing to the people with debt relief and, in Diaeus' case, arming 12,000 slaves. Critolaus marched north against Heraclea in Thessaly but was defeated by Quintus Caecilius Metellus at Scarpheia in Locris and disappeared. Metellus advanced towards the Isthmus. The consul Lucius Mummius then took command and defeated Diaeus at Leucopetra on the Isthmus. Diaeus killed his wife and himself. Mummius sacked Corinth, killing the men, enslaving the women and children and razing the city on the Senate's orders.

The ten senatorial commissioners dissolved the Achaean League and other leagues (later partly restored), abolished democracies, set up property-based oligarchies, and imposed tribute on some cities. Greece was placed under the supervision of the governor of Macedonia, although it was not formally organised as the province of Achaea until 27. Polybius, who helped with the settlement, regarded the year 146 as the end of the period covered by his history and blamed the 'madness' of the Achaean leaders and the masses. Pausanias (7.11-16) is the main narrative source, with Polybius (38-39) in fragments. Modern historians (Gruen, Kallet-Marx) debate whether Rome deliberately sought to break up the League or reacted to Achaean provocations, and stress the social dimension of the Achaean rising.
achaean_war.debate: Gruen argued that Rome did not seek the war and that the Achaean leaders miscalculated; Polybius blames the demagogues.
scholarship: Gruen, 'The Origins of the Achaean War', JHS 96 (1976)
Kallet-Marx, Hegemony to Empire (1995)
Gruen, The Origins of the Achaean War, JHS 96 (1976)
Fuks, The Bellum Achaicum and its Social Aspect, JHS 90 (1970)

numantine_war.detail:
The Numantine War (143-133) was the final phase of the Celtiberian wars, centred on Numantia, the main town of the Arevaci, on a hill at the confluence of the Douro and Merdancho near modern Soria. In 143, encouraged by Viriathus, the Arevaci rose again. The consul Quintus Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus (143-142) subdued much of Celtiberia but not Numantia and Termantia. His successor Quintus Pompeius (141-140) suffered repeated defeats at Numantia and made a secret peace with the Numantines, which he then denied; the Senate repudiated it (139). Marcus Popillius Laenas (139-138) was defeated.

In 137 the consul Gaius Hostilius Mancinus, panicked by a false rumour, was surrounded with 20,000 men by 4,000 Numantines; his quaestor Tiberius Gracchus negotiated a treaty that saved the army. The Senate repudiated the treaty and handed Mancinus, naked and bound, to the Numantines, who refused him (136). Marcus Aemilius Lepidus Porcina (137-136) attacked the Vaccaei without authorisation and failed at Pallantia; Lucius Furius Philus and Quintus Calpurnius Piso (136-135) achieved nothing. The war caused a crisis of recruitment in Rome, with tribunes imprisoning consuls in 138.

In 134 the people elected Scipio Aemilianus consul in breach of the law prohibiting second consulships. Scipio restored discipline in the demoralised army, ravaged the land of the Vaccaei, and surrounded Numantia with a circumvallation of nine kilometres, with seven camps, towers and a barrier across the Douro, with 60,000 men against perhaps 8,000 defenders. After eight months of famine and cannibalism, Numantia surrendered in 133; many inhabitants killed themselves, the rest were sold, and the town was razed. Scipio took the name Numantinus. The siege works excavated by Adolf Schulten are among the best preserved Roman camps of the Republic. The war's failures and its cost in manpower were part of the background to Tiberius Gracchus' reforms. Appian (Iberica 76-98), based on Polybius' monograph, is the main source.
scholarship: Schulten, Numantia (1914-1931)
Astin, Scipio Aemilianus (1967)
Simon, Roms Kriege in Spanien 154-133 v. Chr. (1962)
Schulten, Numantia I-IV (1914-1931)
Dobson, The Army of the Roman Republic: Polybius and the Camps at Numantia (2008)

first_servile_war.detail:
The First Servile War (135-132) was the largest slave revolt in the ancient world before Spartacus. It broke out in Sicily, where wealthy Sicilian and Roman landowners had acquired large numbers of slaves, many recently enslaved in Rome's eastern wars, to work vast estates and herds; according to Diodorus (following Posidonius), the masters treated them brutally, branding, chaining and underfeeding them, and allowing herdsmen to rob travellers for their food. The revolt began at Enna, where the slaves of Damophilus, led by Eunus, a Syrian slave from Apamea who claimed prophetic powers and breathed fire, killed their masters and seized the town. Eunus took the royal name Antiochus, formed a council and minted coins.

A second revolt led by Cleon, a Cilician herdsman, broke out near Agrigentum; he joined Eunus as his general. The rebels, said to have numbered from 70,000 to 200,000, defeated several Roman praetors (Lucius Hypsaeus among them) and took Tauromenium and much of the island. Rome, occupied with Numantia, responded slowly. Revolts inspired by the Sicilian example broke out at Minturnae, Sinuessa, in Attica (Laurion mines) and on Delos. In 134 the consul Gaius Fulvius Flaccus and in 133 Lucius Calpurnius Piso Frugi fought the rebels, Piso besieging Enna.

In 132 the consul Publius Rupilius besieged and starved Tauromenium, where the defenders resorted to cannibalism, and took it by treachery; he then took Enna, where Cleon died fighting. Eunus fled, was captured and died in prison at Morgantina. Over 20,000 slaves were crucified, according to Orosius. Rupilius, with ten commissioners, drew up the lex Rupilia regulating the administration of Sicily. The war was part of the social crisis of the period: Tiberius Gracchus' reforms of 133 aimed partly to address the replacement of free peasants by slaves. Diodorus (34/35.2), preserved in Byzantine excerpts, is the main source. Modern historians (Bradley, Shaw, Urbainczyk) debate whether the revolt aimed at a new kingdom on a Hellenistic model or at ending slavery.
first_servile_war.debate: Start date (136, 135 or earlier) and the scale of the revolt (Diodorus' 200,000 is surely inflated).
scholarship: Bradley, Slavery and Rebellion in the Roman World (1989)
Shaw, Spartacus and the Slave Wars (2001)
Morton, Eunus: The Cowardly King, CQ 63 (2013)

aristonicus_revolt.detail:
The revolt of Aristonicus (133-129) followed the death of Attalus III of Pergamon in 133, who bequeathed his kingdom to the Roman people, except the city of Pergamon and other Greek cities, which he declared free. Aristonicus, claiming to be an illegitimate son of Eumenes II, contested the will and took the royal name Eumenes III, minting coins with that name. He first won support in coastal cities, taking Leucae, Phocaea and Colophon, but was defeated off Cyme by the Ephesian fleet. He then turned inland, appealing to slaves and the poor, whom he called 'Heliopolitae' (citizens of the City of the Sun), an idea associated with the utopian fiction of Iambulus and the Stoic Blossius of Cumae, Tiberius Gracchus' adviser, who joined him.

Rome was slow to respond, sending a commission of five senators in 132. In 131 the consul Publius Licinius Crassus Dives Mucianus, pontifex maximus and jurist, arrived with an army, supported by the kings of Bithynia (Nicomedes II), Cappadocia (Ariarathes V, killed in the war), Pontus (Mithridates V) and Paphlagonia. In 130 Crassus was defeated near Leucae and captured; he provoked a Thracian guard into killing him to avoid capture. The consul Marcus Perperna then defeated Aristonicus, besieged him at Stratonicea on the Caicus, and captured him; Aristonicus was taken to Rome and strangled in prison, and Perperna died at Pergamon. Manius Aquillius, consul in 129, completed the pacification, reportedly poisoning the wells of rebel towns.

With ten commissioners, Aquillius organised the province of Asia (129-126), giving Greater Phrygia to Mithridates V (later revoked) and Lycaonia to Cappadocia; he built roads, some milestones of which survive. The province's wealth, its tax-farming by Roman publicani under Gaius Gracchus' law (123), and Roman exploitation would contribute to the massacre of Romans in 88 under Mithridates VI. The revolt has been interpreted as a social revolution or a dynastic war; modern historians (Gruen, Kallet-Marx) emphasise its dynastic character. Sources are scattered: Strabo, Justin, the Livian Periochae, Florus, Orosius and inscriptions.
aristonicus_revolt.debate: Whether Aristonicus led a social revolution or a dynastic war is debated; the 'Heliopolis' utopia may reflect Stoic ideas (Blossius of Cumae).
scholarship: Kallet-Marx, Hegemony to Empire (1995)
Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)

allobrogian_war.detail:
Rome's first war of conquest beyond the Alps grew out of its alliance with Massalia, the Greek city whose territory was harried by the Celto-Ligurian Salluvii (Salyes). In 125 the consul Marcus Fulvius Flaccus answered Massalia's appeal and defeated the Salluvii; his successor Gaius Sextius Calvinus (124-122) destroyed their oppidum at Entremont and founded a garrison at the hot springs that became Aquae Sextiae (Aix-en-Provence), the first Roman settlement in Gaul.

The Salluvian king Teutomalius fled to the Allobroges, a powerful people between the Rhône and the Isère, who refused to surrender him and who also attacked the Aedui, recently recognised as 'brothers and kinsmen' of the Roman people. In 121 Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus defeated the Allobroges at Vindalium near the confluence of the Sorgue and the Rhône, using war elephants that terrified the Gauls. Later that year the consul Quintus Fabius Maximus, grandson of Aemilius Paullus, defeated the combined Allobroges and Arverni under their king Bituitus at the confluence of the Isère and Rhône; the ancient figure of 120,000 Gallic dead is fantastic, but the victory was decisive. Bituitus, lured to Domitius for negotiations, was arrested and sent to Rome, where he walked in Fabius' triumph in his silver armour, then interned at Alba Fucens.

Fabius took the cognomen Allobrogicus and built the Fornix Fabianus in the Forum; Domitius rode an elephant through the province and set up trophies. The Allobroges were annexed, the Arverni left free. Domitius built the Via Domitia linking Italy to Spain, and in 118 the colony of Narbo Martius was founded against senatorial opposition. The territory, called simply 'the Province' (hence Provence), became Gallia Transalpina, later Narbonensis.

The war secured the land route to Spain and made Rome a power in Gaul two generations before Caesar. Its new province bore the brunt of the Cimbric invasions a decade later.
allobrogian_war.debate: The dates of the battles of Vindalium and the Isara (both 121) and the founding of the province are debated.
scholarship: Ebel, Transalpine Gaul: The Emergence of a Roman Province (1976)
Rivet, Gallia Narbonensis (1988)

jugurthine_war.detail:
The Jugurthine War arose from the succession crisis in Numidia after Micipsa's death in 118, when Jugurtha, adopted nephew of the old king and a veteran of Numantia with Roman friends, killed his cousin Hiempsal and drove out Adherbal. The Senate divided the kingdom in 116, but in 112 Jugurtha besieged Adherbal at Cirta and massacred the Italian traders who had defended it. Under pressure from the tribune Gaius Memmius and the equites, Rome declared war in 111.

The first phase was marked by failure and scandal. The consul Calpurnius Bestia accepted Jugurtha's nominal surrender in 111; Jugurtha, summoned to Rome as a witness, had a rival, Massiva, murdered in the city, and left saying Rome was a city for sale. In 110 Aulus Postumius Albinus' army was trapped at Suthul and sent under the yoke. The Mamilian commission of 109 condemned Opimius, Bestia and others for corruption.

Quintus Caecilius Metellus (109-107) restored discipline, won the battle of the Muthul, and took Thala, but could not catch Jugurtha, whose guerrilla war exploited Numidia's steppes and fortresses. His legate Gaius Marius won the consulship of 107 by promising a quick victory, recruited the capite censi, and campaigned deep into the south, capturing Capsa and a royal treasure fort on the Mulucha. Jugurtha allied with his father-in-law Bocchus I of Mauretania; their combined armies nearly defeated Marius near Cirta in 106. Finally Marius' quaestor Sulla persuaded Bocchus to betray Jugurtha in 105.

Sallust's Bellum Iugurthinum makes the war a study of senatorial corruption and the rise of the new man; modern historians are more sceptical, stressing the logistical difficulties. Its political legacy was immense: it made Marius, introduced Sulla, and began their enmity.
scholarship: Paul, A Historical Commentary on Sallust's Bellum Jugurthinum (1984)
Morstein-Marx, 'The myth of Numidian origins in Sallust', AJPh 122 (2001)

cimbrian_war.detail:
The Cimbri, a people from Jutland, and the Teutones, joined by the Ambrones and Helvetian groups (Tigurini, Tougeni), migrated south about 120, perhaps after storm floods, wandering through central Europe. In 113 they reached Noricum, a Roman friend, and the consul Gnaeus Papirius Carbo attacked them treacherously at Noreia and was badly defeated. They moved west into Gaul, and asked Rome for land in return for service; refused, they defeated Silanus in 109, the Tigurini killed the consul Lucius Cassius Longinus near Burdigala in 107, and in 105 the Germans annihilated the armies of Caepio and Mallius Maximus at Arausio, with the sources claiming 80,000 Roman dead.

Rome expected invasion of Italy. The people elected Marius to five consecutive consulships (104-100). Fortunately the Cimbri turned to Spain, where the Celtiberians repulsed them, and the Teutones roamed northern Gaul, giving Marius two years to train his army in the Rhône valley. In 102 the invaders divided. Marius destroyed the Ambrones and Teutones at Aquae Sextiae. The Cimbri crossed the Brenner, drove Catulus back from the Adige, and wintered in the Po plain; in 101 Marius and Catulus annihilated them on the Raudine Plain near Vercellae.

The war was the gravest threat to Italy since Hannibal, and in Roman memory it revived the terror of the Gallic sack of 390. It transformed the Roman army: the levy of the capite censi, professional training, the eagle as legionary standard. Politically, it established the precedent of repeated consulships for a saviour general, and Marius' hold on popular favour.

Captive Cimbri and Teutones were sold as slaves; some may have fought for Spartacus. Caesar's later war in Gaul was presented in part as preventing another such invasion, and Caesar claimed the Atuatuci were descended from Cimbric survivors.
cimbrian_war.debate: The causes of the migration and the size of the groups are unknown; ancient figures are exaggerated.
scholarship: Evans, Gaius Marius (1994)
Evans, 'Rome's Cimbric Wars (114-101 BC) and their impact on the Iberian peninsula', Acta Classica 48 (2005)

second_servile_war.detail:
The Second Sicilian Slave War began in 104, triggered indirectly by the Cimbric war. When Marius asked allied kings for troops, Nicomedes III of Bithynia replied that most of his men had been carried off as slaves by Roman tax-farmers. The Senate decreed that free allies held as slaves in the provinces be freed. In Sicily the governor Publius Licinius Nerva freed 800 in a few days, then, under pressure from the slaveowners, stopped. The disappointed slaves rose.

In eastern Sicily the slaves chose Salvius, a soothsayer and flute-player, as king; he took the royal name Tryphon, after the Seleucid usurper, and built a capital at Triocala in the west. In the west another revolt was led by Athenion, a Cilician slave estate manager and astrologer. They combined forces, perhaps 40,000 men, and the revolt spread over most of the island; cities were besieged and the countryside ravaged, causing famine. Nerva and his successor Lucius Licinius Lucullus failed to end it; Lucullus won a battle at Scirthaea in 103 but could not take Triocala, and both governors were later convicted. Tryphon died and Athenion succeeded him.

In 101 the consul Manius Aquillius, Marius' colleague, defeated the rebels and killed Athenion in single combat; he hunted down the remaining bands in 100. The last thousand surrendered on promise of their lives and were sent to Rome to fight wild beasts; they killed each other in the arena instead, the last killing himself.

Diodorus' account, preserved in Byzantine excerpts and derived from Posidonius, is our main source. The war shows the dependence of Sicily's grain estates on slave labour and the violence it generated. It was the second of three great slave revolts in seventy years.
scholarship: Shaw, Spartacus and the Slave Wars (2001)
Bradley, Slavery and Rebellion in the Roman World (1989)

social_war.detail:
The Social War (from socii, allies) was fought between Rome and a confederation of Italian peoples who had long been Rome's allies, providing more than half its armies. Their grievances were exclusion from citizenship and from the rewards of empire, subjection to Roman magistrates' abuses, and the threat to their occupation of public land from the Gracchan reforms. Proposals to enfranchise them by Fulvius Flaccus (125), Gaius Gracchus (122) and Livius Drusus (91) failed; the lex Licinia Mucia of 95 expelled those who had illegally claimed citizenship. Drusus' murder in 91 was the trigger, and the massacre of Romans at Asculum began the war.

The rebels, mainly the Marsi, Paeligni, Vestini, Marrucini, Picentes and Frentani in the north and the Samnites, Hirpini, Lucanians, Apulians and Campanian towns in the south, created a state, Italia, with its capital at Corfinium, a senate, consuls and coinage. They fielded about 100,000 men, battle-hardened in Roman service. Rome raised a similar number, with Latin, Etruscan, Umbrian, Greek and provincial support. In 90 the rebels won many battles; the consul Rutilius Lupus was killed on the Tolenus. Rome responded with the lex Julia, offering citizenship to loyal allies and those who laid down arms, then the lex Plautia Papiria.

In 89 Rome's armies under Pompeius Strabo, Sulla and Cato regained the initiative. Asculum fell after a long siege, the Marsi surrendered, and Sulla took Pompeii, Stabiae, Aeclanum and Bovianum. By 88 only the Samnites and Lucanians held out, and Nola resisted until 80.

The war cost perhaps 100,000 lives. Its result was the enfranchisement of all Italy south of the Po and the transformation of Rome from a city-state ruling allies into a nation-state, though full integration took decades. It trained the armies and generals of the civil wars.
social_war.debate: Whether the allies fought for citizenship or independence is the central debate.
scholarship: Mouritsen, Italian Unification (1998)
Dart, The Social War, 91 to 88 BCE (2014)
Brunt, The Fall of the Roman Republic (1988)
Gabba, Republican Rome: The Army and the Allies (1976)

first_mithridatic_war.detail:
Mithridates VI of Pontus had built an empire around the Black Sea, taking the Crimea, Colchis and Lesser Armenia, and contested Cappadocia and Bithynia with Rome's clients. In 89 the Roman legate Manius Aquillius incited Nicomedes IV of Bithynia to raid Pontus. Mithridates struck back in 88, routing Nicomedes on the Amnias and the Roman forces. Asia welcomed him, and he ordered the massacre of Romans and Italians, the Asiatic Vespers; Aquillius was executed with molten gold. Athens joined him, and his general Archelaus seized Delos and Greece.

Rome was distracted by the Social War and the struggle over the command, which Sulla secured by marching on Rome in 88. He landed in Epirus in 87 with five legions, besieged and sacked Athens and the Piraeus (86), and destroyed Pontic armies at Chaeronea and Orchomenus (86). Meanwhile the Cinnan government sent its own army under Valerius Flaccus, who was murdered by his legate Fimbria; Fimbria defeated Mithridates' son at the Rhyndacus and nearly captured the king at Pitane. Lucullus' fleet won at Tenedos.

Sulla and Mithridates made peace at Dardanus in 85: Mithridates evacuated his conquests, surrendered 70 ships and paid 2,000-3,000 talents, but kept Pontus and was recognised as Rome's ally. Sulla eliminated Fimbria, fined Asia 20,000 talents, and left for Italy in 84.

The war revealed the depth of Greek hatred of Roman exploitation and the vulnerability of the East. Its lenient peace, dictated by Sulla's need to return to Italy, left Mithridates able to fight two more wars. It also made Sulla's army and fortune the instruments of his victory in the civil war.
scholarship: McGing, The Foreign Policy of Mithridates VI (1986)
Keaveney, Sulla (2005)
McGing, The Foreign Policy of Mithridates VI Eupator (1986)
Mayor, The Poison King (2010)
Kallet-Marx, Hegemony to Empire (1995)

first_sullan_civil_war.detail:
The First Sullan Civil War (88-87) began when the tribune Sulpicius Rufus transferred the Mithridatic command from the consul Sulla to Marius. Sulla marched on Rome with six legions, the first time a Roman general had captured the city with a Roman army. Marius fled to Africa; Sulpicius was killed. Sulla passed laws restricting the tribunes and left for Greece, after Cinna, elected consul for 87, swore to respect his acts.

In 87 Cinna revived the proposal to distribute the new citizens through all tribes. His colleague Octavius drove him out of Rome after a battle in the Forum; the Senate deposed him and replaced him with Merula. Cinna won over the army at Nola, raised troops among the new citizens and the Samnites, and recalled Marius, who landed in Etruria. Together with Sertorius and Carbo they besieged Rome, cut off its grain supply, and took it in late 87. The senatorial commander Pompeius Strabo hesitated and died of plague. The victors massacred their enemies, including Octavius, Antonius the orator and two Caesars.

Cinna and Marius were consuls for 86; Marius died days into his seventh consulship. Cinna ruled Rome until 84, holding the consulship four times, with Carbo. His regime enrolled the new citizens in all tribes and passed debt relief, while Sulla fought Mithridates and was declared a public enemy.

The war marked the collapse of the Republic's internal restraints: twice in two years Roman armies took Rome, and political murder became normal. Appian's account sees it as the start of an age of violence. The polarisation between Sullani and Mariani would dominate the next fifty years.
scholarship: Lovano, The Age of Cinna (2002)
Keaveney, Sulla: The Last Republican (1982)

second_sullan_civil_war.detail:
In spring 83 Sulla landed at Brundisium with about 40,000 veterans, determined to overthrow the Cinnan-Marian regime, which had declared him a public enemy. Cinna had been killed by his own troops at Ancona in 84; the government, led by Carbo, the consuls Scipio Asiaticus and Norbanus, and later the younger Marius, mobilised perhaps 100,000 men, including many Samnites and Italians who feared Sulla would reverse their enfranchisement.

In 83 Sulla defeated Norbanus at Mount Tifata and won over Scipio's army near Teanum by negotiation. He was joined by nobles, including Metellus Pius, Crassus and the young Pompey with three private legions from Picenum. In 82 Sulla defeated the younger Marius at Sacriportus, besieging him in Praeneste, and took Rome. In the north, Metellus and Pompey defeated Carbo's generals at Faventia and elsewhere, and Carbo fled to Africa. The Samnites under Pontius Telesinus and Lucanians made a final attack on Rome itself and were destroyed at the Colline Gate on 1 November 82, with thousands of prisoners massacred afterward. Praeneste surrendered; Marius killed himself.

Pompey pursued the remaining Marians to Sicily, where he executed Carbo, and Africa, where he defeated Domitius Ahenobarbus and the Numidian king Iarbas. Sertorius held out in Spain for a decade. Sulla took the dictatorship, proscribed his enemies, devastated Samnium and settled his veterans on confiscated land in Etruria, Campania and Latium.

The war cost tens of thousands of lives and devastated Italy. Its outcome was the Sullan restoration, which tried to make the Senate supreme but was undone within a decade. It made the reputations of Pompey and Crassus.
scholarship: Keaveney, Sulla (2005)
Hinard, Les proscriptions (1985)
Keaveney, Sulla: The Last Republican (1982)
Santangelo, Sulla, the Elites and the Empire (2007)

second_mithridatic_war.detail:
The Second Mithridatic War (83-81) was a brief, inconclusive conflict provoked by the Roman commander in Asia, Lucius Licinius Murena, whom Sulla had left with Fimbria's two legions. The peace of Dardanus had never been ratified by the Senate. Mithridates was preparing to reconquer the Bosporus and Colchis, which had revolted, and Murena claimed that the king's armaments were aimed at Rome, and that Mithridates had not evacuated all of Cappadocia. Archelaus, Mithridates' former general, who had defected to Rome fearing the king's suspicion, encouraged him.

In 83 Murena invaded Pontic Cappadocia and raided the rich temple city of Comana, plundering the sanctuary of Ma. Mithridates protested to Rome. A Senate envoy, Calidius, told Murena to stop, but apparently without written instructions, and Murena continued his raids in 82, crossing the Halys. Mithridates' general Gordius and then the king himself defeated him decisively on the Halys, and Murena fled to Phrygia. Mithridates expelled the Roman garrisons from Cappadocia.

Sulla, now dictator, sent Aulus Gabinius to order Murena to stop, and to reconcile Mithridates with Ariobarzanes of Cappadocia. Mithridates betrothed his four-year-old daughter to Ariobarzanes and kept part of Cappadocia. Murena nonetheless celebrated a triumph in 81, which Cicero mocked.

The war was a minor affair but showed how Roman commanders in the provinces could provoke wars for personal glory, and how the peace of Dardanus failed to resolve Rome's relations with Pontus. It left Mithridates confident and Rome's position in Anatolia unsettled, preparing the third war in 74.
scholarship: McGing, The Foreign Policy of Mithridates VI Eupator (1986)
Sherwin-White, Roman Foreign Policy in the East (1984)

lepidus_rebellion.detail:
Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, a former Sullan who had profited from the proscriptions, was elected consul for 78 against Sulla's wishes, with Pompey's support. After Sulla's death he attacked the dictator's system, proposing to restore the grain dole, recall exiles, return confiscated land to its former owners, and restore the tribunes' powers. He opposed Sulla's state funeral. When dispossessed farmers at Faesulae in Etruria attacked Sullan veterans, the Senate sent both consuls to restore order; Lepidus joined the rebels.

Lepidus refused to return to Rome to hold elections and demanded a second consulship. The Senate, on the urging of Lucius Marcius Philippus, passed the senatus consultum ultimum against him in early 77, entrusting the defence of the state to the proconsul Catulus and to Pompey, who received a special command as a private citizen. Lepidus marched on Rome from Etruria and was defeated by Catulus on the Campus Martius near the Milvian Bridge. His legate in Cisalpine Gaul, Marcus Junius Brutus (father of Caesar's assassin), was besieged by Pompey at Mutina, surrendered and was killed. Lepidus fled to Sardinia, where he died of illness, reportedly grieving over his wife's infidelity.

Perperna took Lepidus' remaining troops, some 20,000, to Spain to join Sertorius. Pompey refused to disband his army and secured the Spanish command as a private citizen.

The rebellion showed the fragility of Sulla's settlement. Lepidus' grievances, the tribunate and land, became the agenda of the 70s. His son Marcus Lepidus was the future triumvir; his other son Lucius Aemilius Paullus was consul in 50.
scholarship: Seager, Pompey the Great (2002)

sertorian_war.detail:
The Sertorian War (80-72) was the last stand of the Marian cause, fought in Spain by Quintus Sertorius, a Marian general who had gone to Spain in 83 and been driven out in 81. In 80 the Lusitanians invited him back. With a small Roman force and Lusitanian and Celtiberian allies, he defeated a series of Roman commanders and built an alternative Roman state in Spain, with a senate of exiles, magistrates, and a school at Osca for the children of Spanish nobles.

From 79 the proconsul Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius campaigned against him in Further Spain with little success, outmanoeuvred by Sertorius' guerrilla tactics, as at Lacobriga. In 77 Perperna brought Lepidus' remnant army, and Pompey received a special command against Sertorius. Pompey crossed the Alps and in 76 was humiliated at Lauro, which Sertorius burned before his eyes; Metellus destroyed Hirtuleius at Italica. In 75 Pompey won at Valentia but was defeated at the Sucro, saved only by Metellus' arrival; the combined armies won at Segontia. Sertorius made an alliance with Mithridates, exchanging Roman officers for money and ships.

From 74 the Romans ground down Sertorian towns in the Ebro valley and Celtiberia. Sertorius grew suspicious and harsh, and in 73 or 72 Perperna murdered him at a banquet at Osca. Pompey crushed Perperna and executed him. The last towns, Uxama, Clunia, Calagurris, fell in 72.

Pompey reorganised Spain, set up his trophy on the Pyrenees, and returned with a large clientele. Sertorius became, in Plutarch and Sallust, a romantic figure, a Roman patriot forced into exile. Archaeology has revealed destruction layers at Valentia and other sites of the war.
scholarship: Konrad, Plutarch's Sertorius (1994)
Spann, Quintus Sertorius (1987)
Spann, Quintus Sertorius and the Legacy of Sulla (1987)

third_mithridatic_war.detail:
The Third Mithridatic War began in 74, when Nicomedes IV bequeathed Bithynia to Rome and Mithridates, allied with Sertorius, invaded. He defeated the consul Cotta at Chalcedon but was halted at Cyzicus, where the consul Lucullus besieged the besiegers until famine destroyed the Pontic army (73). Lucullus then conquered Pontus, winning at Cabira (72) and taking Amisus, Sinope and Heraclea, while Mithridates fled to his son-in-law Tigranes II of Armenia.

When Tigranes refused to surrender him, Lucullus invaded Armenia in 69 with a small army, won a famous victory at Tigranocerta, and in 68 defeated the kings again on the Arsanias, but his weary soldiers mutinied near Artaxata, incited by Clodius. Lucullus also restricted the publicani and moneylenders in Asia, making powerful enemies in Rome. Mithridates recovered Pontus and destroyed Triarius' army at Zela (67). Lucullus' provinces were taken from him.

In 66 the lex Manilia gave Pompey the command. He defeated Mithridates at the Lycus, received Tigranes' submission at Artaxata, and pursued the king through the Caucasus, fighting the Albanians and Iberians (65). Mithridates escaped to the Bosporus, where, facing his son Pharnaces' revolt, he died in 63. Pompey annexed Syria, captured Jerusalem, and reorganised the East.

The war was Rome's longest against a foreign enemy in the late Republic. It created the provinces of Bithynia-Pontus and Syria, a ring of client kingdoms, and a vast increase in revenue. It made Pompey the greatest man in Rome and set the stage for the politics of the 60s. Lucullus retired to his gardens and his fish ponds, a byword for luxury.
scholarship: Sherwin-White, Roman Foreign Policy in the East (1984)
Keaveney, Lucullus (1992)
Seager, Pompey the Great (2002)
Keaveney, Lucullus: A Life (1992)
McGing, The Foreign Policy of Mithridates VI Eupator (1986)

sources.w: De imperio Cn. Pompei (Pro lege Manilia)

third_servile_war.detail:
The Third Servile War (73-71) began when some seventy gladiators escaped from a school at Capua, led by the Thracian Spartacus and the Gauls Crixus and Oenomaus. They took refuge on Vesuvius, defeated the praetor Glaber by descending the cliffs on vine ladders, and then the praetor Varinius. Slaves and rural poor flocked to them. By 72 their army numbered perhaps 70,000 or more, divided between Spartacus and Crixus, who led a group of Gauls and Germans.

In 72 both consuls, Lucius Gellius and Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus, were sent against them. Gellius destroyed Crixus' group at Mount Garganus in Apulia, but Spartacus defeated each consul in turn in Picenum, sacrificed 300 Roman prisoners in honour of Crixus, and marched north, defeating the governor of Cisalpine Gaul, Cassius Longinus, near Mutina. Instead of crossing the Alps, he turned south. The Senate gave Marcus Licinius Crassus, praetor, a special command with six new legions plus the consular armies.

Crassus restored discipline by reviving decimation in a unit that fled. He drove Spartacus into Bruttium, where Cilician pirates failed to ferry him to Sicily, and walled off the peninsula. Spartacus broke out in winter. Crassus destroyed a breakaway group at the Lucanian lake, then defeated and killed Spartacus at the Silarus in spring 71. Six thousand captives were crucified on the Via Appia; Pompey, returning from Spain, killed 5,000 fugitives and claimed credit.

The revolt was the largest slave rising in Roman history and terrified Italy. In modern times Spartacus became a symbol of revolution, from Marx to Kubrick's film. Ancient sources, mostly hostile, nonetheless admired his ability and humanity.
scholarship: Shaw, Spartacus and the Slave Wars (2001)
Strauss, The Spartacus War (2009)
Urbainczyk, Spartacus (2004)

cilician_pirate_wars.detail:
Piracy flourished in the eastern Mediterranean after the decline of Rhodian and Seleucid naval power, encouraged by the demand for slaves at Delos and in Italy, and by Mithridates, who used pirates as allies. The pirates' strongholds were in Rough Cilicia, with its mountainous coast and harbours, and in Crete, but they ranged across the whole Mediterranean, sacking temples, kidnapping travellers for ransom, including the young Caesar in 75, and disrupting trade.

Roman responses were intermittent. In 102 the praetor Marcus Antonius received a command in Cilicia; a law of about 100, known from inscriptions at Delphi and Cnidus, ordered allies to close their ports to pirates. Publius Servilius Vatia campaigned in Lycia, Pamphylia and Isauria from 78 to 74, earning the name Isauricus. In 74 Marcus Antonius Creticus received an extraordinary command over all coasts, but was defeated by the Cretans and died. Quintus Metellus conquered Crete in 69-67. Meanwhile the pirates raided Italy itself, burning a fleet at Ostia, kidnapping praetors, and threatening the grain supply.

In 67 the lex Gabinia gave Pompey command over the entire Mediterranean and coasts for three years, with 500 ships, 120,000 infantry and 24 legates. He divided the sea into thirteen sectors, cleared the western Mediterranean in forty days and Cilicia in forty-nine, winning at Coracesium. He offered surrender on generous terms; some 20,000 pirates were resettled as farmers in depopulated cities such as Soli, renamed Pompeiopolis, and Dyme in Achaea.

The campaign was a model of organisation and clemency. Piracy declined sharply, though it revived during the civil wars under Sextus Pompey. The wars established the precedent of great extraordinary commands that led to the Principate.
scholarship: de Souza, Piracy in the Graeco-Roman World (1999)
Ormerod, Piracy in the Ancient World (1924)

sources.w: De imperio Cn. Pompei (Pro lege Manilia)

catilinarian_war.detail:
Lucius Sergius Catilina, a patrician who had been a Sullan killer, was defeated in the consular elections for 63 and 62. Deeply in debt, he gathered a coalition of bankrupt nobles, ruined Sullan veterans, dispossessed farmers and the urban poor, promising cancellation of debts (novae tabulae). After his defeat in 63 he planned a coup: his ally Gaius Manlius raised an army of veterans and farmers at Faesulae in Etruria, while conspirators in Rome would murder the consul Cicero and set fires.

Cicero, informed through Fulvia, the mistress of a conspirator, obtained the senatus consultum ultimum on 21 October. An attempt on his life on 7 November failed; on 8 November Cicero denounced Catiline in the Senate (the First Catilinarian), and Catiline left Rome to join Manlius. In December the conspirators led by the praetor Lentulus Sura approached envoys of the Allobroges, who reported to Cicero; their arrest at the Milvian Bridge with incriminating letters exposed the plot. On 5 December, after the debate between Caesar and Cato, the Senate voted death, and five conspirators were executed in the Tullianum.

Catiline's army, about 12,000 men but only a quarter properly armed, tried to escape to Gaul but was trapped in the Apennines between Metellus Celer and the consul Antonius. In January 62 at Pistoria (Pistoia), Marcus Petreius, commanding for Antonius, who pleaded gout, destroyed it. Catiline died fighting at the front, found far ahead of his men, still breathing.

Sallust's Bellum Catilinae and Cicero's speeches made the conspiracy one of the most famous episodes of Roman history. Modern historians debate whether it was a revolutionary movement, a desperate coup by a bankrupt aristocrat, or exaggerated by Cicero for political gain.
scholarship: Rawson, Cicero (1975)
Levick, Catiline (2015)
Odahl, The Catilinarian Conspiracy (1971)

gallic_wars.detail:
Caesar's Gallic War (58-50) brought Gaul between the Pyrenees, the Rhine and the Atlantic under Roman control. In 58 he blocked the Helvetian migration at Geneva and destroyed it at Bibracte, then defeated Ariovistus' Germans in Alsace. In 57 he crushed the Belgic coalition at the Axona and the Nervii at the Sabis, and his legates received the submission of Armorica. In 56 he destroyed the Veneti in a naval battle in Quiberon Bay, while Publius Crassus conquered Aquitania. In 55 he massacred the Usipetes and Tencteri, bridged the Rhine and made his first expedition to Britain; in 54 he crossed again with five legions and forced Cassivellaunus to submit.

In winter 54/53 the Eburones under Ambiorix destroyed fifteen cohorts at Atuatuca, and other tribes rose; Caesar suppressed them in 53 with savage devastation. In 52 the Arvernian Vercingetorix led a general revolt. Caesar took Avaricum, was repulsed at Gergovia, and finally besieged Vercingetorix at Alesia, defeating a vast relief army. In 51 he and his legates subdued the last resistance, culminating at Uxellodunum, where the defenders' hands were cut off.

Plutarch, from Caesar's own figures, says he took 800 towns, subdued 300 peoples, fought three million men, killing a million and enslaving another million. The figures are inflated but suggest the scale. The war enriched Caesar and his army, created a loyal veteran force of ten legions, and gave Caesar military glory rivalling Pompey's.

Caesar's Commentarii, seven books plus Hirtius' eighth, are our main source, a masterpiece of self-presentation. The conquest added a vast and rich province, organised by Augustus into three provinces, and began the Romanisation of northern Europe. Modern scholars debate the morality, the numbers, and the extent to which Caesar provoked the war.
gallic_wars.debate: Casualty and population figures are much disputed; recent work treats the conquest as including episodes of genocide.
scholarship: Riggsby, Caesar in Gaul and Rome (2006)
Goldsworthy, Caesar (2006)
Holmes, Caesar's Conquest of Gaul (2nd ed. 1911)
Goudineau, César et la Gaule (1990)
Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (2006)

crassus_parthian_war.detail:
Marcus Licinius Crassus, the richest man in Rome, obtained the province of Syria for five years by the lex Trebonia of 55, intending a war against Parthia that would give him military glory to match Pompey's and Caesar's. There was no clear casus belli: Parthia was divided by a succession struggle between the brothers Orodes II and Mithridates IV, and Gabinius, Crassus' predecessor, had intervened briefly. The tribune Ateius Capito cursed Crassus as he left Rome in November 55.

In 54 Crassus crossed the Euphrates, occupied Greek cities in Mesopotamia, and withdrew to winter in Syria, where he plundered the temples of Jerusalem and Hierapolis. His son Publius joined him with 1,000 Gallic cavalry. In 53 he crossed again with seven legions and marched across the desert toward Seleucia, rejecting the advice of Artavasdes of Armenia to go through the mountains. Near Carrhae the Suren's 10,000 cavalry, horse archers resupplied by camel trains and armoured cataphracts, destroyed his army. Publius was killed; Crassus retreated and was killed during a parley. Twenty thousand Romans died, ten thousand were captured, and the legionary standards were lost.

Gaius Cassius Longinus, Crassus' quaestor, escaped with 500 cavalry, organised the defence of Syria and in 51 repulsed a Parthian invasion under Pacorus near Antigonea. Bibulus, the new governor, sat out the threat in Antioch.

Carrhae was one of Rome's greatest defeats, a trauma that shaped its eastern policy for decades: Caesar planned a war of revenge, Antony attempted one in 36, and Augustus finally recovered the standards by diplomacy in 20 BC. It also broke the triumvirate, leaving Caesar and Pompey to confront each other.
scholarship: Sampson, The Defeat of Rome (2008)
Traina, Carrhae (2010)
Sherwin-White, Roman Foreign Policy in the East (1984)

caesars_civil_war.detail:
Caesar's civil war (49-45) arose from the failure to agree on the terms of his return from Gaul. Fearing prosecution if he became a private citizen, Caesar demanded to stand for a second consulship in absence; his enemies, now allied with Pompey, insisted he lay down his command first. After the senatus consultum ultimum of 7 January 49, Caesar crossed the Rubicon with one legion. Italy fell within weeks; Pompey and the consuls evacuated to Greece from Brundisium. Caesar took Corfinium, pardoning Domitius Ahenobarbus, seized the treasury, and defeated Pompey's legates in Spain at Ilerda; Massilia fell after a siege, but Curio was killed in Africa.

In 48 Caesar crossed to Epirus. He blockaded Pompey at Dyrrachium but was defeated, retreated to Thessaly, and destroyed Pompey's army at Pharsalus on 9 August. Pompey fled to Egypt and was murdered. Caesar, pursuing him, became involved in the Alexandrian War and the affair with Cleopatra; in 47 he defeated Pharnaces at Zela.

The Pompeians regrouped in Africa under Metellus Scipio, Cato, Labienus and Juba; Caesar defeated them at Thapsus in April 46, and Cato killed himself at Utica. Pompey's sons raised Spain; Caesar defeated them at Munda in March 45, his hardest battle.

The war was fought across the Mediterranean. Caesar's clemency toward defeated Romans contrasted with Sulla's proscriptions and won him support, though many pardoned enemies later joined his assassination. The war ended in Caesar's dictatorship and monarchy. Our sources include Caesar's own Civil War, the continuators of the Alexandrian, African and Spanish Wars, Cicero's letters, Lucan's epic, Plutarch, Appian and Dio.
scholarship: Gelzer, Caesar (1968)
Goldsworthy, Caesar (2006)
Morstein-Marx, Julius Caesar and the Roman People (2021)
Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (2006)
Gelzer, Caesar: Politician and Statesman (1968)
Raaflaub, Dignitatis contentio (1974)

alexandrian_war.detail:
The Alexandrian War (October 48 to March 47) began when Caesar, arriving in Alexandria in pursuit of Pompey with only 4,000 men, tried to arbitrate the dynastic conflict between Ptolemy XIII and his sister Cleopatra VII, as executor of their father's will, and demanded repayment of debts owed to him. He favoured Cleopatra after she came to him secretly. The regent Pothinus and general Achillas, with the Alexandrian population and 20,000 soldiers, including veterans of Gabinius' army, besieged Caesar in the palace quarter.

Caesar held a small area by the harbour, burned the Egyptian fleet (the fire possibly damaging book stores), and seized the Pharos. Arsinoe IV, Cleopatra's younger sister, escaped to the Egyptian army and had Achillas killed; her eunuch Ganymedes took command and tried to poison Caesar's water supply with seawater. A naval battle and fighting over the Heptastadion mole followed, in which Caesar had to swim to safety. Caesar released Ptolemy XIII, who joined his army.

Relief came in spring 47 from Mithridates of Pergamon, with an army from Syria and Cilicia and 3,000 Jews under Antipater, who stormed Pelusium. Caesar joined them, and at the battle of the Nile in March 47 the Egyptian army was destroyed; Ptolemy XIII drowned. Caesar made Cleopatra queen with her younger brother Ptolemy XIV, left three legions in Egypt, and sent Arsinoe to Rome.

The war delayed Caesar for months, allowing the Pompeians to regroup in Africa and Pharnaces to invade Pontus. It began his relationship with Cleopatra and her role in Roman politics. The Bellum Alexandrinum, probably by Hirtius, is the main narrative.
scholarship: Roller, Cleopatra (2010)
Hölbl, A History of the Ptolemaic Empire (2001)
Roller, Cleopatra: A Biography (2010)

war_of_mutina.detail:
The War of Mutina (44-43) was the Senate's attempt, led by Cicero, to crush Mark Antony after Caesar's death. In June 44 Antony, as consul, had a law passed giving him Cisalpine and Transalpine Gaul for five years, in place of Macedonia, and recalled the legions from Macedonia. Decimus Brutus, one of the assassins and governor of Cisalpine Gaul under Caesar's arrangements, refused to hand over his province. In November two legions defected from Antony to Octavian, who had raised a private army. Antony marched north and besieged Decimus in Mutina in December 44.

In Rome Cicero delivered the Philippics, urging war. In January 43 the Senate gave Octavian propraetorian imperium and sent the consuls Hirtius and Pansa with Octavian to relieve Mutina, after a failed embassy to Antony. Antony was declared a public enemy. On 14 April at Forum Gallorum Antony mauled Pansa's recruits, but was defeated by Hirtius; Pansa died of his wounds. On 21 April Hirtius and Octavian attacked Antony's lines at Mutina; Hirtius was killed, but Antony withdrew over the Alps with his remaining forces.

The victory proved hollow. With both consuls dead, the Senate gave command to Decimus Brutus, slighting Octavian. Lepidus, Plancus and Pollio, governors in the west, joined Antony; Decimus was abandoned and killed. Octavian marched on Rome, took the consulship in August, and in November allied with Antony and Lepidus at Bononia.

The war marked Cicero's last great political effort and the Senate's last attempt to control the Caesarian generals. Its failure led directly to the Second Triumvirate and the proscriptions, in which Cicero died.
scholarship: Osgood, Caesar's Legacy (2006)
Manuwald, Cicero, Philippics 3-9 (2007)

liberators_civil_war.detail:
The Liberators' civil war (43-42) pitted the triumvirs Antony and Octavian against Caesar's assassins, Marcus Brutus and Gaius Cassius. After leaving Italy in 44, Brutus took Macedonia and Greece, raising legions from Caesarian veterans and recruits, while Cassius seized Syria, absorbing the armies of Caecilius Bassus and others, besieged Dolabella at Laodicea, and forced the cities of Asia to contribute vast sums. The lex Pedia of August 43 condemned them; the triumvirate, formed in November, prepared to fight them.

In 42 Cassius took Rhodes and Brutus sacked Xanthus in Lycia, where the inhabitants killed themselves rather than surrender. The two met at Sardis and marched to Macedonia with nineteen legions, taking a strong position at Philippi astride the Via Egnatia, with their fleet controlling the sea. Antony and Octavian crossed with nineteen legions, short of supplies.

In the first battle of Philippi, in October 42, Antony took Cassius' camp while Brutus took Octavian's; Cassius, wrongly thinking all lost, killed himself. On the same day the Liberators' fleet destroyed triumviral reinforcements at sea. Three weeks later, pressed by his officers, Brutus gave battle and was defeated; he killed himself. Many nobles died or surrendered.

The victory gave the triumvirs control of the empire. Antony took the East, Octavian returned to Italy to settle veterans, and Lepidus was marginalised. For many Romans, Philippi marked the death of the Republic. The Liberators' coinage, including the EID MAR denarius, documents their claims. The survivors, including Messalla and Horace, eventually joined the victors.
scholarship: Osgood, Caesar's Legacy (2006)
Tempest, Brutus (2017)
Tempest, Brutus: The Noble Conspirator (2017)

perusine_war.detail:
The Perusine War (41-40) arose from the settlement of veterans after Philippi. Octavian, responsible for Italy, confiscated land from eighteen cities and many individuals for some 50,000 or more veterans. The dispossessed protested, and the veterans demanded more. Lucius Antonius, consul in 41 and brother of Mark Antony, and Fulvia, Antony's wife, presented themselves as champions of the Italians against Octavian's illegal confiscations and as protectors of Antony's interests, perhaps fearing Octavian's growing power while Antony was in the East.

Mediation by officers and veterans failed. In late 41 Lucius occupied Rome briefly, then retreated north toward Antony's generals in Gaul, Ventidius, Pollio and Plancus, who hesitated to commit themselves without Antony's orders. Octavian's generals, Agrippa and Salvidienus Rufus, trapped Lucius in Perusia (Perugia) in Etruria, which Octavian besieged through the winter, building a wall and ditch around the town. Lead sling bullets with obscene inscriptions survive from the siege. Starvation forced Lucius to surrender in early 40.

Octavian pardoned Lucius and his troops, but executed the town council and, according to hostile sources, sacrificed 300 senators and equites at an altar of Divus Iulius on the Ides of March. The town burned. Fulvia fled to Greece, where she died. Antony's generals withdrew; Octavian took over Gaul and its legions after the death of its governor Calenus.

The war almost caused open conflict between Antony and Octavian, averted by the Treaty of Brundisium in autumn 40. It consolidated Octavian's control of Italy and the West.
scholarship: Osgood, Caesar's Legacy (2006)

sicilian_war.detail:
Sextus Pompeius, younger son of Pompey the Great, escaped from Munda and built a naval power in the western Mediterranean. Outlawed by the lex Pedia in 43 and proscribed, he received a command of the fleet from the Senate in 43, then seized Sicily, which became a refuge for proscribed men and runaway slaves. With a large fleet commanded by freedmen such as Menodorus and Menecrates, he blockaded Italy, causing famine in Rome. He called himself son of Neptune.

The Treaty of Misenum in 39 recognised his control of Sicily, Sardinia, Corsica and the Peloponnese, in return for ending the blockade; the proscribed were allowed to return. But in 38 Menodorus defected with Sardinia, and war resumed. Octavian's fleet was defeated off Cumae and wrecked by a storm at Scyllaeum. Agrippa built a new fleet in 37, at the Portus Julius, training 20,000 rowers; Antony provided 120 ships at Tarentum.

In 36 a triple invasion of Sicily began. Octavian was defeated off Tauromenium, but Agrippa won at Mylae and decisively at Naulochus on 3 September 36. Sextus fled to Asia, where he was killed in 35. Lepidus, who had landed in Sicily with twelve legions, tried to claim the island, but his army deserted to Octavian, who deposed him from the triumvirate.

Octavian presented the war as a war against pirates and slaves, returning 30,000 slaves to their owners and crucifying 6,000 more. The victory secured Italy's grain supply and Octavian's popularity, earned him tribunician sacrosanctity, and left him master of the West. Modern scholars (Powell, Welch) have rehabilitated Sextus as a Republican leader rather than a mere pirate.
scholarship: Welch, Magnus Pius (2012)
Powell, Sextus Pompeius (2002)

parthian_war_of_antony.detail:
Antony's Parthian war began with the Parthian invasion of 40, when Pacorus and Quintus Labienus overran Syria, Asia Minor and Judaea while Antony was in Egypt and Italy. His legate Publius Ventidius Bassus drove them out in 39, defeating and killing Labienus at the Cilician Gates and Pharnapates at the Amanus, and in 38 killed Pacorus at Gindarus. Herod, named king by the Senate, recovered Judaea with Sosius in 37.

Antony then prepared a great invasion to realise Caesar's plan of revenge for Carrhae. In 36, with sixteen legions and allies, about 100,000 men, he marched through Armenia to Media Atropatene. Phraates IV destroyed his siege train, Artavasdes of Armenia withdrew, and Antony failed to take Phraaspa. His retreat through the mountains in winter cost some 24,000 men. In 35 the Median king, quarrelling with Parthia, became Antony's ally; in 34 Antony captured Artavasdes of Armenia, annexing the kingdom, and celebrated in Alexandria, followed by the Donations. He betrothed his son Alexander Helios to the Median princess Iotape.

The Parthian campaign was a costly failure, though Antony salvaged Armenia. In Rome Octavian concealed and exploited it, contrasting it with his own victories over Sextus Pompey and in Illyricum. Antony's dependence on Cleopatra's resources after 36 fed Octavian's propaganda.

The war shows the difficulty of attacking Parthia across mountains and desert, and the limits of Roman power in the East. It ended with Antony's defeat at Actium; Armenia was lost again. Augustus recovered Crassus' standards by diplomacy in 20 BC, a settlement that lasted for generations.
scholarship: Pelling, Plutarch: Life of Antony (1988)
Bivar, CHI 3.1 (1983)
Sherwin-White, Roman Foreign Policy in the East (1984)

octavian_illyrian_war.detail:
Between 35 and 33 Octavian campaigned in Illyricum, partly to secure Italy's north-eastern frontier, partly to train his army, and partly to win military glory to compare with Antony's eastern campaigns. In 35 he attacked the Iapydes in the Julian Alps, storming their towns Terponus and Metulum, where he was wounded leading the assault and the defenders burned themselves with their families. He then marched into Pannonia, besieged and took Siscia (Sisak) on the Save, and left a garrison of twenty-five cohorts there.

In 34 and 33 he turned against the Dalmatae, who had destroyed Gabinius' army in 48 and held its standards. He was wounded again at Setovia; Promona and other strongholds fell. The Dalmatae surrendered in 33, returning the standards and providing hostages. His generals Agrippa, Statilius Taurus and Messalla campaigned against the Salassi and other Alpine tribes and the Liburnian pirates.

The campaigns were well publicised in Rome. Octavian displayed the recovered standards in the Porticus Octaviae, built from the spoils; Agrippa, aedile in 33, spent lavishly on Rome's water supply and public works. In 29 Octavian celebrated the first of his three triumphs, for Illyricum.

The Illyrian war gave Octavian military credentials and secured the land route between Italy and the Balkans. It laid the foundations for the later conquest of Pannonia and the Danube frontier under Augustus and Tiberius. Appian's Illyrian book, based on Augustus' memoirs, gives a detailed account, which inflates Octavian's achievements.
scholarship: Wilkes, Dalmatia (1969)
Šašel Kos, Appian and Illyricum (2005)

war_of_actium.detail:
The War of Actium (32-30) was the final civil war of the Republic, between Octavian and Mark Antony with Cleopatra. Relations had worsened since 36: Octavian deposed Lepidus and took his provinces, refused Antony recruits, and attacked his relationship with Cleopatra and the Donations of Alexandria (34). The triumvirate's legal basis expired at the end of 33. In 32 the consuls and some 300 senators fled to Antony; Antony divorced Octavia; Octavian published his will. War was declared on Cleopatra alone, presenting it as a foreign war, after all Italy swore an oath to Octavian.

Antony gathered about 500 warships and nineteen legions in western Greece, with bases from Corcyra to Methone. In 31 Agrippa seized Methone, Leucas, Patrae and Corinth, cutting Antony's supply lines from Egypt, while Octavian landed in Epirus and camped north of the Gulf of Ambracia. Antony's army, trapped at Actium, suffered disease, hunger and desertions. On 2 September Antony's fleet broke out; Cleopatra and Antony escaped to Egypt with sixty ships and the treasury, but most of the fleet was destroyed or surrendered, and the army capitulated a week later.

In 30 Octavian invaded Egypt from Syria and Gallus from Cyrenaica. Antony's forces deserted. On 1 August Octavian entered Alexandria; Antony killed himself, and Cleopatra followed some days later. Caesarion was executed, and Egypt annexed.

The war ended the civil wars and left Octavian sole ruler of the Roman world. Augustan propaganda made Actium the victory of Rome, its gods and Apollo against the East and Egypt's animal gods. In 27 he became Augustus.
scholarship: Gurval, Actium and Augustus (1995)
Lange, Res Publica Constituta (2009)
Syme, The Roman Revolution (1939)
Goldsworthy, Antony and Cleopatra (2010)
Murray and Petsas, Octavian's Campsite Memorial for the Actian War (1989)

cantabrian_wars.detail: The Cantabrian and Asturian wars (29-19 BC) completed the conquest of the Iberian peninsula, two centuries after the first Roman landing in 218 BC. The Cantabri and Astures of the north-western mountains, raiding the plains of the Vaccaei, Turmogi and Autrigones, were the last independent peoples of Hispania. Statilius Taurus fought them in 29 BC and Calvisius Sabinus and Sextus Appuleius triumphed in 28-26, but the main effort came in 26-25 BC, when Augustus himself took command with seven or eight legions (I Augusta, II Augusta, IV Macedonica, V Alaudae, VI Victrix, IX Hispana, X Gemina, XX), the largest concentration of the era. From a base at Segisama, three columns advanced into the mountains while a fleet from Aquitania landed on the coast. Augustus fell ill and retired to Tarraco, and his legates Antistius and Furnius won the battle of Vellica, besieged the Cantabri on Mons Vindius, where they starved, and took Aracillum; Publius Carisius took the Asturian stronghold of Lancia. The temple of Janus was closed in 25 BC and Augusta Emerita was founded for veterans. But the mountaineers rose repeatedly, in 24, 22 and 19 BC, enslaved prisoners killed their masters and returned home, and the Roman troops became demoralised; Agrippa finally ended the resistance in 19 BC with brutal measures, killing most men of fighting age, forcing survivors down to the plains and disgracing a legion (I Augusta, which lost its title). Florus and Orosius, drawing on Livy, record mass suicides by poison from yew trees and captives singing as they were crucified. Three legions stayed in the north-west, and the gold mines of Las Médulas and elsewhere were opened under Roman control. The province of Hispania was reorganised into Tarraconensis, Lusitania and Baetica. Modern archaeology has identified Roman camps and siege works at sites such as La Espina del Gallego, El Cincho and Monte Bernorio, but the identification of ancient place names is often uncertain.

roman_kushite_war.detail: The war between Rome and the kingdom of Kush (Meroë), 25-21 BC, was the first major conflict between Rome and a sub-Saharan African state. In 25 BC, when the prefect of Egypt Aelius Gallus had taken part of the garrison on his ill-fated Arabian expedition, a Kushite army of some 30,000, led by the "one-eyed queen" (the Kandake, probably Amanirenas) and her son Akinidad, attacked Syene, Elephantine and Philae, enslaving the inhabitants and throwing down statues of Augustus. The prefect Gaius Petronius counter-attacked in 24 BC with fewer than 10,000 infantry and 800 cavalry, defeated the Kushites at Pselchis (Dakka), took Primis (Qasr Ibrim) and advanced to Napata, the old royal capital, which he sacked in 24 or 23 BC, enslaving its people, according to Strabo. He fortified Primis with a garrison of 400 and two years' supplies. When the Kushites besieged it in 22 BC, Petronius relieved it and the Kandake sent envoys; Petronius sent them to Augustus, who received them at Samos in 21/20 BC and granted all their requests, including the remission of tribute that Petronius had imposed. The frontier was fixed at Hiera Sykaminos (Maharraqa), with the Dodecaschoenus as a Roman buffer zone. The famous bronze head of Augustus found at Meroë in 1910, now in the British Museum, was buried beneath the steps of a victory temple, apparently taken in the raid on Syene. Meroitic inscriptions, including a stele of Akinidad and Amanirenas (in the British Museum), may record the war from the Kushite side but cannot yet be fully read. Modern scholars see the peace as a negotiated compromise that reflected Kushite strength and Roman unwillingness to commit forces so far south; Res Gestae 26 nonetheless claims that Roman armies reached Napata. The frontier remained quiet for centuries.

alpine_wars_augustan.detail: The Alpine wars of Augustus (25-14 BC) subdued the peoples of the Alps, securing the passes between Italy, Gaul and the Danube and preparing for the advance into Germany and Illyricum. The first step was the destruction of the Salassi of the Val d'Aosta in 25 BC by Terentius Varro Murena, who sold 36,000 of them into slavery and founded Augusta Praetoria. In 16 BC Publius Silius Nerva subdued the Camunni and Vennonetes in the central Alps. The decisive campaign came in summer 15 BC: Drusus advanced from Italy through the Adige valley and the Brenner, defeating the Raeti at Tridentum, while Tiberius advanced from Gaul, using boats on Lake Constance against the Vindelici, and won a battle near the source of the Danube on 1 August, the anniversary of the capture of Alexandria. The two armies met in the Alpine foreland, and the region was organised as the province of Raetia, with Augusta Vindelicum (Augsburg) as its later capital; Noricum was incorporated peacefully around the same time. The Maritime Alps were subdued in 14 BC. Horace celebrated the victories in Odes 4.4 and 4.14. The Tropaeum Alpium at La Turbie, dedicated in 7-6 BC, lists 45 conquered Alpine peoples in an inscription preserved by Pliny the Elder. Strabo stresses the strategic importance of the conquest, which ended raids on northern Italy and opened routes over the Great St Bernard, Little St Bernard, Brenner and Reschen passes. Dio mentions the deportation of young men of military age from the Raeti. The Cottian kingdom remained a client state under Cottius, who built an arch at Segusio (9-8 BC), until annexed under Nero. Recent archaeology has found traces of the campaign of 15 BC, including a battlefield at Döttenbichl near Oberammergau with Roman arrowheads and catapult bolts, and Roman camps at Dangstetten on the upper Rhine.

bellum_pannonicum.detail: The Pannonian war (14-9 BC) brought the lands between the eastern Alps and the Danube under Roman control, linking Italy with the Balkans and creating the province of Illyricum, later divided into Pannonia and Dalmatia. Earlier campaigns by Octavian in 35-33 BC had taken Siscia and subdued the Iapydes. Unrest broke out in 14 BC and Marcus Vinicius and Agrippa intervened, Agrippa's arrival in winter 13/12 BC being enough to halt the rising. After Agrippa's death in 12 BC Tiberius took over the command, campaigning for four years against the Pannonian tribes, especially the Breuci, with the help of the Scordisci; he used harsh methods, selling the young men into slavery and deporting others, and Dio says he took their arms. In 11 BC Illyricum was transferred from the Senate to Augustus because of the war, and the Dalmatians were subdued as well. Tiberius was awarded an ovation in 9 BC (the Senate voted a triumph but Augustus allowed only an ovation) and triumphal ornaments; Augustus claimed in the Res Gestae (30) that he had brought the Pannonian peoples, never reached before, under the empire and extended Illyricum to the Danube. The sources for the war are thin (Dio's brief notices, Velleius, Suetonius and Florus). The conquest was not secure: the levy imposed on the region and heavy tribute provoked the Great Illyrian Revolt of AD 6-9, led by the Breuci and Daesitiates whom Tiberius had subdued. Later Roman colonies and municipalities at Emona, Siscia, Sirmium and Poetovio and the legionary bases at Carnuntum and Poetovio grew out of the conquest. Modern historians (Wilkes, Šašel Kos) emphasise that the war was a series of punitive and pacifying campaigns rather than a single conquest, and that Roman control of the Danube line itself was only established under Tiberius.

augustan_germanic_wars.detail: The Augustan Germanic wars (12 BC-AD 16) were Rome's attempt to conquer Germany between the Rhine and the Elbe. After the Clades Lolliana (16 BC) and Augustus's stay in Gaul, Drusus campaigned for four seasons (12-9 BC) from bases at Vetera, Novaesium, Mogontiacum and elsewhere, digging a canal to the North Sea, attacking the Sugambri, Bructeri, Chatti, Cherusci and Marcomanni and reaching the Elbe in 9 BC, where he died. Tiberius continued in 8-7 BC, deporting 40,000 Sugambri across the Rhine. Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus crossed the Elbe c. 3-1 BC. After an "immense war" (immensum bellum) from AD 1, Tiberius campaigned in 4-5 to the Weser and Elbe, with a fleet sailing to Jutland, and in 6 prepared an attack on Maroboduus's Marcomannic kingdom in Bohemia, abandoned because of the Illyrian revolt. The archaeological evidence of camps at Haltern, Oberaden, Anreppen and Hedemünden and the civil town at Waldgirmes, with a gilded equestrian statue of Augustus, shows that the region was being organised as a province with towns and markets. The project collapsed in AD 9, when Arminius destroyed Varus's three legions in the Teutoburg forest. Tiberius restored the Rhine line in 10-12, and Germanicus, with eight legions, campaigned in 14-16 against the Marsi, Chatti, Bructeri and Cherusci, recovering two eagles and winning battles at Idistaviso and the Angrivarian wall, but with heavy losses from storms and ambushes. Tiberius recalled him in 16, saying that the Germans could be left to their internal quarrels, and the Rhine became the frontier. Modern historians debate whether Augustus aimed at the Elbe as a permanent border, whether Germany was already a province before AD 9 (Dio says so), and why the conquest failed: the decentralised Germanic societies, the military effort needed elsewhere, or the shock of AD 9. The consequences shaped European history by leaving Germany outside the empire.
augustan_germanic_wars.debate: Whether Augustus intended to annex Germany to the Elbe and whether a province existed before AD 9.

great_illyrian_revolt.detail: The Great Illyrian Revolt (bellum Batonianum, AD 6-9) was a rising of the Pannonian and Dalmatian peoples against Roman rule, described by Suetonius as the most serious foreign war since the Punic Wars. It broke out in AD 6 when men summoned for auxiliary service for Tiberius's campaign against Maroboduus turned their arms against Rome, led by Bato of the Daesitiates in central Bosnia and by Bato and Pinnes of the Breuci in the Sava valley. The rebels, numbering according to Velleius 200,000 infantry and 9,000 cavalry, many of them trained in Roman service, killed Roman citizens and traders, attacked Sirmium and Salona and raided Macedonia. Rome responded with an enormous mobilisation: Tiberius, Germanicus and the governors of Moesia (Caecina Severus) and Galatia (Plautius Silvanus) brought up ten legions, more than seventy auxiliary cohorts and fourteen alae, plus Thracian cavalry, while Augustus raised freedmen and slaves for the army. The war was fought in difficult terrain with forts, ambushes and famine: the Romans nearly lost a battle at the Volcaean marshes in AD 7, when five legions were surprised. Tiberius preferred a strategy of attrition, devastating the land and wearing down the enemy. In AD 8 the Breucian Bato betrayed Pinnes and was killed by his Daesitiate namesake, and the Breuci surrendered at the river Bathinus. In AD 9 Tiberius and Germanicus reduced the Dalmatian strongholds of Raetinium, Splonum, Seretium and Andetrium; Bato surrendered and was interned at Ravenna. The war cost Rome heavily in money and manpower, and news of victory came days before news of the Varian disaster. Tiberius celebrated his triumph in AD 12. The region was divided into the provinces of Pannonia and Dalmatia, with legions at Poetovio, Siscia, Burnum and Tilurium. Dio is the main source, with Velleius, an eyewitness officer.

tacfarinas_war.detail: The war of Tacfarinas (AD 17-24) was the most serious resistance to Roman rule in North Africa in the early Principate. Tacfarinas, a Numidian of the Musulamii who had served as a Roman auxiliary and deserted, organised the semi-nomadic Musulamii and their neighbours, the Cinithii and the Mauri under Mazippa, into a force with regular infantry and cavalry units on Roman lines and mobile raiding bands. The war was a reaction to Roman expansion into their grazing lands, the building of the road from Ammaedara to Tacapae by the legion III Augusta in AD 14 and the demarcation of land for taxation and settlement. In AD 17 the proconsul Furius Camillus defeated him in a pitched battle and won triumphal ornaments. In 20 he resumed raids and besieged Roman forts; Lucius Apronius decimated a cohort that had fled and won a victory at Thala. In 21-22 Tacfarinas demanded land for his followers and threatened endless war; Tiberius refused to negotiate with a deserter and bandit, and sent Quintus Junius Blaesus, Sejanus's uncle, who used small mobile columns and winter forts, offered amnesty to all except Tacfarinas and captured his brother, earning the last imperatorial acclamation given to a commander outside the imperial family. After IX Hispana was withdrawn, Tacfarinas reappeared in 24, supported by Moors discontented with the rule of Ptolemy of Mauretania. The proconsul Publius Cornelius Dolabella, with Mauretanian help, surprised his camp at Auzea and killed him; his son was captured. Tiberius refused Dolabella the triumphal ornaments out of deference to Sejanus's uncle, Tacitus says. Tacitus's account (Annals 2-4) is the only narrative. Modern historians see the war in terms of conflict over land between pastoralists and the expanding Roman agricultural frontier, and the military lessons were reflected in Caligula's decision in 39 to place the legion of Africa under an imperial legate.
tacfarinas_war.debate: Bandit insurgency (Roman view) or a struggle of pastoralists against the agricultural frontier.

roman_conquest_of_britain.detail: The Roman conquest of Britain began with the Claudian invasion of 43 and continued for four decades. Aulus Plautius, with four legions and auxiliaries, defeated the Catuvellauni under Caratacus and Togodumnus at the Medway and Thames, and Claudius received the surrender of eleven kings at Camulodunum. Vespasian with II Augusta subdued the south-west, taking Maiden Castle and other hillforts. By 47 the province extended to the line of the Fosse Way. Client kingdoms, Togidubnus of the Regni, Prasutagus of the Iceni and Cartimandua of the Brigantes, protected the flanks. Ostorius Scapula (47-52) disarmed the tribes, crushed the first Iceni revolt and defeated Caratacus in Wales (51), who was handed over by Cartimandua; the Silures continued the struggle. Didius Gallus and Veranius held the line, and Suetonius Paullinus attacked the Druid centre on Mona (60) before Boudica's revolt (60-61) forced him back to win a desperate battle.
