Fearing that Romanus' accusations would turn the emperor against him, Firmus revolted in 372, gaining the support of Moorish tribes and some Roman units, and was perhaps proclaimed emperor. His forces sacked Caesarea, the provincial capital, and attacked Icosium.

Valentinian sent his best general, the magister equitum Theodosius, father of the future emperor, who landed at Igilgili in 373 with a small army of Gallic veterans. Theodosius waged a difficult campaign in the mountains of Kabylia and the Atlas, negotiating with tribes and punishing defectors, including Roman soldiers, by mutilating them or burning them alive. Firmus' brothers were divided: Gildo sided with Rome, while Mascezel, Mazuca and others joined Firmus. After two years of war, the Isaflenses under King Igmazen, who had sheltered Firmus, agreed to hand him over; Firmus hanged himself in 375 to avoid capture, and his body was delivered to Theodosius on a camel.

The revolt revealed the tensions between Roman officials, local elites and Moorish chiefs in late Roman Africa. Theodosius' victory was followed by his own execution at Carthage in 376. Gildo became comes Africae and himself revolted in 397-398. Ammianus' account (29.5) is the main source; some historians (Frend) see links between Firmus and the Donatists, a view others reject.
scholarship: Kotula, "Firmus, fils de Nubel", Eos 56 (1966)
Matthews, The Roman Empire of Ammianus (1989)

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

quadi_sarmatian_war_374_375.detail:
In 373 Valentinian ordered the building of a fort on Quadic territory north of the Danube. When the Quadic king Gabinius protested, the dux of Valeria, Marcellianus, invited him to a banquet and had him murdered. In 374 the outraged Quadi, joined by Sarmatians, crossed the Danube and devastated Pannonia and Valeria during the harvest. They nearly captured Constantia, the daughter of Constantius II and bride of Gratian, who was travelling to Gaul and was saved by the governor Messalla, who rushed her to Sirmium in a public carriage. The praetorian prefect Probus, at Sirmium, organised the defence of the city and cleaned out its ditches. The Sarmatians defeated and destroyed two legions, the Pannonica and the Moesiaca, while the young Theodosius, dux of Moesia Prima, defeated the Sarmatians in his sector.

In 375 Valentinian moved from Trier to Pannonia, crossed the Danube at Aquincum and ravaged Quadic territory, killing indiscriminately. In November the Quadi sent envoys to Brigetio to seek peace, claiming that the fort-building had provoked them and that the invaders were foreigners not under their control. Valentinian, enraged by their arguments, fell into a fit of fury and died of a stroke on 17 November 375.

The war illustrates Valentinian's aggressive frontier policy of building forts and bridgeheads across the rivers, which provoked conflicts with peoples beyond the frontier. It also shows the fragility of Roman control over the middle Danube on the eve of the Hunnic arrival. Ammianus (29.6 and 30.5-6) is the main source. The death of Valentinian left the west to the 16-year-old Gratian and the four-year-old Valentinian II.
scholarship: Lenski, Failure of Empire (2002)
Matthews, The Roman Empire of Ammianus (1989)

gothic_war_376_382.detail:
Pressed by the Huns, the Tervingi under Alavivus and Fritigern were admitted across the Danube in 376, while the Greuthungi of Alatheus and Saphrax crossed without permission. Exploitation by the Roman commanders Lupicinus and Maximus provoked a revolt; early in 377, after the attempt to murder the Gothic leaders at a banquet at Marcianople, Fritigern defeated Lupicinus nearby. Gothic soldiers in Roman service at Adrianople and miners from Thrace joined the rebels. In 377 Roman forces under Trajanus, Profuturus and Richomeres fought an indecisive battle at Ad Salices, and the Goths, reinforced by Huns and Alans, broke through the Haemus passes. Frigeridus and Sebastianus won smaller successes. On 9 August 378 Valens attacked the Gothic camp near Adrianople without waiting for Gratian and was killed with two-thirds of his army.

The Goths failed to take Adrianople and were repulsed from Constantinople, partly by Saracen cavalry; in the east the magister Julius massacred Gothic recruits and hostages. In 379 Gratian appointed Theodosius as Augustus for the east. Theodosius rebuilt the army, recruiting widely including Goths, and fought a war of attrition from Thessalonica; his general Modares, a Goth, won a victory in 379, but in 380 Theodosius was defeated in Macedonia, and Gratian's generals Bauto and Arbogast had to intervene. Gratian settled the Greuthungi in Pannonia in 380, and in January 381 Athanaric came to Constantinople and died there.

On 3 October 382 the magister Saturninus concluded a peace by which the Tervingi were settled in Thrace and northern Illyricum under their own leaders, providing troops when called upon. The war transformed Rome's relations with barbarians and is often seen as the beginning of the end for the western empire. Ammianus' book 31, Zosimus, Themistius and the church historians are the main sources.
scholarship: Heather, Goths and Romans (1991)
Lenski, Failure of Empire (2002)
Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)
Heather, Goths and Romans 332-489 (1991)

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

civil_war_387_388.detail:
In 383 the army in Britain proclaimed Magnus Maximus, who crossed to Gaul; Gratian's army deserted near Paris, and Gratian was killed at Lugdunum on 25 August 383. Maximus established his capital at Trier and controlled Britain, Gaul and Spain, while Valentinian II and his mother Justina ruled Italy, Africa and Illyricum from Milan. Theodosius, occupied in the east, recognised Maximus, and Ambrose conducted negotiations at Trier. Maximus presented himself as a champion of Nicene orthodoxy against the Homoian Justina and had the heretic Priscillian executed in 385.

In 387 Maximus invaded Italy, crossing the Alps behind envoys sent by Valentinian; Valentinian and Justina fled by sea from Aquileia to Thessalonica. Theodosius married Valentinian's sister Galla and prepared war. In the summer of 388 he advanced with an army that included Goths, Huns and Alans. Maximus' forces were defeated in two battles: at Siscia, where Theodosius' cavalry swam the Save and routed the enemy, and at Poetovio, where Maximus' brother Marcellinus was defeated. Theodosius pursued Maximus to Aquileia, where his soldiers handed him over; he was executed on 28 August 388. In Gaul, Arbogast killed Maximus' son Victor, and his general Andragathius drowned himself.

Theodosius restored Valentinian II in the west under the supervision of Arbogast and spent three years in Italy, visiting Rome in 389. Pacatus' panegyric of 389 celebrates the victory as the overthrow of a tyrant. The war showed the continued importance of the western armies' ability to choose emperors and the growing role of barbarian troops and generals, such as Arbogast, in imperial politics. Zosimus, Pacatus, Orosius, Sulpicius Severus and the church historians are the main sources.
scholarship: Matthews, Western Aristocracies and Imperial Court AD 364-425 (1975)
McLynn, Ambrose of Milan (1994)

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

civil_war_394.detail:
After Maximus' defeat Theodosius left Valentinian II, then about seventeen, in the west under the Frankish magister militum Arbogast. Valentinian, residing at Vienne, resented Arbogast's control; when he handed Arbogast a letter of dismissal, the general tore it up, saying he had not received his command from the emperor. On 15 May 392 Valentinian was found hanged, whether by suicide or murder is disputed. Arbogast, unable as a barbarian to take the throne himself, proclaimed the rhetor and former official Flavius Eugenius emperor on 22 August 392. Eugenius, a Christian, sought recognition from Theodosius, who refused and in January 393 raised his younger son Honorius to Augustus.

In the west, Eugenius' regime allied with the pagan senatorial aristocracy, especially the praetorian prefect Virius Nicomachus Flavianus, who restored temples and festivals at Rome, and Ambrose left Milan to avoid contact with the usurper. In 394 Theodosius marched west with a large army including 20,000 Gothic federates under Gainas and Alaric, Huns, Alans and Iberians, with Stilicho and Timasius as generals. He crossed the Julian Alps unopposed and on 5-6 September 394 fought Eugenius and Arbogast at the river Frigidus. After heavy losses among the Goths on the first day, a fierce bora wind on the second day helped Theodosius' attack; Eugenius was captured and executed, Arbogast and Flavianus committed suicide.

Theodosius became sole ruler of the whole empire, but died at Milan on 17 January 395, leaving the east to Arcadius and the west to Honorius under Stilicho's guardianship. Christian writers presented the war as the final defeat of paganism, a view Alan Cameron has criticised as exaggerated. The heavy Gothic casualties contributed to the revolt of Alaric in 395.
scholarship: Cameron, The Last Pagans of Rome (2011)
Croke, "Arbogast and the Death of Valentinian II", Historia 25 (1976)

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans
Panegyric on the Third Consulship of Honorius

gothic_war_395.detail: The war began when Alaric's Gothic federates, embittered by their losses at the Frigidus and by unpaid subsidies, rebelled on the death of Theodosius I in January 395. It falls into four phases. In the Balkan phase (395-397) the Goths ravaged Thrace, Macedonia and Greece; Stilicho twice confronted them, in Thessaly (395) and at Pholoe in Arcadia (397), but was restrained by the eastern court, which bought Alaric off with the command of Illyricum. In the first Italian phase (401-402) Alaric invaded Italy and was checked at Pollentia and Verona. An interlude of uneasy alliance followed (402-408), in which Stilicho planned to use Alaric to annex eastern Illyricum. The decisive phase began with Stilicho's execution in August 408: reinforced by thousands of barbarian federates whose families had been massacred, Alaric besieged Rome three times, extracting a vast ransom in 408, setting up the puppet emperor Priscus Attalus in 409 and sacking the city in August 410. After Alaric's death at Consentia, Athaulf led the Goths into Gaul (412), took Narbonne, Toulouse and Bordeaux, married Galla Placidia (414) and briefly revived Attalus, but was driven into Spain by the naval blockade of Constantius, who starved the Goths into submission. Under Wallia (415-418) they returned Placidia, fought the Vandals and Alans in Spain as Roman allies, and in 418 were settled in Aquitaine. The war thus ended not in the destruction of either side but in the transformation of a Gothic army into a federate kingdom inside the empire, the model for later settlements. The main sources are Zosimus (from Olympiodorus and Eunapius), Claudian, Orosius and Jordanes.
scholarship: Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)
Heather, Goths and Romans (1991)
Heather, Goths and Romans 332-489 (1991)
Burns, Barbarians within the Gates of Rome (1994)

gildonic_war.detail: Gildo, a Moorish prince and brother of the rebel Firmus whom Theodosius the Elder had crushed in 375, had served Rome loyally and was made comes et magister utriusque militiae per Africam around 386. During the civil war of 394 he stayed neutral, and in 397, encouraged by the eastern court under Eutropius, he transferred his allegiance from Honorius to Arcadius and stopped the grain fleet that fed Rome. The Senate, at Stilicho's prompting and in a rare revival of its old authority, declared Gildo a public enemy (hostis publicus), and Stilicho prepared an expedition. Command was given to Gildo's own brother Mascezel, whose sons Gildo had murdered and who had fled to Italy. Mascezel sailed in late 397 with perhaps 5,000 veterans of the Gallic field army, a small force by any standard. Orosius, who saw the campaign as a miracle, says Mascezel stopped at the island of Capraria to collect monks to pray for him, and before the battle on the river Ardalio between Theveste and Ammaedara in spring 398 dreamed that St Ambrose promised him victory. Gildo's much larger army, made up mainly of Moorish tribal levies, dissolved after Mascezel struck down a standard-bearer; Gildo fled by sea, was driven back by contrary winds to Thabraca and was captured and killed or committed suicide. Mascezel himself died soon after, drowned in Italy, rumour said on Stilicho's orders. Claudian's poem De Bello Gildonico celebrates the war as the restoration of Africa's grain to Rome. The war showed the dependence of Rome on African grain and the dangerous competition between the two courts, and Gildo's vast estates, confiscated, required a special official, the comes Gildoniaci patrimonii.
scholarship: Cameron, Claudian (1970)
Modéran, Les Maures et l'Afrique romaine (2003)

radagaisus_war.detail: In late 405 the pagan Gothic king Radagaisus crossed the Alps into Italy with a following whose size the sources greatly exaggerate: Zosimus says 400,000, Orosius 200,000; a modern estimate of some 20,000 fighting men with their families is more plausible. The invaders came from the middle Danube and probably represent the movement of peoples displaced by the Huns, in the same wave that brought the Vandals, Alans and Suebi to the Rhine in 406. Radagaisus divided his host into three groups and with the largest advanced into Tuscia, besieging Florence in the summer of 406. Stilicho, with thirty numeri of the Italian field army (perhaps 15,000-20,000 men) and with auxiliaries from the Hunnic king Uldin and the Goth Sarus, relieved Florence and drove the invaders onto the heights of Faesulae (Fiesole), where he blockaded them until starvation forced their surrender. Radagaisus was captured trying to escape and was executed on 23 August 406. The other groups were dispersed. Some 12,000 picked warriors were taken into Roman service, while the rest were sold as slaves in such numbers that, according to Orosius, prices collapsed. Christian writers emphasised that Radagaisus had vowed to sacrifice the Romans to his gods, and that he was defeated without battle by God's will. The war had important consequences. Stilicho's prestige reached its height, but the concentration of forces in Italy left the Rhine exposed. The 12,000 Goths, settled with their families in Italian cities, became one of the federate groups whose families were massacred after Stilicho's fall in 408, leading them to join Alaric.
scholarship: Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)
Halsall, Barbarian Migrations and the Roman West (2007)

constantine_iii_civil_war.detail: The British army raised three emperors in succession in 406-407, the last being the soldier Constantine III, who crossed to Gaul in 407, took over the Gallic army, secured the Rhine through treaties and made Arles his capital. The war against Honorius's government passed through several phases. In 407-408 Stilicho's general Sarus defeated and killed Constantine's general Justinian and besieged Constantine at Valence, but was driven back across the Alps by Gerontius and Edobichus. In 408 Constantine sent his son Constans and Gerontius to Spain, where they defeated Honorius's relatives Didymus and Verinianus, whose private armies of slaves and peasants had held the Pyrenees. In 409 the hard-pressed Honorius recognised Constantine as co-emperor; Constantine may have crossed into Italy in 410 with the aim of supporting or replacing Honorius, but retreated after the murder of his ally Allobichus. Then Gerontius rebelled in Spain, proclaimed his own emperor Maximus, apparently brought the Vandals, Alans and Suebi into Spain, defeated and killed Constans at Vienne, and besieged Constantine in Arles (411). Honorius's new general Constantius then marched into Gaul; Gerontius's army deserted and he died in a final siege of his house. Constantius defeated a relief army under Edobichus with Frankish and Alamannic auxiliaries, and Constantine surrendered, was ordained priest, and was executed on the way to Ravenna in September 411. Jovinus and Sebastianus, proclaimed at Mainz in 411, were defeated with Gothic help in 413. The war cost the empire Britain, allowed the Rhine invaders into Spain, and brought Constantius to power.
scholarship: Drinkwater, 'The usurpers Constantine III and Jovinus', Britannia 29 (1998)
Kulikowski, 'Barbarians in Gaul, usurpers in Britain', Britannia 31 (2000)

roman_sasanian_war_421.detail: Relations between Rome and Persia had been peaceful under Yazdegerd I (399-420), whose tolerance allowed the organisation of the Persian church at the synod of 410. But the destruction of a fire temple by a zealous bishop, Abdas of Hormizd-Ardashir, led to persecution of Christians in Yazdegerd's last year, which intensified under his son Bahram V from 420. Christians fled to Roman territory and Theodosius II, under the influence of his pious sister Pulcheria and in an atmosphere of religious enthusiasm, refused Bahram's demands to return them. There was also a dispute over Roman gold miners and over Persian merchants. In 421 the Roman general Ardabur invaded Arzanene, defeated the Persian commander Narses and besieged Nisibis, which he abandoned when Bahram approached; Bahram then besieged Theodosiopolis (probably Resaina in Osrhoene), where, according to Theodoret, the bishop Eunomius killed a Persian prince with a stone from a catapult. The Persians were defeated in several engagements, and Socrates tells of a Roman champion, Areobindus, killing a Persian champion in single combat, and of the destruction of a force of Lakhmid Arabs under al-Mundhir, who panicked and drowned in the Euphrates. The Persians, also facing the Hephthalites, made peace in 422, negotiated by the magister officiorum Helion. Its terms included mutual tolerance of Christians in Persia and Zoroastrians in the Roman empire, and perhaps an undertaking not to build new forts on the frontier. Socrates and Theodoret present the war as a Christian triumph, while the bishop Acacius of Amida ransomed 7,000 Persian prisoners with church plate, an act that impressed Bahram.
scholarship: Greatrex & Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars, Part II (2002)
Greatrex, 'The two fifth-century wars between Rome and Persia', Florilegium 12 (1993)
Holum, 'Pulcheria's crusade', GRBS 18 (1977)

joannes_civil_war.detail: When Honorius died on 15 August 423, the eastern court delayed in naming a successor, and in November the western officials at Rome, led by the magister militum Castinus, proclaimed the primicerius notariorum Joannes. Joannes, a capable civilian who tried to tax church lands and subject clergy to secular courts, was recognised in Italy and Gaul but not in Africa, where Bonifatius held out for the Theodosian dynasty, and in Gaul his praetorian prefect was killed by soldiers at Arles. Theodosius II decided to restore his cousin Valentinian, son of Galla Placidia, then a refugee in Constantinople. Valentinian was made Caesar at Thessalonica on 23 October 424. In 425 an eastern army, under Ardabur, his son Aspar and Candidianus, invaded Italy. Ardabur, travelling by sea, was shipwrecked and captured by Joannes's men, but treated well and used his captivity to subvert Joannes's officers. Aspar, with the cavalry, took Aquileia, and Placidia and Valentinian settled there. Guided, according to Socrates, by an angel in the form of a shepherd through the marshes, Aspar's men entered Ravenna; Joannes was captured, taken to Aquileia, his hand cut off, paraded on a donkey in the hippodrome and executed in summer 425. Three days later Aetius, sent by Joannes to recruit the Huns, arrived with a large Hunnic army; after fighting with Aspar, he was reconciled with Placidia, who paid off the Huns and made him commander in Gaul. Valentinian was crowned Augustus in Rome on 23 October 425. The war restored the Theodosian dynasty in the West and showed its dependence on eastern support, but also introduced Aetius and his Hunnic connections into western politics.
scholarship: Oost, Galla Placidia Augusta (1968)
McEvoy, Child Emperor Rule in the Late Roman West (2013)

vandal_war_429.detail: In May 429 Gaiseric led the Vandals and Alans, some 80,000 people according to Victor of Vita, from southern Spain into Africa. They advanced east along the coast through Mauretania and Numidia, encountering little resistance, and in 430 defeated the comes Africae Bonifatius, who withdrew into Hippo Regius. The siege of Hippo lasted fourteen months (430-431), during which Augustine died; it was lifted for lack of supplies. Reinforced by an eastern army under Aspar, Bonifatius was defeated again in 432 and recalled to Italy to fight Aetius. Hippo was abandoned and occupied by the Vandals. Aspar remained in Africa until 434, holding Carthage. In 435, at Hippo, the envoy Trygetius concluded a treaty: the Vandals were recognised as federates in parts of Mauretania and Numidia, paying tribute, and Gaiseric's son Huneric was sent as a hostage to Italy. On 19 October 439, while Aetius was in Gaul, Gaiseric seized Carthage by surprise and expropriated the senatorial estates of Proconsularis, distributing them to his warriors as sortes Vandalorum. He then raided Sicily (440) and besieged Panormus. A combined eastern and western expedition assembled in Sicily in 441, but the eastern troops were recalled when the Huns invaded the Balkans and Persia attacked. In 442 Valentinian III recognised the Vandal kingdom in Proconsularis, Byzacena and eastern Numidia, keeping the Mauretanias and western Numidia, and Huneric was betrothed to Eudocia. The loss of the richest provinces of the West, its grain and taxes, was decisive for the fate of the western empire. The chief narrators are Victor of Vita, Possidius and Prosper.
scholarship: Merrills & Miles, The Vandals (2010)
Merrills and Miles, The Vandals (2010)
Courtois, Les Vandales et l'Afrique (1955)
Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)

gallic_wars_of_aetius.detail: From 425 to about 439 Aetius, first as magister militum per Gallias and from 433 as supreme commander, fought a series of campaigns to hold Gaul for the empire, relying on his relationship with the Huns, who provided auxiliaries. The main enemy was the Visigoths of Theodoric I, settled in Aquitaine in 418, who tried to reach the Mediterranean: Aetius drove them from Arles in 425-426 and again in 430, and in 436 they besieged Narbonne, which was relieved by Litorius in 437 with Hunnic cavalry, each horseman carrying two measures of grain. In 439 Litorius, boasting and consulting pagan omens according to Prosper and Salvian, attacked Toulouse and was defeated and captured; a peace was then made by the prefect Avitus. On the Rhine Aetius defeated the Franks of Chlodio around 428 and again at Vicus Helena (c. 448), where the young Majorian distinguished himself. He fought the Juthungi in Raetia and the Norici (430-431). In 435-436 he defeated the Burgundians of Gundahar, who were then destroyed by the Huns (436), with Gundahar and, according to Prosper, 20,000 Burgundians killed, an event remembered in the Nibelungenlied; the survivors were resettled in Sapaudia in 443. In 435-437 Litorius suppressed the Bacaudae of Armorica under Tibatto. Aetius settled Alans around Valence (440) and Orléans (442) to control unrest. These campaigns prevented the collapse of Roman rule in Gaul and created the system of federate kingdoms and alliances that allowed Aetius to assemble the coalition against Attila in 451, but they also meant that the West could not intervene in Africa when the Vandals took Carthage in 439.
scholarship: Stickler, Aëtius (2002)
Hughes, Aetius: Attila's Nemesis (2012)
Halsall, Barbarian Migrations and the Roman West (2007)

hunnic_wars.detail: The Huns established their power on the Hungarian plain in the 420s, and under Rua and his nephews Attila and Bleda extracted increasing tribute from the eastern empire. The treaty of Margus (435) doubled the annual payment to 700 lb of gold, required the return of Hunnic fugitives and opened markets. In 441, while eastern troops were in Sicily for an expedition against the Vandals, the Huns crossed the Danube, using the pretext that the bishop of Margus had robbed royal tombs, and took Viminacium, Margus, Singidunum and Sirmium; in 442 they sacked Naissus and Serdica. The Peace of Anatolius (443) raised the tribute. In 447, after Attila had become sole ruler by killing Bleda, he invaded again during a plague and after earthquakes had damaged the walls of Constantinople; he defeated the eastern army on the Utus, where the magister militum Arnegisclus was killed, and raided to Thermopylae. The new peace imposed arrears of 6,000 lb of gold, annual tribute of 2,100 lb and the evacuation of a five-day-wide strip south of the Danube. In 449 an eastern plot to assassinate Attila failed. In 450 Marcian refused to pay tribute and Attila turned west. In 451 he invaded Gaul and was stopped at the Catalaunian Plains by Aetius and the Visigoths; in 452 he invaded Italy, sacked Aquileia and the cities of the Po valley, but withdrew. His death in 453 led to the revolt of his subject peoples, the Hunnic defeat at the Nedao (454) and the collapse of the Hunnic empire. Sources include Priscus, Jordanes and the chronicles.
scholarship: Maenchen-Helfen, The World of the Huns (1973)
Kelly, Attila the Hun (2008)
Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)
Thompson, The Huns (1996)
Kim, The Huns (2016)

roman_vandal_war_455.detail: After the sack of Rome in June 455, the Vandals, released from the treaty of 442 by the end of the Theodosian dynasty, launched annual raids on Sicily, southern Italy, the Dalmatian coast and Greece from their bases in Carthage, Sardinia, Corsica and the Balearics, which they seized in these years. Procopius says Gaiseric sailed each spring wherever the wind took him, 'against those with whom God is angry'. The western government under Ricimer fought back: in 456 Ricimer defeated a Vandal fleet near Agrigentum and off Corsica; in 458 Majorian defeated a Vandal raid at the mouth of the Garigliano in Campania. Majorian then prepared a great expedition, assembling 300 ships at Cartagena in Spain, but in 460 Gaiseric, warned by traitors, destroyed most of the fleet in the bay of Elche (Portus Ilicitanus), and Majorian made peace before being overthrown by Ricimer. Gaiseric, who held Valentinian's widow and daughters, supported the candidacy of Olybrius, husband of the younger daughter, and kept up raids, extending them to the eastern empire after 467. The second great Roman attempt came in 468: Leo I and Anthemius sent a combined force under Basiliscus, Marcellinus and Heraclius, but Basiliscus's fleet was destroyed by fireships at Cape Bon. In 470 a further offensive in Tripolitania was abandoned. Finally, in 474 Zeno concluded an 'eternal peace' recognising Vandal rule over Africa, the Balearics, Sardinia, Corsica and Sicily, and the release of captives. The war showed that the Vandal fleet, built in the shipyards of Carthage, dominated the western Mediterranean and that the West no longer had the resources to recover Africa.
scholarship: Merrills and Miles, The Vandals (2010)
MacGeorge, Late Roman Warlords (2002)
Courtois, Les Vandales et l'Afrique (1955)

revolt_of_illus.detail: Illus, an Isaurian general, had helped Basiliscus overthrow Zeno in 475, then changed sides to restore Zeno in 476, and became his most powerful minister, magister officiorum and consul in 478. His relationship with Zeno and the dowager empress Verina was poisoned by mutual plots: Verina tried to have him murdered, and he imprisoned her in Isauria; in 481 or 482 an assassin, apparently sent by Ariadne, cut off his ear, and he wore a cap thereafter. In 483 he was appointed magister militum per Orientem and left the capital. In 484, as Zeno moved against him, Illus rebelled with the support of pagan and Chalcedonian elements and of the Isaurians. He freed Verina, who crowned the patrician Leontius, a Syrian general, as emperor at Tarsus on 19 July 484, and they established themselves at Antioch, seeking support from Persia, Armenia and Odoacer, who refused. Zeno sent an army under John the Scythian and Theodoric the Amal, which defeated Illus and Leontius near Antioch in September 484. The rebels retreated to the Isaurian fortress of Papyrius (Cherris), where they held out for four years; Verina died there in 484. In 488 the fortress was betrayed, perhaps by the brother-in-law of the commander, and Illus and Leontius were beheaded, their heads displayed in Constantinople. The revolt was the last major attempt to overthrow Zeno, and its suppression made possible both Theodoric's departure for Italy (488) and the reckoning with the Isaurians after Zeno's death in the Isaurian War of 492-497. The circle of Illus included the pagan philosopher Pamprepius, whose role the Neoplatonist Damascius discusses.
scholarship: Elton, 'Illus and the imperial aristocracy under Zeno', Byzantion 70 (2000)
Kosiński, The Emperor Zeno (2010)

theodorics_war_489.detail: In 488 Zeno, who had struggled for a decade with the Ostrogoths of Theodoric in the Balkans, commissioned him to overthrow Odoacer, king in Italy, who had expanded into Dalmatia and attacked the Rugi on the Danube; if successful, Theodoric would rule Italy on Zeno's behalf. The Goths, with their families, perhaps 100,000 people, set out from Novae in autumn 488, fought the Gepids at the river Ulca near Sirmium, and crossed the Julian Alps. On 28 August 489 Theodoric defeated Odoacer on the Isonzo near Aquileia, and on 27 September 489 again at Verona, after which Odoacer withdrew to Ravenna. Odoacer's general Tufa deserted to Theodoric, but then returned to Odoacer, betraying the Gothic troops with him. In 490 Odoacer took the offensive, retook Milan and besieged Theodoric in Ticinum (Pavia); but a Visigothic army sent by Alaric II helped Theodoric defeat Odoacer on the Adda on 11 August 490. Odoacer retreated to Ravenna, which Theodoric blockaded for three years. A night sortie by Odoacer's Heruli on 10 July 491 failed with heavy losses; from 492 Theodoric's fleet blockaded Classe. Meanwhile, the Burgundians raided Liguria (490), and in Sicily the Vandals were expelled. On 25 February 493, with the mediation of Bishop John, Odoacer and Theodoric agreed to share power, and Theodoric entered Ravenna on 5 March. On 15 March he killed Odoacer at a banquet. Theodoric's followers proclaimed him king, and in 497 Anastasius sent him the palace insignia that Odoacer had returned to Constantinople in 476. The war founded the Ostrogothic kingdom of Italy.
scholarship: Moorhead, Theoderic in Italy (1992)
Wolfram, History of the Goths (1988)
Arnold, Theoderic and the Roman Imperial Restoration (2014)

isaurian_war_492.detail: After Zeno's death in April 491, the Isaurians, who had dominated the court and army, were displaced by the new emperor Anastasius, who was chosen against Zeno's brother Longinus. Riots in Constantinople in 491 led to the expulsion of the Isaurians from the capital, the confiscation of their property, and the cancellation of the subsidy of 1,400 lb of gold a year that Zeno had paid to Isauria. Longinus was exiled to Egypt. The Isaurians, under Longinus of Kardala, Lilingis, governor of Isauria, Athenodorus and later Longinus of Selinus, rebelled and invaded Phrygia with an army that the sources number at 150,000, including peasants. In 492 the imperial army under John the Scythian and John the Hunchback, with Gothic and Hunnic contingents, defeated them at Cotyaeum, where Lilingis was killed. The rebels retreated into the Taurus mountains, where the war became a series of sieges of mountain fortresses, lasting five years. In 493 Longinus of Kardala was defeated, in 497 Athenodorus and Longinus of Kardala were captured and executed, their heads displayed at Tarsus and on poles outside Constantinople, at Sycae. In 498 John the Hunchback captured Longinus of Selinus and Indes, who were paraded in Constantinople, and Longinus was tortured to death. Many Isaurians were deported to Thrace. The victory freed Anastasius from Isaurian pressure, allowing him to carry out his financial reforms. It was celebrated in the Hippodrome, and the poet Christodorus of Coptos wrote an epic poem, the Isaurika, now lost. The war also marks the end of Isauria as an autonomous power within the empire.
scholarship: Haarer, Anastasius I (2006)
Elton, 'Illus and the imperial aristocracy' (2000)
Feld, Barbarische Bürger: Die Isaurier und das Römische Reich (2005)

anastasian_war.detail: Kavad I, restored to the Persian throne with Hephthalite help in 498-499, needed money to pay his allies and asked Anastasius for financial contributions, citing the joint defence of the Caucasus passes. When Anastasius refused, Kavad invaded Roman Armenia in August 502, taking Theodosiopolis and Martyropolis, and besieged Amida in October 502. The siege lasted three months in winter; Joshua the Stylite and Procopius describe the resistance of the citizens, the monks who failed to guard a tower, and the Persian entry over the walls in January 503, followed by a massacre and the deportation of the survivors. In 503 Anastasius sent a large army of 52,000 men, under three generals, Areobindus, Patricius and Hypatius, whose lack of coordination led to defeats: Areobindus at Apadna and the others at Siphrios. Kavad besieged Edessa and Constantina in vain. In 504 the Romans under Celer besieged Amida, which the Persian garrison surrendered in 505 for a payment of 1,000 lb of gold. A Hunnic invasion in the Caucasus forced Kavad to make peace; a truce was concluded in 506 for seven years. The war revealed the weakness of the Roman frontier in Mesopotamia, where Nisibis had been Persian since 363, and in 505-507 Anastasius built the fortress of Dara (Anastasiopolis) near the frontier, opposite Nisibis, which became the key Roman bastion and a cause of Persian complaint, being in breach of the treaty of 441. The Chronicle of Joshua the Stylite is a uniquely detailed contemporary source, describing the sufferings of Edessa and the region, including famine and locusts.
scholarship: Greatrex, Rome and Persia at War 502-532 (1998)
Trombley and Watt, The Chronicle of Pseudo-Joshua the Stylite (2000)

frankish_visigothic_war_507.detail: By the early sixth century Clovis's Frankish kingdom had expanded to the Loire, facing the Visigothic kingdom of Toulouse under Alaric II, which extended from the Loire to Spain. The two kings had met on an island in the Loire near Amboise around 502. Theodoric, linked by marriage to both, tried to keep the peace, writing letters to Clovis, Alaric, Gundobad and the kings of the Heruli, Warni and Thuringians (Cassiodorus, Variae 3.1-4), threatening to intervene. In spring 507 Clovis attacked, with Burgundian help under Gundobad's son Sigismund and the support of Anastasius, whose fleet raided the coast of Apulia in 508, preventing Theodoric from sending troops. Gregory of Tours presents the war as a crusade against the Arian heretics, with miracles at the tomb of St Martin at Tours and St Hilary at Poitiers. Clovis defeated and killed Alaric at the Campus Vogladensis near Poitiers. The Franks took Bordeaux, where Clovis wintered, and in 508 Toulouse with the royal treasure; his son Theuderic took the Auvergne and Rouergue, while the Burgundians took Narbonne. In 508 Theodoric's army under Ibba and Mammo intervened, relieving Arles from a Franco-Burgundian siege and recovering Narbonne and Septimania; Jordanes says 30,000 Franks were killed. Alaric's illegitimate son Gesalec was proclaimed king but was deposed by Theodoric's forces (511), and Theodoric became regent for his grandson Amalaric. The war gave the Franks most of Gaul south of the Loire, with Aquitaine; the Visigothic kingdom was reduced to Septimania and Spain, with its centre eventually at Toledo; and the Ostrogoths gained Provence.
scholarship: Mathisen and Shanzer (eds.), The Battle of Vouillé, 507 CE (2012)
Wood, The Merovingian Kingdoms (1994)

revolt_of_vitalian.detail: Vitalian, a commander of federate troops in Thrace, son of the officer Patriciolus, rebelled in 513 against Anastasius, demanding the payment of the annona to the federates, which the magister militum per Thracias, Hypatius, had cut, and the restoration of Chalcedonian orthodoxy and the bishops deposed by Anastasius, including Macedonius of Constantinople and Flavian of Antioch. With an army of federates, Bulgars and Huns and local peasants, he marched on Constantinople three times. In 513, the first time, he reached the Hebdomon and withdrew after Anastasius promised to restore the bishops and pay the soldiers. When the emperor appointed a new magister militum per Thracias, Cyril, Vitalian killed him; Anastasius declared Vitalian a public enemy and sent Hypatius with a large army, which Vitalian defeated near Acris in 513, capturing Hypatius, who was later ransomed. In 514 Vitalian marched on Constantinople again, by land and sea, and obtained the post of magister militum per Thracias, 5,000 lb of gold and the promise of a church council with the pope's participation, which met at Heraclea in 515 without result. In 515, the third time, Vitalian's fleet was destroyed near Constantinople by the praetorian prefect Marinus, who used a chemical substance, perhaps sulphur, prepared by the Athenian philosopher Proclus, according to Malalas. Vitalian fled. After Anastasius's death in 518, Justin I recalled him, made him magister militum praesentalis and consul (520), but he was murdered in the palace in July 520, probably on Justinian's orders. The revolt combined religious and military grievances.
scholarship: Haarer, Anastasius I (2006)
Meier, Anastasios I. (2009)
Ruscu, 'The revolt of Vitalianus', Classica et Christiana 3 (2008)

iberian_war.detail: Relations with Persia deteriorated in the 520s. Kavad I asked Justin I to adopt his son Khosrow (525), and the negotiations failed. In 524 or 525 the king of Iberia, Gourgenes, revolted against Persian attempts to impose Zoroastrian practices and appealed to Rome; the Persians conquered Iberia, and Gourgenes fled to Lazica and Constantinople. In 526 the Roman generals Sittas and Belisarius raided Persarmenia, with little success, while the Persians attacked Roman forts in Lazica. Justinian's attempts to build a fortress at Mindouos near Dara led to a Roman defeat in 528, and al-Mundhir III's Lakhmids raided Syria as far as Antioch's territory in 529. In June 530 Belisarius won a major victory at Dara, defeating a Persian army of 50,000; in the same year Sittas defeated the Persians at Satala in Armenia, and the Romans gained the Persarmenian forts of Bolum and Pharangium. In 531 a Persian and Lakhmid army invaded Commagene; Belisarius forced it to retreat, but was defeated at Callinicum on 19 April. In autumn 531 the Persians besieged Martyropolis, but withdrew on the death of Kavad (September 531). His successor Khosrow I, who needed to secure his throne, negotiated with Justinian's envoys Rufinus and Hermogenes, and in 532 they concluded the 'Eternal Peace': the Romans paid 11,000 lb of gold, withdrew the headquarters of the dux of Mesopotamia from Dara to Constantina, and returned the Persarmenian forts, while the Persians returned the Lazic forts. The peace freed Justinian for the conquest of Africa and Italy, but lasted only until 540.
scholarship: Greatrex, Rome and Persia at War 502-532 (1998)
Greatrex and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars II (2002)

vandalic_war_533.detail: Justinian decided to invade the Vandal kingdom after the deposition of his ally Hilderic by Gelimer in 530 and the conclusion of the Eternal Peace with Persia in 532, against the advice of John the Cappadocian and his generals. Revolts in Sardinia, under the Goth Godas, and in Tripolitania, under Pudentius, both encouraged by Constantinople, diverted the Vandal forces; Gelimer sent his brother Tzazon with 5,000 men to Sardinia. Belisarius sailed in June 533 with 15,000 soldiers in 500 transports with 92 warships, stopped in Sicily, where the Ostrogothic regent Amalasuntha allowed supplies, and landed at Caput Vada in Byzacena in early September. Marching up the coast, he won the battle of Ad Decimum on 13 September, where Gelimer's plan of a three-pronged attack failed and his brother Ammatas was killed, and entered Carthage on 15 September. Gelimer gathered his forces, recalled Tzazon from Sardinia, and attacked, but was defeated at Tricamarum in mid-December 533. He fled to the Moors on Mount Papua, where he surrendered in March 534 to the Herul Pharas. Belisarius returned to Constantinople with Gelimer, the Vandal treasure, including the Jewish Temple treasures, and thousands of Vandal prisoners, celebrating a triumph in the Hippodrome in 534, the first granted to a private citizen in centuries; Gelimer, on seeing Justinian, repeated 'Vanity of vanities, all is vanity'. Africa was organised as a praetorian prefecture with seven provinces in April 534. Sardinia, Corsica, the Balearics and Septem were also recovered. The Vandal kingdom was destroyed in less than a year, but the Moorish wars and military mutinies followed.
scholarship: Merrills & Miles, The Vandals (2010)
Hughes, Belisarius (2009)
Merrills and Miles, The Vandals (2010)
Pringle, The Defence of Byzantine Africa from Justinian to the Arab Conquest (1981)

moorish_wars_534.detail: After the fall of the Vandal kingdom, the Moorish tribes of Byzacena, Numidia and Tripolitania, which had already been gaining independence under the Vandals, attacked the new Roman province. The eunuch Solomon, praetorian prefect and magister militum, defeated the Moors of Byzacena at Mammes (534) and Mount Bourgaon (535), but failed against Iaudas in the Aurès mountains (535). In 536 a mutiny of soldiers, angered by the confiscation of Vandal lands they had married into and by the prohibition of Arian worship, broke out under Stotzas; Solomon fled to Sicily, and Belisarius returned briefly to relieve Carthage. Justinian's cousin Germanus restored order by paying arrears and defeated Stotzas at Scalae Veteres (537). Solomon, returning in 539, conquered the Aurès and built a network of fortresses, many of which survive, as at Ammaedara, Theveste and Thamugadi; Procopius describes the following years as a period of peace and prosperity. But in 543 the plague struck, and in 544 Solomon, after the murder of Moorish envoys by his nephew Sergius in Lepcis Magna, was defeated and killed at Cillium by the Levathae and Antalas of Byzacena. Sergius's incompetence, the revolt of the dux Guntharic, who seized Carthage in 546 and was murdered, and Moorish advances followed. In 546 John Troglita was sent from the East; after a defeat in 547 at Marta, he decisively defeated the Moorish coalition of Carcasan at the Campi Catonis (548), as celebrated in Corippus's epic Iohannis. Fifteen years of peace followed. The wars show the limits of Roman control in Africa beyond the coastal plains and the dependence on Moorish allies.
scholarship: Pringle, The Defence of Byzantine Africa (1981)
Modéran, Les Maures et l'Afrique romaine (2003)
Conant, Staying Roman (2012)

gothic_war_535.detail: The murder of Amalasuntha in 535 gave Justinian the pretext to invade Ostrogothic Italy. The war, lasting nearly twenty years, had three phases. In the first (535-540) Belisarius took Sicily (535), Naples (536) after a siege in which his men entered through an aqueduct, and Rome (December 536), which he defended against Witiges for a year (537-538); after the relief of Ariminum and the fall of Milan to the Goths (539), where the male population was massacred, and the sieges of Fiesole and Auximum, he took Ravenna in May 540, capturing Witiges and the Gothic treasury. In the second phase (541-550) the Goths, under the able king Totila, recovered almost all Italy by appealing to the peasants and slaves against the landowners and the imperial tax collectors. They defeated the Romans at Faventia and Mucellium (542), took Naples (543) and Rome (546), which they partly depopulated. Belisarius, sent back with inadequate forces (544-549), recovered Rome briefly (547), but Totila retook it in 550 and invaded Sicily. In the third phase (551-554) Justinian sent Narses with a large army, mostly of foreign troops; he defeated Totila at Busta Gallorum (Taginae) in 552 and Teia at Mons Lactarius, and destroyed the Frankish-Alamannic invasion at the Volturnus (554). The last Gothic garrisons held out until 561-562. The Pragmatic Sanction (554) restored the property of the landowners and the authority of the Senate. But Italy was devastated by war, famine and plague, and within fourteen years the Lombards invaded. Procopius's Wars books 5-8 and Agathias are the main sources.
scholarship: Wolfram, History of the Goths (1988)
Heather, Rome Resurgent (2018)
Moorhead, 'Italian loyalties during Justinian's Gothic War', Byzantion 53 (1983)
Hughes, Narses (2017)

lazic_war.detail: Khosrow I broke the Eternal Peace in spring 540, invading Syria, sacking Antioch and extorting ransoms from cities. Belisarius was sent east in 541 and raided Assyria, while Khosrow invaded Lazica, at the invitation of the Lazic king Gubazes, who resented Roman monopolies, and took the Roman fortress of Petra on the Black Sea coast. The war in Mesopotamia continued with the Persian siege of Edessa (544), and the Roman defeat at Anglon in Persarmenia (543), until a five-year truce in 545, renewed in 551, for which Rome paid 2,000 and then 2,600 lb of gold, but which excluded Lazica. In Lazica, the war became a long struggle. Gubazes returned to the Roman alliance in 548, alienated by Persian plans to deport the Lazi and convert them to Zoroastrianism. The Romans under Dagisthaeus besieged Petra (549), and Bessas took it by storm in 551 after a long siege. The Persians under Mermeroes attacked Archaeopolis (551), defended by the Romans with the help of a panic among the Persian elephants, and established themselves in the region of Kutatisi and Mukheirisis. In 555 the Roman generals murdered Gubazes, provoking a crisis; the Persians besieged Phasis but were repelled (555), and the Romans defeated them at the fort of Onoguris. A truce in 557 led to the Fifty Years' Peace of 562, negotiated by Peter the Patrician and the Persian Yazdgushnasp, whose text is preserved by Menander: Persia evacuated Lazica, Rome paid 30,000 solidi a year, trade was restricted to designated cities (Nisibis, Callinicum, Dara), and Christians in Persia were granted religious freedom. Agathias describes the war in detail.
scholarship: Greatrex and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars II (2002)
Braund, Georgia in Antiquity (1994)
Börm, Prokop und die Perser (2007)

spanish_war_552.detail: In 551 the Visigothic noble Athanagild rebelled against King Agila and asked Justinian for help. Justinian sent a small expedition under the elderly patrician Liberius, who had served Odoacer and Theodoric, landing in southern Spain in 552. The Romans helped Athanagild defeat Agila near Seville in 554, after which Agila was murdered by his own men, and Athanagild became king. But the Romans remained, occupying the coastal cities from Cartagena to Malaga, perhaps with Córdoba, Medina Sidonia and some inland territory organised as the province of Spania under a magister militum. The extent of the province is uncertain and it varied over time. Athanagild and his successors tried to expel them. Leovigild took Medina Sidonia (571) and Córdoba (572), and campaigned in the Bastetania (570); the Roman governor Comenciolus fortified Cartagena around 589, as an inscription shows. Under Reccared (586-601) and Witteric (603-610), the Visigoths made further gains, and Pope Gregory searched the imperial archives for the treaty of Justinian with Athanagild, without success. Sisebut (612-621) took Malaga and other cities around 614-615, and corresponded with the Roman patrician Caesarius. Suintila completed the conquest around 624-625, earning Isidore's praise as the first king to rule all Spain. The province of Spania, lasting some seventy years, was a significant Byzantine presence in the West, and an important conduit of eastern culture, the Byzantine influence being visible in Visigothic royal ceremonial, coinage and art. Its archaeology, at Cartagena with the theatre district and Begastri, is still being studied, and recent excavations have revealed the Byzantine-era occupation of the theatre at Cartagena.
scholarship: Thompson, The Goths in Spain (1969)
Wood, 'Defending Byzantine Spain', Early Medieval Europe 18 (2010)
Vallejo Girvés, Bizancio y la España tardoantigua (1993)

roman_lombard_wars.detail: The Lombard invasion of 568, led by Alboin, rapidly conquered most of northern Italy (Milan 569, Pavia 572), and Lombard groups pushed south to establish the duchies of Spoleto and Benevento. The Roman government, short of troops due to the Persian war, held Ravenna, Rome, Naples, Genoa, the coastal cities and the islands. Justin II's son-in-law Baduarius was defeated in 576, and the empire turned to diplomacy: Tiberius II bribed Lombard dukes during the ten-year interregnum after Cleph's murder (574-584) and financed Frankish invasions. Maurice paid Childebert II to attack the Lombards (584, 585, 588, 590), and in 584 the Lombards restored their monarchy under Authari, who fought off the Franks. Maurice created the exarchate of Ravenna, combining civil and military power, first attested in 584. In 590 a coordinated Frankish and Roman offensive under the exarch Romanus retook Modena, Mantua and Altinum, but the Franks withdrew. In 592 Romanus retook Perugia and the corridor between Rome and Ravenna, which Agilulf recaptured in 593, threatening Rome. Pope Gregory the Great negotiated a separate peace with Agilulf, despite imperial opposition, and in 598 the exarch Callinicus agreed to a truce. Agilulf took Padua (601), Cremona and Mantua (603) after Callinicus seized his daughter. Truces were renewed in 605 and later, with the Romans paying tribute of 12,000 solidi. The result was the division of Italy into Lombard and Roman zones, a fragmented political map that lasted until the eighth century, when the Lombards took Ravenna (751) and the papacy turned to the Franks. Paul the Deacon's History of the Lombards is the main source.
scholarship: Christie, The Lombards (1995)
Brown, Gentlemen and Officers: Imperial Administration and Aristocratic Power in Byzantine Italy 554-800 (1984)
Wickham, Early Medieval Italy (1981)

roman_sasanian_war_572.detail: Justin II's refusal to pay the annual subsidy under the treaty of 562 and his support for the Armenian revolt of Vardan Mamikonian, together with his alliance with the Western Turks, led to war in 572. Its first years were disastrous: Marcian's siege of Nisibis collapsed in 573, Khosrow I took Dara in November 573 while Adarmahan raided Syria, sacking Apamea, and Justin went mad. Sophia and Tiberius bought truces for Mesopotamia (574-578), while fighting continued in Armenia, where Khosrow, invading in 576, burned Sebasteia and Melitene but was defeated by Justinian son of Germanus near Melitene, his army losing its baggage while crossing the Euphrates. The Romans were defeated in Armenia in 577. Maurice, magister militum per Orientem from 578, raided Arzanene and Persia, but his expedition with the Ghassanid al-Mundhir toward Ctesiphon (581) failed, leading to al-Mundhir's arrest. Maurice won at Constantina (582) before becoming emperor. Under his generals John Mystacon, Philippicus and Priscus, the war continued with mixed fortunes: Roman victory at Solachon (586), failure at Chlomaron, a mutiny in 588 over pay cuts, the loss of Martyropolis by treachery (589), and Roman victory at Sisarbanon (589). Meanwhile, the Persian general Bahram Chobin defeated the Turks (588) and was defeated by the Romans in the Caucasus, and rebelled; Hormizd IV was overthrown and killed (590), and his son Khosrow II fled to the Romans. Maurice restored him by the victory of the Blarathon (591), and in return Persia ceded Dara, Martyropolis and most of Persarmenia and Iberia. Theophylact's history covers the war in detail.
scholarship: Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and his Historian (1988)
Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and His Historian (1988)
Greatrex and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars II (2002)
Howard-Johnston, Witnesses to a World Crisis (2010)

balkan_wars_of_maurice.detail: The Avars, who had entered Pannonia after the Lombards left in 568, and the Slavs, who had raided across the Danube since the 520s, exploited the empire's preoccupation with Persia. The Avar khagan Bayan besieged Sirmium from 579 and took it in 582. In 583-584 the Avars took Singidunum, Viminacium and Augustae and raided as far as Anchialus, while the Slavs raided to the Long Walls and settled in Thrace and Greece; the Chronicle of Monemvasia dates their occupation of the Peloponnese to 587. Thessalonica was besieged by Avars and Slavs in 586. Roman resistance under Comentiolus achieved little; in 587 his army was put to flight by a misunderstood cry ('torna, torna'). After the peace with Persia in 591, Maurice transferred troops to the Balkans and took the offensive. In 592-593 Priscus campaigned against the Slavs north of the Danube, defeating the chiefs Ardagastus and Musocius. In 594 Maurice's brother Peter replaced him, with less success. In 595 Priscus defended Singidunum against the Avars, who then raided Dalmatia. In 597-598 the Avars besieged Priscus at Tomis and advanced to Drizipera, where plague struck their army; a peace in 598 recognised the Danube as the frontier and the Roman right to cross against the Slavs. In 599 Maurice broke it; Priscus crossed at Viminacium and won major victories, killing the khagan's sons. But Maurice's refusal to ransom 12,000 prisoners led to their massacre (599), and in 602 his order to winter beyond the Danube led to the army's mutiny and his overthrow, ending the offensive.
scholarship: Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and his Historian (1988)
Pohl, The Avars (2018)
Curta, The Making of the Slavs (2001)
Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and His Historian (1988)

heraclian_revolt.detail: In 608 Heraclius the Elder, exarch of Africa, and his brother Gregory rebelled against Phocas, whose rule had led to military disasters in the East and executions in Constantinople. They stopped the grain supply to the capital and struck coins showing the exarch and his son as consuls. The revolt had two arms. Gregory's son Nicetas led an army overland from Africa to Egypt, which he reached in 608 or 609; with the support of the Greens and the local population, and after fighting near Alexandria and in the Delta, he defeated Phocas's general Bonosus, who had been sent from Syria, and controlled Egypt by 610, as narrated by John of Nikiu. The younger Heraclius sailed with a fleet in 610, stopping in Sicily, Thessalonica and the Aegean islands, gathering support, including that of the general Priscus, Phocas's son-in-law and commander of the excubitors, who was in secret contact with him. On 3 October 610 his fleet arrived at Constantinople; the Greens rose, and Priscus abandoned Phocas, who was captured and brought before Heraclius, who had him executed on 5 October. Heraclius was crowned the same day by the patriarch Sergius and married Fabia-Eudokia. Phocas's brother Comentiolus held Anatolia with an army until he was killed in 611. The civil war weakened the empire at a critical moment: the Persians took advantage to cross the Euphrates and take Edessa, Antioch and Caesarea, and the Avars and Slavs advanced in the Balkans. The revolt founded the Heraclian dynasty, which ruled until 711, and demonstrated the importance of Africa and Egypt as power bases.
scholarship: Kaegi, Heraclius, Emperor of Byzantium (2003)
Olster, The Politics of Usurpation in the Seventh Century (1993)

roman_sasanian_war_602.detail: The last and greatest of the Roman-Persian wars began when Khosrow II, avenging his benefactor Maurice, declared war on Phocas in 603. In the first phase (603-610), helped by the Roman civil wars, the Persians conquered Mesopotamia and Armenia, taking Dara (604), Amida, Theodosiopolis and Edessa (609). In the second (610-621), they crossed the Euphrates: Shahin took Caesarea in Cappadocia (611); Heraclius was defeated near Antioch (613), splitting the empire; Damascus (613) and Jerusalem (614) fell, the True Cross being taken to Ctesiphon; Shahin reached Chalcedon (615); and Shahrbaraz conquered Egypt (618-621). The Persian armies raided Anatolia and the Avars threatened Constantinople. In the third phase (622-628) Heraclius, financing the war with church treasures, took the offensive: after a victorious campaign in 622, he invaded Persarmenia and Atropatene (624), destroying the fire temple of Adur Gushnasp, and fought in the Caucasus and Syunik (625). In 626, while the Avars and Persians besieged Constantinople without success, Heraclius allied with the Western Turks; in 627 they besieged Tiflis, and Heraclius invaded Assyria, defeating the Persians at Nineveh (December 627) and sacking Dastagird. Khosrow was overthrown and killed in February 628; Kavad II made peace, returning all Roman territory, prisoners and the True Cross, which Heraclius restored to Jerusalem in 630. The war exhausted both empires: Persia fell into civil war, the Roman provinces were devastated and their loyalties weakened, and within a decade both empires were overrun by the Arabs. James Howard-Johnston has called it the last great war of antiquity, and its course is reconstructed from Sebeos, the Chronicon Paschale, Theophanes and George of Pisidia.
scholarship: Howard-Johnston, The Last Great War of Antiquity (2021)
Kaegi, Heraclius (2003)
Greatrex and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars II (2002)

arab_roman_war_634.detail: The first clash between the Muslims of Medina and the Romans was at Mu'ta (629), a Muslim defeat, followed by the expedition to Tabuk (630), which won the submission of frontier communities. After the Ridda wars unified Arabia, Abu Bakr sent four armies into Syria and Palestine in 633-634, under Amr ibn al-As, Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan, Shurahbil ibn Hasana and Abu Ubayda, reinforced in 634 by Khalid ibn al-Walid after his desert march from Iraq. The Arabs defeated the Romans at Dathin near Gaza (February 634), took Bostra, and won at Ajnadayn (July 634), Fahl (January 635) and Marj al-Saffar, and took Damascus (September 635) and Emesa (636). Heraclius assembled a large army under Vahan and Theodore Trithyrios, which was destroyed at the Yarmuk (August 636). Heraclius abandoned Syria. Jerusalem surrendered to Umar (637 or 638), followed by Aleppo, Antioch (637), Caesarea Maritima (640), and Roman Mesopotamia (639-640), where the governor John Kateas had briefly bought peace. Arab forces also took Dvin in Armenia (640). In December 639 Amr invaded Egypt, took Pelusium (640), defeated the Roman army at Heliopolis (July 640), and took the fortress of Babylon (April 641) after Heraclius's death. The patriarch Cyrus signed the Treaty of Alexandria (November 641), and Alexandria was evacuated in 642. In less than ten years the empire lost its richest provinces, about two thirds of its revenue, and was reduced to Anatolia, the Balkan coasts, Africa and Italy. Historians attribute the Arab success to Roman and Persian exhaustion, religious divisions, Arab mobility and leadership, and the Arabs' policy of negotiated surrender.
scholarship: Kaegi, Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests (1992)
Donner, The Early Islamic Conquests (1981)
Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007)
Hoyland, In God's Path (2015)
